I really enjoyed this game's story greatly but I don't feel like playing another similar Telltale story ever again. Here's why.
See, it's a rather simple game, there's a story, set in Walking Dead setting, about a single man Lee Everett whose decisions and actions are under your control as zombie apocalypse unfolds, and then there's a whole bunch of other characters that you meet over duration of like five episodes. They're all fleshed out, sympathethic characters and good people you wish you'd have along you during an apocalypse, except for few douches who deserve everything terrible that happened to them. And that's the best thing in this game. Characters. They're nice, they feel like real people, and their stories are tragic, even of those few you never witness dying in this game. I even got all teary in the end, so sad it was.
Meanwhile, the game itself is... well, this format TellTale at the moment of writing is still milking dry is great for creating drama, but eventually it feels like nothing you do matters. You can see the railroading on your first playtrough, grinding your teeth as all given dialogue options aen't what you would have said to defuse a heated situation (can't complain because games are linear most of time, but, you know, it still feels like hard railroading), or witnessing bad things happening irregardless of what you choose. And half the time situations aren't even the sort where you really can't do anything, it's like, even if you spare a person, somebody else will stab them the very next second, or you defuse a situation with somebody being super mad at you just for them to still be mad at you to do something dumb later on. You'd expect this would have improved since then, with them earning from mistakes of original game, but seeing how Telltale are currently working on season two of a freaking MINECRAFT ADVENTURE GAME, I say they lost their mind since then. Also there are QTEs, in all of these games, this one included. While it does add some tension and are well-paced distraction from figuring things out or dialogue, there's not much satisfaction in completing them as all you have to do is mash specific buttons. And sometimes you have more railroading pop up even there, say in this game there are several scenes where you enter an FPS mode to shoot up some zombies, except there will be a few zombies you will never hit despite shooting straight at them because the storywritters just really needed a scene where character X saves another in the last moment and no way you'll be stealing a spotlight from them, ok player?
Also, must remark that this game had some ocassional lagspikes which is odd because it's older than my computer, is not an ancient pre-DirectX relic and has very simple graphics and tiny setpieces which are all separated by loading screens. It's really odd seeing a game that looks like it was made to run on potatoiest of potatoes to still lag once in a while. Talking about simplicity of graphics, I must comment artists on recreating a comic book aesthetic very well. Black inky lines and all. And not just that, they also have created extremely expressive human faces with such a low poly-count. Marvelous. It's kinda obligatory to mention sound too, so while soundtrack was appropriate but not remarkable, I have to commend voice actors for their work too.
Anyways, if you gonna play this, do it for the drama, don't expect genuinely meaningful choices because they're all an illusion, the story is emotional and well paced but it's railroaded so hard that the binary choices you make won't matter for long. I'm giving this game thumbs up but, if Telltale employee ever reads this, this is not an encouragement to keep cranking out the same thing.

The figures above are not right! I've played hundreds of hours on this game usually through PAMM. It is basically the only game that I play nowadays and I have a large library of games. Also I only play single player against the AI, too many people keep saying that it is a multi-player only rts game, it is not. I have found the skirmish mode to be a lot of fun with so much to do while playing it and I always play it on absurb difficulty. There are a ton of mods to use, from AI mods to eye candy mods to map mods etc. there is also a mod on it's way for another faction. Though I don't play online there is a great community that do and most of them are very helpful if you need help with anything. My favourite game was TA but now PA is my favourite. There is a learning curve at least for me and I'm still learning, what with planets being round and not flat (makes the game very interisting when you get used to it), unit cannons, nuclear missiles, planet smashing, titans, annihilaser, asteroids, unlimited units (I think there might be a limit of 3000 but I'm not sure, if there is it can be changed in the ai_config.json using any text editor), four layers of units (land, sea, air and space) and so much more. No two games ever seem the same to me, you can play on just one planet or several, with or without moons. For me PA is very stable, and it saves and resumes ok so that I can play the long games that I like. I should also mention that you can rewind the game you are playing and start from the position you rewound to, so it is like one continuous save. If you like playing skirmish games such as TA, C&C Generals etc. then you should like PA. I don't miss not having a campaign as I don't usually play campaigns and as I mentioned before, I don't play online very often so I can't coment on them. I don't play Galatic War either (maybe I will give it a go at a later time) so I can't comment on that. But the skirmish mode keeps me entertained for ages and as far as I am concerned that is what a game should do.

As a cub, Stoundbar's bright colorful fur astounded everyone, and shined bright against all the other tigers around her. Tigers everywhere thought she would be the legend among them.
As she neared adolescence, her outstanding talent showed itself. Were there already fast tigers in the community? Sure, but Stound was faster. Were there tigers who were experts at hunting? Sure, but she brought in more game than anyone else. It became clear that she had potential.
And then it happened...
A circus came to her habitat and was swiping up other tigers, but when they saw Stoundbar, they stopped in their tracks. They released the other tigers and took her instead. Off to the circus. The circus... named "♥♥♥♥leChish"
At ♥♥♥♥leChish, her talent was displayed. Her best qualities; her running, her hunting skills, and others were all showcased for small audiences at first; introductory gigs where people got an exclusive glimpse of Stoundbar's excellence. Other acts, performances; other animals fell in her shadow. All people wanted to see was Stoundbar.
After awhile, ♥♥♥♥leChish began a fundraiser to develop Stoundbar's talents even further. Apparently, word of StoundBar's unique talent and glory had spread internationally, so their fundraiser raked in millions. By that time, they had their own place for their increasingly popular shows, but they decided that, with these new funds, a change of location was in order. Over almost the course of a year, they moved to a new location, and excitement for StoundBar waned the longer they took.
When they finally moved, however, ♥♥♥♥leChish Circus' popularity died, and with it, Stoundbar's did too.
And then came the abuse...
With Chucklefish--err, I mean.. ♥♥♥♥leChish seeking a desperate revival of Stoundbar's audience and notoriety, they began to beat and batter the last remnants of her brilliance out of her over time. They spent months at a time between shows pumping her with harmful steroids and hormones to try and boost her lore. Enhancements which seemed amazing on the surface were soon revealed to be harmful for her in reality. For about a month after Stoundbar, with her brand-new enhancements, were exposed to the world, her fans returned to the stadium. However, they got bored and stopped attending shows once again.
Eventually, ♥♥♥♥leChish fell into a depressing pattern; a downward spiral of desperate enhancements for Stoundbar which slowly began to kill her. The fans, however, rush back temperarily (in increasingly small numbers) and then retreat to other shows in only a matter of weeks.
Stoundbar's fur suddenly didn't seem so bright;
Her talents.. no longer special.
Starbound's era passed prematurely, and for that... all thanks can be given to the poor management of Chucklefish.
I was one of her fans; there from the first show she gave to the massive, cheering crowds.. and now all I can say is.. show's over kids, now it's time to move on to the next great act.

This review is more of an argument and is long, but in my opinion, is necessary. I have always enjoyed the Fallout universe. Its vast lore, storyline, content, and immersion are just a few of the amazing qualities that this series has to offer.
My arguments against negative reviews:
1. Paid mods and dlc do not destroy the game. I know multiple people that have played this game, time and time again, never using mods or dlc, and have enjoyed it immensely. Furthermore, paid mods and dlc are around in a wide variety of games, and are not that uncommon. They aren’t a signature feature of Fallout 4. They do not destroy the overall game, especially because of the quality this and other games have to offer nowadays, and especially because buying mods and dlc is a choice.
2. The FPS feeling of Fallout 4 was its intended style. This FPS style was the style that the developers intended for this game to play as. It was meant to feel like you were struggling to survive, having to fend off enemies everywhere and anywhere. Moreover, play style still varies. You can play as both a sneak character, as well as an aggressive character. You can be a sniper, as well as a melee character. The play style varies, as it was intended, and as it should. Unlike Fallout and Fallout 2, this game, in its 3D style, is intended to be played similar to an FPS, so I don’t exactly understand the point of this negative argument. Skyrim would be the exact same way, if it had guns.
This game is an amazing game, plays as it’s supposed to be played, and being a AAA game, isn’t destroyed by the optionally-purchased mods and dlc it has to offer.

As a fan of the point and click genre when I saw this crop up I just had to give it a go, and for the most part I wasn't disappointed.
By that I mean I wasn't expecting great things from it. It's been made by one person whom from what I can tell, hasn't made a game before. It's got all the thing you expect as standard in a point and click game. Although it was refreshing to not have to do the "try to combine everything with everything else in your inventory" trick.
This actually game actually has you checking around your surroundings, though those are small and it's not exactly hard to work out what's important in the room.
I like the fact this game was created using actual physical materials and animated in stop motion. As I mentioned above it does mean that objects of importance are very easy to spot though.
The sad thing is that the weakest element of the game is what it sells it self as, it's a musical. Unfortunately the songs grate quickly and the the singing isn't exactly at a professional standard. I don't know if that's intentional (due to the storyline etc) but I found I had to actually turn off the speakers at times.
The storyline is interesting, but I found quite easy to guess the plot twist. The game is also quite short, I completed it in just over an hour. I would not recommend getting this at the current price (£3.49) wait until it comes on a steam sale.
So my verdict. Get it if you want something unique and interesting. But don't expect a lot.

Modern Tales poses almost no challenge as a hidden object game, but it is a fun, thrilling adventure in the truest sense of the word.
If we took a sci-fi adventure novel from Jules Verne, rewrote it into a 1940s pulp story, and ran it through a hidden object game creation kit, we would end up with Modern Tales: Age of Invention. This entire game dedicates itself to the concept of an adventure, as we jump into the role of a scientist girl who tries to rescue her father, his clandestine collection of colleagues, and their inventions from the clutches of a greedy French businessman.
This approach also meant many clichés and some famous real-world people ending up in unrealistic supporting roles, but it all pales to one important thing: the story is fun!
It has to be fun though, because the gameplay is so ridiculously easy that it is almost non-existent. Every important object is easily distinguishable, hidden object scenes have large items with minimal clutter, and even the standard puzzles are child’s play. Essentially, they just add enough gameplay to let us enjoy the rest of the game for what it is: a simple, yet incredible adventure.

And it has finally been released.
Just Cause 2 Multiplayer Mod is basically what it says, it's a Multiplayer Mod. Out of the two test sessions I've played, you can have 1000 players in a single server (depending on the server), but the highest I've been with is 520 people, and surprisingly, it keeps incredibly stable and in-sync. When not in-sync, the craziest things can most likely happen, so I can't really even count that as a con for myself. Even with 520 players, select areas doesn't feel full even besides such a high player count. With more than 500 people, you're basically in for mayhem, competition, and murderous players. You have racing, parachuting, competition, deathmatches, and much more, including with more people hosting servers this time around.
Your first experience can probably be a bit bleak, you might be confused or overwhelmed to what's happening around you, including if you spawn in a crowded area. You could be being shot at, you could have people following you, or you might just be alone, which is why it's always good to look at the FAQ
and the in-game help menu. (F5) Though, both aren't to detailed on what you can possibly do, they help out with some commands that you might want to know. It's also nice to know that you can put yourself in a Faction, which is basically a group for people. Or, you can make your own faction, which also helps in sitting yourself in a server. (EDIT, 4:38 PM 12/17/2013: The devs have not released the Factions script yet, so look out for it! No one's actually too sure where the script is actually, so we'll see soon.) I also believe it's great to find your favorite server, and keep with it unless if you want to try something new. Because JCMP uses SteamIDs instead of unique IDs for players, Servers can keep track of your in-server stats including your money, so your progress will be always saved unless if the server has been reset.
So far in-game, I have experienced Deathmatches, Survival matches, Boat Races, Plane Races, Skydiving Races, Road/Dirt Races, Destruction Derbies, Dogpiles, Stunt Events, and MANY more game modes thanks to the open LUA script system that allows server admins to add these scripts to their servers. Though, a lot of the scripts are still stock / basic because of the game only now being released to the public to host and mess with, I believe as the devs update this game, it'll have a lot more gamemodes and functionality in the future once people start getting comfortable with how it works. There might be more to what I named, but I'm not sure yet. I'll also update this once time passes by!
Besides activities and gamemodes, the destruction a full server can have is amazing. From blowing up random landmarks to just plain randomness in a field, there's plenty of mayhem to last until another update, Including at places like 'airport' 1 and 2, 'Pie' Island, and 'racetrack'. If all of those aren't your thing, cruising with friends also works out too since even with a crazy amount of players, there's still many other places on the map to travel to with people.
A big con is that a good amount of the original game's menu's are still possible to back into, but it wasn't as much as the tests, I'm glad they managed to get rid of most of the menu's.
In general, you might be overwhelmed by too many things and the open world aspect might be too much for those who like to start off with instructions instead of going out of your way to throw yourself into explosions and others, but you're up for a SAMP like experience after you figure it out here, JC2 style. It's defiantly a SAMP competitor, and I cannot wait for what people come up with using the LUA code system, and I can't wait for what the developers have in mind for the next update. Keep in mind that the game just launched and there's still a good amount of things they should fix / add, (which is also why you should report these things to the JC2MP bug report forum! just sign in and steam and make sure your issue isn't server related!
but I'm very confident that this mod will take of even more in the future.
I would defiantly recommend this to those who own JC2 and enjoyed it.

It is somewhat difficult to recommend Kindred Spirits on the Roof due to how niche it is. It has a number of love scenes with nudity, so that can be a reason for some people to avoid it. Then the quantity of such scenes is relatively low and they do not appear until several hours in, so it's not for people who just want porn either. Furthermore, the majority of the main cast are lesbians, so people who have a problem with homosexuality would have a problem with this title. There isn't much of an engaging central plot or gameplay elements, so it also is not for people who need such things to enjoy a visual novel.
All that said, Kindred Spirits on the Roof is an upbeat yuri romance visual novel with a character-driven story that is very highly recommended to everyone who is interested in such things.
What makes Kindred Spirits on the Roof feel so praiseworthy is the quality of its character writing. The main cast is relatively large and yet every character was relatable in some way and felt very believable. These characters have a good amount of depth and many undergo an appreciable amount of growth over the course of the story. The writing also does a fantastic job of conveying emotions. While not everyone will have the same experiences as those portrayed in this visual novel, the emotions that result from them are universal and this story presents them in a way that anyone can easily empathize with.
Unlike most other romance visual novels which feature one protagonist with multiple potential love interests and routes, Kindred Spirits on the Roof instead presents a single story with multiple couples. This allows the reader to view all the different sorts of relationships portrayed within the visual novel without having to read through it multiple times. At certain points in the story, the main storyline will stop and the reader will be presented with a few different scenes to select that focus on the various couples from the point of view of one of the characters involved. The main storyline will not resume until all scenes for each couple are viewed. There are dialogue choices to make, but the story is ultimately linear and the choices only impact the dialogue immediately following the decision while all choices must be viewed to unlock every extra scene after the main story is cleared.
As far as overall presentation, Kindred Spirits on the Roof has a respectable level of quality. Each character has a decent number of sprites and even multiple outfits. There are also over 50 event images and the art looks pretty good overall. The soundtrack consists of 11 background tracks, an opening, an ending, and one insert song as well as instrumental versions of the opening, ending, and insert song. The quantity is not particularly impressive, but there are enough tracks to convey all the emotions needed and they are put to good use. I personally enjoyed listening to each track. Translated lyrics for the songs that have them can be found in the music player accessed from the scene selection screen. In addition to the main story and couple scenes, there are over 70 extra scenes that become available after completion and provide even more content. My time on Steam is a bit off since I had a habit of leaving the program open so I could listen to the music as I took care of chores and such, but I feel confident in saying I spent over 40 hours with this title.
Kindred Spirits on the Roof is among my favorite visual novels and the best I have read on Steam. There are some aspects that would turn some people off from it, but for everyone else it is a title that I very highly recommend.

When you see the thumbs down on this review, you'll probably be ready to either click "not helpful" or just scroll on past it. Fair enough!
Fact is, my feelings for this game are very, very mixed, but the reason I settled on giving it the negative rather than the positive were, believe it or not, mechanical reasons. And I don't mean the bug that forces you to quit the game every 10-20 minutes if you launch the game from Steam.
If the visual novel worked differently, I would probably recommend with much less hesitation, but because of how it works, not only am I instead giving it this negative review, but I may not even finish it (or at least not after a break) because I ended up just flat out getting fed up with it.
If that sounds strange, as I'm sure it does, then read on.
Truth be told, the writing in Kindred Spirits on the Roof isn't all that bad. The art, while not exactly incredible, is actually quite charming, and the characters are all look distinct from each other while still not having designs too outlandish or stereotypical.
The story is about a girl who comes to find she can see two ghosts who have fallen in love and who want to help other girls find love at their school. The girl comes to assist their quest, and slowly but surely helps a handful of couples get together and stay together over the course of the story, eventually finding love herself along the way.
It's light hearted, and those without much experience with how these types of stories are written or how homosexuality is viewed in Japan might experience some culture shock when reading some of the dialogue, but the game is overall pleasant in tone and develops all of its characters fairly and in a decent enough manner.
On the negative side, the soundtrack only seems to have a little over half a dozen or so songs (it feels like half that for the first few hours), and it reuses this same pair of peppy tracks in scenes where they really don't belong over and over again. The tracks that start to appear later in the game during more emotionally driven scenes are much more enjoyable and immersive, but that same pair of peppy songs always come in no matter what.
Looking at these things, the game probably doesn't sound too bad, right?
Well, if it was just this, I would be giving the thumbs up rather than thumbs down right here.
When you go into a visual novel, usually you expect to progress through the story from scene to scene, occasionally making choices along the way. If that sounds about right, as it so happens, there are actually exceptions to this that incorporate different types of gameplay or ways of moving from scenes: Kindred Spirits is in the latter category.
In Kindred Spirits, the player progresses by viewing scenes through a planner. First, they'll view scenes about the main story of the protagonist and two ghosts who want to help the students of the school they're haunting find love, and then progress in the main story is halted so that scenes from the perspective of the other characters can open up on your planner on the relevant days.
At first, this seems like a cool and novel system. You open up your planner, which serves as the game's menu, and not only look at any scene you've already seen, but progress through the story with a sense of time alongside you! As you start helping more and more couples, you'll have more and more scenes to go through between each portion of the main story, all taking place on different days, some taking place on the same days, which can really make your planner feel full and...
And that is where one of the big problems with this system starts.
I appreciate the system the game offers. The idea is interesting, and letting players see different perspectives this way could work, in theory.
But to me, it presented a big problem. As I see it, the problem could be taken in one of two ways: It makes problems for players who are either more interested in the main story and would like to keep following that, but it also makes it even worse for players don't care for whatever flavor of the day couple(s) the game insists you need to focus on before you can return to the protagonist.
Because you
proceed with the main storyline or even with
further down the road until you see the scenes the novel wants you to see in more or less the order it wants you to see them. In a normal visual novel, this sort of thing is usually handled in a few ways: multiple routes, unlockable
side scenes, or just being flat out kinetic.
By Kindred Spirits giving players the planner, it makes them feel like they have a level of control that the game doesn't actually give them. I would almost say the planner not only seems to only exist to give players the
of having input in the story, but I might even go as far as to say that it takes control away.
There were too many times where I found myself not enjoying the game because the game yanked me back into the planner and told me I needed to stop reading the story I might have been enjoying or invested in and go back and see what other characters were doing during this same period of time. The narrative had me jumping all over the game's different times, going back and forth from the end of the week to the start of it to earlier that month from various unrelated perspectives, and it created an experience that felt disjointed on more than one occasion.
This could all have been avoided if there were an option to let me come back to these scenes at my leisure, or just not get to see them if I progressed past the points they were relevant. Presenting and writing them in a way where I didn't have to keep jumping back and forth to the planner would have worked out, but as it is, it feels like the author wasn't able to make scenes that flowed together as well, and so they needed to create a system that could circumvent them having to have every scene naturally move into the next. The fact that many scenes include recaps far more lengthy than necessary of what's going on in that character's life only adds to this issue.
Putting the scenes into entirely separate routes would have even worked better. It might have meant players wouldn't get the whole story in one sitting, but you would get fuller, more fleshed out experiences as opposed to the slapdash back and forths you may not even want to read about that you have here.

If that were the case with me, I would not be writing this in a negative light. It wastes your time doing that.
You may finish a scene and be ready to go on to the next, then find rather than another scene of the main story, you have to play as the other girls for a while. And that may be it for you. Another classic I played many times on
.  This takes the concept from the first game and gives you a sideview perspective rather than a top down, and it also adds new toys to destroy Creeper with.  The missions get progressively harder as you go on and you aren't always allowed the luxury of consolidating your power before going on the offensive.  It's a tactical and strategic masterpiece of a game wherein it seems simple on the surface but becomes very complex as the game goes on.  Furthermore you learn to anticipate the unexpected and make ready for it.  You also learn to restrain your desire to build everything at once and maximize your energy usage to build more efficiently to deal with rampages, particularly the drones that spawn on the later maps.  Probably one of the best additions to the game that wasn't present in the original was the inclusion of conversion bombs, which allow you to turn pools of creeper into your own anti-creeper lakes.  This can come in extraordinarily handy at times, though the missions that this wonderful tool exists are counted on the fingers of one hand.  Still, the thing that really made this game different from the first other than the perspective was the inclusion of the Nullifier weapon which lets you destroy the Creeper Emitters and spawn-gates for the drones and phantoms.  No longer do you just have to perform lockdown, now you can actually destroy the sources directly.
All in all, it is a fun game that will eat up a ton of your free time and not leave you feeling like you didn't do anything, unlike some games.  It's not a job, it's not a chore, it's a challenge.  A challenge of your skill and adaptivity.  It definitely doesn't disappoint and I highly recommend it to anyone looking for something fun and frustrating at the same time.  You'll be glad you bought this little gem.  The soundtrack is also very fitting and driving like the first game, but even more so.
It's rare to find a game that has very few flaws.  Well-balanced, well thought out, and more than meets the eye best describes it.  There's even a code mode which lets you run random maps after you finish the story and the bonus missions, so on top of the hours you'll sink into conquering the Creeper you'll have more to do if you're interested in continuing with this experience.  This has always been one of my favorites that I kept going back to, and with the Anniversay Edition you're getting the full story for the campaign, better writing, and a great game for a reasonable price.  Buy it!

Enough about the past, here we are in the present with Deca Games, I would almost call this the beginning or the re-creation of Realm of the Mad God, Deca Games seems to be a very player-friendly company actively collecting player fed suggestions and by far and most notably hyping up a dead community.
Deca Games is creating a new Realm of the Mad God therefore I refuse to leave a review slandering the game for what it has been the past four years and would rather like to leave this review focusing on what Deca Games is doing right now, and as far as I've seen, no one has been upset with their progress thus far.
Not too much can be said for the moment because the future is yet to come. However what I can say is that most (including myself) are content with the changes being made (<3 UB Ring re-color) and events going down. The fact that Deca Games are able to (thus far) revive such a dead game is astounding, I've seen players on that I haven't seen in years and I've talked to players I haven't talked to in years. Basically I'm a big fan of Deca Games so far, I love the changes few changes they've made so far, the events they come up with, using the player-created content, their reactions to duping & hacking & multibox'ers have been better than a significantly larger company (Kabam), and much more.
All in all Realm of the Mad God has so much more potential. just looking at the reddit posts I see so many well-thought ideas (ex: Evaluation Stages for events = solution for steamrolling events?). I can't wait to see what Deca Games has planned for RotMG throughout the next ten years and I wish them the best of luck in the future!

Game of the year for me. Incredibly sincere and heartfelt, chock-full of infectious emotion that you simply can't help but feel as you read on. Simply a pleasure to read every single scene - from the amusements of daily life, to heart-thumping romance, anticipation, tense moments of drama and anger. Art is perfect for what it is: not overly cute (or "moe"), not overly serious, just some pleasantly designed characters that are easy to look at. The background music and theme song contribute to the game's atmosphere and are assigned to scenes appropriately.
It's the writing that makes this novel so good, though. The novel was fantastically tasteful, even for such a sexually-charged premise. In fact, the focus on building friendships/relationships provided so much characterization for every character that you feel like you know them as intimately as a close friend would - a rarity in yuri works. Even the erotic scenes contributed a lot to building the characters, which I enjoyed so much more than the very well-written and well-drawn scenes themselves.
I have no idea how liberal the interpretation is from the original, but I honestly don't care. Liar-soft and the MangaGamer translators have done a stellar job writing a very well-made yuri story that, although far from novel or original, can speak to your heart and make it feel a whirlwind of emotion.
Absolutely worth every penny if you are a fan of the yuri genre. Thank you so, so much for this experience.

First off, I did get this for free - thanks Humble.
I didn't know what to expect with this game.  Sure, I love the show but from what I had been told the game was "point and click"?  Sounded a little weird, I would expect FPS or at least some sort of survival horror.
I was pleasantly surprised.  I also died a number of times in scenes, as the pace shifts from gently letting the plot unfold to OH GOD OH GOD click click....dead.  It works well, though.  I think it only works because it is done so well - the writing is good, the people management is a tough thing to juggle and the story develops nicely.  The atmosphere is creepy at times (we all know to expect zombies but you no more get innured to them than you do in the tv show) and the characters are well enough voiced that you do start to care what each thinks.  At one point I did (trying not to use a spoiler) leave someone behind and I felt guilty about it for a while.  Still wonder if I could have chosen differently, what would have happened?
The achievements at first glance seem too linear (complete chapters) but on reflection I would rather have that than be driven to make certain choices like in visual novels - those in themselves become linear.  At least in this game the choices you make DO affect the results rather than being forced to hunt out choices on a list.
I would say if you are going to get it, though, make sure it is on sale - I am most of the way through and it is clearly not going to be a 50 hour game.
Edit: completed and I am seriously considering the DLC.  You can't get 100% of achievements without the DLC for one thing - for another, I really enjoyed this game.

I know game devs hate it when their game gets compared to another, but this game is a lot like Terraria, and I'd urge any terraria player to play it. It keeps in tact the 2D voxel building and platforming mechanics and gameplay while adding a whole lot of cool♥♥♥♥♥♥in reference to other games of the sort. It's not a quick rip off of Terraria if that's what you think it is, but instead an entire game build of the same game style.
In Starbound things are more futuristic and sci-fi, whereas Terraria seems to focus on a more fantasy feel. And you'd expect that when you realise that in starbound there are hundreds (if not thousands) of planets to explore.  Certain aspects of the game are a lot more fluid than Terraria's. For example: The map circles all the way around, as apposed to terraria where you are stopped at a dead end. I find this feature especially pleasing since I've had to tolerate Terraria's version of this for so long. There are even quests to guide you so that you don't wander mindlessly around the galaxy for eternity (though there's nothing stopping you if that's what you wish to do)
One thing I'd have to complain about however would be the platform mechanics. You have to press down and hold space to pass through the platforms. That's not it though, when passing through the platforms, you don't stop or slow down at every platform like you do in Terraria, no, you pass through them as long as you're holding down both buttons. You pass through them without slowing down; without friction. This leads to the player often falling to their death in randomly generated areas underground or elsewhere. In fact, the platform mechanics are so bad that I hardly ever use them with building, even going out of my way to avoid using them when traveling. Also, There isn't a map like in Terraria, unless I just haven't found it yet.
Tl;dr Pros and Cons section:
Pros:
-huge universe with many planets to explore
-map scrolls around when you've hit the edge
-sci-fi instead of fantasy (if that's your thing)
Cons:
-platform (block) mechanics are absolutely terrible
-no map (though not a big deal to me I figured it may be worth listing)

I like it. I found this for a steal on
($9.99 +$1.00). The Total Annihilation feeling is also there for those who still reminisce about the good old 1997 Cavedog game called Total Annihilation. I was just wondering, where is the D-gun? The general feeling about the game is that the developers went into boring mode story-wise but got much of gameplay mechanics right. Gameplay > Lore, right? It can't get max points but it's definitely a play in my book.
1. Big Bots
The most attractive thing about this game are the big walking tin cans. Who doesn't want a mega Gundam?
2. Interplanetary Combat
Truly one of the highlights of the game.
3. The Annihilazer
Loved it. Build 5 Catalysts to activate the ENTIRE METAL PLANET and fire a beam to destroy any other planet. It warms my heart to know that I can build a Death Star without starting from scratch.
4. Titans
Super Area-of-Effect attacks. Fantastic.
1. No Impact
Shooting peas and lasers just don't simulate major combat. What I'm talking is the big vlada-boom from firing from a tank. The units don't have the "oomph" when they shoot. It feels like shooting peas at each other.
2. Too Many Units to Micro
You can build over 100 units and it's a hell of a problem to manage.
3. Rotating Views of the Planets
It's difficult to comb/scout the planet as you're trying to search the surface area of a sphere. The good thing is that scout planes are cheap and radar coverage is huge.
4. Orbital Transport
Due to the Astraeus' single unit limit, it is a chore to move units from 1 planet to another. It would be far better for the Astraeus to have multiple troop transport capabilities or to combine it with a teleporter.
5. 1 Capital Ship?
Only robots and 1 Capital Ship. There's a kind of limitation here. There is an Omega orbital ship but that's really limited. The defense satellites don't count.
6. Building over Ore Dots
I built an Air Factory over the Ore Dots and the next thing you know, you couldn't build an ore extractor over it.
7. Campaign
Very dull. Move from point A to point B, play a skirmish. There isn't a campaign at all. It's just skirmish after skirmish. I completed each map is less than 20 minutes.
8. Teleporter Facing
You have only 1 entrance to the Teleporter. The orientation is extremely important if you don't want your troops taking an additonal 5 seconds to get into the Teleporter.
9. View Orientation
A sphere with fog of war is really hard to focus on. If not for the large radar, it would be near impossible to locate your enemies.
10. Orbitals
It's quite hard to keep track of your orbitals. All you have is a thin line that shows you where your satellite is. It's like a balloon where you only focus on the string.
11. Naval
WTF is this for? You need water? Who the hell cares?
1. Singularity Commanders
You hedge everything on 1 single commander. This is not diversifying your risk very well. While I enjoy the quickness that games will end, I note that the same could also happen to me.
2. Ore Dots
Surprisingly, this is a great idea. However, I would prefer to reduce the number of dots by at least half and increase the metal production by x2 on each dot. I do not enjoy having to play Bob-the-Builder for resource structures.
3. Commander Loadouts
Good idea but executed poorly. It is most boring to see Air, Orbital or Vehicle Commanders. I would suggest looking at Company of Heroes 2 for a good example of how to have commander loadouts.
1. Bring in Space Combat
I was hoping for Battle Cruisers, Capital Ships, Warp Jumps and Orbital Bombardments. The Omega is not sufficient.
2. Big Boom Units
Just like how the commander goes nuclear when he dies. Perhaps some units that will cause a mushroom cloud explosion, a crater, earth split, shockwave or a void hole.
3. Upgrading the Factories
A Tier 1 factory is always stuck at Tier 1. I would allow a Tier 1 to upgrade into a Tier 2 Factory so that all the factories are the same and you don't waste space. Tier 2 Factories are not unique and still produce Tier 1 units either way, so upgrading is definitely a good idea.
4. 1 Large Planet
Instead of a tiny planet, how about 1 gigantic planet to fight on?
5. Energy Shields
I would have enjoyed looking at an energy shield dome.
6. Terrain & Weather
Not sure if you can render snow, electromagnetic clouds and desert sand storms.
7. Orbitals
Turn them into autonomous drones. It is extremely tedious to have to micro 3 separate levels. Level 1, planet surface
Level 2, orbital
Level 3, planetary
If they are drones, you can actually make them orbit instead of being geostationary.

So that trailer looks pretty cool right? Well you're probably alright stopping there. Not to jump on the negative review train; the game is a pretty harmless and innocent hour and a half with nothing egregious, but what's in the trailer is pretty much all there is to the game, albeit with a predictable detective story tacked on.
First off let me just list off why the game intrigued me enough for an impulse buy, so we can compare expectations and see if the game actually lives up to them. I bought this game because:
-it's a musical
-it's claymation
-its themes include gender, which is particularly tender and interesting to me
-it apparently did well in IGF nominations
-it's only an hour and a half long, which for someone with a massive backlog is actually an incentive
Now that I've played it, my positives are:
-it's one continuous musical adventure, with each screen change being accompanied by new music. The vamp technology
leading into each character's singing parts isn't perfect but is cool nonetheless.
-it has a lot of trombone
...And that's about it. Let's break this down further.
The musical element is the game's most unique and as mentioned above, works well enough. I don't actually have a huge problem with the "grating" voices: to me it along with the point and click mechanics create somewhat of a nostalgic experience. It really feels like a stage show, which is neat. At the same time, there's nothing particularly complex about the compositions, and the game doesn't really embrace the "musical" idea fully, it's just kinda there.
The claymation is very crude and pretty much a gimmick. It's very low resolution assests with no graphic options to speak of.
The gender theme isn't near as prominent as I expected and rather forced, thankfully it's not offensive but it's also not trailblazing.
As far as gameplay goes there's very little to speak of, just exhausting dialogue options. This isn't inherently bad, there are great games like Attack of the Friday Monsters that use this so as to not feel gamey or proprietary in any way. But that's the thing, you'll still be navigating basic menus for most of it so the fact that this is a very shallow, simple game will always be in the forefront of your mind. That said, it is simple enough for anyone to play and you won't get frustrated or stuck.
The story is the primary focus of the game, and it's pretty disposable. For one it's indulgent; you're thrown in with little context and immediately expected to care about the characters with no concept to guide the experience. The game constantly repeats information you've just heard back to you. It's pretty humorless; there are bits of overdone social commentary here and there that are really random and don't fit in with anything else: this is unfortunately the extent of the game's themes. And in general it's all pretty incidental, with a lack of finese to the storytelling, and it's just not at all cohesive! For all its twists and turns it never does anything unseen in other point and clicks or noir. The ending at least had potential to satisfy and bowtie all the elements but it feels unfinished, like the last 15 minutes are part of a different game.
So yeah in the end it's just kinda boring, you know? It's one of those cases where you have to take a step back and realize that just because it's cool as a trailer doesn't mean it'll be cool as a game, especially since it never explores any of its enticing elements. Still, on sale for a quick runthrough you can do a lot worse.

This game of deception and mental strategy can be fun if you're willing to look past the glaring issues. That being not only the fact that the developers have slowly transitioned into a format of pay-to-win mechanics, some being subtle and others not so much, along with the fact that a few issues with the overall gameplay have been ignored since the beginning of development. Classic Mode is fairly easy to understand, just watch a few YouTube videos made by experienced players and you'll get the hang of it. The process of slowly finding out other people's roles and intentions while also working your way towards victory is very fun, and it is indeed exciting when you actually come out on top as some of the more difficult roles like the Serial Killer. Considering the game can be played for free on a browser, you don't need me to explain to you what makes it fun. However, I don't plan on ignoring the problems with the game, which I will touch on in the next paragraph.
Before the Coven expansion and all that, Town Points (TP) would be racked up by playing matches, with extra TP being awarded if you win. TP could also be bought with real money, but this was in no way mandatory. You could spend TP on the shop for things like new character skins (the newer ones are admittedly very good-looking) and pets, houses, maps, and more recently profile pictures. Overall, this system was very okay in my opinion. But as of recently, the devs have locked your TP amount and instead made it so you earn a different "silver" currency by playing. A few store items (definitely not the best and most impressive ones) can be bought with large amounts of silver, or whatever it's called, but it is glaringly obvious that the devs' intention is to get you to spend real money, get TP, and buy stuff. I might've been okay with this had it not been seen as a complete 180 degree turn from the old system, where TP was earned through playing. Along with that, the devs already earned money from the Coven expansion, and they've been using Kickstarter to fund not only a card game, but an RPG of sorts as well. We have no info to suggest how much they earned from TP purchases and Steam store purchases, so we can only assume. Admittedly, there has been a slight increase in content since these new restrictive systems, but I mean it when I say "slight." I bought this game from the Steam store, and am not ashamed to say that I even purchased TP sometimes back before the new system was made. I, as a decently long-time player, do not appreciate these currency changes, to the point where I almost feel cheated.
As for base gameplay, it's about as how you'd expect from a browser-based, free, discussion-based game. Hate speech, spam, and overall lack of good communication are not rare, even if sometimes they are meant to back up one's in-game role. Many friends of mine who play the game, along with myself, are rarely bothered by the things people say, but it doesn't dismiss the fact that it often messes up the game and can lead to unfair results. I've seen two of the three members of the Mafia leave the game before it even starts, leading to the last Mafia member willingly getting himself lynched just to get the game overwith. When your playstyle and chances of success are entirely determined on whether or not your teammates leave the game or not, it gets frustrating. That doesn't even touch on how bad at communicating some players are. The system of how to punish leavers has changed much since the game came out, but even today, it is still far from perfect, or even acceptable for a game at this state of development. Custom games are a joke, where I cannot even recall the last time I entered a lobby without at least three votes to repick the host, simply because one or two people didn't get the roles they oh-so wanted. All-Any and Vigilantics are intended to be creative, but they just end up being RNG-based, that is if you can even find anyone inhabiting those lobbies. Competitive can be fun sometimes, but like any other game with competitive elements, it can be a cesspool of toxicity. I've seen people say "go back to classic/practice" more than a few times in comp. I'm sure you can figure out the other things wrong with gamplay on your own by watching videos or playing yourself.
Despite what I've said, my review for this game will still be marked positive. That is because I find Town of Salem fun and interesting, whether it be with friends or otherwise. It doesn't mean I support the devs' newest decisions, or even the decisions they've been making since launch. My suggestion is to try out the game on a browser if it truly does pique your interest. But keep watch of what you do, so that you don't end up giving the devs more than they deserve. That's it for my review, I hope this helped or at least gave you some insight.

Capcom well release a free DLC for the modes that the game is lacking such as the challenge mode.
The game, on the surface looks simple, but on the conterary it is a deep game which needs a high skill level; it is easy to get into but hard to master. There are no safe dragon punches anymore if you have to do a move you have to commit. The game demands from you to learn fundementals and neutral game; as scrubs and mashers get punished hard. Every character playes really differently from one another and that adds to the depth of the game. The V system is unique as it adds a different prespective to the game and how it is played because it changes how the characters are played.

"Twitch combat"
No, there is no twitch combat.
The space combat is slow and plodding, it is literally just lining up your mouse with an enemy and shooting till it dies.

Very odd game concept in my opinion. There is pretty much zero tutorial (only a brief introduction to the UI) followed by some introduction pages for the games one can open. The introductions are insanely confusingly written, most I've read twice or three times and was still not clear how the game works. So I learned the rules pretty much every case finally by trial and error. Not good.
The individual games are either puzzles (just click on the one you want and it just opens) or missions (it asks to do something, bit like a mini-quest, sometimes it ports you somewhere for this). The minigames are diverse but rather pointless besides "play a game, get a little bit of money, rise the skill level which seems to have not much impact on anything". At least so far I haven't found anything to motivate you to play a game besides that you hopefully want to play that particular game. Many of the games are not accessible without paying money for Doubloons or grinding enough ingame currency to buy Doubloons from the bank. Individual game sections (crafting, monster hunting, ship navigation & gunning etc) are all split into "pay with Doubloons for 30 day badge".
Most money comes from pilfering trips with other players on a player owned ship, you can have up to ... (25?) players on a ship, individual tasks are all minigames. If you are on a ship you can't just leave (bad style) and if the game/task you like is already occupied by enough others you have to do another one (freeloading is frowned upon). So you basically spent hours doing the same minigame over and over for very little money to hopefully encounter other ships often enough and then try to plunder them (or be plundered). There are treasure chests and crafting goods besides the money, but it seems those stay exclusively with the ship owner? So you get money to buy Doubloons or maybe other clothes or weapon or resources.
Crafting minigames do not yield any resources or items. You just lend a shop(pe) your workforce and receive a little bit of money in exchange.
All very puzzling honestly, the minigames are to some degree not too bad but it feels to me somehow pointless. I've played a lot of FreeRealms and minigames gave resources there which I could then use for crafting in other minigames. Usually I played the minigames for the sake of the minigames but there was a meta game on top that made it feel more like an actual world and overarching motivation. Completely lacking here.
Oh and if a shop does not have items pre-made available (the norm) then you can order it for ingame money - but it usually needs to be "delivered" (despite you showing up at this island and shop) for Doubloons usually. Which means you are either spending real life money for a few pixels or you grind ingame currency to exchange for Doubloons. Just to give you an idea: puzzles give 25ish coins, plundering a ship 500-800 coins maybe initial (and a bit more at port if you stay so long) - and a Doubloon is roughly 4000-5000 coins. But you need 5 Doubloons to have the monthly crafting badge activated and simplest clothing or furniture cost 1-5 Doubloons to "deliver" usually. Besides clothing and furniture there seems very little to buy anyway (besides the ship you want, but for which you need for navigation an officer badge ... more Doubloons).
So no, I don't really recommend it. Wouldn't mind paying a monthly fee if this whole Doubloon extra charging was then gone, but it isn't. Feel like an insane nickle and diming with barely any explanation and no point to grind.

To be honest, I expected only to come for the yuri and then, er,
for the yuri, if you catch my drift. But despite my misgivings regarding potential fanservice and to-the-point meet-'n'-flick that all of the news sites seemed to expect of Steam's first uncensored game of "frank depictions of sex", this visual novel turned out to tackle issues related to struggling romance, including but not limited to struggling with sexuality, age gaps, and the idea of valuing other close relationships against romance, not to mention a social and fairly deep discussion on what it means to feel love. It is superbly well written and, at times, poignantly heartfelt; some of the dialogue comes off as awkward in a realistic way, in the scope of anime and manga, but it rarely ever feels cheesy. None of the referenced (meaning named and drawn) characters are cookie-cutter personalities; no obvious tsundere, dandere, yandere, whatever. Rather, they are all multifaceted, organic creations, and the underlying theme regarding the main character almost perfectly fits an Uncle Iroh quote:
I surprised myself by becoming very emotionally involved with the characters and their stories, and ended up reading through this VN twice consecutively, and plan to listen to the drama CDs (by which I mean read the subtitles) when #4 is subbed and when they go on sale. Honestly, the explicit scenes are definitely not the end goal; they're nice to have and certainly demonstrate the different levels of experience, clumsiness, and passion between the different couples, but ultimately I found myself wanting to know more about the relationships themselves. There are uplifting and embarassing moments, heated and heartbreaking moments, funny and eye-rolling moments.
The technical side is also very charming and fitting with the theme of high school romance. Only the more important scenes are voiced, which is a feature I tend to like since it gives an enhanced sense of emotion and climax to certain story arcs. Each main story arc has a number of side story arcs focusing on the individual couples intersecting it. In this case, the planner approach is a stroke of genius. My one complaint on this end would probably be the difficulty in attaining the extra scenes, which are unlocked after completing the game and through selecting different choices throughout the game (the choices are very minor and only affect these extra scenes and some immediate dialogue; the story itself is linear). The music, though somewhat limited in choice and looped a little poorly, is tasteful for the different emotional stings throughout the game, from simple and melancholic to upbeat and driving. My two personal favorites are "Together", played during pivotal scenes in each relationship, with its melody seeming to display a collapse of willpower and the sort of heartthrob one gets from a perfect relationship, and "My Territory", which is a somewhat cheeky tune without any particularly distinct mood that plays a lot during important character-building scenes involving the main character at home.
In short,
is a well-written game that deals with relationships, longing, and the sort of struggles that arise because of each character's unique dealings and personal hurdles. It's a little expensive at $35, but I believe it to be well worth the price.
My personal relationship ranking:
. Although, I have to say, it's pretty hard choosing.
Edit: I write this at the end of my third time through the main story. Right now, I think my personal relationship ranking has changed to:
, but it's still damn hard choosing an order.
Edit 2: My, oh, my, the extras. I've played through the story three times now, but it's currently 2 in the morning because I've spent the last ten or so hours(!) playing through all of the extra scenes. In my previous two playthroughs, I thought I played them all, but apparently that was not the case. The extra scenes add multiple layers of depth to every character, and they tie the entirety of the story back together in satisfying and emotional ways, sometimes heartwarming, and sometimes heartbreaking.
That being said, this was the first time I encountered the 30-minute freezing glitch/bug. It certainly is annoying, but I did not seek a fix. I imagine you could uninstall and reinstall the files to try to fix it, but it's not something that bothered me that much.

This game is a hit or miss thing. It's a puzzler, entirely. Each puzzle is unique to each one, even though they do share elements. Something like bilging is for your match 3 type of people. Something like patching is more for people who like mazes. Being f2p in the game isn't bad once you get going, and if you're really good at the puzzles, you will easily be able to advance through the game at a relative pace. The community is still pretty lively, albeit the number of voyages available have dwindled since I first ever played this game. Over all, there's a number of good things, but a few quirks in the game.
Pros:
*Technically not P2W. You can get different things, but only being good at puzzles will make you win
*Music is good when it's there
*Puzzles are diverse
*Crews work nicely if you can find an active one
*Learning how to do the puzzles better is very rewarding
*There's not really much wrong with the game, if you find it enjoyable
Cons:
*Music isn't always there
*Advancing can seem slow if you aren't very good at puzzles
*It's a time sink
*Only the Emerald Ocean is all that lively.
Conclusion: Definitely a yes for people who like puzzlers. They're all unique, they're all enjoyable, even if you don't do very well, and they all have a nice atmosphere. Also, it's free, which is definitely a good thing.

Hey everyone,
A little background: I had PA since the alpha stage. I chose to move to PA Titans with the special offer for 10 bucks. I do have and play SC2.
I have read some of the reviews, and I agree that, maybe, dev wanted to make some money out of the Titan “expansion”.
Now, I believe that some of you got the wrong idea of this “strategy” game. Most of the strategy games work with a balance of attack and defense, true. PA is a strategy game where I see Attack as the only key of the game. There is
here.
Let’s have a look at another game, SC2. Some of you have mentioned that would gladly go back to play SC2, and I understand that -- I love SC2. But these two games are completely different. See, SC2 has a great deal of “defense”. If you push the AI to very high difficulty and they are located in a floating island, you can’t really get to them. At the same time you can spend 30 min building your own defenses, and you would know that you are secure under your shield generators and turrets for the next two (human) hours.
PA is nothing like that. There are no shield generators, and buildings such as turrets are destroyed very easily. There is most probably very little defensive strategy programmed in the AI. The game is all about how fast you are to build and destroy the other. It may come to a surprise to you, but it’s called Planetary
.
Here comes the fun part. If you think that it is too easy for you, just create your own planetary system, set it up as you like. Then play alone against 5 AI! You can also set your own strategy to ANNIHILATE other commanders! :D
5 AI, which means that you could destroy each of them in a different way:
The game is really fun to play. It’s not a game that would last long (like SC2) unless you decide to. Against 1 AI you could win in 10 min, sometimes in 3 min if you are fast enough.
For who is interested in purchasing this game, consider this as a VERY fast-paced game. Within the first minutes, your fabricators will already be half the way around the planet building mass extractors. 2 min in you will have multiple factories building an army. 4 minutes in you will already have a nice army (
) and will be building the advanced factory. 7 minutes in you may already have advanced builders and would be start building advanced technology (such as the cool titans). Compare this to the slow-paced SC2, and you will understand why some people are not comfortable with it.
Finally, everything depends on you. Do you like long games? Select harder AI and more AIs. Do you want to build titans? Well, one is normally enough to ANNIHINLATE your enemy! You need more enemies to have more fun! ;D
Side note: Someone said that Galactic War is the same as Skirmish. That’s false -- Galactic War is different from Skirmish. A normal battle in Galactic War is you against one opponent. Only if you start fighting the faction commander (“mini boss”), you will find yourself against multiple enemies. When you start you will NOT have all the technology – you need to destroy other commanders to find technology (usually, when you start, you can ONLY build base vehicles). Additionally, there is some special technology which is not available in skirmish, such as 50% off production costs for Titans, 75% off energy for artillery, faster commander, faster (type) of units, faster building, stronger units, and way more! You can even find other “remains” of commanders that you can activate to have an allied AI with you in the battles. You will start with nothing, and you can end up with the most powerful combination for a
Enjoy.

I don't feel like reviewing Starbound is worth my time, so instead, I'll tell you the story of a tiger; a glorious tiger named "StoundBar".
As a cub, Stoundbar's bright colorful fur astounded everyone, and shined bright against all the other tigers around her. Tigers everywhere thought she would be the legend among them.
As she neared adolescence, her outstanding talent showed itself. Were there already fast tigers in the community? Sure, but Stound was faster. Were there tigers who were experts at hunting? Sure, but she brought in more game than anyone else. It became clear that she had potential.
And then it happened...
A circus came to her habitat and was swiping up other tigers, but when they saw Stoundbar, they stopped in their tracks. They released the other tigers and took her instead. Off to the circus. The circus... named "♥♥♥♥leChish"
At ♥♥♥♥leChish, her talent was displayed. Her best qualities; her running, her hunting skills, and others were all showcased for small audiences at first; introductory gigs where people got an exclusive glimpse of Stoundbar's excellence. Other acts, performances; other animals fell in her shadow. All people wanted to see was Stoundbar.
After awhile, ♥♥♥♥leChish began a fundraiser to develop Stoundbar's talents even further. Apparently, word of StoundBar's unique talent and glory had spread internationally, so their fundraiser raked in millions. By that time, they had their own place for their increasingly popular shows, but they decided that, with these new funds, a change of location was in order. Over almost the course of a year, they moved to a new location, and excitement for StoundBar waned the longer they took.
When they finally moved, however, ♥♥♥♥leChish Circus' popularity died, and with it, Stoundbar's did too.
And then came the abuse...
With Chucklefish--err, I mean.. ♥♥♥♥leChish seeking a desperate revival of Stoundbar's audience and notoriety, they began to beat and batter the last remnants of her brilliance out of her over time. They spent months at a time between shows pumping her with harmful steroids and hormones to try and boost her lore. Enhancements which seemed amazing on the surface were soon revealed to be harmful for her in reality. For about a month after Stoundbar, with her brand-new enhancements, were exposed to the world, her fans returned to the stadium. However, they got bored and stopped attending shows once again.
Eventually, ♥♥♥♥leChish fell into a depressing pattern; a downward spiral of desperate enhancements for Stoundbar which slowly began to kill her. The fans, however, rush back temperarily (in increasingly small numbers) and then retreat to other shows in only a matter of weeks.
Stoundbar's fur suddenly didn't seem so bright;
Her talents.. no longer special.
Starbound's era passed prematurely, and for that... all thanks can be given to the poor management of Chucklefish.
I was one of her fans; there from the first show she gave to the massive, cheering crowds.. and now all I can say is.. show's over kids, now it's time to move on to the next great act.

There are actually a couple of reasons to recommend this game to others. First of all, although it doesn't neccesarily follow an 'RPG' type storyline completely, the game is very good in itself. While creation club is kinda trash, it doesn't affect gameplay any and I don't see the big issue about it everyone is complaining about, as it really doesn't affect the game's experience in the slightest. The game itself has a pretty darn good storyline, with quests to keep you occupied and entertained for years, and the immense open world in the game is fun to roam around, with random places and settlements and people popping up all over the place each with their own stories that you can explore and sometimes even pursue. One of my favorite aspects of the game is how much the player is in control. The enormous amount of choices ensure that no-one's playthrough experience will be quite the same, with multiple interesting endings that can be achieved. The graphics are very well done and the amount of detail put into the game is massive, with tons of hidden locations and features. Mods or not, this game is truly a must have for any level of gamer. It combines elements of horror, humor, RPG, FPS, Simulation, Design, Strategy, Building (You can build your own settlements in the game with hundreds of items, furniture, decorations, resources, and even trade stands to choose from for the ultimate experience of building your own small city (I recommend getting the build limits nullifying mod)), and a storyline tailored to your own choices. The mods are a great addition to the game with lots of fun and interesting content, especially Nuka-World and Far Harbor, yet you really don't need them for the true game experience. This game never gets boring for me, with so many possibilities and so many things to do. In short, you should definitely buy this game.

"A delayed game is good eventually, a rushed game is bad forever" -Shigeru Miyamoto
The original release for this game was to be December 4, 2013. A bit late, eh?
Sure, Chucklefish may not have been able to deliver on time, but look at Valve's record. They weren't bashed for being late because of Valve Time.  The game is getting much better, and is almost to it's official release (2 updates until) and is really good compared to what it may have been if it released when planned.
So what I am saying is that putting this game off because of the heaps of negative reviews in the "Most Helpful" section isn't what this game deserves.
Now that I got that out of the way, let's make an actual review, shall we?
Overall: It's doing what it's set out to do.
When the beta first came out, it was so much different, monsters actually need to do attacks to damage you, the snow infantry armor was overpowered, and you could die of hunger, and freezing.
The Novakids didn't even exist in the game.
Today, that's all changed: Questing, ship upgrades, colonies, and really smooth generation of planets. This game managed to keep me interested in mining, which for some reason, Minecraft couldn't get me interested in that.
This game has done exactly what it aimed to do in the first place: let people explore.
Although, it is still in beta, with many additions, bosses, quests and mechanics yet to be created in the universe. (with whips being planned in the next update, upon writing this.)
However, this game is not flawless; the AI is quite stupid, with pathfinding that matches an acrobat missing their inner ear, and the game making some parts of itself feel unneccessary, and the framrate dying at certain buildings made by the devs (which is being fixed).
Conclusion: You should try it, sometime, at the least.

Have you ever played a Point and Click game? how about a Point and Click game with every animation made out of clay? What if i ask, if you played a Point a Click Musical game. If you answered no to both of those questions i wouldn’t be 100% surprised. Dominique Pamplemousse is probably the first of it’s kind that i have ever seen. A point and click detective musical game. it’s sort of hard to picture it while i even write it down; and I’ve played the game. But Dominique Pamplemousse has heart thats heading towards the right direction of innovation, creativity and a bit of nonsense.
First of sure Dominique Pamplemousse is NOT a fun game to play. It is as basic as a point and click game can be. You see something out of the ordinary and “boom!” you click it. The only difference in this game, is that almost ever dialogue is sang in a musical tune. Crazy as it sounds the game does have plenty of character. Although it seems that there is only one voice actor for ALL 9 or so characters, you can tell that the developer of this game had a blast making it. As i said earlier the game is all animated in clay. As odd as it is, the animation sorta fits with the musical theme. sorta not that great. There isn’t lip moving when the characters talk, instead they just move the mouth up and down over and over. The singing in the game is extraordinarily terrible! A lot of off keys, and most of the time it feels like the singing is forced into saying words really quickly just to keep up the tune.
Aside from all of that i was really quit interested in the story. Sure a lot of points the story is very cliche, but once the game was over i was feeling for some more Pamplemousse action and of course singing. I hope the developer doesn’t quit on this style of game. Unfortunately we live in a time where there isn’t as many creativity in video games as there use to be, and this game really brought a smile to my face to know it’s not gone. I’m glad a game like this exits and i hope to see more, but maybe next time, i would like it longer then 1hr and of course with more voices.
I definitely want people to play this game, it’s $5 right now for the deluxe edition which includes the SHEET MUSIC (come on, how many games come with sheet music) and soundtrack. As i said, i WANT people to play this. I don’t expect people to like it and i understand but it just seems like a game, personally to me, that i did not want to miss.

I hate doing this kind of thing because I have been both a game developer and reviewer, so I know how hard it is to do an amazing game. The idea is sound enough, and the trailer is tempting, but the execution is lacking soul and substance.

Space stations are for deploying and making money from while you are away doing someting else, not blasting level 1 pirates!
This game is not as terrible as some reviews would suggest, and even though there seem to be periodic updates, there is no info on the steam channel about what those updates are doing.

Huge universe, twitch flight/combat, fly fighter ships, merchant ships and capital ships.....yes, maybe it's not as pretty as some of the new AAA games but awesome gameplay.
LONGER VERSION:
I've played Fairspace for awhile now (since way before it came on steam) and love it each time I log in.  I've seen many improvements/updates made to it, and each time the dev has listened to the players, made changes they wanted or needed.  The community is a big deal in this game, and luckily it's a good community.
The combat/flight side of the game is smooth and well executed and it's a breath of fresh air to play a space mmo that gives you direct control of your ship.
Trade and exploration is a big aspect of the game.  Your map starts out fairly empty and planets, stars, nebula etc only appear as you find them.  So if you want to make the money by finding the really good trade routes you will have to head out into the unknown.
The game could benefit from some updated sounds and graphics, but even as it stands, it is a solidly playable game.

The end decision is I do in fact recommend this game, but wait until more of the content and features are available. Right, so anyway, to keep this review short and sweet this VN is good.
The main story focuses on our protagonist, Yuna, who is spurred into action as an undercover matchmaker by two gay ghost girls to subtly meddle in the love affairs of gay girls in her all girl's high school. So the premise is fairly simple, but with solid writing and letting us see events from the different girls' perspectives (who have different personalities and are all fairly likeable) makes for an immersive, at times emotional, story. Of course, when combining several romantic stories some might appear more solid than the rest, but which one you like is for you to decide.
Being a visual novel the gameplay is not too interesting. You will be given choices here and there, but the story is linear and the only impact is some slightly changed dialogue and
.
"As for the music, it's okay." 10/10 - [insert-gaming-site-here]
No seriously, it's just ok. Some catchy tunes, but overall ok.
The artwork is fairly good. The character designs are cute and varied and fit the characters pretty well. Some of the sprites can be amusing at times. The backgrounds, though, are rather generic with a few exceptions. The CGs used for the "intimate" scenes are rather tame, but I really don't think they are meant as fap material either way. Strangely enough I would say they are cute, emotional and intimate first and foremost. As something to be remembered fondly. That being said, the CGs can sometimes appear to be somewhat, eh, weird when portraying characters from certain angles. I noticed one CG in particular, but overall it's fairly solid.
You will probably want to buy this one for the story and while it has a simple premise the execution is well done. I got a little hooked, or emotionally invested so to say, and continued through the night. Then I got a bright idea, and turned off the in-game music for a piano cover of Celine Dion's you-know-which-song during the climactic last scenes. And tried not to cry. But cried alot. Sleep deprivation and exhaustion can do miracles sometimes.
So, there you have it. In not-so-short-but-sweet terms. Yeah. Buy it.

I don't feel like reviewing Starbound is worth my time, so instead, I'll tell you the story of a tiger; a glorious tiger named "StoundBar".
As a cub, Stoundbar's bright colorful fur astounded everyone, and shined bright against all the other tigers around her. Tigers everywhere thought she would be the legend among them.
As she neared adolescence, her outstanding talent showed itself. Were there already fast tigers in the community? Sure, but Stound was faster. Were there tigers who were experts at hunting? Sure, but she brought in more game than anyone else. It became clear that she had potential.
And then it happened...
A circus came to her habitat and was swiping up other tigers, but when they saw Stoundbar, they stopped in their tracks. They released the other tigers and took her instead. Off to the circus. The circus... named "♥♥♥♥leChish"
At ♥♥♥♥leChish, her talent was displayed. Her best qualities; her running, her hunting skills, and others were all showcased for small audiences at first; introductory gigs where people got an exclusive glimpse of Stoundbar's excellence. Other acts, performances; other animals fell in her shadow. All people wanted to see was Stoundbar.
After awhile, ♥♥♥♥leChish began a fundraiser to develop Stoundbar's talents even further. Apparently, word of StoundBar's unique talent and glory had spread internationally, so their fundraiser raked in millions. By that time, they had their own place for their increasingly popular shows, but they decided that, with these new funds, a change of location was in order. Over almost the course of a year, they moved to a new location, and excitement for StoundBar waned the longer they took.
When they finally moved, however, ♥♥♥♥leChish Circus' popularity died, and with it, Stoundbar's did too.
And then came the abuse...
With Chucklefish--err, I mean.. ♥♥♥♥leChish seeking a desperate revival of Stoundbar's audience and notoriety, they began to beat and batter the last remnants of her brilliance out of her over time. They spent months at a time between shows pumping her with harmful steroids and hormones to try and boost her lore. Enhancements which seemed amazing on the surface were soon revealed to be harmful for her in reality. For about a month after Stoundbar, with her brand-new enhancements, were exposed to the world, her fans returned to the stadium. However, they got bored and stopped attending shows once again.
Eventually, ♥♥♥♥leChish fell into a depressing pattern; a downward spiral of desperate enhancements for Stoundbar which slowly began to kill her. The fans, however, rush back temperarily (in increasingly small numbers) and then retreat to other shows in only a matter of weeks.
Stoundbar's fur suddenly didn't seem so bright;
Her talents.. no longer special.
Starbound's era passed prematurely, and for that... all thanks can be given to the poor management of Chucklefish.
I was one of her fans; there from the first show she gave to the massive, cheering crowds.. and now all I can say is.. show's over kids, now it's time to move on to the next great act.
