Yuritopia is real.
At first, the game might start out a little slow but that's only because it's fleshing out the characters and introductions. Once I got through that small bump, I honestly loved every second of the game.
The protagonist is easily likeable even from the getgo (it doesn't take long before you utterly love her, really) and the girls that are introduced afterwards are all rather unique in their own way and easy to become fond of. Their relationships went in ways I didn't expect but definitely had me grinning as they developed. Nothing about it feels rushed or awkwardly forced. It all seems really genuine even with the realism they seem to add to it (a crush that starts out entirely one sided, age difference, etc.).
In terms of content, it definitely has quite a lot in my opinion. Even after you finish the "main" story line, side stories are unlocked that show the other girl's feelings and their perspective. It's also important to point out that while Yuna (the protag) has a large role in aiding the start of their relationships, you also see how these girls come together from their own perspectives. With the side stories, you see what the other person was thinking at the time and how they were feeling, so in a way you get to see both sides. That was utterly amazing, honestly.
As for the nudity, none of it feels perverted or done in the purpose of trying to get more views/customers. They arrive to that point naturally in their relationship, and not every couple goes as far as some. Even then, everything feels warm and loving. These scenes were made to show their feelings for each other, rather than to just draw naked girls, which is a definite bonus.
Final thoughts: While the price can be a bit... well, pricey... for what they're offering you, I honestly think it's definitely deserved and worth it. If you truly love Yuri, girls love, or just love seeing cute relationships blossom and develop, then this game is definitely for you.

This is by far my least favourite game from Nickervision. Doesn't make it bad.
If you're not familiar with that developer, gist of those games is: arcade-like, very simple and quick. Well done and fun. Rest of the review will just be complaining, so go get the game (or better yet, grab Orbt XL which is better). It comes from a place of love though - I like the game, but see how much better it could be and it bothers me.
Some of the issues here were also present in BitBlaster XL, but weren't as important, as BitBlaster felt "less endless". It felt like a game that one could be eventually done with and fine with that. This is a bit like super hexagon (or Orbt XL), meaning you will want to replay it a lot more.
Control: there's something wrong with how the controls work. Pressing buttons while transferring between nodes affects your speed, which is somewhat not intuitive in some scenarios (eg. when you are going right, but want to go up soon if you press up before hitting the node you'll slow down. If you press left, you somehow won't).
Simplicity: It's just not very simple, the concept feels either forced or not fleshed out enough. Games like this work, because they have very simple rules. Think super hexagon. Move right/left and don't hit stuff. This one has aspects that took me 1h of play to discover. Granted, this is because it's fast paced and you tend to not pay attention - it's still rather simple.
Content: this game ends too soon. I get the strategy behind this: it's a $.5 game that makes everyone happy. But I want something that will push me to actually get good with it. Be it achievements or unlocks. After 1h of play you have to motivate yourself. This is very much true for all Nickervision games and I see that it's a viable strategy - everyone gets a nice feeling of completing the game and it's hard to justify a negative score for something that cheap. And I'm still recommending it, cause yeah, the price is right and the game is fun. It just could be so much more.
Progression: This is the same issue as Bit Blaster XL. You just get better stuff. Once you unlock the next thing, you won't ever have a reason to go back. I can't stop myself from feeling like this was intentional to serve the part of the audience that maybe isn't that great at games but they want all the achievements nevertheless. You grinded enough, you get the best player character, best is better than what you've been using, better high score, yay progression. I think that's a bit patronizing to gamers and super hard games like super hexagon made big bucks to prove my point. I'd rather see skins, like in Orbt XL.
Overall I feel like the concept isn't all it could be. The game is still good. I think the pricing is very sane (some indie companies would sell a game like this for a lot more - I feel like Nicks sale quantities prove them wrong). I like the sound and the visuals. I love that it works flawlessly on linux (well, the leaderboards don't work but who cares).

Kindred Spirits on the Roof is charm personified and if you're not careful, it will suck you right into its core and never let you leave the planet known as Yuritopia.

Very few pieces of media with the 'Yuri' tag can admit to being more than just 'fanservice'. If I was asked to describe 'Kindred Spirits on the Roof' in terms of my anime experiences, I would have to say that it reminds me of a cross between " Kuttsukiboshi" and "Sakura Trick" mixed in with a cross between "Maria Sama ga Miteru" and "Strawberry Panic".

The two ghosts - or 'Kindred Spirits' as they prefer to be called, may as well have been drawn from the likeness of Sachiko and Yumi. Not to mention, Matsuri and Miyu - the track and field sempai - look an awful lot like Sei and Yōko. This led me to believe that the design choice may not have been entirely unintentional. Considering how big a part "Maria Sama ga Miteru" has had in the Yuri/Shoujo ai genre it doesn't really surprise me. In fact, it almost felt as if the game was paying homage to these roots, expanding on them and going into an area that was not possible 10 years ago.

I very rarely play a game through more than once – feeling as if once I've done the main story there are too many other games out there to try so no need to do all the "side stuff". Kindred Spirits on the Roof however is a visual novel that made me want to not only experience all the "side stuff", but made me want to re-experience it again and again - in the same manner as one would re-read parts of a favourite  book or rewatch parts of a movie that left an impression.

As flaws are part of any review, I do feel obligated to touch upon them. Although, in my opinion, the main flaw here is simply the lack of voice acting. While all the main scenes have voice acting – it would've been great to see it in the side stories as well. The voice acting in this game is so exceptional that it's truly a shame that there's not more of it.

In conclusion, if you're looking for an experience that will put a smile to your face and make you feel good about life, love and the human race in general – then look no further. Kindred Spirts on the Roof will do just that – and more. In my 100 + hours with the game I got the 'full clear' icon with all the extras unlocked – yet I'm still keeping it in my favourites so that I can come back to it whenever I need a 'pick-me-up'.
This game is REALLY fun! The new unlock system is also really nice and isn't grindy like his previous games! I highly recommend this!

This review is for the full series (1-4)
Sorcery has been around for more than 30 years now, I remember playing around with the books as a kid with dice and pen at hand. Remastered digitally it hasn't lost any of its charm. If you ever had a knack for complex choose-your-own-adventure games, this one will be everything you ever wished for. Just buy it whenever you want and start chipping away at it.
If you are an avid RPG fan with a knack for visual novels and are thinking about picking up this series, there's a few things you should know and consider though. First and foremost, the difficulty of Sorcery contains a lot of trial and error. The source material wasn't altered for the game, which means that decisions that theoretically are perfectly viable are going to fail every single time, just because the rule-set says so. It also means that in quite a few situations you will be railroaded into a particular turn of events because you aren't meeting the item, stat or simply story decision criteria to take even the most obvious of alternate paths. This can be extremely frustrating, especially to gamers which aren't used to frustrating game-design. Just imagine 'Tomb of Horrors' for D&D : Left path or right path? Left. ... ... ... Rocks fall, everyone dies. No trap detection, no saving throws, no further decisions, just death, final death. Next time around, remember not to go left, ever. Sorcery by far isn't as harsh as that, but it does remind of the golden age of total failure without any repeat option. So if you don't want to be frustrated at all, don't play Sorcery.
As for the visual aspect: The graphics are there, but they don't play a major role, as most of the story is supposed to happen in the players mind, which leads to rather minimalistic graphical design. It's not a bad thing per se, but if you dislike reading a lot of text, some of it over and over again until you get your decisions right, you might want to steer away from Sorcery.
If I still didn't manage to discourage you from playing Sorcery, than there's a massive chance you'll just love the entire game series and will have quite a few dozen hours of fun with it, even if you knew the original material. It is difficult to crystallise my thoughts on this game into a simple thumbs up or thumbs down because the game has some great aspects but also some out right bad elements.
The game starts off really well, you are basically playing as Captain Archer in Quantum Leap inhabiting some guy's body. However Brother Cavil doesn't turn up with a computer made out of LEGO to tell you what is going on so you have to try and ask people to explain things without giving away that you an imposter. The voice acting is excellent, the characters feel natural and the world building is thorough.
This does lead me onto the first thing I didn't like; during my first conversation I asked about something and was effectively told to just Google it. This makes sense from the perspective of how a real person might react but from a game play and immersive story telling perspective it does not. Having to sift through pages of dry text on the in game information system does not help me feel like I'm part of this world. It is also rather tedious, I tried on a couple of occasions to look at all of this information to get a fuller picture of the universe but each time gave up caring.
Once the game got into the murder mystery it again started well but didn't really reach a satisfying conclusion. As you talk to people there are various things that vaguely point your suspicions in one direction or another and keep you guessing but then out of nowhere it stops and the game just straight up asks you who did it. So I just had to guess and guessed wrong. After a couple of play throughs I looked up who the murderer was and even with that knowledge I couldn't see anything that would point more suspicion at that character more than any other. I was forced to conclude that you were supposed to just play through again and again until you guessed the right character. Only after a good few more playthroughs did I find the vital piece of evidence. It turns out that I almost found it in my first attempt but I missed it due to the terrible inventory system. I can't explain better without spoilers,
This brings me onto the worst part of this game, the inventory system. Whoever built the inventory clearly wandered into the sprint planning for a completely different game and built this overcomplicated mess. This game is all about the dialogue, combat is a minor side part of the game so all this game needed was a health bar, a lethal weapon and a non-lethal one but instead you have multiple weapons with different firing modes and ammunition types together with an unintuitive system where if you fully charge your battery you can't carry anything. The most telling thing about this system is that there is a community guide on how to use it. If someone has to write a guide for your basic user interface it is not an intuitive system.
Now onto the other big thing I didn't like. The game makes a big deal about how much your choices matter so after I completed the game I immediately started it again to play through doing the opposite of what I did in the first time. And sure enough just like The Walking Dead and Silent Hill Shattered Memories before it your decisions really don't matter. Yes you get different dialogue and a couple of events pan out differently but the core flow of the narrative is the same.
Usually I like achievements as they give you an incentive to go back and find bits you have missed or play the game in a different way but here I found to get many of the achievements you had to play through so much of the game again it quickly became repetitive and tiresome.
I haven't talked about the story yet which is for the most part good with some novel 4th wall breaking which I liked but it does drag a bit. Towards the end of the game it builds but to what is either going to be the end of game cliffhanger or onto the next big chapter of this game. So here is what finally tipped me to give this a thumbs down, I was relived that it was the end of the game. That is not the feeling you want to leave a gamer with on a cliffhanger ending so I am not going to buy the sequel.

You will choose how the story plays out, by actions or by what you say.  You will also have to explore whatever place you are in in order to progress but it's not that hard, althought this can make the game a little boring to play to some people.
Nonetheless it's a really good game, a must play!

The story was what kept me intrigued and playing along in a genre I was unfamiliar with. I'd watched many mystery movies and television shows, but never played one. Where it fails for me is the out of genre gameplay they shoehorn in. The fps shooter mechanics are a primitive and unwieldly mess. The non-lethal weapons seemed to be mostly ineffective despite the   target restraint system. It's difficult to tell if it's merely designed poorly or glitchy. There's another detour in the...flight mechanics? I'm not sure what else to call it, but I'm being very generous there. The instructions are entirely unclear and the interface is not a first-person cockpit/turret view liked you'd expect from the rest of the game. It reminded me more of minesweeper, only more tedious.
These short forays into other genres could be excused if they didn't impact the outcome of the rest of the game. Unfortunately, what you do in them has consequences. If you fail on your first try, you're going to have to go through them again despite the focus of the game being character interaction.
The voice acting was solid and the characters were likeable or engaging. Snippets of diary, journal, and email entries would have been great. I don't understand what's up with all the negative reviews that have hundreds of hours of gameplay. What, were they having a terrible time but couldn't put it down? Give me a break. I think some people might be expecting a little too much from a video game... 900 hours played yet downvoted? lol
Anyway, on to an actual recommendation.
It's Fallout. Sure, a bunch of stuff is different but the gameplay (the stuff you'll spend the majority of your time going; like exploring, killing, looting, strategizing your skilltree) itself is still very much the same. So if you enjoyed Fallout3 or New Vegas, I'd say there's like a 90% chance you'll enjoy Fallout4.
It took me a while to get used to the new GUI, but overall I like it just as much as the old way. There are a few instances where circumstance makes it a little hard to do finely tuned environmental interactions (since there are lots of "A.R. floating menus") but those rare occurences aside, it's fine.
The settlements system is addictive and satisfying in a "Fallout Shelter" mobile game kinda way. So if managing that little mobile game was fun, you'll probably enjoy the new addition of managing your settlements.
I can't speak for any of the DLC since I still only just play vanilla Fallout4. And seeing as how this is a recommendation / review for just this one title (the base vanilla game) I don't think this is the place for a critique of DLC, player-created-content, or the companies overseeing any of that stuff.
So yeah... it's more fallout. It's fun. People are sinking hundreds and hundreds of hours into it.
I like it, it's neat. If you like fallout, you'll probably like this.

Let me just open by saying that Kindred Spirits is Good.
For some context: I read a lot of visual novels, and I regret that. There's not really any other way to put it. I like the medium in theory, but the vast majority of what you can find is just bad. Pacing in particular is a problem, followed up by tendency to throw in reprehensible content.
Kindred Spirits is novel right off the bat because something actually happens in the first hour. While it's not immune to pacing problems, Kindred Spirits' plot moves along fairly regularly, aided by the device of the planner breaking the story into discrete chunks. Another thing that stops Kindred Spirits from feeling like it's stalling out is the fact that it follows a handful of couples, so someone's story is always advancing meaningfully whatever you're reading.
The couples are what is going to make it for you if you like the game. The characters are all unique and fairly well written, and the game for the most part does a really good job of differentiating the characters' internal monologues when there's a scene from their perspective. Yuna is an interesting character and one who I feel a lot of kinship with, but seeing the antics of the various couples as they fall in love and strive to start a relationship is bulk of the draw.
Well, I guess there's one other potential draw. The elephant in the room.
According to one of the translators, sexual scenes are only roughly 6% of the script. Having read all of it, I'm surprised it's even that high- and if sex scenes are 6% of the script, then things like "nngh" and "ahn" have to be at least 3%. I'm not a huge fan of sex scenes in these kind of games to begin with, but if you're going to have them Kindred Spirits' ones are fairly good. They do a decent job of making the people actually seem like teenagers who have no idea how to bone, and the CGs never get more explicit than a few anime tiddies. Unless you're incredibly morally offended by euphemistic reference to heavy petting you'll probably be fine- it's not like people are breaking out the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for a 50 page orgy.
One complaint you can level (aside from the pacing and editing, which, while WAY above VN standard, is still a little long sometimes)  is the "extra scenes". Once you finish the main story, you're only about half way done. Various scenes pop up all over the planner, and the main way they're unlocked is making choices in the main game. This is sort of a hassle, so I'd recommend just going back and choosing the other option every time you see a choice to get it out of the way early. The extra scenes are nice, but they're where the game threatens to outstay its welcome. Personally I was charmed enough to enjoy it right up until the final extra scene, but I suspect a lot of people will be done about halfway through the extras.
Also, the game makes you think it might have alternate routes, but that's a lie, choices only affect the extra scenes. Which is a shame, but there's nothing wrong with there being one story you want to tell.
In summary, Kindred Spirits is a cute little game that's a lot of fun. It lasted me about a month and I enjoyed my time with it.

I've been shilling for the Sorcery series for a while now - writing walkthroughs and FAQs, doing an LP, recommending the series to fellow posters - but I've reached the conclusion that I don't much care for Sorcery 4.
Mind, it's a really complex game with an excellent climax. It keeps track of and reacts to the disguise you're wearing (out of 4-5 options), the level of alert you've left behind - not just in this game, but in previous installments as well - and to time shenanigans. Can't imagine how hard all that stuff was to map out.
Your endgame can vary greatly depending on exactly which people you've met and left alive 2-3 games ago!
But, with all that in mind... I have the most fun in these games when I keep rewinding a situation to see how different solutions can shake out. Some of the weirdest outcomes in these games result from pursuing a marginal and seemingly irrelevant tangent. And Sorcery 4 kinda puts a stop to that. At some point, as a part of raising the stakes, your rewind ability is sharply limited. You can no longer ♥♥♥♥ around and try everything :(
Now, the above is a matter of taste - I'm sure most people play "fairly", just accepting whatever outcome the game throws their way and carrying on if they haven't died. What's actually a problem are the towers of magic. They're basically a series of puzzle rooms that you'll have to solve if you don't have specific information / allies from a previous installment. They don't react in the slightest to your disguise, the guards alert state, or time stuff. Basically, every time you replay, the towers are exactly the same, and it gets annoying quickly.
Still a game with a very impressive bunch of scenarios. Just... not as much fun to replay as 2 or 3.
Also, on a petty personal note; the fact that I've spent a long time hunting for spelling and grammar errors, yet never got a response from the developers and the errors remain unfixed in the final update is fairly discouraging.

Sorcery! Part 4 is a great conclusion to the series.  There are many hidden secrets in part 4, and I enjoyed exploring and unlocking many of them.  The finale is hard-won and highly satisfying, worth every effort to work towards.  I know there are multiple endings, good and bad, so I am interested in seeing what other endings are available.  If you have played the other parts, you know what to expect.  This is more of the same, which I was very happy for.
Some users have complained about the rewind mechanic being removed for much of part 4.  I found that removing this feature made the game more intense and rewarding when you succeeded; I couldn't use the rewind as a crutch.  I enjoyed the challenge and the uncertainty of my choices.  I cheered when I was able to make my way through a desperate situation, and I came back with a determined resolve when I failed.  If this sounds like it would be more trouble than it's worth, please realize that the game designers made it so dying without the rewind isn't all that punishing: you still retain all the items and knowledge you found, and you start back at a checkpoint that isn't too far from anything.  It's easy to get right back to where you were, and you often find new secrets on the way back, anyhow.  It all makes sense lore-wise, also.  Retaining all the items and knowledge you found is important, because you can use them to overcome obstacles later in the game.  I never felt like the game was unfair or overly punishing.  They also give you a rewind after you finish the game, so you can go back to any point of your playthrough to try a different route or a different ending, which is a nice touch.
Overall, I enjoyed every minute of Sorcery!, and I highly recommend it.  I am excited to play through all of the parts again on New Game Plus, once it's added, to see if I can uncover more secrets and unlock new endings.

Quite simply if you liked Steve Jackson & Ian Livingstone FF books then this is a MUST BUY. Inkle has produced far and away the best game going. The entire Sorcery! series has been an amazing production of Steve Jackson's epic series and this final part has been utterly awesome.
Each game has become progressively bigger and better, so that they are so much more than simply an on-screen copy of the gamebook. (Some fighting fantasy games are available from other developers, but are basically just the original book with the highly limited options that a 400 page book allowed.)
There is a massive amount of new material & also rearranging of original material from the books, however all the new material has an authentic feel, in keeping with the source material.
The combat system is a little strange at first, but way better than randon dice rolls once it is mastered. The use of disguises woz another great idea for this final part.
The great thing about these games is the ability to retrace your steps and return to areas already explored (apart from in part 1) and what you find can be influenced by your previous actions. This gives massively more scope than the original game books ever could.
The lack of the standard "rewind" option once inside the fortress is great as it builds the pressure on the player, really leaving you with that feeling that your next mistake will be your last!
I asked Inkle if they intended to make any other FF books in this same format, but sadly they said they had no plans at this stage. But we can live in hope! Please, please, please Inkle, produce some more of these amazing games - "House of Hell" would be my first choice. The ability to backtrack & explore would be great for proper exploration of the haunted house.
In the meantime, these games are so massive that after several months there are still so many more options that i could chose in the game that it remains interesting. Thank-you Inkle! (The Sorcery! 4 launch playthrough evening woz great fun as well!)

I want to like this chapter, I really do.
The complete randomness in the choices provided this game detract from what could have continued be an interesting tale. Much of the game involves guessing what you think the designers want you to do--instead of choosing your own path--and you are often punished for choosing incorrectly, even if you follow gameplay logic already presented to you. The story is also stymied by situational puzzles that bear little if no connection to the larger story.
Navigation, sadly, is also a mess. Once you pass through a location, sometimes you are able to backtrack, and other times you are not. And then, sometimes when you are allowed to, there is no purpose to it, as the game indicates that there is nothing more that can be done here. The mix between linear progression and choice of movement is, again, unfortunately, stymied by an overall lack of structure and greater intent.
What was once a charming little adventure has collapsed upon itself, lacking the structure of a cohesive story and consistent gameplay rules; often, too often, random situations are presented to you with random choices to select -- with no consistent logic. Options in one situation for example, are often not presented in another, similar situation. Good games create an environment with a set of rules and provide interesting choices within that structure. This chapter lacks that systemic structure.
The primary weakness of this chapter is a lack of focus of intent. There is scant evidence of a lead designer, as the volume of random situations and random choices scatter what could have been--what I hoped would have been--a satisfying conclusion.

Pros:
1. Several different fighting styles that each contain their own unique moves and combos.
2. Very good dodging and grappling system.
3. Autokicks afk room leaders pretty quick if they afk in a room full of ready people (unlike Rumble Fighter).
4. Kicking someone from a room requires a vote (so it's harder to rage kick).
5. Freezone channel (only opens during a specific short window of time) makes everyone balanced stat wise. Not to be mistaken with the Free channel.
6. Lots of creative potential for combos (especially from something like Taekwondo).
Cons:
1. One of the problems is, once you hit level 20, you can no longer enter the Beginner channel and you're forced into the Free channel. And that's not even the main problem; at levels above 20+, you're able to wear really strong armor (especially rares) collected from arcades (boring PvE) or purchased from other players who have already obtained the items from tedious arcade grinding. But the degree to which your stats can be increased from the really expensive or hard to obtain rares is insane. Some people could have 1.1k hit attack and 20k hp due to having spent days or weeks of farming arcades, and they could be pit against someone with, like, 800-900 hit attack and 10k hp who only plays arcade casually. The gameplay (PvP) itself is really good and it has a lot of potential, but if it were managed in a way that made it less stat based, it would be significantly better. A fodder tier person (skill wise) shouldn't be able to beat a skilled person just because he farms more.
tl;dr: very stat-based in the Free channel even though it's PvP. This channel can only be fully enjoyed if you don't mind pouring way too much $$$ or farming PvE a lot. The first channel (Beginner) and Freezone (different from the Free channel; everyone's stats are regulated here) will be fully enjoyable though.
2. Inputs are somewhat delayed for pretty much everyone (I think). Still, even with that, the gameplay is still pretty good since you can still play fluidly, just requires a bit more prediction--which isn't all that bad. It would just be better if we had more control from inputs being registered instantly.
3. The special E sets (which require level 25) can be a bit of an issue because of how much better the E's they provide are compared to normal E's (the ultimates you can do once you fully charge your sp bar). Get someone who's stacked high sp with arcade gear plus a good E set to walk around getting those item boxes for SP refills while spamming E whenever he approaches a large group, and there's a high chance he'll get first place without much skill. Not too much of a big deal, though, because you can just set a room to have the E ability disabled.
4. There's an item you can buy called "Super Room Master" that makes your character unaffected by room master kicks. If they obtain the position of Room Master, it also lets them keep their position even if performing poorly in a match. Someone with it could join a room, just stay there, refusing to ready for childish reasons, and pretty much annoy everyone in the room because the room master can't even kick him out. It's happened.
Overall, the quality of the gameplay is good enough for you to ignore the cons. All I do is log on for Freezone these days.

I had played Puzzle Pirates since about 2005, shortly after it was released. The game is now 13 years old and it's age has shown. Puzzle Pirates was released in the early days of MMO's, and for many years kept me interested for its involving fun puzzle gameplay and live econemy that was effected by the players. It also helped that for the years of WoW's massive popularity, every other MMO in existence was a WoW clone or so it seemed.
The game offers a wide variety of fun puzzles, both single player and multi player, and a large amount of missions such as tournaments and raids to profess your puzzling skill.
Many things feel terribly dated and strange compared to the way game are played today, such as the way we move around islands (you could click to walk to areas for no reason or simply teleport to important areas on the map). Large raids could be very difficult to pull off as finding 50 people online to sail into Atlantis could be vastly difficult.
If you are a fan of puzzle games, you could have a lot of fun here. The game has aged heavily, and it shows. No amount of updates and polish could save it in that regard unfortunately. It comes down to how you rate a game. Rating this for its time I give it a hearty 5/5, and for today, I could reccomend it only to puzzling fans and more casual gamers. How I dream for a modern re release of this game..

Hmm, What to say about Starbound. I usually don't bother to write a review, but i'll make an exception.
For those expecting something like Terraria, you'll get just that. While it is similar, Starbound goes beyond Terraria in some area's and falls short in others. Like Starbound has a seemingly endless amount of worlds to explore but after 150 hours they start to look identical. Fortunatly the most recent update improved that by adding in a new combat system that at times feels very rigid. Personally I love Starbound and often play with mods for more fun. Although modding is not especially difficult it can break character saves and you'll lose countless hours of gameplay. Which is not nessecarily the modders fault, as they often outline possible bugs and the results or recklessly deleting mods. Anyway back to the game. Starbound falls short of Terraria because it thoughly lacks the excitment of spawning a pumkin moon or fending off a pirate invasion. In Terraria you have to farm for items to get them, anyone who has successfully made and Ankh Shield would probably agree. Instead you  farm for better guns and melee weapons, traversing each world in the hopes of finding a sword that has the effect you want or a gun that has the right secondary fire. the difference between them was that in Terraria you could easily make a monster farm and in Starbound you have to travel planet after planet in the hopes of finding exactly what you want. All in all the gameplay of both are fun and you can easily waste countless hours crafting, wandering and smiting the mobs in the games.

Keep in mind that this review is from someone who played the game when it first released with OGP, years ago.
This is a game that I grew up on, and it indeed has it's ups and downs. For one thing, I can see why people think the game is pay-to-win (Dirty-X, which is a paid fighting style, has insane spams), but I honestly don't think this is true. Sure, paying is an easy way to improve, but that is really the case with every free to play game. I feel like this game is actually a lot about skill as well - I play online often, and always get beaten by people that aren't using any paid items, despite the fact that I have spent some money on this game.
To me, this game is one of those games where you play it a lot for a month or two, stop playing for a while, and eventually get back on. This isn't really a bad thing to me though, because the main reason why I decided to get back on this game was because of different events.
All in all, I feel like this game deserves more praise. For the people that give this game bad reviews, try to rethink the type of game it is. It is free to play, which obviously means paying will help you improve faster. However, I don't find this game pay to win. In fact, even before I spent money on this game, I was playing pretty well against other players, payers and non-payers alike.
Give this game a try, if you have the time! You probably won't regret it.

I love Starbound, but I tend to play it for a while and then give it a break for months before playing again. It has been in early access for a very long time, meaning I have seen a lot of changes, most of them for the better. My main disappoint has been the disappearance of "hunger" - food now simply restores your health, so I find I have much less incentive to grow it. The game progression has also become rather more linear, which in my mind is a bit of a disappointment.
However, the developers continue to work on the game, streamlining it and adding features that keep me coming back. My husband loves the building aspect and I enjoy exploring. With the addition of the colonies feature and the ability to make towns, he is happy and with extra biomes and items regularly added, there is always something new to discover.
That is one other aspect that is a bit frustrating- multiplayer has yet to be built into the game so you still have to use Hamachi or some other linking client (I haven't been able to do it with anything other than Hamachi, but I am not very savvy about these things). It would be nice to be able to just boot up and play multiplayer without having to do all these workarounds.
I'd definitely recommend picking it up on sale and giving it a go. I've had a lot of fun playing this game.

Inkle's Sorcery! series has definitely been one hell of a ride. Part 4 takes everything from the previous games -- from the plot twists and revelations, to the items and friends you've accumulated along the way -- and wraps it all up in one exciting, climatic finale. Very few games make you feel like you’ve embarked on a journey, which something I felt is always was lacking from other fantasy titles that boast “epic quests.” However, if you’ve played the previous 3 titles, then you’ll be rewarded with fulfilling conclusion to the story and a real sense of self-achievement.
The game really makes you feel under pressure of failure, without making victory seem impossible. Upon entering Mampang you feel the weight of your quest really fall hard on your shoulders, but the game never toys with you. Despite all the hardships I had throughout the game (including but not limited to; losing all my provisions, losing my legendary sword I paid 40 gp for, and dying at least 7 times), I never felt like the game would rip the carpet from under me and try to make me fail. It puts everything you know about the game to the test, and it makes the story all the more exciting and the victory rewarding.
If you’ve played the previous 3 Sorcery! games, then you know what you’re getting into with gameplay; there’s still the fantastic spell casting system, dice games, rewinds (albeit very few this time around), and some simple time travel mechanics. I would say that there’s much more backtracking this time around, even more so than Part 3, which can get tedious at times, but in the end it’s worth it.
Overall, Sorcery! Part 4 is a fantastic final game that puts you to the test and makes the journey here worth it.

A overall good part of a 4 part game series. However I can't help but feel that they rushed through the process of making this simply to put it out there.
The visuals: Plain and simple, it does not contain as much details as the previous parts, which is sad because I had hoped the parts would only become better along with the experience this rather new company got from the 3 last parts of Sorcery. Most of the map is simply mountains that you can not go to, and the inside of Mampang does not contain much more than large deserted areas of dust and crops. Once you enter the buildings inside of Mampang, you get a little better view of what's inside, yet you still feel isolated. You can hear a hint of people surrounding you everywhere you go, but visually you only see a open field of dust. So imagination is the key here I think.
Aside from lack of visuals, the visuals that do exist are pretty good, I like the way they draw everything and use pictures from the orignal books to describe characters appearences (perhaps more pictures of characters for the future though? Newely drawn of course).
I'm not a big fan of the 3D elements that they incorporate like the timewarp towers or the large tower of Mampang, mainly because the timewarp towers fly around the screen when the game decides to steer the camera around for visual effects, and that the high tower of Mampang is quite chunky, you can see that they tried to make the tower round but it came out more like a stop sign than a circular shape, however this may just be a difference in taste.
The sound: Not much to get here either I'm afraid, mostly the sounds you will hear outside are the whisperings of the wind. Once inside of the fortress the background sound effects like the laughter of the townsfolk gets dialed down enough to barely be heard, you will mostly sit in the quiet and read the story that is written in this game, until you turn your volume up, only to fly out of your seat when you open your spells which has this loud bang that will wake up the dead on that kind of volume. So unless you feel comfortable turning your volume up and down every time you go to your spells (in a game called SORCERY), then you will have some trouble with this.
However some soundeffects are rather nice, for instance the soundeffects in the sewers are well made, there are areas where the sounds are quite good, but this is still a big concern for me.
The story: Really good, this is where the game truly gets brilliant, and the reason for why I personally play it. They've taken the story from the famous books "Steve Jackson's Sorcery" which makes this game come together so very nicely. They've managed to incorporate the story of the books nicely into this game, you feel free as there is no lack of decisisions to make, and you keep your interest from the story which you get to read, and take part of above all.
Tips: One thing you should be vary of when playing this game, you can never be quite sure if your game will be saved if you press "Quit" in game. Personally I played for quite some time, I ended coming far into the game when it got very late and I decided to press "Quit" in the game (There is no save button which is a major flaw), and I woke up this day to open sorcery when I got to the main screen and apparently had to choose adventure all over and do it all again. So my advise is to test it a few times to make sure it will save, and perhaps if you can leave the game on at all times until you've finished the game.

It's almost bittersweet that I've reached the end of this so relatively quickly, though that has much more to do with spending the entire week dedicated to finishing through it.
A couple of things to note first off. I think the price-tag is still a bit steep, and I'd highly recommend watching this like a hawk for sales if you're truly interested in experiencing it. The demo will give you about the first 2 hours of story and introduce all of the characters. You can even carry over your save state from the demo since they're all held in simple files.
The other issue I've run into was performance. There's nothing about this VN that should cause stutters or lag, but I found consistently that I'd get about 20 minutes into a session and suddenly text speed would halve and the minimal on-screen movement of sprites would diminish even further than that. This problem might be localized, and it's ultimately a minor gripe, but I figured I'd give the heads up.
That said, I do highly recommend checking this out, especially if you're a fan of romance in any way. There's a lot to get into and there's a surprising amount to digest. The base game covers about 21 hours and the extra content delivers as many or more scenes in a smaller format for 5 hours.
Not a single moment is wasted driving the narrative. There are multiple points of comedy (Ano is an absolute trip), there are chances to cry, and there are points of pure catharsis. This novel is a bit unique in that sex drives the narrative, yet is never solely the focus. It would be unfair to say the erotic scenes don't serve their own purpose in character development, but they are simply moments where everything comes to a head.
I think the thing that impressed me the most in this is how organic the development of the main character is. I won't tell much, but it's very clear from the beginning that Yuna is not living entirely as herself. Her story perhaps more than any of the others is worth being read and appreciated.
Really, the thing that will make you enjoy this game is the sheer realism behind it in spite of its crazy, spirit-driven premise. A wide range of situations reach all of the characters, from the couple that have been in love for years but have had to hide it, to a new, entirely taboo affair between a teacher and student, to a 2 out of 3 couple that overthinks absolutely everything.
If it were any use, I'd write paragraphs on paragraphs about the merits of each individual character, and that's really where the biggest strength of Kindred Spirits on the Roof lies.
In summation, when two ghosts tell you to make girls have sex with each other, you'd best damn listen. Happy hunting, cupid

It's quite an addictive little MMO... I downloaded it on Friday night, played it for most of Saturday and a fair portion of Sunday... now I'm about to go back on for the start of my bank holiday Monday. It's first and foremost a roleplay game, where you have a character. You can get to all of the features without paying any cash if you're sensible and patient, which suits those of us in austerity-stricken Britain.
All of the tasks in the game are represented by addictive little minigame puzzles - so when you want to repair your ship, it's a fill-in-the-holes puzzle, when you're in a sword fight it's a "send things to your opponent's board" Tetris-type game... all the puzzles are imaginative and varied, keeping the pirate theme quite well.
My one complaint is the screen resolution. It runs in 800x600 and always in a window, with no scaling options. On a 1680x1050 monitor, that makes it pretty small. Even if the game's native resolution stayed the same, a little upscaling algorithm and full-screen option would be awesome.
(Edit: Said algorith has since been added)

It was a pleasant surprise to play Nickervison Studios previous arcade-style games and find something so entertaining for such a small price.  Diamo XL steps up as their next title falling right in line with the arcade design that I enjoyed so much before, but this time, it may be missing a little of the magic that made Bit Blaster XL and Orbt XL so enjoyable.
Diamo XL's core premise is essentially to trace the lines of the diamond shape on screen with a gamepad (or keyboard) controlled cursor.  Once you cover all of the lines, you'll be awarded five base points which can be multiplied by a modifier that increases as you continue moving the cursor.  The obstacles are a series of red squares that come hurdling in from all sides to collide with your cursor and end the run.  As you progress, additional enemies appear that do things like temporarily destroy a line in the shape or make a corner inaccessible.  You increase your potential score by maintaining your movement, but too much movement can have you colliding with obstacles much more frequently and ending your run.
One thing that Diamo does very similar to its predecessors is limit player control.  Bit Blaster had it so you could only turn your ship without controlling thrust. Orbt only let you raise or lower the orbit of your cursor while you maintained your movement in orbit. In Diamo, once you've committed to moving down a line to a corner, you can't stop – you can only increase your speed by pushing the button for that direction.  This is actually where I find my biggest issue with the game.  The problem is that you're working primarily with a 'diamond' shape, though the center is filled with a perpendicular crossing.  When using a controller, it's often difficult to use the d-pad to move on the diagonal lines.  It's possible to use “up” to go diagonal and upward to the right or left depending on which side you're on, but logically you try to press the d-pad diagonally which can often register as a press either to the left or up.  This could potentially be resolved by just using a keyboard to dissuade yourself from even having access to a “diagonal,” but I just like I can react faster using a gamepad.
I can't really say that Diamo XL is bad, but I can say that it doesn't really live up to its predecessors on a number of levels.  Even beyond the control issue, it just doesn't seem quite as fun as Bit Blaster or as engaging as Orbt.  I'm not sure what exactly is missing from the experience, but I can say that when I do lose a run, I am nowhere near as compelled to restart and try again.  However, in general, it's a solid game for its minuscule price, and certainly one worth recommending as a time killer.  I'm sure a future sale could easily take this down to 50 cents and grabbing all three titles in the “Arcade Bundle” is still definitely something I suggest doing.  I just hope that whatever Nickervision has planned for the future has more of what made the their first two titles such enjoyable games.

I hear a lot of whining and complaints from fans of this game. Some are true and others are just nonsense. I'm gonna list a few Frequently Heard Complaints and state my opinion on it, based on how the game actually works.
Complaint 1: "There is no proper PvE in this game. Only really survival and it sucks"
Opinion: I agree partially, the game DOES lack PvE a bit. Street Fighter in itself is NOT meant as a PvE game. If you want a game with a story and play against computer, then try some rpg game similar to Naruto. However, Survival is a nice idea and the only thing it lacks is consistency with supplements. If you came here for the PvE to begin with, then the fault is on your side.
Complaint 2: "Servers keep crashing and lack stability."
Opinion: I can not speak for everyone, but after playing quite a lot of games online and offline (pve and training), I have only rarely had the occassion that the game got a wee bit unstable, nothing that didnt fix itself within a few minutes though. So if I play 2 hours without issues and then get a 5 minute interruptance, that is no big deal at all and all complaints are unjustified.
Complaint 3: "Online sucks cause people disconnect on purpose"
Opinion: I have NOT yet encountered any of those (currently around 1200 LP), maybe I'm just lucky. Capcom however already announced that they will be seeking out sinners and punish them adequately. Nothing to be worried about in the near future (I hope).
Complaint 4: "This game is grindy as f***"
Opinion: Depends how you see it. If you only want to play online mode (which is totally legit), then yes, you will be grinding fight money, rank points and experience forever. However, if you combined PvP and PvE, you will get a lot of easy earned fight money and experience quickly. Capcom really wants to make some bucks with microtransactions aswell. I am totally against making online so extremely grindy though. The rewards right now for winning online are absolutely outrageous and I can understand this complaint deeply. Also farming for colors for EVERY costume of EVERY character in survival mode is plainly idiotic.
Complaint 5: "Capcom promised us a full fledged AAA game and all we get is an unfinished piece of s***"
Opinion: Whoever says this, has never really played an unfinished game. I would go into details as to WHY the game is actually a finished title already, but that'd make this post to long, so I'll keep it as short as possible.
- Smooth stable gameplay
- Hardly any bugs at all (didn't find any myself yet apart from some graphic glitches like long hair wiggling around on the floor)
- Awesome unique soundtracks
- Stunning graphics and art
- Extremely detailed Training Mode
- Many different unique characters
- Challenging AI (Survival mode mainly)
- Progressive Character/Profile development (EXP + Fight Money)
- Very smooth and accessible User Interface
Overall I would say that Capcom did a good job of an early release of this game, the price tag however is slightly too high. I myself got the game for 35€ and I think that would be a much more valid price tag.
I really hope the March and June update are going to be satisfying enough to validate this price tag.

If you're a hardcore Street Fighter/ fighting game fan, or you have the ambition to be, this is the game for you. The systems are refined enough to present  a deep experience while also allowing new players to get into the thick of it fairly quickly. Sure, there are some little niggles present, like the lack of certain training functionality and the inability to make a private session with more than two players, but these will be fixed in an update soon after I write this review, and I will update it as such. Also, a much bigger issue is the fact that any controller besides Xbox 360 compatible ones will
work with the game without a wrapper program like x360ce, and this introduces a slight bit of lag, so please take that into account. This is also being worked on, apparently, but it's unknown when the fix will be implemented.
But, let's address the elephant in the room: The lack of singleplayer content. In the game currently, there's only slideshow-esque story modes for each character (Think Street Fighter IV and Street Fighter xTekken's story modes) and a near-impossible survival mode, with an actual story campaign on the level of the recent Mortal Kombat games coming for free in June. Yes, this is a little pathetic, but there's a method to Capcom's madness. See, Capcom's running a tournament series called the Pro Tour, which is based on a very particularly scheduled set of tournaments. Said schedule basically depended on SFV coming out on February 16 on the mark in order to get the independent tournament owners and pro players up to speed on SFV, otherwise there'd be a huge shift in scheduling that would cost the tournament organizers, pro players, and Capcom a whole lot of money in rebooking flights, venues, staff, etc. Now, if you don't care a bit about what I just said, and you just want to play the story mode and button mash online, I'm sorry to say that you're not in the target demographic, and you're a casual. I sincerely hope you can make a full recovery and join us all in the FGC. But, in all seriousness, the game's not for you. If you really only care about the story that much, just ignore the game for now and pretend it comes out in June. There'll probably be a hefty discount, and it'll save you some effort from going onto forums and complaining about the game being unfinished. You'll be missing out on a fun and engaging game in the meantime, but hey, some people can't be convinced.

While this would seem kind of obvious, basically if you enjoyed the other Sorcery! games you should enjoy Sorcery! Part 4 as well. Basically part 4 is just more of the same. The game mostly focuses on the choose your own adventure gameplay which was prevalent in the other Sorcery! games with the occasional battles and puzzle solving.
Part 4 introduces two new mechanics. First you are able to wear disguises which change how different characters react to you. You can tell that the characters react differently based on what you are wearing but I don't know how much this impacts the game.
The other "new mechanic" involves limiting your ability to rewind time after you reach a certain point in the game. Basically the game creates checkpoints and when you die you are sent back to these checkpoints. You retain all knowledge that you acquired but you will have to repeat encounters like they never happened. This allows you to approach situations in different ways if you didn't like the outcome the first time. I have mixed feelings about this. It creates quite a bit more backtracking but it also ups the stakes since you can't just rewind every mistake you make in the game.
Basically my recommendation comes down to whether you liked the other Sorcery! games. If you haven't played the other games I would recommend waiting on part 4 until you do since the game will just feel like you jumped into the end of an adventure. If you didn't really like the other Sorcery! games, part 4 is more of the same so you probably won't like part 4 if you didn't like the other games. If you enjoyed the other Sorcery! games though I think you will really enjoy part 4 as well.

So after this game appeared in my store dash a couple of times, I decided to download it on a whim to see what it was like. I grew up playing games like runescape, but was dissatisfied with OSRS because of its extremely limited free-to-play model. The game practically forces its premium membership down your throat. I expected RPG MO to be similar. However, I was completely wrong. After I finished the tutorial I was left to my own devices, whether it be fishing, mining, fighting or literally farming, there was always something cool for me to do.
One of the really nifty appeals to this game, at least for me, is how barebones it is. A grid map, enemy mobs don't move, your character slides to its destination, and you take turns with the enemy hitting each other. Each damage calculation is simple, and figuring out your combat level from your stats is really easy. The map is broken into chunks, each with a town to go to, and there are many, many chunks to visit. With this game, you never have to worry about your computer's capabilities. Your computer can run it. Trust me.
Another thing I found especially great about this game is the really, really strong sense of community. In the EN general chat, new players ask questions about the game all the time, and mods, premium members, and other players all help the new player get to what they need to know. Everyone is super friendly, abide by the rules, and make sure to appropriately handle someone who says something out of line. This is a complete 180 from the moba community I'm used to, and boy am I happy about that.
One last thing that I'd like to touch on is a bit of a gray area for the RPG MO community as a whole, and that is Captchas. In this game, when you complete an activity (like mining or fishing), theres a small chance that a box will pop up with a captcha code inside it. Players who fill out the code and submit it before the timer is up will be rewarded with extra EXP in a category of their choice, while those who ignore Captcha will eventually accumulate enough negative points that they will be thrown in "jail". In this game, jail means you can't do anything until an admin or game master busts you out. I personally love captcha for two reasons.
1: It gives free experience. Who doesn't like free stuff?
2: It stops people from botting. The one big emphasis in this game is "you work to get what you want". Botting brings players anything they want with little effort, making all those positive feelings of hard work paying off meaningless.
I know this is a bit of a niche game, very simple and monotonous, but I find this game to be really fun. I hope you do to!

After a LOOONG wait, it's finally out of Early Access. And it's a success.
It finally has an actual story, which is sort of good, could be better, but good.
The amount of races is pretty nice (6 races with story relevance, 7 total), ranging from your average, run-of-the-mill spacefaring humans to plant people and the aforementioned Novakids, which are essentially sentient stars.
All races are statistically the same, only difference being their looks and interactions with other characters.
The combat system is simple, but has a surprising amount of depth to it (like Terraria/Minecraft, but removes on-contact damage if you hit an enemy, also includes dual-wielding for 1-handed weapons and special attacks for 2-handed ones)
Second to last thing I'll mention is the near-limitless supply of worlds to explore. There's a good bit of variety on planet generation, ranging from your average, grassy, calm world to an absolute fireball of a planet with nothing but lava and robot castles of pure, hard steel.
For the hard-working and perfectionist builders out there, Starbound's got ya covered with "lifeless" planets, where the only thing there is you, your tools, and the canvas that is the planet itself.
Finally, at last, the boss battles and the lore.
The bosses are mostly unique, every one of them has a low chance to drop their signature weapon, and they feel simple yet fun to fight, with most having actual relevance to either the story itself, one of the races' backstories, or even both.
Speaking of lore, there's quite a lot of lore surrounding each race (save for one, but they're most likely going to be fleshed out in the near future), ranging from funny little codex entries to engaging, interesting stuff.
TL;DR All things considered, Starbound's a great game and you should get it if you'd like a 2D adventure game with building elements, an interesting story and lore, and an all-you-can-choose posse of playable races.

I don't think there ever has been or ever will be again this much adorable in one package.
Although the basic premise of the game revolves around sex, the story focuses on friendship and romance and overcoming life's challenges.  The actual sexual content is almost incidental, although I would still recommend for adults only.
While the game is expensive, it is also quite lengthy for a single route with bonus content, between 30 and 40 hours.  Normally I like to read for just a few hours at a time, to let a story marinate and let me immerse in its setting and characters and situations.  Although each scenario is relatively short, there's always something happening or something to look forward to or some reason to read just one more!  After the main route is completed the game opens up bonus scenarios equal to a small fandisk, which is good because no fandisks were made so this is all there is.  I wish there had been more of Hina's "wawawa" moments, but what there is is very good.
The music is suitably cute with a decent variety of tracks.  Early on they got repetitive, and the way they faded out then got loud again when they looped to the beginning was kinda distracting.  Days later though I will sometimes hear them sneak into my consciousness at relevant times.
The characters are central to the experience, and everything about them is spot-on: their basic design, art, poses, expressions, outfits, actions, and voices are all perfectly suited to them.  Sure some of them are a little stereotypical or tropic, but the story at least gives reasons for them to be the way they are.  The characters share moments that are cute, sweet, touching, and occasionally surprisingly hilarious, all while staying in character.  I couldn't help but cheer for all of them.
Two characters deserve special mention:  Hina is the most adorable ever, and Yuna's voice actress nailed it with a sweet-sounding voice I could listen to forever.
When it's all over, you're left with an ending theme by Rita that will keep me nostalgic for a long time to come.
Sachi-san, Megumi, Yuna, every day with you was so much fun.

I fully expected something like that from this game, just another excuse to ogle at fictional girls. To my surprise it was not like that at all, at least in the time I've played it thus far. No gravity breaking tities, no brain-less bimbos smutting up the place, no (well, almost no) hyper exagerated archtypes. It's almost as if Kindred Spirits wouldn't be a typical anime *gasp*
Joking aside there is an interesting story here to enjoy, unless you don't like visual novels then see the above note, and the characters I feel are well written so that everyone actually becomes a character and not a one note prop to move the story. Best of all this is an actual game with choices. I don't know how the choices affect the later story, but it does give some agency to the audience which I think too many types of these games forget. The story is told different angles so I also didn't feel stuck with the main character through the whole ride. A nice thing also is that I don't think the game makes blanket statements about homosexuality, there are characters who question such pairings, maybe not enough to be more realistic but enough that the audience knows this isn't a completely common thing.
The one problem I have with the game is the voice acting. I am one of those anime fans who prefers anime subbed rather than dubbed which this game is, so if you have a problem with japanese voice acting that is something to note. My problem comes from the voices they chose for some of the characters. Everyone has a VA to them so that's nice, but some of them sound like kids in elementary or middle school. That's my thoughts though.
It's a nice game with a good story and more character than a stereotype anime. If you enjoy these things then this might be up your alley.
Bottom line: Good characters help make a good story, bad characters help it become porn.

35 bucks is actually pretty reasonable for the amount of content you're getting in this visual novel. It's at least as long as a season of your typical anime series. It's also very well written. Despite the cast including two ghosts, the story is pretty down-to-earth and it's not as melodramatic as a lot of yuri stories. It also comes closer to the real world of LGBT-land than typical yuri stories; the word "lesbian" (or the Japanese equivalent, anyway) is actually tossed around, some characters worry about coming out of the closet to their families and friends, etc.. If you like visual novels and you like slice-of-life romance stories, Kindred Spirits is about as good as it gets. The only possible dealbreaker I can think of is that there's no male characters--if you suffer withdrawal and lapse into a coma when deprived of boys, then Kindred Spirits isn't for you.

Alright, first of all, fair warning for those who would buy the game because it's the first 18+ uncensored game in Steam, don't buy it. The R18 stuff is not much, with 1-2 CG per pairing with nothing much going on, along with conveniently placed stuff to cover the private part. You can see nipples, but that's about it. So again, don't buy this if you're looking for the R18 content
If you're not just looking for that, then maybe wait for a sale or something. The price is a bit daunting indeed, but for me personally, i did not regret buying at launching discount, at all.
Gameplay:
Nothing much, it's just your usual VN. The kicker here is that everything is already predetermined, so no matter what choice you make, the ending is still the same. The choice however would unlock more extra stuff for you to see after the main game complete, which makes the playtime more than worth it. Unlike usual VN where you go in a straight line, this VN enables you to go parallel, meaning there's one main story, and several side story that you happens at the same time in the timeline. So you'll be playing as several characters, seeing it from their own perspective, which makes the depth of the story really hits home. Of course, this can leads to several moment where some story ended up on some not-so-likeable note and you need to wait for the story to progress to see the continuation. So far it's not a problem to me, but it's definitely not something i'm used to.
Story:
If you're buying this not for the story, then you missed out a hell lot. The story here is well written and nicely paced, and with the unique cast of pairings, well maybe not so unique, but some is, you can't help but like most of the cast. This is not your perfect utopia where everything went smoothly, which means every character have their own conflict to deal with, adding more realism to the story. This game is one of the few games that actually managed to make myself cry, despite being a R18 yuri VN. Overall, i cannot reccomend the story enough. Definitely a must buy if you enjoy School Romance and Yuri genre.
Oh and the supernatural part do comes in and out of the story, but in the end it doesn't really affects the realism.
Graphics:
Your standard VN style CG and sprites. Can't really comment much on this part, but if you like what you see in the screenshots, you won't have any trouble liking the art-style. The R18 CG is pretty well done though, i must admit. Definitely more detailed than the screenshots provided.
Sound:
The VA is great. Every voice fits with the character, and the acting quality is really good. You won't be disappointed with the VA quality. What you might be disappointed with might be with the amount of voiced lines.
. All the main point of the story is voiced however, so in the end it's not much of a problem. The R18 section is voiced, so yeah.
The soundtrack is nice and all, but there's nothing more to it. It fits the mood well, but i won't go as far as to reccomend it. The OST isn't so bad either, but yeah, just decent. One of the insert song was quite good however, which i would reccomend listening to it.
TL;DR:
You like good storytelling? You like yuri? Buy it, it's worth the money. Don't buy it if you're in it for the R18 stuff.

If you've played any of the other Burnout games, you'll be familiar with the aggressive racing style that involves destroying your oponents' cars to win the race.  Unline the previous games in the series though, Paradise is free-roam, so you're not limited to driving the set track that you were given in the earlier games.  That being said, because there are only half a dozen points that the races end at, you pretty much end up driving the same couple stretches of road very often, simply because they're the fastest way to get to each end point.  While the routes may be a bit tedious, you're given completely free reign over what cars you drive in each event.  The advised method would be to pair up tougher cars for destruction-style events, and boost-style cars for race events, but if you really want to try to beat a supercar in your van, go ahead (I would suggest trying to continually take it down before it can get up to speed).  Alternatively, switch to a stunt car and get ahead by back-flipping over the tops of your opponents.
Paradise also gives the option of driving motorbikes.  This is completely separate to the cars though, and feels like a tacked-on thing at the end.  You can complete the whole bike component in quite a short period of time (it was either in about an hour, or an afternoon, can't remember which).

I would really love to have give this game a good review but is sad I cannot.
This game had really great start but has go into lower and lower over time. The GMs at first did pay attention to what people got to say and tried to make changes around it, but lately the only time you see GMs around are during the time with PVP with GM is here.  Even then is hard to present your feedback to them without receiving obligatory "Thanks for your feedback (But clearly we are not interest)".
I see a lot of people say the game pay to play but that is the least of the issue here. Not so hard to make Zen without pay for currency.
The larger on the scale for problem is more on the side of the content/gameplay.
1. They released a majority of the content in the beginning of the game, did not give time to progress  and let us have something to look forward to. Aside from the latest content, a hard mode difficulty arcade and one new special attack set but I will return to make points with this in another section.
2.The new ladder system. Sure, its nice to see new things but this was something they should have left alone.  With this revamped ladder system, sre is easy earn your ladder that's nice but it broke PvP. Not only did this make it so that playing with friends practically become useless since there is no way to gain ladder but it has a negative effect as well. When you play in beginner1 its more than possible to leave it with 8-10 Stars in ranking. its almost the average now before entering Free1 Channel.
How does this effect gameplay? Well, if you want to earn ladder you are forced to play Auto-Team Balance, which in turn sometimes you are paired with a level 20 with 7-8 stars or so that does not actually know how to play. They earned their stars from winning just enough or being paired by someone who has maybe put an alternate in beginner 1 to make new class/help a friend level. And when you are paired to these person in pvp then chances are you will lose due to the amount of deaths they take and/or lack of ability to assist. So ranking means nothing. Also with this system its heavily abused from people leaving the room to prevent ladder loss.
3.Content missing that was supposed to be here. With daily events half of them are broken. Warfare was suddenly taken in a patch and never did make a return even though it was supposed to in the last patch. The increased drill rates that do nothing. Unless the already incredibly small rate was increased by incredibly smaller amount, I do not see any difference.
(etc)
The Hard mode arcade was a nice addition but its one of the very few things here you have to pay for to enjoy, or buy from a selling player.  But you need VERY good stats to stand a chance. For this you have two options. Grind heavy and buy good items or farm cow suit (Takes 30 days with once daily event.) or you can put cash and buy what you need. Either way its likely you will need to refine these items as well. So more grinding, or more money spent. Your choice.
Lastly, I feel that since this is intended as a Global server, they should make investments into something much more powerful. That, or invest in servers for each area (EU, NA, South America, Asia etc.) And I feel the GMs should interact more with the players and at least listen and consider the feelings and suggestions of the players regarding how the gameplay experience should be.
Until this happens, my review will remain negative.

Agent Walker manages to pass the threshold of being enjoyable (mostly thanks to its visual presentation), but with large warning signs for its disjointed story, childishly simple puzzles, and strangely overcrowded hidden object scenes.
The hidden object games made by Brave Giant tend to be small hits or big misses—Agent Walker: Secret Journey sits somewhere between those, in a rather uncomfortable position.
Theoretically, this game should be awesome: set in the middle of the World War II, we play as an agent sent on a mission to retrieve the Spear of Destiny before the Axis does. However, the premise quickly falls apart under the myriads of few-second video clips that have little connection to each other, completely killing any flow the story could have had.
Gameplay also show some concerning duality: the hidden object scenes are overcrowded and pretty challenging, but the conventional puzzles, including the point ‘n’ click style item hunting, are insultingly easy. I understand that this is a casual genre, but Agent Walker is just a tiny step away of dragging along the player instead of letting them do anything that resembles gameplay.

Agent Walker: Secret Journey takes us into the German-occupied French countryside during World War II, where we have to recover and destroy the Spear of Destiny. The setting is quite unusual for a hidden object game and the location is also interesting, but despite these, the game falls into mediocrity.
The game starts out pretty good with all the aforementioned countryside scenery and by us finding - surprisingly fast and easily - the sought after artifact
. Then it is quicky taken away from us and throughout the rest of the game we'll spend our time tracking it down. The nearby French town is a beautiful sight as well, but after a short boat trip (which is executed through a set of minigames) we'll be crawling around in dungeons and in a pretty dull castle.
The minigames are fine and there are some clever item related puzzles, like the one where we have to stuff a sack and place it under a lamp post, so the bottle placed on it (how did it get there?) won't shatter, when we knock it off. This however only applies to the first half of the game, because after we manage to leave the town, the quality of these puzzles also deteriorate. Not the numbers however, which seem to increase as we progress, but this concerns the hidden objects scenes only and this is where we get to the Achilles' heel of HOGs: the overused hidden object scenes, the ones we have to go back to twice or even three times without any hints (if played on expert difficulty). Seriously, it's better just to have the necessary items placed somewhere along the way, than reusing the same hidden object scenes over and over. The other annyoing element is the morphing object: it's fun to use them from time to time, but when we have to wait for the third or the fourth time in a single scene for the actual item to turn into the one we need, it gets quite bothersome.
There are also hidden relics we can find (they aren't mandatory and are there only for achievements) such as figurines of WWII leaders, uniforms, and models of war machines. These miniature war machines are usually quite hard to spot since some of them tend to be at very abnormal locations, not to mention that they can be turned upside down too (very hard to find a battleship model for example, when it looks like a stick in standing position). Fortunately the game is forgiving enough, so the miniature collectibles we collected will be stored and we only have to look for the remaining ones in the next playthrough. Pretty neat feature achievement-wise. (By the way the 'Fast Tapper' achievement's description is wrong, we have to find 5 items - instead of 3 - in a hidden object puzzle in 5 seconds.)
Since violence is usually very mild in hidden object games it should be noted that in this one sometimes we have to kill other human beings (soldiers actually). There's no blood of course and the situations kind of require that we should deal with our enemies this way, but still, it looks awkward to spare the life of predators, but kill humans without remorse. The only reason I mention this is because these games are usually family friendly (even though I prefer the ones with horror involved :)).
As mentioned before the graphics is nice for a hidden object game, at least for most of the time. Both the countryside and the town areas look great, it's a shame we don't get to see more of these locations. The castle where the endgame takes place is
ordinary-, some might say boring looking. Also the captain's character model was reused from Demon Hunter: Chronicles from Beyond, but I'm not complaining, it's a pretty authentic looking captain :)
The music is a mixture of lethargic and annoying scores, which is strange, because other Artifex Mundi games usually have relaxing ones, which at times I'd listen to separately without playing the game itself. The voiceovers are awkward too for some of the characters: the kid in the caves sounded like a girl and a ghost in addition to that (maybe he
a ghost?). Something I loved was the chirping of the birds (though it only appeared in the rare countryside/forest areas obviously).
Agent Walker: Secret Journey treads in the footsteps of Demon Hunter 1 and 2: while isn't particularly bad, it's not a game I would recommend. Artifex Mundi has so many great titles one can choose from, that this game can only fit in the runners-up section. If you have no more hidden object games to play, this might be worth a look. I really hope the developer's next game will be a better one.
PROS
+ nice, colourful scenery (at least in the first half of the game)
+ some interesting item related puzzles
+ unusual setting for a HOG
CONS
- repetitious hidden object scenes and morphing objects
- languid plot
- dull second half
- annoying music
RATING
4/10
