This game is really well written, I'm usually not big on plots, in fact, most of the games I have don't even have a singleplayer story mode because of that reason. However, Bastion was different for me, since the moment I began playing the game, I felt really immersed. The narrator speaking as you play is probably my favorite part of the whole game, it really makes you feel like you're part of the game and I wish more games would do the same.
As for the gameplay, it's rather good as well. There are quite a few number of weapons as well as skills throughout the game making it pretty simple to develop your own style of play. The game itself is rather easy in my opinion, it only gets a tad difficult if you invoke all of the idols (Items that add various effects to monsters that make the game more difficult, but giving you extra EXP to compensate). The only part that I had some real difficulty with was the Stranger's Dream with all idols invoked, and even that only took me two attempts. However, if you have difficulty with these sort of games, there's a No-Sweat mode which allows you to continue unlimited times no matter how many times you die. Though of course, some of the achievements can't be obtained via No-Sweat mode.
I'm usually not big on music in games either, but the soundtrack is also another thing to love about this masterpiece. It costs $10 to buy the soundtrack here on Steam for download, which sounds a little pricey, but I personally thought it was well worth the price. The music in the game is just amazing, and I can't get enough of it, just like the rest of the game, it's extremely well done.
If you're big on achievements, like I am, the achievements in Bastion aren't too difficult, to 100% the game, all you really need is time. I estimate that it would take most people 16-18 or so hours to perfect this game, I took a little while longer since I spent a lot of time messing around in the game, it took me a little over 20 hours. Each playthrough takes roughly 6-8 hours, New Game+ should take a little less than that, though if you haven't done the dreams, those might add on a bit more time. Then you have to play Score Attack, but you only need a million points and that doesn't take the entire storyline if you do the dreams with idols invoked.
There's not much else to say about this game, it has beautiful art, music, gameplay, story, and it has decent replay value. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone and everyone. I think this game is more than worth it at normal price, but it goes on sale every now and then as well, so if you really want to, waiting for it to be on sale is a pretty good option too. (Currently 40% off as I'm writing this review.)

Puzzle Pirates (hereafter refered to as Y!PP) is basically, if you're looking for less description and more TL;DR, an online multiplayer puzzle game with cards, gambling, monarchies, democracies, autocracies, familiars, and the occasional zombie or 24.

If you have the money at all, it's probably a better idea to use P2P oceans (servers), else Y!PP might be ruined for you with dubloon inflation prices, as currency can be exchanged between pieces of eight (PoE) and dubloons (dubs). I've had experience with pretty much (almost) every ocean they've offered in history, but all I can say here is choose based on your wallet.
Do I recommend it? Yes. However, I'd only recommend it if you enjoy 2D virtual chatrooms that turn into PvE/PvP puzzling on the fly. Basic listening skills and the ability to commit are highly recommended as well, as no captain will keep you on their ship if you disobey them or slack off.

A very old game that like previous reviewers have said, is past its prime. That isn't to say its bad though, there's a lot of aspects to the game that keep you coming back, like its pretty big variety of puzzles and politics relating to certain areas (islands).
The game has two kinds of ways you can play, subscription based servers, and microtransaction based "doubloon" servers, needless to say, subscription servers are pretty much dead. Subscription servers allow you to pay a monthly fee to have unlimited access to everything in the game, while doubloon servers require you to pay doubloons to access parts of it. You can purchase doubloons in game or pay real money for them, but earning them in-game is pretty tedious, as doubloons cost a decent amount of gold (known as PoE, or pieces of eight). The doubloon servers are populated a bit, due to it costing no money to access all the game content,
The game has a lot of depth to it, thanks to island politics, sea adventures, and crew management, I myself can't speak on behalf of politcs, as I have never been the "king" of a flag (a political party basically), but sea adventures and crew managment really bring the game to life and add replayability. There are multiple sea adventures you can embark on (Cursed Isles, Atlantis and a couple others I forgot the names of), and usually require a crew of up to 60 people to do, but are usually plagued by AFK's (lazers), which hurts the experience.
There's a lot more to the game, but it's 3AM and I'm too tired to go through it all, perhaps I may revise this in the future.
Overall I recommend this game, but dont expect a spectacular MMO, as the game has a relatively low population and high paywalls.

I have played a great number of MMO's, ranging from First person shooters to RPGS and one game stands out amongst them all.
Puzzle Pirates
This is an incredibly well-made game, with a surprising amount of depth in it. The entire game is ran by players, from the economy (you can own your own shop, from blacksmiths building swords and cannonballs to shipyards building ships) to the politics and warfare. Various player- ran crews can form a flag, wage war on another flag, and even blockade an island in hopes of capturing it for the flag.
But if you have no desire to get in to all that, there is really no need to! (Aside from the fame and wealth) Casual players alike can hop on, do a few fun puzzles (There are competitive puzzles from sword fighting another player, to loading cannonballs as the ships gunner, to navigating a ship in a tense sea battle) and make some loot.
Money (Pieces of Eight or POE) can be spent on anything you like, from fancy clothes, ships, pets, houses, swords etc.
I can't reccomend this game enough if you have an interest in MMO's, Pirates, or Puzzles.

From developer Liar-soft, creators of the "Steampunk" series of visual novels! If you're a fan, you'll be pleased to know that popular voice actors from the Steampunk series return to fill out the cast. Sakurai Hikaru (also of Gakkou Gurashi, Fate/Prototype fame) returns as an assistant writer and Kawashima Rino (from Dies irae and Shikkoku no Sharnoth) voices the protagonist, Toomi Yuna.
Colorful characters - all fulfilling certain yuri tropes - are present, as well as a bubbly OST and mostly on-point translation. You'll find little bits of "Westernization" here and there, but nothing that'll really disrupt the dialogue. Decently long... and watch out for mood whiplash!
There's the issue of a high price point, but maybe you'll be willing to forgive that for the sake of R-18 nudity.
Enjoy!

Sleeping Dogs, just like Just Cause and Saints Row, was once a pretender to the GTA throne when it was called True Crime but just like those other two game series its easily topped anything the recent GTA games have done. Though in this case its by actually managing to pull off a (mostly) serious crime game with an actual likeable cast of characters and an interesting plot that actually gels with the sandbox gameplay well. (Wei Shen is not a very good cop or nice man.)
The gameplay is a beat-em-up style akin to the Batman Arkham games and while it may take some getting used to once you do it becomes real fun and it can be really brutal, with the ability to break legs, chucking thugs into open furnaces, and sending a guy careening into a table saw.
The game is also not afraid to have some fun and be a bit silly,  you can dress up as a luchador in a tux or play a mission where you have to perform karaoke badly for example. There's also DLC where you fight Jiang-Shi.
Alongside Red Dead Redemption Sleeping Dogs is one of my favorite sandbox games and I heartily recommend it.

"Yuritopia!"
That aside, Kindred Spirits on the Roof is a great lighthearted visual novel. There really isn't much to say about the game since it's pretty straightforward and full of fluff for you to discover. The premise is very simple though - Toomi Yuna assists two "kindred spirits" (yurirei, a play on words that literally translates to lily spirits or otherwise known as lesbian spirits) on the roof in hooking lesbians up at her school. Everything is very lighthearted and soft though. But don't forget this game is 18+ for a reason...
In any case, if you are looking to buy this game, be aware that some parts are not voiced in this game, so that MAY take away from your experience. Typically, introduction scenes (for new characters and the whatnot) and important ones (romantic CGs, certain scenes, etc) are voiced, but the common chitchat scenes are not voiced.
I would recommend this game for anyone who likes visual novels in general and is appreciative of the yuri genre.
Yuritopia Simulator 2016 is a go!
EDIT: WOW, after playing through the entire game, I feel absolutely compelled to play it all again. Everything about this game is simple - the art, the story, the music - but yet, I was just so moved and enjoyed every minute of it. In this case, Okujou no Yurirei-san really proves that simplicity is not a bad thing at all. In fact, it is what makes this game so good in my opinion.
I won't go into any spoilers, but all I can say is I really loved the moral of the story and how so many things are connected with one another. Truly a work of art.

I wasn't 100% sure what to expect playing this game. I knew it looked like the sort of thing I'd enjoy playing, as usually I like games with player driven narrative, but the details on what happens during the game are kept to bare minimum (understandably). I ended up playing through to the end it about 9 or 10 times in total, and had a whole bunch of reloads in between as well just see what other interactions I could have. After all that time I was still encountering new dialog as I did my final mission to be a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to everyone for the final achievement.
I won't spoil the story as I think it's something that is worth playing through at least once without really knowing what to expect, but it was an interesting sci-fi story and very meta in terms of who you are in the game. I look forward to one day playing the next chapter.
The game does have combat if you want, and even this has an impact on the story and what others think of you. Kill everyone outright and some people will not be too happy. It did feel a little bit underutilized in this game though. Like they went to all the trouble of giving you these weapons and cool inventory system, but I guess the way the plot for the next chapter is being set up this will be used more.  There is a virtual training scenario which was obviously created to allow you to use these aspects more but I would look forward to seeing what actual impact the equipment side of things can have in the game.
If I had any complaints it would be that the game world is very small, literally confined to the 12 or so areas on the ship, it's not too serious though as the focus is on the dialog and story, and the game does a good job on that, but a bit more change in scenery wouldn't go amiss.
All in all, a well executed game that is a lot wider than it is long, and I look forward to continuuing the story in the future.

Game #4 - Burnout Paradise: Ultimate Edition (PC)
November 5, 2014
In the world of Racing games, the Burnout series is more about creating chaos and less about the racing skill. This type of experience is not unique to just racing; in Football games you have NFL Blitz, and Basketball has NBA JAM. As with the others, Burnout Paradise offers over-the-top speed, jumps and crashes. This entire experience is similar enough to it's predecessors, but offers players the newer concept of exploration in an Open World environment. The updated game design, graphics and expanded multiplayer makes this a game that needs to be played.
The overall experience of Burnout Paradise is somewhat discounted from the other games in the series. Luckily this was neither a good or bad move on an already fun game, but a choice to try and update for the future of the franchise. Although there are changes like the Open World exploration, a majority of events made there way to to Paradise. Players can stop at many traffic singles and hold LT and RT to begin events like Racing, Wanted Man and Takedown. Additionally, there are events specific to each vehicle, which are acquired by taking down cars after major races. The final addition to Paradise was the introduction of Motorcycles. While not as simple as cars to maneuver through the city; they create a unique challenge for even the most seasoned Burnout racer.
Burnout Paradise release on January 22nd, 2008 for the Xbox 360 and PS3. A little over a year later EA brought it to PC on February 8th, 2009. At full price of $59.99 many people would have snatched it up immediately. This also lends to the Metacritic score of 87 making it a very well received game. In my experience, which is being familiar with the franchise and game mechanic, I would give it a solid 8. In today's market, you can probably pick up the
Edition for $15-$20, and depending on the PC key sale, you can pick up the Ultimate Box edition for less than $10.  Well worth the money, the introduction of Open  World exploration, and the quick and painless way to find a new race event, made this a better experience.

This game is really well written, I'm usually not big on plots, in fact, most of the games I have don't even have a singleplayer story mode because of that reason. However, Bastion was different for me, since the moment I began playing the game, I felt really immersed. The narrator speaking as you play is probably my favorite part of the whole game, it really makes you feel like you're part of the game and I wish more games would do the same.
As for the gameplay, it's rather good as well. There are quite a few number of weapons as well as skills throughout the game making it pretty simple to develop your own style of play. The game itself is rather easy in my opinion, it only gets a tad difficult if you invoke all of the idols (Items that add various effects to monsters that make the game more difficult, but giving you extra EXP to compensate). The only part that I had some real difficulty with was the Stranger's Dream with all idols invoked, and even that only took me two attempts. However, if you have difficulty with these sort of games, there's a No-Sweat mode which allows you to continue unlimited times no matter how many times you die. Though of course, some of the achievements can't be obtained via No-Sweat mode.
I'm usually not big on music in games either, but the soundtrack is also another thing to love about this masterpiece. It costs $10 to buy the soundtrack here on Steam for download, which sounds a little pricey, but I personally thought it was well worth the price. The music in the game is just amazing, and I can't get enough of it, just like the rest of the game, it's extremely well done.
If you're big on achievements, like I am, the achievements in Bastion aren't too difficult, to 100% the game, all you really need is time. I estimate that it would take most people 16-18 or so hours to perfect this game, I took a little while longer since I spent a lot of time messing around in the game, it took me a little over 20 hours. Each playthrough takes roughly 6-8 hours, New Game+ should take a little less than that, though if you haven't done the dreams, those might add on a bit more time. Then you have to play Score Attack, but you only need a million points and that doesn't take the entire storyline if you do the dreams with idols invoked.
There's not much else to say about this game, it has beautiful art, music, gameplay, story, and it has decent replay value. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone and everyone. I think this game is more than worth it at normal price, but it goes on sale every now and then as well, so if you really want to, waiting for it to be on sale is a pretty good option too. (Currently 40% off as I'm writing this review.)

My one piece of advice to you if you decide to pick up this game; never stop expanding and attacking your enemy or you will soon face total annihilation!
On the topic of the game's re-release,
Ultimately I feel like it was a bad call for the re-release, developers should have worked on the game they had and earned back the respect they lost during the early life of the game. I feel like if they released Titans at a much cheaper price, or perhaps just let it loose as a free DLC it would have driven many more sales and the steam reviews would've started to turn around. The developers had their reasons for doing things how they did, and ultimately I've chosen to forgive them over what I believe is a minor transgression. Don't let the drama stop you from coming in as a new player, chances are we'll only have a better game from here on out.

While the change in artistic theme isn't an option, the different ways to play was many. You can build nothing but builders and defenses, then nuke the world into submission (like the terran's from StarCraft). You can spam cheap units early on and try to rush them (Zerg). Or you can build a massive air army and slowly glass the planet (Protos). So, while you're not forced into options, you're also not giving away your play-style with your faction. Give and take. Would recommend.

Let me just say that I absolutely love this game, but every great game has it's... Downsides.
There are many great things to behold in Starbound, Like the sheer amount of weapons and the ever-thickening, Delicious plot, and even when you have downtime and take a break from all the fighting and falling and dying and dungeoning and Falling and dying... On the Downside, however, Every-so-often there are updates (Btw, Fantastic job on the combat update!) and in some of the previous updates, You got your character dropped into the Cybervoid or Electrohell... Deleted. Now some of you may be thinking, "But hey, you couldn't have gotten that far." Well, sometimes people get attached to their characters and put alot of work into making them, But im sure they had excellent intentions in mind while doing so, like character models or different sounds and such. Now enough about how I feel, Now onto the facts.
Professional Review:
The Good:
- Insane weapon collection. (I got swords overfloing from my pocket)
- Rich, intriguing lore with an everchanging plot. (I like good stories)
- Fun dungeons (Fungeons!)
- Challenging challenges with challenging boss fights at the end. (I miss bone dragon though)
- Humorus dialog with Guard/Citizens.
- Endless hours of play.
The Bad:
- A Tonne of updates that change nice and intreting features. An exaple would be the old Star map with the different Sectors and the old-ish bosses.
- That one year.
- Endgame gets boring.
- Bugs, Glitches (See what I did there?), and annoyances are common.
The End:
*Warning* This reveiw will most definately change along with the game.
Overall: This game has its ups and downs but that doesnt stop it from bee-ing a bad game.
If platforming adventure or actaion games dont suit you, then don't play it, simple as that.

For the sake of sanity in this review, I will be covering the Classic gametype played in the game, since it's the most popular. Keep in mind there are other gametypes that add additional roles and chaos to the town of Salem.
This game starts with up to 15 players picking names, then receiving roles at random that dictate their objective to win within the game. There are many roles and 4 alignments/teams - Town, Mafia, Neutral, and Serial Killer. The Town is the initial majority of players, whose objective is to find out bad guys (mafia and SK) through investigation, interrogation, and any other means possible. The Mafia is a team of 3 who will try to kill and frame people at night until all town/SK is dead. The Serial Killer (SK) is a one-man team who only wins when all town/mafia are dead. Neutral roles add chaos to the mixture, because you have a Jester who is trying to deceive people into hanging him (if a Jester hangs, he wins and gets to kill one of his guilty voters that night). You also have someone as Executioner, whose goal is to try and get his target (who is always a townie) hung.
Town of Salem is appropriately named, because there will be many accusations thrown around in attempts to get people killed. And you rarely know if the accusations are legitimate until you start hanging a few people, since people's roles are revealed when they die. Thus, Town of Salem lives up to it's name. This game is quite in-depth and I could go into great detail about each role, who is immune at night, strategies that are common for each role, etc. But instead, I suggest if this game appeals to you, visit the Wiki and learn the classic roles. It will make lying as a bad guy much easier at times, and give you a better understanding of potential liars/motivations within the game.
There are only a few drawbacks to this game I can think of. First, because it is free-to-play, you occasionally get the trolls that intentionally throw games, or just act like idiots even if they are town (idiots are normally Jesters being way too obvious, but not always). Also, the Mafioso just takes orders from the Godfather, and risks getting caught by investigative roles. It's a horrible role, unless the Godfather gets killed somehow, then you can kill whoever you want. Also, the Jester is a boring role. The best way to get yourself hung is to just afk and hope the town notices and hangs you. It's the only role where the best way to play it is to not play at all.
Overall, a great game with lots of fun to be had. You can play it with friends too, but I find that the best way to play with friends is to randomly pick a name and not tell each other your names/roles until after the game is over. If you know your friend's role, it's actually cheating. Plus enough people collude with their friends already, and help them even if they're not on the same team. Don't be one of those guys, please.

I'm going to say some bad things about Sleeping Dogs even though it was a stellar game. Here, watch:
GTA fanatics have been wanting a GTA Hong Kong (or a GTA Japan) for years now. Everyone says that this is a sequel to True Crime, but I know that it can't be, because it doesn't crash every ten minutes. This game isn't the GTA Hong Kong game I've always wanted, but it might be the GTAHK game we deserve.
Though they've condensed Hong Kong's layout down well into a manageable size for gameplay purposes, I didn't like the lack of ridiculously tall buildings in this game. I understand that this had to happen for budget reasons; however, I would have killed people for a Kowloon Walled City DLC.
Action-wise, this game plays a lot like Yakuza, with occasional shooting interludes, which makes it hit some odd notes at times. Though it intentionally pays tribute to Johnnie To's movies (with the Fulltime Killer outfit unlockable in-game), the movies it steals from aren't known for long, protracted martial arts scenes. At no point in any of his movies does Lam Suet bust out with any fancy kung-fu moves. At no point in Infernal Affairs does Tony Leung bicycle-kick a dude. Thematically, though, this fits with my other complaint, that all the triads in this game are filled mostly with 'roided up rejects from a Fast and Furious movie rather than middle-aged detective types. I choose to take this as an intentional criticism of the newest generation of triads rather than a series of unfortunate casting moves. It makes more sense for people with steroid issues to be fistfighting, even if it's not what you'd see in Election.
The soundtrack is just what I wanted from this game, with the unexpected inclusion of Daptone radio, which ends up popping up during car chases at the absolute perfect times.
In conclusion, ignore all the bad things I said and BUY THIS GAME. The DLC is all kinds of fun, and you'll get it cheap during a Steam sale, so go ahead and buy it too.

The side missions are pretty much more of the same, just with more driving. The driving isn't awful, but again it's pretty boring. The story is perfectly fine too. Nothing special. There are one or two slightly interesting plot points, but it's far from anything which surprised me in any way. This game I assume is based on the Mafia party game that is really fun to be played in big groups of people. However, this is a playable steam game with a different time of place setting and with potentially more possible classes that you can end up as in a game.
Before you start each new match, you select your character's name. Afterwards, you will be given a random role that you must keep to yourself or reveal carefully as depending on your role, revealing it too soon or at the wrong time can result in your untimely death. There are generally 3 different factions in a normal game of Town of Salem. There is Town, Neutral, and then there is Mafia.
If for example you end up as serial killer, your job is stay hidden which may include bluffing about your actual role the entire game while killing the entire town during each night which would include both the good guys and bad guys.
If you're town, you'll want to get rid of both the Mafia members and the serial killer in order to win.
Mafia wants to basically kill all non mafia members so they must convince the town to lynch the serial killer as the serial killer is immune at night while they also will be killing the town members during the night.
To keep a long story short, try this game out for free on your web browser. Do the tutorial, try out a couple matches. If you like it and want it on steam (if you get it on steam you also get some in game funds that you can spend on cosmetics or scrolls), then all you'll need to do is just link your original account to your steam account which is pretty easy.
It's most fun queuing up with some friends and it shouldn't be hard to convince them since they can literally play the game for free through their web browser. Anyway, good luck on winning your games with ...whatever role you may become!

Realm of the Mad God (RotMG) is an incredibly addicting game which features perma-death. Whilst many dislike losing everything upon death, it's also a very rewarding game. When you start up it is quite difficult, but the more you play, the better you get. You eventually learn tactics and figure out the best course of action for you and your character. It's important to focus both long-term and short-term, as anything could happen at any given time. Being reckless is one of the main reasons why people lose characters, so it's important to always stay calm. Don't let your greed for loot get in the way of your character's safety.
I personally enjoy RotMG because it allows me to do whatever I want. If I want to feed and upgrade my pet, I do that. If I want to max a knight or a mystic, I do that. If I want to do dungeons, I do that.

Okay, this game was not nearly as bad as I was expecting. A friend decided we needed this game in our lives, so he got it for us. The game progressively gets harder as the nights go by, similar to fnaf, but i'm sure you already know about that game, and it's similarities to this game. Alright, here goes nothing. The game's visuals are pretty low quality, and quirky at times. That does give the game a negative impression at first glance. Now, time for game play. The game play is quite impressive, with one major flaw, i'll come back to that later. The game play is pretty much fnaf. It is surprisingly fun, and the jumpscares are quite effective. The fact that the game has little to no ambiance makes the jumpscares even better. Now, back to that flaw. You can't save. The game also crashes when you run out of sanity. Basically, you have to restart when you run out of sanity. Or just if you want to quit the game, come back, and back to night 1. The game also does not have a main menu. I think if the game had an alternate death sequence for when you run out of sanity, instead of crashing, and if you could save the game, this would be an incredible game. Not to mention it's only 66 cents as of right now. By the way, this review was not meant to be sarcastic, i decided to point that out, as many of the reviews on here are. I hope this game gets improvements and updates, and I hope this game becomes so much more than one of those mostly negative reviewed games for 60 cents on steam. Also, the game has 10 nights, not 1. Have a nice day!
EDIT: Okay, so I guess the game was having some issues, my friend decided to test out what happens when you run out of sanity, and the game crashed. I suppose that was coincedence, as I ran out of sanity while playing, and all that happened was that the door opened, and there was nothing I could do about it. Basically recreating the power element in fnaf. At that point and time, all you can do is hope you win. I find that pretty cool, and I take back what I said about it crashing when out of sanity.

Puzzle Pirates is an excellent MMO puzzling game that is past its prime, yet still very playable and a good way to amuse yourself for hours. It is also a game I have played on and off for over 9 years now.
You get to be a pirate, and you perform your tasks(Sailing, carpentry, navigation, swordfighting and many more) by playing puzzles. The puzzles done interact with eachother, making it a unique challenge to run a functional ship together with others. While you can play it for the social aspect of puzzling together and having a great pillage among friends, it is equally possible to just puzzle on your own, or to join easily accessible pickup groups('Jobbing') just for the puzzling.
Sadly, due to its age it is now unlikely that you'll find a large amount of people - An issue in any social game.
With your rewarded or pillaged money you can buy outfits for your pirate, customising your pants, hat, shirt and boots with plenty of different clothing and colour options - As well as allowing you to buy a fancy house, paint it, furnish it, and just have yourself a humble abode, a shack, or a magnificent mansion. The customisation in the game is excellent, with many years of content to keep you busy furnishing, clothing, painting and customising every bit of your pirate, house and if you have the money even your ships.
But sadly, you won't be able to do too much with it, as the ingame economy has almost wrecked itself. This game has a very good economy model, with supply and demand, freight trips, and commodities being produced and moved all by players, fashioned into their end products by players, and bought by players. However, to deliver anything but the most basic of goods you need to pay a delivery cost. There are two currencies, Pieces of Eight(PoE), and Dubloons. PoE are the money of the world, you get PoE from your pillaging, from working for the navy, and as payment for labour(Also a puzzle!), and Dubloons, a currency you can only buy with physical money from your own wallets outside of the game.
Of course, nothing is ever truly fully free, is it? There are two kinds of servers for Puzzle Pirates. The first is a subscription ocean, where you have to pay a monthly fee to have access to just about anything(But you do get to play and puzzle for free as an unlimited trail), the economy on there is actually pretty decent, but if you aren't subscribed and do not plan to subscribe you will be locked out from a large amount of content. The other is dubloon oceans, where you are free to play - But you need dubloons to deliver anything more fancy than a broken crate and a bedroll, and you need to buy badges with dubloons to unlock content such as anything rank based in your crew(Read: Pirate version of a guild/group), Sea Monster Hunting, and playing some of the puzzles and parlor games(All shipboard working puzzles are always free. On-shore labour and parlor games are free only a few days a week depending on the specific puzzle).
Luckily, dubloons can be bought using PoE in a market system, so you can technically get everything without ever paying anything for a dubloon but your ingame currencies. Sadly, this means that you will need to spend -A LOT- to get them. As demand for them is set incredibly high, with almost everything of any note costing you dubloons and a large part of the remaining playerbase being rich their prices have gone up to nearly 4000 PoE. To give that some context, you gain about 20 for an average performance with the NPC navy for one league point, on a trip that lasts 20 or so minutes. At this rate, you have korean MMO levels of grinding just to be able to afford the basics for your pirate, and it is not at all uncommon for an item's cost in PoE to be negligible compared to the dubloon costs. Dubloon costs for everything has sunk the economy for all but a few, but at least the puzzles themselves are enjoyable, even if the MMO part of the game is a mess.
As long as you have your expectations right this is not a problem, with well designed puzzles you can surely find ways to enjoy yourself
Edit: I wrote a guide to help you enjoy the game, all the way at the bottom
As you might tell from the economy bit up there, it is not very friendly to newcomers, mostly thanks to the prices becoming impossible. Aside from that though, it is a very friendly game and easy to pick up. Easy controls, easy to learn but difficultt o master puzzles and an appealing artstyle are part of the draws. The population on server is friendly, helpful, and tries their best to enjoy a good game, but without reaching for your wallet it is unlikely that you will ever get far these days - And if you plan to make your own crew you are out of luck as this is one of the most expensive (in dubloons) things one can do. In addition, if you do not buy dubloons or subscribe, you have around 6 weeks since your last login to come back. Else your pirate will be deleted.
As amusing as the chatfilter is with pirate-y-fying your swears, and as amusing as the puzzles are, as friendly as the community on server are, and as satisfying it is to build up your home and move somewhere bigger over countless pillages, Puzzle pirates is on a straight track to the cliff of abandonned old games and nobody seems to know if the developer has plans to slow down and save it, or given up hope to just let it fall while hoping to get some final payments out of it for dubloons.

This game was a complete surprise. I don't even remember why I bought it. I guess generally favorable impressions at
plus a decent Amazon deal was reason enough. Let me start out by saying I'm very glad I did.
You play as Wei Shen, returning to Hong Kong after a stint in the US, where you are acting as an undercover cop policing the local triad war.
While I don't really care much for the way a story unfolds in a video game, the character of Wei Shen was still highly memorable to me. The voice acting was unique and well done and there were scenes ranging from touching to badass and he felt really fleshed out in his relationships with his family and other characters.
The pc version is a very well done port and can simply look great at times. I wish I had bothered to take screenshots as I played it.
The gameplay itself is solid, highly interesting as long as you aren't holding a gun, and even then the gunplay is inoffensive. The driving mechanics are very well done. I remember hearing that ex Need for Speed developers worked on this title and it shows. It's simply enjoyable, despite perhaps too high a frequency as the main story unfolds. The melee combat is fun at well, which seems unique for a game of this type. The poilice/triad duality also puts an interesting twist in your typical morality system. There's a strong online component where you can replay missions or challenges and share scores and such though I never put in the time to explore that much.
The amount of optional objective is varied but limited. This is good in some ways because it doesn't simply overwhelm the experience, like Riddler Trophies in Arkham City, but at the same time it leaves little to do outside the main story if you simply want to explore. I suppose it might help make the game more replayable.

This game I assume is based on the Mafia party game that is really fun to be played in big groups of people. However, this is a playable steam game with a different time of place setting and with potentially more possible classes that you can end up as in a game.
Before you start each new match, you select your character's name. Afterwards, you will be given a random role that you must keep to yourself or reveal carefully as depending on your role, revealing it too soon or at the wrong time can result in your untimely death. There are generally 3 different factions in a normal game of Town of Salem. There is Town, Neutral, and then there is Mafia.
If for example you end up as serial killer, your job is stay hidden which may include bluffing about your actual role the entire game while killing the entire town during each night which would include both the good guys and bad guys.
If you're town, you'll want to get rid of both the Mafia members and the serial killer in order to win.
Mafia wants to basically kill all non mafia members so they must convince the town to lynch the serial killer as the serial killer is immune at night while they also will be killing the town members during the night.
To keep a long story short, try this game out for free on your web browser. Do the tutorial, try out a couple matches. If you like it and want it on steam (if you get it on steam you also get some in game funds that you can spend on cosmetics or scrolls), then all you'll need to do is just link your original account to your steam account which is pretty easy.
It's most fun queuing up with some friends and it shouldn't be hard to convince them since they can literally play the game for free through their web browser. Anyway, good luck on winning your games with ...whatever role you may become!

I tend to play this game similarly to Dark Souls.
ROLLROLLROLLROLLROLLROLLROLL.
The fact that you can abuse the combat roll in the same way as Dark Souls is already a 10/10 in my book. But this game has many things going for it. For one, the general style is brilliant. You can't go wrong with tiny humans using pure energy to knock each other out with weapons that, without the energy motif, fit right into Call of Duty. SMGs, RPGs, revolvers, you name it. But the combatants are CHILDREN and there is no sense of death, plus it's all staged in a holographic battlefield with bright vibrant colours and great visual appeal. The music is cutesy and colourful too, but maaaaaaaaaaayyyyy get a bit repetitive and annoying if you play it enough.
The controls are solid (did I mention the combat roll?) and there isn't a single hitscan projectile anywhere in this, so DODGING BULLETS IS POSSIBLE, and in some cases, really easy to do. Makes the combat more kid-friendly, but the weapons system is deep enough to engage anyone. Yeah the quest list barely passes 20 entries, but this game is multiplayer-oriented, so you'll have more fun there honestly. It isn't even first-person for god's sake.
Ultimately, if you like shooters but want something different, then this'll be something great to try. I'm having fun with it so theoretically, anyone can.

I was initially on the fence about this game but I'm glad I got it. Although it is inexcusable for a fighting game to release with major standard features missing and a host of launch issues, I think the number of negative reviews don't do it justice. The fighting mechanics are brilliant - hard-hitting, "meaty, easy to pick up and play, good selection of characters (i.e. they're different and not "too much choice"). It is much less technical in terms of execution and combos than (Ultra) Street Fighter IV, making it more accessible. The characters feel refined, and have smaller move lists. There seems to be less emphasis on execution and combos than on fundamentals, which is a good idea but I personally find long combos to be more fun. However, the game has more juggling than Street Fighter IV despite the removal of Focus Attacks, which makes it more accessible. I can definitely commend Capcom for this.
My primary concern was initially with performance. The game is locked at 60 FPS - i.e. the game logic is tied to the framerate because that's how fighting games work. But if you can't get 60 it goes into slow-motion at 30 FPS usually. My "PC" (Alienware Alpha - i5-4590T, custom GTX 860M, 8GB RAM, v300 SSD) can run the game fine on Medium-High settings at 60 FPS. I also haven't encountered any server connection issues that plagued the beta and its release.
The online is generally solid and the game plays really well overall. There have been some more comprehensive tutorials added in the "Challenges", and even tutorials for each character. There are also 10 trials for each character, but as I said the execution barrier in this game is non-existent compared to SF4 series so they're significantly easier. The major downside to this game is perhaps the Survival mode, which has 4 difficulties which require you to fight through 10, 30, 50 and 100 AI fights respectively; with the difficulty increasing as the rounds go up. This is an extremely frustrating mode and is how you unlock some colours and additional fight money, and is done on a per character AND per-costume basis. The AI is ridiculously cheap on Hard and Extreme, and even on Normal in the last few rounds. It is time-consuming, boring and grindy and in desperate need of updating. Unfortunately, as it stands, it is the only substantial piece of single-player content besides the short character stories.
I definitely trust Capcom and they have been releasing updates every week. More content will be added in the future for free - much of which can be purchased with in-game fight money. And the content that's here isn't bad at all. Sure, it needs CPU versus and a more comprehensive story mode, but overall it's good. It is a multiplayer focused game as you'd expect, and it has cross-platform play with PS4 so it's easier to find matches, which is definitely commendable. The downside to this game really comes down to content and some optimisation issues. In its current state however it's passable, but not for £45. I picked it up for £25 and don't regret it.

I've been playing this game for the last 3 years I guess, but not here on steam, and now I feel comfortable to write a review. Sorry for my English and long review. Happy reading:
The Beginning:
New players can struggle in this game. I think that 90% of new players leave the game after the first death. I did it. I only started playing more than a year later... Apart from that, I think the game should be completely remodeled for the new players. It's hard to get better gear as a new player and that is the most important thing to do in the early levels. But you keep dying and losing your stuff and then you see that awesome gear in the nexus that you can buy for cash and what do you think? Stupid P2W game! I'll quit!
Believe me, this idea is completely wrong.
Is it a Pay 2 Win game? A little bit, but not how new players see it. Buying gear for gold its non-sense, because you
die and lose your money. Seriously, don't ever buy gear with gold. It can take some time to understand the mechanics of this game, but once you do, you'll realize that the "Stats Potions" are the most important items in the game, not expensive gears. And, so far, they aren't selling these for cash.
If you are a new player, don't give up on the game until you get your first Stat Potion, because these potions are the currency of the game. Yeah, it's kind weird a game without a standard currency, but I'll discuss that on the Economy section. Once you get the potions, you will be able to trade them with other players in exchange for decent gear, and you’ll start killing gods, which drop more potions and gears... And after this point you'll be playing the "real" game.
It’s not going to be easy to do this though, you'll die many, many times and you'll want to punch your monitor and keyboard. But if you have patience, you'll be able to dodge the shots better, you'll learn the shot patterns of the enemies, you'll know when to nexus (it's ok to be a coward), etc. It may take some time, but you will progress. Maybe you'll lose all your items and characters, but in this game, your skill as a player is worth more than your characters.
The Economy:
Everyone knows this is an important topic when playing an MMO. RotMG economy is a little different than usual because there is no standard currency, you can't sell items to npc nor anything like that. The only thing you can do is trade your items for other items with other players. So the community end up adopting really wanted items as currency, like Stats Potions, UBHPs, etc. This is a little bit weird at first but you'll get used to it, and it will feel natural after a while.
But there is no trade post, action house, grand exchange or whatever the name. To find the items you want to trade, you have two options: Going to the trade server and shout out what you want, or searching on the RealmEye for offers. I personally have mixed up feelings about this system because it's not very fast to get the items you want (you can only trade with online people), you need to know English and you can get scammed. But it also adds that feeling of good old trades, of meeting people and having to talk to them, etc. It's a good and a bad system at the same time for me.
Ah, and I have to mention dupes. RotMG has suffered a lot of duplications attacks and currently there are hundreds, maybe thousands of super rare items running around, messing up with the prices of the high end gears. It’s sad that the previous owners of the game were incapable of dealing with this.
The Loot System:
The loot system has only one problem in my opinion. It favors DPS classes and completely ignores support ones. So everyone pretty much just play with DPS classes like Warriors and Knights because you can’t get loot otherwise. It sucks.

The drop rates in this game are pretty high (except for UTs, of course). I used to play Tibia and Ragnarök in my childhood and those were friggin hard games to get loot. For example, most dungeons bosses have a guaranteed stat potion drop. That means you will always get a decent drop if you are alone in the dungeon. And this doesn’t inflate the economy because of the permadeath feature, which continually removes items in the game, as people get killed every day. Maybe gods should have better drop rates (they were nerfed after pets were introduced), but I don’t know if that would be good or bad for the economy.
Pets:
Oh, pets…. The most complicated part of the game. I didn’t play the game before them, so I can’t comment how the game was before pets. But I can imagine, and I agree with the older players, I think it was a lot more fun. But they are here, and won’t go away, so we have to deal with them.
The good thing about pets is that they are the only thing that remains after death. That helped me out a lot in the beginning: knowing that even if I lost everything I still had a pet to aid in my rebuild. I would have probably quit the game if it weren’t for them. But…
… they are the absolutely Pay to Win feature of this game. Seriously, they are extremely over powered and expensive. It can cost hundreds, if not thousands of dollars to make a divine one. They also destroyed the class balance and everyone just play melee nowadays, because damage taken doesn’t matter anymore, only DPS. I won’t go any further in this discussion because it’s so complicated, especially because without the pets, this game probably would have been shut down years ago, due to lack of income.
Overall:
This is a good game, but it needs a lot o work to become a great game. Class and pet balancing, hacks, bots, multiboxers, dupers, rewrite the code (its Flash, even Adobe said to stop using Flash)…. There are many, many problems to be solved so that this game can be fun again.
I hope the new developers can make it right, cause this game has potential, and is unique, beautiful and cruel.

I like the game personally, but after 11 hours of play time I'm starting to notice some flaws that may not be fixed with more updates.
First, your fun relies on having a good captain. If you don't have a good captain you probably won't have any fun. This is probably the biggest weakness of this game, it relies too much on 1 to 3 people per team being any good for the rest of the team to have fun. This usually won't be a problem if you're playing on a populated server but I've had instances where nobody on my team of pirates were actually decent.
Second, you're probably wondering why I didn't step up and try my hand at being a captain if nobody else was any good. I did. I sucked. I was mutinied. I was never given another chance to get any better. You're probably thinking this is where I'll say the community itself is a flaw, but I don't really blame them for their actions. They paid $20 to have fun not to patiently wait for a captain to learn the ropes. If this was a free to play game then I would totally blame the community, but in this situation the blame shifts to the developers. There aren't any incentives given to be patient with new captains or to give them a chance and relying on people to overlook their $20 spend to train up someone they don't even know and may never meet again... that'd be high expectations of good people, and we're gamers.
Third, it just gets old over time. This is coming from a player who sunk thousands of hours into Team Fortress 2, this gets old after 8 hours. Five dollars. Only a few hours of gameplay. 16-bit graphics compared to the flashy 1080p stuff in standard games.
But... wow Angry Birds Space﻿ blew me away. It doesn't need flashy graphics or even fanservice to falsify its enjoyment. It just does things right, and boy that was one immensely enjoyable experience.
I think most of the magic of this game comes from knowing absolutely nothing about it. I got this game from a friend and just decided to play it since it looked very interesting and it was getting good responses. So I went in completely blind, knowing nothing but the game's name. And I'm glad I did, because everything the game presented to me was unexpected, notably dark in places, and very emotional, which would have been lost entirely if i watched someone else play it. So, if you happened to have been flooded by everything Angry Birds Space on tumblr (god help us) and the entire story's already laid out for you, the magic has been lost and the game won't be as incredible of an experience. I'm sorry.
Angry Birds Space's ability to completely turn the tables of its story depending on your actions is massive. Upon your game's startup, every little thing you do will be set in stone in the game's story pathing. If you're the type who immerses yourself into the game's charming music, laughs at the childish but hiliarious anctics, and is willing to hork down healing items just to prevent yourself from killing a monster just because a fight is difficult, the game rewards you. It opens up a very character-developing and world-unfolding story, along with some of the most emotionally invested boss battles I have ever experienced. You know a game is good when it breaks the fourth wall so well that you're shaking in your seat in true fear and can't stop the shivers, all while having to fight a hopelessly overpowered god of a boss. The amazing writing only starts once you beat the final few bosses, and the story doesn't stop being good from there onwards.
On the other hand, what makes this game different is that it keeps its dark side from you, and its entirely your choice to experience it. If you scoff at the game's sparing choice since you're too cool or grown up to possibly be nice to people, you can go around and intentionally sink your weapon into a monster who just wants to be a friend. And unlike many other games, this isn't just a simple "Oops, I killed another unnamed enemy, let's reset the game and nothing changes" moment... the weight of a dark choice is huge. It forever changes your playthrough. Reset the game, and the characters know. Events change. And with each curious kill, you, in turn, turn from the only human in a land of monsters into the biggest monster in a land of innocents. In the end, ignoring what Angry Birds Space sets out to do, which is to let you experience childlike innocence and fun, only makes it delibrately change the game into a quieter, more grim story. Very little character development, and the world isn't explained to you, nothing. There's very little reward for going through this route. Yet it is a choice you can do. Granted, you get two of the hardest boss battles by becoming the murderer and will be forced into Game Overs repeatedly from them, but even that is a message from the game... It's trying to stop you from getting to the end of this route. Before its too late.
It's as if you're doing deeds in an actual living, breathing world. And that's what makes it even more terrifying when you decide to become a murderer instead of a savior, because only you know that you're willingly going forward to obliterate every weakling in front of you. It's a test of your willpower, and it's your choice. The worst thing? The damage cannot be repaired. Go clean, or go home tainted. The game even gives you the choice to completely delete everyone's happiness after the most satisfying happy ending. The happiness you worked so hard to earn. And you can even become the murderer after saving the world, which will only permanently taint your game and never let you have a satisfying ending again. That's absolutely brutal, and yet that's still a choice. Amazing.
Yes, this game might not be for everyone. The humour may become dry after a while for some people, and tons of gamers nowadays like to bash at popular games instead of trying it out, just because they feel accomplished by doing it. But, if like me, you are willing to experience why everyone's been talking about this game, give it a shot. This game does the morality concept so well that other games can only dream of doing the same, and it is one not to be forgotten.
It is a sin to call Angry Birds Space a game. Doing that would categorize Angry Birds Space into the bland and consequence-free "kill-em-all" genres that a lot of games are falling into now.
Angry Birds Space a story-driven, emotional experience.

Even back when the game was young, it was already breaking the norms and creating something entirely different among games of its time. It continues to do so, now more than ever,  being a sandbox MMO that offers something no one else can.
Skindeep, the game floats on dozens of different puzzles representing combat, keeping your ship seaworthy, crafting, harvesting, and just having a good time in the inns. The game is still much more deeper than that; the game is built on the shoulders of its players with a constant world heavily impacted by the politics of massive crews and flags and the entrepreneurship of individuals.
The path you choose is entirely up to you. As many will find, you will probably start off getting jobs aboard ships but this can quickly branch off into what YOU would like to do. You can continue to keep jobbing for crews or join your own doing the same thing, work at shoppes, run your own pillages as an officer in a crew, become a trader sailing island to island, become an adventurer or monster-hunter sailing to unknown dangers and looting giants, join the polticial scene among many of the top flags and crews who run a good fraction of the ocean, or even conquering entire islands owned by other players.
It's presented with a 2D setting and environment, but its very stylized and clean. The only true downside is the lack of effort put in by the developer's interest; the game has constantly taken blows due to poor management and bad decisions. You'd think a game like this would absolutley THRIVE in the current situation we are in now where puzzle and casual games rule. Alas, even Three Rings botched that up making a failure of a transition to mobile.
Still, what the game truly needs is more player activity. It's a highly social, very detailed yet entirely simple game that may be the best MMO made as of yet. If you're looking for something new and fresh, that is skill-based, detailed but without a steep learning curve, easy to learn but hard to master, or simply just one of the best casual games there is, then I highly recommend this to you.

TLDR: Think of this as a single really long level from Deus Ex. There are a bunch of characters, a single unifying mystery, some systems and mini-games, and ties to a (frustratingly obtuse) larger conflict.
The setting is jaw-droppingly complex. Sure, you can understand the core mystery (who is the traitor onboard?) without knowing the setting, but if you want to immerse yourself, you need some ritalin and a lot of patience. Be prepared to play an entire ARG, read thousands of words of backstory, and dive deep into the 'discoveries' folder (free DLC.) And even then, nothing is resolved; you've got a Byzantine world of intrigue and near-future politics. The story you play (a murder mystery) is a tiny fraction of a greater conflict that Adam Jensen could never hope to understand. We're talking ancient aliens, future churches, megacorporations, rogue AIs, machine revolutions, and multiverse theory.
I'll let you down easy; once you go into the briefing (towards the end of the game) about the next mission, that's it. You've got one more scene and then you're done. This game ends right when you're expecting to continue playing, and in a bad way. It's not just a cliffhanger, it's a frustrating and abrupt ending that leaves all the major questions unresolved.
I think there are only two ways to dive into Consortium:
1. Play through the game. Interact with the crew. Try to ignore the setting. Enjoy the mystery.
2. Dive deep. Read the documents. Play the ARG. Go on the forum. Read every kickstarter update. Spend hours on the in-game infodump terminals. Lose sleep over abstract concepts and the constant repetition of the number 21. Wait for the sequel in 2018.
With all that said, I only write the review because I like the game. It's got lots of interesting character moments, some decent voice acting, and a fantastic soundtrack.
I think you should pick it up if you like investigation or mystery games, because it's a neat little experiment within the genre.

If you're familiar with
, this is basically the same game but streamlined. For the uninitiated, Left 4 Dead is a multiplayer FPS where four survivors must work together to survive a zombie apocalypse, fighting hordes of fast-moving Common infected and Special infected with unique abilities.
In this original iteration, only the Hunter (fast pouncer), Smoker (long-range snarer), Boomer (kamikaze horde summoner), Witch (extremely dangerous if alerted) and Tank (it is what it sounds like) appear.
There are four modes in L4D: Campaign (play through one of a number of 'campaigns' in the story), Versus (like Campaign but additional people can control the Special infected), Survival (the hardest mode, where you must hold out for as long as possible against the Infected and set time records), and singleplayer (Campaign with bots on your computer).
The gameplay is directed by an AI system named The Director, who spawns items & enemies, and changes the level depending on the status of the survivors. The harder the difficulty, the more contempt it has for you.
The presentation, as befitting most Valve games, is stellar. The campaigns are presented as movies, with 'credits' after the end displaying gameplay stats and a separate music Director controlling the incidental music. It does a good job of creating a zombie-film like atmosphere.
Only thing of concern is the community. It's not abysmal, but it's relatively small and you'll run into some toxic players, given how cooperative and intense this game can be. If you want to play Expert at all, be prepared to do some janky metagame stuff to fit in - killing players who are below 50 health when they reach the safehouse so they respawn at 50 being one example.
Now you might be wondering: with all of the official L4D campaigns ported over to the sequel, why should I play this? Well, there
a number of differences that for make L4D unique and worth playing for me and others even today, and even if it lacks Workshop mod support.
Regarding weaponry and equipment:
* The weapon animations are simply better than the sequel's. Fortunately, there are mods that
to L4D2. There is also an
for the pump shotgun.
* The pistols are M1911s, which I much prefer over the L4D2 pistols. There is also also an
for them.
* There are less guns, which means more meaningful weaponry choices. Tier one only has the pump shotgun and Uzi; tier two has the auto shotgun, M16 and hunting rifle. The shotguns function the most different: if you reload them from an empty magazine you must rack the chamber before firing. This makes a difference on the harder difficulties.
* The melee in non-versus games does not suffer from fatigue; you can keep doing it as long as you need. This is helpful when there are no melee weapons to choose from!
* There are only pipe bombs and Molotov cocktails; and no adrenaline shots, defibrillators or ammo packs. Which, again, can make for more of a challenge.
Regarding your enemies:
* Less Special infected (no Jockey, Charger or Spitter) make for a different and some say harder experience, not in the least because the SI that remain are more dangerous here.
* The Common infected appear different and more true to what Valve had in mind.
Regarding performance:
* The game runs better than L4D2.
* The HUD is streamlined and looks better.
Regarding aesthetics and other stuff like that:
* There are different achievements in L4D; for example you do not get achievements in L4D2 for beating the original campaigns on Expert. If you want credit for doing so, you'll want to do it here.
* The little touch to the bot AI's weapon selection is missing in the L4D2 ports. In L4D2, Zoey uses assault rifles as well as hunting rifles, Louis uses shotguns, and Francis uses snipers. This is in contrast to their behaviour in L4D, where Louis would use the Uzi/M16, Francis uses shotguns, and Zoey would usually pick up the hunting rifle.
* L4D2's campaigns and aesthetics are action-horror oriented. L4D's are more horror-oriented. While this is largely carried over in the L4D2 ports of the original campaigns, the optimal experience is playing them in L4D.
* For those who enjoy glitches, there are a number in the original campaigns that have not been fixed. The Jesus Rock in Death Toll's finale is a prime example.
* You can see your legs when you look down.
Basically, Left 4 Dead distills the formula to its essence and consequently makes this first entry into the series a classic. I suppose this right here is why it's still being played in a nutshell.
Not to say that Left 4 Dead 2 isn't bad, because apart from the weapon animations and its larger but more toxic community it's really not worse - just different. If you want a different Left 4 Dead experience, or you want to ease your way into the franchise by picking it up at the source, I'd recommend this.

GOCCO is basically a shooter that replaced bullets, blood, and death with cute anime chibis and toy guns. As far as mechanics go it is very different from modern military shooters where fights are won by 'he who shoots first'. Instead the projectiles move slowly enough to dodge and sidestep, and both the player and enemies are a little spongey (only in comparison to military shooters, less spongey than say, borderlands) making the game much more forgiving. Fights are more about the ability to run and gun, landing multiple shots accurately while never standing still, 'duck and cover' is also viable.
On the downside, the game is short and lacks progression beyond equipment. Also, if you don't speak chineese, you won't be able to understand the vast majority of the players online, which isn't the games fault. On the whole I'd say with the current content $20 is too much, but if it's on sale, grab it, it's short and fun, especially if you have friends.

Caligula is a 1979 Italo–American erotic biographical drama film directed by Tinto Brass, with additional scenes filmed by Giancarlo Lui and Penthouse founder Bob Guccione. The film concerns the rise and fall of Roman Emperor Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, better known as Caligula. It was based on a screenplay by Gore Vidal, co-financed by Penthouse magazine and produced by Guccione and Franco Rossellini. It stars Malcolm McDowell, Teresa Ann Savoy, Helen Mirren, Peter O'Toole and John Gielgud. It was the first major motion picture to feature both eminent film actors and pornographic scenes. It remains one of the most infamous cult films ever made and remains banned in several countries to this day.

Game is just too rough around the edges. The online works (sometimes) but only in ranked. Battle Lounges are busted for a lot of people and players sometimes don't show up in CFN name searches which makes inviting difficult anyways. Despite living in the mid-west and requesting 4-5 bar connections only I still often get matched with people too far away (central and south America, west coast) to have a solid match and have to deal with rollback teleporting. It also takes too long to load into matches. 1-2 minutes for match making, 1-2 minutes of loading to and from the match when the actual makes takes 2-3 minutes. And if all that isn't enough there's the rage quitters.
1P content is practically non-existent. Story mode will take even the least competent players less than an hour to finish and survival mode is just a bore with an awful difficulty curve where the first 80% will be incredibly easy and then the difficult suddenly spikes for the last 5-10 matches. No alternate costumes at launch and colors are locked behind survival mode and some idiot decided you need to unlock the colors per costume.
So the single player experience sucks, the online mostly sucks (with netcode that's worse than Skullgirls, KI and MKXL and lacking features). The only bright spot is the great training mode and even that is inexplicably missing some features that have been in other games for years (hitboxes, frame data).
There's a lot of potential here and I'll keep playing it, and probably rewrite this review in the future, but there's no way I could possibly recommend this game to anyone in its current state and it really does pain me to write that as a huge SF fan.

This is a good racing game.
But instead of just racing, you can also take down your enemies, easily the thing that sets the game series Burnout apart from others. And it's very fun. Another unusual thing is that, while you're racing (or are playing the other modes), there are no arrows to guide you, no boundries. You must rely on your mini-map and / or compass to get to the finishing line.
The game has a massive open world with over four hundred shortcuts that you can learn in order to get to the finishing line quicker than the others can. There are also some other "collectibles". You also find events (Racing, Marked Man, Road Rage...) only by exploring the map. The main goal of the game is to get a Burnout Driving License, which you can only get by winning the aforementioned events. You get cars every time you upgrade your license, and when you shut down certain cars.
The game also has an online mode, where you can play the same events that you can on singleplayer, but with actual people. Sadly, Race is the only properly made event, as the other ones really haven't had much love given to them. When you're not doing an event in multiplayer, you're on freeburn, where you try beating other people's records (no. of barrel rolls, air distance, etc.). It's quite fun, even if it has its flaws.
Now, let's talk about the port: it's bad. The online mode doesn't even have a chat. You can only communicate with other people with voice chat. The menus are really odd too. The optimization is alright. I do have some FPS drops in areas with lots of cars and action, but you can kinda blame it on my PC (although I expected it to perform a bit better regardless). The fast menu is also impossible to access unless you have a controller, which is a problem because that's the menu that allows you to change teams in certain multiplayer events such as Road Rage.
Overall, it's a good game. And it's cheap. You don't really need a controller, the keyboard works just fine. It has its flaws, but overall you should get it if you're a fan of racing.

Are you looking for a different racing game, or planning to get into the racing genre? Then this might just be the game for you!
isn't your usual racing game, but will still supply you with hours of fun!
The racing genre has many subcategories, and the burnout franchise might just be an entire subgenre on it's own. You still have the basics like racing of course, but EA has a different look at racing. You can crash into things, crash other racers, make stunts while still aiming for the first place.
The main concept is still the same. You are in a car, dropped in Paradise city, have fun. The physics aren't too different from other games, but I felt that drifting has been kept to a minimum. Which isn't necessarely a bad thing, especially not in a city full of buildings and other cars.
Like I said before, you are able to crash into everything, breakable or unbreakable. Remember however, that it doesn't mean your invincible. At least, not in most events. Fortunately, there are several repair stations around Paradise City so that shouldn't be the biggest of your problems.
You start off with a basic car at a junkyard, and the game will teach you several things before you start the journey. However, it does barely to not teach about the controls, which is something you have to find out yourself unfortunately. If you're familiar with racing games, then this won't be any problem for you, but it may be annoying for new players.
Each car has 3 stats, being Speed, Boost and Strength. It is up to you to seek the best combination which both fits your driving style and is the most useful in events. Events are scattered all around Paradise City, of which I have a few examples below:
When you complete an event, it sometimes occurs that there's a new car racing through the city. You can take it out and add it to your own collection! Also, you get a new car every time you upgrade your license. Your license gets upgraded every time after you have completed a set amount of events.
The game is still part of the racing genre, but still does many things different from other games in the same genre. Instead of selecting events, you are racing through Burnout Paradise, which is the overworld itself!
I won't touch the graphics however. Graphics is something strictly personal to people, so I can't give my opinion on that. For me however, the graphics are pretty good and fitting of the game. You can see far ahead of you and I haven't experienced any lagg or framedrops during my playthroughs of the game.
We now have Steam music, but I still want to mention that the music selection in Burnout is pretty good. There is music for everybody, from metal to opera to classic. Of course, there is also the narrator, being the dj of this radio station, who will give you advice during the game.
There are a few things I have to mention, that may not be appealing to several people. For example, cars aren't customizable. The only things you can change to your car are the colours. I personally don't mind this but I can understand that other people do.
To go online, you are also required to have or creat an EA account. It's not too big of an issue, unless you are strictly against it of course.
Beating the game isn't too hard. It only requires you to complete events until you got the final license. I would recommend trying to take on as many different events as possible, because otherwise it might become boring/repetitive over time.
Completing the game however, turns out to be a more difficult journey. The game does not have Steam Achievements, but there are in-game achievements called Paradise Awards. They are technically the same as Achievements, only that they won't show up on your Steam profile.
I myself am not a completionist, but it does bother me that the game handles collectables rather poorly. There are Super Jumps, Billboards to destroy and Fences to drive though. Unfortunately, When you achieve a colletable, it does not show up anywhere on the map for example. You will most likely have find them all by the end of the game, but it's still a nitpick which I can't overlook.
Burnout is a really fun game that I would recommend to anyone looking for a new fresh experience. People familiar to the racing genre might find a few nitpicks, but may still find a lot of fun here. And while this may be different from most racing games, this may still be a good starting point for newcomers to the genre.

I'm filing CONSORTIUM under "Games that are not for me"
Do you read all the books in Elder Scrolls games? Was your favourite part of Mass Effect when you wandered around the Normandy talking to the crew? CONSORTIUM might be for you, then.
Finally got around to trying CONSORTIUM because I'm in the middle of binging on The Expanse, and I was in the mood for some sci-fi gaming. That was a mistake. Story/dialog in video games always suffer in comparison to other media, and CONSORTIUM is mostly dialog and backstory. Apparently multiple playthroughs are required to get the full story. The dialog, while reasonably well acted, is not written well enough to get me to sit through it once, let alone multiple times.
Oh, and everyone has a callsign(?) consisting of a chess piece and number. Some people might have no problem with that, but I very quickly lost track of who was Pawn 17 or Pawn 44 or Pawn 32 or whoever. Made it hard to get invested in the story when I generally had no idea who was being discussed.
Story aside, the game is also generally klunky. For example, I kept getting hung up on doorways; it honestly felt as though my avatar was bonking his head on the lintel each time, and having to stoop a bit to get through on the second attempt.
So, yeah. Not a bad game, necessarily, just not one for me.

All commanders have access to the same units regardless of what commander you pick.. there is no "Faction" based units that are similar with differences.. such as in starcraft. which i dont mind at all really.
in addition to the traditional LAND and AIR units... you now also have BOT units.. which act like a group all their own.. less durable and less damaging than the rest by far.,.. but easily manufactured fast and in great numbers... there is also the ORBITAL units which orbit the planet or you can send them off to another planet.
You can build teleporters to easily transfer troups from one side of the galaxy to another.. which is nice and its not a very big galaxy.. it might sound more daunting than it really is... for example... a radar plane would probably be able to travel a full revolution around a plant in about 30 seconds or so.. while obviously taking longer for ground units.. maybe a few minutes... traveling from your planet to anotehr can take a minute or two depending if its in your system or an outlieing planet.
The battles can be massive... the troups are amazing.. and the overall gamepplay feels great..
THE BAD
In multiplayer games... the spawn system needs work.. if there are 3 plantes with 5 starting locations or more.. for a total  of 15 spawn points and you have say 8 players... the odds you are going to end up picking the same exact spawn point as an enemy commander is a posibility... and it sucks when that happens.. Hopefully they will turn the spawn system into a draft kind making it so no 2 players can spawn at the same location but maybe highlight whereb your teammates have picked if they are going before you so you can spawn close to them if you want.
There is a serious lack of customization in multiplayer set up for custom games.. all you really have control over if the map (or star system) which you can also customize i think. But you cant say... restrict the game to only LAND units.. if you wanted.. or only air.. and you cant turn off devastating effects like Nukes.... there is also a unit if you build it.. and complete it... it destroys the planet it is on.. which is neat.. but not fun when you are on a planet that gets wiped out.. there is another unit that will essentially thwor a plant at your planet destroying both... which is also not fun.. there needs to be an ability to turn these types of units off..
The ORBITAL units are neat.. but annoying after a while.. the abilitiy to turn off specific units is also missing so you could use only transports and radar vehicles from the orbital structures.. that would be nice.. but sadly.. you cant do that.
The matchmaking is bad right now.. not many players online... most i have seen is 3000... but once it really gets gooing that will hopefully pick up... almost no one does ranked.. ive only managed to do one ranked match withoiut waiting for more than 10 minutes..
there is no campaign... there are galactic battles where you travel from star system to star system on a map unlocking aditional paths when you beat one and then unlocking tech that will benifit you later in the planets from then on.,. there really isnt a goal for that. i dont see the point.
the tutorial feels only about half done.. it doesnt touch on most of the units or special units.. it doesnt tell you what to do with gas planets and i had to find ouyt on my own watching other players use them for energy sources from orbital units.. and i was like OHHH..
OVERALL i woulkd recommend this game.. but not for more than 20 dollars.. i got it 70% off and i was happy with the purchase.. wait for a sale or watch a lot of gameplay before you decide to get it.. hopefully since its still early access that it will get better.. but its a good waste of time right now.
