This is one of the few games where I bought it during a Steam Sale, beat it and felt like I would have gladly payed full retail for it.  This game sort of sits in the middle of the GTA - Saints Row spectrum of seriousness; overall the main story is fun in that Johnny To triad film sort of way.  The hand to hand combat in this game is very satisfying, it's a dumbed down version of the combat found in the Arkham games.  You can buy some cheap DLC that will add other martial art styles to the game, which can be a fun way to change things up.  Shockingly gunfights while driving are fun, as you go into bullet time and there are many different ways to disable a car.  Nice to see some thought put into this part of the game.
The biggest complaints I have about the game also stem from the combat.  The quicktime events to escape certain attacks are annoying and the timming can be vague.  Also the gunplay in the game is not so great, with aiming seemingly arbitrary.  Often you're better just to blind fire wildly.  Fortunately the gunplay is only near the end and very limited, so it's only a minor annoyance.
The bottom line is, for a game that almost never got released this is a super fun game.  I'd strongly reccomend buying it at full retail and you have no excuse not to own it if it goes on sale.

Realm of the mad god is an 8 bit mmorpg/bullet hell game with an emphasis on getting stronger by loot and artificial stat boosting potions instead of leveling up (The max level is 20 and is obtained in less than an hour). Death is permanent and you lose your chararcter with all the loot he or she had on him and the stat increases, but you don't have to start from scratch since there is a vault where you can store items and this gives you an opportunity to try out of of the many different classes from warriors, knights and wizards to ninjas and tricksters who mostly play differently.
Despite the abundance of microtransactions, you can enjoy the game without spending a single cent like I did and since there is no pvp aspect, you won't be at a disadvantage compared to other players. A huge part of the fanbase left because of the microtransactions and the lack of updates coming from the old owner Kabbam, but with the recent takeover by DECA games promising a wave of new content and their generosity with free items going out to everybody who is playing, now is the best time to start a new character and plunder dungeons with both new and old players.
The pros: Immense amount of replayability
Original loot system which encourages teaming up with other players instead of fighting between eachother.
Varied locations, bosses, dungeons and the dungeon layoutt are always ranomized.
Challenging difficulty that is only surmountable by quick reflexes, skill, knowledge of the game and loot.
Can be played in both short and long sittings.
Seeing your character becoming stronger is very satisfying and rewarding.
Encourages being social and joining guilds.
Minor nitpick: Much more enjoyable with friends you already know.
Lag is almost never fault of your computer, but because of the server and is very noticeable, especialy when teleporting a large number of players at once or there simply being a large number of players.
Not very beginner friendly, watch some videos like those made by bickuribox12, Balkaneser or SLVRDLLR to learn, most other youtubers like Markiplier had no idea what they were doing when they made a video.
Con: Death can be very frustrating, especialy if it's for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t reason like lag or teleporting to the wrong person and dying instantly.
Grinding for loot and stat boosting potions can become boring and repetitive.
Lack of music other than the main theme which becomes so repetitive, you have no choice other than to turn it off.
All in all a very enjoyable, although slightly flawed game. It's free and takes up almost no space so you have nothing to lose. The pros far outweigh the cons and nitpicks.

My inititial review of this was a negative, I got some feedback, tried it again....my opinion of this game hasn't changed.
The game is enjoyable for a short while, new game feel. But then you figure out what it really is (repetative, grindy, and uninspiring). There's no  'I just want to play it a bit longer feel'. Frankly after 4.5 hours I never want to play this again, ever.
After hitting the esc key I was able to change settings, too bad that you're not told that ingame...like the tutorial.
The game asks you for your first & last name, email address, and birthday in order to be able to reset your password. I see this as wanting too much personal info. Hell, why don't you also ask for my SSN while you're at it to make your request complete, that way you can verify my correct age with the SSN office. So really, you need to know my age, for legal purposes only. How do I know that's all you'll use my personnel info for? I don't know you, I have no reason to trust you.
During my game play I was plagued by ingame popups asking me to click a check box to verify I wasn't a robot, then I had to select items (like all the mountains) from another pop. I found this to be quite annoying. Who the hell wants to be interrupted during their game play by useless system monitoring?
As far as game play, I got thru the tutorial and got to the first town and that was it, I had enough. In the tutorial you learn combat and crafting. There are no hotboxes, so you have to click on your inventory, then select the item you want to equip and you have to do this for everything in your inventory, every time. For a crafting game it's a pain in the you know what. Plus you'll click the item you want to equip, but the command never actually takes, so you must click the inventory and do it al lover again.
I find that trying to figure out which merchant accepts what is a pain, so you're constantly running from merchant to merchant trying to figure out who is going to buy your stuff, unless you memorize all that and where they're located in the city. Why not just be able to sell anything to any merchant and keep the specialied stuff to certain merchants. Even games from the 90's had that. Again what year was this made in?
When sell to a merchant I found it to be a bit confusing, everything has a purple border, I couldn't tell what was or wasn't selected. Other choice is to click you inventory again, then right click the item, click sell, etc..
There's not much excitement to the game, the same exact monsters always respawn in the same exact spot. And there's always patches of the same NPCs. Combat is automatic (what you have equipped is what you fight with), and then just wait to see who wins, no strategy involved here, heck, you can't even heal yourself during combat. You're only attacked by the aggressive ones if you move next to a square next to one. Combat is either weapon or magic.
On auto run to a spot, your character goes in a straight line, no exceptions, often causing unnecessary combat when there are aggressive NPCs in the way.
You have an unlimited supply of resources in exactly the same spot every time. It's very grindy, go fish, catch fish, cook it, sell it or keep it, go do it again, etc, etc. Tired of fishing endless fish in the same spot, go chop a tree that never gets chopped down.
I see a lot of posts say this is a lesser copy of Runescape (released 2001). Never played that game but I believe it. After playing this I felt like I time travelled back atleast 15 years.
Finally...
Yes I know it's EA, but you chose to sell it here, so you get reviewed on how it is and not what mythical potential you think it will have.

To reiterate my friend Cydran's review, Terraria in space. But let's go a bit more in-depth with that. The majority of Starbound's gameplay is drawn from Terraria. Although I honestly think Terraria does everything just a little bit better. That being said, Starbound still stands strong with some added features that Terraria doesn't have. It adds a vast universe (to say the least) complete with countless star systems and planet types. It tries to establish a lot more lore. More quests (albeit fairly shiттy ones). More in depth crafting (which can be kind of a drawback at times). The ABC music adds the perfect amount of that nostalgiac 8-bit feeling. Also, the immense amount of decorational items which are just beautiful. The story as it stands right now is lack-luster, but hopefully they'll tweak it some more. Overall, I'd recommend you get Terraria before you get Starbound. It's cheaper, and it's just generally better. But if you've gotten your fill of Terraria and are looking for something a bit more, I'd recommend getting Starbound.

A friend and I bought this after seeing it's basically a miniature PSO and the rather positive reviews. Before you continue reading, I have to say that I understand that this probably wasn't made by a huge game studio and it's something I feel had a ton of potential to stand out.
Gotta say, it's not actually as fun as people in the reviews say. I don't mean it in a particularly bad way, but it was hyped up a lot in the reviews so I expected more.
I wouldn't say it's bad but just within the first 2 hours of playing with a friend it's pretty clear it's really repetitive. Really repetitive. I wanted to make sure I could get the refund (as the game has a decently notable price tag). While it had charm and appeal for the time I played, it wasn't enough to keep my friend and I coming back.
The car that's driveable is probably the most fun part (my favourite, anyways) and it isn't even included on a lot of levels. I felt that more direct-coop things like that would have made the game a lot more exciting. Vehicles, teamwork-based objectives, riveting and dynamic levels- stuff like that. The customization was nice but I felt held back because literally everything costs a certain amount of ingame money that actually takes a while to collect. There's no way to get loot, ever. You just grind money and spend it all, and not to mention those materials you gotta collect for stuff too. Unlike a game like Borderlands or even PSO (which this game seems the most similar to), there's no satisfaction of ever getting a rare item or just interesting equipment because all the loot comes in the form of money or materials and little else.
The gameplay as a whole works pretty fine but a part of me says that the 'air' energy/stamina system is being used for too many things, having to recharge a bit too frequently. I want to use the gun camera for the melee attacks as well but there's no way to change that, and it feels really clunky the way that it is. All of the combat feels really floaty and doesn't have that satisfying feeling when you defeat enemies, it's like hitting balloons. Really tough balloons.
There's very little enemy variety, most of them making up of recolours and remodels of enemies that basically do the same thing. The level design is also pretty poor in certain levels while other ones are more appealing in both visuals and gameplay, but overall it feels somewhat cheap, which was disappointing because there's a lot of potential. Since I didn't want to play over the two hours we had for the refund, I haven't seen the later levels so I did some research and it seems even later on you're doing basically the same thing.
The game's pretty hard to look at sometimes with all the bloom on, and drop shadows only appear when you limit the framerate to 30 from 60 (at least if I recall properly, anyways- it was a particular video setting I'd rather not turn down). Without the shadows, it really is hard to look at the game with their harshly stretched textures and ultra-vibrant colours.
The sound effects aren't really all that varied and you'll hear the same stuff a lot. You won't really hear any music in game like the trailer's, either. It felt really bland playing for extended periods of time, and I seriously don't want to hear any more of that rolling sound.
To summarize and some other stuff:
-Yes, it's cute. Yes, it has charm.
-The assortment of costumes is nice, but comes at a price of more grinding.
-It suffers terribly from repetitiveness and lack of variety, in almost all departments- from monsters, level design, game modes, sound effects, equipment.
-There's an overall cheap feel to it all and a lot of it feels same-y.
-Serious grinding of the same missions involved for money and materials.
-Small community.
-Visuals can be hard to bear with for long periods.
-Sound design is lacking.
-Game feels floaty, slow, almost.

I finally managed to finish the game.
Half Life is a game that is composed of "set pieces" that as you progress through the game become more, and more elaborate, as difficult, as spectacular, as insane.
The whole game is a Science Fiction adventure, and one incredibly memorable at that, the whole thing feels like a journey that you're clearly taking part in.
This illusion gets created by letting the player play through the eyes of the game's main protagonist Gordon Freeman, that though you never hear him speak, or react in any other way than the one you want him to, it still has managed to become a "gaming" icon.
This is because however unlikely certain situations may appear to be possible to overcome, enemies to defeat, or obstacles to surpass, the game always finds a way to make it seem pausible that you may succeed, and you have to if you want to finish the game, obviously.
Now the problem that I have with some of this sequences is that at first their design seems brilliant, and simple, but as you keep progressing through the game, this "set pieces" can become jarring, disorganized, and, or messy, and frustrating to complete.
It is not only the fact that you'll have to repeat certain sections over and over again, some that simply rely in pure "trial, and error".
but also, there are ones that are incredibly cryptic, and while they simply do require a bit of patience, and thinking on the players side, more often than not, even whilst comprehending what is it that you need to do, the controls, and systems, simply work against you.
At one point I was done with a massive firefight against a couple of soldiers and a tank, since the game is an "old-school first person shooter" I had to rely in getting health pickups, my health was all the way down to four, of a hundred...
Right when I got through a doorway that was supposed to allow me to continue, I immediately got killed by a turret that was placed to edge of the door I had just walked through, luckily I had a saved right before it happened.
But tell me?
How the f**k are you supposed to know that was going to happen unless it had happened to you at first?
There's no way to know about it, the only thing that could give you some input that the turret was there, is a sound that they produce when they're active, but in the midst of everything crumbling around you, the explosion of the tank, the gunfire, and the flow of adrenaline that that leaves you with, you probably won't be able to listen to that.
There are other cases, other examples, near the end of the game there's a section that requires you to shoot at an enemy enough times you scare it away from you so it can destroy a wall and form a path through which you can continue.
First time it happened tho, the enemy didn't react, I had to reload another save file in order to get through it.
And then the last couple of sections, they require some horrible form of platforming, that doesn't even feel like it was designed with the systems the game had presented at that point in mind, it feels much more as if it's one of those cases you have to do everything in your power, whether it is what the game requires you to do, or not, in other to complete those parts.
Other times the enemies simply fill in the screen, and you don't get enough ammo to take all of them at once, even if you have to, it gets frustrating after a while, it is annoying, and most of the times, you have to improvise.
Whether this was intended or not, that's besides the point, it is not enjoyable for me.
However...
This where mere moments near the end of the game that turn an otherwise incredible experience in a bit of a "slog", crazy part is that when finishing the game though, as frustrated as I was, not even from loosing, but just from playing it, I felt this incredible sense of accomplishment that surpassed any sort of high score, or challenge in any other game I have played recently, it became clear to me that this game's brillance comes from offering the player a journey in which you actually feel you're part of, in which you feel as the hero, that partake in every event leading to the imminent continuation of an incredible narrative, that didn't come in the form of a cutscene, or text.
But instead, in pure gameplay experience, everything in this game you get to experience it through the players eyes, it is an incredible masterpiece in videogame design because of it, and even if it hasn't aged that well in some aspects, it has in plenty of others, and it still manages to trascend, and offer, the same experience that made it timeless in the first place, it is in my opinion, a clear example of what videogames can offer when handling the medium, with the respect, and care, it deserves.

This is, quite simply, the best co-op tower defense game ever made. That's not a huge claim because there aren't that many of them in the first place, but for someone who really loves the gerne like me this game really is a blessing.
Its production values are high, which means that the ingame comics, the graphics, the sound and the effects are all top-notch (especially considering the price when it was on sale or in the Humble Bundle).
The way the game is played is simple, it's a Dungeon Defenders-esque TD+shooter where you place blocks in squares on the map in a way that makes the enemies lose as much time as possible.
Those blocks act as walls and as tower bases, which means you can either leave them there or build towers on top of them.
There is also a metagame, as you can level up and unlock more weapons, more towers/tower slots, more weapons and more perks/perk slots.
There is not much grinding as far as I have seen: you won't need to endlessly repeat old levels to be good enough to make it to the next one, although you will occasionally hit a wall where you're going to need to replay previous stages.
The variety in weapons, enemies and towers is more than satisfactory, and you're going to find out each enemy's weak spot soon enough, as they try to make it as obvious as possible (for example, there's one type of enemy that will take literally 0 damage from the front, so you need to distract him with something else as you hit him from behind).
One thing I will say about the difficulty though is that finishing the game solo is pretty much impossible. This game was made with co-op in mind, and if you don't have anyone to play with you better either find someone or join public servers, as it's really the only viable way to play this game.
And speaking of public servers, you MIGHT have a problem with latency with this particular game. I couldn't connect to any pub games without horrific lag, and couldn't even play with a friend that lives relatively close to me.
However, if you happen to stumble upon this problem, I have a solution for you: Tunngle.
Just download it, google "Sanctum 2 Tunngle" and play there. It is not illegal in any way, so don't worry. It will create a fake LAN server for you to play on, without lag (assuming your co-op buddies don't have terrible internet).

You hold your ground against of hordes of monsters that will attack your core, should they reach it. You do 2 things to avoid this, shoot them, and build towers. Shooting is straight forward, but it should be said that you have infinite ammo. You can place towers on an overlaying grid on the map. Some towers attack, and some towers buff others. you must then hold out against the horde with whatever you have.

Realm of the mad god is an 8 bit mmorpg/bullet hell game with an emphasis on getting stronger by loot and artificial stat boosting potions instead of leveling up (The max level is 20 and is obtained in less than an hour). Death is permanent and you lose your chararcter with all the loot he or she had on him and the stat increases, but you don't have to start from scratch since there is a vault where you can store items and this gives you an opportunity to try out of of the many different classes from warriors, knights and wizards to ninjas and tricksters who mostly play differently.
Despite the abundance of microtransactions, you can enjoy the game without spending a single cent like I did and since there is no pvp aspect, you won't be at a disadvantage compared to other players. A huge part of the fanbase left because of the microtransactions and the lack of updates coming from the old owner Kabbam, but with the recent takeover by DECA games promising a wave of new content and their generosity with free items going out to everybody who is playing, now is the best time to start a new character and plunder dungeons with both new and old players.
The pros: Immense amount of replayability
Original loot system which encourages teaming up with other players instead of fighting between eachother.
Varied locations, bosses, dungeons and the dungeon layoutt are always ranomized.
Challenging difficulty that is only surmountable by quick reflexes, skill, knowledge of the game and loot.
Can be played in both short and long sittings.
Seeing your character becoming stronger is very satisfying and rewarding.
Encourages being social and joining guilds.
Minor nitpick: Much more enjoyable with friends you already know.
Lag is almost never fault of your computer, but because of the server and is very noticeable, especialy when teleporting a large number of players at once or there simply being a large number of players.
Not very beginner friendly, watch some videos like those made by bickuribox12, Balkaneser or SLVRDLLR to learn, most other youtubers like Markiplier had no idea what they were doing when they made a video.
Con: Death can be very frustrating, especialy if it's for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t reason like lag or teleporting to the wrong person and dying instantly.
Grinding for loot and stat boosting potions can become boring and repetitive.
Lack of music other than the main theme which becomes so repetitive, you have no choice other than to turn it off.
All in all a very enjoyable, although slightly flawed game. It's free and takes up almost no space so you have nothing to lose. The pros far outweigh the cons and nitpicks.

Multiplayer Mod is an unique experience where up to thousands of players can compete with each other on single server at the same time. All NPCs are removed, so you will meet only human players. Mod weights a couple of megabytes and of course requires original Just Cause 2 game. DLCs are not required but recommended. Graphics remain the same.
In JC-MP Mod the only aim is to have fun, with no goals or missions. The most suitable definition of this kind of entertainment is mmo sandbox. Every player spawns in the air in random parts of Panau Islands with random weapons. One of important aspects of the game is money gathering. You can earn money by killing other players and winning races/destruction derby. You can spend them on weapons, vehicles or character models (by default, every player's model is Rico, my favourite is ninja). Vehicles are also available for free in game world, like in original JC2, but not weapons (you have got a lot of ammo at start).
Fighting with other players is the basic thing you can do in this game. Shooting is quite frustrating due to high ping (players are from all over the world) and blind shots are very common. If you get used to it, it's fun. Many vehicles are two-seated so you can pick up someone with you, but (with some exceptions) driver is a shooter too. Funny feature is the speed boost activated with Shift key which allows you to fly using you car :) You can fight with others using all kinds of vehicles which makes you powerful, but you need to pay attention on other players. If someone is close enough, he will probably hijack your vehicle, which is too simple in my opinion - QTE sequences are removed.
Another playmode is racing - pure fun with no downsides, the same with destruction derby race - aim here is to smash each other :) Rewards are high so you can earn much money that kind of play. You can also set up fraction and others can join it. You can compete with other fractions, and there is no friendly fire beetwen members of the same fraction. Instead of using grappling hook and parachute to move, you can teleport to your fraction member using simple command. You can also teleport to some well-known parts of the islands, like airport or city, which helps a lot.
Overall, Just Cause 2 multiplayer mod is an awesome experience, in which many people put a lot of effort. It's worth to appreciate it, expecially because it's non-profit. However, I got bored after a couple of days - it's only a crazy thing, a variation of original Just Cause 2. Best tastes in short sessions.

I've played a little over 5 hours of PA:T, and I still don't really get the mechanics of it. In the Wargame franchise, there's a system of units that counter other units that results in interesting gameplay. As far as I can tell, PA:T has none of that. There are strong units and there are spam units. Spam units just die, and strong units massacre everything.
Beyond that, gameplay (I think) is limited to one type of game, where you have to destroy the enemy commander. By spamming one type of bomber, I was able to win every game against the AI that I played. There were no consequences for just spamming and saying "f*** off" to strategy and tactics. Really, this is a real time spam game.
I briefly enjoyed the campaign, until I made the mistake of picking the "Subcommander" perk, which gives you an AI to help you. Seems cool, right?
Not if you actually enjoy playing the damn game! The allied AI commanders are way faster and way more efficient that you could ever possibly be, which makes the game kinda pointless to play- I literally couldn't mobilize my forces fast enough to get into combat at all.
The game offers a fairly deep base building mechanic, but you almost never get to build your base up. On every map, I tried to actually build a "titan" unit, and usually the AI won the game for me before it was even done building. Ugh.
On other games without the AI commander, I  was able to build my titans, and, well, they're kinda game ending. What do I mean by that? Well, I sent one to an enemy planet and told it to kill the enemy commander. I then ignored it for about five minutes until the game notified me that I had won.
Whoo?
On the positive side, the game has some seriously cool things to it- I love the concept of combat on multiple levels- Ground, air, undersea, and orbit. Orbital mechanics are neat and don't require KSP levels of knowledge. It's fun waging war across an entire solar system all at once, provided that you can actually keep track of the action. Some of the units are legitimately badass to look at. The art style is neat, and the music is good.
Really, I wish that the developers would take a little more from RTS games like Homeworld and Wargame. It needs more strategy, and the gameplay mechanics have a lot of potential. It just needs to actually be a strategy game that's fun to play, and I'm yet to really have fun playing this.

Let's look at some arguments.
The quality is sub-par:

It divides the modding community:

I am not sure if you people are stuck in the 80's, but we demand higher quality games every day and we get butthurt if it doesn't mean our standards. Newsflash, higher quality games means more time spent making them, more people working on the games. This means extra costs for the company, and yet we demand the game publishers keep the retail prices the same as they've always been or we will complain.
Creation Club charges money for existing content:

Luckily there are a number of active players online so you can always find a stranger to help you through the level.

In this game, you are randomly assigned one of the many roles and land in a town with a group of players such as yourself. The rules are: town wins when all evil roles die, evil roles usually win if they're the last men standing. There's also neutral roles and certain exceptions, but you should read a wiki or experience this by yourself.
Town has an ability to lynch one person a day. Technically simple, right? Everyone reveals their roles and the game ends in 2-3 days?
Wrong.
There's no way to prove if someone is telling the truth or lying with 100% certainty. You can only be ALMOST sure.
You have to deduce, guess correctly and be smart about using your exact role - and other players.
It's difficult to win if you don't eliminate crucial enemy roles quickly, but you can get demasked and killed if you rush it.
Overall, it's a brilliant game of cat and mouse, similar to all kinds of Werewolf and Mafia games. Great idea.
It's important to note this game has a browser version. What changes in Steam version? Slightly less lag, better resolution, decent stability and you get a small bonus for buying the game.
My recommendation is: try it in browser and if you like it, come over and buy the Steam version.
In my oppinion the developers deserve every penny.
The graphics and audio... kind of "are there", they're not crucial, but they aren't annoying, so it's all good.
There's endless variations of games because of randomized matchmaking and roles, so you're not about to get bored anytime soon.
In short: I'd recommend this game at any time of day or night. The thing with scrolls (being able to almost choose the role for $$$) kind of ruins it sometimes, but there are many interesting roles to play - I'm not complaining.
Buy it if you like it, and it's a MUST HAVE when it's on sale. See you in the Town!

Perfect game from a simpler time.
One thing that annoyes me the most about modern games, yes I'm looking at you Metro, is the fact that you are basically only watching cutscene after cutscene and you're barely even allowed to do anything yourself.
Everything that looks remotely like it could be fun happens in cutscenes.
In Half life everything story releated happens while you're playing, without ever being interrupted. Characters talk to you when you run past and if you don't wanna listen to what they have to say you can just run by without caring, it's up to you.
Also the game doesn't bother explaining everything to the point that even a 3 year old would understand it, the leveldesign is so well thought out that you'll never even end up asking yourself what to do. If you can't take the most obvious route (because of a locked door for example), all you have to do is look around and you'll find other paths to take, or at least clues of what you are looking for. That is much better than markers all over the map or an annoying AI running with you telling you the same hint over and over again.
One thing that bothered me a little bit would be how ridiculously inaccurate certain guns are, but overall the gunplay and movement feels very solid and obviously familiar for cs players.
It's a tiny download, you can grab it for under $2 during steam sales, it runs on every toaster and is an absolute pillar in the world of gaming, why are you even reading reviews?

I have been playing this game since it was released in 2008, and still absolutely love it. To me it is the definitive arcade style racing game that nothing else since has come close to.

Even though they run it at 60fps, the visuals are only now starting to get surpassed by rival games, but the gameplay is still king.
It was a divisive game when it came out due to its open world sandbox style that immediately alienated the majority of people who tried the demo and I think it never got the recognition it deserved because of that. The sandbox world is actually the games strength, rather than be another arcade style race from a-b on a set route, in BP you needed to learn your way around the game world, the more you learned, the better you get. The game world is a staggering achievement, and even now after playing it for years, I am still finding new things.
As the game is very cheap now, I would recommend it to anyone who likes arcade style racing games, put the effort in to playing and learning it, and it will reward you with one of the best games ever.

Strictly speaking, I can recommend this game - but there are two major caveats, which is why I'm writing this review as a warning.
People have been complaining of crashes. I experienced the same. The issue turns out in most cases to be that the game is poorly optimized, graphically, such that even if you're getting great frames on any given setting, the game might overload the memory and crash. So you might be forced to play at lower settings than you'd like to avoid this.
Second (and for me this is quite frustrating), multiplayer does not work. Or, rather, if you're going to play with anyone, make sure you do finish the game within thirty hours (of real-life, not in-game, time). Why? Because Ubisoft, in its infinite propensity for poor decisions, has taken the validation servers offline, but online profiles are given a thirty hour grace period during which they aren't validated. Thus, once you make a profile, you have just over a day until it tries to validate with Ubisoft only to find out that they've managed to ruin yet another online experience.
Apart from that, it's a wonderful game. A substantial step up from Anno 1701, with just the right additional mechanics, and a beautiful setting.

Oh my god. This game is amazing.
Also known as Anno 1404, Dawn of Discovery is a city-builder with many RTS elements. I've only played the Master Builder scenario, which has taken me almost 70 hours, and the game has literal dozens of scenarios with different goals, so consider that as you read the review.
Dawn of Discovery is a resource/economy management game that manages to feel really unique. I've only dabbled in the other Anno games, so I can't weigh it against the previous or current Anno games, but this game is amazing on its own. You are given a set of random islands at the beginning of the game and through trade, exploration, and conflict, you are to build a thriving kingdom. The game has a lot of depth in managing land that rivals juggernauts like SimCity 4 and Cities: Skylines, but also places a large emphasis on trade. The key to winning this game is networking your islands in a manner that lets them support each other. There are a plethora of resources available that differ from island to island, so making sure that the needs of your citizens are met requires you to take advantage of all of the land that you have available to you.
The resources mentioned above are of course used by the populations of your islands. Your people start off as peasants, but as you build more structures and obtain more resources, your lowly peasants can become rich nobility. This is more than just a title, though. As civilians elevate to different levels, their needs change and keeping them happy becomes more challenging. Your economy can easily go into the toilet if you have inefficient trade routes or a lack of services. Civilians also damage structures and move down in their ranks when needs aren't met. This manages to be fun despite the challenges and there is a lot of variety in how you can manage these civilians due to there being two major types of civilians with very different needs.
Combat is fun and easy to get into. There is a diplomacy mechanic that allows you to trade or war with other AI or human players. Much of the combat is sea based, but there is also land based RTS-style combat to keep things interesting. Warring can be extremely expensive, though, and can be frustrating if attempted too early.
Building in this game is really, really flexible. You want an island dedicated to making beer and wine? It's doable. You want to make a mansion the size of a continent? Go for it. There are dozens of structures that can be built and managed, and the game becomes a city-builder fan's wet dream after a short time of playing.
The music and visuals are phenomenal. The music is extremely pleasant and adds an atmosphere of beauty to the game. The game looks amazing and runs well on my GTX 960m. The only problem with this game is that by default it only uses 2 GB of Ram. This almost always causes the game to crash on highly populated kingdoms. There's a fix for it, but it's 3rd party which is a tad disappointing.
This game is a must-buy for any city-builder fan. Even if you do not like RTS games, the game is phenomenal and allows you to play without having to worry about combat at all. Buy it. It and the expansion are definitely worth the $15 price tag.

This game is a charming mix of Dwarf Fortress, The Sims and Sim City Ants.  Confusing?  Allow me to explain.  In A Game of Dwarves, you are a young dwarf prince who has just been told by your father to strike out on your own and re-capture a magic crystal that will help you defeat the evil wizards who banished your kind from the world above.  To do so, you will command a group of dwarves, whom you will assign a role and give orders to with the goal of growing your community and building an efficient and productive colony.
There are several different types of roles these dwarves can fill, but the first ones you will encounter include, warriors, workers, diggers and builders.  Most of these roles are self-explanatory, for instance warriors defend your home from creatures and monsters that hide in the forgotten ruins and tunnels underground.  Workers harvest food and other resources from fertile patches of earth you find underground to keep your dwarves fed.  Diggers are the primary workhorses in a dwarven society as they expand your colony by digging new tunnels and excavating long lost ruins which may contain treasures and other useful tools.  Then there are builders who craft the various beds, tables, benches and decorations you will use to keep your dwarves fed, well rested and happy.
This game has a good sense of humor and doesn’t take itself too seriously most of the time, but don’t let that fool you.  It is easy to lose track of your dwarves as you are off in another part of the colony, and you will return to find them dead and a gravestone left in their stead.  This happens usually because a digger falls in a hole and starves because there is no ladder there for them to escape, or they unearth a monster and you don’t have any nearby warriors to assist them in fighting it.  So while the game seems simple at first glance, you have to pay attention and plan out your expansions so that there is a food source (table) near your frontline diggers, as well as a military member and builder to assist them when they need it.
Each dwarf needs food, rest and has a level of happiness to keep track of.  Like Sims, they will try to take care of these needs automatically, but know that they will have to travel to the nearest food source and bed so it is a good idea to have plenty around your colony so that the dwarves can work where assigned and quickly resume working once their needs are taken care of.  Additionally, dwarves are vain creatures, so they want to see decorations and tributes to their greatness to keep them happy and working at maximum proficiency.
This game is nowhere near as complex and crazy as dwarf fortress, but it is also much more accessible.  I did not encounter many issues or bugs while playing this game, except for the fact that I could not get the client to go full screen.  I am not sure what was causing this to be the case, and I tried several resolution settings without any luck, so this may just be something going on with my setup.
Overall, I think this is a fun game.  I have played it for 2 hours, which was just enough to complete the tutorial missions, which btw I think are very good and taught me how to play the game in an engaging way.  I am currently doing a Steam Run, where I play every game in my Steam Library for at least 2 hours, but I plan on coming back to this one for sure.

An absolute marvel at storytelling and character development. This is not just a game, it’s an experience to behold. Your choices shape the story.
The “Artwork inspired by the original comic books” makes the game look very unique compared to others, but it heavily sacrifices that ‘unique’ look for potentially better-looking graphics that could’ve been implemented. But the uniqueness of the visuals gives the game a nice charm to it; scoring it slightly above average.
This is where this game truly shines. It excels in not just presenting you with a great story, but it also gives the characters in the story some life and value. Ultimately, your choice determines the outcome of the story; whether that choice was right or wrong.
From the main menu soundtrack; up till to the credits, it was beautiful. The only minor downsides are the soundtrack that play in a couple of the “puzzle” scenarios or more like the lack of soundtrack in those scenarios. It would’ve been nice to hear a subtle backdrop tune instead of just silence and the sound of you walking from place to place.
For the most part…it’s okay. I mean, you can’t move the camera whenever you like which means 70% of the time you’re stuck in an awkward angle and for some reason you can’t choose to run or walk any faster, Lee’s slow pace may throw you off a bit when solving some of the puzzles. But this is passable for a point and click story-adventure game, so this much is fine. Then again you buy this game for its story, not for its gameplay.
You’re definitely paying a premium if you buy it for £18.99. I really think this is worth around £14.99. But you can always wait for a Steam sale or buy the game elsewhere for cheaper if you’d like.

I'll admit, it's not the best looking game and is a little awkward to watch (the Dwarves/enemies often "slide" along surfaces, especially up and down ladders), however you get used to this and it actually is a little charming after a while.
The game has some pretty clever mechanics, where you have to continue to build Dwarven items and decorate your hold the deeper you delve, otherwise your Dwarves become unhappy. This keeps you pushing forward and gives you a reason to actually "conquer" and turn the mineshafts and caverns into actual Dwarven homes. Also, the game has a clever "question mark" system to encorage you to mine in different directions. The leveling and variety of your Dwarven warriors is also a cool way to add depth and variety to combat, plus naming each of your Dwarves gives you a connection to them and their exploits as your colony grows.
The story missions are quite extensive and become challenging, so there's plenty here to keep you busy for hours. Or you can just run wild with a custom game.
Overall, while this game isn't the most polished and could have more features, it's still an incredibly fun and fairly unique base-builder/dwelver game that has plenty of character and charm. It's definitely worth the current price, especially if you snag it on sale.

I bought this game at the last summer steam sale and I must say, I'm kicking myself for waiting this long to play it.  This game is basically everything grand theft auto wished it could be.  The gameplay, story, graphics are all top notch.
Speaking on the gameplay, I was expecting a GTAish game with an interesting plot twist(where you are actually in fact an undercover cop),  What I wasn't expecting was the very well thought out and executed melee combat system instead of the usual bland cover based shooting mechanics you see in these games(there are still times in the game where you use a gun, but very few and far between)  It makes the game feel like a Chinese action flick.  Controls are tight, side quests and missions constantly mix up gameplay from racing, to hacking, free running chases of dead beats who owe your gang money and so much more.
Graphics are very good indeed(make sure you download the high resolution texture pack), from the textures to the brilliant lighting and shadowing effects.  The only thing that breaks the immersion is the less than steller character animations. (it amazes me how many games STILL haven't caught up to Half-life 2 in that regard.)
As far as story goes, I don't want to spoil anything but expect a very gritty, well written, and emotionally scarring thrill ride.
TLDR, Great GTA style sandbox with excellent melee combat, amazing graphics(download the high texture pack off the steam store) and a story that will absorb you and possibly scar you for life.

Awesome game I almost missed out on because the first load took ages and was ready to quit when it finished.
The plot, setting, and characters are excellent. You're a traveller to a parallel universe's Earth where you play as a Bishop (lorewise, something between secret agent and one man army) on his first day on duty, aboard a plane called the Zenlil. From the start, you will be exploring highly branching conversation options with many of the crew's members. The only thing I had heard about the gameplay before going in was that "everything you do has a consequence", and I found that to be largely true.
The somewhat limited duration of the narration means you don't get to know all of the characters in depth; the lower-ranking servicemen in particular can be one-dimensional. For those you do get to know, you learn enough of to really want to see how they'd react to future situations as well. The voice acting is solid throughout.
Everything in the graphics department feels source engine-ish. On the bright side, even as a player who will sometimes not play certain games solely because of the graphics, they didn't bother me too much. They got the job done well enough, and there was enough detail put in that they weren't bland.
The combat is clunky at best, and is by far the game's weakest point, but its presence does help with the setting, which was lovingly crafted (in that it'd be harder to believe your tough enforcer background without the combat scenes to prove you're as good as they say you are/should be).
Also, there's a news article database where you can read articles on the world's lore, many of them simply there for the curious.
Overall, this was a very pleasant experience for me. I'd say it's a must-play for anyone looking for a great narrative delivered in a fresh way.

I just can't stand these people complaining in these reviews about things that were known months before the game was released. One cannot expect to have his or her hand held 24/7 and just buy things without being first properly informed about it. That is just irresponsible.
Definitely the best SF right now. And not only because it is new and has plenty of players, but because it is closest to fast paced 3rd Strike without being a copy-paste. The combat system is the best in all of SF's to date, with plenty of depth.
The game is lacking content, yes, but that's just filler content. The most important bits of a fighting game, that is fighting and being able to fight with other players, is working perfectly. A valid complaint is the lack of lobbies at the date of me writing this, but this should be changed in March. Not to mention, if what Capcom said is true and keeps its promises, more coming the next few months. And stuff that is important (characters) you can get for free, just by playing.
Graphically, the game is running on UE4, and it shows. Lightning, shading and textures are crispy and beautiful. There is really not much to say about this other than the stages looking poor. But in the end they're still just backgrounds and the focus will be on your opponent regardless. Also, thanks to sound effects making punches sound meaty, as well as small screen shakes after every hit, or block, makes them feel and look much more powerful, which is a very rewarding feeling.
In the end, this is a game for the fan, and because of the changes that I am not properly knowledgable about I cannot properly list them, the game is very rewarding even for low level of play (scrubs and newbs), and because it is fresh, there is plenty of people to play with at any level.

It's not entirely intuitive with the in-game wiki, when it comes to finding new information on items, formulas for crafting, or even how to progress. Fortunately, though, this is still being developed and there are online wikis to support.

CONS:

Ok seriously, I do not understand what the problem is here. People are complaining about the paid mods like it's actually something serious. Has anyone actually LOOKED at what's actually IN the creation club's mod menu? There's like 6 mods there, and literally none of them are that good. Same goes for Skyrim. There's an ENTIRELY DIFFERENT SECTION DEDICATED TO UNPAID MODS. Bethesda never said that ALL mods were going to move to the creation club, and the majority of people who make mods aren't buying into it anyway. Fallout 4 is a great game, love the gunplay in this one, the wasteland is infinitely more dangerous and navigable than Fallout 3 OR New Vegas, and they added some amazing improvements to the existing game. The only thing I can say is I wish there was a way to refuel the fuel cores, and guess what? Someone did that with an UNPAID MOD. Also, the dialogue needs improvement (which they've already said they're planning on fixing in the next installment), and I'd like to see the morality system more clearly (they didn't actually remove it from the game, just made it less apparent it was happening, so your choices still matter). Don't scrutinize the game solely based on the fact the developers are experimenting with new models because what they actually did was make a great game and absolutely streamlined the modding process so it's way less of a headache to install and uninstall mods. And as for the radiant quests, I like them. I'm the type of gamer that enjoys the building and resource management stuff and all the extra radiant quests that come with it. It makes the 200 year old wasteland feel like you're actually rebuilding instead of being completely dead. If you don't like that stuff, then probably don't play it, but if you do, I highly recommend it. It's very enjoyable and probably my favorite in the series.

Pluses:

At first I installed it for the puzzles. When I first opened the game, I couldn't stop myself from whistling along to the intro music. And then it was only better.
The atmosphere of the game is admirable. The music and sounds are nice and not distracting, graphics are nice to watch. The world is wide and there's plenty to do - you can sail on different kinds of voyages, run a workshop, take care of your house. Things are generally cutomizable, starting at your clothes and ending at your ship, when you earn enough for one. The variety of puzzels is wide enough not to get bored. Your character is constantly developing and you can see the progress as your reputation and trophy board grow. And last but not least, people. There are gamers of all ages and from all corners of the world, so for kid's sake there are some manners enforced, but not to the point where it could destroy the "piratness" of the atmosphere. Players are generally helpful, newbies can ask any question and get a solid answer.
The only minus are doubloons. In game you earn Pieces of Eight which are used to buy things. Problem is that you also have to pay a fee in doubloons, which is usually 3-4 times higher than the prize of an item itself. You can exchange PoE for them, but the course is really high - about 3000:1, when on an average pillying you earn a bit less than that. Or... you can buy them for green cash. So if you decide to start the game, be prepared that either you'll pay, or spend the first week of playing on earning for a decent bed. Despite that, you can still play quite freely if you're just there for the puzzels and sailing.

How to avoid trouble on the main channel (EN):
- Don't talk about other games
- Don't say anything offensive, according to the current PC culture
- Avoid controversial topics, including politics
- Avoid cursing
- Avoid long discussions in general
- Avoid drug suggestive or explicit language
- Avoid sexual suggestive or explicit language

The walking dead is a game based on comic book series. We are in a post-apocalyptic world that has been dominated by a strange disease through which dead people return to life and want to devour our brains.
The Game casts us as Lee Everett, a convicted murderer on his way to the prison. However, before Mr. Everett can trade his denim shirt for an orange jumpsuit, the zombie apocalypse breaks out and gives Lee a new goals in life such as surviving at all costs and protecting a little girl named Clementine.
It's an adventure game, but it’s not the kind of adventure game you’ve come to expect. Okey, you'll need to figure out how to get a radio working and how to distract walkers here and there, but you are choosing your own adventure. The big moments come when you choose how Lee responds to situations and what he says in conversations with his fellow survivors. Choices and dialogue pop up on screen with timers, and you have seconds to pick exactly what you’re going to do or say, you choose, and the game moves on – adapting its story to each decision.
Will our endings be completely different then? No. The Walking Dead is telling us the same story and thus taking us to the same conclusion, but it allows us to experience it in different ways.
All of the characters are very well written and voiced as individuals, which makes you care about whether or not they get munched on by the walkers. The game has a special painting, such as comics. Telltale wanted to use the style that the comics used, developers likes to stay true to the source material.
The walking dead is something special. By giving players the option to craft relationships and make choices that fill out the story, the game wraps you up in its events and makes you care in a way only a few video games can. It's a tale no one should miss.

All right, so here is my first impression review/initial constructive critique.
Let me begin by saying, normally, I don't usually find myself interested in fighting games, or games with a lot of influence on PvP. Under most circumstances, I'm typically a sort who enjoys a casual, laid-back, PvE atmosphere. I also don't usually find myself interested in games with an "anime/manga" feel to them (generally speaking, anime/manga just isn't much of my area of interest). That said, those are mostly personal biases. However, I wanted to give praise to the fact, that what attracted me to this game to "try it out" was the presence of the fighting form known as "Capoeira". It is an Afro-Brazilian form of fighting that I studied in real life for 7 years, and enjoyed very much. Upon seeing Capoeira as an option in this game, I could not refuse at least giving it a try, especially since it's free-to-play. All right, so here we go...
Let's start with the positive:
- Free-to-play: Always a plus. I know a lot of people gripe about it, and you are entitled to your opinions, and I respect them. However, I don't have anything against free-to-play titles, and I enjoy them extensively.
- Simple graphics and low sysreqs: The simple graphics and low system-requirements make this game playable on just about any machine made within the last decade or so.
- Easy controls, easy learning: The controls to the game are easy, and quickly learned, with a very quick, simple, and straight-forward tutorial. And even the tutorial gives a few rewards to get you on the ground running.
- No account registration necessary - At least, I think, for Steam users. I was kind of surprised when it didn't prompt me to create an account with a username, e-mail, and password. I'm assuming it uses my Steam account, and from there, I just make my characters. Not sure how it works, but it's very simple to get started.
- Low HDD space: This game's file size is not very large, which is good for those still using smaller HDDs.
Now let's go onto some aspects that I feel could use some improvement:
- Could use a little more PvE content: There is some PvE content, yes, but I feel it could use a little more, especially early on. I'm not one who enjoys PvP a lot. Also, I feel that some of the PvE content could be geared towards solo play a little bit more. I realize building a social gaming community is the goal. But I feel it should still be an "opt in/opt out" sort of thing. Perhaps rather than make a team-designated PvE arcade automatically "team difficulty", instead, how about scaling the difficulty according to number of players present? Example: One player = easy; 5 players, etc = much harder. Or even by level of the team leader; the higher the level of the team leader, the higher the zone's difficulty (and based on level-gap the lower players get less XP, to avoid power-leveling abuse).
- Full screen mode?: Maybe I just wasn't finding it, and it was just well hidden, but I would like to see a full-screen or maximized-windowed mode.
- Other audio and graphics settings options?: Again, if it's already there, maybe I just couldn't find it. Perhaps an in-game notice during the tutorial phase could be be added to point where the settings are, at least the first time around.
- Translations: This I am going to express understanding with. I have a passion (and compassion/empathy) for languages. I love studying them, and learning them, and even teaching the ones I know. So please understand, that I know translation can be troubling at the best of times. Sometimes, some languages have words, or even whole expressions, that have literally no definitive translation in another language. And finding the "more or less equivalent" words and expressions in another language, all the while trying to account for grammar, punctuation, spelling, and syntax, is no easy task, especially for someone whose first language is not the language they're translating to. And it's already known that English is the most difficult language to learn if you are not already a fluent speaker of it. This game has a lot of English translation issues with it, and I know it's still very early on. I also know that most likely, the game is of origin in a non-English speaking country. Let me say that I understand. English is challenging. But I have faith that with some hard work, and determination, the translations can be worked through.
All in all, this game has some interesting potential. I'm interested in following it further and seeing how it develops.

When I first saw this game, I thought it was adorable but didn't think it had much to it. I was right on both thoughts. The game is truly adorable and very fun to play but the amount of content it has is fairly limited. In my 8.5 hours of gameplay, I haven't finished it yet, but, If you rush through the quests on the easiest difficulty, you will have it completed in less than 8 hours, If you take your time and just play casually, you can make the fun last longer and longer. To my knowledge, there are only 18 quests and, as of this post, I just recently completed Quest 12. The game is about grinding to get outfits and weapons, but the grind isn't tormenting like many games.
The only real downfall this game holds is its very small community. It is rare to ever see a public server on the server list which seems to discourage people from playing online. This game seems to be a game you play with a group of friends, or solo, rather than meeting friends on it. If you choose to make a server, it is likely that a few people will join, but it might not be a lot. I do not know too much about the community so it could be more active than I am seeing. When I joined a few servers in January, I had no idea what I was doing but the community I met was very helpful; I never once met a troll. (I could just be lucky.)
In my opinion, $20 is a stretch to spend on this game, but, if you want a very casual game, this is the game for you, though it can get hectic at times. I impulse bought this game but I do not regret it. There is  a demo you can try out if you're skeptical, it will teach you the basics and show what the game is like. If you're considering this game, try the demo first.
Do I recommend this game? Yes. I will update this review when I play it more. Hope this helps.
Edit: I am, currently, at 11.1 hours into the game, and I finally beat the final quest. There are 20 quests in the game but each are fairly unique, despite most using the same level layouts(never the same). I liked the game storyline, it was cute. Despite my completing the game, I only played on Easy Mode, which is the easiest of the three difficulties. There are also items called badges for stat benefits, but I never used any. I also never enhanced my weapons, but it is possible to do so. There is so much of the game that I have not yet experienced.
I still recommend this game to anyone who may be interested.
Edit2: I am, currently, at 16.7 hours into the game and I found the community! My problem with finding people playing was mostly because I was playing at around midnight, EST, when most people are in various timezones around the world. The people I met were friendly, helpful, and all around fun to talk to. There is a community, albeit a fairly small one, and the developers often pop into the game to talk with their players to get personal, chibi to chibi, feedback about the game.
Though I am 16.7 hours into the game, I am still learning a lot with each passing minute. This game is far beyond worth it to purchase at its price and I expect great things for it based on what I have seen.

Half-Life is said to be one of the best FPS games ever created. It has spawned multiple sequels, a number of them having been made by lesser-known developers than Valve. The frachise is likely responsible for certain rules of asthetic when it comes to FPS and driving home the 'action' part of a game.
Experiments are being conducted at the Black Mesa facility, likely under the supervision of the mysterious Briefcase Man. When something goes wrong, it is up to you as Gordon Freeman, Theoretical Physicist, to  stop the alien invasion caused by the malfunction. You'll find plenty of guns and ammo to stop the alien horde, from Assault Rifles and shotguns to laser-trip Claymores.
I only recently purchased this game on Steam after having already played Half-Life 2 a few years ago. I saw the discount on the Half-Life Complete package and took advantage of the deal. This was definitely worthy of a package purchase, but I would gladly play full price if I had to. The jumping may be a little clunky, but that's a small problem that called be solved with something called "duck jumping"; just before you are about to jump, hit crouch and you should be on top of your obstacle.
Buy Half-Life Complete AND The Orange Box while they're on this limited-time deal. I know where I'll be spending my next $10.

In Left 4 Dead and its sequel, Valve tried and succeeded in creating a game that felt like a traditional zombie horror film, complete with film grain. The game originated out of Valve designers recognizing the fun of defeating melee-only enemies by way of  ranged weapons. To maintain a challenge, Valve added special enemies that work to seperate you from your friends.  Certainly a very gore-filled game, but also very rewarding play and a solid story. If you're one of those people who groans and/or screams at the movie characters "Don't go in there, the zombies are in there!" or "Don't seperate, they're waiting for you to be alone!" or "Don't have a shower now, the zombies are coming!" tis game was made for you. Now you can re-enact those moments, except YOU will be going into the room while your friends scream at you while being eaten by the zombie hordes. This game is worth it, even if it's jsut to show you how big a hypocrite you are. Enjoy, and turn your flashlights off.

What I find most interesting, is how the captaincy mechanic plays out. As a captain you bear the weight of responsibility of not just the success of the ship, but whether or not your crew actually enjoys the game. You'll get blamed for everything, even when it's the crews fault, or no one's fault. For this reason though, good captains will get a lot of support from their crew, a crew will passionately follow a good captain from round to round. It's an ugly, yet satisfying job that will teach you humility. You'll quickly learn if you've got what it takes to really... lead. Despite being a fairly average captain myself, I've won games against much better captains simply because my crew likes me more than the enemy crew likes their captain, because my crew are fixing my holes and firing my cannons much more enthusiastically, and more importantly, faster, than theirs. It's not all just steering and aiming.
Though it must be said, the game itself isn't very complex, has bugs, and lacks in content, and the experience is much derived from the community rather than the game itself. The game will constantly remind you its an alpha.
On an interesting technical side, this game is actually 100% playable on 350 ping, and the lack of servers in Australia isn't a problem.

Sanctum 2 is billed as the sequel to Sanctum 1, but I'd say it's more like an evolutionary remake along the lines of what Doom 3 is to Doom 2.
The basic idea of FPS/Tower Defence hybrid is still here, although the balance - which back in Sanctum 1 was 50/50 split between FPS and TD - is more like 60/40 in FPS/TD stakes. Every level pits you against waves of lumes and you're given an array of turrets and weapons to handle them - so far, so sanctum.
Where it differs in design is the idea of progression, and enemies. The lumes fight much like any other alien enemy in an FPS rather than Sanctum 1's weird ignore/punt back approach, with ranged, melee, and anything in between making up the hordes. Sanctum's clever enemy design comes back with a vengeance, with some genuinely original enemy designs coming through, and the DLCs keep adding to it. This originality extends to the turrets and guns - staples like Assault Rifles and Beam Laser towers rub shoulders with drone launchers and mind control spires, and your choice of 4 (5 in the DLC) characters allows you to specialise in most FPS class roles. Perks allow further customisation, to such an extent that the number of options available for any one mission is insane. Want a no-scope close combat sniper? Pick your build.
The downsides of this game are few, but do tend to rear their head from time to time. The aforementioned progression means that early levels can be disproportionately difficult, due to the lack of unlocked items and guns for use. To their credit, Coffee Stain Studios patched this so you unlock stuff much faster, so it's not that big a deal. Difficulty can sometimes spike and trough with little warning - bosses in particular can make a level trivially easy or extremely difficult depending on whether  you know they're coming.
But these are nitpicks. The gameplay is solid and orginal, and the Unreal Engine 3 has been used to fantastic effect, producing a world that looks like a mix of James Cameron's Avatar and Minority Report, seen through an anime lense.
Heartily recommended.

For those of you who haven't heard of it already, Bastion is an isometric action RPG, and the first game released by American game development studio Supergiant Games. Set in a colourful hand-painted post-apocalyptic world, you play as the Kid, a silent protagonist who wakes up to find himself and not much else floating on a piece of what was once Caelondia. Setting off for the Bastion, the civilization's refuge in times of calamity, you create, find and fight your way towards an unknown future.
Bastion is unique in that you discover the story and the backstory behind the characters by playing through levels and having the narrator speak to you. The narrator reacts to your actions in the game with contextually-appropriate comments. There is very little reading to slow you down in-game, as Bastion plays like a narrated storybook. Its musical score (described as "acoustic frontier trip hop"), art direction and narration have been universally praised, and I find the story to be compelling. Other people may disagree on whether or not the story draws you in but I think it's interesting to explore the after-effects of surviving an apocalypse. There is a great deal of customization in the form of weapon and alcohol combinations, and the combat is responsive.
Unfortunately, the levels tend to blend so well with the background that you have difficulty telling where the ground ends. Falling off edges is not penalized excessively, though; you only lose a bit of health. And while combat is responsive, it can become repetitive since the only way to scale the difficulty of the game is through invoking gods, which goes from easy to brutally hard. Bastion is also a really short game, clocking in at about 8-10 hours for a single playthrough. However, there is a new game+ mode, where you get to keep everything you collected in previous saves. The story also supports there being a new game+ mode so there is added replay value.

Yes, a few things have to be improved but this game is the most balanced first release of a street fighter series yet. Every character is actually fun to use and learning their unique styles adds to the game's scope. Sanctum 2 is billed as the sequel to Sanctum 1, but I'd say it's more like an evolutionary remake along the lines of what Doom 3 is to Doom 2.
The basic idea of FPS/Tower Defence hybrid is still here, although the balance - which back in Sanctum 1 was 50/50 split between FPS and TD - is more like 60/40 in FPS/TD stakes. Every level pits you against waves of lumes and you're given an array of turrets and weapons to handle them - so far, so sanctum.
Where it differs in design is the idea of progression, and enemies. The lumes fight much like any other alien enemy in an FPS rather than Sanctum 1's weird ignore/punt back approach, with ranged, melee, and anything in between making up the hordes. Sanctum's clever enemy design comes back with a vengeance, with some genuinely original enemy designs coming through, and the DLCs keep adding to it. This originality extends to the turrets and guns - staples like Assault Rifles and Beam Laser towers rub shoulders with drone launchers and mind control spires, and your choice of 4 (5 in the DLC) characters allows you to specialise in most FPS class roles. Perks allow further customisation, to such an extent that the number of options available for any one mission is insane. Want a no-scope close combat sniper? Pick your build.
The downsides of this game are few, but do tend to rear their head from time to time. The aforementioned progression means that early levels can be disproportionately difficult, due to the lack of unlocked items and guns for use. To their credit, Coffee Stain Studios patched this so you unlock stuff much faster, so it's not that big a deal. Difficulty can sometimes spike and trough with little warning - bosses in particular can make a level trivially easy or extremely difficult depending on whether  you know they're coming.
But these are nitpicks. The gameplay is solid and orginal, and the Unreal Engine 3 has been used to fantastic effect, producing a world that looks like a mix of James Cameron's Avatar and Minority Report, seen through an anime lense.
Heartily recommended.

This might be the best Street Fighter entry.
The gameplay is increadibly tight. Each character is well balanced and only a few match-ups are strongly oneside (Zangief vs Dhalsim) which is a hallmark of a great fighting game. The new v mechanics are well designed and help make each character feel truly unique. The execution skills required are very friendly to new comers compared to past entries.
The netcode is mostly fantastic with a few occasional issues with rollback. Match making during the early stages of a game always lead to occasional skill mismatches but from what I can see that shouldn't be the case once more of the good players continue to ascend the ranks and the many different leagues become more evenly populated.
The character background stories are fine, nothing special. Short, easy matches to help give you the background of the character you're interested in and unlock a story oriented costume (you'll still have to buy this costume in the store, once the store is open). Survival is beatable, there were issues early in the release because of the server issues which have been largely eliminated. Survival could be alot better, the need to use each costume for each character to unlock all possible color options is frustrating. Survival also has entirely too many matches of disparate skill levels.
With free updates coming (new characters, new story and challenge modes) I can't help but be excited. If you're new to fighting games and have a desire to play multiplayer (not playing multiplayer is like playing a CoD game just for the story, the multiplayer is the real meat of the game) I strongly recommend this game.

: If you generally love SciFi and tactical fights, this game has an amazing atmosphere for you, though its mechanics still needs some serious refining. In the lightspeed edition, the grind has been reduced to a much more tolerable level.
: This is a tactic RPG in a Star Trek setting, with basically XCOM 2 base management. It's not a roguelike, so the comparisons to FTL are extremly misleading. Nor is it a 4X-game.
----
The core gameplay loop of Halcyon 6 are its 3 vs 3 space (and ground) fights, which use an initiative system. Core mechanic in the fights is inflicting debuffs (e.g. crew panicked - unit will use a random attack ability) with one attack and exploiting that debuff with another for 2.5x damage. To mix things up, the battlefield may prevent certain debuffs (-100% chance).
Sadly, this doesn't really prevent that the system has a surprising low variation of attack sets you will use, e.g.:
Knock out sensors -> exploit + knock out weapons -> exploit
or
Knock out engines -> ram/flak
Some debuffs are also extremely tricky to inflict, even though there is many abilities exploiting them. That part of the fighting system definitely still needs polishing, to increase the interaction between the classes and allow for interesting chaining of abilities.
The 3v3 fights have a strategic overlay, where you increase resource generation, build new ships, skill up your officers and research ship buffs. Sadly, also this system has a major design flaw: Since you end up only using 3 to 6 officers, its generally always the same three ships and officers fighting. So upgrading a ship 'class' (+x% damage) is nice, but as soon as you upgrade to the next tier (five ones), those upgrades are effectively obsolete. Biggest problem here is that the enemies upgrade to the next tier as well, so the opportunities of using lower tier ships quickly disappear.
I think this and the repetitiveness of the combat causes or caused all the complains about the game being grindy. It feels like a wasted opportunity, in which the artists did an amazing job creating a lovely atmosphere, but the mechanics being a bit of an afterthought.
The Lightspeed Edition apparently tuned down the grind, which is actually pretty good. As someone who dislikes grind, I managed to stay engaged for the whole first act (of two), which took around 10 hours. There is probably another 3 hours of gameplay to be had, but somehow the game overstayed its welcome due to the combat.
Even with its problems, considering the price, I have no problem recommending the game. The atmosphere they created is quite enjoyable for a SciFi fan - including all the SciFi tropes of weird alien races, expendable redshirts (I mean green shirts) etc. It's just sad they didn't quite get the mechanics where they should be. Also I wished, there was much more interaction with the other races in act 1.
I personally wouldn't mind a sequel, which expands the existing art assets, but completely reworks the core gameplay loop. Why not generally make even officers a little more expendable and allow for things like a desperate 'ramming speed' option that will probably nuke both ships. To improve the chance of creating good 'war stories', including memorials (see XCOM 2 - War of the Chosen). Why not allow high rank officers to auto-resolve fights, in which their allies and their enemies have lower tier ships? This way you could increase the scope of the war thats going on and improve the aspect of fleet management without making the game grindier. Right now its basically three ships vs the rest of the universe, and losing officers is quite punishing. Etc..

Yes, only purchase this game through Steam if you would like to help support the devs. Otherwise, go to their website at
and play it free there. If you use info sheets and the ToS Wiki during the game like I do, press the ESC button to resize the screen when playing through the Steam client. You can then cycle through your needed tabs with ease.
If you like detective games you may love ToS. I've never played an in-person version of Werewolf or Mafia but I have tried other versions that were or are out there on the web. I keep coming back to ToS. The other ones are too confusing to navigate, have a stiff learning curve or you get in trouble by longtime regulars for having a new account by threatening to report you for just trying to play because you couldn't possibly be a brand new player. And their games typically last only about 5 minutes. While that can be a good thing, I find that it's just too quick for me to be as deceitful as possible in only a couple of minutes.
Each game in ToS takes around 30 minutes to complete and I personally do not believe that there are any boring roles. Each role is unique and while some are more aggressive roles, that means there has to be a balance of more passive roles. But each role plays an important part when played correctly or creatively. The only thing that makes a role boring is if you die on the first or second night. Those deaths are usually just the luck of the draw. But, that's just part of the game. Join another one and try again.
I love getting creative with roles. For example, when I'm Survivor I like to be as vocal as possible. When I'm Jester, I like to be as quiet as possible. It's all in how you want to play around with human psychology within the rules of the game. I've seen games with just two Mafia members win and games where seven Mafia lost (All Any mode).
I've seen my fair share of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ry ingame but the dev team cares about their community and are very responsive. There are now profanity filters that you can choose to have on and there has always been a report button for cheaters and the really out-of-hand players. Mostly, people are just playing a personality role while they are alive and if they stick around while dead, you can have some sane and interesting conversations.
In the end, it's just a game. If someone is being a♥♥♥♥♥♥ /ignore them and move on to the next game when the time comes. Each game is different and that's what is so enjoyable. Just remember to have fun and play your part as best you can.
