You know what you're going to find here?  One heck of an immersive game with plenty to do, and you're going to enjoy every bit of it.  What really drives this game is the narration.  The primary voice acting really pulls you in and makes the characters alive.  Along your travels you'll pass plenty of others that have some very interesting conversations.  You'll want to revisit some areas and live out people's issues.  The mom and daughter outside your first apartment are your first soap opera.
The action in the game is fun and can get tricky at times.  It's action, it's quick time event, and it's environmental.  Get creative and look around, you can really do some interesting things.  As you learn moves, you can punish your foes with greater effect.
Music!!  Plenty of varying stations to listen to that offer a style thier own.  Not sure if other games offer this, but you can even control the volume.  Rock, rap, classic, Hong Kong locale, techno, it's all there.
With the going price now, you won't be disappointed and really wishing for more.  There is some DLC that adds to the story (not essential), and helps polish the experience.  I completed in 24 hours (doing most, but not all side quests), am greating looking forward to a sequel, and actually want to 100% this game.  I can't remember ever caring about that before.
Do it.  Buy this.  Thank all the recommenders later.

Overall, I can't recommend this game for the following reasons:
- Account uncertainty
- The need more microtransactions
- The pure repetitious gameplay
- Questionable community
The first is explained above. The issue with microtransactions is that they are around every corner. Some things can be purchased with in-game currency but not much and the amount of grind to just get a "badge" for 30 days saying you can play a feature in the game is ridiculous.
Which leads into my next point: repetition. In order to get anywhere you need to up your skills, which in turn means you are playing the exact same tetris puzzle over and over and over again. It's so mind numbing it actually starts to become physically painful. You get the idea.
Finally we have the community. If the repetition and wallet-poking don't run you off, you might be ok with the community. The players in game are an odd mix, comprised of the following demographics:
a) Those that will talk to you and try to recruit you
b) Those that ignore chat or are too stupid to use it
c) Trolls
d) Jerks and all-around unreliable people who take up a slot on your crew and then disappear

Consortium is a FPS/RPG, a bit akin to Deus Ex as the setting is futuristic, there is an inventory system with a character sheet, multiple lines of dialog to choose from, and a sub-par shooting experience.
In Consortium, the player "controls" a soldier in an intervention outfit. There is a very interesting hierarchy in that group, as if each person was a chess piece. The game takes place in the aircraft of that outfit undergoing an assault from an enemy militia. Discussing with anyone lets the player choose how they respond (play dumb, flirt, and so on) and stand in a positive or negative way relative to each character. The dialogs are to me the meat of the game, quite interesting with well fleshed out characters.
Sadly, the First Person Shooting is so bad that I could not go much further in the game. Enemies have too much health and the combat is stiff and uninteresting. There are lots of opponents that can easily pin down the player (the combat takes place in an enclosed space), and it feels frustrating that such a bad shooting experience is also so difficult to overcome.
Overall I think the game is an interesting and well written piece, but the FPS part is so badly executed that it prevents from appreciating the rest of the experience.

If you actually like playing fighting games competitively, Street Fighter 5 has fixed a huge number of the issues with 4's gameplay. The V skill and V trigger systems enforce a level of uniquity for each character in a similar way to the Drive mechanic in Blazblue. Unintended mechanics that became overwhelmingly prolific in SF4 such as crouch tech are removed, and the game has a hard priority system which tie breaks when moves would normally trade in SF4, encouraging the use of normals other than lights. Light normals also confirm into less. There is a 3 frame buffer that makes impractical links a thing of the past, and the crush counter system ensures you are aptly rewarded for respecting your opponent's DP or going for the risky counter hit. The new characters are all interesting and fun to play (extra special shoutouts to Fang, a character with an extremely unique keepaway playstyle revolving around poison that clears if you successfully attack him, and Rashid, who breaks a number of the series' established rules, having multiple ways to change trajectory in the air and a dash with no fixed distance from which he can attack), and the game is graphically a lot more pleasing than 4, if still a little behind most AAA games. Don't let poor steam reviews decieve you, it's captivated the genre's fans, and has already broken the record for most sign ups at the biggest fighting game tournament of all, Evo. Rollback netcode has done wonders for the game, and while those on poor connections might have a bad experience in neutral, lag will no longer fear with your combos or wakeup game (unless you're connected to the internet by carrier pigeon).
However, if you find competitive fighting games difficult to penetrate or don't want to put down the large amount of time required to learn them, there's little for you here. That's not me trying to be insulting, there's factually no worthwhile learning tools for concepts beyond basic controls, or anything to appeal to audiences that aren't experienced with the genre. Lacking proper single player options or even a decent tutorial (with the promise that these are coming later), this game was clearly rushed out for the existing fighting game community to be ready for the Capcom tournament season. Story mode is a rushed demo of the full story which won't be in the game until June, and survival mode is an uninteresting grind.
Recommended for stellar multiplayer experience (in terms of both gameplay and online infrastructure) and a fresh and inspired take on a beloved franchise, but if that alone isn't worth £45 to you, you should skip.

Aweful, aweful game. First playthrough expect to spend *alot* of time in the dark, literally and metaphorically. Some objectives are very vague, some are so easy to fail simply because you didn't notice something, some seem to be impossible to pass.
Examples, I was told to "defend the crew", shot or incapacitated maybe 8 attackers, 2 of them standing infront of a wall yelling but not moving, searched the entire plane and couldn't find anyone else, objective is still the same 15 mins later. Ummm... huh? Reload game from the last auto save, this time 12 attackers where I found the first 8 and I move on. Okay so major bugs in that mission that they didn't fix.
Another mission I am supposed to rescue the pilot when he is at risk of being electrocuted. Objective says to go through the access point in the cockpit. I do that and people are yelling "help him! quick! get out of there!" I look around, it's a small room with an access door that I came through and a door to the infirmary where some of the people are yelling, but the door is locked. I think "okay, they already got him to the infirmary and I am supposed to go there. I go back through the cockpit and people really freak out. "Go back in there and help him!" Except now the access point is locked. Oooookay? what was that about? Second playthrough I find out he is in the corner of that small room. That would have been nice to know before you wasted my time.
Another easy to fail mission because they didn't make things clear, those 8 attackers that I said I found in that mission? That was technically my second time playing that mission. the first time I was told to follow a crew member to a weapons lockup. she walks 20 feet and a door opens, she turns and looks at me, I walk through the door, it closes and locks behind me. Huh? she didn't follow? where are my weapons? The objectives just read "protect the crew" and tell me to go to the hanger bay. I go there, unarmed, and think alright I'm supposed to knock out an attacker and take his gun. nope, punching them does nothing. I spend another 5 mins searching for that mysterious weapons catch I was promised, no where to be found. Reload, Oh! she was walking up to (and blocking) a small panel built into the wall with some weapons, and I'm not supposed to go through the door, just wait until she opens it. lame.
Finally a mission that I'm apparently not supposed to succeed? I'm supposed to convince the pilot that there is a virus in the system. Ok, easy! Except when I get the mission I am standing next to the cockpit door and it is locked. A woman walks in and locks it behind her again. You can see through a "window" to one side and they are making out, they tell you to go away and there is nothing else to do. The woman doesn't come out until you leave the area, and when you return the pilot is already down below where he gets electrocuted, so you are notified that you failed the mission. Oookay? So why is that even a mission?
Oh yeah, so as for being in the dark literally, for some reason you spend at least 30% of the game in near or total darkness because the lights are malfunctioning. As you can imagine, that makes it a bit difficult to navigate the ship, especially with out a map, since sometimes you have no idea if you are even moving or just stuck at a poorly made doorway that you have to walk at just right to walk through.
Now a word on game length. I've played through twice. 7 hours on record. The first playthrough took over 5 irritating hours of being left in the dark wondering "what am I supposed  to be doing?" Which means the second playthrough, now that I know what I'm doing, only took 2 hours even though I tried different options and unlocked some things that either weren't available or simply bugged during the first playthrough.
Finally, the game has a few bugs. Some of them irrelevant, like the pilot saying that he is going to check some systems, you go into the cockpit and he is sitting in the air acting like he is pushing buttons 5 feet from his chair. Some of the glitches halt your progress, like the 2 enemies staring at and pointing their guns at the wall while yelling at you then nobody else shows up and you can't move on.
Overall, a terrible game. I'll try it once or twice more to make sure I'm not missing something major that caused others to give this game a high rating, but it looks like it's a waste of time.

This is a great racing game that's all about driving in the open world of people-free Paradise City, of which the title song claims has green grass and pretty girls.  Along the way, you'll be bombarded with advertising billboards for such things like Burger King, EVGA motherboards, Crash FM, and this very game.  Sadly, you can only demolish one of these billboards, which keep reappearing continuously.  Somehow, I feel real sorry for the cleanup crews having to fix up the damage caused by driverless cars.  It's like Twilight Zone stuff, man!
While you repeat the events that you've already cleared with each new license, you get to hear a selection of licensed songs that usually repeat a pretty good deal.  Or you can listen to past Burnout songs from a time Acclaim published those games.  Maybe you just feel like listening to that Avril Lavinge song over and over.  Did you know that song was also in Burnout Dominator AND in multiple languages?  There are also classical songs in the game, but nobody listens to those. ;)
The damage model is quite glorious, parts flying off, cars flipping about, and [my favorite /s] the game going into super slow motion because you were too slow in reacting to a barrier right in front of you.  It's like you know you're going to be taunted mercilessly, especially if you crash mere seconds before the time trial expires.  But if you feel like crashing into things and causing mass destruction, there is a Showtime mode.  It's not quite like the crash modes in previous games, but it counts for something.

Despite the FPS/RPG trappings its more like an adventure game than anything else; aside from some virtual reality training levels there are only two real firefights in the entire game. Thankfully the adventure game stuff is pretty interesting, with the entire game playing out on a single sci-fi aircraft that's like a cross between Star Trek and Thunderbirds where everyone has goofy uniforms and chess-based rankings and you do everything from solve a murder mystery to negotiate with terrorists to man the ship's defenses and do repairs after a battle. It's only towards the end when it tries to introduce a metanarrative involving terrorists and AIs and characters speaking to the player directly that the story starts to fall apart.

Complex, complicated, frustrating at times, but oh so much fun.  Lacking in content right now, but its supposed to change in the near future; and still, despite the lack of modes, the heart of the game, the fights themselves, are the best you'll find.

I've played a lot of the classic edition offline so I have more time in this game then it shows. Basically you rebuild a star base, build space ships, recruit commanders for said ships and send them on missions to either support or rebuild resource generating colonies, defend against hostile fleets, or to to quests or away missions or diplomacy with the alien races. You're ultimate goal is to survive the onslaught of a hostile alien race known as the cruul.
One of the things I like a lot about this is in combat, instead of just brute forcing your way as is typical in most jrpg style games(using the same powerful attacks over and over in repetative battles where the only goal is to push an xp or currencey number up), this game has a system where conditions your attacks apply can be exploited by another ships attacks, creating chained combos and interesting emergent and dynamic puzzles. For example, one ship might cause 'engines down' the equivalent of slow or cripple in another game, and a second ship will 'exploit' that condition and apply another your third ship can exploit. You may find yourself thinking do i want to keep the 'sensors down'(blind) condition or try to exploit it for a killshot.  You'll have to scan an enemy's weakness and resistances, a sector's bonuses and penalties, and plan a fleet loadout that will overcome the threats presented.
The stakes in each battle are high, letting a ship explode before getting cloning tanks means you lose not just an expensive ship but the commander, letting enemies hit your colonies deprives you of much needed resources, there will be many battles but few were trivial xp grinding. There is a hostile alien race that you can attack at will for xp but they'll come at you as well.
You may find yourself occasionally watching the fast forwarded action if you get resource starved or are waiting for projects or fleets to complete their tasks, and setting those tasks can become somewhat repetative in mid-late game, but I find the music and art in the game charming enough to take the stress out of those situations, and you'll get slammed by action eventually.
The music is excellent, the battle music is invigorating, the map theme is chill and each alien race has their own theme music. The art and sprites are excellent as well, the ships show battle damage as they lose health, the aliens in away missions explode in gooey chunks, and the attacks and effects are very spectacular.
If any of the above sounds interesting you should try this game.

Very recently a new company, DECA Games, purchased the rights and has continued developing the game and being very active with the community, it looks like ROTMG can finally be a great game again.
If you've never played ROTMG, here are some pros:
- Very easy to pick up and start playing, great variety between classes and easy to learn, hard to master gameplay
- Very unique niche in the MMO world, as it is both a multiplayer co-op bullet hell and roguelike in one
- A lot of interesting and varied content, and likely more to come in the future from DECA
cons:
- Somewhat young community
- Plagued by multiboxers and hackers
- Hasn't had a new dungeon in like 3 years, endgame content can feel repetitive
If you can overlook these flaws you will find an amazing and unique game with a very strong community

NOTE: Many reviews for this game are negative solely because of the developers' choices, not on the game itself. I will agree that the devs have overall cheated many people of their money, especially early backers, but that has nothing to do with the quality of the game itself. I will talk about the game only in this review.
I've put up a kind of funny review of the base game Planetary Annihilation, but it wasn't too helpful. I will make a legit review here.
What is this game exactly? This game is an RTS that takes place across a solar system. Each solar system varies, most provided in-game are only 1 planet big, but can be many planets big as well. But what does that mean? Essentially, you can start on one planet and build up your economy and an army and all that. However, with the help of orbital units, which I'll get to later, you can travel to another planet and start to expand there. This is the most unique thing about this game, in my opinion.
So, how diverse is this RTS? Not as diverse unit-wise as Supreme Commander or other RTS's, but enough to compete. There are 5 unit types: Land, Bot, Sea, Air, and Orbital. Bots are just smaller, less powerful versions of Land units, but very easy to mass-produce. Orbital units are units that, as the game stated "rain death from above on units that rain death from above." Orbital units are not the best at fighting, but they are mainly used to gain access to other planets and other uses. The economy is essentially the same as the other well-known RTS's: Metal, to be gotten from specific metal spots on planets; and Energy, which can be generated wherever you like. The Titans are essentially the Experimentals from Supreme Commander 2, so not a whole lot to talk about there. All and all, the game is a solid RTS,  so yeah.
Demolishing planets? Yes, you saw right. There are certain "game-ending" things that you can do, such as destroying entire planets. For example, you can build giant thrusters on a moon and crash it into the planet that your enemy's on. These thrusters are a pain in the butt to make, but they're worth it. One of the screenshots looks like the Death Star that's shooting a giant laser. This is another means of planetary annihilation (hence the name). If the metal planet (Death Star) is present in your game, you can build 5 special structures at 5 special points to gain control of it. These special structures are even more of a pain in the butt to make, but once a player gets their hands on the metal planet, it's essentially game over. Or you can crash a moon into the metal planet and just not worry about it.
Oh yeah, there's also a System Designer where you can make your own systems to play in. If you like designing maps, you'll like it. If not, just don't use it, simple as that.
Is this game worth it? On a sale, yes. $40 is steep for this game. Unless you REALLY want this game, I would wait for a sale. This game is so fun, especially with some friends to play with. The people reviewing this game negative only because of the devs should really vent somewhere else, just not in a review.

The main issue:
Even with no mods this game will crash at completely unexpected times without any warning, just like Skyrim (another big Bethesda title). This issue is widespread and everyone will experience it eventually, albeit some users more than others. It has nothing to do with computer performance because even users with specs far exceeding the requirements still experience the random crashes. Since Bethesda is no longer willing to update the game except to push PAID MODS (no more bug fixes) in a MANDATORY update that adds Creation Club and happens to break existing player mods, the random crashes are permanently a part of the game. If you do purchase this game (I'd recommend waiting for a sale, don't pay full price to Bethesda), SAVE OFTEN. Some areas of the game may become permanently inaccessible to you because it crashes every time you enter it, requiring you to load a save before you entered the area or to accept that you can never visit that specific area again.
The storyline:
There are four dialogue options for every conversation, but the options are superfluous because the vast majority of the time they elicit word-for-word the exact same response from whichever NPC you are speaking to. Your choices have absolutely no impact on the storyline other than a handful of faction choices towards the end. As countless others have said, the main storyline is weak and disinteresting compared to previous Fallout titles.
The gameplay:
Unless you play on normal or easy the entire game consists of collecting ammo and then wasting all of it shooting a single enemy hundreds of times. Higher difficulties don't enhance the enemy's tactics, they just absorb more bullets necessitating either mind-numbingly repetitive hit-and-run, hide-and-repeat tactics or spamming constant (costly) automatic fire which THEN necessitates mind-numbingly repetitive ammo collecting. Combat is supposed to be a core mechanic in this series, but Fallout 4 does a terrible job at making it interesting.
As many others have said, if you want an enjoyable, rich storyline with great gameplay, play Fallout: New Vegas. If you just want newer graphics and settlement management at the cost of game stability and boring repetitive tasks, buy Fallout 4.

I really WANT to recommend this. But... I don't know. Once the sequel comes out it might be worth it.
Basically, it's 5 hours of walking around and talking to people with conversation trees that aren't clear what their outcomes will be. You will think you know the right response and NOPE, they'll get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you. But is it REALLY your fault? Maybe... or maybe it's the hit-and-miss voice acting, script, and dialog.
And the conversations wouldn't be so bad if everyone wasn't EXTREMELY similiar looking. And using NUMBERS AND NAMES to separate everyone? That's horrible! People have both a Callsign AND a name, and people use them interchangably (So you have to learn both!) and the ship has like 20-30 people so you don't even begin to recognize names until a few hours in. At that point, the game is 90% over. Moreover, the conversations move (even with subtitles on) WAY TOO FAST.
I ABSOLUTELY support the indie devs for reaching for the stars. But the actual gameplay is 5 hours of that "5 minute period" of most games where you wait for the actual action and fun to begin.
They have an entire "combat system" that... and I can't believe I'm even saying this... that you never actually use. I went through the entire game with ONE BATTLE. ONE. FREAKING. BATTLE. Why even have an inventory system? Why have me manage and decide what weapon to use?
The game is very hard to pin down. It makes it very difficult to naturally feel and understand WHAT the game is asking you to do. It's a game that you have to play to the end before you realize any of the boundaries and scope of the game. That's great if you want to make the world "seem" huge and beyond what you actually play in. Gemini Rue did that BEAUTIFULLY. But when done wrong, it leaves the player feeling very unsure and constantly "thinking" (more like guessing) about what he's doing.
This game is a GREAT EXPERIMENT from a new group. But it's also a deeply flawed experiment. So I both applaud them, and look forward to the sequel, but I can't really recommend the average person to play it.
If the game is cheap, it's WORTH risking a couple of bucks to support these guys. But if you're strapped for cash, and don't like flawed-but-original games, I wouldn't recommend this.

Full review:
Pros:
- New systems deepen the mechanics of all characters
- Cross-platform gaming and good netcode
- All DLC characters would be acquirable through gameplay
Cons:
- Sparse content, at least for now
- Intimidating to newcomers
The new Street Fighter is based on the same principles from the last three decades of franchise’s existence – two fighters dueling on a 2D side-scrolling backdrop using a combination of 6 strikes. But this is far from being a simple, shallow game.
The game ships with 16 characters to chose from, four of which are newcomers to the series, and Capcom plans to add more through DLCs (it’s possible to win them by playing the game). Although it sounds like there’s too few when compared to Ultra Street Fighter 4, we should remember that SF4 also had less than 20 fighters and that all the game changes and new characters were added through re-issues of the game at full price which fragmented the player base. The decision to make the game a basis to add new content on to over time is far better than the Capcom’s earlier practice with the series and we fully support it.
Variable System is a completely new addition with which every character gains an additional set of moves. Namely, the V-scale will fill up as you get hit or perform a chosen character’s specific move, and it has a different number of increments for each fighter. By filling up the scale, you’ll be able to activate the so-called V-trigger which enables your character to perform a specific move and temporarily strengthens his special attacks. Also, now you can block an opponent’s relentless assault, followed by a combination of buttons with which you can unbalance your opponent for a brief counter-attack window. This whole system is great and you’ll spend a lot of time discovering all of its applications and finding new move combos with familiar characters.
The current campaign is a sore excuse for a story-mode, because it isn’t a challenge like the former Arcade mode, nor does it last long – it takes about ten minutes to go through each of these stories. Although Street Fighter was never primarily a solo game, some players might be bothered by this “bare-bones” release from Capcom. But still, the game is mainly targeted as a multiplayer game for playing with friends or online, and for which there’s no lack of modes.

Note: If you're using a keyboard and mouse, you'll have a much better experience if you go into Options > User Request Options and turn
Camera move interpolation and turn
V-sync. This removes the "floaty" feeling the camera normally has.
For the price, GOCCO OF WAR is absolutely a worthwhile purchase. Fans of Monster Hunter-style games will recognize familiar mechanics such as crafting, questing, and multiplayer lobbies, but the combat has a neat twist with the inclusion of the "Air" resource. "Air" will deplete with attacks or dodges and fill back up after a brief period of doing neither. It's pretty cool and never feels like it gets in your way, even when you run out of it. The game also has "badges" which seem to take the place of equipment buffs, allowing you to make a look without worrying about stats.

Cons:

GOCCO OF WAR is a pretty 'grindy' third-person shooter. Normally, something being described as 'grindy' wouldn't sound all that great, but here it works pretty well. In a similar fashion to a certain Japanese game where you hunt monsters, much of your time on GOCCO will be spent playing then replaying the numerous quests to get that ONE LAST MATERIAL or THOSE FEW MORE COINS you need to build/buy an outfit part, weapon or other material. There's enough action to keep it from getting stale though, even when you're replaying Quest #20 for the fifteenth time to try and find that frickin' Dragon Blood.
Quests can be played either by yourself on Offline mode, which typically grants you an AI teammate to follow and help you out, or Online with up to 4 players. Thankfully, material drops are 'instanced' for each player, so you don't have to worry about that guy with the max level weapon charging through everything and taking all the treasure.
An assortment of clothes and costumes are available to customise your character with. Military uniforms, t-shirts and shorts, alien outfits, pretty much anything. If you decide that you don't like the look of your character or just want a new hairstyle, you can also edit everything about your appearance at any time when in a lobby except for gender, but with 16 character slots that really shouldn't be an issue at all.
The weapons are fun to use, looking as bright as the rest of the game and having secondary uses such as charged shots or alternate attack functions. Each of the weapons can be upgraded to deal more damage, or evolved into a new form to add status effects (fire, lightning, poison, etc.) or just beef up the damage even more.
Overall, GOCCO OF WAR is a nice way to kill some time after enduring some of the other offerings Steam has available. Now if you'll excuse me, I'm trying to save up a few hundred thousand more for that shiny new gun...

This game does have some good things going for it but they're not enough to make the game fun enough to play.  The art is nice and retro feeling and the space combat feels like it's strategic but it's really more like a puzzle game.
You use the powers/abilities which your opponent is vulnerable to, and make up teams based on that. All the while juggling base expansion and research.
Some of the events are kinda neat, but a bit hard to tell what decisions are safe to take at times, results seem to be randomised. The character tech trees are neat but If you lose a character/ship early on it's a bit of a speed bump, and constantly having your base under attack seems arbitrary and not fitting for the story.
Far far too many notifications for events early on. Not enough down time to consider strategy or to really make my own way in space. I just wanted some breathing room to make decisions now and again but the game kept sending pathetic fleets to bombard the base, for reasons that amounted to "we feel like killing you humans now".
Nothing the player does seems to have an affect on what the AI does, I don't feel like the universe responds to my presence, i'm forced to respond to it.
Speaking of the story I didn't feel attached to the characters or my base. Decisions are made on a practical basis and I haven't really felt like I was really feeling how my characters were responding to events. Everything seems very "go to X pick up Y and return to recieve reward".
That said it is satisfying beating strong enemies with your ships and struggling through some encounters but the enemy ships seem to have a cookie cutter design to them so they're rather easy to predict and as a result your own strategy seems to stagnate.
Player ships seem to be reliant on the character abilities (random upon recruitment from a pool of abilities which they can upgrade and acquire over time) which I dislike.
Long story short there's just a lot of little things about the game design that don't seem to come together and the game isn't really excelling in any particular area to make up for that.
You might have some fun if you stick with it but I would recommend a few other games before trying this one if you're looking for games in this genre of space/base colony management and combat.

Just bought this game today and have to say that it's been one of the most effective games I've ever played at creating a total immersion factor.   Several games in this genre attempt it, but very few are successful, usually because they get one or two parts of the game right and the rest fall into mediocrity.  In this case, I think the game does a fantastic job creating just the right mix of ship/personnel/station progression with an exceptionally balanced combat system.  Think x-com with the majority of the battles being in space, combined with much more fluid (and interesting) mechanisms for managing everything else.  While it's a really nice touch to include the on-planet battles with your crew and the aliens that inhabit whatever planet you're on (it certainly does add to the immersion) the majority of your time will be spent battling other ships and managing your space station.  Add in a compelling story with plenty of humor, and you end up with a very enjoyable experience overall.
I'm not sure what the game was like before the lightspeed edition, but it's sure a blast to play now.  Thanks to the devs for making this game.  Back to space!

I was close to recommending this game, but then I realized I can only recommend it, when the price is as low as it is currently (11,09€ at 70% off). Since this review will stand longer than the sale I should give an honest opinion.
I don't know anything about the dev issues or the former game, I was also not a kickstarter participant. My friends and I found this game, thought it looked interesting and it was on sale, so we got it (thanks Jason!).
So this is an unbiased opinion, not from the view of someone slighted by the Uber devs.
For a lower price, this game is fun. Moving the units about, building stuff and the planet hopping is quite entertaining and the RTS elements themselves are semi-solid.
The game would not be worth the original price though.
Pros:
- Multiplayer RTS game with AI, what else can you want. It should be standard these days, but with indie developers, you often find it isn't.
- Quite a lot of different units, buildings and things to do.
- The planet hopping is done interestingly and well.
- Instead of micro management, this game is more set to macro combat, a concept I quite like.
- The game utilizes a window-in-window kind of news system, where you can easily and quickly see trouble, problems and points of interest.
But now the sad parts, some of them game breaking when you forget them.
Cons:
- Some units are downright useless, even if you spend a majority of your resources on them. A good example are the highest orbital ships you can build. With just the tiniest bit of micro management, a few smaller ships or even a few ground units can, for some stupid reason, kill your entire fleet. Yes, the ships can be helpful in a big war, however they can easily be caught unaware since they're so slow.
- In conjunction with the previous con, the army movements are... lacking. A simple command like moving as slow as the slower member of your army is not easily found, the pathing is... weird... (sometimes a ship can't fly over debris??).
- The AI difficulty curve is STEEP. A "Normal" AI won't even fight back much, you can annihilate them with pretty much a single unit (a titan or a commander building the Annihilazor on a metal planet, all alone). While one difficulty higher, they'll shower you with atom bombs and when you finally have some defenses up, bombard you with everything else, never relenting, always knowing where your buildings are.
- Too many insta-kill buildings/things. While you CAN planet hop and escape insta-kill scenarios, humans are, by and large, settlers. The home planet is usually the place where you build the most and keep the most. Insanely stupid insta-kill things can happen to you, like building the right titan, dropping a moon on you or building on a metal planet and shoop-da-whooping you out of the sky.
To show you just how frustrating that can be let me tell you how me and my friend spent a few hours this morning.
First game, Normal Difficulty, wrecked AI with stupid stuff like Annihilazor, dropping Titans or simply showering them in 200 ships for giggles.
Second game, Hard Difficulty. Before we even had any kind of orbital defense, the AI settled on our planet and began pelting us with 2-3 atom bombs a minute. After losing half our buildings we finally had some anti-atom missiles done. slowly defending our♥♥♥♥♥♥while being thrown in a pool of "ATOM BOMB LAUNCHED" notifications. Those notifications sadly went over the notifications that someone had build catalysts on the metal planet, we heard the sound of a laser revving up, leaned back and watched our planet explode.
Third game, Hard difficulty, this time we're prepared, orbital defense ALL UP ON THIS PLANET, ♥♥♥♥ yeah, slowly gather resources and plan our revenge....... when a planet hits us.
Nope, wasn't the AI. Nope, wasn't something random. The map is just built so that THE TWO PLANETS HAVE THE SAME ORBIT AROUND THE SUN. HOW DID THEY EVEN FORM. THOSE PLANETS SHOULDA BEEN DEAD A LONG TIME AGO.
While this sounds funny.. inside the game it was just frustrating watching everything we worked for randomly explode...
So yes, this game CAN be entertaining for a couple of hours. But not for the full price. Wait for at least 70% off before buying it.

This game was brilliant. Much better than other titles that Square Enix has made that are not Final Fantasy such as Just Cause which has serious audio syncing problems.
Combat system closely related to that of Batman Arkham Asylum and Arkam City. graphics are quite impressive.
But besides the great fighting mechanics, the endless amount of things that you can do in Hong Kong, the customisation with clothes and the many many cars there are to purchase and show off. What is most impressive about this has to definitely be the storyline. Unlike typical games of this genre such as Grand Theft Auto and Saints Row, the main protagnanist of the game,  Wei Shen, is not just a character that comes off as just the average, out to get money and destroy stuff for the sake of it.
Wei Shen is the heart of the game. He is a well respected polie offica with the San Fransico police department that heads back to his home city, Hong Kong, to try and assist the local PD with taking down the Traids in the citty. It is immediatly obvious that your character has history with a fair amount of the people in the Traids, seeing as they use one of your oldest friends, Jackie to get Wei into the Triads to begin his undercover operation. Though as Shen gets pulled further in to the seedy underground workings of Hong Kong. It becomes more apparent that his motives of ether helping the police take down the Traids, or working with the Triads become extremely blurred.
In conclusion, as I have seen with other reviews of this game, we are all confused as to why people are not paying enough attention to this brilliant title. Yes there are a few bugs in the game, but what game doesn't. Even if you do not like the look of the game, I absolutely recommend this game just for it;s in depth and "keep you on the edge of your seat" storyline.

A very interesting game that features both offline single player and online cooperative play with friends or random strangers. I can vouch that the multiplayer is great... if you can find people to play with (I for one plan to buy gift copies for friends).
The game features cute chibi like characters, and various monsters to fight in various missions. From symple "Defeat the boss", "Rescue the NPCs" or "Defend this object", each mission alone doesn't give an entirely unique gameplay element, but those are standard in your ordinary RPG genre.
After playing the game for about 4 hours, I noticed the missions are not exactly randomly generated. Each mission re-uses the same landscape with different obstacles placed around, to try to give the game a fresh feel between different missions. For some people, this may detract them from such a game, but this simple setup should not discourage you from trying the game.
Weapons are standard. You can upgrade the weapons in a straightforward path, and they only change when using specific items to upgrade them with.
There are more clothing options than initially shown to you in the character creator. Other clothes are obtained by either buying them at the shop, or from synthesizing various items you obtain from completing quests.
As far as I am aware, the main items of the game that affect your stats are weapons, and badges. You obtain badges from either the shop, or from completing missions. The harder completed mission, the more likely you get a higher ranked badge.

Sanctum 2 is a firstperson shooter mixed in with tower defense mechanics. It sounds like its gonna be messy, but the way its excuted is very smooth and makes sense. You begin by choosin your charater, a loadout, the towers you wanna build that round, and a few other options to enhance the game and bring diversity to the match. Then, you start the mach with resources to build your towers, lay down walls to divert the enemies route, and time to figure out what to do. the match begins, and  you just go to town with your loadout. The weapons are pretty diverse, and i enjoyed how there's a primary and secondary shot to all of them. Another interesting thing they did to kind of keep the action pumping, is when you need to reload, you can just switch instantly to you secondary weapon, burn all your ammo, and switch back with another full Mag in you primary weapon, making it very easy to just continually lay down the hate on your enemies.
Speaking of enemies, ive seen about 4 or 5 differnt kinds, and they all bring a little challenge to the map. And, if having standard enemies isn't enough, you can gain more experience by choosing to enhance your enemies' strength, durability, speed, etc. This is a nice touch that brings a little bit opf replay value and challenge when you might feel like testing your trigger finger.
All in all, im having fun playing this well-made hybrid. The towers are upgradeable, and diverse and functionable, the maps are just as ranged in their layout, and the FPS portion of the game have tight controls and mechanics. My only complaint would have to be the weak Story.....honestly thers not really a story at all, just comic drawn cutscenes to go from map to map. And the character models look whack noit gonna lie. But, when you're actually playing a stage, the characters seem to be more detailed and look better than when in the transition screens.
If you are not gonna play this game with ny buddies, than you're losing out on a great experience, lack of a solid story for campaign mode is made up almost singlehandidly by the amount of fun you have WITH FRIENDS! So if you get this game, i encourage you to just hop into a match, and have fun! People are friendly and want to play with others here on Steam!

I thought it took me 14 hours or so to finish Halcyon 6, then I checked on Steam and it actually took me almost twice as much--which is awesome, because that means it lasts for quite a good while
time flows fast while you're playing it, which in turn means it's fun.
Your base is an ancient civilization's spaceship (no spoilers here, the game tells you this right away) and it works very much like the latest X-COMs'. You build reactors, hangars, etc. in its rooms and assign people to work in [some/most of] them. You gotta manage your resources and building space carefully or you'll get screwed,
Final Fantasy style. You lead a fleet of up to 3 ships into battle (or 3 dudes, on the much rarer occassions when you fight on the ground) against up to 3 opponents. Each of your pilots have their own skills that can be used in space/ground battle, and each ship category has their own as well. The battle takes place in turns,
,
,
and
are all present, and the latter (debuffs/status effects) are your main weapon against your enemies. Some skills cause debuffs, and others
them, inflicting extra damage.
There are 3 main character classes: Tactician, Scientist and Engineer. There's a specific ship for each class, and each one of these is subdivided into two sub-classes: Strategist/Can't-remember-what, Biologist/Physicist and Inventor/Mechanic, each with their own skill tree. Everything you can wrok on/research inside your base will require one or more of the 3 main classes' attributes, meaning you must have all 3 of them (unless you wanna lose the game.)
Your base stands at the center of everything, surrounded by star systems on which you can install extractors to gather resources (there are 4 of them: crew, fuel, materials and dark matter, and they can also be produced by working in your base.) There's also some diplomacy, quests offered by your neighbors, attacks on your base and random events. So... there's some lite-4X to Halcyon 6 as well.
I got through the game on my first attempt (well, "first" after the usual "learn-the-game/screw-up initial-play) on Vice-Admiral difficulty (that's the middle difficulty, although tagged as "Very Hard" in the game) with Ironman Mode on. Halcyon-6 is not hard, but I lost some ships and crew a few times, and once or twice felt there was a real chance I might get defeated but... no, it was ok. Anyway, it's not so easy either, so I'd say it's well balanced.
I think that covers most of the game. So... is Halcyon 6 good? Yeah, I had a blast playing it. If you think you'll like it, buy it--you won't be disappointed.

The game itself is divided into three main parts: space/fleet/resource management (similar to Master of Orion), space battles (also similar to MOO) and land battles. I backed this on Kickstarter, and I'm glad to say it turned out to be a fun little game! It's got nice pixel art and some fairly dry and humourous writing, and the music does the job considering the setting and all.
Most of the game is built around a basic combat system where up to three ships (crewed by officers) on each side line up across from one another and shoot abilities at each other. Some abilities apply debuffs and others consume those debuffs to boost their own power, so a big part of tactical thinking involves trying to chain combos of debuffs on your targets, and spreading damage-over-time effects optimally across the enemies. It's a pretty good system, not especially deep but enough to allow for some variation over the course of the game.
Outside of combat, there's a very simple strategic layer where you gather four core resources from various nodes around your territory, and occasionally interact with other starfaring factions through quests or the occasional raid on your facilities. Much like combat, it's a simple and fairly shallow system that manages to stay interesting just long enough for you to finish the game. I was even able to ignore resource management about halfway through the game, after which I focused mainly on quests and levelling my officers before wrapping up. There are essentially three acts to the game that frame some major quests and a few gameplay elements, but the story is simple and mostly only serves to string everything together.
My main problem with the game is that it felt quite linear, which wasn't quite what I was expecting when I first backed it. As soon as you unlock a new tier of ships, the last ones become completely obsolete. Quests are fairly simple overall and once you do a few easy quests for each faction, they love you forever. My biggest challenge was at one point I only had one trio of officers of high enough level to perform any of the research or fly any of the top-tier ships, so I ended up having to grind a second trio up to spec by throwing them at more dangerous foes. Nothing unexpected ever really happened.
Still, it was fun enough while it lasted, and it didn't quite overstay its welcome. Give it a spin if you like the style, and get ready to chain some spaceship combos.

A long time ago, I was sitting in a press room chatting with the guitarist from a band called I Mother Earth and a dude walked up to the singer who was standing a couple people over and asked if IME was trying to sound like Jane's Addiction. That was met with mild disappointment from the singer, who obviously had heard it before despite not really sounding like Jane's Addiction at all. However, I Mother Earth's sound was such a unique fusion of funk, rock, and metal that people didn't know what to make of it and so drew comparisons from bands that were at least marginally similar.
Such is the way of Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander (LIGHTSPEED EDITION). It is very uniquely its own game but seems to pull from obvious influences such as FTL, XCOM, various old school JRPG's, Mass Effect, and so on. The mesh of influences helped Massive Damage, Inc create what ended up being an interesting and concise adventure.
The story in Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander (LIGHTSPEED EDITION) is definitely a hodgepodge of some sci-fi elite: Battlestar Galactica, Star Trek, Stargate, Hitchhiker's Guide to the Universe, Mass Effect; taking elements from each as influences for this one. Essentially, humanity has expanded outward and that resulted in conflicts with other races. A new threat emerges (the Chruul) and destroys the bulk of humanity's remaining fleet leaving only those people left on an ancient precursor race derelict space base that they were researching at the time. From there, you (the people in the space base) must build a couple ships and start looking for any other survivors while also trying to figure out what happened and where the new alien species appeared from. The was a nice twist at the end that was fun.
The writing is however more in the vein of what you would expect from Monty Python if they teamed up with Douglas Adams (RIP) to write Hitchhiker's Guide to the Universe crossed with the Holy Grail on the Starship Enterprise. Tongue in cheek dry humor rather than serious and brooding story telling. The various races were developed quite well and bore similarities to the Ferengi (Yabblings), the Borg (The Coolective), Klingons (Xlar-Yanthu), and so on, only with the obligatory humorous twist. Plus there are pirates. Lots of pirates.
All in all, I thought the writing was pretty good and the lore of this part of the universe was surprisingly dense. There is actually quite a bit of dialogue and that was always pretty entertaining.
8 out of 10
The gameplay in Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander (LIGHTSPEED EDITION) is split between 3 major activities and some sub activities as well.
The most important aspect of this game is base building. You are humanity's last known survivors on a mostly unexplored alien space base. As such, you have to explore the base and then build up the base to suit your needs. This is set up very much like XCOM in application. You have a variety of structures that supply power, training, supplies, build ships, and so on. Most of these rooms have tasks that are available which upgrade your facility, your ships, your soldiers, etc....However, each of these tasks must be accomplished by an officer. All of your officers are also pilots, and managing who is on missions versus who stays behind to accomplish these tasks becomes a bit of a mini game.
There is also a research section which simply requires supplies to fund. These allow you to build new structures, new ships, upgrade your abilities, and so on. This is attached to base building as a sub activity. By the end of the game, you will have fully explored and upgraded everything on your space station as well as have researched all possible research trees.
You also have to keep your crew's morale up. This can be accomplished via battle victories, saving colonies, completing certain tasks, and via on board therapy and team building sessions. A happy crew is a constructive crew.
Did I mention that your base will come under attack periodically and has health points that must be monitored and repaired as needed so everybody doesn't die?
Combat is handled very much in straight forward, JRPG style turn based style. Your (up to) three ships or soldiers line up to face the enemies (up to) three, ummm....enemies. All of your officers level up and can choose abilities based on their class. Their class and level also impacts which types of ships they can pilot and which level of ship as well. There are six classes and three prestige classes all told. There are likewise six types of ships available for each tech tier (of which there are five). Higher tier ships require higher levels.
Everything your officers have learned are represented with abilities. You can take only a certain amount of items (you will be able to find and use many useful ship upgrades such as healing drones and better hull armor, etc....) and powers with you into battle though. You can set up three configurations however to take advantage of different combos. The power selection in both ground and space combat is pretty diverse. They are also quite entertaining to watch. If you dont have enough officers available for ground combat, "Green Shirts" will fill in. These are basically like Star Trek's security people that die in every episode of the original series. They start out under powered but can be trained to become super soldiers.
With space combat however, you dont get the support of the Green Shirts. Whatever ships you have with you is what you have going into battle. Battles can get quite strategic in nature as you figure out which combination of powers from your ships will win the day. When to heal and buff, when to attack, etc....This is the bulk of combat in Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander (LIGHTSPEED EDITION) realistically. Probably upward of 95% of the battles in the game are space battles.
There is a map overlay which reminded me a little of Mass Effect 3's map. As more of the galaxy is revealed and you establish more colonies, your map grows. This is where you will do most of your resource gathering (you get resources from battle and completing quests as well) as well as exploration and of course initiating battle. It's very user friendly and easy to grasp.
8 out of 10
The graphics in Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander (LIGHTSPEED EDITION) are more old school in nature and look great. Low texture, PS One era type graphics, but obviously done much better. I thought in particular the battles and abilities were super cool to look at. The ship designs were neat. The rest were fun (character animations, map design, etc....).
7 out of 10
The audio in Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander (LIGHTSPEED EDITION) was for me a bit of a mixed bag. The soundtrack very definitely conveys that 1950's style sci-fi vibe and sounds, from the music to the actual tracks used for battle, the good B movie sci-fi feeling is there. However, they do get quite repetitive after 20 or so hours. I wish more had been done with this. That said, it was still well done....just less variety than would have been ideal.
7 out of 10
Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander (LIGHTSPEED EDITION) is a game that you can easily sink 20 or so hours into. There are multiple difficulties available though for new playthroughs and the actual choices you make in the game interacting with aliens can also change things up in new playthroughs. You can be their enemy, their ally, and can pick and choose making for galactic chaos or stability depending on how you handle things. I'm thinking you could as such get many playthroughs  out of Halcyon 6 if you were so inclined. Ultimately, I had a really good time with it. As much as its varied influences shine through, it is still it's own game through and through.

Dawn of Discovery Gold (The original including the Venice add-on) is the American version of Anno 1440 AD Gold Edition which was released in Europe.  The game is identical and I could find no changes apart from the game title.
Graphics are well implemented and fully customizable to suit player's hardware and operating system environments.  Sound is atmospheric, NPC's are well vocalized and have convincing characterization, music is of good ambience and is non-intrusive.
There are four difficulty settings and the game supports both single player and multi-player.  There are a number of campaign missions with pre-defined victory conditions, and a sandbox mode for infinite play.
Starting conditions may vary significantly depending on difficullty settings and gameplay mode.
Essentially the player is tasked with exploring islands, establishing a colony, expanding the settlement and ensuring that resources are acquired to meet the needs and demands of the colony.
The player can place fishing huts, lumber yards, mines, quarries and a variety of farms and manufacturing plants to generate resources.  Various facilities such as places of worship, fire departments and taverns will increase the safety and status of the colony.  As the game progresses additional storage and manufacturing and mining facilities become available.
The player can adjust tax rates and either approve or deny colonists access to building materials.
There are NPC's (Non-Player Characters) that will offer quests from time to time, these will usually be either fetch and deliver, find and deliver (Zoom in on the town and find a person or persons), explore an island, escort a ship, or sink a ship.  These missions usually have a time limit and need to be completed before the time expires.
The islands are of two main types (Northern/Occidental or Southern/Orient).  The resources that can be cultivated will differ depending on the type.
Players can trade to purchase goods, or opt to produce and sell goods.  Trade routes can be automated or the player can manually operate a trading vessel.  Trading can be set at each player harbour.
Players may during mid to late game decide to acquire additional expansion potential by evicting one or more competitors by force and taking over their islands.
Pirates will occassionaly be either a help or a hinderance depending on difficulty settings and diplomatic status.
Dawn of Discovery has a lot of depth and is a great time-waster.  The game has a sense of progression and accomplishment and will unlock features and rewards.
Dawn of Discovery is a highly addictive and fun to play game that comes highly recommended.

Okay, I don't normally review games, but after seeing these reviews I felt the need to.
While creation club is not the greatest, it in no way hurts your gameplay. The game has not suddenly become worse. I appreciate the need to tell Bethesda that this isn't okay. But saying the game is bad because of creation club is just plain dishonest.
The game itself is good, very good, in fact. It isn't the best Bethesda has done, but I feel that a lot of the problems with the game revolve around the voiced protagonist, which necesitates a lesser degree of choice on the part of the player. This wouldn't have necessarily been bad for some other games, but it definitely doesn't work well in a Bethesda style game.
The content which is present is all very good, and I would recommend all of the dlc. This was even the general opinion of people on this site up until this whole Creation Club fiasco. I don't feel the need to talk more about this content; you can find all of that in older reviews.
Now for Creation Club, the reason for me writing this review: don't let this turn you off of the game. It really isn't as big of a deal as people are making of it. Most people look at it and see the old paid mods thing, which was a much worse system. Creation Club itself isn't the problem; however there are problems with it. Currently, things are VERY overpriced.  The content does not, however, hurt one's gameplay experience in any way. If you don't like the content, if you don't think the prices are reasonable, don't buy it. It doesn't affect the game. I know people think that it will ruin mods in the future, but I don't think that will necesarily be the case. Bethesda needs to see these reviews, and adjust the Creation Club accordingly. If they either contract out larger content, or lower their prices, Creation Club could actually be good for the community. If people are motivated to make large mods with lots of content because they can sell it to bethesda for a good amount of money, I think that's great. The system itself isn't the problem.
TLDR Creation Club as it currently stands isn't a good thing, but it doesn't make the game bad. Don't avoid buying the game because of it.

Early Access Reviews are very hard to make when you don't know what the final product will be. It's a good thing that Starbound is one of those titles that at this point, are shooting straight upwards to 1.0 release. I can probably make my say as to where it's at now (as with the combat update), and what it'll become on release (which at the time, still needs a revamped quest system and the like).
So it's definitely getting better now that we really are getting all these changes that improve the play, and things that hampered it in the beginning are starting to vanish. However, enough elements on the screen at once, Starbound will feel slow, and this may be one damning reason why it really needs some optimization before coming out. Because of the way Starbound uses assets, nothing is pre-processed, and this can really deteriorate how the game operates.
On the bright side, it makes Starbound easier to mod, to the point you could use a free program that does alpha channel PNGs
, and notepad. Also with JSON formatting for dead simple programming of objects, you can even take old mods and update the darn things yourself.
I'd like to see some Workshop for Starbound as well. I mean it's just one folder, right? Get the people going with the mod scene, and if it's not easily implemented, that's fine, but community content will keep it thriving, and that's definitely one thing I want to see now, and further on in development.
But besides all that, where's the meat? Exploration, mostly? You'll never find that perfect planet, because I still can't find time to build myself a nice hut in the middle of the goddamn nowhere, all because my ship may be a little... TOO useful? I don't know. You do run out of space fast in that tin can, but upgrades make it so you don't. But dungeons are rad, bosses are pretty cool, and if you break the game, it'll tip it's hat and close itself FOR you, so what's not to love?
TL;DR - I recommend this game on the principle of "IT GETS BETTER!" - and it does. It has. It can. It will. Cheers.
[NOV 2017 UPDATE]
So. Golly. The game is done, I feel kind of accomplished. Does everything I say hold up? I'm not very sure. I actually kind of hate everything I said because I was kind of dumb back then. Starbound definitely got the "it gets better" that I was talking about, but very incrementally. After 1.0 all bets were off. Starbound was a complete experience for the time. And it was good. Despite some of its major flaws, it's still great to waste time with. You go at your own pace. I guess that matters to me a lot to be perfectly honest.
So yeah. Play Starbound. It might fit you. I can't say. You'd have to give it a shot.

This game tries to scratch the itch dungeon keeper and dwarf fortress have long since stopped scratching for me. (hundreds of game hours can only do so much.)
Unfortunately, where those other games are like a Velcro nose scratcher inside a spaceman's helmet, this is more of a damp sponge. You can try as hard as you want, it won't scratch.
I only managed to stick with this game due to the mild amusement of designing a very simple dwarf base, but that gets old FAST; it was pure stubbornness after the first 3 levels. You don't have the challenge and satisfaction of making something like in dungeon keeper or dwarf fortress, and it's not much fun aesthetically because the near non-existent challenge the game does provide wrecks your design.
The major problem with the game is how unfinished the final product is. The potential is definitely there, but it was rushed into final product for obvious financial reasons. Hence the cash grab DLC rushed quickly out.
The biggest clue to this being an unfinished mess is the falling animation. When your dwarves tunnel into a large cavern, or are falling for some reason, they panic, fall one Z level, stop in mid air, Panic again, Fall another Z level; rinse, repeat till the bottom. Come on guys, didn't have time to fully program that one?
The second clue is the half-hearted attempt at making your dwarves happy. You can decorate your entire dungeon with minerals you find, but this is purely aesthetic. Rough wooden walls and floors do the job just as well as Dragonite ore, the rarest mineral in the game. Come on devs, was the balancing too hard? Dwarf fortress had that coded!
If we are talking balancing, the teleporting mechanic breaks the game so hard it physically hurt me sometimes with boredom. You can teleport your dwarves anywhere on the map you have visited, as many times as you'd like, and as fast as you'd like. Sure they TRIED to nerf it by only letting you do one dwarf at a time, and by having special fields you need to send your dwarves to destroy, but you can work around them easily, usually by tricking the stupid AI.
If I send a dwarf tunneling into a unknown cavern, I should fear for his safety, or for the safety of my base, not watch bored with my hand on the teleport button to whisk him away from the slow moving enemies. (The combat AI is so bad they even take a second to spin and position in a North-south or West-East pattern before hitting each other.)
I never had any fear for my main base while playing the game. You can stop intrusion by deleting a ladder. Enemies try to circumvent this by randomly teleporting around, but half the time they stood there stupidly. Depressingly, I never had the chance to use all the nifty traps they game had available for me. By the time you can afford the traps you already have the appropriately levels fighters, making them useless.
I was REALLY angry at the half-coded ending to the game. Anti-climatic, with rushed animations; even the writing was half-hearted. Did they even expect anyone to get through the entire game?
There are more problems, Terrible AI, bad animations, ETC; but this game has taken enough of my time already.
I know some of you out there are desperate for easy to play games that scratch that itch I mentioned above, but don't come here. You will leave wanting, and with less money in your wallet.

Finally came around to change my review from my native language German to English :)
Perhaps some people might hate me for my opinion, but I do recommend this game, even though not at it's full price. I love "A Game of Dwarves" a lot and I continue to play it from time to time (at about 200 hours playtime for now). I really like the general gameplay, the isometric view, the animations and also the weird kind of humour.
Problem is that the game is still a bit buggy and shows unused potential, but the developer's company Zeal doesn't exist anymore... Players have condemned Zeal for selling over-priced DLCs before even fixing the main game, which is absolutely understandable in my opinion. But was it the small Swedish indie-company Zeal who came up with that idea or their international distributor Paradox Interactive?
Some reviewers recommend to teach "them" a lesson by not buying the game until the bugs have been fixed. However that would be completely fruitless since Zeal has already dissolved a long time ago, only a short while after the release of "A Game of Dwarves". On their Twitter-page
the last entry was about the early access (!) release of the game in October 2013...
Paradox Interactive on the other hand has not given a d*mn about low sales and boycotts up until now, as they still continue to charge extra-money for the DLCs on Steam. More smaller DLCs can only be ordered from within the game though, and perhaps that cannot be changed without developers? Well, it's not like you are going to need the DLCs anyway!
* the "Star-Dwarves"-expansion pack can only be played in "free-style" mode, not during the story-mode-campaign. The Star Wars-like fighters might be a little bit stronger than the "ordinary" dwarven fighters, but with not much visible difference
* the "Ale"-pack is absolutely not necessary to keep your dwarves happy. Instead it's totally easy to get them all to 100% happiness forever by regularly crafting additional cheap storage-cupboards and/or decorative wall-tiles and floor-tiles made by wood (renewable) and/or stone
* the "Pets"-pack is mostly decorative. Even though some pets will also help with fighting, they are very weak in the beginning and it takes a lot of patience until they have levelled up
* the rest of the DLCs are just completely "cosmetical" additional items
Perhaps I am just lucky but I have stumbled over only very few bugs during 200 hours:
* ranged attackers sometimes have troubles with positioning themselves, and sometimes they can miraculously fire through walls or corners :D
* there have been a number of crashes during the ending-sequence in the last "chapter" of the campaign - seems like this has been the last part of the code before Zeal gave up
* very rarely my dwarves have somehow managed to get (fall) into small closed or secluded spaces so I had to teleport them out of there manually before they could starve to death
* sometimes dwarven fighters wouldn't attack enemies by themselves if too far away; but it always helps to station them close to critical areas beforehand (just like in "Craft the world")
* generally it will help to save and relog every few hours (will prevent most fighting-AI-bugs), as well as to make copies of your savegames once in a while just to be on the safe side
* in my (PC-)version of the game I've never spotted any dwarves falling from ladders or getting inactive while fighting. They seemed to have troubles with staircases though as far as I remember, so I have long refrained from building those. They are too pricy anyways :p
* very rarely the camera suddenly "fell" below the current level and got stuck - but that could always be fixed with a relog
* I personally like the random and sometimes mean level-designs with a few tough enemies placed closer to the starting-area, as this poses a bit of a surprising challenge sometimes. Not everybody is going to like that though I think
* the ending wasn't really bad, but it underlined the feeling that Zeal once had more in mind previously, but just couldn't make it into a reality before dissolving
* the German translation also is quite good; even much better than in many other games I've played, with very few mistakes or bugs :)
All in all the few bugs I have experienced have not been able to kill the major fun I had and still have while playing "A Game of Dwarves" :)

I have multiple problems with this game. The framerate is low (locked at 30fps, and I know I can get 60+ on ANY other game), the controls are very clunky on both keyboard and controller, and the game is unnecessarily difficult due to a combo of bad controls and steep difficulty curve. These all contribute to a poor experience.
Customization options were welcome, but a convoluted crafting system makes obtaining cosmetics a chore. Combining two items could give you one of the same items you used to craft, with no added perk. There were only 3-4 people online for both of my 20-30 minute sessions, so not many to show off the few cosmetics I had.
The English translation is choppy, and the story baffles me. It seems to be a lighthearted kids' game, but in the first level, Satan makes an appearance AND themes such as death, evil in its purest form, and the apocalypse are brought up. IN THE FIRST LEVEL! But I don't think this game is meant to be played for the story, anyway. It is definitely gameplay-centric. So no big deal. But overall, the game is simply not worth its current price.
EDIT: Whoa, the dev responded to my review minutes after me posting. And with that, I realized my original review was a bit too harsh, so I edited it accordingly. It was kinda unfair to judge a game immediately upon its release. I mean, even big companies like Bethesda launch patches directly following release. I figured this was a lazy port of a Japanese game, but now my gut tells me I'm wrong. The developer cares about their game, stating a desire to continually improve the game. And, maybe when the game is a bit more polished, I'll come back, as the concept is promising. Until then.

This game is AMAZING.
It presents itself as a sort of combination of X-Com and FTL, and it lives up to that admirably. The combat is formatted like a JRPG. Much like Darkest Dungeon, Halcyon 6 has a mechanic where team members reduced to 0 hp do not die immediately, but instead have a chance to die with every subsequent damage they take. The combat system is very focused on status effects, forcing the player to think at least a couple of moves ahead instead of just having every ship use its best skill every turn. The music is excellent. The pixels are typical low-resolution indie fare, but the art direction is very charming.
The death animations for greenshirts (yes, the game has faceless, nameless away team members as a mechanic, and they do die very often, it's great) are absolutely great, this is early 2000s newgrounds cartoon gore, and it's every bit as funny now as it was then.
There's like eight difficulty levels, which for me isn't great, because I'd rather a game just present itself to me as it's intended to be played and let me bash my head against it until I can git gud, but if you like a fine degree of control over how hard the game is, this game certainly has that. I'm pretty sure the intended difficulty is higher than "commander," the only difficulty i've played so far, because I can see in the way the game is set up a lot of opportunity for resources to be stretched thin and the player always having to accept losing some things and trying to figure out what losses are most acceptable, but the game hasn't put me to that point yet.
There's a lot to take in at first in terms of managing resources and such, but the tutorial does a fine job of teaching you those basics, and it feels pretty natural quickly.
Loving this game, I put it on my favorites list after like an hour and a half.

I highly recommend this game to anyone that likes 3rd person shooters combined with anime style chibi characters.  As for cost vs. gameplay time, you will definitely get your moneys and more.
The gameplay is basic, there arent many things you have to memorize which i think is a great thing and wgich keeps the game simple.  The game has an "mmo feel" to it, but is not one.  You are placed into a hub where you can accept quests, craft, and purchase items.  There is no story, you go to an NPC, grab a quest, do said quest, and earn rewards.  And that is it, you can also repeat quests on same or higher difficulties to earn gold.
Combat gameplay is fun, not the greatest, but is solid.  Although it does feel a bit sluggish, possibly due to the 30fps lock(?), but nonetheless still playable.  Controller is recommended to play this game.  Im a mouse and keyboard person, but the game feels better for controller.
***The keyboard and mouse controls have been updated.  It feels much more smoother now and there is no drag when aiming with the mouse.  I now suggest using the keyboard and mouse for playing instead of controller :) ***
Now for the good stuff, where I feel the game shines is its character customization.  The crafting system is excellent.  With the materials you have gathered you can discover and make new outfits, head, body, and legs.  Also, you can upgrade your weapons and make them more powerful.  Lastly you can earn things called badges which give you stats, as far as i can tell the stats are random so there is much fun in trying to find the perfect one.
Downside which may be a turnoff for some is the "air" mechanic.  Shooting/slashing and doging use up air, so think of it as ammo and stamina combined.  As you drain your air meter you either have to let it recharge by not shooting or dodging for a few seconds or pick up air orbs.  But there are badges which give you increased air and air recovery so this mechanic is a little less frustrating.
Another turn off to some is that quests have a time limit, currently at 15 minutes. Now i hate time limits myself, the feeling of being pushed is not fun, but in this game it is bearable...and doable.  You do get a bit of time back by clearing monsters out in a given area.  If it werent for the other good things this game offers this would have been a deal breaker for me, so do keep this in mind.
***this has been updated, the devs have added about 10-15 minutes to all missions.  The quests are much more bearable now for solo play and hard mode solo play***
And last downside is there is no local co-op.  Only one person can play at a computer, but is multiplayer capable by joining online game rooms and joining up with others to complete quests.
Overall this game is excellent and one of a kind.  If you have an interest in this game, dont hesitate to buy it, you wont regret it.  I hope my review is thorough and helps you decide if you want to buy the game or not :)

GOCCO OF WAR:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Welcome to the Gocco Studio Japan, an incredible theme park where you can be part of an imaginary war and fight against enemies created by a hyper-holographic simulator. All you have to do is to pick up one of several ecological weapons available to you which are powered by air and jump into battle on your own or with friends via the online mode.
GOCCO OF WAR is an action/co-op type of game. First, you have to create your Chibi (Japanese slang to describe a person who is vertically challenged) which is really fun especially when you have a fair few options to choose from. Then you have to decide if you want to play online or offline. Either way, you will end up in a lobby. There you will have Chibis you can talk to and find a little bit more of what to do. Also, you will have 3 stands and a billboard.
To do a quest, just go to the quest stand. There you will be able to activate one. There are 21 quests available to you in the game but you have beat the quest to get access to the next one. During the quest, you will be able to pick up items and gold. At the craft stand, you can enhance or create other weapons. If you accumulate enough gold during your quest, head straight up to the shop stand where you can purchase more powerful weapons. The billboard is a tool for the online mode where you can join a party of 4 on a quest.
The combat system is very easy to master and the levels are well designed. This is a really cute, fun game to play by yourself or with your friends. I would recommend this game to anyone already familiar with the RTS genre that's interested in trying out a concept that turns the idea on its ear and asks "how big can a RTS be?"
There are a variety of modes and ways to play against friends and AI - there's a lot to offer here. Will it turn into the best RTS of all time? no, probably not, but I do applaud Uber for forging new ground and making us all reconsider how grand war gaming can be.
