This is a good Fallout game to play if you havent played the other installments. This just feels like a reskinned Skyrim with many of the skyrim assests reused in this game(animations, sounds, textures). Fully voiced player character has no personality, making it really hard to follow along with the story. You can be a suck up one second, but the next dialogue choice you do a 180 and come off as if you were a salty elderly person.
Companion AI is horrible, so not really fixed since Fallout 3. If they dont block your passage during a fire fight, they push NPCs that you are talking to out of the way, making dialogue impossible. Only three notable companions while the rest you could essentially play the entire game and only meet them once.
Hardly any side quests, making most of your playthroughs defending and building settlements. Coming from New Vegas, the gun selection is pretty lackluster. You either spend your playthrough using one gun and always modding it, or you carry maybe a sniper rifle that you use 4 times...maybe.
Sprinting is now a thing which is a big plus. Now instead of waiting 10 minutes to get to one location to another, you spend 5 minutes and another 5 minutes at a loading screen. Despite what kind of processing power you have, you will spen most of your game in a loading screen.
The game gives you overpowered weapons and armor within 20 minutes of the game. Remember Deathclaws? They can be dispatched as quickly as feral gouls....on survival.
If you dont buy the DLC you dont get patches, meaning most parts of the game is bugged. I am unable to complete the institue ending and no mods are loaded. DLC also comes out to more than the game itself as well. If you plan on getting Fallout 4, you must be ready to spend at least 100 dollars.
I only recommend this to Fallout fans who can deal with these negatives. The game provides more lore and was more immersive than the last installment.

Alright, so currently I don't have a huge amount of time into the game, but I'm currently crossing the bridge from "new player" to "skilled player" Back when I first started, I died constantly to early monsters and was pretty jealous of all the players walking around with top-tier and UT gear. It was really frustrating how easily I died, even if I paid money for equipment (which I only did once, mind you). Then after many hours, days even of useless slaughter, I realized that just playing with what I thought I knew wasn't enough. So, like Counter Strike, I started researching everything. What monster dropped what, What bosses had what patterns, etc. So, eventually... I actually ended up living long enough to start potting my character. ...Then he died. BUT, from that character, I had learned MORE stuff I needed to learn. So, I learned that, and I started trying to farm an early dungeon, the Snake Pit. I died in those. A lot. BUT, after working on it for a long time, I started just outright NEVER dying in them, and now I'm to the point I can rush with practically any character. I know the boss's patterns, I know the Treasure Room Boss's patterns, and I barely even get hit. I kept working from there, and now I'm to the point where I am today: Almost past Dark Blue star, Partially maxed character, multiple character slots, and a whole lotta player skill. Alright, now that I've got my cheasy story out of the way, here's the Pros and Cons of this game:
Pros:
•KABAM IS GONE AND DECA ROCKS
•...Did I already say Kabam is gone? ..o. I did. Moving on. (Kabam was the previoous owner of the game for those who don't know)
•Awesome learning curve
•Rewards you for getting better and taking more calculated risks, giving you either that sense of "Crap, I wasn't ready for that", or "YESSSS!!! I DID IT BB!!!!"
•The community is in general friendly (As usual, expect there to always be a few jerks)
Cons:
•Practically EVERYTHING is overpriced
•On that same note, in the shop you can buy tops (Top-tier equipment) for considerable amounts of money. This in general is a terrible idea, as some noob will think "Oooh! If I pay la muns and get this op gear, I won't die!!!" Then, they'll go and end up dying with that character due to a lack of player skill, and there goes the $25-$30 they spent on that character. This is more of a tip than a con: DO NOT BUY ANYTHING in the game until you've played for at least a few weeks and are sure you're going to play
TIPS:
When you do decide you like the game enough to buy something, DO NOT BUY EQUIPMENT! You'll just die with it and lose all your money. Instead, buy Vault Chests and Character Slots. I currently have 3 character slots, and that is honestly all that I need. I have 1 for my main character that I'm potting, 1 for my farmer that I plug any extra pots into, and 1 for my party/guild character for doing dungeons with my friends. I also currently have 3 Vault chests. I really, really need more than this for the point I'm at, but 2 is great for early on. I'm pretty sure that when you start out, there a deal for a chracter slot and a vault chest for $10, which you should definately do. Alright people, thanks for reading this far, and have fun

So I've been playing this game on and off for four and a half years now and I think it's finally time I give my review on it (Vault challenge).  Anyway, this game is like crack. Pros
- Extremely addictive

Cons

Overall I probably can't think of too many pros and cons off the top of my head but I would recommend this game to anybody likes bullet hell games.  I've spent 50-75 dollars on the game and I don't regret it. Personally I would rate this game a 8.69/10 but that's just my opinion.

Consortium is a little bit of an odd duck - the best way I can decribe it is as a 'poor man's Mass Effect'. Both have similar main ships, both have similar multiple choice dialogue systems and both have the choices and consequences of words and actions.
Consortium's graphics are very different tho, they sit firmly on the blurred line between serious and cartooney, but I personally like that. I also liked the fact that it felt like you had complete run of the ship, it felt like interactions between yourself and other crew members was more natural and less forced/scripted. I also liked the fact that lots of things were there to discover or not, it didn't really matter.
On the downside, I didn't like the fact that once in a while I would feel a bit lost, not helped by the fact that some crew are 'unavailable' for interaction at certain times, without any sort of rhyme and reason. I didn't like the fact that accidently pressing the wrong key meant a conversation (and who knows how much else) was terminated and irretrievable. Even tho I liked that fact that it didn't matter to the game whether you found out stuff or not, I didn't like the fact that I finished my first runthrough with a measly 5 achievements!!
All in all, a fun little (short) game with decent graphics, a decent, well thought out story with replay value and a nice little cliffhanger at the end - after all, it IS part one of a planned trilogy!

CONSORTIUM is an odd beast. I can honestly say I had a great time with it, and can tell that the developers put a lot of time, effort, and heart into getting this indie creation to function like it does. I'd compare it favorably to the sections in MASS EFFECT where you just chat it up with your crew on the Normandy, learn a little bit about every one, affect their lives in little ways.
In CONSORTIUM, the crew is a lot less diverse (sometimes, I had trouble telling them apart), but the reactivity is absolutely fantastic. Going through the achievements, I can see so many different outcomes to choices that I made half-heartedly at the time. There's a lot of opportunity for replayablilty here. That is if you're on-board with the game's premise of spending 4-5ish hours getting to know its cast of characters in a confined flying command center.
If you love the dialog/choice-heavy sections of modern RPGs, here's a great little game that's built entirely around that. As someone who always puts points into charisma in RPGs (I know, I know), CONSORTIUM was right up my alley.
It's definitely not perfect. There are entire systems (inventory and ammo management) built around its very clunky combat mechanics, but I can only think of a few times when you have occasion to use your gun. You'll probably see more combat in the combat training scenario than in the rest of the game combined. It gives the impression of a game that's trying to "check a box" rather than make it a key part of the experience. It is a-okay to not have combat in a game like this. When CONSORTIUM was at its best, it reminded me of TITANIC: ADVENTURE OUT OF TIME. No combat, intriguing story, interesting characters, worthwhile investigation sections. An all-around great game.
There was also a bit of story-bending to an ARG that I didn't know existed, but apparently does. In the moment, I felt a little lost, like there was a crucial part of the story I was missing.
Overall, really enjoyed my experience. Confined and relatively brief, though it was, the game is also very dense. I can easily see myself playing through this a couple more times to see different outcomes. Eager to see how Part II of the trilogy eventually plays out!

In my opinion, they've been doing a great job.
Yes this game has no arcade mode, yes there is no trial mode, yes survival mode is boring...
But that's not the core of the game, those are superficial things.
The netcode is amazing, the game mechanics are great, the characters are fun to play, the new ones fit perfectly the street fighter universe, they improved the ranking system, they improved the lobby system (even if it's still ongoing) ...
They did an excellent job delivering a core game that would be able to live for a long time (depending on the popularity of course...).
The thing people tend to forget is that Capcom tries to copy the economic system and community system of mobas , mmo, all the games from the new generation.
And when those games were released, they had huge problems as well, server wise, in-game bugs, ...
And I think they're trying to adapt it to their franchise to give the opportunity for the community to grow ! Of course more money for them, but also more players for you to play against, more people to learn from,more possibilities in the games ...
So, that being said, SF5 has still a lot of room for improvement, specially to get new/casual players on their side.
- Arcade mode,
- Trial mode,
- other modes (I remember a final fight like mode in a tekken game if my memory is correct)
- More costumes,
- Cinematics,
- More characters,
- More character customisation
- More levels
- More customisation for everything (Life bar, super bar, vtrigger, levels, ...)
- access to account from your browser and phone
- spectator mode : being able to move camera (orbit control like)
And for experimented players too :
- 8 persons lobbies
- Online tournament creation
- Hitboxes visualisation in training mode (that would be awesome)
- training room with a friend online (I didn't look for it in the game, so I don't know if they already added it)
- Browser statistics tracking (get online replays, check ranking from your browser/phone)
- In-game notes
- send replay on youtube, or save replay in mp4 (I didn't look for it in the game, so I don't know if they already added it)
- Rage quitter in ranked should have their LP reduced... and the LP of their opponent increased for the "waste of time"
etc... etc...
So yes there are room for improvement but :
- The game is easy to get a hold on
- The netcode is great
- The game mechanics are incredible
- The game is gonna keep evolving (frequent patches)
- The training room has been much improved (record dummy)
- The core game is almost flawless
Capcom, you're totally on the right track, so thank you for what you're doing !
TL;DR
For casual gamers and non-patient people : Wait for July (The full story mode release date)
For people who want to pick up fighting games : Go for it, go online, make some friends, and make your way to the top, I'll be on the same path
For sf4 players :
- if you played for flashy combos with your friends : Go play tekken because you won't be happy with this game. (Maybe Ken or Nash though, I think I've seen some flashy stuff with them, and I'm sure some more flashy characters will come)
- if you played for the game itself, the feelings it gave you ... run for it, the game mechanics are even better than sf4

I recently played through the campaign for A Game of Dwarves.  I'm giving it a thumbs up, but a qualified one.
The game is something of a builder/manager game: you control a settlement of dwarves and guide them in both mining out the area around their settlement and building the things they need to be happy and do well.
I really liked the potential of this game: I find it a fun thing to occupy myself with while watching TV or just winding down in the evening, and there is some challenge to it too — more than once I restarted a scenario to come at it from a better angle.
Overall, I'd say it's a decent enough game when it's available at a reasonable price.  Less than $10 is certainly OK, but around $7 might be more appropriate.
Why would I want to knock the price down further?  Well, the game certainly has its flaws.  For one, while there are Steam achievements for the game, some simply cannot be earned because some of the levels won't give you full credit for completing them.  (Paradox knows about this bug but has said that, with developer Zeal no longer in existence, no further development will be done.)  So, for achievement hunters: you'll never be able to get 100% for this game.
There are several other little problems that, while they are not game-breaking, can be annoying as well.
I'll also say that, tone wise, I'd have preferred fewer puns and pop culture references (example: one resource is "dragonforce", with the tooltip, "the hardest metal known to man") and dialogue that was worthwhile reading — instead, it frequently pauses your game mostly to waste your time.  Some of that is, I think, poor translation work (or non-native English at the very least), and it tended to annoy me to some degree in that I generally expect a bit more polish from a game I've paid to play.
Yet, all that aside, I really did enjoy the game itself.  That is, despite its slap-dash feel and poor finishing.  The pacing is relaxed, and the graphics cute enough that you can spend time just enjoying digging around and making nice settlements.
There are some DLC available for A Game of Dwarves, both add-on packs (Pets, Ale Pack, and Space Dwarves) plus some in-game purchases of furniture available.  I got a few of the in-game furniture packs, but they seemed a little overpriced (about $0.99 USD for three pieces of furniture).
Overall: the game can be fun, and I can entertain myself for an unreasonable amount of time laying out settlements and making attractive rooms for my dwarves to enjoy.  Just know that the game is not really "finished" in a sense, and try not to pay full price for it.

To be honest, I first purchased this game a few years ago, and was not impressed. I had been playing a lot of Terraria, and Starbound was getting some hype, so I tried it out, and even though there was a lot of potential there, it just wasn't particularly 'fun'. Fast forward to the Glad Giraffe update when I jumped back in, and Starbound has come a long way toward being an incredible game (and is still getting better on the road to what the devs are considering the official 1.0 update).
Pros:
- Just going to get this out of the way, if you like Terraria, play this one too.
- Endless worlds means tons to explore, I've found worlds that seem barren and boring, only to discover a massive scientific outpost under the surface, and worlds that have a peaceful glitch (medieval robots) village, seemingly paranoid and oppressed apex (Planet of the Apes style race) military compound, and a town full of murderous mushroom men, 30 block tall mushroom trees, and giant mushroom houses, all just a short jog from each other, and that was just one pair of planets around one of the 4 star systems I explored with that character, out of the ungodly number of total possibilities
- Combat is fun (YMMV), there's still some work to be done (and a lot of complaints about damage on contact with enemies that might result in changes), but there's some really fun variety in the swords, axes, daggers, spears, grenade launchers, machine pistols, shotguns, assault rifles and more, especially with all of the special abilities offered by the latest major update. I seem to always find some OP weapon that wrecks fluffly little alien rock monsters on one planet, then I fly off to another and have to run for cover from the locals until I find something better
- Construction/decoration options are satisfyingly varied, with tons of lighting, furniture, storage and knick-knacks to create anything your heart desires, with each race embodying a different theme that can be mixed and matched
- Still in development, so it's still getting better!
Cons
- It's still a bit unstable, for examply I got to the fourth(?) ship upgrade on my most recent character, fighting ufo-piloting  penguins and gathering rare extravagant materials for some kick♥♥♥♥♥armor and staves, died and now my character won't load. It's not like Terraria either where it's easy to go right back to the same world with a new character, all of that progression was just lost because I didn't think to make a back-up
- Controls still feel a bit odd, using the scroll wheel to select your equipped items from the hotbar, selecting your default set-up, left and right handed items, switching to the matter manipulator etc, all feel really overwhelming sometimes (that might just be me, but it feels like I'm given too much control over my hotbar to the point I just can't keep all of it straight)
- It needs a lot of polish, for example in combat with certain weapons (almost anything two-handed), if an enemy gets too close for your shotgun to hit (???) they can just wreck you and there's not much you can do unless you have movement tech equipped sometimes, and there's a lot of little things like no easy way to organize chests (quick-stacking or anything like that), fetch-quests that still feel clunky, etc.
-It's still in development, so a lot of that polish, a lot of the glitches, and entire systems still need to be fixed/updated/completely revamped between now and 1.0, so while there's a lot of improvement still to come, it's still sometimes painfully obvious that it's an early access title
Buy this game if you like Terraria
Buy this game if you like the idea of a 2D-Minecraft in space with much more satisfying survival mode (IMHO)
Buy this game if you like open sandboxes always enticing you with 'hey, what's that over there?' moments
Buy this game if you don't mind things shifting a bit on the way to 1.0 (which might be coming up here 'soon')
Don't buy this game YET if you want to play a fully stable (as much as possible), fully fleshed-out experience and won't tolerate the imperfections that come with Early Access titles

HALCYON 6: STARBASE COMMANDER
*NOTE: Has had a number of patches, including a major overhaul, since this review was published*
PUBLISHER/DEVELOPER – Massive Damage
GENRE – RPG/STRAT/ROGUELITE
THE BASICS:
You are in charge of Starbase Halcyon 6 and a small complement of officers – you are some of the last few survivors of the human race, after Earth was devastated by an alien race known as the Chruul. Your mission is to explore your little sector of space, looking for other enclaves of humanity in nearby star systems, nebulae, and asteroid clusters, while protecting them from the predations of the merciless Chruul invaders. In the meantime, you also need to explore neglected areas of your own starbase, excavating the areas and clearing out any lingering alien presence within them. Research new facilities and ships, level up your officers, and clean house. If you're lucky, you'll even make some new friends along the way from among the nearby alien cultures.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
You begin with yourself – the standard unseen overmind/leader –  plus one “Legendary” officer of your choice (meaning, one who can unlock a special, unique skill later on), who comes with their own ship; and one other officer, each chosen from among the three types: Science (support, debuffs, and healing/repairs), Tactical (high offense and buffs), and Engineering (high defense and mix & match powers). You will need to recruit more officers as you go, and each of them has their own complement of both ship-to-ship combat and ground combat abilities; each set of three recruits (one of each class) can be re-rolled up to two times if you don't like what you see (save for the Legendary starter and any unique officers you find as part of the story). Officers will come with some passive abilities (whether boon or bane), and will learn more over time as they encounter specific enemy types. In addition, they will each earn skill points as they level up, which are used to improve their active combat abilities. The crews of individual ships will also distinguish themselves after enough fights, adding minor bonuses to their vessels. Unlike the officers, they stay with their ships, and cannot be reassigned. Each officer has their own unique grouping of abilities, drawn from a specific pool based on their class. The ships, however, all have pre-set abilities based on their type, and each Tier has two ship types to choose from; you will have both of them to draw upon in combat.
Combat is turn-based, with a clear row of icons at the bottom of the screen displaying the current turn order. Space combat abilities will range from DoT (damage over time, such as Bleeding) and AoE (area of effect/multiple-target) attacks (better yet, some do both!), messing with enemy sensors, raising your team's shields, supercharging your weapons, setting up repair drones, and the like. Many attacks serve a dual purpose, setting up a debuff or a DoT on the enemy; Certain other attacks will “exploit” an existing DoT, thus doing significant extra damage in exchange for canceling the DoT early. It's up to you whether to let the DoTs run their course, or to use an Exploit attack and hope it does enough damage to kill the enemy right then. If it doesn't, you'll have ticked it off when it's ready to counterattack. The game keeps track of aggro/which character or ship each enemy hates the most, and the enemies will tend to focus on that character when the time comes.
You need to seek out and gather resources from the local star systems; if survivors are present, they'll continually produce Materials, Dark Matter, Fuel, and Crew members (via cloning, perhaps?), all of which are needed to keep your fleet going as it gets bigger and badder. Naturally, the enemies are getting bigger and badder, as well, while opening portals to allow more of their their buddies access to your star system. You'll need to destroy the fleets guarding the portals in order to shut them down. Later on, you'll get more advanced “bases,” such as Spires, which have tougher defenders and more of them, and also require that you send in a team of ground troops to neutralize the enemies running the base. Meanwhile, any enemies left unchecked will seek out your active resource-gathering locations and attempt to destroy them. Once you get into the meat of the game and complete the first major section, diplomacy with nearby alien factions will come into play. Play your cards right, and you could end up with some really good new officers and ships to help you out. Screw it up, and you could find yourself fighting a multi-front war with only one or two squads of experienced officers to handle them all.
CONTROLS:
Primarily mouse-driven. Click on an unexplored area to send an officer there to check it out; click on an established facility to use it; click a celestial body to send ships out there to collect resources and/or fight whatever baddies may have taken up residence there. You get up to three ships for each fight in space combat, and you will always have three members for ground combat – redshirts will fill up any open spots when the time comes. Just as you might expect, they're basically cannon fodder, and they die spectacularly; but, better them then you.
GRAPHICS:
16-bit style graphics done right! Incredible amounts of detail for the medium. Attacks and other Ability effects range from your basic “pew pew” lasers to massive explosions to drone swarms and laser barrages. All of them do their job, and many feel “meaty”, giving a sense of impact. Widely-varied backgrounds for the space battles and many different ships, on all sides. Your ships will tend to get bigger and “chunkier” as you progress through the research tiers and create new models.
SOUND:
Modern chiptune music and sound FX which fit well with the milieu.
OVERALL:
Fun times, plenty of sci-fi book/TV/movie puns (especially in the cheevos). Excellent sense of atmosphere. Fun combat, different officers are distinct, even from others of their same basic class.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS: Nominal
STORY: 75
GAMEPLAY: 90
GRAPHICS: 85

FUN FACTOR: 85
ATMOSPHERE: 95

The devs are involved with the community in Steam, and very responsive – They've come out with a major patch and two hotfixes (with improvements based on player feedback) in the time it took me to play and review the game.

A very nice X-Com-lite at a decent price.
Halcyon 6 combines a lot of features (space/ground combat, base building, exploration, resource gathering, diplomacy, etc.) into a small package and while none of these gameplay aspects is very deep individually they work well together to make for a fun game.
Combat is in the JRPG style and is based around skill synergies where you apply debuffs to enemies and then trigger them with a different ability for extra damage. Using this system is essential for winning the game. Ground combat is pretty much a reskin of space combat but it's admirable it even exists, this being a small indie game, so it's ok.
Personally I find JRPG combat systems quite repetative and the game began to wear on me as I approached the end even with the Lightspeed Edition's reduced grind but there's an option to skip combat animations which helps a lot. Your mileage may wary depending on preference.
Story and characters are full of charm and the writing, imo, manages to be funny and endearing even though it very much relies on the usual pop-culture references and trope derivatives.
Overall a competently put together game with no glaring flaws (personal preferences aside) with a lot to offer for a low price.

It's Angry Birds. How can you say anything bad about it? But honestly, the game does have a couple glaring flaws.
1: Excessive 3-star Scores
You've just managed to destroy everything (and I do mean everything), with two birds, and you even get 10k bonus points for having a spare bird. You still don't get that third star. It's at this point that you realize you're going to have to repeatedly restart that level after you launch your first bird. Again. Again. And yes, again. I'm no logistics expert, so this is more often an exercise in awkward shots where you hope beyond hope that everything goes perfect, with chaotic randomness going in your favor 1% of the time. It eventually works, but it's extremely frustrating when you realize your spare birds are useless. At least on the less demanding levels you get to try more than once before hitting the retry button.
2: Stop Showing the Pigs!
Yes. YES! I know! They're there. So stop jerking the controls away and showing me the pigs. Okay?! It's extremely irritating when you're retrying a stage again and again only to have 1/10 attempts (or more) slowed down or even ruined by the game wanting to show you the pigs. Sometimes I'll be trying to get ready to launch and the camera jerks me around so much that the bird gets launched in some wild direction. >.<   Every Angry Birds game seems to be like this. Unless you leave the level and come back later I don't see any point to showing you the pigs unless you manually push the view over there yourself. It's pointless and irritating, especially in the excessive 3-star levels I already mentioned.
So there you have it. Two flaws. That's not bad really.
This particular Angry Birds title changes things up a bit by adding a new bird that can freeze objects it hits (it expires with a freezing explosion), gravity zones, and 'clinging' structures. The clingy structures can either be interesting, challenging, or just downright annoying. Arches in particular. Clinging structures are very difficult to destroy because their pieces stick together and they are often rooted at multiple points.
There's a lot of gameplay (200 levels), replayability due to hidden secrets (that you'll likely miss the first time through) and rescoring. There's nothing quite like the mindless destruction of poor little green piggies with explosives, falling blocks, and well placed shots of perfect chaotic destruction. So if you like satisfying explosions, demolishing structures (often structures of a hideous and pointless design, but still...), as well as the comical pigs and birds that are ever present in every Angry Birds game then I believe you'll enjoy this one.

It's just another Angry Birds game... with 2D gravity instead of 1D gravity.  It's quite fun and can be somewhat challenging on some levels.  If you like Angry Birds, you'll like Angry Birds Space.
Pros:
The game is child-friendly.  The birds are memorable and very popular on clothing, even amongst people who aren't fans of the video games.  The controls are simple, allowing anyone to play the game without much effort as long as they can use a basic computer mouse.  The game has a lot of levels and will provide many hours of entertainment if you like the game in the first place.
Cons:
The cutscenes are not entertaining and are poorly animated. I wish it had more of a story and also less repetitive music.  It would also be nice if the game didn't use the scroll wheel for navigation and instead let us zoom out on the menu like it does the levels.  The zoom feature is also broken on some levels, and the camera likes to move on its own too much.  Some of the levels are too easy while some other levels seem to be easy but give you only 1 star for some unknown reason.  It is unclear what the goals are on some levels.  Once you beat a level, there isn't much reason to replay it.
Overall recommendation:
If you want something casual, this is worth the $5.

From the developers who brought you ModNation Racers, a kart racing game that makes Mario Kart seem unsuitably violent for children, comes Sleeping Dogs; the brutal, ultraviolent action game you've always anticipated would rise up gallantly, to try to compete with the popular GTA franchise, only to fall short by an unsurprising stretch.
Not to say it's not an entertaining game, Sleeping Dogs reaches certain standards, most of all when it comes to innovating the field of satisfying your homicidal urges. After all, its progressive skill system is based on 'Face points’ that are awarded accordingly by how creative you are on your quest: to reduce the bodies of your enemies to the least identifiable shape possible (the important thing to know about evidence is that it’s best if there is none). You get the option to use the vibrant urban environment to your advantage, being given difficult choices like whether to crush all the bones in your opponents’ bodies with easily accessible car engines, or the equally effective maneuver of putting them gently down in a trash container.
The story is set in the metropolitan jungle of Hong Kong, and you have the privilege of following Wei Shen: the spiritual successor to every character Jackie Chan has ever played in films. He is an undercover cop and a master of martial arts before he even enrolls in the in-game martial arts class, and an unrelenting champion of doing the right thing. Like spending blood money on fancy clothes.
Throughout Wei Shen’s journey, you will face difficult moral choices, encountering moments where you’ll have to decide whether a character or scene is merely stereotypical, inappropriately prejudice or straight up racist (for example: why it seems like every fighting individual seem to possess knowledge of, and skillfully demonstrates, advanced martial arts just because it’s set in Hong Kong).
You will be taken on an adventure where, as a servant of the law, you will rise in the ranks of organized crime through vicious acts, lie to near everyone you come across, and enthusiastically murder almost every goddamn person that stands in your way, be it suspects, gang members or policemen, and still getting to keep your job as a cop. Oh, and you also get the option of using ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s posing as masseurs for in-game bonuses, tasteful! An excellent social commentary on how the modern execution of justice is flawed and better handled by a single, unstoppable psychopath, who also enjoys karaoke.
Your toughest enemy throughout the game will be the agony of a typical, nightmarish PC port. Before I start with the review, I'd like to make it clear that although I'm not the best player, I have been playing for nearly four years. The time does not show up on my steam profile because the game was originally a flash game, and my account is linked to that, not Steam.
Basic Info:
Realm of the Mad God (Rotmg for short) is a top-down pixelized roguelike rpg. A bit of a mouthful but I think that covers it. The main bulk of the gameplay comes from entering "realms" in order to fight the monsters within them alongside your fellow players. As you progress the monsters you encounter will become more difficult until you're fighting alongside the pros in the toughest areas and dungeons. Seperate to the realms, there are many elite groups who choose to split themselves from the rest and take on the toughest challenges in small parties. And other still choose to live a tradesmen's life and devote much of their time to buying and selling items (although trading in rotmg is usually so that combat is made easier for the marketer).
Combat and Gear:
Rotmg has 14 classes: each class has it's own ability and weapon types are split between class groups. Weapons and abilities are divided by tiers. Tier 0 is starter gear and Tier 13 is the best (tiered) equipment available. Seperate to the tiered items are UT (untiered) items which may be even stronger than some of the best gear OR may have unique aspects to it.
Combat is very reliant on what gear you have. If you have bad gear, you won't stand a chance against the strongest dungeons and monsters. All combat is done with left click (your primary weapon) and the spacebar (your class' ability).
Market:
Believe it or not, the trading system in this game (although primitive) is the base for a very sophisticated market. Prices are dynamic and based on what is high in demand, and almost everything is tradeable. There are dedicated "trading servers" where the bulk of the hubworld (the Nexus) is filled with people advertising their wares with speech bubbles. FOr most players, combat alone won't get you through to the late-game; you'll need a good share of trading ability to succeed.
Late Game:
Since this is a more general description of what you can find in Rotmg, I'll be skimming over some things like the dungeon system and guilds since they work exactly like you think they would.
After grinding monsters and slowly raising your stats, you'll be practically invincible. Invicible to everything except the strongest monsters. As a skilled character with maxed stats, you would be joining the most grueling dungeons in order to hunt loot so rare that it rivals the strength of the strongest tiered loot. The late game phase of Rotmg is considered by many to really be the beginning of the game, with everything else just being preperation. This may deter you from the game if you aren't patient (fair warning!).
The not so good stuff:
- This game is a roguelike, so upon death you will lose everything on the character you died with. All the stats you've put into it and all the gear it had will be gone. This is a huge turn off to the game if you are still unskilled and are prone to dying.
- Rotmg used to be owned by Kabam, who promptly turned it into a pay2win by putting the rarest items on sale (at a very high price) for premium currency (gold).
- Spambots are prevalent in the game and it can be difficult to shut them up unless you filter your chat. Otherwise, the chat function becomes moot.
- Rarer loot is very difficult to obtain due to low drop rates and relative difficulty to obtain in relation to character strength.
Final rating: 8/10
It's very difficult to compare this game to triple a titles and the like, but it is definitely one of the best games in it's genre. The gameplay is addicting and the risk of permadeath adds to the exhiliration. The co-op is tremendously fun and the difficulty will put your skills as a player to the test, but provide very worthwhile rewards.

The core game is good (this is Street Fighter after all), however this release is so barebones (and the few modes featured in the game so poorly implemented) that I would not recommend purchasing it for at least a few months until Capcom has hopefully gotten their♥♥♥♥♥♥together and fixed everything.
One of the features in the launch version of the game is an extremely short story mode with costumes that you "unlock" but can only use in story mode until a future update, at which point you will have to purchase them using in game  currency. There's also a survival mode where you battle computer controlled opponents for a set number of matches in order to unlock colors for the character you complete the mode with. This is a poor substitute for arcade mode as it takes muuuuuuuuuch longer to get through. This is the first fighting game that has required grinding.
The online was barely functional at launch, and, though a little better now, is still horribly implemented. For example, there is no punishment for ragequitting. There was a sweet spot of about a week between when they fixed the unplayable launch servers and when people started realizing it was punishment free to disconnect. As of now I get rage disconnects on about 30-50% of matches I am about to win.
There is a Battle Lounge which you can use to invite friends or other players to battle. This would be where I spent the majority of my time if it weren't for the fact that the netcode in this game is horrible so my friends and I all experience constant rollback and framedrops when playing with eachother. I've spent more time troubleshooting this than should be necessary as I have fantastic ping in every other game I play with them.
Aside from the above mentioned modes, there's also a basic training mode.

Capcom was open in telling people that the single player content would not be ready in time, but a lot of people missed that because it didn't say anything on the Steam page, and most people don't take the time to watch all the trailers. For newer players, I'd recommend waiting until after March to buy the game, when it should be finished. In the meantime, it doesn't support keyboards or arcade sticks very well, which is a major issue. They said they're working on a patch to iron things like that out though, and it should be fixed pretty soon.
Anyways, just saw a lot of negative reviews and wanted to clarify that Capcom did tell the community it wouldn't be done on their website months before they released the game, and that the single player content will drop on schedule in March. Feel free to hold off on buying it (or refund it if you didn't spend 2+ hours on it) but I hope you'll all come back and enjoy the game when it's done.

CONSORTIUM is a heavily story based and very conceptual game. It has this slight feeling of leaning towards AAA games, but instead of being a few hour long rollercoaster ride with splosions and lols, it focuses more on ideas while providing more gamplay than usual indie titles.
Story is the main point in the game, but it has so many branches that it would require a dozen playthroughs to get them all.  In one conversation you can change the whole outcome of the game, then in the next one, you might change it all again, everything depends on your choice. You can be a modest doing-my-job guy or a cocky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or a complete weirdo. And again, this may or may not impact the outcome. Honestly before this game I did not think you can make so many changes in story with  2-5 dialogue choices.
While the game has combat which is moderate (and that's what makes the game lean towards AAA FPS rather than being full chit-chat indie title), it can completely avoided through dialogue OR you can turn the game into a bloodbath.
Graphics aren't impresive but bearable (though somewhat unusual, thus giving some originality to the game), same about sounds.
CONSORTIUM combines FPS, RPG and mystery solving while being heavily story driven, and makes me wish more AAA titles would adopt such ways of story telling. Not just 2-3 outcomes and call it best game ever with multiple endings, but story that changes with every choice you make.

tl;dr: A tepid recommendation. If Steam had a "neutral" recommendation, or an X/10 system, this game would rate right in the middle. Younger children or newcomers to RTS looking for a very shallow, slow start may enjoy this for its gameplay, most others will find it a casual experience at best.
Vaguely reminicent of Dwarf Fortress, if DF was designed for younger folks instead of psychotic, bloodthirsty engineering aspirants.
It's cute and cartoony, but the game's economy is broken the moment you discover the wood->gold->wood loop, leading to a significant decline in challenge (unless you hurry through). Unlike DF, this game is less about keeping your dwarves alive (usually a trivial task) but in providing beautiful surroundings with the fruit of their labor. Even here, however, the game is lacking. Simply slapping up massive quantities of wooden-covered walls and wooden flooring (again, infinite wood->gold->wood loop..) is enough to keep your dwarves beaming from ear to ear, if you're consistent about it.
That leaves building a palace for yourself differently on THIS level because you like the pink flooring instead of the black, and playing through the story. The story's not bad, but the characters become long-winded and repetitive at times, and it's not a particularly strong story.
Lengthwise, the game feels short, unfortunately. Once you've learned how to break the economy, levels are reduced to mere delay while you wait for your military to be strong enough to steamroll a few foes, then a few more. It's not a bad game, but it's a casual game for new gamers.
tl;dr: A tepid recommendation. Not a challenging game, more of a casual building game with a few vestigial combat and research elements.

I did not enjoy this game.
The Walking Dead is basically an interactive movie, so the story and how it's presented is the most overwhelmingly important factor. In that case, it does fantastic. Telltale gave the story the primary focus and the presentation is very well done. In that aspect, it can be complimented.
Where the game fell apart and where I ultimately disliked it is the characters. It is utterly baffling to me but there are literally only two characters in the entire game I like -- it's probably not a coincidence either that the two characters happens to be children. Every single other character in the game, including Lee, are very hard to sympathize with.
They all act in ways I find utterly illogical, they're generally despicable with little to like about them, they all generally act in the most incompetent ways possible, and you can't help a single person without them later backstabbing you. It's really like the game is trying its hardest to make you dislike every single character in the game
Having never watched the TV show, I'm guessing this might be how it is done and how Telltale believes is the best way to create drama and keep the story engaging...but the end result is that it's also very hard to enjoy the game. When you don't like most of the characters and they do things which you can't make sense of, how do you enjoy the story? I do see how it keeps the drama up, but without a character that I could back and support, I just end up not caring about anyone (save for Clementine).
Overall, I got The Walking Dead for free so I can't complain too much. If you can get it for free too, I'd say give it a shot. Otherwise, definitely don't bother.

Halcyon 6: Lightspeed Edition by developer Massive Damage is a turn-based strategy game set in space. In it, you play as the newly appointed commander of the Terran Federation after the previous command (and most of the federation outside the space station you start in) is destroyed by a new alien threat known as the Chruul race.
As opposed to most movies and games where humanity fights against an outside alien threat, this game begins at a point where other alien races (aside from the one you’re fighting) have made contact with humanity. In fact, according to the game’s story, the Terran Federation was actually strong enough to keep these races from fighting each other before the emergence of the Chruul. As such, your units and the units of the Chruul are on a much more even playing field.
Combat in the game is, as previously mentioned, turn-based. A turn order for all units can be found at the bottom of the screen. While there are plenty of moves that deal pure damage, there are other moves that inflict status conditions on the enemies or buffs on your own units. In fact, many of the attacks in the game will deal double damage if the enemy it hits is suffering from a specific status condition. For example, one of the strongest attack moves I had—called “Flak Cannon”—dealt 120 damage normally and dealt double damage when it targeted an enemy with the status condition “engines down.” I would equip another one of my ships with an attack which—while not nearly as strong as “Flak Cannon”—would inflict the condition of “engines down.” Then I would attack with “Flak Cannon” and do a whooping 240 damage to the enemy ship I was attacking. Exploiting combos such as this can make a huge difference in battle.
Halcyon 6: Lightspeed Edition also has ground battles, but these play out more or less the same as space battles. The moves and status conditions are different, but the combat is still turn-based with a focus on status condition exploitation. As this is a space game, you will not see ground-based combat nearly as often as space combat, but it still doesn’t hurt to make sure an officer you select has good ground abilities.
Halcyon 6: Lightspeed Edition’s units are “officers.” At the beginning of the game you have a choice between one of three officers—a tactical officer, an engineering officer, and a science officer. Engineering officers usually have the largest, most powerful ships, but at the expense of not having nearly as many turns as the other two officers (turn amount is decided by ship speed). Science officers, on the other hand, have light, fragile ships that are able to take the most turns out of the three. Every time you get a new officer, you are again given a choice of one of the three types to have. I found it effective to go into battle with one of each type of officer.
The game has 4 resource types: dark matter, fuel, materials, and crew size. All 4 of these are generated by space stations found in the remnants of what used to be Terran Federation space. With these space stations, you can either send ships out to collect the resources generated by them, or you can build a satellite drone at the station which will then periodically send resources to your base.
Additionally, you can gain dark matter and materials from winning space battles. When you collect a resource through a collection of ships, the ships will hold the resources and the resources will be unusable until the ships dock at your base.
Throughout Halcyon 6: Lightspeed Edition, you will occasionally be contacted by ships from the other races. While sometimes (usually when contacting the Chruul) these conversations don’t change anything, most times they end with deciding whether or not to take on a quest. Other times, they force a quest on you and you can make a decision on which way you want to handle the quest. These decisions also occasionally appear mid-quest (although I only saw a decision appear during a quest once).
Overall, I think Halcyon 6: Lightspeed Edition is very well put together and something that fans of turn-based strategy games would enjoy. As such, I think a fair rating for this game would be 8.5/10.

*It's impossible to split fleets once they're made. Just sent a fleet to defend outpost, and now want one of your science officers to upgrade that outpost while the others return to base? You got your ship construction screen, your ships stats and powers screen, your officer screen (which doesn't show the powers of the ship they're on), your ship equipment screen (you can't view the equipment from the map, though you can view the rest of the ship's stats)... Want to know how much power your stations uses and generates? Tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ kid, that isn't on the display. You need to start building something, and it'll tell you. *Bugged as♥♥♥♥♥♥ Want to send a fleet to defend a world that already has a science officer sitting there, upgrading it? To be honest, I first purchased this game a few years ago, and was not impressed. I had been playing a lot of Terraria, and Starbound was getting some hype, so I tried it out, and even though there was a lot of potential there, it just wasn't particularly 'fun'. Fast forward to the Glad Giraffe update when I jumped back in, and Starbound has come a long way toward being an incredible game (and is still getting better on the road to what the devs are considering the official 1.0 update).
Pros:
- Just going to get this out of the way, if you like Terraria, play this one too.
- Endless worlds means tons to explore, I've found worlds that seem barren and boring, only to discover a massive scientific outpost under the surface, and worlds that have a peaceful glitch (medieval robots) village, seemingly paranoid and oppressed apex (Planet of the Apes style race) military compound, and a town full of murderous mushroom men, 30 block tall mushroom trees, and giant mushroom houses, all just a short jog from each other, and that was just one pair of planets around one of the 4 star systems I explored with that character, out of the ungodly number of total possibilities
- Combat is fun (YMMV), there's still some work to be done (and a lot of complaints about damage on contact with enemies that might result in changes), but there's some really fun variety in the swords, axes, daggers, spears, grenade launchers, machine pistols, shotguns, assault rifles and more, especially with all of the special abilities offered by the latest major update. I seem to always find some OP weapon that wrecks fluffly little alien rock monsters on one planet, then I fly off to another and have to run for cover from the locals until I find something better
- Construction/decoration options are satisfyingly varied, with tons of lighting, furniture, storage and knick-knacks to create anything your heart desires, with each race embodying a different theme that can be mixed and matched
- Still in development, so it's still getting better!
Cons
- It's still a bit unstable, for examply I got to the fourth(?) ship upgrade on my most recent character, fighting ufo-piloting  penguins and gathering rare extravagant materials for some kick♥♥♥♥♥armor and staves, died and now my character won't load. It's not like Terraria either where it's easy to go right back to the same world with a new character, all of that progression was just lost because I didn't think to make a back-up
- Controls still feel a bit odd, using the scroll wheel to select your equipped items from the hotbar, selecting your default set-up, left and right handed items, switching to the matter manipulator etc, all feel really overwhelming sometimes (that might just be me, but it feels like I'm given too much control over my hotbar to the point I just can't keep all of it straight)
- It needs a lot of polish, for example in combat with certain weapons (almost anything two-handed), if an enemy gets too close for your shotgun to hit (???) they can just wreck you and there's not much you can do unless you have movement tech equipped sometimes, and there's a lot of little things like no easy way to organize chests (quick-stacking or anything like that), fetch-quests that still feel clunky, etc.
-It's still in development, so a lot of that polish, a lot of the glitches, and entire systems still need to be fixed/updated/completely revamped between now and 1.0, so while there's a lot of improvement still to come, it's still sometimes painfully obvious that it's an early access title
Buy this game if you like Terraria
Buy this game if you like the idea of a 2D-Minecraft in space with much more satisfying survival mode (IMHO)
Buy this game if you like open sandboxes always enticing you with 'hey, what's that over there?' moments
Buy this game if you don't mind things shifting a bit on the way to 1.0 (which might be coming up here 'soon')
Don't buy this game YET if you want to play a fully stable (as much as possible), fully fleshed-out experience and won't tolerate the imperfections that come with Early Access titles

This is my first review ever, and I'm writing it because I believe the indie developers need more help in that regard. That said, I am coming down from 3 year Skyrim binge and needed something new. Gave this a try and I immediately loved the old school feel to it, the fact that its free to play and the open world sandbox style made me give it a try. So far, my character is level 43, I use the market but have yet to spar with other players or go into PvP world (if you die there, other players will steal your stuff). Still definitely a noob but I'm already addicted. Some of the good and bad, in no particular order:
-pick up and play, easy to learn but extremely difficult to master
-controls take some getting used to, some bugs here and there but not enough to affect gameplay
-Prepare to grind. I like to play this game while I'm doing other things on my computer, watching TV etc. Not truly set it and forget it while maxing out your stats but if you empty your inventory into the chest and devote time to gathering/crafting skills, it can get take a long time. Utilitze the 2x Exp events wisely.
-You will have to do captcha checks every so often to prove you aren't a bot. I do understand why they do it and they give you free exp for doing it (and penalize you for getting it incorrect or ignoring them) but I wish there was a pause function instead of having to log out if you need to step away for a while but not want to stop playing.
-free to play, but you can buy MOS points with your steam wallet and get some ridiculously great items early game. $5 will go a long way, especially when you are grinding mining/forging to make mediocre gear. Of course, you can go through the whole game without paying anything.
-The cost of entry to skills like Archery, Carpentry, Jewelry, Fletching and Breeding is very high, as you will need to aquire licenses and deeds to level these skills. (Just the deed for the island is 35,000 coins, which is a lot early game, but not bad as you progress in level and better loot. I have chosen mining to specialize in and I am getting loads of money for all of the silver chunks I have been mining. Choose a skill to specialize in, sell on the market to make money. Enemies do not drop money, but they will drop loot, sometimes the loot is valuable. If you die, you lose all of your loot except 2 items, unless you store in a chest. The chest space is limited as well, so choose what items you are hanging onto wisely.
I may update this review as I get further in-game but for a free game, it gives you a hell of a lot. Hopefully this helps some people out, I already got a couple of my friends to give it a shot.

This game's pretty good. I didn't play the origional, I found this game a few days before it was release and then followed it and then eventually bought it.
PROS:
-I can play the game on the highest settings even if there is a lot of movement on screen.
-I have never ever have the game crash.
-Overall very creative.
-All factory-type robots are balanced. Example:
*Bots are quicker to make and are excellent infantry.
*Vehicles do more damage and are harder to kill, but are slower to move and build.
*Air has the best mobility, but probably the easiest to kill (in my experience).
*Orbital has the least amout of choices for robots, but can only be targeted by certain defences and bots.
*And Naval (My favorite), Extreme range, damage, health, targeting abilities (some of them can defeat orbital), and submarines, which also can only be targeted by certain defences and bots. Downside is that you need to have water, which can sometimes be abundant. I prefer to start of on planets with water because the naval units (along with an upgraded radar and a few Holkins) can defend you well.
CONS
-So far only bug fixes, no major updates.
-Starting off is hard due to the lack of resources.
-There is no tutorial, which kinda sucks.
-The game is basically over the moment someone gets all 5 catalysts in a machine planet, although some guy I played with kept on nuking a catalyst the moment I was almost done with the last one about 3 times, but unfortunately, I was still able to finish it and destroy the rest of the planets.
Overall, it's great, but get it on sale. Not worth 40 bucks unless they add some new content, because some of the players who had the original said that there was barely anything new added.

I have 2174 hours into this game at the moment of writing this, and I have to say I am disappointed.  The game has been out for more than two years, and there are still massive bugs in the vanilla version that you have to use free mods to fix on PC.  The control layout is great for those who use a controller, but needs more mods to make it halfway decent for a PC.  The storyboard changes are conflicting with even their own previous version of the game Fallout 3, and the lore inside is quite inconsistent.  The addition of a voiced protagonist ripped apart what little RP would have saved it.
On the good side, if you like building up settlements in game, or using your character as a dressup doll, and have fun with first person shooters, this game is great for you.  Sadly for a game that lists itself as an open world RPG, there is extremely little of that to be found.
Add on that they added in microtransactions by way of the Creation Club before fixing the extensive list of known bugs, and you have a train wreck that has made it impossible for me to purchase anything listed by Bethesda or Zenimax in future.
In summary, don't play this game if you cannot afford to mod it, and want a fully functional RPG right out of the box.

Dawn of Discovery aka Anno 1404 is a fantastic, detail-driven city/economy simulator with a bit of RTS. DoD is relaxing, gorgeous, and a great example of sandbox citybuilding with a challenge. You're encouraged to make multiple cities/islands and trade route them together, micromanage and setup production lines and creating a very pretty visual balance between the environment and buildings, which all look incredible and detailed. For what it is, and with no major flaws in my play experience so far, I'd say DoD is pretty dang good.
Sadly it's not on sale on Steam at the moment cause, to the best of my knowledge anyway, Ubisoft's last patch for the game never made it to Steam, so Steam pulled it, saying it's an incomplete game. Unfortunately the last patch means Steam versions are incompatible saves with non-steam, so you can't really play much with non-steam owners of the game. Hopefully it goes up for sale again soon... However, Anno 2070 is almost identical and highly reccomended.
EDIT: DoD is back on sale! I very much reccommend it still, although there does still seem to be the issue of occasional crashes or multiplayer disconnects, if anyone has an idea why, I'd be happy to hear it. If you are looking at this game you probably enjoy RS, UO, and the like; well, from one player of these games to another you have just found a gem in RPGMO.  Given the coding platform of the game I would like to first say I enjoy the color and shape of the items, places, pets and characters in RPGMO.
A few observations about the game (by no means an exhaustive list):
The market system allows for a single user to become a baron in the market or use the market to sell/ collect items to continue your adventure.
Having your own personal island where you can chose to farm, breed pets, or just create a house adds a little special something to the game that is enhanced by going to see other islands and by the fact you can expand the dimensions of your homeland.
There are basic elements of the game like PVP and Quests that you find everywhere on the net.  I think the PVP in the game is respectable and I have seen others enjoy the quest system (it eludes me from time to time).
I want to close with yapping about a critique I see from other players: chat moderaters.  If you want to speak freely be in channel 18.  If you want to learn about the game and be restricted in your words join channel EN.  Either way, make your choice and enjoy the crafting, enchanting, searching, looting, killing, trading and chat that is RPGMO.

There are subtitles available, but they are horribly coded - the entirety of what the person is saying flashes on the screen all at once, then disappears line by line BEFORE the character is even finished reading the line. I get the idea of throwing you into a situation you're not prepared for and having you figure out what's going on, Quantum Leap style, but the game doesn't even tell you what most of the controls are. At one point, my quest flashed up on the screen, while at the same time, FOUR other pieces of text information flashed up, AND there was a disembodied voiceover telling me what I should be doing (on top of which, the background was occasionally flashing with a painful white light). Unable to process any of that since I didn't know what to focus on, suddenly ALL the informaion disappeared (other than the painful flashing, of course). I still had no idea what my quest was or even how to find out. Nothing is explained until way too late - fine for storytelling, BAD NEWS for gameplay. I could only tolerate about 30 minutes of this before I could feel myself going into sensory overload and had to turn it off. I've been playing video games my whole life and never once have I had that happen.
It's possible there is a great story and a really interesting game in there, but if you have ANY kind of sensory issues whatsoever, don't go anywhere near this one unless you're prepared to have a meltdown or a seizure, because you will.

Video Overview:
Halcyon 6 is very star trek and Xcom in its concepts. You're managing a star base that is made up of red, blue, and yellow shirt officers in the vein of star trek. So Red shirts have the highest damage, blue has the highest speed, and yellow has the highest defense. Each have their tricks and advantages; they even have their own ships as well. You'll need a good mix of each if you want to effectively explore and build up your base; while also building up the surrounding planets. Ground and Ship combat is turned based RPG style with it's own status effects, but there are shot chance % like in Xcom. The Xcom side of things is exploring and building in your base like in the newest Xcom games. You're also sending your officers around to build up and handle situations with time going by like Xcom. There will be a number of races and factions to interact with; befriend and anger them at your peril. But there is one race that will appear in your space on occasion that will get stronger each time that you will want to deal with.
The music and art is very star trek; if you're a fan of space games, you'll enjoy this for sure. The variety of races, ships, and quests are very fun as well.

Decent story, good art, trailers make it look great... but the actual experience is rather lacking.
I bought it on sale and under no circumstances should someone pay full price for this game.
I love the story and look of the game, but I would never encourage one of my friends to buy this.
List of issues:
1 - Combat is rock/paper/scisors based on the Status Effects. Combat is all about applying a status effect with one unit, and the next unit using an attack that expliots(and removes) that status effect from the target for a +150% damage boost. SInce not all units can apply & exploit all ststus effects you MUST have one of each class in a fleet for maximum effect.
Once you find a rotation of attacks you like, you stick with that and never change it.
Because of this combat options feel extremely limited and always feels like a grind/chore.
2 - Researching and building higher tier ships never really feels to give you an advantage. Specifically, random enemy fleets will ALWAYS have ships relatively equivalent to yours in tier. You just built a new fleet of all new Tier 3 ships? All random enemy fleets will now have all Tier 3 ships.
This mechanic of enemies always advancing to be your equal always feels crappy to me.
Specific story encounters are exempt from this rule. Enemy fleets in main story missions seem to be locked, so it is possible to be slightly over/underpowered for these encounters.
3 - Base building is rather lacking. I'm close to the end of the game and I'm pretty sure I'll never use 1/3 of the rooms on the station. There's just nothing useful to build.
-addition - Just finished the game and there are some unique useful items you get to build.  Still didn't use 20% of the rooms at the end.
4 - Numerous attack animations are VERY bright. Some people may not even notice this, but I find it rather annoying. Many attack animations are extremely bright white for portions of them and take up a decent portion of the screen (15-20% or more). This difference between the game's base brightness level and when these animations happen is so drastic that you can easily tell even with your eyes closed.
Combat animations can be turned off in options, but then combat just becomes a boring game of clicking icons and making numbers appear without any visual entertainment.
-Edit - Just finished the game and it leaves me giving it a solid "meh." Not bad, but not exactly good or impressive.

Do you want a feature complete game? Do not buy this.
Do you want a fighting game? You might want to consider reading more before buying. And please make sure to read more reviews before deciding whether to buy this! Use this as a second opinion!
This game is not feature complete. There is no real story mode; no real singleplayer. There are no lobbies (there is something called a battle lounge, but its 1 on 1). There is no challenge system and while I have not played survival, its pretty quick and lame from what I have read. All this stuff is coming in the free March update. The games mandatory tutorial does not tell you much aside from that your fists can punch, you can throw out a fireball if you are Ryu, your legs can move and kick, and you can block stuff. The tutorial, however, fails to mention more crucial things: did you know you can quick recover from a knockdown into a roll by double tapping left when you hit the ground? You can also quick rise by double tapping down. They acknowledge throw breaks, but don't tell you how to do them, which might seem like its common sense to most people but someone brand new to the series wouldn't get it. The tutorial overall is just very vague for a game that is trying to bring new blood into a niche genre.
As a fighting game, I'm enjoying this. I think right now its a solid experience if you want to hop in, train, and fight live players. I play them pretty casually, so I'm no expert at the systems present, but it does change quite a bit from the last title I spent time with (SFIV). The new Variable Gauge system creates more identity to the characters, as activating your V-Trigger will alter your moveset, giving them new properties or creating new moves entirely. Every character now has a V-Reversal while allows them to escape pressure through a knockdown as well as a V-Skill that alows characters to dissipate projectiles or other perks unique to the character. The Variable Gauge system changes a lot from the last system, but people who have played the Alpha series or Third Strike might feel right at home with it.
Links and execution in this game also feels much easier than 4, making it a breeze to get in and start practicing your bread and butters until your thumb or wrist hurts. This also means this game is very accessible to new fighting game players, so long as they take the neccessary steps to get outside information, have a proper mindset, and a willingness to learn from their mistakes.
Overall, I think Street Fighter V can only get better from here on. At $60, its a very tough decision for a lot of people. If you wanted a feature complete game, you should wait until March or maybe April at the latest before jumping into the fray. If you know all this, and don't care, you have a fighting game that is very solid when the servers aren't acting funny. Here is hoping Capcom keeps it up and makes this game fantastic, because it has the potential to survive for a really long time if they play their cards right.

I have 2174 hours into this game at the moment of writing this, and I have to say I am disappointed.  The game has been out for more than two years, and there are still massive bugs in the vanilla version that you have to use free mods to fix on PC.  The control layout is great for those who use a controller, but needs more mods to make it halfway decent for a PC.  The storyboard changes are conflicting with even their own previous version of the game Fallout 3, and the lore inside is quite inconsistent.  The addition of a voiced protagonist ripped apart what little RP would have saved it.
On the good side, if you like building up settlements in game, or using your character as a dressup doll, and have fun with first person shooters, this game is great for you.  Sadly for a game that lists itself as an open world RPG, there is extremely little of that to be found.
Add on that they added in microtransactions by way of the Creation Club before fixing the extensive list of known bugs, and you have a train wreck that has made it impossible for me to purchase anything listed by Bethesda or Zenimax in future.
In summary, don't play this game if you cannot afford to mod it, and want a fully functional RPG right out of the box.

RPG MO is an old school MMO sandbox game. Be warned that it is very grindy, meaning you will spend hours going through the same few motions, but it is a rewarding kind of grind that leaves you with a satisfying sense of progression and accomplishment.
PROS:
- Strangely addicting. The game is very simple in concept, yet I can't stop playing it. I spent around 50$ on new games in the steam winter sale and here I am, still playing RPG MO.
- Housing. Once you buy a deed, you get your own little island to build on as you wish. You can craft your own house, design it however you like, make farming plots and even breed your very own pets!
- Decent crafting system. Simple and straight-forward, your character can specialize in however many crafting professions you chose and there's plenty of recipes (or formulaes) available for each.
- Great community. The playerbase is nice and helpful. There's always people online so the game feels very much alive. I have seen people complain about moderation in their reviews but in my 20+ hours of playing, I have yet to see one abuse their powers. Just follow the chat rules, obey the laws of common sense and be respectful, it's all they really ask of anyone.
CONS:
- Lackluster visual design. The world itself doesn't look like much. There isn't much of a design going on, nothing visually appealing that would entice you to go and explore. The character models and monsters could use a visual upgrade as well. I appreciate the retro feel, but the visuals could be improved.
- Questing in its current state is uninteresting and unrewarding. So far my quests have been nothing but kill quests. Kill X number of monsters and then move on to the next, slightly harder monster. The rewards are pretty trivial as well so far. I feel like the questing system could add so much more to the game but is far too simplistic at the moment to achieve much of anything.
- Confusing UI. You can't drag items around in your bags and the buying/storing interface is just confusing and annoying to use.
Overall, RPG MO is a fun little game that I recommend to anyone suffering from a mild to severe case of nostalgia or simply looking for a time waster. You can play it as an F2P player or invest some money to support the developpers, you'll have a fun time either way.

I felt compelled to write a review for Sleeping Dogs, as it is a game that gave me more bang for my buck than most ever have.  I'm a huge fan of open-world games with driving (GTA, Saints Row, Far Cry).  With that said, I 100%'d Sleeping Dogs at about 30 hours in, and my current playtime is now nearing the 118 mark.  I can count the number of games I've 100%'d on less than two hands.  So, I think the important question is, why do I still keep playing?  What caused me to learn this game inside and out, to the point where I know all the mechanics, glitches, and how to mess with every piece of AI?
The answer lies in that to me, Sleeping Dogs is just pure fun.  The melee combat is something that almost no other game has done as well, and really the only one that comes to mind is the Arkham series.  Even with Arkham, I find the combat takes too long, whereas in Sleeping Dogs it gets things just right.  It's visceral while remaining simple.  Enemies react in momentary fear to bone-crushing martial arts moves, and the protagonist Wei Shen can masterfully counter and take out hordes of gangsters.  Wei also moves around Hong Kong with basic parkour moves, as he can survive falls of impressive heights and slide over all manner of objects smoothly, if timed right.
The other aspect is driving.  Let me preface this section with two things: one, that I vastly prefer arcade style driving (if I want real driving, I'll go take my real car out), and two, the weapon-based DLC car singlehandedly has given me hours upon hours of extra time with the game.  I'll put this bluntly; if you want realistic driving, go play another game.  Ramming cars at high speeds, tearing through the Financial District with a nearly indestructible bus, and blowing out the tires that sends cars flying like a Hollywood movie... all of its is insanely fun.  Add in the DLC car that pretty much breaks the game, and it just gets hilarious how awesomely you can dominate Hong Kong.
Sleeping Dogs is far from perfect, however.  Some of the things the game does are laughably bad, like how the police are handled.  I'm not going to mince words here, the police are just terrible.  They're so bad that they're funny, like with how awful horror movies work.  The biggest issue I have is that they literally pop into an area.  You could be in a desolate alley and shoot someone, or beat up a bunch of people in a quiet street with no police anywhere nearby.. and they will literally pop in like they used a portal gun or stepped through a dimensional rift.  If they weren't so easy to shake off and mess with, this would have ruined any sense of immersion the game had.
While I thoroughly enjoyed the story with a satisfying ending, which took me about 15-20 hours with exploration and side missions, you could tell that in some sections, the developers did not have the time to implement other features they wanted.  It's pretty obvious that they wanted to include deeper connections to Hong Kong with Wei with how much exploration and collection there were, along with Wei's serial hit-it-and-quit-it attitude with women.  Wei's struggle with his identity and corruption, both in the Triads and the police force, was a compelling reason for me to finish the story, however.
Finally, don't let the DLC scare you.  The DLC mostly adds things in to make the game a little more fun, and none of it is necessary whatsoever.  I know some people who wouldn't sneeze at Sleeping Dogs for the amount of DLC it has, but I doubt they ever actually took a look at what it does.
I really believe that Sleeping Dogs is a game that every fan of this genre should play.  Hong Kong's a relatively fresh setting from similar games, and Sleeping Dogs finds its identity in mechanics that are just fun.  Not crazy whacked up purple♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bat fun like Saints Row, and not maniacal, realistic Trevor fun as in GTA, but just super tight, simple, attractive combat with good pacing and a pretty beautiful world.
