It is unfortunate that this game is being lambasted this heavily in its current state. For all the negative attention the game is garnering we might receive 100k of fight money as compensation but in turn we are turning away millions of potential online players and future free DLC characters. We are essentially telling Capcom that their hard work and effort for creating an impeccably crafted fighting game that was built from the ground up for the community is not even close to being worth the price of admission. I would personally rather have all my characters and balance patches as free upgrades than having to pay $15 to upgrade revisions every year to satiate the demand for an arcade mode at launch.

There has been a common belief that Capcom has lost their edge over the years as a game developer. They have a reputation for nickel-and-diming consumers and passing development responsibility to any third party developer that comes knocking at their door. Street Fighter IV for instance has gone through many revisions and the majority of the development was done by the studio DImps.
In an unprecedented move Street Fighter V's development largely took place at the offices of Capcom. In this arrangement Capcom still took and acted on advice from the creator of Street Fighter to ensure that they were headed in the right direction when it came to creating the game design. What we received from this engagement is a game that has 16 wildly unique characters with their own combat systems in place.
Normally when you include a multitude of unique character specific systems into a single fighting game you are left with an imbalance across the roster. What we ended up with is one of the most balanced fighting game rosters ever seen in a single video game. R. Mika for instance has a skill where she can grab a microphone and cut a pro wrestling promo that increases the strength of her next command grab; if the opponent attacks her in this instance she has a frame of armor to negate damage and she can also cut her promo short at any point and throw her microphone as a projectile. Not even getting into her ability to call in her tag team partner as her V-Trigger you can see that this character offers a unique attribute that accentuates her grappling style and fits into her pro wrestling moniker in the process.
There are a lot of small quirks that make this game accessible and approachable. There is damage scaling for combos, there are no 1-2 frame links, the ranking system appropriately matches you up with opponents around your own skill level, crush counters can heavily damage people who spam in predictable or unsafe fashion. Simple things like dragon punch maneuvers can now be effectively punished by players of all skill levels.
In an era where we have to continuously purchase update after update to keep up with every balance patch and future character addition we can finally keep our minds at ease that our day one purchase will not be outdated for at least an entire generation. This is the best deal Capcom has offered in ages and the negative reception pointed towards them at this time will only push the company towards an anti-consumer mindset in the future.

I would definitely recommend this game. It is absolutely addictive and hours of fun. There are so many different roles to play, achievements to unlock, and friends to make. You'll never play the same game twice and events will never unfold the way you think they will. Essentially, you're given a role and you're either part of the town, part of the mafia, a lone serial killer, a jester, or an executioner (at least at the beginning). If you're part of town, you'll have to work with your group to lynch the mafia and the serial killer. If you're mafia, you'll have to work with other mafia members to kill the town and convince the town to kill the serial killer. The serial killer has to kill everyone without drawing suspicion to herself. The jester has to convince the town, mafia, and serial killer to lynch her. The executioner has a target (who is always a member of town) and must convince the town to lynch this innocent player. There are many other roles as well, so you'll never get bored.
Once you get to ranked, the pace will pick up and you'll be faced with even harder challenges, but it will just make the game more exciting. My only complaint about this game is that sometimes the community can be very cruel to newcomers who are still learning the ropes or even to seasoned vets who just make a mistake. For this reason, I recommend playing with a group of trusted friends. That way, if the bad guys win, you'll have a much easier time of laughing it off. I also recommend using a different username each game. That way, nobody targets you because of a mistake you made or because you killed them previously! You should definitely buy this game!

An amazingly polished sim styled game, with a nice blend of informative UI and beautiful attention to detail.
The gameplay is a classic supply chain styled game, similar to early Settlers games and the Stronghold series. However unlike those games where it felt more as though you were, to some degree, directly in control of each individual unit, this one abstracts it. Such as armies aren’t individual units, but whole groups which are move around, forming camps from which attacks can be launched.
There is a sense of not wanting to compromise gameplay, while also wanting to keep a believable level of "realism". Keeping the two in a good balance, and while each mission can on occasion feel a little slow to progress, it's a good idea to try the free play. Where like a Civilization game, you customise victory (if any) conditions and just sit back and watch your island cities grow.
A slick, well executed and well crafted game.

They had to put in the "you've been playing for two hours" warning for a reason!  Just don't ever expect a quick game.
DoD (or known elsewhere as "Anno") for me was the right amount of challenge and relaxation.  This meant that I could spend a good deal of time on it without being frustrated or bored.
The challenge part stems from managing all the complex supply chains that you'll need to get your cities up and running.  From harvesting crops to gathering fuel, from smelting to ship building you'll be constantly checking your stocks, trying to predict impending shortages and clear out stuffed wearhouses.  Or when you're not doing that the game throws random quests at you, which lead to rewards that are actually worth pursuing.
Yet if you want to you could also always pull back a bit, and spend some time on urban renewal.  Plant some trees.  Build a part in the city center.  Watch the waves lap on the shore.  The music definitely helps this portion.  And then when you're feeling less stressed, back to the never-ending grind of supply and demand!
The military gameplay is pretty lackluster, but if they made you play a RTS and this game at the same time that would be simply overwhelming.
If you play co-op, you and your friend can fight over where to send precious building materials or what development plan to pursue.  This is all the more fun since you share all your units and resources, and both of you can control the same unit at the same time.
Overall this was well worth the money I spent.

Fallout 4 is a game that had a lot of hype and a REALLY good first impression. This however changes as you get into the game. For someone new to the Fallout series it is definately a fun game to play and easy to get into, because the game was watered down severly from its previous iterations of Fallout:New Vegas, a game which I thoroughly enjoyed published by Obsidian, because its style of improving upon the style of Fallout 3 and previous qualities of the Fallout series. Fallout 4 blatently removed a large quantity of the vital compenents to the Fallout series. This happened on a variety of fronts, from the full removal of the skill system, and the repair system (The repair system is not the reason I am leaving a bad review) as well as the change of V.A.T.S. "Vault-Tec Assisted Targeting System" farther from the turn based, first person shooter hybrid, than that of Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas, which offered, in my opinion the best gameplay experience, to a bullet time first person shooter style mechanic. Even though I loved the graphics of Fallout 4, this did not compensate for the massive defecit of QUALITY story. I found Fallout 4 had a very shallow storyline and really failed to deliver on the side quests of the open world game which really identified the Fallout series. There were many side quests, but they lacked the flexibility that the player would have wanted by giving us the abysmal  Arrow speach selector, and not giving us an option to be evil or letting us know what kind of nonsense our character was ACTUALLY going to say when we picked "Sarcastic". This lack of personalization was furthered by the perk system not actually unlocking new gameplay styles for the majority of the game. The player is forced to choose perks like Lone wanderer and Big Leagues if they actually wanted their character to be stronger than a molerat. A player feels much more like a tool to execute a story rather than the player, as they are voiced by one of two people (Male, Female). This game is good if you want to shoot at things that look pretty, like an open world Call of Duty, or want to get an easy to learn introduction to the Fallout series. However for anyone who has played Fallout prior to these point, I would like to say you are going to be disapointed with what you find. Bethesda should have focused its resources into developing story that it decided to devote to Graphics rather than mechanics. It is thought by many people, including myself that the best Fallout game so far was New Vegas, and it is my opinion Bethesda should either move towards the roots of the series or allow a 3rd party (Hopefully Obsidian) to do it for them.

a game from 1991. I got it in a bundle of 3D Realms games I think.
First of all, to set the tone, here are some other games released in 1991:
Civilization 1

with a whole 4 colors. WOWEE!! TOO MUCH GRAPHIX
So, despite being incredibly subpar compared to the vast majority of good games released in the same year, how is the gameplay?
In one word – Mushy.
Each level is the size of the screen, if you die, you start at the beginning. You have unlimited lives, but limited shots that carry over between levels. When you jump it isn’t a consistant distance. When you jump and grab a ….triangle (for points? I’m not sure) you immediately stop your jump height (unlike getting a power up in Mario) which can totally screw up a jump. Sometimes you fall slightly through the ground when you jump/fall though it has very complex animations to bring you back up. Complex, heh. It’s a puzzle game more than anything and it isn’t always clear what you can shoot. One instance I was stuck because I didn’t know this set piece of here was something I could shoot. And you have very limited shots so you don’t want to waste them. Level elements are also invisible. One time I was entirely stuck until I went one particular way and magically triggered something.
I played a little under half an hour. Some of the puzzles are satisfying enough to solve. But overall, this is kind of a stinker. I can’t even say it was good for it’s time because it clearly wasn’t. There is a reason this is a forgotten game. If the release date was 1986 it would get a pass, maybe. But probably not, the original Metroid is better than this by far.

In "Monuments of Mars" you explore the red planet in order to find out what happened to former astronauts not coming back from their mission.
This game from 1991 is an Apogee title I did NOT play during my childhood (I played a lot of Apogee games) so 31 year old-me experienced this crude-looking mars mission first-time.
Every screen you enter and leave is its own level. So you have to make your way to the exit but every level gets a bit more challenging. Either its aliens, laser guns shooting at you, other lasers (or electricity, it depends), spikes or other traps, you should survive it all. And also think your way out in order to open closed gates or use moving platforms wisely. And that's pretty much it.
And the control is very basic and easy, so no complaint about that.
Sure, it looks very dated and barely even has sound but if you like playing games like this one for nostalgia and don't feel bothered by all this you can get some nostalgic, cool sci-fi entertainment out of this.

Based on the FAST engine, Monuments of Mars takes most of the best elements of Pharaoh's Tomb and adds new challenges. Astronauts have been disappearing in ruins on Mars, and your job is to discover the secrets and rescue the survivors. Gameplay is quite different from the Nevada Smith series because many areas only become accessible after tripping invisible switches, and there are movable blocks. Having a changeable environment is a great twist. Your character has infinite lives, but it's still a good idea to save in case you get stuck somewhere and can't die. Poor collision detection makes some of the later levels more frustrating than necessary. Developed by Scenario Software, Todd Replogle misspelled the name of his own company, listing it as "Scenerio Software" on the title page! There are 20 levels in each volume, which must be played sequentially because there is no map screen. There are 4 volumes in this game, with only the first volume playable in the shareware version.

Halcyon 6 combines the best parts of XCOM with the best part of turn based RPGs.  Progress is a choice between building out your resource generating planet systems, or base exploration and training.  How easily you can upgrade your ships or crew depend on how well these seperate aspects are managed.
Both ground and ship combat is a turn based JRPG style combat system, with the emphasis being on debuffs and status effects.  Each of the three classes have several debuffs they can afflict the enemies with, and their teammates have abilities to expend the debuff in exchange for heavily increased damage.  At higher difficulty levels, choosing the debuffs that correspond to enemy type and star system buffs makes a large difference.
The game would benefit from more than three class types.  As it stands, I see very little benefit from not running with one of each, as there are no gaps between status affliction and spenders.  Providing more depth to the team building would allow for nuanced interactions between ship types.
I may be missing this in the UI, but it appears possible to paint yourself into a corner when building your base.  There is no readily available option to upgrade the tiles to modern technology, or demolish the structure and build a new one.  This has not created an issue on my playthrough, but I will finish with only 2 spots to spare.
Playtime is worthwhile for the price, and the midgame mechanic additions increase complexity.

This is a reccomendation with a caveat- this is not going to be a universally loved game. There are a lot of aspects that can be frustrating, or even infuriating, to certain types of gamer personality. Let me explain.
Halcyon 6 is several games at once. It's a resource management and base building game. And it's pretty good at that. But it's also a choice-and-consequence kind of game, with branching paths and options and events, sometimes random, sometimes not. It's... not so good at that, but it's good enough, I suppose. And it's also a turn-based space combat game. Personally, I enjoy the combat, but it's sometimes a bit lackluster.
Halcyon 6 does all of these things well. It doesn't do any of them amazingly, but it does a solid job on each of them. And they're all tied together- your choices affect how much you can upgrade your base, which affects your armada of ships, which affects your resources, which affects the choices you can make, etc. This does serve to make the experience more cohesive, and I enjoy the overall result.
But, well, look at some of the negative reviews. The game can feel a bit grindy, especially on the lower difficulty settings. On higher difficulty, there's less time to spend on being frustrated at the grind, because you're spending more time panicing about oncoming doom, but even then it can be frustrating. So, tl:dr, if you are easily frustrated by things that look like grinding, this game is not for you. Otherwise, if you like resource management, choice-and-consequence games,  and space combat, this game is pretty good.

This is probably my favorite RTS out all the ones I've played. Probably because it gets rid of that always irritating unit limit (or at least I find it irritating). The game also allows you to do some pretty insane and fun things such as fly planets and moons into your enemies and even build the equivalent of a Death Star to blast your foes with massive beams of light.
The game is fairly simple to get the hang of almost right away, the tutorial may still need some work but that's something most people can probably get around if they've played an RTS before.
While I haven't played the previous version of the game my research shows that it didn't go over so well with its lack of content, this version fixes that with the addition of new smaller units and units that are the namesake of the games title, TITANS. The Titans are, as shown in the trailer and screencaps, colossal units that can be quite devastating to your enemies, but require a lot of resources to build. Though there may be at least one Titan that isn't too useful-at least not on its own-which would be Helios, who sits in orbit and attacks things on the ground with some fairly decent laser cannons, Helios is more useful when  it comes to securing certain locations such as the bases for Catalysts to build the Annihilaser.
I have encountered some issues with the game, however. Such as random crashing in the main menu and the game crashing when you try to load large systems, there may have been some minor things but I can't quite recall. I can also say that I wish the planets could be larger and more diverse in their climates, maybe even some life on them other than simply trees but that's something I can also live without.
With that said I can definitely recommend this game to new, moderate, and veteran RTS players. It's got some some minor irritants and some things I wish could be implemented but the good things about the game far outweigh the bad.

So I should start out with saying something nice. My three year old absolutely adores this game, and consequently we've played it quite a lot. This is his first experience with the series, it may well be my last. He has no concept of how many aspects of the series were sacrificed in the insane pursuit of an 'open-world' approach to racing games. He will perhaps never grasp how hollow every aspect of the game now appears in the light of a proceedurally-based sunrise, from the crashes, to the super jumps, to the minor variations on 3 routes that win all the races, to the billboards the game begs you to smash, defiling it's own logo OVER and OVER and OVER, as if the developers were working through some emotional issues. If the obvious cover-up done on the Van's paintjob is any indication, it was a cukolding experience for them. Oh, Criterion, remember when you were making Burnout 2 and Black? What led you to blue barrels and yellow construction signs acting as surrogate blues clues for toddlers?
In any case, by 'Ultimate Box' what EA meant to say was "Box full of DLC for you to pay for", as this content isn't even Downloaded, it came with the game, you just have to pay to use it. That's right, there are several packages of cars just waiting to be unlocked for extra money, including the hovercraft delorean which makes every other car in the game seem lame. Oh wait, it's not actually a delorean, because EA had to slavishly rip off a bunch of brands without accrediting them. The car that looks like a Bel-Air has freakish air-time, making it the only candidate for completion of several achievements/unlocks.
And they put motorcycles in this game, probably to taunt you with how much you can taste an awesome Road Rash remake, but rest assured it's completely neutered, uninspired, and honestly looks like they just walked away before they got anywhere with that particular aspect of the game.

Both casual and in depth at the same time.  A sisyphean grind for money and stats, but in a good way...  lots of suspense over drops, some good ones rated at .02%.  The RNG is a bit merciless.  You could accidentally break a really expensive item trying to enchant it, for instance, and some items you can only craft at a 1% success rate, losing all resources if you fail--but for a free browser game that you can also play on your cell phone (and the cell phone version is pretty damn good, I think), it's nice to have a game where you can feel like the time you put into it is actually building towards something, but also having a casual feel since you're not going to get ganked or anything, like you would in old school UO which, let's face it, is the best game of all time.  If you miss that kind grind with a deep in-game economy, then you'd probably like this game.  Another good thing is this:  since there are no skill caps, you can't really ruin your character or anything.  This let's you feel pretty free to try different things in the game without feeling like you need to start over.  There's nothing to lose in trying the game out.  And the in-game purchases are more fairly accessible to players without spending real money than any other game I've played with such things.  So, give it a shot.  It's pretty slow-paced, but I find it relaxing.

While I wasn't a big fan of the original edition of the game ( too grindy,  lack of customization options for officers,  was a bit boring ),  I find myself really enjoying the Lightspeed Edition.
The new changes help refine what the game is and what it isn't.  It's not a 4X game and no longer gives the feel that it is a poor substitute for one.  There's no burgeoning sense of awe and wonder in exploring unknown space,  no sense of expansive satisfaction in the building of a mighty warfleet.  No euphoric rush of your scientists succeeding in their experiments to unlock a critical technology that will turn back an alien menace.
What it is though is an engaging scenario of science fiction "what if " that combines light versions of 4X elements.
I love 4X space games, but Halcyon 6  is not a 4X game and giving it the gameplay of one (as in the original version ) was killing it.  The new Lightspeed Edition shaves off the 4X bloat and helps the game become more itself.
Events occur at a pace that keeps you engaged without being overwhelmed or bored. Resource acquistion is more balanced, making you consider where to apply resources instead of just amassing overwhelming amounts and having nothing to spend them on.
Is the game perfect, no.  But it is engaging, and I am enjoying it.
If you're looking for a 4X fix, look elsewhere.  But if you're looking for an engaging, space scenario with a sense of humor give Halcyon 6: Lightspeed Edition a try.

This is a very well-made game.  It feels like the XCOM base manager mashed up with a turn-based combat system using FTL-like graphics and a Star Control 2 sense of humour and storytelling.  The harder difficulties offer a great challenge for those who want it, while the lower difficulties are quite enjoyable for casual players. Overall I'd give it a 8/10.

A video game that's not really comparable to other video games, because there really isn't anything like it. I've played through it once already and just started a second playthrough, and I think I'll continue playing it beyond that. No point in explaining what the game is (just read the store page), but I will say that they ♥♥♥♥ing nailed it.
Starting off with the writing, I was blown away. The lore is insanely extensive, which you can find by just playing the game or accessing the terminal on the ship or reading the "iDGi-1 Discoveries" compedium (included with the game for free). It's rare to see a game take its lore as seriously as this one does. The actual writing in the game's story is great as well, with characters having their own distinct personalities (as they should) - and the way you interact with (or don't) with these characters actually has an impact on the way they treat you and even the outcome of the story. The branching paths of the story not only make replayability possible, but they seem designed around taking advantage of replayability (and replaying actually fits the lore!) - a good comparison (apparently) is Undertale.
Gameplay-wise, the game is mostly talking to people. There are a few combat scenarios, one being in a virtual world, but for the most part you won't do much shooting. The combat itself can be approached in multiple ways, offering lethal, non-lethal, or a little of both. This also has a noticeable impact on the game and its world. The actual combat mechanics aren't anything amazing and are rarely used, so you probably shouldn't waste what little inventory space you have trying to carry an entire armory.
Now the complaints! At times, the voice acting was particularly hammy - sometimes even outright bad. Most of the time it was just decent. Visually, the game was a headache - at least at first. I can appreciate an art style but the shadows and lighting just seemed to detract from everything, and it just felt like they were progressing backwards in their art direction. To quickly address the length, it is short. I can see how some might think 3-5 hours is petty for a $15 game, but with the amount of replayability and the fact that replaying actually changes things, I'm alright with that price.
Is it worth the money? Absolutely. I'm actually ashamed I got this for free, and would have gladly paid for it had I known it was this good (though I did back the sequel on Kickstarter, as should you if you're reading this within 24 days of posting).

If you liked Starbase Commander, you will still like Lightspeed Edition. It's better.
Going in, I was slightly worried about the UI re-skin. When Interstellaria (my previous favorite Steam game) changed the UI, it resulted in a bunch of bugs and acted more as a side-grade in atmosphere. Halcyon 6 didn't have those problems. The new skin looks more hi-tech and more polished. It feels like an upgrade.
Officer progression keeps getting better. I remember the days when you leveled up and got to pick one of four powers to upgrade. Starbase Commander gave you more control over which power to upgrade, and gave you a nice interface to plan with. Lightspeed gives you a whole skill tree to explore, with more than just power upgrades. (Bonus XP from combat, anyone?)
Legendary officers used to feel like the officers you built your strategy around just so they wouldn't be useless. Now, you can customize which character, class, and epic power you get, so they fit into
strategy. There are now 15 different epic powers to choose from, instead of the 6 we had before.
Before entering combat, you can now choose which powers to put on your ships. Combine that with the boost to the base chance of inflicting status effects, and combat feels more fluid and less "spam that one power." The new prestige classes also add exciting new powers that can change things up a bit. Does your ship spend a lot of time in Critical Condition? Use Dimensional Inversion on it to boost damage output tremendously! (Or use Guard Ally so that it can't die...)
For all of you concerned that content was removed to shorten the game, never fear. Waiting until you had enough resources for that shiny new hanger or ship wasn't content. The only things that were removed were forced grinding (you can still grind if you like doing it) and two Ground Combat healing powers that aren't needed anymore. Every science officer
have a healing power, no matter how hard you look.

While when I first read that the Lightspeed Edition was going to be created, I was skeptical about the whole ordeal. As time went on, I warmed up to it. But after the full game's re-release, I can't say that I'm entirely satisfied, or that I feel the game is in any better of a state than it was before.
First off, I like that things are sped up a bit. There's a lot of grind in the game, but speeding up the game also puts a lot of pressure on newer players. Why couldn't he have a simple toggle? Another problem is the 'customization' system. It's little more than picking a portrait. Only a small number of the custom officers have any sort of detail or backstory, and it can't be changed for fluff or flavor. On that note, not to sound like it's a major complaint, but a TINY fraction of those custom officers are female, which kind of stings because I always wanted a main officer that was female, but not Isolde.
I've noticed that combat was significantly changed, as well. Critical State is no longer a 'do or die' situation for my ships, but that just feels a little cheap. It takes the urgency out of combat, and while I'm sure there are consequences (I noticed abilities gained cooldowns), I haven't noticed anything serious thusfar.
The most painful change, to me, is the way the UI shifted. I don't like the new bulky, huge radial buttons. They interfere with clicking and targeting on other objects in the world, and it's just too distracting. A simple toggle would be all it takes, but I don't see one anywhere in the game.
Honestly, I love Halcyon 6. I like my Trek-COM 4 game, and I like it's art, witty humor, and direction.
What I can't say I like, is how this didn't come out as an update for the 'classic' game as a toggleable difficulty shift, such as FTL's major 'DLC' addition, with an option to use the new UI or the old one. Instead, I'm forced to play the old game, with none of these features, or the new game with all of the flaws. I can't say that I currently reccomend people to play Lightspeed Edition, even if I suggest they buy it. Go play Classic Edition first. Learn the game. Then come play Lightspeed. And maybe I'm nitpicking, maybe I pulled a Sterling and jumped the gun, but if anything changes... I'll be sure to come back and change my vote.
Edit: Alright, I've now lost ships to the critical state. I can't say that I'm not still frustrated by it, however, as the new mechanic isn't really detailed anywhere and I'm forced to change my old playstyle just for the new one. I've also noticed that your 'prestige class' is locked in to what your sub-class is. A Tactician is always a Counselor, and I'm not really okay with that. Again, I don't mean to sound like I'm nitpicking, but I realy love this game and don't want to see it fall out of favor.

To preface this; I have over a thousand hours in Fallout 4 on the Xbox One, but even with my time played on Steam I think I've played enough of the game to give an informed review.
If you fill a pool with toxic waste I'm sure you'll find one person who would swim in it. Those are the people writing positive reviews. Not to discredit anybody who enjoys the game, maybe I just prefer clean water over skin-melting bile. To start with the positives: the gunplay is fine. The gameplay itself isn't horribly broken, except for the times that it is and you have to rely on user created content that fixes it. It can be quite pretty to look at, especially if you're relying on user created content. There are around four guns, two of which are the same gun (the combat shotgun and the combat rifle) unless you rely on user created content. And the settlement system, which "just works" and can be a bit of fun if you rely on user created content.
Gunplay being the only thing that is competently put together in the game would be fine if this were Call of Battlefield: Medal of Modern World War X, but it isn't. It wears the skin of a series cemented in story, a coherent narrative and meaningful player interaction; of which the game has none. Underneath that skin are the hollow bird-like bones of a game created by Bethesda with organs, nerves and muscles created by the community. I've got two main points to hit: a weak story and the anti-consumer policies being put into place by Bethesda.
The Story: The story, since I should avoid profanity is a complete pee-pee doo-doo pile of baby vomit that; when one tries to understand it: falls apart like a house made of twigs in an apocalyptic flood. Or a nuclear war. I guess that's more appropriate: the story is like an atomic war on your senses. But without the flash, destruction and meaning and more a wave of mind numbing dribble. Bethesda assumes you're invested in your son, making you either a lawyer mother or a soldier father. No roleplaying in this RPG, no sir, you've gotta find your son. New Vegas, a game by adults who have a grasp on solid storytelling and an understanding of what the R stands for in RPG put you in the shoes of a courier. The story in New Vegas unfolds around you yet you're a key factor in the state of the wasteland. Character interactions are rich, and every faction is compelling in their own way. When you ask Caesar why he does the things he does he gives you an explaination, it cements the fact that he believes in his cause and that his cause has a set of beliefs that drives them to do what they do. It's presented in such a way that you as the player might even believe in what he's saying. In Fallout 4 when you ask Father (your son, moral dilema alert, very compelling narrative ahead) why The Institute is kidnapping people and replacing them with synths he says "you wouldn't understand." The player is never given a chance to care about The Institute, the only reason they're given to choose that faction is "this is your son. He is the goal of the game. Will you be a parent, or a HERO?" And on my first playthrough I had been duped into thinking the writers for the game weren't huffing glue so I chose The Institute foolishly thinking that as their leader I could make meaningful decisions that would paint The Institute in a more positive light. I was wrong, and I was wrong for ever touching the story or any of the side quests, each as well thought out as marketing a cereal box full of live bees to children. I feel like I've been saying "it's poorly written" and banging on about that but it still gets me fired up, and when Pete Hines was confronted about this his response equated to "it's just a game bro :)".
The Anti-Consumer Practices: Bethesda games do have a unique quality to them. The vast open world and the promise of it all at your finger tips seems enticing, but its as wide as a river and as shallow as a puddle. User created content is the bread and butter of their games, and with the Creation Club they have "created" a problem. If it is successful and people pay for these mods I promise you that in ten years the mod tools will only be handed out to a select few creators and free mods will be a thing of the past. That'll set the precedent for the rest of the industry, so I hope you don't enjoy new countries in Civ, missing features returning in The Sims or bug fixes for any broken game (expect to see Fallout Bug Patch: 1,000 Creation Club Bucks). Bethesda is a company, profit is their bottom line. Skyrim released in 2011 and it's had five different releases (Skyrim for 360, PC & PS3, XB1, PC and PS4, Nintendo Switch and Skyrim VR) and Fallout is about to have it's second release in the form of Fallout VR. If you own the game don't buy from the CC, you can download it all for free, risk-free and with little effort from the Nexus. Bethesda gives users 100 CC points for free, which is virtually worthless. If you want something substantial it's going to cost you a minimum of eight dollars. Eight dollars for a gun is outrageous, especially considering you could have it for free and donate directly to the creator on the Nexus. They tried paid mods before and it failed, but it's a slippery slope and if they get enough people using CC don't expect the mod tools to get released for Elder Scrolls 6.
Fallout 4 is riddled with issues, half-baked ideas and a completely raw story. The only reason I play it is for the settlement building, which is fun but poorly integrated into the game: and no you cannot just ignore it. When Todd said "it just works" he meant it. It JUST works, barely enough to squeak by into the "finished" product. I wouldn't recommend this game unless you're a glutton for punishment. Oh, and in this game difficulty equates to bullet-sponge enemies, making for a game that's less "tough but fair" and more "I'll just sit on this bus and lay into this legendary deathclaw for a couple of minutes, maybe I can get a video up on my phone and just watch that". Survival is the only way to play and it had to be patched in a year after release. I would rather just play the box, not recommended.

I have 46 hours and bought the game on release day, so I think that it's time for a review.
Before we begin, my review makes it seem like the recommendation doesn't match up, but it should be explained near the end.
To start things, off:
The rollback is AWFUL. I can't stand losing because i land a hit confirm on my side, but get hit by a CA on my opponents side and lose the match. Straight crap.
Also, no reprecussions for rage quits. I've lost out on a lot of points from people with 3.8k points because they rage quit so they get to keep their fake online e-peen. No one respects players with bad skills and a high rank.
That said though, it's kind of hard to punish rage quitters when the netcode for this game can be so awful at times, that it isn't even playable.
For the competitive local players however,
This game has very strong mechanics and has excellent gameplay. The only real problem i've had is it is the stubby normals that all of the characters have, but that's not even really a gameplay issue. If you're looking to play this game locally with the versus mode, or if you're a competitive player, then sure, this game is downright amazing.
However, for the Casual market:
Before I go too far into this, I know that capcom has been telling us that this game will have featues accessible down the line, and that the release copy will most definitely feel incomplete. However, with poor marketing decisions, I'm afraid for this game's PC support, as fighting games rarely get revisited for reviews, so a lot of major gaming news outlets already have mixed reviews for this game, which is very scary. Now, sorry for going off topic for a second there, but for the casual market - as it sands February 2016 - the game is very, very lacking. You get what's essentially a neutered story mode, and a survival mode that has some of the worst difficulty spikes of all time. Not very healthy, but that being said, Capcom did release this game early for the competitve market, and Capcom Pro League.
Overall, it's not a bad game. The mechanics are strong, The fighting is crisp; but it feels like what we got is a neutered version of the game, that's basically almost a beta at this point. As mentioned, I feel really scared for the PC support when the updates roll out, as I feel like we'll get another Diablo 3 situation, or another MKX. It's genuinely a good game, I really like it, but there are a lot of issues with this that make it really frustrating to play. Luckily, we're past the first three days of the game, as the game not only needed a day 1 patch, not only a day 2 patch, but a day 3 patch.

Sometimes the characters do feel a bit shallow but it does a good job at making you care for them and there are nice side missions(including KAROKEEE !!!!).
I would give it a 8/10 because the gunplay is bad, even if you focus on melee then you still should make sure that guns feel alot more powerful and the quick time events feel so boring and annoying.

Sleeping Dogs is a solid 7/10. The game really doesn't do anything new, but what it does do it does pretty a-okay. The fighting, shooting, and driving are all solid. The story is enough to get the player interested, and the characters are all pretty well-written. It also looks pretty damn pretty, like probably the best-looking GTA-like game I've played. I'm sure many critics have mentioned the rain-slicked streets of Hong Kong, and I can't blame them, it all looks damn nice.
Now even though I say the game is solid, it also is a disappointment in a way. Nothing in the game feels special. You play as an undercover cop. There's a LOT that could be done with this if given the right treatment. Unfortunately, Sleeping Dogs never plays that out enough. The conceit of playing as an undercover cop is one that should be given to a game that allows for more choices, something like TellTale games or even Quantic Dream. If a sequel is made where you play as another undercover cop, I would be more than okay with it so long as they give the player is given different choices and branching story paths. Do you kill the cop to keep your cover, or try and find a way out of having to kill him? Do you help out an old cop buddy with taking someone down within the triad, or do you deny him and risk having him hold a grudge? Simple choices, but ones that could lead to interesting story developments. Sleeping Dogs as a franchise has a lot of potential, and it has a storied development history, so I look forward to seeing what the future holds for it.

People criticize Sleeping Dogs on PC for: Having wierd driving mechanics, ♥♥♥♥ed up driving camera angles, and being a bit linear. I'm going to go and just say they're wrong on all counts, except that ♥♥♥♥ed up driving camera thing.
The game looks good, it handles good, the voice acting's spot-on, and even though there's assloads of hand-to-hand, it's the right mix of challenging and simple, with QTEs only if grappled. The side-diversions are generally entertaining ("You gotta learn to drive if you're gonna keep doing this") and vehicular combat is, while a little lacking in diversity, not hard.
There are few to no painfully slow escort missions, the plot is good, the environmental attacks are satisfying and effective, and the world feels Hong Kong. You feel like an undercover cop walking the fine line between brutal violence and not wasting civilians.
Minor issue: Realism goes right out the window in parts. You wouldn't think a triad would have sixty million motorcycles and cars to throw at you to destroy on the highway, but apparently they do. Also the car-hopping, and walking off disgusting injuries.
Basically, they tried mixing a bunch of stuff into this game: Third person shooter, martial arts combat, vehicular combat, an open-world sandbox, and a story. I reckon they succeeded where it matters, and for me, it was worth the money I paid for it, at least. Make sure you have a controller, though, and set the game to controller only so it gives you controller button prompts.
Only downsides: No post-game unless you're a completionist nut, and because the Parkour button is the sprint button, you have to check yourself when you go sprinting about or you might wind up climbing on top of cars/sliding over your cover by accident. I also had trouble spending money, and was wading through almost a million dollars in cash by the end of it.

An equivocal review of an intriguing game with one critical flaw.
The characters of CONSORTIUM are each unique, supported by adequate-to-good voice acting, and they combine nicely with an interesting story to create a plausible and exciting environment. There is also an impressive amount of player agency within the small bounds of the scenario. The game's simple aesthetic mostly works well, though the bare animations do detract from immersion.
Unfortunately the core experience of this game explicitly relies on save scumming (saving and loading to explore different gameplay options) and while saving is quick, the slow loading times are immersion-breaking when you try to follow the game's instruction to explore conversation trees. This is the main issue with the game as it stands: exploring the many complex branching conversations central to the game is changed from an exciting and fun experience into a slog.
A few other, mostly minor, issues also detract from the game. Many conversations seem to just involve finding what to say to each character to increase their alignment- though many obvious exceptions make this a minor gripe and the game is still miles better than most other games in this regard. Combat is also limited, but functional, and given the scope and tone of the game the slight awkwardness may be appropriate. Finally, game-breaking bugs do exist but fortunately the developer seems to be active in supporting and fixing those as they are encountered.
CONSORTIUM is pushing forward the boundaries of the art, and is certainly worthwhile. The game brings some intriguing ideas and a good story to the table, but sadly the load issue combined with other mechanical shortcomings were enough to push it slightly over the boundary to 'not-fun' for me. In my opinion it is worth supporting this game solely for the direction it is headed, but I would not recommend it to friends as a fun way to spend some time.

Consortium is a short, dialogue-driven indie drama defined by the choices you make. Short, because its length feels like an episode rather than a full game (took me four hours to complete a run-through). You have the ability via some satellite thingy to travel into the future and inhabit the body of someone else in that future. You wake up in a cabin aboard a plane / airship and have to immediately come to grips with your new surroundings. The entire game is spent aboard this plane; you'll look for a traitor among the crew, negotiate with a mercenary, and try to keep the plane repaired and running. The moment gameplay starts, the conversations and choices begin.
You can
.
Which are two of the primary strengths of Consortium. Choices abound, and result in genuinely different outcomes – NOT the same out come with minor variations. This means that, though short, replayability is high. There are a lot of dialogue options, with staying silent being a valid choice as well. With so much talking, the voice acting needs to be top-notch, and it is. A few characters seem a little flat, but the primary characters are unique and reactive. There are some very funny sci-fi references as well; like when you find someone dead, one of the conversation choices is, “He's wearing a red shirt; why should I care?” (Star Trek fans will know.)
A supporting strength of Consortium is the lore. This is never forced on you – you have to go find it – but there are questions that can be asked, and bulletins to read that explain a lot of the world you find yourself in. Ranks are modeled on chess pieces (you play as a “bishop,” while answering to a “rook,” and primary crew are “pawns”). And gun play is good, though shooting doesn't need to happen much if you don't make certain choices. I did choose the more violent route, and the shoot-out on three decks of a plane / airship, blacked out, with only red emergency lights pulsing on and off, was a creepy yet exhilarating setting for a deadly game of cat and mouse.
The three decks of the plane / airship are fully explorable (including the crawl spaces). Characters are generally well-modeled, though assets are re-used frequently (while every character's face is different, all men have the same body type, as do women). The graphics and environment are fully 3-D, which is an interesting choice since the game could have gotten away with being a 2-D point-and-click (would have lost that feeling of freedom to explore if the devs had done that, though). The graphics quality is plain but utilitarian; it fits the setting.
Usually a game's shortness would count heavily against it, but the high level of replayability counters that. Go into Consortium expecting dialogue-driven drama, and you'll easily get your money's worth. The game ends on a cliffhanger, but with the sequel recently Kickstarted, I hope the next episode comes soon! Value-wise, worth getting on sale for around $5, but if you want to support the developers, consider purchasing at full cost. Highly recommended.
Note about crashes:
I had a few where the game would just lock up and CTD. I set the game to run in Windows XP SP3 compatibility mode, and the crashes disappeared. The load times are long, though, and if you open the Task Manager it will say Consortium is “No Longer Responding”; ignore that and be patient, the game should eventually load.

Time to rewrite a review, as the original was stupid!
Planetary Annihilation:Titans is an RTS game developed by Uber Entertainment.
Design: The game is very futuristic, which, the pictures make quite obvious. However, is the game nice to look at? Running on high, or "Uber" settings, yes it is. I haven't run it on any other settings, so I can't say much about them.
Core Gameplay: Single Player: The single player unfortunately feels very lack luster, and even somewhat broken at times. You are given a solar system, and a bunch of planets. What do you do then? Well you attack the planets of course! Basically the story is some factions or whatever want more power, so you fight for planets to gain said power. Wait, is that it? That can't be it. It seems like a game like this should have a great story! But no, it doesn't. The story is by far the most dissapointing aspect of the single player "campaign". However, it doesn't end there. The tech system is flawed, and makes it hard for you to amass an army that is strong, and powerful on all fronts. However, sometimes, you can become completely overpowered, and break the single player even more! See, the tech system does in fact have some varied parts to it, including an AI team mate! So the AI team mate is useless, right? Nope, not all. It is better than you most likely. It can build units, a base, and attack the enemy before you make your first unit. TL;DR: Don't buy for the campaign, it sucks balls.
Core Gameplay: Multiplayer: Hard to write about something when it's dead. Hardly anyone plays the multiplayer, or the game at all, for that matter. The problem is, unlike some other RTS games, it lacks significant depth. It won't keep you there for more than thirty hours, in general. However, playing the AI skirmish was fun, and is where likely twenty-six of my twenty-seven hours went. Varied enough planet's, good AI (In most cases) I enjoyed myself there.
TL;DR: Fun, altough the multiplayer itself is nearly dead, and the game lacks overall depth.
Side Gameplay: Map Creator: Shame it wasn't more complex. Although it works just fine, map makers, and or modders just won't find enough depth here. It may be a side dish, and wasn't really even shown in screenshots, it still deserves critisism.
TL;DR: Just use the randomized planets, don't bother with this.
Side Note: It should be noted that this game, was not the first Planetary Annihilation game. The first one was abandoned, and screwed over the people who payed for the kickstarter. This split the fan base, and ♥♥♥♥ed over anyone who bought the first version. Total♥♥♥♥♥♥move, and it shouldn't be forgotten that Uber did this.
TL;DR: Careful Uber, people won't put up with this again.
Quick Summary and Overall Rating: This game was so close to being great, but so far at the same time. The single player is terrible, the multiplayer is dead. Although the AI Skirmish mode is pretty good. Do NOT give this company your trust, they will screw you over. As much as I would love to add what Uber did into the overall score, I won't, as that wouldn't reflect the game's overall quality.
RATING: 3/5.
(Also, please add in a neutral/in the middle thing for ratings, it's annoying to say good or bad, every time. BTW, yes I do very much so realize that the developers can't add this to thier reviews, I'm not stupid, only dumb.)

Fallout 4 is a game that had a lot of hype and a REALLY good first impression. This however changes as you get into the game. For someone new to the Fallout series it is definately a fun game to play and easy to get into, because the game was watered down severly from its previous iterations of Fallout:New Vegas, a game which I thoroughly enjoyed published by Obsidian, because its style of improving upon the style of Fallout 3 and previous qualities of the Fallout series. Fallout 4 blatently removed a large quantity of the vital compenents to the Fallout series. This happened on a variety of fronts, from the full removal of the skill system, and the repair system (The repair system is not the reason I am leaving a bad review) as well as the change of V.A.T.S. "Vault-Tec Assisted Targeting System" farther from the turn based, first person shooter hybrid, than that of Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas, which offered, in my opinion the best gameplay experience, to a bullet time first person shooter style mechanic. Even though I loved the graphics of Fallout 4, this did not compensate for the massive defecit of QUALITY story. I found Fallout 4 had a very shallow storyline and really failed to deliver on the side quests of the open world game which really identified the Fallout series. There were many side quests, but they lacked the flexibility that the player would have wanted by giving us the abysmal  Arrow speach selector, and not giving us an option to be evil or letting us know what kind of nonsense our character was ACTUALLY going to say when we picked "Sarcastic". This lack of personalization was furthered by the perk system not actually unlocking new gameplay styles for the majority of the game. The player is forced to choose perks like Lone wanderer and Big Leagues if they actually wanted their character to be stronger than a molerat. A player feels much more like a tool to execute a story rather than the player, as they are voiced by one of two people (Male, Female). This game is good if you want to shoot at things that look pretty, like an open world Call of Duty, or want to get an easy to learn introduction to the Fallout series. However for anyone who has played Fallout prior to these point, I would like to say you are going to be disapointed with what you find. Bethesda should have focused its resources into developing story that it decided to devote to Graphics rather than mechanics. It is thought by many people, including myself that the best Fallout game so far was New Vegas, and it is my opinion Bethesda should either move towards the roots of the series or allow a 3rd party (Hopefully Obsidian) to do it for them.

EDIT:
Here's a more fleshed out review for marxgames:
Cons:
- Everything feels very dead. Basically nothing moves, the NPCs rarely have dialogue and the quests are "kill x of y". Runescape had a very lively world in comparison, and it's quests were always something special.
- You can't rearrange things in your inventory. You need to manually equip a forge hammer to use the forge (In RS2 it auto-equips and RS3 the hammer was removed).
- The game's ugly. I know this is a rather touchy subject and a bit of opinion. But from the towns full of people in the exact same pose to the UI that covers half the screen without providing much useful information, it's just not pleasing on the eyes. The tiles get that subtle weird flicker thing in between tiles when you move, and depending on your window size you can see where the tiles stop being drawn at the edges. They need to expand the window of drawn tiles a little further out.
- I don't feel like the progression really made a lot of sense. I felt like to fight the monsters surrounding iron i needed to already have iron to beat them. You could technically just walk around the monsters (they don't move), but that just reinforces my first point.
- I really hope they figure out a better anti-cheat system than the timed Captcha that pops up every now and then. Sure there's a reward for filling it out but I don't really want Captchas to be part of the game loop.
- An extension of the last point: I feel almost like I *am* a bot when I play the game. Cycling between the same [insert color] wizard over and over until my defense reaches [x]. This is a flaw in RuneScape too but at least the things you were hitting moved sometimes it didn't question you about your humanity every hour. It almost feels like they're pointing out how much better the game would be if you were botting.
- Chat takes up half the screen and I can't type things like "Rainbow2:Wave2:Trimming Armour 100k."
- Everything in the starting areas drops a Tomato. Tomatos don't stack or anything. There's not a lot of reason why all the bats in the cave drop Tomatos. It might be a joke but really it just comes off as a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ loot system.
Mixed:
- Infinite Skills. More to do but less to aim for IMO. reaching 99 in RS meant you could go do something else. 99 in everything was a very exciting time. The leader-boards in each skill was good though.
- There are a lot of rules in chat that aren't really made clear to you. One of the rules is that you can't mention other games (like: "anyone excited about the PoE update") unless you're in channel 18 or above (i think). No one uses those channels. I just feel like being a part of the community was too much of a hassle to bother.
Pros:
- The map looked kinda big but I couldn't explore most of it. (things scale fast and your stats grow slowly)
- Probably some other things i didn't get to experience.
- There's home building which sounded cool but like I couldn't dedicate myself to getting to that point. All the recipes looked insane and I've been let down by mmo home-building before. Definitely the coolest feature in the game that I saw though.
I don't usually like comparing games to other games but this game describes itself as inspired by RuneScape and really it just feels like a worse RuneScape. It doesn't really feel like it *improved* much of anything from the source material.
At the end of the day, there are just better games that do the same thing at the same price point.  I only recommend this game to people who somehow like the graphics or are interested in an MMO with leaderboards for grinding skills.

This game was one of the few gaming experiences I will not soon forget.  The attention to detail is incredible.  The visuals are absolutely stunning (especially with the texture pack at night in the rain).  Calling the city an "urban neon jungle" seems like the most appropriate description.  The music selection is also great.  It really suits the theme and mood of "Hong Kong" (yes, the city layout is nothing actually like Hong Kong, but it's done so well who cares?).  The open world is set up in such a fluid and dynamic way that every action you take feels like it was tailored to your specific decisions.  Items and NPCs react to you in a direct and seamless manner.  There are extremely linear games which don't feel as fluid and natural as this one.  The story, while not entirely original, is very well paced and well written.  I waited a while after release to pick up this game and I was very pleased.  It has a GTA/Skyrim type feel to it that keeps you playing.  I completed most of the side missions, which netted me about 30 hours to complete the game.
There are a few minor gripes, though.  I encountered scenarios where an important NPC would get stuck in a doorway or certain mission objectives could not be completed when NPCs wouldn't show up.  A reload did remedy these issues, however.  Also, the story was slightly predictable and cliched but still highly enjoyable.  The gun-play was a little awkward, perhaps due to the odd controls, but the melee action is the real star of this game anyway and was masterfully done.
All in all, this is a worthwhile title.  Seems redudant at this point, but I highly recommend this one.

Now yes, these developers are kind of shoddy for releasing this game twice for full price, but the game itself is
extremely fun. This is one of my first RTS's, and now I plan on playing more from the genre.
Theres nothing more fun than to build a huge army to annihilate other players, and also with the newly added "Titans". The titans literally stomp on anything in their way, and you would need alot of firepower to stop them. There are also a good variety of them, and all of them are unique. For example: The orbital Titan, Helios, can link with a teleporter, fly to another planet, and teleport other units while attacking at the same time. There is even a system creator where you can make your own solar systems.
Unfortunatly, some things have been done slightly wrong. Solar systems seem very empty, only supporting up to 4 planets stably. It can go up to 16, but thats only if your cpu can handle it, and you need a VERY heafty cpu to do that. My cpu so far seems to only support about 8 max. This would be okay if other players spawned more spread out, but on the randomly generated maps there is only 1 starting planet for each system. This is EXTREMELY frusterating because players can spawn really close to you since the planets cannot really support more than 4 people, and having the max amount of players in a game (10) spawn on the same planet can be way too hectic for the size of 1 planet. I once spawned in and I had another commander spawn right next to me. The default maps are a little better in terms of starting planets, but playing the same map over and over again can get repetitive really fast.
You would think the system designer would fix this issue, but it really doesn't. On my PC, it crashes a lot when all the planets generate, making it really difficult to actually make a system.
I also didn't like the lack of options in the game. Compared to Supreme Commander, there are very little options and difficulty levels for AI Skirmish. There is way too little customization for AI Skirmishes

Recently I looked on the store page wondering what others thought of this game, and looking over the reviews I could only see ones that did not recommend the game, and in all seriousness I strongly disagree with these claims.
The game, much like any managment game, plays very slowly, you start off with a barly functioning settlement and create a thriving dwarven city/stronghold/research lab, really whatever you want to make as long as it involves dwarves. From the start you must gather food and minerals, level up your dwarves as you go, fight off monsters, decorate your town/city/fort etc and make sure your dwarves are happy, you need specific materials for specific pieces of furniture and so you should really look to dig everything you can, you can make traps, barricades, grow food and create an army of adorable little dwarves.
Honestly I love this game, it is slow but when you finally finish your 10 story all-marble throne room with pillars and suits or armour it is extremly satisfying. At one time I literally filled up the largest map with a city which I named Moria after the lord of the rings franchise.
The game is slow but satisfying and is NOT for people who do not like both trial and error and having to choose wallpaper for bedrooms...oh also you need to be patient, very patient.
Now, the game itself is only 10 dollars and I got a pre-order of it, it is fairly cheap comparing to most games and much better than a lot of more expensive ones *cough* infection survivor stories *cough*. All in all that is around pocket money price for the average teenage male/female assuming you don't spend it on something else.
As any proper review does, I need to point out the bad. The main point being that it is repetetive, very much so...to the point where the only reason you play story mode is to see what the ending is, which brings me to my next point, terrible writing. The story isn't immersive and feels like it was rushed, VERY rushed. But the levels are thought out well and allow a fun time while you struggle to understand what the hell is going on. And the worst part are the DLC's....ill just leave it like this.
All in all it a very fun game, it sqanders is potential a LOT, however I still love the game, and I love playing it, right now I am still trying to get enough dragonstone to finish my grand treasure chamber so I have to go, but seriously check the game out.

This game is horrendously addictive.
I will initially start with the one thing I really don't like about the game - and that's the conversations between King and Prince - and only because it usually interrupts me as I'm either moving an object or placing one to build - having to click the arrow to continue the conversation is, for me, a niggle.
Other than that, it's quite a simple premise that is developed very well indeed.  I find myself thinking "oh I'll just clear this area here, just a few blocks" and when I eventually look up it's been several hours and let's just say more than just those few blocks, because those few always lead to more, and more, and more...
The storyline itself is quite funny, and if you take the time to read the conversations when they appear, it carries that dry humour through the game.
I've seen some people complain about the DLCs/Stores items that are purchasable with real life pennies - well all I can say to those it what do you expect when the game itself is so cheap for what you get - the small (and it really is!) amount for the extras help create more revenue for the developer, and in my mind that means the developer can afford to spend more time on updates - which is a win!  However, you don't need to buy anything from the shop - it's fluff stuff.  Instead of bed A that is 3 smileys and 4 Z's you can purchase bed B that is 3 smileys and 4 Z's.   Each item you purchase usually cost the same resources as one of the items (from the same group, ie beds) you already have.  So to repeat myself here, you don't NEED to buy anything from the store, you can play just fine without them.
I have only found a 1 bug, but found that others had noticed it as well, reported it, and the developer acted upon it incredibly quickly - so if you do find one, just report it as best you can on the forums.
Now if you don't mind, I'm going to leave this review short and sweet, as I really want to go back in and look after my dwarves :)

First thing I've got to say, I'm more into Hidden Object Games than Point and Click Games.
And while this game was a nice waste of time with relatively easy puzzles, it's infuriating to try over and over because a damned thing won't fit in his spot. Sometimes you need to put it somewhere it doesn't belong for the game to accept it's position.
One example: (not that much of a spoiler)
4 books need to be put in 4 different positions with no clue which colored book goes in which slot. The thing was: more than 4 slots, each with a (seemingly) 5px wide hitbox and a book that changed color while putting it where it should have been. After 3 minutes drag and dropping I finally finished the task but stuff like this surely doesn't make games fun.
But the other riddles were to my liking, especially the puzzles.
The story is... ok-ish I guess. Nothing that you will want to share because 'damn it's awesome', I've heard worse, but the way they told it was quite uninteresting.
One thing that caught my attention: When in fullscreenmode and tabbing out, the game instantly crashes. I don't know if it's just my pc, but it's fairly annoying.
If it weren't for the lousy hitboxes I would have finished this game in way less time than those 2 hours it took me to. Also it would have been a good 1-1.5h time-waster, totally acceptable for 2-3€ at a sale.
But in a state like this, I just can't get myself to recommend it.

Great little horror game.
- Starts off scary but gets less and less scary as the game goes on.
- Can be beat in 15 minutes if you know what you're doing but is about 2 hours long otherwise.
- Has puzzles.
- Does not run very well and may crash when loading saved games after death.
- Has twist ending if you do obscure things. Likely you'll not do them in your first run so there's replay value in trying to get the other ending.
- You can cheat at getting the 'never hit by an enemy' achievement by loading from checkpoints if you get hit.
- Don't try to reattached the leaver from where it came from because it can fall out of the world. It's easy to get stuck at this part since the door forward locks. Bring the leaver back to the wall-box thing.
- There's 2 difficulties: normal and nightmare. Just skip normal because the only differences is normal gives you an unlimited-battery flashlight. You only need the flashlight in monster areas and they're far apart and short. Plus there's an achievement related to beating the game on nightmare.
- The game tells its story mostly with blurbs of text on screen given by clicking on books and papers on the ground. It's 'meh.' There's just background info and vague info about back stuff that happened in the past before the game like basically every horror game.
Over-all I'd recommend this game. If it's on sale and you think you might like it: buy it.

This game is probably one of the best part games out there. It's very fun in the sense of murder mystery and pretty much every role is essential in the game towards helping catch the bad guys or if you're the bad guy, getting rid of the good guys. No matter which side you play on it's a lot of fun. In terms of pros I would say ;
+ good variety of roles each with their own abilities and attributes
+custom gamemodes where you can add multiple roles/ ban roles for added chaos
+ stuff such as the will system, talking to the dead, questioning as jailor, etc. make it somewhat complex and more interesting
+fairly easy to pick up
+there is a cash shop HOWEVER you can earn free coins through acheivements and first wins of the day. These coins can be used to unlock cosmetics and scrolls which give you a higher chance to land on whatever role the scroll is for
However despite how fun this game is, it still has some flaws;
-for a mainly text based game with fairly simple animations it still sometimes lags which can be annoying considering the game revolves around typing so if you're about to be lynched and you need to type up something fast in your defense and a lag spike hits it's annoying as heck
-the community for this game sometimes makes me question humanity. Not only will you get lynched for the stupidest things but also some of these people can't put two and two together. Also a lot of bad trolls such as mafia who will reveal other mafia members, vig purposefully shooting people like mayor, etc.
All in all it's a pretty good game. Keep in mind though that the steam version only unlocks acheivements and some points for the cash shop but you can play this game for free on their official website. I'll give this game an 8/10, I would personally recommend playing with friends if you can as thats when it is the most fun

Squids From Space:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Captain . . . have a listen to this squishing sound - I’ve never heard this sound from space before! Captain . . . have a look at my monitor - it’s the weirdest thing I’ve ever seen in my life! Look in the middle of the screen, it looks like a squid and its getting bigger and bigger every minute; what do we do, Captain? By Poseidon’s mercy, it’s a full alert - we’re being invaded by Squids from Space!
Squids From Space is an action, PvP (8 vs 8) top down tactical shooter where you can play as a soldier to defend the earth or as a squid and try to conquer it.
You will be greeted with a fun 1950’s-style menu with a newspaper headline, reading, “The Squids Are Here!” From that point, you can either checkout the server lists or just press play. Essentially, you have eight contestants playing in each of the races and the your goal is to pick up either the human general or the squid brain from their own base to yours three times in the raw to win the game.

Each of the races has their pros and cons. The squids are better at harvesting than the humans. What do their harvest, you might ask? Well . . . barrels, tables, lights, dresses, car doors and many other things within the map. Each of these items has a points value, and you have one dedicated drop spot per race at the start of the game. There are another two drop spots but you have to gain and retain the spots to be able to use them.  Let me tell you that it will be an ongoing battle and these drop spots will swap hands every few minutes.  Each of the races can unlock four upgrades within the battle by accumulating resources as fast as possible.  A few times during the fight, citizens will need to be rescued (if you play for the humans) or abducted (If you are the squids). These citizens carry the biggest points in the game and can help you reach your level four upgrade very quickly.
You have six different weapons on each of the races when you reach the fourth upgrade. As I mentioned above, the Squids have an advantage in harvesting and they also have a crawling tank, which is so much fun. They also have the invisibility skill but it can only be used for about ten seconds. The humans have great weaponry, including powerful explosives and stand-alone machine guns which can be very deadly. If you play the humans, you must make sure to hit the squid head to register your kill. Be aware though, these squid heads can role and jump on your head to take control of your body.  It’s really fun!
This game is currently on early access and offers one map to play at this stage.  You will be able to find a game very easily, but might be playing against bots most of the time. I did manage to play with other players and boy, it was fun! This is a game to look at closely – It could become something special, in my opinion.
Graphically, the game looks great and runs very well. I personally didn’t have any issues playing it. The controls are very responsive. I really like the 1950’s theme - it’s just great!
Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Great graphics
-	Game runs smoothly
-	Fun and easy to play
-	Good weaponry and upgrades on both races
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Need more maps, only one at this stage
-	No Achievements or trading cards
To be honest, I can’t wait to see more content for Squids From Space. I reckon this could become something special.
8/10

War. War never changes. Unless of course you're Bethesda. This game is so good. I remember I got it almost a year ago for Christmas, and it took forever to download (understandable) but when I played it, I got about 15 FPS. Yeah. You can't play a Bethesda game at 15 FPS. Lukcily, I got it for PS4, so I'm going of that version.
The good: Although the title has "4" in the name, Fallout 4 is it's own game in the same universe as it's presecessors. I remember when I booted up the game, put in my S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats and my name, and Codsworth said it, I legit thought I was part if the game. It just sucks you in. And it's also so addicting, being my most-played PS4 game. But if you want better graphics for that version, and don't care about trophies, then there's a mod you can get that improves texture quality, and the lighting, so it looks like a post-apocolyptic nuclear fallout. Also, the story is pretty good. Now, this is the 1st- and only- Fallout game I've played, so I can't compare it to 3, or New Vegas. But there are REALLY laughable moments in the writing. And I never laughed from writing in The Elder Scrolls. Now, what's bad about Fallout 4?
The bad: Creation Club. Just, really? WTF are you trying to pull, Bethesda? I've already bought the game, and I wouldn't have a problem with paying for the season pass, but paid MODS? Why? Also, speaking of mods, the library on PS4 is really limited.
That's about it. And I highly recommend Fallout 4, because war. War never changes.

Pahelika puts you in the shoes of a man finding a magical book and set on the trail of a mighty one used by a king to defeat  his evil enemy.
The game is a little adventure one, you find objects, you combine with others, you use them and you solve some puzzles (sliders, codes, jigsaws, etc..). You visit different "worlds" (fairies, ice, an old wizard's tower, etc...). While the gameplay is well balanced, there is however a big problem with Pahelika.
It's a problem of hitbox. I was trying to put an object where it should have been to see it being refused. I was on the glittering zone but nothing was working, unless I click a little more above or a little more under. Also, it was not always easy to understand what to do.
I was even stuck at one moment because I couldn't find the switch, that was so tiny, that I thought that the game was bugged. I did a new profile and I wasn't stopped, yet, I realized that sometimes, it was not easy to spot. I don't know for you but when you have to rely on a walkthrough because you're tired of some non-sense, it's not satisfying. I mean, Pahelika falls into the category of games where I feel like I don't need to look for a guide - it's been like that since I play casual games. And having to look for the walkthrough on the Internet is frustrating.
The graphics and the soundtrack are correct, the story is told like a comic, which is a nice feature.... though the guy you're incarnating is different from the header on Steam and drawn in the cutscenes.
Anyway, I can't really recommend this game. Despite a good gameplay, I didn't quite enjoy the game like I should have if it was more polished.

Does SO much right, with a small setting and distinct characters and visuals and good acting and a central mystery to keep you interested, but doesn't have the self-belief to own that and tell a self-contained story. A lot of people writing games seem to feel that stories have to be "Epic" to be interesting, while the opposite is almost never considered, like there's some kind of shame in telling a story reminiscent of a stage play or short story. It's not that less is more, it's that less is more relatable, and thus often less is simply better. CONSORTIUM is one of my new favorite games. The focus is directed entirely towards areas that most games don't get enough love in. Graphics are passable, and there are some minor glitches, but this game is all about the story. With a playtime of 3-5 hours and a multi-dimensional story line, replay value is through the roof. The short playtime also makes CONSORTIUM fairly easy to play in one sitting, which highlights another of its greatest strengths: the way you influence this world really is entirely based on the decisions you make. Each playthrough you are encouraged to adopt a new approach, and seeing the story all the way through in one sitting allows you to stick to the personality you have assumed. There are only a few instances where combat is required, and even then you can avoid lethal force. Or you can kill everyone, but be prepared for there to be consequences.
In summary:
PROS
Excellent voice acting
Smooth writing
Real impact from your decisions
Replay value 11/10
CONS
Below average graphics
Glitchy, but improving with patches
