I used to love the old "Dungeon Keeper" game, but my dungeons always got destroyed when I broke through to the hero's lair because I couldn't keep up with the attacks. "A Game of Dwarves" is styled after "Dungeon Keeper" but has what amounts to a sandbox mode (so you can play and dig and build to your heart's content without being attacked left and right), is brighter (one of my complaints about DK was that everything was dim and dark, being in a dungeon, and that I couldn't see what was going on half the time), is 3D so you can dig up and down as well as sideways, and retains the humour that made DK fun to play.
It's not perfect. The voice acting is a bit weird in places ("what does it take for me to get somebody to listen to meeee"), though in a way that's generally amusing rather than off-putting. The dwarves can be slow to react - especially the military. (I miss the DK Call to Arms banner which at least told your dungeon's inhabitants to respond immediately to attacks. There's something similar in GoD but it's more like a garrison flag, a "mill around here until told otherwise" banner, rather than something you can use to make them react quickly to invasions.) The controls are not always intuitive or explained well (it took me forever and an internet search to figure out how to rotate objects. While I'm not averse to using walkthroughs when I'm stuck, I shouldn't have to look to external sources for
).
You also spend a
of resources on placing tables and beds for your dwarves to lay about doing nothing (they need to eat and rest frequently and die if you put said food and beds too far away for them to reach after their work shift), compared to DK where you'd just build a lair for each creature to live in. Despite that, I still find it easier and less labour intensive to play GoD than I did DK, which had you constantly digging for gold to pay your monsters. With GoD, as long as you've got workers operating your "farms", you can just sit there and let your dwarves take a long holiday.
I haven't gotten too far into the campaign side of the game so I don't know how much harder it gets to keep your dwarves alive. My biggest complaint so far is that the resources are scattered so it's next to impossible to have symmetrical farms that aren't scattered in small pockets all over the place, but that's not a complaint so much as a personal peeve I have with keeping everything compartmentalised.
All in all, I'm enjoying Game of Dwarves more than Age of Mythology, which I paid at least twice as much for,
you can get a few freebie DLC to go with it, so I'd definitely recommend.

I honestly don't know how to feel about this game, as I've only played Fallout: New Vegas before. It's a good introduction to the Fallout universe, considering your character's backstory, so it's easy to get into. I'm having fun. There's a cute doggie. But there are, as with most games, problems as well.
If you like to shoot things (and boy, do I ever) you'll like the way you hardly do anything but shoot in this game. The conversation system is really annoying though; people walk up to you and start conversation trees all at once and it's a bit hard to prioritise. It'd be better to have people approach you one by one, and to mute the surroundings a bit more when they do. Or just keep the old system. That'd work too.
The crafting system in this game is awful! There are hardly any pieces to use, they lock onto each other so rigidly that it drives you crazy and, aside from stores and some crafting stations, you can't upgrade your building skill with perks to unlock more pieces or anything. No architectural skilltree, no blueprints to find in the wilderness - nothing! All you can build are lousy sheds that are full of holes. The rain falls right through the roof, how is that anything like a permanent settlement?! I love crafting systems in games (all of my most played games are heavily focused on crafting) but this is ridiculous. When you can't make a crafting system that rivals even SPORE, why even include it? I would've prefferred to just have a couple of houses that you can buy, like in Oblivion, just make them furnishable; that's enough to make you feel like you've made a little saferoom. The current crafting system seems to have been a little too ambitious, as if they wanted you to be able to create a whole little Sim City, but it feels pathetically unfinished. I wanted to be able to build a little diner for the barman - not a shed. I wanted people to have little brick houses with ruin surroundings to sleep in, like an old abandoned hotel - not a shed. I wanted pretty houses that were kept as clean as possible considering the sad fate of civilisation, like Cabot House - NOT A SHED! I shouldn't be able to build better Fallout villages in The Sims 2 (with mods) than I can in the actual Fallout crafting system!
Fun game, but it doesn't keep its promises of fun crafting. 6/10 - buy it on SALE!

Inspired by classic Hollywood and Asian cinema style action thrillers, Sleeping Dogs is a gritty open-world cop drama set in the vibrant city of Hong Kong. Sleeping Dogs catapults players into the role of undercover cop Wei Shen, tasked with taking down one of the world’s most fearsome criminal organizations from the inside... the Hong Kong Triads. As players explore the bustling and crowded Hong Kong island, through its neon-lit side streets and sprawling street markets, an incredible story unfolds of loyalty and betrayal where Wei begins to question his own motives as he is sucked in deeper than he could ever imagine.
Offering players an island packed with action, every street corner, market stall, harbor dock or city skyscraper can become an opportunity for intense shoot-outs, adrenaline-fueled street races and intense, brutal martial arts combat. Featuring one of the most intuitive and imaginative combat systems, Sleeping Dogs empowers players to perform an extensive set of martial arts moves, singlehandedly taking on numerous opponents. Players perform bone-crunching kicks and combos, vicious counters and a cinematic set of environmental takedowns making use of countless real-world items from circular saws to phone booths, incinerators to refrigerator doors.

Overall Sleeping Dogs is a love letter to Hong Kong cinema; I’ve been mesmerized by its tiny immaculate detail which gives this game so much charisma and charm. Truly one the great gems of this generation.
On a last note, the PC version is just amazing, advance PC options and day 1 HD textures really show that United Front is committed to the PC. Listening to Ninja Tune radio while driving a motorbike down a wet and rainy neon lit sky is just pure bliss.

Ok, initially, I thought this game was really stupid. It seemed really easy. The difficulty kicks up at a good pace, though. Hoverers and Bobbleheads are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, though.
You have the option of playing as 4 (5 with the DLC), possible characters , each with a different specialization.
Skye is the rifle-wielding, double jumping, increasing damage as long as you maintain accuracy character,
Sweets, Skye's sister, is the MASSIVE Rocket Launcher-wielding girl who can set fire to enemies she hits for a nice DoT
Haigen is a rough rider with a shotgun who don't need no man and is willing to get all up in the lumes' business
and SiMo is the sniper who has great accuracy and does more damage to weak spots (orange/red colored areas of the enemies)
If you have the DLC, there's also Tsygan who is very overpowered with the right set up. Moreso than anyone else. She does more damage on the shot that clears the clip.
So you get to make mazes through tower bases in this game and your goal is to defend the core from the attacks of Lumes, the alien enemies on a rampage to get rid of cores for seemingly no reason.
You also can place towers to help you dispatch any Lumes that might come your way.
So this game is basically a tower defense game. It's a really good one, though.
There is such a large variety in towers and there's so few towers you can carry at a time (4, I think). But that's not all. You're also a tower. As such, you can unlock perks that give you special abilities ranging from extra damage to making it so you can GOOMBA STOMP enemies. There's also a plethora of guns you can use to give you more possibilities with how you want to play a particular wave. At level 20, even, you unlock everyone's primary as a possible secondary.
The enemies vary from small suicider to giant heavily armored behemoths. There's a lot of diversity among the enemies, but it's all really generalized to (Fast/Slow) (Ranged/Melee) (Low/Med/High Health) (Light/Med/Heavy armor) (Fly/Walk). What is that, something along the lines of 144 possibilities? Something like that.
Overall, very interesting game with some unique gameplay. Solid purchase.

is a fun tower-defense game that lacks any true innovation but is very well-crafted across all of the fundamental aspects of the genre.  Anyone who is a fan of the genre should find this game enjoyable, and should be happy to have it in their library.
This game is a large improvement over the first one in the franchise.  All of the core gameplay from the first game is still evident in this, with many tweaks and improvements.  Anything you could find in the first game, you can find in this one— but better.  There is also significantly more variety to game modes and level design.
Great fundamentals are at the heart of this game; everything a good tower-defense game needs to do right,
does right.  Also, the wide variety of game modes, map designs, and difficulty levels all contribute to the diverse and enticing core gameplay.  The lighthearted nature and cartoonish humor inherent in the graphics and soundscape encapsulate a charming identity that makes the game unique.  A ridiculously large amount of towers to unlock, random event bosses, and achievements add a satisfying amount of replay value.
has a lot of good things going for it.
The game can be quite difficult at the highest difficulty.  Normally, not a bad thing.  But some levels require an extremely specific solution that, for the average gamer, can take away some of the fun of trying to solve the levels via your own experimentation.  If you get stuck on a level and don’t want to look up the solution online, you can grind coins by playing the game and then buy items or unlock new towers to facilitate your victory.
is a good game, and a great tower-defense game.  There may be no groundbreaking features, but it does have a charming, unique identity and sound fundamentals.  Anyone who truly is an advocate of the genre should enjoy playing this.

I honestly don't know how to feel about this game, as I've only played Fallout: New Vegas before. It's a good introduction to the Fallout universe, considering your character's backstory, so it's easy to get into. I'm having fun. There's a cute doggie. But there are, as with most games, problems as well.
If you like to shoot things (and boy, do I ever) you'll like the way you hardly do anything but shoot in this game. The conversation system is really annoying though; people walk up to you and start conversation trees all at once and it's a bit hard to prioritise. It'd be better to have people approach you one by one, and to mute the surroundings a bit more when they do. Or just keep the old system. That'd work too.
The crafting system in this game is awful! There are hardly any pieces to use, they lock onto each other so rigidly that it drives you crazy and, aside from stores and some crafting stations, you can't upgrade your building skill with perks to unlock more pieces or anything. No architectural skilltree, no blueprints to find in the wilderness - nothing! All you can build are lousy sheds that are full of holes. The rain falls right through the roof, how is that anything like a permanent settlement?! I love crafting systems in games (all of my most played games are heavily focused on crafting) but this is ridiculous. When you can't make a crafting system that rivals even SPORE, why even include it? I would've prefferred to just have a couple of houses that you can buy, like in Oblivion, just make them furnishable; that's enough to make you feel like you've made a little saferoom. The current crafting system seems to have been a little too ambitious, as if they wanted you to be able to create a whole little Sim City, but it feels pathetically unfinished. I wanted to be able to build a little diner for the barman - not a shed. I wanted people to have little brick houses with ruin surroundings to sleep in, like an old abandoned hotel - not a shed. I wanted pretty houses that were kept as clean as possible considering the sad fate of civilisation, like Cabot House - NOT A SHED! I shouldn't be able to build better Fallout villages in The Sims 2 (with mods) than I can in the actual Fallout crafting system!
Fun game, but it doesn't keep its promises of fun crafting. 6/10 - buy it on SALE!

Sleeping Dogs has a great storyline and engaging characters you can't help but feel attached to. There isn't much to dislike about this game, it has plentiful side missions and activities. while not as massive as say, the GTA series is, it is respectable and it is a fresh perspective on free-roam crime games. The sequel (Triad Wars) will hopefully build off what I feel was a great success in Sleeping Dogs. The DLC gives it further replayability although I found 'Nightmare in North Point' to be a bit boring (combat, dialogue, run to next checkpoint. Repeat) Although it may be a preferential thing. The comedy in that DLC however was quite funny. The only gripe I have with the game's story is the ending. Not saying it is bad or ruins the story, it fit quite well but I just have the opinion that it could've been made better.
Price: At the time of this review (Dec, 1, 2013) the price is $25. You'll easily get your money's worth with this game. The story alone is worth it.
Story: While not exactly the best storyline ever written, it is a gritty crime drama and it easily draws you in with a cast of colorful characters (Wei, Old Salty Crab, Jackie, Dogeyes, Big Smile Lee, etc) The only small problem I have with the game is it fails to introduce some characters properly and you're left wondering who is that. Thankfully the game has a sort of codex where you can read stories and bios such as Wei's sister Mimi's bio. I personally feel the story could've been expanded upon and legthened a bit but it is still good regardless.
Gameplay: Gun-play is fluid, has a Bullet-Time mode Wei can activate by jumping over cover or falling down, slows time and allows you to aim and see the red mist from a headshot so you can feel proud of killing an 18k ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. hand-to-hand fighting is even better in my opinion, reminds me heavily of the Batman: Arkham series, you can feel the strength of the punches/kicks and there is a side quest that lets you collect statues to learn more fighting moves. Driving mechanics are decent, and a fresh spin on driving with the 'action hi-jack' allowing you to tail behind a car and jump onto it while driving at high speeds.
RATING: 9/10

I played through the game once and resolved nothing. (Also note, there might be some slight spoilers in this 'review')
My name is Bishop so I figured I am higher in rank than the Pawns and equal to the Knights.
The Rooks are doctors and pilots and the Knight is the commander, so the titles make no sense in regards to power.
I guess if who ever is closer to the king is higher in rank it would go  Bishop -> Knight -> Rook and then it could potentially makes sense, except when I identified with being the security guy (think Adam Jensen from DeusEx) because I found that that slot was vacant on the plane and then me being higher in rank than the Knight makes no sense since she orders me around.
Honestly trying to figure this out took up most of my time playing the game, all I was listening for was references to what my role is. I expected to figure this out quickly so that the game could continue and I could first of all understand the questions in relation to who I am and then answer them as I would like my character to do.
I actually never found out exactly what role I inhabit in the game and when choices come up I am left guessing, I thought 'Oh well if my character is the security guy or special ops or a soldier then I guess that he finds killing people to be a necessity, so I am going to go all out lethal'  and so I did that and what happened then is that I got shouted out by people that I thought were below me in rank.
And all of this is certainly not helped by the utterly confusing titles where everyone calls each other by their rank and number "Rook 13" or "Pawn 44". The numbers have no relation to each other, Pawn 1 is on your plane but Pawn 2 is somewhere else out in the world. I guess the developers want us to know there is more to this organization than our plane, but it just adds so much to the confusion. Also, why do we even have a "Rook 13" to begin with? There are not 13 Rooks on a chess board. There are 4, or on one side only 2. There is only one King and one Queen in the game so why can you have an unlimited number of Rooks? The game does not even have to call this Rook "Rook 13" as there are only 3 Rooks on the plane and one of them insists you call him by his name, Wade, so the developers are already playing within the limitations. (Also as a side note there is only 1 bishop and 1 knight on the plane so that is also within the limit.)
There are some references to other characters which would take this above the limit but none of them are on the plane so it is easily solvable by adding the first letter of the name of the plane (for our crew Z as in Zenlil) as a prefix to their number. So for example "Bishop Z-2".
Now if these two major issues were to be addressed then I am sure the rest of the game would be tremendous, although there was a situation very close to the end where I am asked if I have played the accompanying ARG game and when I answered no I got berated for it and there was no effort made to catch me up on what I had missed and even if they did it wouldn't have made any difference because the question was asked way too late in to the game.
Technically there is nothing wrong with the game, I found no bugs or game breaking issues other than that the game temporarily freezes up between (the admittedly very rare) loading screens. I played through it in one sitting, the voice acting wasn't bad and there is a good pace of breaking up all the talking with some varying action.
Unless I find a reason to play through the game again and I learn a bunch more about who my character is then I don't think I would buy the sequel and as to whether or not this game is worth it, it's fairly short (which can be a good thing), it's mostly about talking and the ending is very abrupt. I personally, even if my review has focused on the bad things, think 15€ is worth it because I appreciate the game the developers have created even if it is flawed in some ways.

Just completed my first run through and this is a great forray into the realm of how interactive and engaging the art of videogames can be.
It is not as polished as other games attempting similar, but for what it attempts, it does it well and is absolutely worth picking up (Especially when it is on sale).
The story for a first timer probably takes about 3-4 hours on the easiest setting.
All of the side missions are easy enough to do and add to the main story.
The music is really good.  I mean, really good.  The end credits for whatever reason remind, at times, of A New Hope or various serious 80s SciFi scores.
It is not an action game though, so don't expect it to be Half-Life.  It is a story game first with rare, brief moments of light FPS-ing.
The only real cons I might have for it are;
Unless you're really in to the lore, you probably aren't going to sit through reading all the data logs in the game, and their bricks of text, that aren't particularly pleasant to sort through when you are looking for something.
If you are sensitive to screen static, it is purposely part of the story and experience, and while not distracting, it is not exactly subtle either.

But there´s no "middle-rate"-finger and that´s why I have to give, like it or not, a negative review. I fully understand that after a game comes out, you´re not so ambitious as a dev to debug the game you made during a long period of time. Squids From Space is a top down 8v8 from the company Fun Bits Interactive. In this universe, squids from space invade Earth and you must fend them off of your land or help them take a new world to call home. Each team has a uniqe set of abilities, weapons, and possible vehicles meaning there is a lot of variety in gameplay.

In Squids From Space you have can choose from two teams, squids or humans, and you can swap any time. The squids have foreign weapons and abilities. This includes, but is not limited to: Massive tanks, guns that blind humans, guns that freeze humans, guns that deconstruct humans and reconstruct vehicles, and invisiblity. All this might sound overwhelming but they arn't the only species that can pack a punch. The humans don't have access to vehicles but make up for it in superior weapondry. They have rocket launchers, machine guns, grenades that heal, grenades that kill, flamethrowers, and many more.
The goal of the game is to capture the enemies objective three times. To do this you must get to the enemy base, take the objective and get it back to your base all without dying. But what if you do die? If this does happen then you drop the objective and it will go back to your enemy's base over time, but you can still take it further. To do this you simply pick the objective back up and take it as far as you can, if you drop it again it will reset the timer for going back to you enemy base. Why not always carry it? Because while carrying the objective you cannot use any weapons or abilities meaning that you must rely on your freinds to protect you. But there is another goal as well, it might not win you the game but it will help. There are various items around the map that can be taken back to your base for resources that bring you closer to leveling up. But why level up? It will give you new weapons, abilites, and if you reach level four your enemy can't. You can just rush the enemy base without worrying about leveling up or you can take your time and slowly grow in power.
Currently in the game there is no customization, one map, and around 6-7 guns per team, but they are planning of adding more of all of that. Beyond that it has a very nice community and wonderful player base, but if no one is on you can still play against AI. They are planning a large update every two months and various bug fixes in between those larger updates.
To me the game is worth every penny but if you are worried about if you would like it, there are tons of videos on youtube that can help you decide. If you think that you would like it but it doesn't have enough content for your liking then you can come back periodicly to see if you are pleased with their new aditions. Overall the nine person dev team are great and will help you if help is needed. If you want to chat with other people that like the game or have questions they have a community discord:

Short, sweet and intense. Pretty good horror game.
Good:
- Very good music. Always fit to the terror or suspense level.
- New game mechanics of rearranging the rooms you visit. Pretty fresh, but only briefly utilised.
- Definitely scary and thrilling. The enemy has very good AI, and really behaves the way it's supposed to. Doesn't really feel like it uses any cheap tricks to damage me.
- Very atmospheric. All locations in the game are well built with no redundancies or annoyances.
- The few puzzles that there we're, were good.
Bad:
- Bugs. Atleast 5 times, when I reload my save, the game would freeze and I would have to force exit. Also a weird bug where one of the 'rooms' came off the table and started floating in mid air where I couldn't reach it, so I had to reload my save which took me back a while.
- Save files. Not anywhere as useful as they need to be. The game should be saved after every completed puzzle, or room completion, or finishing of the next main hall part. As I said, I had a bug which forced me to reload a save, which took me back to the beginning of the previous level I had already completed.
- Lag, screen tearing and FPS issues. It doesn't really matter how powerful your PC is, this game is not optimized well. Most of the game runs fine, at near 60fps for me. But there are a few moments where mini freezes occur during an intense part which is where I need my focus. Also freezes for a second or two whenever it saves.
- Quite short. If you really get into horror games, and into the intensity of them, you might get a good 2 hours of going slowly through and experiencing everything. But once you beat it and know what happens, you can run through the entire game in about 20 minutes.
Overall: 7.5/10 - If you get it on sale
The only reason I wouldn't pay full price is because of how short it is. This doesn't mean it's a bad game or isn't worth your time - it is. The development team here, if given enough of a budget, could really make a hugely successful horror game franchise if they focused their efforts. They definitely have great ideas.

As a game, I don't think it really works.  If you're looking for terror, this game is a great thriller though... but that's it.  In the gaming category it isn't so great.  If that's what you're aiming for, look around a little harder (first-person puzzle/adventure and drama/terror game - you wont find that here, sorry).
Why is it that I don't like it?  Please read...
Well, so it begins... you're dumped somehow in an old manor without any clue as to how you fell in such predicament.  It's almost like you woke up from a bad dream and there you are.  With that, you are left with a flashlight (awesome, and if you choose the hard-game option it may not even work), and you've somehow forgotten how to touch, grab, look, observe, hit, examine, etc. anything that isn't pertaining to your game's progress... no "biggie".  As you explore you find that you're ALL alone.... or are you?  Nope... and this is a spoiler (so don't read further if you don't want to know this) you find something that may "possibly" be alive... a mannequin.. not just any mannequin, but one made out of copper (what the heck?!... copper for real?).  I haven't yet been to the attic, but I already know what the subject of the game might be.... the murderer, the keeper of the manor has been manifesting itself in that mannequin (don't know for sure yet but clues do suggest that).  As you move on, you will probably decipher the fact that guests in the manor were pretty much killed by the keeper at some point.
Be careful with most of this game's reviews.... they DID lead me to take the mannequin lightly.  Don't let it happen to you, the mannequin is VERY MUCH lethal.
Whew, I took that out of my chest!  Well, the biggest issue I had was the fact that the mannequin is indeed lethal, but there are mechanics that just didn't seem to agree with me.  Having played games like Zork, Montague's Mount, Riven, etc (and loved them) you do assume the mechanics will be similar.  I have to blame myself... I hate spoilers so I didn't look for sample videos (I should've).... anyway, there is no inventory, basically as you would in real life you carry things in front of you, BUT this is what is not very real-life-like... remember the above mentioned? (look, observe, hit, etc) you will soon realize that you are DEFENSELESS in every possible which way.... except for room models, I don't think you can actually carry anything else... a key perhaps, but not much else.  That means that if you're attacked in a dark room, you can't swing... despite the fact that the bedroom and library are full of books (and that books have been amazing murder weapons in the past) you can't simply grab one of the damn things and swing them at the dreaded mannequin.
There is no "real" save game feature (I hate that in games).... ok... that's not a big problem for certain games, you complete certain puzzles and there; they save.... NOT this one.  This game sometimes saves RIGHT when you're about to enter a room and sometimes, not even.  That's a problem when you're done getting a model and just want to put the game down.  Such is the case with the bedroom, I am not happy I have to do that sequence again!  It should save everytime you place a model on the main counter.  Why doesn't it do that?!!!
Anyway, it appears you can't really swing that model at the mannequin's face either (if you needed to).... I imagine myself in this game as a disabled person with a mechanical (crane, hand or device) to carry things with... pretty much.
I am not done, and quite frankly, I am unsure whether I want to play this game again :( The issue is not the fact that is scary (not the biggest problem), but when things are scary and you're somehow stupid or disabled, that's just not nice.

At the time of writing I've played Burnout Paradise for a couple of hours. Overall I would recommend it but it has its problems and it is by no means the best Burnout game I've played. The arcade-style driving is really good fun, so much so that on the strength of it alone I will recommend the game. The cars are easy to handle even at the preposterous speeds you will normally be travelling and the game is fairly forgiving when you hit into walls and barriers. There are a large variety of cars of various types and you unlock them at a pleasing steady pace. There are no real world cars but that doesn't bother me becuase cars are boring.
To try out events you simply stop at an intersection and press a button. On the whole the event types are good. There are a few subtly different types of races and a mode in which you have to destroy as many cars in a time limit  There's also a mode that's new to me called 'marked man' where you have to get across the city in one piece while a load of other cars try to destroy you. It's good fun if (so far) a bit easy. One let down is the crash events. In older Burnout games these would be carefully choregraphed sets which required ingenuity to score high damage. Now you simply crash into whatever happens to be in the section at the time. Success in this mode now feels more luck than design.
Throughout the city there are tonnes of jumps and shortcuts. Just driving around with no purpose but to find these is very fun and this is when the open-world setting is really played to its strengths. On the other hand, the open world setting also has the effect of turning races more into exercises of navigation than driving skill or tactics. So far whether or not I have won a race has depended almost entirely on which route I take and not really how I take it. Every race has proceeded thus: the race starts and within 20 seconds at most I have a healthy lead, then I'm not sure where to go because the mini-map is so zoomed in so I take a road which heads in the general direction of the finish line, that road turns out to be a windy road with no exits which takes me back in the opposite direction, then it either it takes me too far out of the way and I quit the race (and annoyingly there is no way to restart the race) or its a minor enough inconvience that I can make up the difference over the other races who all drive incredibly slowly. Now in time I can see that I will get used to the layout of the city and this problem will dissipate as the city is reasonably small. But I imagine this will lead to boredom at the familiarity of the tracks and the setting.
The game is well presented though the menus can be a bit confusing to navigate and I hate being bugged all the time to register online. The soundtrack is reasonably small and consists mostly of bland rock music (but with notable exceptions). Additionally, the DJ who talks to you frequently has already started to grate on me. I imagine he will become insufferable if I put many more hours into the game.
Overall still a good arcade racer but I can't help feel it would have been better to ignore the trend of the time for open world locations and just give us another solid entry in this enormously enjoyable franchise.

A good short game that makes you think and has a lot of replay value.
The visuals are stunning, especially during the cut scenes, and the sountrack is outstanding (I bought it as soon as I finished the game).
The gameplay is fluid and easy to catch onto, and the game itself is really all about choice, where there are no wrong or right answers.  What weapons you choose to customize, with what perks, and which weapons and skills you choose to equip will change your strategy and how you battle.  All of this is completely cusomizable with no real direction or advice from the game.  The game gives you limitations (you can only have two weapons and one skill equiped at a time) and it is up to you how you will work around these limitations to make them work against you or for you.
Furthermore, the story of the game makes you think philisophically, especially towards the end of the game, where you wonder what choise you would make in real life and what the consequences of that choice would be.  The very last choise you make in the game is especially difficult, but unfortunately, it doesn't seem to make much of a difference to the overall game, asides from which cutscene you get at the end.  I have only played the game through once, so I don't know if your final choice has some effect on the next time you play the game in "New Game Plus" mode.
Either way, I really enjoyed this game and highly recomend it.  If you have a thing for games with a retro or indi feel while still being very original, this if for you.

I found this game to be marginally entertaining at best and in no way worth the full price.  However, that is a subjective criticism based on my own criteria for what makes a worthwhile RTS.  So, I'll try to break it down Barney style using less subjective observations and let reader decide if this is a game worthy of a place in their library.
The Good:
- A multitude of units to build.
- There are many methods at the players disposal to destroy the enemy (nukes, zerg tactics, celestial collision, etc.)
- Scale of environment and units is impressively broad.
- Many unlocks and buffs in campaign mode.
- Graphics and animations are good.
- Ample amounts of action and explosions.
- Simple, easy to learn gameplay.
- Voice dubbing was tasteful for an indie developer.
The Bad:
- Expensive (real money) reskins of the commander unit.
- Overhyped game.
- A critical lack of immersion.
- Building an army becomes a chore very quickly.
- Game crashes on the regular.
- Game desynchronizes on the regular.
- Why is this game so buggy?
- Questionable Ethics of the development team.
The Grey:
- Everything is expendable.
- Simple & unimaginative resource gathering system.
- Simple story and plot.
- A thousand ways to achieve one outcome; 'Annihilation.'
- Music is creatively repetitive.
- The music.
- Rounds are over very quickly most of the time.
In short, this game does what it was meant to do very well- be an easy to play sandbox of creative destruction on an unparalleled scale for the casual RTS enthusiest.  Unfortunately, I cant recommend that readers make a full price purchase of this game until Uber tackles the bugs that riddle PA.

Honestly?  Fallout 4 was alright as a shooter/action game but it is NOT an RPG and definitely not a "Fallout" game.  Replay value is meh and the variety of choice (and consequence) is basically controlled by the game.  The new Dialogue system is a disgusting joke and very misleading, the NPCs are about as cool as cardboard cutouts with gimmicky voice boxes (they seem fun and interesting for the 1st 5 minutes but lose their appeal and fun value quickly).
The new VATS system is annoying and worthless, there is almost no character story development or growth.  In addition, the modding system is unnecessarily cumbersome and non-intuitive and the lack of creation tools is almost a deal breaker.  I get Bethesda is trying to grow their player base but for the people who are fans of the previous installments, distance yourself and approach 4 as just a shooter/action game based in the world.  Almost everything that made Fallout what it is was removed.
Overall, if you're wanting a new Fallout, avoid this.  If you just enjoy post-apocalyptic games and action/shooters, then you'll probably like this.
Since the "recommend/don't recommend" doesn't actually help, I would give this game a 5/10 (I enjoyed it but haven't touched it in about a year), and if you're using the Fallout series as a guide, I would give it only a 3/10.

While theres nothing inherently wrong with A Game of Dwarves theres nothing all that good about it either.  I was looking for a Dungeon Keeper-esque/ general RTS game that would fill waste some time and I did find it in AGoD (kind of an interesting abreveation, no?).  The gameplay itself is not terribly revolutionary, you dig out and settle an area, collect resources, do research and train and build an army.  The thing that kills the game for me is the AI, especially in combat.  To intiate combat you must dig into certain areas where monsters may or may not be waiting.  If they aren't you may find a few resources and go along with your day, if there are monsters they usually kill one, if not two, of your diggers because your army is perpetually late to the party.  Your supposed to be able to place down these flags that your army is supposed to stay stationed at but they just dont care about them.  So wherever they are they have to run to meet the goblins or orcs or spiders or republicans or whatevers killing you this time and stop them from stomping your♥♥♥♥♥♥  90% you can dominate them, rebuild your diggers, take their stuff and move on.  10% of the time your army gets wiped out and its game over.  If you lose a battle there is no coming back, theres not enough time to train new units, there simply isn't.  So really the combat consists of coin toss on wether or not enemies show up, a tense few seconds of them stomping around killing whatever they see till your army shows up and then a fierce but usually short battle that either allows you to move on or completely ends your game.  And I just dont think thats fun, probably because it isnt.
Luckily combat is a minor part of the game overall, in my playtime I would say only a sixteenth of it was actually spent fighting anything.  Most of the game is mining and building and on this aspect the game does a bit better (though only a bit).  The minecraft like cubeness of the blocks seems like fun at first until you realise its a pain to fill in any dug up squares and covering them with wood is costly and ugly.  Using the resources you get from mining allows you to build all sorts of things dwarves need in a variety of models.  I made a little barracks once and was really proud of it until I realised I had to dig out the floor to try to find gold so I could continue progressing the story.  So anything you do build on either wastes the resource its built on or has to be gotten rid of eventually which kinda sucks.  Still its fun to be creative and make death pits for miners and cellars full of random cleaning supplies that no one can get to no matter how hard they try.
The art style was okay but it wasn't something I really liked looking at, its cute for a while but it got old for me pretty quickly.  The music got old even faster however, I had to mute it within an hour or so of my first game and pull up something on itunes just becuase it was so bland and repetative.   And there are some glitches that are pretty annoying, though nothing game breaking that I found which in a way was to bad, it probably would've been something fun.
But the reason I cant say I hate this game is that it really pulled me in.  It didnt really mater how boring it got or how annoyed with it I was I just kept saying, "One more area to clear then I'll (shower*eat breakfast*eat lunch*go meet my friends*eat dinner*sleep*etc)."  But no matter how many times I told myself that I would always find something else to do, this archer sucks, better make him practice, if the walls in here were covered in decorative stone it wouldnt look so bad, etc.
I guess ultimately if you need a time waster, this is it, its not the best but its not the worst I've ever seen.  I just think for the money you could find something a bit better.

Not an awful game, but not good. Lets start with the pros first.
Pros:
- Unique and charming graphics and soundtrack
- Decent arcade style gameplay
- Cooperative player interaction
- Unique Progression system
- Good class balance
The thing is the objective is to get better gear to beat better monsters to get better gear and so on. Not my type of game but it gets worse, lighten up your wallet and BUY some of the best gear in the game from the hub shop. Not to mention you cannot have more than one save unless you pay money too.
The whole hub is filled with people spamming the chat offering deals on ingame items, this is not occasional either, Ive NEVER been to the nexus without a spam bot advertising. Also some things are way too dangerous if you arent high enough in gear and level, meaning you can get one shot, and this game punishes HARD for dying, meaning say goodbye to ALL your gear, you cant even go back to your grave, it just deletes your stuff.
Youd think a game about loot would have a good looting system, not the case. There is no auto loot button you have to double click each item, and its limited, meaning if you and a friend kill a boss you will scramble to see who gets the good item. Prepare to be frustrated by doing a team effort against a big boss and only one person gets a reward. Infact now that I think of it, the looting system is nearly identical to that of minecraft, basically meaning it has no place in a mutliplayer face paced arcade game.
All in all its cute, but there is not alot of depth to the gameplay, and you can bypass the point of the game by paying real money. Its a loot game with a bad loot system. Its worth a try only because its free and I pity those who play the game consistently. Go spend your time on a better game.

I honestly don't know how to feel about this game, as I've only played Fallout: New Vegas before. It's a good introduction to the Fallout universe, considering your character's backstory, so it's easy to get into. I'm having fun. There's a cute doggie. But there are, as with most games, problems as well.
If you like to shoot things (and boy, do I ever) you'll like the way you hardly do anything but shoot in this game. The conversation system is really annoying though; people walk up to you and start conversation trees all at once and it's a bit hard to prioritise. It'd be better to have people approach you one by one, and to mute the surroundings a bit more when they do. Or just keep the old system. That'd work too.
The crafting system in this game is awful! There are hardly any pieces to use, they lock onto each other so rigidly that it drives you crazy and, aside from stores and some crafting stations, you can't upgrade your building skill with perks to unlock more pieces or anything. No architectural skilltree, no blueprints to find in the wilderness - nothing! All you can build are lousy sheds that are full of holes. The rain falls right through the roof, how is that anything like a permanent settlement?! I love crafting systems in games (all of my most played games are heavily focused on crafting) but this is ridiculous. When you can't make a crafting system that rivals even SPORE, why even include it? I would've prefferred to just have a couple of houses that you can buy, like in Oblivion, just make them furnishable; that's enough to make you feel like you've made a little saferoom. The current crafting system seems to have been a little too ambitious, as if they wanted you to be able to create a whole little Sim City, but it feels pathetically unfinished. I wanted to be able to build a little diner for the barman - not a shed. I wanted people to have little brick houses with ruin surroundings to sleep in, like an old abandoned hotel - not a shed. I wanted pretty houses that were kept as clean as possible considering the sad fate of civilisation, like Cabot House - NOT A SHED! I shouldn't be able to build better Fallout villages in The Sims 2 (with mods) than I can in the actual Fallout crafting system!
Fun game, but it doesn't keep its promises of fun crafting. 6/10 - buy it on SALE!

Half-Life. The very first game Valve made. Without this game we wouldn't have all of Valve's other games, and neither would we have Steam. And besides that, it layed much of the groundworks for 3d first person shooters. Because of all of this, Half-Life may very well be one of the most important games ever.
I got Half-Life in the Valve Complete Pack, on a summer sale, so it was more of a bonus than anything. This is probably how most people will want to get Half-Life, since it will cost next to nothing and comes bundled with some more popular games (cs:go, l4d2, etc). If you look at it that way, the question becomes more if it's even worth your time anymore, since the game is more than 20 years old at this point. I'm going to say Half-Life is definitely worth your time, if only just to get a greater understanding of Valve and its games. Just know that Half-Life has become slightly antiquated over the years , and some sections are a bit unfair (mainly on the last levels), but it'll give you enough good gameplay and a solid, though simplistic, story to enjoy to keep you going for the 30 of so hours it lasts.

A good short game that makes you think and has a lot of replay value.
The visuals are stunning, especially during the cut scenes, and the sountrack is outstanding (I bought it as soon as I finished the game).
The gameplay is fluid and easy to catch onto, and the game itself is really all about choice, where there are no wrong or right answers.  What weapons you choose to customize, with what perks, and which weapons and skills you choose to equip will change your strategy and how you battle.  All of this is completely cusomizable with no real direction or advice from the game.  The game gives you limitations (you can only have two weapons and one skill equiped at a time) and it is up to you how you will work around these limitations to make them work against you or for you.
Furthermore, the story of the game makes you think philisophically, especially towards the end of the game, where you wonder what choise you would make in real life and what the consequences of that choice would be.  The very last choise you make in the game is especially difficult, but unfortunately, it doesn't seem to make much of a difference to the overall game, asides from which cutscene you get at the end.  I have only played the game through once, so I don't know if your final choice has some effect on the next time you play the game in "New Game Plus" mode.
Either way, I really enjoyed this game and highly recomend it.  If you have a thing for games with a retro or indi feel while still being very original, this if for you.

If you are reading this before the March update, please be aware that there will be additional content in March and additionally in June. I will update this review accordingly for each update.
02/25/2016:
This is another title in the Street Fighter universe. The appeal of this game is the new game mechanics during combat called the V-System. It allows for different features such as a two different reversals for each character called "V-Reversal", a special move(s) that can apply in combos or as an escape route called "V-Skill", and finally each character has the ability to activate their "V-Trigger" which can allow someone like Ryu to have electricity applied to his fireballs which allows him to charge these fireballs to "break" an opponents gaurd if they're planning on blocking the said fireball in this mode. The combat in this game is great, fresh and fluid. Capcom made sure each character had a flash Critical Art or as SF veterans would call them "Supers" which take a full 3 bars of your EX gauge. This is just the tip of the combat in SF as each character has their own set of combos that you'll eventually learn if you favorite/"main" a specific character. Everything as far as the combat goes has been improved and expanded upon. Nothing feels stiff and depending on how you viewed the "focus attack" of SFIV, it's removal is noticed in SFV. The graphics of SFV make the game shine. Even the music in SFV really stands out as you can enable all songs via options during the menu while you wait for a match, ranked or casual. There are even "endless" lobbies that allow you to set the match conditions. Want to go first to 10? You can do that. Yes, you can rematch for another FT10 if your heart desires. I would recommend this game to anyone who has grown to love SF.
However, this game is bare bones. For what it's worth, SFV is solid in gameplay but the noticable lack of content puts a damper on finding out how great the gameplay is. Story mode is very short. I understand that the current story mode is prologue stories of each character and maybe Capcom should have a description of that as you hover over "Story Mode" in the menu to make people aware. There's no challenge in the prologue story at all. You start with max super/Critical Art bar and max V-Trigger bar against a punching bag AI opponent. Maybe Capcom wanted everyone to get to know the story of V so that it's not so hard to understand the upcoming June update Cinematic Story Mode. Either way, you get Fight Money and levels for each character story you complete. When you level up, you also get Fight Money that you can later use to purchase DLC characters or even character costumes with the upcoming March update.
Survival mode is where Capcom must want the single player focus to go towards until the Cinematic Story Mode comes out. This is said to be due out in June and will essentially be an overall SF5 story mode that ties together everyone based on the events that happen in V. In Survival mode, there are 4 difficulties; Easy -- This puts you against 10 AI opponents. Completing this difficulty will unlock color #3 for the character you beat the mode on and a title for said character. So, you beat it with Ryu? Great. You get a title and #3 costume for Ryu. Sounds easy, right? Sure. For easy mode. Next difficulty is Normal -- This difficulty puts you against 30 AI opponents. You get a few colors this time. #4, #5, and #6. Next we have Hard. The game just throws more AI opponents at you but this is where you can tell the AI doesn't play around. I don't want to say it cheats but they have on demand reactions against you if you whiff, don't punish them or if they get dizzy they will mash out of stun/dizzy state in 1 second. Be fast. You get suppliments each round. Make sure to use the health and power up respectively. Be careful the later opponents as they really good and actually do damage.This will feature 50 AI opponents.  If you manage to beat this difficulty you will get colors #7, #8, #9 and #10. If you are only aiming for colors, you're done. However, there is another difficulty; Hell/(Achievement calls this mode Extreme) and it's no joke. It's HELL. 100 AI opponents. They are challenging from the start and won't be afraid to push your $#!T in.
It's sad to see that the only content in this game is survival or multiplayer. SFIV had more content than this on launch back in 2009. If you're wondering why this game has the rating that it current does as of 02/25/2016 (43% out of 3,511 reviews) then my review is a good reflection of that. I like the gameplay and thus would recommend this game to people who do their research. If you've grown up playing Fighting Games like I have since SFII in arcades, then you'll love this game. If you like fighting games but like fighting games with content, wait until this summer. Capcom launched this game so that 2016 could kick off Capcom Cup with a new game and SFV is that game. The closer we get to Capcom Cup and even after, this game should be filled with content. The beta tested audio content if you were happened to be matched up with a qualifier, finalist or even winner of Capcom Cup and even EVO, so be sure to play around those times to see how neat this game can be. If you're new to fighting games and this would be your first fighting game, I would wait until June when this game will complete.
tl;dr Only buy this game if you do your research and are okay with a barebones game now that will be complete by June, 2016. If you want my opinon, I would buy it and recommend it to those who have played SF before, even just button mashing.

Every time you want to craft items and sell it in your shop, you HAVE to play a mini-game. You can hire other players to 'work' for you. Every amount of orders they fill, you pay them. The puzzles are challenging but simple as well.
Prices for commodities go up and down just like in real life. You need these commodities to fulfil orders in your shop.

Overview: Traditional Tower Defense
The Good:
+ Bright colorful graphics. Towers, enemies and special effects are unique, vibrant and can be easily distinguished from one another especially when a lot is happening on screen.
+ 25 levels spread across different game modes and 3 difficulty levels. Each map provides a different entry/exit points along with different obstacles/hazards that you can use to your advantage.
+ Multiple game modes: Survival is your traditional tower defense game. Time attack has you killing a certain amount of enemies before time runs out. Sudden Death pits you against a never ending massive wave of enemies, forcing you to kill a certain amount. Puzzle mode is a twist on the standard tower defense formula by changing some of the rules forcing you to think very carefully where you place towers on the map.
+28 different tower types, 23 different types of enemies and 5 rare elite enemies that randomly show up in certain maps. Each tower is unique and has its own strengths and weaknesses.
+The game has items that can be purchased with coins that you get by completing levels. These itmes are completely optional as every level can be completed on the hardest difficulty without them. The items are a good way to perfect your strategy and provide some help on some of the harder maps.
+ The achievements are much more bearable than its predecessor. Only a limited amount of achievements require grinding
+ Good difficulty balance
The Average:
The game is an ios port and that may turn some people off. In order to get items and some of the new towers you first must purchase them with coins. Coins are collected after every map. These however are strictly optional and are not required to finish the game. In app purchases have been removed from this version and the cost of each item/tower is significantly reduced over the ios counterpart. You will gain a lot of coins simply by playing the game and I never felt the need to grind for coins other than for an achievement.
The Bad
- Does very little to innovate the genre
Conclusion
This is a great tower defense game and makes some significant improvements over the first one. Anybody looking to get into the genre or is looking for a new game to play, this is a great game to check out just to expect anything new or exciting.

I've thought a lot lately about why I like this game so much. It's the emphesis on being part of a crew. Of knowing every job on the ship and jumping to it before the captain has called an order. Keeping the guns primed and firing, keeping the ship afloat and not treading on other crew member's toes to do it all. Running a boat crewed with a group of friends is, pardon the pun, a blast.
The satisafction of a well timed, well aimed long range canon shot when you rely on another player to steer the ship to aim the canon, while you factor in fuse burn time and the rolling of the ship in the waves to judge the perfect moment to take the shot - its challenging in a different way to most shooters I've played. Of course you still have the close quarters action when ships ram and board each other, aiming your muskets to snipe across the water, timing your sword strokes, lobbing grenades onto enemy decks as you pass in a fairly well realised melee system.  It's different though, and that's the appeal. I'm playing something that doesn't feel like everything else and I'm really enjoying it.

I write few reviews, but I wanted to put in a good word for this game.
Firstly, this game more then met my hopes and expectations.  I was dubious because it tries to do many things and seemingly faces some huge tech hurdles for such a small team, but it does deliver.  I think it's the best naval combat experience out there, even in it's slightly buggy not quite polished EA form.
But more noteworthy, it's the first game where teams have captains/squad leaders/commanders/whatever that really lives up to the primise of that feature/structure.  A good captain makes the game great fun.  A crew that all works together wins much more often then not, and crews where everyone ♥♥♥♥s off and does their own thing do fail and fail hard.
Perhaps it's the fact that this game does not have the hundreds of thousands of players that Battlefield and the like have, and so it's a self selecting community of people who really want to give it a go, but in my first 4-5 hours I've had almost entirely crews that do work, and it's been great. I'm happy to man the guns and patch the leaks and help board etc.  I'll captain a ship eventually, but first I have more learning to do.  As it should be.
So, if you are on the fence, as I was for a while, I hope I can nudge you to get on board, it's a lot of fun.

Don't let my playtime fool you (as I write it currently sits at 8.8 hours), I played hundreds of hours of this bloody game on the PS4.  That may make it seem like I like this game.  And I do.  But it's terrible.  Hear me out.
It's got the addictive quality down thanks in part to some of the new features added to the game, like crafting and settlement building.  They add a new dimension of management and of course, game breaking.  Basically what you do is level up your science perk, build a bunch of industrial water purifiers in Sanctuary, then every day or so, take the hundreds and hundreds of cans of purified water down to Diamond City to flog the lot.  You will never ever run out of caps.  Then clean out all the shops of their ammo and go around shooting things.  THAT is what kept me coming back.  I didn't care about the story, I just wanted to shoot things to level up so I could shoot things deader.  That's all.
Basically what I'm saying is the combat is the best thing about this game.  Much better than 3 and New Vegas, and don't get me started on 1, 2, and Tactics.  Helping the combat mechanics are nice enemy variants that scale with your level: as you level up you find tougher and tougher enemy viariants that in turn reward more XP.  Awesome!
The environments and music are much nicer this time around and the dynamic weather system is the♥♥♥♥♥♥
But that's where the good ends.
Where do I start with the issues.  I know.  I said I didn't care about the story?  The reason is that Fallout 4's story is execrable.  And I mean it.  Total first grade garbage.  Not that it doesn't have nice ideas, but the worst execution imaginable.  The writing is the worst of it, and I mean this is some next level crap.  It wastes no time in showing you up front how terrible the writing is gonna be when the protagonist drops the line "war never changes" FOUR TIMES in the first five minutes of the game.  Sorry did I say protagonist?  My apologies, if you're a lady player what I MEANT was the soon-to-be-dead husband character who gets top billing on the narration.  Bethesda makes it totally clear that they INTENDED you to play as a man, which is absolutely unprecedented not just for an RPG, but even for a Fallout game.  The intro demolishes any semblence of "making your own story" by telling you what your story is then asking you to fulfill the story they've already written for you in this open world RPG with emphasis on player freedom.  Seeing the issues yet?
I'm not going to sit here and keep poking holes in the story because I might as well write this into a book if that were the case, look up Joseph Anderson on YouTube and he'll do it for me.
The dialogue system literally could not be worse.  I have never seen a mechanic with so little effort put into it, it is beyond any shadow of a doubt the worst dialogue system I have ever seen, it could even compete with Dark Souls, which wasn't SUPPOSED to have a dialogue system.  The reason for this is that it may as well not exist, the conversation will move forward the way the writers intended no matter which option you choose.  Some scenes will have all options lead to the same line, but all, without fail, no matter what your character says, will end in your conversation partner carrying on the same way.  You are a totally useless pawn in this system which is essentially a bunch of cutscenes with interlaced QTEs.  Yes it is that bad.  It is an indefensible disaster of a dialogue system.
The game is utterly broken, so broken I'd hesitate to even call it finished.  Everywhere is people levitating, clipping through scenery, AI running into walls, more recently I had control wrenched away from me to show a conversation between Piper and her sister that I could barely hear and wasn't even happening anywhere near me.  I'm not kidding.  Patches have not saved this broken down mess of a game.
Preston Garvey can die.
So can Mama Murphy
So can Trashcan Carla
The weapon crafting system is deceptively limited, you'll exhaust all the options rather quickly.  It's fun, yes, but could be better.  Same with armor mods.
There was this big marketing thing about recording thousands of common names so you could be called by name in conversation?  Remember that?  Did you notice after playing it that it was lierally only Codsworth who would do that and the devs deliberately misled you?  Or how about the new facial animations and body language that's only shown in one scene.  Effort be damned!
Also, the leveling system is shallow and vastly inferior to previous games, abdicating a specialized character and just replacing the idea with the sole goal of having all the stats and perks at once and essentially becoming a demigod.
Also the intro is still too long.  Take some pointers from Obsidian because New Vegas' intro was perfect.
I am shocked by the positive reception this game got.  I still play it because it's possible to have fun with it.  But Bethesda can and should do way, WAY better than this.  This kind of horrendous design should not be encouraged.  To that end, and especially because New Vegas exists and is way cheaper and is definitely world's better, I'm not going to recommend this one.

As someone who, admittedly, has been both on the "whiteknights" and the "haters" sides of the neverending argument, I can tell you that, as always, the truth is in the middle... but definitely at least inclined towards the negative side.
If you buy this game as it is now (don't mind the "early access" disclaimer, after this long it doesn't matter anymore) you get a very limited experience with one of its few redeeming qualities being that it looks pretty. If you want to buy the game anyway in hopes that the full version will be better, as someone who has followed development from day one, I think I can almost safely say that these people lack the means and direction to make it the great game they promised it to be, and it's flawed at its core.
I still kind of enjoy it, I wish it was better, I wish it was at least 10% of what they promised, and I have some hopes residing in the fact that after a bit of time after the game will be out of beta will have passed, the devs plan to hand it over to a b-team for constant updates, so there's a (still unsafe) bet for the game to express its full potential then I guess.
Too bad that at this pace we'll get to see the result of said coin flip in 2088.
Anyway, don't get me wrong: it's not like it has 0 content, but the core game is lacking and the devs have taken the abysmal path of trying to develop its basic features and at the same time try to release more pretty furniture and stuff that will get old fast to keep the fans pleased until """release""". Basically, they are hoping to buy time but in the process they are wasting time, progressing at a snail pace and showing multiple times that they are still unsure about the game's direction.
They still get at least a bit of my respect for being relatively new at this and aiming so high, but as of lately they seem like they have relaxed a lot, especially since they can just publish other games to sustain themselves (sounds familiar?).

Blackwake is a fairly simple game focused on pirate ship combat, akin to other games like Pirates of the Caribbean Online and Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, only with the focus being shifted to a more in-depth look at how a ship is maintained in a combat situation by the way of fully-player-manned workings, in order to give the most realistic idea of how a ship runs. This means that multitasking, communication, and skill are much more important in this game than in those similar, as a well-oiled crew in this game can result in an astronomical advantage in a fight.
When you spawn into a regular ol' server (across a widening array of gamemodes with a maximum playercount of 54), you are given a choice between joining a British fleet, or a group of pirates. You will then choose a ship to join on whichever side you chose, where you will typically be promted with a loadout menu that includes primary and secondary weapons, along with some special items with an array of uses (like health items, grenades, etc.) and a melee weapon. Once you choose that, you are free to move about your ship. It will also ask you if you wish to nominate yourself as captain, your previous experience will be shown in the public vote as a reliability %, and you can add a description if you so choose. Captains mostly just pilot the ship and issue orders using a command wheel or voice chat, regular captain-y stuff I guess.
As a regular crew member, you are in charge of keeping the ship in working order by doing one of the following tasks:
- Reload cannons using a supply box located near it (Powder>grape shot/cannon ball/grappling hook (if the captain orders it)>ramrod the contents inside>push it into position), and obviously use the cannons
- Go to a predetermined spot on the ship to pick up and replace supply boxes if they are low
- Repair holes in the hull (if left unrepaired, the ship will sink)/a broken nose (ramming, disables ship movement)/torn sails (slows the ship)
- Pump out water at a pump
- Smother fires using water buckets
- Use side-mounted swivel cannons to destroy enemy sails (no reloading needed)
- Fight if boarded or is caught in the act of boarding
- Repair cannons destroyed by enemy cannon fire
- Steer if the captain is not doing so
Most of those tasks that can be awarded with a set number of points, leading to leveling up (and gaining cosmetics) and climbing the leaderboard. 4 special players are called out at the end of a match for extra merits (most deaths by cannons/ best captain (determined by number of crew hits on enemy ships)/ most repairs/ most ship hits).
In the game there are currently 4 ships (2 more planned currently)
- Hoy/Sloop (smallest ship, 4 guns on each side, 7 men)
- Junk Ship (medium sized, new so info come later :3)
- Schooner (medium sized, new so info come later :3
- Galleon (largest ship, 2 decks, 8 cannons on the bottom deck (2 in the front and back) and 2 on either side of the top deck)
The captain can choose the name of the ship and its colors when they are elected
I'll be adding some more info in the future, but that's really everything that needs to be said for something thinking about getting the game. In conclusion, it's a very good game for someone looking for a more in-depth look into ship combat, and you do get what you pay for, free updates inculding (and still coming). While the playerbase in considerably smaller than other similar games, you won't have trouble finding at least one server per gamemode that has a good amount of players in it (if it isn't already maxed), so that issue is negligible. It's worth it if you think it'll be; there's a lot of good times to be had, mate.

If it's on sale for $5 or less, there's no reason to avoid it, but there's also not a lot of reason to invest more than a week into it.
The fps element added to the tower defense adds less than one would expect.  The game gives the player an empty field.  The player makes rows with pylons to maze the monsters.  The player upgrades one of his towers between rounds and pew pews in fps mode during them.
There are only a few monster types, and despite having different strengths and weaknesses, the tower placement strategy is no more interesting than making sure the right types of towers are built for the right monsters.  The fps strategy is similarly simple: shoot them in the weak spot until they die.
The level of challenge is good for most levels, and the multiplayer is pretty fun.  Nevertheless, I can't think of a reason to prefer this over Dungeon Defenders, which has a lot more tower and character configuration strategy involved in addition to a more compelling levelling system.

I've thought a lot lately about why I like this game so much. It's the emphesis on being part of a crew. Of knowing every job on the ship and jumping to it before the captain has called an order. Keeping the guns primed and firing, keeping the ship afloat and not treading on other crew member's toes to do it all. Running a boat crewed with a group of friends is, pardon the pun, a blast.
The satisafction of a well timed, well aimed long range canon shot when you rely on another player to steer the ship to aim the canon, while you factor in fuse burn time and the rolling of the ship in the waves to judge the perfect moment to take the shot - its challenging in a different way to most shooters I've played. Of course you still have the close quarters action when ships ram and board each other, aiming your muskets to snipe across the water, timing your sword strokes, lobbing grenades onto enemy decks as you pass in a fairly well realised melee system.  It's different though, and that's the appeal. I'm playing something that doesn't feel like everything else and I'm really enjoying it.
The main reason I highly recomend this game is because I want there to always be populated servers to join. I really like it and I think a lot of people would too if they gave it a bash.

I write few reviews, but I wanted to put in a good word for this game.
Firstly, this game more then met my hopes and expectations.  I was dubious because it tries to do many things and seemingly faces some huge tech hurdles for such a small team, but it does deliver.  I think it's the best naval combat experience out there, even in it's slightly buggy not quite polished EA form.
But more noteworthy, it's the first game where teams have captains/squad leaders/commanders/whatever that really lives up to the primise of that feature/structure.  A good captain makes the game great fun.  A crew that all works together wins much more often then not, and crews where everyone ♥♥♥♥s off and does their own thing do fail and fail hard.
Perhaps it's the fact that this game does not have the hundreds of thousands of players that Battlefield and the like have, and so it's a self selecting community of people who really want to give it a go, but in my first 4-5 hours I've had almost entirely crews that do work, and it's been great. I'm happy to man the guns and patch the leaks and help board etc.  I'll captain a ship eventually, but first I have more learning to do.  As it should be.
So, if you are on the fence, as I was for a while, I hope I can nudge you to get on board, it's a lot of fun.

Blackwake is a fairly simple game focused on pirate ship combat, akin to other games like Pirates of the Caribbean Online and Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, only with the focus being shifted to a more in-depth look at how a ship is maintained in a combat situation by the way of fully-player-manned workings, in order to give the most realistic idea of how a ship runs. This means that multitasking, communication, and skill are much more important in this game than in those similar, as a well-oiled crew in this game can result in an astronomical advantage in a fight.
When you spawn into a regular ol' server (across a widening array of gamemodes with a maximum playercount of 54), you are given a choice between joining a British fleet, or a group of pirates. You will then choose a ship to join on whichever side you chose, where you will typically be promted with a loadout menu that includes primary and secondary weapons, along with some special items with an array of uses (like health items, grenades, etc.) and a melee weapon. Once you choose that, you are free to move about your ship. It will also ask you if you wish to nominate yourself as captain, your previous experience will be shown in the public vote as a reliability %, and you can add a description if you so choose. Captains mostly just pilot the ship and issue orders using a command wheel or voice chat, regular captain-y stuff I guess.
As a regular crew member, you are in charge of keeping the ship in working order by doing one of the following tasks:
- Reload cannons using a supply box located near it (Powder>grape shot/cannon ball/grappling hook (if the captain orders it)>ramrod the contents inside>push it into position), and obviously use the cannons
- Go to a predetermined spot on the ship to pick up and replace supply boxes if they are low
- Repair holes in the hull (if left unrepaired, the ship will sink)/a broken nose (ramming, disables ship movement)/torn sails (slows the ship)
- Pump out water at a pump
- Smother fires using water buckets
- Use side-mounted swivel cannons to destroy enemy sails (no reloading needed)
- Fight if boarded or is caught in the act of boarding
- Repair cannons destroyed by enemy cannon fire
- Steer if the captain is not doing so
Most of those tasks that can be awarded with a set number of points, leading to leveling up (and gaining cosmetics) and climbing the leaderboard. 4 special players are called out at the end of a match for extra merits (most deaths by cannons/ best captain (determined by number of crew hits on enemy ships)/ most repairs/ most ship hits).
In the game there are currently 4 ships (2 more planned currently)
- Hoy/Sloop (smallest ship, 4 guns on each side, 7 men)
- Junk Ship (medium sized, new so info come later :3)
- Schooner (medium sized, new so info come later :3
- Galleon (largest ship, 2 decks, 8 cannons on the bottom deck (2 in the front and back) and 2 on either side of the top deck)
The captain can choose the name of the ship and its colors when they are elected
I'll be adding some more info in the future, but that's really everything that needs to be said for something thinking about getting the game. In conclusion, it's a very good game for someone looking for a more in-depth look into ship combat, and you do get what you pay for, free updates inculding (and still coming). While the playerbase in considerably smaller than other similar games, you won't have trouble finding at least one server per gamemode that has a good amount of players in it (if it isn't already maxed), so that issue is negligible. It's worth it if you think it'll be; there's a lot of good times to be had, mate.

text: This game took me by surprise. I always liked early GTA games, and I thought this game would be a good comparison. And boy was I right. In fact, I enjoy it a LOT more. The story is well-crafted, and surprisingly well-written. The gameplay is solid, the combat feels like those of the Batman: Arkham games, and the driving is really exhilerating, especially if you're using a controller. I guess that could be one downside: the game does play better with a controller. After all, it is a port from Xbox. But other than the controls, it really doesn't show the fact that it's a port. This game plays beautifully, and the graphics are absolutely gorgeous. Turning world density all the way up makes i feel like a real city, and the free High Res Texture pack only adds to the fidelity of this "sleeper" hit. No pun intended. Well, maybe a little. Okay, yes, pun intended. I highly recommend this game.

A beautifully well-written game. It throws you in the deep end plot-wise, but that is actually a plus for this game as you work out just what kind of situation in. Quickly into the plot, it develops into mysterious and, for once, actually believable mystery game. The one (or two, depending on your choices, I hear) proper shooting sequence has mechanics decent enough to make it enjoyable and I assume it's a taste test for the sequel, which will likely have more. Kudos to the developer for making the mystery cohesive and giving the player a truly stumping series of events. I only got it right because I noticed the culprit doing some dodgy acts before the investigation. The culprit was believable and I did not find myself irritated by any cliches. The plotline thankfully avoids many, many cliches. It is also brilliantly well acted, and the variance of accents really gives it a feeling of a futuristic, almost united world. The plot also reminds me of 1984, and gives the player perfect reason to support any of the factions (or neither, like me). I find most games flop when they try to write as intricate plot as this, either falling into cliche or simply being way too over its head to be coherent or well written. This game, however, does it well and gets a high reccomendation from me. A little short, but still well worth the investment. Can't wait for the sequel.
By the way, your choices change a lot. Unlike most games *cough cough* Telltale's Game of Thrones *cough cough*, every choice is significant and you also know when a significant decision must be made. You understand the severity of the events at all time and the game throughout is very intense. I'm so glad this game did its choices and consequences right.
