Alright so I'm not normally the guy to write Reviews but here we go :
I saw this Title for 1,50€ on sale and since I played it countless of hours on my playstation3 I thought might aswell grab it while its practically free (compared to the 1 1/2 burgers you'd get for that money)
While downloading this game I watched the reviews for this game. Normally I do that before I buy games but well I knew what I buy here.
So my shock was even greater when I checked all the negative reviews while downloading this game, speaking of constant crashes, the most abysmal port they have ever seen etc.
Let me tell you this, maybe im one out of a thousand (I don't think so) but so far this game works flawlessly for me. Even better than on console.
Many bad reviews were given because apparently the game is crashing on their side because of some webcam issue because the game wants to take a picture of you for your drivers license.. Did these people never open the configuration before starting the game? You can disable the webcam there. BOOM. Done.
Also I saw bad reviews because apparently the game didn't pick up the xbox controller. I started the game, took my xbox controller in my hand and rocked through Paradise City.
There were also many bad reviews because its an open world racing game and they were saying as how you would get lost and only look at the map while driving.. Yeah, maybe, if you just start the game.. but after years of not playing this game I bought it today on PC, jumped into the game and could still drive like a master through this awesome designed city, I still knew all the shortcuts i basically felt right at home. Just because the game doesn't only give you one simple straight path with no other choices to drive on doesn't make it a bad racing game - it ju
There is one bad point about this game. It seems as if the developers dropped the ingame DLC's you can buy. So you can no longer ingame spend your money on other cars (and lets be honest here, you can get about 6 normal cars and idk 15 toy cars which never appealed to me) but i've heard there is a fix for that which just unlocks all the cars without having you to spend anything. ALSO THIS DOES NOT MEAN THAT ONLINE WON'T WORK ANYMORE. As far as I could see all online functions were still working just fine.
Yes, its a bit different from Burnout 3 (which is still the best in the series imo) but there is really a LOT of fun to be had here. In some aspects I like it even more than BO3 because of the open world you get to know places and even though no race is like the other after and after you learn the city and later missions aren't just harder because the A.I drives more unfairly but also because it becomes hard to combo all the shortcuts you've learned on the whole map into one good run on a race.
I think for 1,50€ it is INSANE value, even for the full price at 6€ I still think its basically stealing from the developers. I played at least 200hours on playstation and I didnt even get into online thaaat far. By the way, Online functions are really great in this game.
To be honest I would still be recommending it for 20€.

Fantastic game. Terrific visual-design, spot-on gameplay that is both fair and fun, great soundtrack, and great players online. It's a 10/ 10, if you ask me.
The reason there are so many bad reviews is because the online service was more or less offline at the time of launch, and there is currently very little single-player content to enjoy. However, even prior to this game's release, CAPCOM stated that there was more content on the way in just 2-3 weeks, so there will be more single-player content soon, and there will be more characters as well, which can either be earned for free by collecting in-game currency, or by purchasing them like the old, simple days.
Instead of going out for a walk, or at least taking a deep breath, everybody came to this review-section with a sledgehammer, wanting to get blood on it.
Despite the rocky start for this game, I appreciate the fact that CAPCOM has made a very well-balanced game that will be fiercely competitive, and that they opted to release what they could as early as possible, for the community of hardcore fans who know no better gaming-situation than a brand new STREET FIGHTER game, prioritizing the competitive community, and simply adding more content which has been so sorely missed by the casual players at a slightly later time --- only 2-3 weeks after release, as earlier mentioned.
I recommend this to anyone, because the game has a smart mix of simplicity in its controls, and depth with strategies and more at the core. The characters' playstyles and visual designs each cater to pretty much all preferences of the general public.

I only paid 2 dollars and 49 cents for this game, yet still I regret that I purchased this complete and utter shash.
Fieldrunners 2 is simply a terrible tower defense game in every single respect. Obviously aimed at mobile money markets with microtransactions removed for PC, this is definitely the worst tower defense game I've played in several years. Generic cartoony graphics don't even attempt to hide the lack of originality or character (but still somehow the game has long load times even on 2500k @ 4ghz, GTX 780, 16gb DDR3, and SSD). The levels, characters, and art design are generic flash TD fodder and have not a single iota of verve, originality, or even competence.
Seriously, I wonder if all the other products that this game rips off even realize it? For example I bet Valve doesn't realize that they stole the TF2 Heavy model and animations almost verbatim (plus the TF2 soldier model and anims, just to name two), and several other models and animations have been copied slavishly from other titles. There are almost no options in the game for anything whatsoever. As far as I can tell there is no hotkey to instantly restart a level, or to bring up the normal ESC menu with the normal options. Apparently you have to click on it, because if you hit ESC it instantly asks you if you want to quit the game. Clueless, greedy, incompetent mobile devs. Yuck.
Beyond the simplistic mobile approach and total lack of creativity, competency, or imagination, the worst failing of Fieldrunners 2 is that it's built entirely around the worst TD grind mechanics you can imagine, and they're all hidden invisibly underneath a layer of flash/mobile simplicity. The waves are seemingly endless, randomly thrown together without thought, and invisibly leveled in HP while still using the same models and animations, with no indication that the enemies are gaining massive amounts of HP. There is no "next wave" button or indication of what the next wave comprises. One of the earliest levels has 50, yes FIFTY equally boring and generic waves, most of which comprised identical looking enemies whose HP scaled invisibly up to the moon. Who likes that? Maybe someone on mobile who has never seen a tower defense game, but even then only for the first hour or two.
I get that the game sucks and grinds purely to drive microtransactions, but I rebel against this negative approach to game design. It creates enemies out of your customers and generally makes people hate you. -I- personally hate you, Subatomic Studios, for this game. You created an enemy out of me, and I will make sure to track your company in the future purely to avoid your products and warn people about how much you suck. This game should have never been released on PC, or anywhere. It is trash. Total, complete, and utter trash.

Fantastic open-world action game! The undercover cop drama story is the perfect combination of tongue-in-cheek Hollywood cliche' and intense, moving drama with memorable characters about whom the player actually learns to care, getting pulled in to the high-octane madness and thoroughly enjoying the ride. It's one of the stories where one kind of knows where it's going, but still intensely enjoys finding out how it gets there.
The city is expansive and interesting, with huge amounts to explore and do, and the driving is extremely good and fun. There's a decent variety of cars and motorbikes with which to get from A to B, and there are cabs for quick-travel if one gets tired of long drives. The combat is ludicrously fun, violent, and satisfying, with a deep and rich combo system and seamless, fluid fights with counters and lots of awesome environmental takedowns, not to mention the good cover system and gunplay. It's never very difficult, but neither is it easy to the point of tedium.
The graphics and sound are great, especially with the hi-res textures DLC (Free), and the game is stable and well-optimized. I never had one crash or really noticeable bug in around twenty hours of game time.
Absolutely recommended, I enjoyed it thoroughly and don't see any reason any fan of the genre would not.
Worth mentioning: the Nightmare at North Point DLC is short but really fun and cheap.

I'm one of the rare few who decided to pick up this game in 2015 and not in 2012 so I'm a bit unvinegared by the past of development issues, but nevertheless aware of them. As of playing this the game is still in beta (with a prospected 2-3 updates until 1.0) but here are my thoughts:
PROS:
- This game is absolutely massive in scope.
- Well written lore that motivates you to keep exploring. To me this is one of the things that makes the game stand out in particular. The atmosphere is very strong in this game.
- Beautiful pixel art and impressionist/chiptune inspired soundtrack.
- You can pick your species!!!
- A LOT of customization, item collecting, and things to do/organize/build.
- Duel Weilding combat and a fairly decent, streamlined UI (compared to other games of this nature)
- Endless Exploration.
- Space is awesome.
- I can be a sentient star flying on a train in outerspace. Honestly that was one of the biggest reasons I bought this game lol
CONS:
- Quests can be a little tedious, though they are a welcome addition to the game.
- Has had a history of development issues and you take that risk knowingly when purchasing.
- Like its cousin games Terraria and Minecraft, the game works on a skinnerbox formula that you can burn out of. As of right now there's not as many tiers of progression as there are in Terraria which is what makes that game so addictive. I believe this will change. 30 hours in and I'm only on the second tier of armor (I know, I'm a slow gamer) though, so there's a lot of content already - not to mention the different species for replayability.
- as of writing this it's still a beta and it shows, with some flavour text missing, a few glitches/bugs, and a couple of limitations that I'm sure the developers are working on.
- needs a few things to be one of the best games ever. my suggestions: More bosses relating to the lore,  more stuff like the Lunar Base mission, and hopefully the developers will include some Novakid (please!!!!) and Hylotl villages in due time.
- Multiplayer needs to be made more accessible.
- FPS rates are really awful and make the game unplayable at times. (unless your computer is fully optimized. as of writing this I've got a potato processor. Either way a game like this should really run a lot smoother than it does.)
OVERALL:
I highly, highly reccomend this game. Even as a beta, there's hours and hours of content already there and more promised along the way. It's cute, fun, unique, immersive, and I am glad I finally gave it a shot.  However, there are many things that need to be added and fixed before I can really say it doesn't have any flaws, of which I listed. I believe they will get this project done (they just updated yesterday as of writing this!) because it's a damn good one. Please give it a try!

I like supporting games like these, exploring the culture and feel of Asia. Games are typically about Europe/USA. Despite this, Sleeping Dogs is a great game, really good action, and it has characters you actually care about. I do feel that the game was too short and needed more content. I don't particularly like DLCs in general but I realize that's the trend nowadays.
The game does has some issues that most of these types of games have, that is, the driving can be clunky, especially on lower end PCs. There are random bugs/glitches and finding things can be downright annoying. But overall, the story and graphics are amazing, the chasing and fighting is really good. Some people are disappointed about the lack of shooting but it IS Hong Kong; guns are very much illegal for the average citizen, so guns would not be plentiful. Plus, physically punching, kicking people is more visceral and entertaining at times.
I would say check this game out, I would (arguably) say that it is not worth buying at full price, but there is a sale on it on Steam right now.
TL; DR? its GTA in Hong Kong, it has fun fighting, the story and graphics are good, even with a few hiccups along the way

Tl;Dr -  A good game with a lot of potential with interesting writing and world building marred by poor combat.  Unfortunately felt like an incomplete experience that ended far too soon.
Consortium is at heart an adventure/rpg tasking players with finding who the traitor is aboard an airsip and bringing them to justice.  The premise alone sounds interesting but the problem is unlike both RPGs and adventure games items in the game world are essentially just fodder to be recycled to provide power for your armor.  Despite a few times the game tryign to bring attention to certain items, at no point could they be picked up and examined making rifling through people's storage lockers and whatnot pretty pointless.  At no point did I feel like I was a detective trying to get to the bottom is a mystery but rather just going around having a casual chat with murder suspects with no actual ability to dig deeper and snoop around their personal belongings to try to contradict their stories.  As a matter of fact most snooping and gathering of information is taken from a newsfeed console that works like a text based "Her Story".  Keywords are used to search for documents and those can be read and new keywords attempted to piece together background and knowledge about characters in the world.
While I liked this in Her Story I found it rather tedious in Consortium.  On the one hand, yeah it's nice to have an abundant amount of lore I can read through and learn from but on the other hand...the console isn't very well explained.  Half of the...articles?  Documents?  Whatever I'm supposed to call them are sometimes written as though they were intended to be actual posted texts and other times are written with action cues in them as if they were works of fiction or we were expected to imagine we were watching a video.  This confused tone gave the overall experience a bit of a amateurish vibe as if they weren't quite sure what they really wanted to do with with console research...so they did everything with it.  Also many documents you can search for are obviously meant to be top secret yet anyone and everyone can pull them up with relatively mundane search terms in terminals found in common areas.  I would of rather much of this information be put into the actual game world such as a paper in someone's locker or personal computer or find some notes that lead me to think they have a background in programming, search under someone's bed and find some other tidbit of information...you know...actually doing stuff with the game world.  Trying to pick up a book or examine something will simply destroy the item and recycle it's energy to power your armor as stated before which...is...mostly pointless.  It seems strange so many junk items are littered around the cramped spaces of the plane when the game has only two or maybe three combat encounters total.
It also doesn't help that when these sparse combat situations happen the FPS elements are clearly lacking.   The entire experience felt as if this game had come from a past generation where early full 3D FPSes were just stepping out of Wolfenstien 3D's primordial FPS ooze.  Gunplay lacks finesse with mindless enemies running at you guns blazing with no real use of cover or indication that the people you are fighting are real people (a story trope that is hammered in a few times) but rather mindless drones sent at you like so many Doom Imps from times of yore.  You are given essentially a lethal and non lethal method of dealing with enemies but without a system in place to aid in actual non lethal combat it becomes an excercise in tedium.  Instead of methodically taking down enemies trying not to alert the hive, you're stuck with a gun having to charge blasts that may or may not take down an enemy down with very little to no feedback as to what's working and why.  Once and enemy is downed you're expected to run over to them and knock them out completely before they manage to get back up lending even more tedium to an already horrible system.  While you are given a generous amount of time to get this done, it's still very likely you're going to have to charge into the middle of the battle to try to snag all the enemies at once before they get back up leaving the rest to keep shooting you.  It's an utterly unrewarding experiance they were better off scrapping from the game entirely.
Thankfully the combat is the least important part of the game as you spend most of your time wandering the plane and getting to know it's crew.  This is the meat of the gameplay and is actually done pretty well. You're expected to respond to people in a timely manner and just about everything you say is remembered and has some degree of impact later on giving a pretty good illusion of dealing with real people.  This attention to detail does come back to bite the game as you are often given a limited set of responces and have found on some occations the only sensible option was to stand there awkwardly and say nothing at all.  It's a shame the world itself wasn't given this degree of treatment as I think they could of crafted something rather special.  Each character's opinion of you is tracked seperately though I have yet to actually see this make any kind of major difference other than an indication of if they like you or not.  Only the officers in the ship seem to actually matter as you spend most of your time talking and consulting with them and some Consortium characters only appear for literally a single conversation (yet their approval is still tracked).  Replaying this game is pretty much mandatory as your first run will mostly be spent trying to figure out what the game wants from you and what you can actually do in the world to effect events going on; while this is all very well and good a full third of the game is tedious tutorial things that was interesting only the first time through yet were unskippable since.
In the end my lack of a recommendaiton came down to one thing;  The original demo for Deus Ex.  You see, throughout the entire game I kept mentally likening this to Deus Ex.  The RPG/FPS elements, the clunkiness of how just about everything works yet is not quite clunky enough to make me want to stop playing and, quite frankly, the very similar plot lines.  Deus Ex was one of my favorite games growing up and I remember being impressed by the size and length of it's demo...which was about as long as this entire game. Suffice to say I can't recommend a game that bills itself as a complete product when it's clearly geared to be an episodic release.  I have to admit the game started off on a bad foot with me when I booted it up, was immediatley told of the kickstarter for the "direct continuation".  So I just got this game and now you want funding for chapter two?  The entire plot of the game felt like it was leading to this long and epic storyline that never came.  The game just ended...on a cliffhanger no less.  A cliffhanger whose conclusion they now want me to go fund out of my pocket so I can go buy the second episode of this game.

Kraven Manor is a short horror game set in a mansion that starts out as a single entrance hall, and grows outwards as you build the layout using a small-scale model in the hall from pieces that you find by exploring. It's an interesting concept, but it's short-lived, both because the game itself is pretty short and because of the fact that unless you go for the somewhat underwhelming secret ending, the game never really uses the feature in any puzzley sort of way except for one point where you're tasked with connecting rooms in a straight line to access one on the end of the board. The core gameplay is based around solving small puzzles in each room, usually while under attack by the game's enemy, a mannequin that you can probably already imagine if you've played Condemned, or any number of the other games that copied the "mannequin that follows you when you turn around" feature. For something made by a group of college students it's a pretty decent horror game, and it's certainly better than all those $20 Slender clones that weren't even worth making, but it is still a bit of a steep sell for $6, given that it ends so abruptly that you're mostly just left with disappointment that they thought up such a novel mechanic and did mostly nothing with it. Kraven Manor is the sort of game that you throw into your cart as a bonus after adding all the games you wanted to buy in a sale because going from $30 to $33 isn't that big of a jump, but I wouldn't necessarily call it the game that you go out and buy on its own.

This game is unlike anything I've ever played.  It has stylings of other branched-dialogue games, like Mass Effect or KOTOR.  The difference is the extent to which the game respects and reacts to your choices as a player.  Your possible decisions are many, and they will change the way characters treat you, and the outcome of the game.
The world is also beautifully realized, with rich (optional) lore for your enjoyment.  After reading a small chunk of the available lore, I had a better understanding of the game world, and found myself more engaged for it.
One thing that may turn off some players is that the game will not hold your hand.  It will allow you to make mistakes and fail, which makes succeess all the more rewarding.
I recommend giving this sleeper a try - you may be pleasantly surprrised.

Nightmare mode is where the fun's at really. Kraven Manor becomes too easy on Regular. Nightmare gives you a rechargable flashlight that can only be turned on for about 30 seconds, after that it needs to be recharged which takes about 10 seconds. While making a little difference, it makes the game way more fun and panic inducing, as running out of batteries in a dark section can be your certain death. To finish my review, Kraven Manor is a worthy experience. The price is kind of high for the amount of content you get. It's really really short, and that saddens me. Street Fighter V is as fantastic a fighting game as one could ask for, the fights feel fast paced and the characters are varied and feel unique. The newly added V-Skill and V-Trigger system makes each fight feel exciting and changes the pace from other fighting games.

As great as the fighting itself feels the game around the fighting is severely lacking. As it currently stands ( as of 2/24/2016) the game modes are training, a story mode which is far too short and easy and consists of 2 or 3 very easy one round fights with static images and and voice over. The slim roster of 16 seems a bit sparse compared to Street Fighter IV which had 25 at launch.
The game also has Ranked and Casual matchmaking and Battle Lounges which currently only hold 2 players and have been not super reliable for even that. The matchmaking however has been super stable with very little laggy matches only one or two of my nearly one hundred matches suffered from lag that made it hard to play.
The unfortunate thing is the game itself feels great and I have been loving every moment playing it but without the arcade mode, trials and other modes you usually get in a full release of a fighting game it is hard to recommend for someone who is not a hardcore fan of the series.
The march update seems as if it will add some of these missing features  which will hopefully round out what the game offers to people not as familiar with the series.
Although I would find it much easier to recommend this game if there was more content in it the stellar improvements over Street Fighter IV and the quality of the actual fighting outshine the rather bare bones package to make it worth your time and money if you are a hardcore Street Fighter fan.

Been playing for a week now, up to about 18 hours, and I have no problem giving this a thumbs up.
-The characters are diverse (and by that I mean F*** Birdie).
-The stages are better than SF4 (and by that I mean SFxT stages).
-The matchups are balanced (unless you lose).
-The mechanics are easy to learn (and by that I mean it's not an Arc System Works Game).
-The connectivity is great (and by that I mean the connectivity of people on YOUR continent).
-The actual "feel" of the game is one of the best fighting game experiences I've seen in a long while (and by that I mean it's one of the best fighting game experiences I've had in a while).
I think the only negatives that irk me on a regular basis is the wonky interface.  Trying to do things like find where to see replays or turning off notifications was confusing at first.  It works, but it can be streamlined.  One week out connectivity issues are mostly dealth with but stat pages don't seem to work.
Really, as long as you've got the patience to learn and study from your mistakes there's no reason pros and casuals alike can't enjoy this game.  The systems and techniques that pros like to use on one another are there, and for the casual player the motion inputs have been simplified and the frame windows widened.  And if you're mid-tier it just seems like the best of both worlds.
I understand some are dissapointed in the amount of alternate modes / extras in the game but, in the games defense, we did know exactly what would and would not be in there before the release.  If this were SFxT or MVC3 you would be able to point to obviously shady practices but in this case Capom is selling a online-based fighter with extra content to come at a later date and has not presented it as anything more than that.  If that's not enough for someone that's ok, but it's up to the consumer to investigate what is and is not present in a potential purchase, so make sure you do that before you consider buying.

This game is fantastic. Capcom managed to make it rewarding to vets, while making some tweaks to make it easier for new players. Overall this is a rock solid product, and instantly one of the best fighting games out there.
Punching and kicking people in the face has never been more satisfying. Street Fighter V feels like an expansion to the Alpha series. Alpha counter is back, powerful level 3 supers are as potent as ever, EX moves feel like Level 1 supers, big counter hit juggles and combos are a core part of the gameplay, and much of the cast got their start in Street Fighter Alpha.
The V gauge system is a welcome change and adds nice variety. This bar governs your ability to alpha counter (aka V Reversal) and V Trigger. You must choose which to use your bar for, which adds a nice layer to the game. Activating V Trigger will spend your whole bar and you cannot V Reversal. Alternatively V Reversal costs 1 chunk of V bar so you cannot activate V Trigger. Offence or Defense, it's your choice.
Many things are just like you'd expect in a street fighter game. The low/overhead/throw mixup game is present, along with things like Trip Guard, Negative Edge, pianoing, frame traps, etc. However, a few key changes were made that players will need to be aware of. Super Grabs can combo. That's right, Zangief can headbutt you and hit confirm into grab super. You cannot die from block damage (except supers!), you take white recoverable damage from blocking medium or hard attacks, and alpha counters can be baited and grabbed with fast recovering attacks.
Currently you can play training mode ( which has lots of tools for creating situations you would want to reproduce), VS mode, story, survival, and a few online modes. The game has cross platform matchmaking PC to PS4 which hasn't been done before. Capcom is still making improvements on the infrastructure of the online platform, and they are being very transparent about that via @SFVServer which is great. My overall experience so far has been positive. Many online matches feel very smooth, and things are only getting better.
A couple of things I'd personally like are to make ranked matches 2/3 and allow player 2 to rematch between matches. Overall those are small complaints though, and this game is a lot of fun. I highly recommend it.

This game is a diamond in the rough. It's an isometric, much-simplified Dwarf Fortress, with a basic campaign and a sandbox mode. The graphics and voice acting are simple but enjoyable, with a good sense of humor. The mechanics are exactly what is needed in this genre; you dig, you accumulate resources, you move up a tech tree, and then you dig too deep and watch your dwarves die terrible deaths. One of my favorite indie games.

I love Left 4 Dead. The atmosphere, the visuals, the pacing, the humor, the maps.
Valve reinvented co-operative gameplay with this title. Sure, there have been multiplayer games that let you mash bad guys as a group, but never done as thoroughly as L4D does it. Your team's survival depends on teamwork. And yet, it's never complicated. L4D rewards you for behaving exactly as you should behave if there really was a zombie apocalypse. Stay together as a group, watch each other's back. Share resources.
The Versus mode exemplifies these themes too, in that the infected team works best if the individuals cooperate and coordinate.
All of this adds up to an awesome "beer & pretzels" alternative to your usual hardcore fare.
L4D2 one-ups L4D in many ways, but the atmosphere of the original is much darker. When Valve adapts all L4D maps for L4D2, there will be little reason left to buy this game... but still. It's on sale all the time. Enjoy a little piece of history.

If you're reading this hoping for a challenging sandbox survival game, look elsewhere. Enemies appear only in air pockets dug out by the player, and keeping a good supply of resources is just a matter patience of not getting careless along the way (forgetting to make farms). This is the fundamental problem with the game if you're looking for a survival challenge.
Aside of these problems a number of other major issues and a significant lack of polish plague the game.
[Combat]:
Enemies lack proper patch finding and will when encountered instead wildly teleport around the level until they find a dwarf to beat up. Your own dwarves cannot be controlled (aside from teleporting them) and soldier dwarves will simply bullrush your enemy they can patch-find their way to, even if they are on the other side of the level and have 1% of their maximum health available (no way to prevent this aside from sealing them in).
Enemies teleporting makes traps useless, and since you can't stop your dwarves from blindly rushing into battle the only factor is having more and higher level dwarves than the enemy monsters.
[Resources]:
Certainly better than the combat, but basic resources are surprisingly rare, while 'rare' resources when found can buy you immense quantities of these resources, which leads to situations where the best way to get "stone" is to find an unholy rock and sell it for a few thousand rocks. Unfortunately you also need to mash the "buy rock" button a few hundred times since you can only buy very small stacks. Aside from this you have a few minor issues like resources sometimes permanently disappearing from your resource tab if they reach 0.
[Graphics & Sound]:
The sound and graphics for the game are both nicely done and get the point across. Aside of a few minor issues designing a good looking dwarf fortress is both possible, fun and fairly easy to do.
[Summary]:
A few major design flaws and a severe lack of polish across the board prevents this game from reaching its full potential. Perhaps the game will change later on, but as the game is now I do not feel that I can recommend it to anyone.

This went from being a game I didn't care about, to being one of my favourite games of all time. Let me explain...
I've made this mistake before, but this time it was ironically the playable demo that dampened my enthusiasm. I couldn't see what was good about the fighting system or the driving, deleted the demo and stopped thinking about it. Journalists continued to go nuts, my friends were bugging me about it, and still I stubbornly ignored the title. And then eventually I played it, and regretted every moment I'd spent putting it off.
Some people have dismissed it as "GTA in Hong Kong", but that's not really fair. It obviously leans on GTA IV very much, but it has carved out a unique place for itself among crime games. For one thing, there's much less shooting in this because there are far fewer guns in Hong Kong than there are in the American cities that are usually the settings for these games. It's a prettier, more colourful world which resembles GTA IV with enhancement mods. The combat is the best of any open world combat game (yes, better than Assassin's Creed, better than Batman). The mission designs are a lot of fun, and there are plenty of uses for all the money you make, with dozens of clothes shops, vehicle dealers and betting arenas. If you're into parkour and exploration, Sleeping Dogs will take you on long journeys around the rooftops to find secret items. There's none of the bratty Cartmanesque dabbling in racism, sexism and homophobia of GTA, and even the motivation of the character fits better with the action gameplay than any GTA. Oh, and if you get the Wheels Of Fury DLC too, you'll play to win a place in your garage for a fururistic car that is quite clearly the Christian Bale Batmobile. You know you want this.

hm, what's the best way to review this?
first let's pretend we don't know any other games.
then this game actually isn't too bad. but far from good either.
while the graphics are browser game quality and the user interface and usability are pretty primitive the overall production chain is relatively decent. the first products are fairly basic and setting up a production takes little effort. after you get around to actually use the game since the tutorial is really basic as well and lacks important stuff like the research system. which is in fact pretty half-as#ed. but sooner or later you will get it to work.
buying machines for your factory costs money and so does importing raw materials and every processing step. exporting finished products out of your factory is the only way to make money. and it works. nothing wrong with that.
however soon after the start you quickly realize how extremely limited this game is. products quickly get more complicated to manufacture and pretty soon you will run out of space. your factory is divided into multiple small factory basements for some strange reason. you have to unlock each new area by paying a good amount of money but there is no way to connect the areas unless you finish the research related. so having two or more areas working together and combining their individual intermediate products into the final product is the challenge (and limitation) you face for the rest of the game. obviously this is done to slow you down and add pseudo complexity but at the same time it adds great annoyance since you lack the means to effectively control the production and item flow between your factories. mass production is needed later in the game but at the same time it is greatly hampered by aaaawefully slow item transfer between areas.
and you can't speed it up!
talking about speeding things up.
i have played the marathon mission only. it took me almost 12 hours to complete all 16 goals, see all the game has to offer and get all the achievements as well. the game was running in fast forward pretty much all the time. still i left the game unattended for up to an hour on multiple occasions because there was just nothing left to do but to wait. i had unlocked all areas, crammed them full of machinery in the most compact way possible, everything was running full throttle but still it took 2 or 3 minutes to complete one single product. in fast forward mode. usually you need to produce 30 to 70 items of a product to meet the goal and get to the next goal. so this takes a while. once even after running the game in afk mode for almost an hour i still was barely half done with my current job. in fast forward mode!
and there is simply no way to speed production up since you have already used all available space in the most sensible way possible. you just can't do anything but wait. that's plain terrible!
the later products are simply too complicated for both the intended and unintended limitations you face in this game. when you can't play a game but just have to wait it out then it's really, really poorly made.
there are other missions with production goals and profit goals and there's even a leaderboard but since i have seen all the game has to offer already i really don't feel like playing some more. ever.
back to the start:
obviously factory engineer is not the only game we know.
in fact it has a bigger brother called FACTORIO and like all bigger brothers it does everything way bigger and better.
yeah, at 20 bucks factorio is double the price but 10 bucks for factory engineer isn't exactly a steal either. especially when considering what it is you actually get for your money.
factorio doesn't suffer from any of the limitations that beat down factory engineer and it's way superior in absolutely every respect.
so if you are interested in belts, inserters, factories, intermediate products, production chains, automation, optimization and logistics BEFORE you buy factory engineer just head over to factorio's shop page and download the demo.
you can thank me later.

There were a few moments that shined and in theory would have worked out great, but the execution was really off. Regardless of who made this and their experience, this is still a product that is asking for money.
For $5.99 the price is barely justified. Even though it is a little over an hour I could not bring myself to finish this. I typically enjoy short bite sized games perfect for killing a couple hours but between everything that was wrong with it I just had to put it down.
First of all the game runs bad.
bad. Graphics set to low and 0 FXAA, it struggled to stay above 24, rarely peaking at 40. This made it ridiculously janky and nigh impossible to stomach. I'll say that if it maintained a steady 60 frames a second on high (which should NOT be a problem for my specs) I would've enjoyed the setting and general look of the game alot better.
Gameplay-wise there isn't anything special. Walk around, solve "puzzles" (so minimal and straightforward they shouldn't be even called that), antagonist pop up at places/follow you/etc. This is how almost all horror games go, except that this doesn't work here all the time.
The bronze mannequin was definitely creepy at certain points and the way it behaved and interacted with you was well done. At certain points you would be stumbling around in the dark trying to keep your eyes on him (otherwise he can move and attack you). Playing on Nightmare, your flashlight runs out and darkness allows him movement. This was the strongest aspect of the game.
Other instances of interaction with the mannequin were sadly laughable and unavoidably comedic looking. At some point you walk into a sideroom in the bedroom and the door shuts behind you. You open a chest and see some pictures and then you hear a loud sound like the door opening. Turn around and the mannequin's leg is halfway in the room. It then "is dragged" out while dramatic music is playing. When you leave the room there is a shadow on the wall of the mannequin that "falls over" when you get close to it. There are many other times like this that unintentionally spark a chuckle, such as the time you spend in the wine cellar, the white medical ish room (the maze was another frustrating sequence that I gave up on when the game crashed), the attic, and the second visit to the library.
The last main point of contention would be the "examine-able" objects, like the notes, books, and pictures. Nearly all other horror games, regardless of being true independent titles or "indie" in the sense that Amnesia is indie, all have notes, books, and pictures being the main source of plot information. Typically when you interact with one you get to view the note, book, or picture, however in this, a tooltip simply pops up telling you the information. Other than this being a way of cutting corners I see no purpose for deviating from the working existent formula. What purpose does NOT showing you the paper serve? Especially with the photos. What were they thinking? Any potential impact of the story was completely wasted this way. Instead of seeing a crime scene photo you are told that this generic looking photo is that of a crime scene. This was not a budget, time, or experience issue, since many other games (even markedly WORSE ones) have the sense to not do this. This was pure laziness.
The music would be the strongest aspect of the game, but sadly this isn't saying much. I love me some dark ambient / borderline drone music but compared to what's in other games, albums, etc. either the score was either generically weak or it was terribly under-utilized. Droning sounds are not inherently creepy. If they are used well in conjunction with elements in the game such as what's going on, interactions, scenes, etc. it has the potential to be creepy, even terrifying. The quality of the music was not unique enough to hold up against it being under-utilized.
While there are some distinct positive aspects to this title, Kraven Manor severely underwhelms for the price. There are countless other games out there that have many things in common (even stuff that at first glance you'd assume to be worse than this) for $5.99 or less. I got it for free and was somewhat willing to look past the flaws but even then I came away disappointed.

This newest edition to the Street Fighter franchise doesn't fail to deliver its classic 1 on 1 bouts, bringing a new set of characters with the old, and mixing it up with new mechanics.  The combat system is more visceral and satisfying than ever, every strike having tons of feedback, and every special attack feeling unique.  The new Variable system gives players new options to spice things up, and it provides every character to be even more distinct from each other than ever before.
The balance of the current roster (on release) is, as far as I can tell, spot on.  No one is glaringly more or less powerful than the rest of the cast, despite the variety available.  Veterans have new tricks and newcomers offer new ways to play.
That said, despite how good the combat feels and how much I love the game, it's clear that the game feels a bit hollow at the moment.
The only UNFORGIVABLE aspect of the game is the lack of non-Xbox controller support and the inability to rebind keyboard controls.  For a franchise that started out in the arcades, not including all manner of input to play is a terrible move.  I know this will definitely change in the future and there are 3rd party workarounds, but to not have it at launch (ignoring whatever else is 'missing') is, as I've stated, unforgivable.
Don't get me wrong, I love the game and I wholeheartedly recommend EVERYONE to try it, but right now it pains me to admit that not everyone will enjoy it.  It's clear that the game was put out for players to get their hands on this new setting to participate in more competitive events, and so the single player side of the game suffers.  While Capcom has promised to deliver in that regard, it has only hurt their sales and image.
Even then, the game can only improve from this point onward.  New characters, new modes, new stages--support will continue for this game for years to come -as it has for previous titles- and this time there is no pressure to purchasae anything else past this current copy of the game to keep up with it.  All gameplay updates will be available for free to everyone that owns the game.  Any new characters added will be available for in game currency.  Stages, costumes, and colors have yet to be determined.
All in all, the core part of the game is there.  It feels great to play, but not everyone enjoys purely online, and what little single player that is available won't satisfy the average player.  Buy it now if you are determined to improve, buy it later if you'll primarily be playing alone or are otherwise uninterested in the online aspect.

Best viewed as a sim dungeon, dwarven style. There's a campaign mode where dwarves seek to reclaim their land from evil magi, but it's pretty rudimentary (I like the Dwarves-Elves angle in the story though!). It does structure gameplay a bit on each level with preset elements and gives some bonus incentive to continue playing, however it's still rather sandboxy experience, in the end not differing all that much from actual "custom mode", which is pure sandbox without the preset storyline elements.
Otherwise, if you want to treat it as a strategy game (real time with pause), you're going to be dissapointed. It's as if creators were aiming to make something like Dungeon Keeper but in full 3D (multiple levels of dungeon not just one), changing the tone from dark lord to sort of supposedly benevolent dwarves, perhaps being inspired by Dwarf Fortress, but in the end they realized they won't make it and dialed down difficulty a lot. It's very basic, no AI to speak of, no challenge, you can do everything at your own pace without being forced to discover (always marked) rooms with enemies until you feel ready. No enemies respawn or surprise you unless you dig your own grave unprepared. Many things feel unbalanced and purely aesthetic in nature (although aesthetics do have gameplay implications of keeping dwarves happy - the more you dig, the more decorative stuff you need for dwarves to feel at home). Early game on a new level is rather slow in terms of trying to push story forward/discover random enemy rooms, because you are too weak. And then, after a bit of building up, you're totally overpowered. Especially once you realize your ability to move stuff anywhere you want by your godly player powers is overpowered on its own.
So yeah, as a sort of sandboxy doll house, err- dwarven dungeon, it can work pretty well. You dig around, gather resources, set up farm for food and wood (ultimate renewable resource that buys you everything), and possibly some shrooms for happiness (yeah.. but I usually just stick to wood for cash and get happiness otherwise :P), build some cozy place for your guys to live, occasionally fight baddies who won't be a problem at all after a bit of building up, push story forward. Can be somewhat slow, and there surely are better sim games, but the overall tone and setting here is pretty unique for such genre I think.
Doesn't work at all as a strategy game, though. And if you want to be picky, animations are bit off, but otherwise looks are sort of cute.
Bonus points for spelling "dwarves" properly (not "dwarfs"). Malus points for broken achievements (one mission is broken and doesn't give you full influence, required for cheevos).
Also take note there are silly in-game cosmetic microtransactions, but many are free and you can easily ignore the rest (of which only Ales DLC is separate on Steam and only gives you ale tree and kegs to increase dwarven happiness). Bigger DLC is Space Dwarves, which changes medieval tone to futuristic, but it only works in pure sandbox (aka custom) mode, not in the campaign mode. No idea about the Pets DLC.
In the end, this title isn't very strong overall, but I still recommend it for its setting, however only to people who like to mess around sandbox/dollhouse style and maybe have some TV series to watch at the same time for slower moments or something xD

This is an absolutely fantastic little game. You're a Dwarf Prince, who is given control of a group of dwarves, and you build fortresses and caves underground and fight bad things who want to kill you. You go searching for materials to build furniture and decorations, and to advance your dwarven army. Once you kill the bad things, you can steal their beds and bunny rabbits and stuff to put in your fortress.
There is a campaign mode with quests which I think is really well done, and great to play. There's also a sandbox 'free' mode so you can build your ultimate fortress without any distractions. In both sandbox and campaign, I love being able to decorate my little dwarven fortress.. thing. There's a whole range of decorations and things to do, and discover.
Killing stuff and making a badass army isn't bad either, theres a fair few enemies and bosses to defeat with your military dwarves.
Theres a skill tree type doohickey that will allow you to give your group of dwarves more powers and items as the game goes on.
It's a great game to play casually and relax with (if you learn not to try and rush through, which made lead to stress and death unless you're quite focused!).
Sometimes your dwarves don't do quite what they're told, plus they're fat so they get stuck behind furniture a lot and then panic and die of starvation.. but it's okay, you can just spawn another one.
I definitely recommend it. It might take a tiny while to get used to (at least, it did me) but once you're there, it's quite addictive. One thing though - Apart from the DLC, there is an in game 'shop' to use your steam wallet to buy yet more decorations. The packs in there arnt expensive, and I think anyone who enjoys building/decorating/creating things like I do will be happy to pick them up for the price they are.. but if that sort of thing annoys you, well.. it's here.

Game for minimalist rpg players (aka rs classic fans. aka people who probably broke a sweat when y2k was a thing)
First of all I'm not 100% sure on the bandwidth use at an in depth level, though any home internet package will definitely do the trick, but I had successfully played this game after using all my high speed data tethering. So this game is perfect if you tend to run out of mobile high speed (and have an "unlimited data phone plan"). As for resource use, it's not too clunky as far as I can tell, but I'm not exactly blue screening while running everything else and say another game. (eg. chrome (3-10 tabs idle), skype, steam, acer bloatware apps, unified remote, task manager, vlc player (audio/video) this game and another game like League of Cancer.
That little perk aside, the gameplay is very simple and very grindy, as you would expect from a simplistic mmorpg like this. Or pretty much any mmorpg really.
For the combat you point and click everything and watch the basic math onomatopoeia fly before your eyes. At times you will feel a little underwhelmed with things, like the fact that even if you totally outclass an enemy to an insane degree, it seems there's still a decent chance you wont 1 hit them. On the flip side of that, it is somewhat more satisfying when it does happen. Let's be honest though, there's nothing like going to the start area of a game after playing for some time and going on an unmitigated, surefire 1 hit killing spree that's so indulgent at times that you don't even care that it's all going straight to your♥♥♥♥♥
The leveling scale is pretty basic, and although no-cap levels are an exciting prospect it's not quite worth writing home for. As is the anti=botting/capcha reward system, although rewarding and straight to the point. Don't want to do anything but combat and still level up skills? Don't be a bot.
There are player markets and while not the most user friendly, which is part of the charm, it's not totally unusable or outrageously foreign. There are no ways of drop trading as far was I know so if you want items you can't get from the npc markets or straight up grinding for them, this is going to be the way to do it.
The "MOS" market where players can buy things using money from real life isn't game-breaking or really unfair, not that this game makes any claim to such balancing. Although, having a $199 package does seem a bit excessive in my opinion, I guess I've seen worse kickstarter rewards (unless you would literally die for a bite of potato salad.)

Our first encounter with a navy ship did not go as planned. The Terminator Y was ravaged by cannonballs, and was left to sink in the cold, open sea. After repairing the ship, our captain blamed our defeat on the "disgusting" name we gave our ship, but we persevered.

This game is fun and a good time killer, but ultimately unpolished and lacking in some categories. Overall it is a good game, and I recommend that you buy it on sale.
Some mechanics of this game are fun to mess around with, especially in the fun-focused sandbox mode, but some of them become a hassle or just plain annoying. For example, arms that grab items from the conveyor belts can only turn 180 degrees to move a product. They should be able to rotate in any direction to enable people to have a well-running factory that looks nice and earns lots of money. However, even in sandbox mode, your factories can end up feeling small and limited because of this game's limited mechanics and factory sizes. While there are many different factory rooms that you can use at the same time, they are all pretty small and oddly shaped.
This game can be fun but needs to be updated and changed. It's a good time killer, but not something to keep you hooked for hours on end. Many games have done what this game is trying to do better. With some updates, changes, and tweaks, this game could end up being another big and addictive simulator. For now, just wait to get a good deal on it from a sale. Not worth the current $10 price tag.

Amnesia certainly inspired a slew of imitators over the years, but few came out as polished as Kraven Manor. Originally a Guildhall student project, this one is a first-person romp through a spooky mansion with a creaky inhabitant and a cool gimmick for navigation. Once you start to dig into it, however, the polish starts to come off in some unfortunate ways. Part of that is in how the monster works, so if you're wary of spoilers you might want to skip this review.
The first thing you come across in the main hall of the manor is an incomplete model of the building. Throughout the game you find pieces of the model that you can fit as you please, freely rearranging the structure on the fly. It's a cool, simple gimmick that is used to unlock the final sequence... and that's it. You're not going to be doing much else in the manor, either. There's no inventory to fiddle with, only some books to get snippets from, items to lift and throw, and buttons to push.
What you are going to be doing is staring down the house's obnoxious bronze inhabitant. The enemy in Kraven Manor is one of those ever-popular Weeping Angel or SCP-173 types that only moves when you're not looking at it. I know that sounds kinda cool, but what that actually means is the moment you turn to work on a puzzle or leave the room, it caves your skull in. Sequences with the monster turn into aggravating games of Red Light, Red Light where you stare at it while trying to blind navigate to whatever the hell it was you were doing. And the thing goes all herky-jerky crazy when it's just out of your sight, resorting to straight-up teleporting if you're too good at keeping eye contact.
Easily the biggest knock against the game is its length. I beat it on Normal in just a little over 30 minutes. There's a Nightmare mode for masochists, because all it does is limit your flashlight and make the enemies kill you faster. If you're a jumpy type like me you'll get a few good rushes out of the enemy encounters and a few of the scripted moments, but it doesn't last. As a student project, Kraven Manor is undeniably impressive, but a paid product needs a lot more than what's offered here.

Kraven Manor was developed by a team of thirteen gradate students within a six month time frame. In some ways that fact is all too apparent, in other ways it's surprising just how much was accomplished with so little.
A first-person horror set within the eponymous building, the game's unique hook is that the structure of the whole manor can be changed dynamically. This is achieved by finding scale models of the individual rooms and setting them onto a board in the main hall, the arrangement of which determines what can be accessed. It's a really clever idea that lends itself well to an exciting scope of gameplay possibilities... or at least it could, it never really gets used to its full potential here. I think there were literally about two or maybe three instances in the whole game where the positioning of the rooms actually mattered in any significant way. Otherwise, the only thing it affected was the walking distance to the room you were heading to next.
I say "the whole game", there's isn't really all that much to it. There's maybe less than a dozen unique, relatively small areas to explore, all of which can be seen in probably about an hour for most players. But at least most of that time will be eventful as various set-pieces are triggered with regularity along the way, the vast majority of these being highly effective at unnerving the player. This is largely thanks to the main threat to your survival in the manor, a life-sized bronze mannequin that appears both lifeless and yet obsessive in its focus on your demise, made even more unsettling by its strange behaviour as it will only move and attack when not being looked at directly, otherwise perfectly playing its role of inanimate object.
So it has a solid idea at is core, a suitably terrifying creature stalking your progress and is well designed with its creepy locations and adequate visuals. But it's not without its issues. As I guess is to be expected given the nature of its birth, there are technical hiccups and bugs, several of which forced me to reload my game on more than a few occasions (sometimes not triggering an event necessary to progress, sometimes essential items couldn't be interacted with, and on a couple of instances closing the game and spitting me back out to Steam). Loading can also take a while, though in fairness, that's most likely due to the fact the rooms aren't in fixed locations, plus it only seems to load once at the start rather than room by room and is seamless thereafter. Movement also feels somewhat sluggish and cumbersome, though whether this is by design to add to the fear, or a result of poor programming is debatable.
Overall this ends up feeling like a very advanced prototype or proof of concept more than a fully-fledged game, and I really do hope it's developed further by the team into a greater experience. Despite its flaws, it really does have so much going for it well beyond a lot of other games in the genre made by more experienced people with more resources and hints at greater things to come for the young talents. So, if you're a fan of horror and have the patience and tolerance to see past its blemishes, then I think you'll be pleasantly surprised with Kraven Manor.

I've just completed Sanctum 2 as I'm writing this review!
Playing this game gives me a lot of satisfaction. e.g. Hitting the enemy on their weakspots, creating an efficient maze, upgrading a tower to the max, overcharging the towers, etc.
My initial knowledge of the Sanctum games was that they were a fusion of a FPS (First Person Shooter) and a TD (Tower Defence). A very strange mixture of game genres. TDs usually give us a point of view where the entire playing field is within sight. FPS' are like it implies, displaying a first person view. Marrying the two together gives quite the interesting feeling of having to manage your defences while being on the battle field at the same time. In a way, you yourself are a tower, but a sentient one, capable of precise manoeuvring and targeting capabilities.
There are two phases in the game, the building phase and the battle phase. The building phase is the time where players can, well, build. It's a phase where players would strategise and create complex mazes, or just fool around and explore the map. The building phase is the TD part of the game. The battle phase is where the game gets serious, especially when you know the next wave has a boss. You lose the ability to build and upgrade towers during this phase. You whip out your weapon and the shooting begins. Enemies have different agility and attacks. I feel clever when I find out their capabilities and work around them, I'm sure you will too.
Sanctum 2 can be played both solo and along side with others. When more people join in, it gets very fun, especially with friends. Even during building phase, people tend to build tower bases or cores onto one another, trying to squash each other. When a big boss appears, it's very cool how everyone would swarm over it. It's nice that veteran players would help by giving tips like pointing out the weakspots or the strengths and weaknesses of towers.
Sanctum 2 is genuinely a very enjoyable game.

After hearing about this game being free for a weekend I decided what could be the harm in trying it out. Man have I been missing out. I have just recently finished my first playthrough and am itching for more. I can't wait for the kickstarter to finish and the boys that develope this game can continue their work on the Consortium trilogy.
Let's go through some pros and cons.
Pros:
-A very rich lore base that will keep anyone who is interested in world building very busy
-The game's setup is fairly unique in it's presentation
-The conversations are engaging and figuring out the big mystery has made me want to keep playing this game over and over.
-The characters all feel fairly unique with their own designs and voices as well as personalities. It is interesting to see who is more eager to turn on someone than help figure out the mystery.
-Speaking of mysteries, boy howdy is there alot of mystery in this game. Multiple times I found myself saying woah out loud.
-The writing for the game is very solid and kept me well engaged through my first playthrough. I didn't even leave my seat before I finished it and I am eager to start my next playthrough.
-Apparently there is the intention to import saves to the next "episode" of the game when it comes out so I feel that that is going to be incentive for many to get the perfect playthrough.
Cons:
-Even though I don't really have a problem with it I know many others will and that's the fact that the graphics are a bit wonky. The style seems a bit cartoonish in appearence but there is also multiple times where the characters would have weird shadows on their faces or certain textures in the environment would just be a bit off.
-The game really just drops you in with no brakes, so to some that can be a turn off.
-At times I felt lost because I wasn't aware of a certain event that happened off screen in the lore of the game, making me go back to the intel databank to read on past or occuring events. To some that is a turn-off.
-The gunplay is pretty basic so don't go into it expecting the next Call of Duty game. I'd say it's more akin to Deus Ex than anything.
-Sometimes I couldn't really figure out where I needed to go or what I needed to do to finish a mission. Eventually I figured out there was a map at the center of the ship that tells you where everything was so that helped out a bit.
-Relatively short but since I got the game for free there is no complaining from me.
All in all I definately think that if you are a fan of a great mystery and some stellar world building than this game is for you. This game was a game I didn't know I wanted and now I keep coming back for more. Do yourself a favor if your into game genres like sci-fi, mystery, and CYOA (Choose your own adventure).
If you do decide to play this game please go in blind like I did. It is best to figure things out on your own and to just enjoy the adventure!
Note: The cons I listed are not explicitly how I feel about the game but are things that people looking to play should be made aware of.

Puzzle Pirates Review
The world of Puzzle Pirates is what you'd expect from a pirate-themed game. Clipper ships and war brigs sail the seas, crewed by all manner of scalawags and sailors. Islands populate the landscape, inhabited by numerous seafaring folk. Like most any MMO, the populace of Puzzle Pirates has to earn its keep by performing assorted labor tasks, like being part of the crew on a ship or taking on assorted tasks for businesses while on land. However, you don't run around killing monsters or collecting rare items like you would in most any MMORPG. Instead, you perform your work via puzzles, and each one is uniquely tailored to the task you're charged with.
For instance, when on land, you can opt to take a job with an apothecary, a distiller, or a shipwright, among others. If you choose the apothecary, you'll see several orders for potions and concoctions that have been placed by actual players in the community. The puzzle itself revolves around rotating a number of pipes leading from colored jars at the top of the screen to a position where they'll pour out into color-coded vials at the bottom. You can create combos to up your rank, but if you screw up, you'll break your jar. Even though you can just play the puzzle as it is without even worrying about the available orders, you'll earn more money and a higher rank by filling the orders. Every task is just like this, featuring a unique type of puzzle that fits the type of work you're doing, and essentially providing you with a way to perpetuate the economy. You earn money for your work; you help a local business fill its orders; and you help other players get the items they want.
From a technical standpoint, Yohoho! Puzzle Pirates is just about the easiest thing in the world to boot up and play. The game starts up instantly and quits out just as easily. It runs on basically any machine, from a high-end PC to a Mac to even a Linux box. Granted, this is because this is just a Java client that doesn't take up more than a hundred megabytes on your hard drive. Make no mistake; Puzzle Pirates isn't bad looking at all. The puzzles all have a nice look to them, and you'll see an appreciably precious art style while you're wandering around a ship or island. Because of the game's visual limitations, you won't find anything especially impressive. However, the visuals are just fine for what they need to be here.
Overall a nice little game and is also free so there is no reason not to try it.

I didn't really care for the first Fieldrunners game, but the developers tweaked, streamlined and improved the game. I am really happy with the improvements. Its not just the same map with a different background. There is an actual campaign instead of just unlocking maps. The game does a really good job of instructing you and easing you into the game without forcing tutorial levels on you. The graphics and animations are also a lot better than the original game. The fun facts / tips make the game feel more alive. There are now items to use and you can pick your own towers that you'll be able to use.
Fieldrunners 2 is a very simple and shallow tower defense game with a cartoon look. The game consists of a campaign of several unique maps. You start with a certain amount of cash to buy your towers. You can place these towers anywhere, well almost anywhere. The enemies don't attack, they just run from their starting gate or gates all the way to your base. The game says your base, by base, I assume they mean your gate, because you don't see a base. These are basically open courtyards. If enough enemies get into your base, you'll lose the game. The limit is 20. I am very happy the game maps don't force you to do 100 waves, instead its 20, 30, 40 and so on waves. It makes the game feel much less of a chore when you can breeze through levels. There are other objectives too, like defeat X number of runners within Y time. The maps are really beautiful with a great art style. Far better and more diverse than the original game.
You're tasked with arranging these towers, making walls of towers, and making a winding path for enemies to follow. Basically make a maze of towers. Can you plug a gap and make an unsolvable puzzle? Nope. The enemies will plod through from left to right. If something blocks their way, they'll path around it, but not intelligently. They'll chose a path that can end up having more of your towers. Some maps have paths already predetermined. There is a wide variety of enemies, standard soldiers, a heavier soldier, they'll eventually get jeeps, motorcycles, tanks, helicopters and giant robots. What do they all do? Just walk. Again they don't attack you. The helicopters and planes will at least fly over your towers in a straight line headed for your gates. There are now troop transports that when they explode, the troops come out and keep running. Your job is to destroy them before they enter your gate.
Now that we've covered the enemies, let's talk about the towers, there are a few types of towers based on what mode you're on. Before each map / level, you'll fill 6 tower slots with towers you've unlocked by buying them with coins you earn for beating levels. This was a great change from the previous game that forced you to have 4 or 6 specific towers. Gun towers with short range, goo towers, that have a longer range, but will shoot goo to temporarily slow enemies down, there are oil towers that do the same thing, but to multiple enemies and the effect doesn't last that long. Next up there are long range missiles, which are great to have, there are bomb spitters that I feel are too similar to missiles. There are new laser towers that don't have an attack radius, but rather can attack up, down, left, right in a line. You can upgrade each and every tower by right clicking it and selecting to upgrade it for a price. Do you want to know which towers do the most damage? The stats are in the help menu item, but they should be hover items that just appear when you go to select which tower you'd like to place. There are new usable items as well, things like air strikes and mines. They're a nice feature in the game. The tower guns turn, but the electro towers don't turn and you'll pay extra for it. You can hit the space bar to pause the game to plop down towers, but there are only two speeds, normal and fast.
The previous game had you type in your name for the high score, this game just uses your Steam name. There are 3 difficulties for every map / level and I think it just adds waves onto the difficulty instead of making the enemies more difficult. The achievements are more time consuming than they are difficult. Its pretty easy to get them, but you'll invest 2 hours for the first one, which is a far cry from the first game where you could achieve the first few within a few minutes of the game. I wouldn't bring up achievements if the game didn't have 50+ and the previous game had 90+.
Overall, its a great upgrade from Fieldrunners 1. Its worth a try, and it might feel more like a mobile game than a PC game, but its still a fun little game.

You find yourself in Kraven Manor, a spooky and unsettling home to God only knows what. You don't particularly know the ins and outs of why you're there, nor do you know too much about the manor itself but you must press on in search of answers. There isn't much in the way of story or narrative here, the crumbs of story which you are fed are genrally found through interacting with old photographs and books that are strewn throughout each of the manor's creepy, harrowing halls and rooms. The gameplay is similar to other games of its kind; You are equipped with nothing but a flashlight and a journal which updates every so often after certain events occure. There are no weapons to speak of, running and keeping your wits about you are the only tools you'll need to survive. Exploration is the meat and bones of the game, whether you're looking for a key to open a locked door or a gear to fix a mechanism, you'll always be roaming room to room.
Soon enough you'll come across the game's antagonist, a bronze statue that will terrorize you throughout certain sections of your journey through Kraven Manor. Keep your eyes on him and he's nothing more than any other creepy part of the manor's decor, but turn your back on him and you'll be terrofied by the loud, clanky footsteps that make their way toward you in the dark. It's a foe that will keep you on your toes throughout. One moment you'll be at ease and exploring, then the next you'll be fleeing in absolute horror as this metal abomination pursues you down darkened hallways.
Arguably the biggest star of Kraven Manor is the manor itself. Dripping in atmosphere with rain splattering against the windows and thunder pounding through the halls, Kraven Manor seldom gives you any peace or moments rest. There were often times that I neglected some books and photographs, instead opting to get the hell out of whatever room I was occupying.
Kraven Manor is  a short game, you'll probably finish up in an hour or maybe an hour and thirty depending on how thorougly you explore.
If you're looking for a short, tense game to play one evening then it's a game you should definitely try. It may not do anything new and it never really strays away from established and tried mechanics, but Kraven Manor's bronze antagonist and gloomy setting are easily worth the price of admission.
2 Years later some pride is finally being taken in making the game better. Hopefully this dedication is kept up this time.

So the creation club is a substandard attempt at cashing in on a title Bethesda wasn't interested enough in to offer long term support or content for, but is apparently willing to try and collect money from in the form of♥♥♥♥♥♥poor, unoriginal "paid mods" that it refuses to call paid mods. their implementation in the deployment of the creation club has been amazingly poor - updating executables every week and pushing locked archives onto player hard drives "in case" they decide to pay for the thin-blooded "Creations" is ridiculous. The best racing game available for those of us who like interesting game modes, well-running software, slow-motion destruction, and an engaging multiplayer. Those game modes are races, missions to wreck other cars, a survival mission, combo stunt missions, and time trials. The next item on the first list is good software. Even on my laptop this game runs super smoothly and at times can surprise with its "beauty". Those slow-motion crashes are fun to watch, especially if it's not you who is crashing. That multiplayer is great. It is centered around ranked matches and the unranked "freeburn" mode. Basically, you can (at any time) jump into the multiplayer version of the normal game. It is organized in lobbies of up to eight players, including one host. The host has the option to begin races, as well as any of the single-player game-modes. The last feature of the multiplayer is a non-instancing challenge mode. This game is definitley enjoyable and my only criticism is that there are not enough people playing!
Also, there is nothing better than taking down other cars while Bach and Puccini are playing softly in the background. (:

Generally,this game is a good game.It has some obvious advantages and disadvantages.
1.Game Difficult:Very challenging
This game is one of the most difficult games i have ever played.It is really fast-paced.In small maps(One planet),it is not too hard to play well.But when you play large maps(more planets),facing more foes,things changed.You need to highly concerated to your ground base defensive forces,attcking forces and  orbital units,even the advance forces to other planets.In Titan,more units are added so it is hard to adapt the game in a short time.If you make a little wrong step,you may possiblely lose advantage or lose the game.
If you do not often play RTS games,I do not recommend to buy this game because it really difficult to play.
2.Game banancing+
There are not many difference between players,the different commanders have different expertises.So,In my opinion,the game balancing is good.
3.Story mode-
This game,with its previous edition,both have no story mode.So the players can not get what the game is talking about such as :why the robots are in a war?Without background information,we can not learn more about the game world,or interested in it.
4.Strategic
In many RTS games,skill tree is an important part of the whole game.But Titan do not have skill trees.But,thanks to this,i am still able to play this game.If it has a complex skill tree,I will be hurry-scurry.However,many units in the game have an upgraded version which can be producted in the upgraded factory.
5.Multiplay
I am a Chinese player.The game experience in the offical server is not very enjoyable.The game can not running smoothly because of the network delay.
So,if you are a player who likes RTS games very much,you can try this game,But if you are not,you may try some other easier strategy games first.

When you first play this you'll probably think 'Wth am I playing?' The mechanics have an old skool feel to them, the graphics are a bit underwhelming and navigating the space is, and remains, something of a frustration throughout. I'm fairly sure this is a deliberate choice on the part of the developers. You can basically forget all of that because what drives this game is story and character. It's kind of like bits and pieces of your favorite sci-fi shows and games pulled together into a coherent whole. The fact you're in the middle of it all as it plays out, whether you like it or not, is just a bonus. You can of course play it any way you like, but you're almost certain to get involved at some point.
One of the smartest things about the game is it's played out in a single environment - a plane you happen to be stuck on. The fact this doesn't get stale at any point gives you some idea how much thought has gone into it. The constant crew banter and the pace of events certainly doesn't hurt either. Overall it's a good few hours of breakneck storytelling and decision making and the claims of replayability are certainly true. My first playthrough was 5 hours odd and I still don't know what the hell was going on...
