However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

A Game of Dwarves is a mixed bag of fun and frustrating; quirky and buggy.
Drawing heavily from Dungeon Keeper, AGoD puts you in charge of a group of dwarves in a small mine. In each mission you expand your starting location by digging outwards and downwards, building new room types to supply your dwarves and advance your settlement.
As you explore further, uncovering new minerals that unlock new rooms and upgrades, you encounter increasingly deadly enemies. AGoD has you constantly juggling between exploration and training so that your military dwarves can always handle what's around the next tunnel bend.
Problems start with the interface. A substandard UI and poor camera controls are mentally taxing.  This wouldn't be such a problem except that the campaign missions become obviously uninspired as time passes.
Campaign missions involve digging your way to Spot X, and then digging your way to Spot Y, but this can be frustrated with the way the developers "walled-in" objectives with impenetrable rock. This often means digging around for a long time, juggling the poor camera controls, just to find the entrance.
Still, there is fun to be had, especially if you can let go of the campaign and focus on building and creativity.
In the end, I can only recommend AGoD to hardcore Dungeon Keeper fans and those who enjoy building epic projects in sandbox environments.

I personally love the gameplay in this game. I like how slow the game is when you are sailing along the ocean but then all of a sudden you get hit by cannons from the enemy galleon and need to fire back at them, repair sails, cannons, and holes, while there needs to be water pumped out of your boat. Blackwake can get really intense and fun when you are in mid-battle. The shooting in the game is awkward but this was probably intentional to simulate how bad the guns' accuracy were.
Different guns and weapons for different purposes, one even reading that it is reasonably good for killing members of your own team. The repair time is respectable. The galleon ships are bigger meaning that they have more cannons but are also a bigger target to be hit, this is also balanced since it can fit more players on it too. While the smaller boats are the complete opposite. You won't recieve any real benefits from leveling besides that you won't look as dumb as your fellow pirate in a gray shirt and pantaloon.
The sounds in the game are very-well-fitting. Cannons flying in the air, swords clashing, gunshots, bombs ingiting, impacts from cannons, swallowing rum, repairing damaged parts, character voices, etc... they all match perfectly in my opinion. Some of the dialogues are quite funny to listen to.
The Blackwake community is the most ideal and optimistic community one could wish for. I haven't heard a single squeaker in the mics yet, usually when someone teamkills everyone understands and votes to kick, and every player aboard the ship usually is doing something that will help their team, no one is really just standing there. I see people loading cannons, using the swivel, carrying supply boxes or steering the wheel. Sometimes there are players up in the ropes using a telescope and reporting to their team what they saw. My favorite part about this game is when the captain of the ship is an intense role player and uses a pirate dialect to give orders. It is honestly elegant and sometimes funny to listen to.
Blackwake is one of my favorite games because of its high performance in each of these categories. Your experience will still be very enjoyable without a friend. I ensure you that this game will definitely provide you with a lot of fun and laughs. Because of all of this, I would recommend Blackwake.

For an Early Access game, it's in great shape.  It's basically a much, much better version of Big Pharma.  You'll see people saying it's like Big Pharma + Factorio, and that's true, but it's much closer to Big Pharma than Factorio.
The basic layout is identical to Big Pharma: you have some small-ish factories of odd rectangular shapes; you import and export goods at the walls of the factories using special machines; and then inside the factory you route to and from various machines with arms and belts to make products and produce a profit.
Like Big Pharma, there's no way for belts to cross each other (like Factorio's underground belts do) so layouts become puzzles.  Also like Big Pharma, you buy your equipment on the market (as opposed to making it, like in Factorio) and money is a constant pressure.
It greatly improves on Big Pharma in several ways. Selling to market is easier and less annoying. The machines are a bit smaller relative to the factory so you've got more room to ramp up capacity.  (And, because the market mechanics are nicer, you have more reason to ramp up capacity).  There's much more of a meaningful research progression and research requires actual products rather than money, which makes for more interesting and dense factory designs.
Overall -- especially for being early access -- it's a more fun and engaging version of Big Pharma. Looking forward to its evolution.

is a great simulation, crafting and management type of game. You can defiantly tell that this game was inspired by Factorio but has put it's own spin on the game itself. As of writing this review (23rd September 2016) I feel like the game is in good shape, but could expand a bit more and have more improvements to implement while it's still in it's early access stage.
is a great management game whereby you are allocated a specific area to build basic machines to start off with. As you progress and slowly make profit on selling products you will be able to make more comprehensive products to sell as well as expanding your knowledge on new machines and new products to produce. As you gain profit on the products that you produce and sell you will be able to expand and buy more area to create more machines to sell more products to gain more profit.
The first 1 to 2 hours is going to be more or less creating the most basic machine to sell a product to gain profit to create more machines. Unfortunately the game doesn't yet have a productive tutorial, only a quick written guide for you to follow to create your first basic machine. I would like to see the game have a tutorial at the start as the first time you play this you have to keep flicking through the quick guide and the game itself and the guide misses out on a points of the game. If you're not going to add a tutorial to the game, then at least make it so the quick guide is detachable so you can read through how to make a basic machine whilst playing the game and expand a bit more on the guide itself. Possibly a tips section at the bottom of the guide.
Making the machines fully automatic from smelting the ore to selling the product is the main way of gaining money. More or less every product in this game can be fully automatic to create the product from it's parts to then selling it at a price. There is a bunch of different machines that are essential to use. Machines such as conveyor, handler, smelter, Assembly machine, Importer, exporter and Product maker.
The conveyor is used to move your products around the factory, if you're not careful with the overloading of products the conveyor can overload on products in a turn and then that conveyor section will be jammed. I feel like you need some sort of alarm or something to let the player know that this area is jammed otherwise you don't know until you find it. Also I find it kind of tedious if you have a rather large row of conveys you have to click every time. Could there possibly be a click and drag mechanic so you don't have to click every square that you have to place a conveyor on? Just a idea.
The other machines (Exporter, Importer, Handler, Smelter, Assembly machine and Product maker.) work perfectly fine, and I don't feel like there is much else to say about the machines. Except that I feel like most of the machines should have a hot key, as the Conveyor has a hot key for the space bar, but the other machines don't. There are other machines that you can unlock with research points but I haven't unlocked enough to really comment on that part of the game as of yet.
The music in the game can get rather repetitive, although I would give some credit to the developer as the game has a rather solid base game for it's current early access stage. I would like some more soundtracks on the game, or the option to turn off the music so I can play my own music when playing the game.
- Not just another factory management game
- For it's current state in early access, I feel like the game has a solid base game that you can have a decent amount of time playing.
- The game has a lot to do and a lot to work towards
- This game currently has a lot of potential
- More game modes such as a challenge mode (less money allocated and products make less money), timed mode (make a certain amount of money in a certain amount of time to pay it off) and sandbox mode (unlimited money and research points to mess about with)
- I feel like you need a tutorial at the start of the game, or make the quick guide detachable so you can create machines and read the guide at the same time.
- The conveyor should have a click and drag mechanic so that you don't have to click every tile.
- Hot keys for all the machines would be a massive time saver
- Need more variety of different music
- The objects have no rewards, maybe have some sort of reward after completing the objectives. More money, research points, percentage increase in products sold ect.
- Game might get repetitive after a while because of the lack of game modes
- No tutorial at the start of the game
At this current state that the game is in, and the price that the game is asking for I feel like the game has a lot to offer even at this stage. Even after playing 7-8 hours on steam (didn't show because I was playing offline) I still haven't unlocked barely anything and still have a lot to work towards. I would recommend this to people who enjoy the factory management type games. This game has a lot of potential and I am looking forward to seeing how the developer will make this game while it's in early access.

The menu and UI is akin to something one might find in a nightmare. The map is, at times, convoluted to the point of insanity. The worst, in my opinion, is the complete and utter lack of racing guidance within the game. During a race, you are given the task of getting from point A to point B, and you must get there first, ahead of all the other opponents you will race. The issue lies in the fact that there is no glowing arrow telling you which route to take, and the world is 100% open during said race. So, while racing, I can garauntee that you will spend 90% of your time watching the map, the compass, and literally every other piece of HUD that MIGHT tell you which way to go. Because one wrong turn, and the race is over for you. Now, I know what you're thinking. "This guy's lame, he doesn't know how to race!" Well, that may be true. Except that as you progress in the game, the speeds increase, and reaction times grow short. The AI knows EXACTLY where to go, and you are busy navigating. So would I recommend this game? No. Because you will not spend your time racing, you'll spend it navigating an unnecessarily complex and open race track.

Although, while I am a big fanboy of Undertale, and have had more fun playing Undertale, that doesn't make this a bad game at all. Infact, it's actually really good.
Although, one thing that undertale takes advantage to in this game, is that it has a satisfying ending, that is actually an ending, if you do it right, and multiple nonsatisfying/terrifying endings if you don't. This game, it all leads up to one confusing sequel bait, "To be continued". It even says so itself. I'm not joking. At the very least the new game they're making (Of which's kickstarter will be avaliable on the 18th) looks pretty interesting.
But let's put it all in a list:
PROS:
+Good story. It confused me at the start, but kept me interested and immersed until the end.
+Very interesting and realistic characters and reactions.
+"Say nothing". It's about time that a game with dialogue, I am now able to say absolutely nothing when I have absolutely nothing to say. Or when there's nothing that I want to say.
+ In all honesty, I think that the combat is fairly nice. Nothing special, just, nice. I had alot of fun in the VR tutorials.
+The ship is laid out like a bloody ship.
+The voice acting is top notch from the characters I've heard.
+ Chess pieces. I like chess pieces.
+ Your armor looks cool.
+ It's, VERY immersive. Seriously.
+Choices.
Alright, you can probably tell that I'm running out of things to say, but that doesn't mean it's a bad game. I'm just running out of things to say. Most of these pros outweigh the mixed points and cons.
MIXED POINTS
*Admittedly, I think the dialogue is kinda limited. You use the first four function keys, function 4 always being "say nothing". It's not nearly as bad as it was in Fallout 4, but it's still kind of limited. However, for the most part, I don't see there needing any more dialogue options, so yeah.
*Also, the dialogue system can be quite clunky for some, as there is the fear of pressing the wrong button, not knowing if you pressed the wrong button, and actually pressing the wrong button, and if you are using a controller, I don't know how you would be able to press anything. But I haven't tried it with a controller. So I'm not sure.
*The graphics, are, well, I don't have that good of a machine, so I can't really complain about it too much, but they aren't the greatest in the world. But in my eyes, unless they are eyesoaringly ugly, I don't think graphics matter all that much.
*Oh. I thought this was going to be in space.
*The UI is pretty wierd. I'm one who despises Cyan, and despises it's use in Science fiction games, and despises hologram UI, but that's an opinion, so I am going to leave it as a MP.
Now for the negatives.
CONS:
-Although I have some subjective issues with the UI, the UI isn't always the most responsive, and can be very, VERY -confusing.
-The AI in this game is terrible. I was fighting this one shady guy, whom I will not spoil, and he all of a sudden just stopped dead, giving me a clear advantage to headshot him until I defeated him. And then when the ship is being boarded by some bad guys, I just had to go around a corner, and then shoot them. They wouldn't follow me, I just stood behind some bars and masscared them.
-The ship you are on gets small when you are used to it. Atleast in System Shock 2 it was a hugemongolous ship with many features. It can get repetetive to wonder around it so much.
-Dear lord can some of the objectives be confusing.
-Short
-The ending. ♥♥♥♥ the ending.
-Admittedly, I got this on a free weekend, but I really cannot see myself paying money for this game. Especially with it's sequel (hopefully) coming out.
-I get it  you wan't to be pacifist, but where did that say you could only have TWO combat sections?
To be truthful, I really like this game's story and atmosphere, and I think its an underrated title. But I can't give it a strong one, seeing as how the sequel (Who's trailer can be found here:
) is going to eventually come out, and then leave this game in the dust, with what seems to be more advanced gameplay and being on an actual mission. Plus it's being developed on UDK 4, as opposed to Source.
But if it's free, or on sale for cheap, get this game.

Kraven Manor is extremely short, and beatable in under one hour. The puzzles are easy, with the enemy evoking a good sense of fear, and there is a slight alternate ending that nets a few extra achievements. It’s horror in the atmospheric, psychological kind, but it’s not the “terror experience” that some people have claimed it to be.
At its current price ($5.99 as of this review), it’s worth the purchase. I picked it up in a bundle myself many months back. At its full price, which I believe was $10 or just above, it would not be worth it, the value for your investment just wouldn’t be there.
+ Graphics. For a bunch of university students, it looks good for the amount of time they’ve put into it. Being university students, you wouldn’t think they’d have a lot of free time for this. But, the game looks fantastic. The mansion is nicely dark and dank, and the animations and lighting are terrific.
+ Sound. The sound and music work wonderfully, from letting you know if the enemy is nearby to the feeling of something bad is about to happen when the music crescendos.
+ Atmosphere. It’s not a jump scare game, and that’s a good thing. Not knowing where the enemy is while you’re running around a darkened room looking for something, it evokes a sense of fear while not relying on crap jumping out of doors to frighten you.
- Length. This is extremely short. It’s almost more of a tech demo than an actual game, and you’ll be done in an hour, if that.
- Puzzles. They’re extremely easy. You will not need a walkthrough, or hints, or help of any kind.
- No replayability. For such a short game, that’s probably expected. There’s an alternate ending that really isn’t that good, that you can get by collecting three items during the normal play. There’s also a ‘Nightmare’ mode, which is slightly more difficult, but aside from an achievement for completing the harder mode, it’s all pretty much the same.
- Save stutter. For some reason, whenever the game autosaved, the game froze for a second or so. Which is odd. I’ve never had that happen in any games made in UE.

I am writing this review on the first day of the game's release, and will update it as the game evolves.
Firstly, the game is VERY early access, for example, it is missing music entirely.  There are sound effects, but no way to control the volume, etc.
However, these items are readily acknowledged by the developer, so I'll put aside those known unfinished items and instead focus on reviewing the values of the game:
It is clearly inspired by Factorio with a bit of Big Pharma tossed in as well!  Like Big Pharma, the map consists of several large buildings in which you can place your machinery.   One building is available at the start, and additional ones require funds to purchase.
To create products, you must first import raw materials, then send them through a production chain via Smelters, Assembly Machines, and finally Product Makers in order to create finished finished goods that can then be sold via the Exporter modules.
Of course, the game wouldn't be complete without conveyor belts and Handlers, which transfer goods from machine to machine to belt.
There is quite a lot of research, which is purchased with points generated by feeding Research Labs with completed products... the same ones you could be selling!  Each product has a research starting value that goes down every time one is processed... so changing the products that go into the labs is a necessity.
Research points are used to unlock further machinery, new product designs, and things like loans and lower interest rates.
I really like that this game has an economic component: one is limited by funds to buy machinery, etc.  My first attempt at the game was to build a long assembly line of several smelters, etc. ... and then I ran out of funds before I could buy an Exporter to sell my goods!
The game has interested me far more than I anticipated, and I'm glad that there is a new factory-building game on the horizon!
This game does need a lot of work, which the developer acknowledges, but they are also asking for player feedback to improve things, etc.  I will delighted to provide that feedback and see where this game goes in the future!
I would definitely recommend the game if you are interested in the genre, and want to see how Factory Engineer develops!

Hello possible commanders,
so I shall "judge" this game. Judging is a personal thing, so here are my impressions:
We all hailed supreme commander. So very different units, so many commander upgrades. With expansions, some things became quite imbalanced if you rushed them. Scale and performance had always been an issue (I had no 1000 $ for a top notch gaming machine). Planetary Annihilation has all those units, but makes them available for all. Now it is up to you to crush your enemy with titans, flood him with mechs, bomb him to the ground, nuke him to death, crush him under the tires and chains of yourt tanks or eradicate the planet he dwells on (preferably you have a transport or "warpgate" if you also happen to dwell on that planet) with an asteroid, a moon, or a planet-killer gun.
It also has:
strategic flexibility
a factor of randomness (galactic war)
balance: if the enemy has warships, you have a simple defense gun that mows the orbit free

Because I am a beta backer, I have no idea how many skins are for free, but they are mostly cosmetic. The available basic commanders have the same armament for free.
Then comes planetary annihilation. I was one of the beta buyers/testers. There were good days, there were sad days. There were bugs. Unfinished units. Planetary travel problems (you had no idea how to do it)... and so on.
Considering bugs (and with the AI):
They fixed them, made it a funny yet sometimes hard game when the AI came killing you wit a super army. (Only one time an enemy subcommander marched directly onto my warships. The idea was good - they had no underwater defense. Problem - massive firepower and single target enemy. So not a real bug but you might think it was one.)
Planetary Annihilation: Titans has not disappointed me. Get it for the special offer price, it is totally worth it. If you like the genre and loved supreme commander - get it as well.
Some thoughts:
Planetary scale - no other game has it.
Warp in reinforcements? Why not fly them from another planet. Or deliver them via planet (not recommended)
Nuclear missile - meh. Why not crush the enemy with an asteroid? Or two? We still have those tough
2d maps, her you get a whole solar system.
As of yet, I have to discover any AI unfairness.
Concerning dlc, i have seen no such thing, just got some free commander skins. Or models.
Scouts are useful. Radar is useful. If you use them, it is very easy to find your enemy. On larger planets tough, it takes some time to find the opposition - because the radar has limited range.
Also, I have yet to play on a world that was covered to more than 40% with water.
As I play the game, i will update the review.
(UPDATE 1)
Great game. Really funny moments, where i died in the campaign, yes, you can call it that, because I pressed the planetary ignition button. Stupid tough, because my escape ship was shot down and the teleport was on the target planet.
Compared to many other games, the "galactic war" is a campaign. I call it that, read the information on each planet and enemy commander, and decide for yourself.
(UPDATE 2)
Played some intergalactic Maps with aquatic planets. Works awesomely smooth. Water land transition is neatless and all working just fine. Teleporters are really useful and fun - even on a single planet when you want to install a beachhead infront of your enemies base because a mountan blocks his artillery. Orbital teleport titans are also really fantastic - invasion on a new level. You should shield the more valuable assault titan with "replaceable" interstallar ships tough - 3 basic space defense buildings wreck your priceless armada in a second.
Also, for the first time, used the planetkiller (metal planet with 5 catalyst units) on a moving planetary object. Really and imply epic. YOu even can deploy or move units off that rock or out of its orbit in mere seconds before the impact.
Awesome game with melee fighting. A must have!

A futuristic Sci-Fi adventure where you work your way through situations by diplomacy and/or action. Graphics and sound are good enough, controls play well enough. If I had to compare it to games I've played, it's a little like a mini Mass Effect with no aliens/exploration, more choices but worse combat? Conversations/actions affect your relationships with characters (via a point system) which may influence the options you have in the story (which branches out well enough).
Probably the best point of this game is the world/lore. It has very extensive lore in the form of ingame articles, out-of-game documents and files, and a website. However, the rest of the story hasn't really been explored because you have to wait for future games to see more (their next game is going through Kickstarter). I think you will be able to carry over your save to the next game so relationships and decisions may hopefully play some part in the next game.
The way I played the game I spent much more time in dialogue than combat (but I don't think there were too many opportunities for combat besides the V.T. simulation). For combat, you have an inventory system with equipment slots and a small variety of weapons to use. You can choose between lethal and non-lethal, though non-lethal is less effective. I think it's a shame you don't get to really play around with it outside of the V.T. sim but the story plays out as the story plays out and combat is limited in this episode.
I think Consortium is a very nice opening chapter/episode to a world that has more going on than what has been presented. If you want to run and gun and skip all the text then there are better games for that. If you're looking for a Sci-Fi world you can immerse yourself in and enjoy reading optional text to flesh out the world (more text than Skyrim/Dark Souls) this may be what you're looking for.

HOWEVER, there are some levels in which there is virtually no risk of losing despite being considered further along in the content (especially the last of the DLC contents), and some where your ability to shoot the enemies is crucial and towers will not be anywhere near as effective.  Fortunately, you can usually use any build that works with your playstyle(s) as long as you include some basic aspects; Focus Towers (or friendship, later on), Core Healing perk, and a well-placed 'Amp' Tower.
Overall, the game is highly enjoyable and levels do have decent replay value, but the game could have included a significantly larger number of maps to play on instead of considering additional difficulty settings for existing levels.

I rarely write reviews, but this game is so very addicting and fun.  The challenge is to win as either Town, Serial Killer, or Mafia.  It is multiplayer, and you have to convince the other players of your innocence without giving your role away unless you absolutely have to.  It is a true witch hunt, where if you do reveal who you really are, it could mean death, where as if you don't, it could also mean death...  It is a challenging game to play, and you can get into some interesting mind games.
The matches last about 10 to 20 mins, and the time really flies by as you are immersed in looking for clues, or trying to prepare defenses (if your on the bad team) and ensure you can trick the town.
The graphics aren't much, but the focus is on the gameplay and so that is totally fine by me.   The game is 'cutely' made.
I have experienced some slight technical issues from time to time, but I think its mostly related to the host disconnecting mid match and messing the game up.
All in all, a very fun, game, and there is a lot more to it than meets the eye.  Each role has an important job to do...

They took a great game and made it 1000% better and more enjoyable, which I didn't think was even possible. Once you get into this game you may very easily be hooked, as I am. The Heroic difficulty is challenging, but after gaining some experience (and unlocking more towers), you'll find they're not nearly as insurmountable as they seem at first.
For those concerned about having to buy coins (with "real" money) in order to beat all levels and earn all acheivements, I totally disagree. I have subsequently started playing on Android and Steam (now my preferred platform--love the large screen experience and the convenient keyboard controls). I have never spent a penny on In-App Purchases (sorry, Subatomic Studios). You can earn plenty of coins simply through normal game play. As for the Steam version, I am only 1 acheivement away from collecting them all--and that one is just a matter of time since it's the "play once a week for 6 months" card. I'll have no problem there, because I can't stop playing. Even after seemingly accomplishing every challenge the game has to offer, there's always room for improvement so my current activity involves finding better strategies to get the highest score possible, and learning new and creative ways to use various towers.
For my tastes, this game is a good as it gets. I would just like to see more maps and challenges to conquer! I would rate it a solid 10 out of 10.

A Game of Dwarves has been described many ways by many people with much more experience in "gamez journalizm" than me, but I will attempt to give a recommendation for you, the reader, anyhow.
This game can best be summed up as Dungeon Keeper and Dwarf Fortress having a big dumb pretty baby.
The game isn't terribly deep, but that isn't to suggest that the game is simple, it has quite a few layers but after your first deep inspection, you won't have much left to figure out.
For those that are going into this thinking this is DF in 3d, it is not, please do not expect it to be as I did. The game is mostly centered around its story mode, with objectives on a series of small maps. You do indeed mine out areas in 3d (with ease might I add once you understand how placement of ladders work) but it is mostly to mine out gold and other resources to fuel your army when you uncover pockets of enemies or other objectives strewn about the map.
There is a non story mode, but even those center around monster spots and other objectives. Do not come into this game expecting a 1000 year fort with multiple generations. The dwarves don't breed, you simply buy more dwarves as you upgrade a spawning pool, and food is pretty much trivialized by being a simple plant and harvest resource set instead of being cooked, processed and so on.
This does not however mean it is a bad game. I am a huge fan of Dungeon Keeper and this takes a good number of bits from that game and enhances them for a new way of doing things. The systems are clean and work together well, are easily utilized, and research isn't made to be a complex chore.
This is very much a straightforward game for people that want to mine a large area, kill a bunch of stuff, and make a couple cool rooms along the way.
Summarizing my rambling thoughts above: If you like Dungeon Keeper and DF, you probably will like this, as long as you go into it knowing that is more on the DK side of complexity rather than the DF.
Definitely worth the price of admission for fans of Dwarven fun!

Half life was a game created by Valve back in 1998, and was considered innovative for incorporating story into gameplay. I never played any Half life game until now and after playing it, this is my opinion on this game.
What Half life did right:
The story of Half life is simple, and it is all conveyed to you through NPC dialogue. You are never taken your controls away, and this is what makes the game immersive. The environment is great, from inside the labortory to outside the canyon, there are a lot of diversity. You are also given a ton of weapon, which you can experiment on. And each weapon gives you the satsifaction of blowing up an alien. Music also kicks in the most apporpriate time during an actions sequence, and it stays ambient and unsettling during exploration/platforming segments.
What it falls short:
Half life is an old game, so we can excuse the graphics as it was considered teachnological advance back in 1998. However, this does not excuse the combat. Combat against aliens are fun, and each one are diverse so it makes them enjoyable to fight. Combat against soldiers, however, is annoying as they never miss their shot, they throw grenades that allows lands near you, and they take too many shots to kill even in medium difficulty. This makes the gun fights tedious, and I usually just skip pass groups of soldiers instead of fighting head on unless it is required. Another problem with the game is the confusing ways to advance the game. So in the level "On the rails", you get to a dead end where  there is a mounted machine gun fires. After you kill the person operating the machine guns, what you are supose to do is to go towards the red blast door on the track and it automatically opens for you. There are 2 problems, first in the earlier level "We got hostiles", the red doors that you open to advance towards the silos requires you to go around the office, and open the door via a button, so you assume you need a button to open said door. Second, the door is in the middle of the tracks. Last time that happens you ram it open using the cart, so it is logical to conclude that this what you need to do. Many maps in Half life are like that, giving vague direction of where you need to go, and ending causing the player to get lost and backtrack unneccessary portions. Third problem, the final boss. For spoiler warning, all I could say is the same problem with some levels, no indication of what you are supose to do and an annoying attack that hinders your progress.
. Also platforming in a first person shooter game is not a good idea, but it is managable in Half life so I let that slide.
Beside all this rant of the problems, I still have fun, a ton of fun. Half life does have its flaws, but I enjoyed it a lot and finished it within 8 hours. Each flawed level is overweighted by good ones like"Black mesa inbound", "Questionable ethics", "Lambda core", and in late game, weapons like the Glueon gun is fun and powerful. I probably won't play Half life a second time, but again there are a ton of mods made for it, so I could have fun modding the game or playing community created maps.
Recommendation: Play it, its problematic but still fun as hell.

*TL:DR Half-Life is an alien shooter with a few minor puzzles and a semi mysterious story. If you enjoy games in this genre, Half-Life is a must buy when on sale for $0.99.
Half-Life takes you on a journey as Dr. Gordon Freeman, a theoretical physicist who has to defend himself when an experiment goes terribly wrong. Being an older game, Half-Life is pretty rough around the edges. The game doesn't force feed you a story. It's up to you to assume whats happening with the small pockets of information that you hear / see as you work your way through the game.
Pros:
- Runs great on low end rigs.
- Can get it extremely cheap on sale.
- Shooter with a story.
- Gets you to slightly think. Not entirely spoonfed.
Cons:
- Odd shooting mechanics:
-> Aim assist /  Aim lock - makes headshots hard on some enemies.
-> Enemies will take damage but bullets hit elsewhere occasionally.
-> Most guns pointless. Found myself using the pistol most the game.
- Odd jumping mechanics:
-> Pressing backwards mid jump stops all momentum.
-> Found myself crouch jumping up most things.
For a game released in 1998, I give it props. If you can get this game on sale for less than a dollar, I would highly recommend it.
Rating: 8 / 10 (If buying as a budget title)

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I usually don't write reviews, and i apology if my grammar fails me somewhere, but this game deserves it.
Town of Salem is a game where 15 people are divided in to 3 groups: Townies, Mafia, and Neutral roles.
Each side has multiple roles befitting that faction, neutral being a special case. Townies are requiered to eliminate mafia and evil neutral roles, Mafia needs to kill all of the Townies (and evil roles that are a treat to the family) while each Neutral role has a specific goal, wheter it is to be the last man standing or simply survive until the game ends.
After joining the lobby the match starts once 15 people are gathered (unless the hosts decides to start sooner with fewer people but please don't do that). You choose the name you'll have during that match, for each match you can choose a diffrent name, and after that you'll get assigned a role and a game can start. In game phases are divided in to day time and night time when each role, if able, performs its ability. During the day all of the players gather to share informations, talk, lie and acuse each other. At the end of a "discussion phase" players vote who to send to the block, and if more than half players vote someone out that someone is given a chance to defend himself. Players then vote if the acused one is guilty or innocent. If voted guilty he is executed and if not he is released. During the night time Mafia gathers to discuss their plans such as who will they murder next, who will be blackmailed, who will be framed and so on. But Mafia members aren't the only night owls, Serial killers, Werewolfs and other evil people are choosing their targets, Sheriffs are looking for bad guys while Doctors are visiting potential targets.
Notable "mods" the game offers are "Normal" and "Chaos" mod. Normal one offers mostly predetermined roles, leaving only a few of them to be random, so you know what to expect in that match, while Chaos mod generates 15 random roles, making the match a lot less predictable, but in a way a lot more fun. There is also an option of joining a Custom made match where the host of the lobby chooses which role will be played.
This game puts your ability to lie at test, but also your ability to tell the truth, as sometimes you will have to convince people to trust you when you're actualy not lying. However if you pull too much attention to yourself you just may make yourself the next target of the Mafia. Connecting dots is the most useful skill.
tl;dr: You like to lie without feeling guilt? You like to trick people? You admire getting tricked? This is a game for you!

Its got all the elements of a modern horro game except one. It has events outside your control, jumpscares, things changing position when you turn away, mandatory puzzle-solving, and a lovable creepy assailant. What it lacks is length, its easily less than 2 hours if there aren't any show-stopping bugs (only saw one - a medallion thar didn't slot into place) for normal, no clue about the tougher difficulty.
If I recall there are two configurable difficulty levels, and I assume the tougher one allows for access to slightly more content, which may make more content accessible with the added challenge (which would make sense because there were some moving parts I couldn't complete on normal).
The one knock I have with the gameplay content is the chase sequence towards the end. Repetitiously running through an I'm-being-chased maze til completing it isn't spooky or scary, its kinda lame and boring. Okay maybe two knocks - ZERO explanation as to why the character ended up in there, who they are, or anything else, so I really have zero connection to the avatar I'm controlling and feel no empathy for it. Other than that, there wasn't much in the way of psychological horror, mostly jumpscares. I have a natural +10 resistance with saving throws against jumpscares, I just laugh at them. :)
That being said, its great for a student project, and definitely has all the atmosphere and elements of a modern horror game. Thumbs up.

If you like RTS and strategy games in general and you are willing to learn, you might want to consider getting this. Has a good amount and variety of units (all are more or less useful, no clear "losers"). Has a deep-ish learning curve. Maps are spheres! Has a flowing economy, meaning that the resources will never run out on the maps. Also the community has made some great maps if the ones in the game are getting a bit dull. Has singleplayer (a campaign wannabe and skirmish) and multiplayer.
So you might be wondering what changed in PA:Titans that is not in vanilla PA. For a slight increase in price compared to PA (which is not even sold anymore) you get the titan units, some normal units and a more balanced game. Also if you have PA:T but your friend(s) only have PA you can still play with them!
I have to admit though that the game has some more or less annoying bugs. Pathing issues (becomes more and more common the more units there are on the map), joining lobbies and ranked games, joining games that you got disconnected from and a few others that i cant remember from the top of my head. But most of the bugs aren't really that common and there are easy workarounds.
The game runs pretty well on my not so good laptop (depends on what you consider "well"). But as always you should check the minimum requirements before you buy anything. The game is not graphics intensive but it takes  quite a bit of CPU (loading the systems for example). I haven't really experienced that many connection problems and it's more than likely that it's your own internets fault than the games fault. If you experience problems with the game you should go and find the games forums and ask for support/solutions there.
PS. I believe that the reason why uber didn't make PA:T a DLC is because the reviews of PA were full of outdated complaints and some unnecessary hate.
PPS. I know there are people who are actively hating the game and Uber. But please, do not hate a good game (if you think it's good) just because the company that made it is not so great. Have fun Annihilating!

Good parts:
-Fun squad based combat.
-Nice art work on people, weapons, and maps.
-Interesting additions to XCOM such as the increased importance of using reaction fire during the enemy's turn.
Not good parts:
-Annoying artistic screen glitches while trying to use the in game menu (why would I want the interface to fuzz out? It's annoying and doesn't add anything to the game. At least give us the option to turn that off.)
-Never ending cut scenes and John Woo-like special effects during missions. (I want to play a game, not sit here for 10% of the time just watching the same special effects over, and over, and over...)
-Artistic camera zooming, swooping, and shaking until I feel motion sick after some of the sequences.
-To get anywhere in the base interface, you need to sit through a 3 second zooming, swooping, disolving screen transition. And you constantly have to navigate through the base interface. It's neat the first time. OK the second. And as annoying as a mosquito in your ear for the rest of the time you're playing this game.
Summary: It's like trying to play with a fun toy, while someone else knocks it of your hands every 15 seconds.... while someone else rocks your chair in random directions.... and you start getting motion sick.... and then after 9.4 hours you just get fed up and close the game and uninstall.

The details on every inch of the game you encounter looks amazing and sets the perfect mood for the game; cozy, yet spooky. Another thing is that you need to properly WANT to survive in order to feel terrified by the enemy, which usually isn't the case with horror games that have monsters with some impressive artificial senses and intelligence. , hailing from year 2003, is the last of the adventure games created by the French developer team, Cyro Interactive. Since then, all rights of Cyro Interactive products - including
- is acquired by Microids, another wondrous name for the adventure game genre. I must declare that it is more than lucky Microids decided to distribute Cyro's old games digitally, so newer generations of adventure lovers may also experience this beauty, based on Gustave Flaubert's original novel with the same name.
It's 241 BC. After the First Punic War between Roman Republic and Carthage, Rome wins the war. An uneasy treaty of peace has been signed between parties, mostly to the benefit of Rome and now Carthage must pay mercenaries that has been recruited from various countries. While the mercenary camps are settled just outside of the city borders in an uneasy wait, a slave named Spendius manages to escape his masters. While he was trying to get out of the city without being noticed, he is stopped by Salammbo, the daughter of General Hamilcar Barca and the high priestess of goddess Tanith. Salammbo pleads with Spendius that he would carry a message to the one she loves, Matho, the Libyan leader of mercenaries. Spendius agrees, and thus begins his long, brutal and laborious climb from a lowly slave to a general of the Mercenary Revolt that would threaten to bring Carthage to its fall.
The original story is written by Gustave Flaubert, after the immense success of his first novel,
. Even though his main source was Polybius's
to establish the story on a historically just timeline, the setting itself is highly fictitious. With its incredibly violent descriptions of war and surreal depictions of ritualistic traditions of Carthage back at the time,
was sensational for the era it was published. It should be also proper to note that the game is based upon Flaubert' work, yet takes a different turn rather than actual recordings; namely prefers to end the series of events with a less gruesome take.
The graphics of the game are simply breathtaking for its era, with futuristic architecture and intimidating character models. The artwork is inspired from French comic artist Philippe Druillet's graphic novel with the same name, and he has been heavily involved with the development of the game himself. The atmosphere is dark, elegant and overwhelming. Everything is intimidatingly surreal and there is a surprising attention to detail when it comes to all and any textures. It is probably nothing impressive for today, but it is simply beautiful still.
The game interface is annoying though, and it works really slowly. Remember really old adventure classics like
series, where you'd have a 360 degree of visual angle, yet to you'd have to click at some direction to move?
carries the same tradition. Since there is no "you are here" indicator or any kind of "useful" map interface, this can get pretty disorienting with all that dark and alien architecture around at the start. If you are not easily discouraged though, you get the hang of what is what and what may reside where after a while.
Gameplay is fairly simple. Collecting items, solving puzzles and some riddles. Fair enough. Nothing is especially hard or boorishly easy. If you are to listen to dialogue implications carefully and get used to making the best of your environment, the game flows fairly. One warning though: even though the story and the gameplay is linear, there are many, many ways to end up dead. You may very well imply the wrong notion to the wrong person in a dialogue or miss a timed puzzle to end up Spendius massacred in various brutal ways. Don't forget that you are a rebel and spy, trying to fight not only against a whole city, yet anyone that may decide it could be beneficial to get rid of you. Luckily, the game restores you to the last point where everything was somewhat okay the minute you screw up and end up dead. So, you won't be facing the labor of playing through a portion of the game just because you forgot to save.
The game isn't for everyone. But for the adventure gamer who'd appreciate a good story, beautiful environment design and some fair puzzle challenges,
is a true gem, even today. It might be a bit frustrating for the history buff, since the environment is futuristic and the events do not match up with the actual recording, but I truly recommend to spare a leisurely evening to give this one a try. Good day, and good gaming to you!

Salammbô is the last game from Cryo, the legendary game studio that made great games like Atlantis, and always had a great eye for detail and valued art and considered games like a new way of expression (back when games were not still considered as such). Cryo was founded also by members of Infogrames, the creators of Alone in the dark (the original)
This last effort of theirs, was troubled in its conception, partly because the studio closed its doors while doing this game (2002). Wich of course affected the development but luckily didn't  affect the game too much so the game was finished and published (2003). And while the game was not the best of the studio it was one of the good ones. The art, still present to the last minute was done in this case by Philippe Druillet an acomplished french artist who did work inspired by the writing of HP Lovecraft. Druillet created originally a series of graphic novels in the 1980s called Salammbó wich were based on the novel of the same name created by Gustave Flaubert in the 1800s. This was a lush and very violent narrative wich depicted historical events about the fall of Carthage during the 3th century (the Punic wars) and the revolt of the mercenaries.
Salammbó is a dark game with weird visuals wich reflects perfectly the character of the artist. The game alltough it is dated now (2016) and has low resolution (it was one of the last full screen games before everyone went widescreen) still manages to this day to show some incredible art from Druillet wich work previously with Cryo doing Ring: The legend of the Nibelungen. I played originally the dubbed english version wich has horrible voices and now the original french one (both on steam) wich is better but still is not the reason why you are going to play this game.
The game has not much support from its present publishers so if you have a problem you are probably going to search for a solution. Personally, the only problem i had was that i had to activate compatibility mode in Windows 7 x64 bit version for the game executable, because if i didn't do that, the game crashed miserably when opening it...but aside from that (it was a very quick solution) the game worked without problems...still, it would be better if you just sold a game that didn't have such a glaringly fatal problem so big and clear in first full view (when you open the game i mean) even if the game is 13 years old, you should check from time to time the games you are selling for any compatibility issues (in this case steam) and fix them before continue selling them... what the heck, i gladly would offer myself to take the job of checking these games if steam would be interested, just for them to to be able to continue selling this classic games...without having crashing issues wich can be solved so easily (but shouldn't be done by players, because when you buy a game it shouldn't be crashing on you....like riven ...another great classic with compatibility issues....)
Anyway, besides that, the game is surely great....i wouldn't necesarily recommend it to a modern age player, because it can be hard to adjust to is gameplay rules.... BUT if you dare to do it...you are going to be rewarded, because theres a nice story and great visual work by druillet.

Having spent over 500 hours total at least on this game (I moved over to Steam not too long ago hence the low hour count on it as I played on the main website), I would count myself as experienced enough to write my opinion on this game.
The community is extremely helpful and any questions anybody may have will most certainly always be answered. Furthermore, there is a moderator or a staff member at most times of the day for any further enquiries. After many years the game is still being played by around 300 or so unique users a day so it is far from dead and is being updated monthly with big patches coming out every few months. The latest big patch was the archery and fletching addition and there was a smaller patch around a week or so ago. There are many things being currently worked on and upcoming additions into the game as well as the anniversary coming up on the 21st or so of July marking the 4th year of RPG MO if i am not mistaken. But anyways, the game is very active and not about to die as long as people keep playing which many will.
The game is NOT pay to win however, you can drop a little bit of cash in order to save the coin costs on certain items like the firelord set, orbs of luck and such. I definitely would recommend this game to anybody who loves spending hours on grinding in a social, friendly environment. I will not lie, it is very similar to RuneScape in many ways but has its own charm and is somewhat different from it. Those who love a grind fest will adore this game. I personally love grinding and spend a lot of time doing so. This game is definitely not for everybody but you can give it a try and may stay for the community if not for the grind itself. The game is not pay to win but pay to profit. You can become rich but you still need to grind to gain levels and use various equipment which has level requirements. You can be as rich as you want but you wont be able to use 99% of items.
The combat system itself is RNG with the factors of Strength, Accuracy and Defence being the main factors of the damage dealt, received and % chance of hitting. There are other mechanics such as Archery and Magic. Magic add magic damage to your next hit but costs money as you need to use spell scrolls to obtain spell charges in your magic pouch while archery will use arrows which you put into your quiver. The combat system itself is easy to understand and you gain XP according to the damage you deal to monsters which is where the grindfest comes in.
There is a "skilling and harvesting" part of the game which is my favourite mechanic in the game. You can mine, cut wood, farm and fish. These, for now, are the main harvesting skills.  (Mining, Woodcutting, Farming and Fishing)
There are also "skilling" or "crafting" skills in RPG MO which are: Forging, Jewelry, Fletching, Alchemy, Breeding, Carpentry and cooking.

I held off writing this review until all the DLC came out because as is the case with many games nowadays community feedback and devoted developers often cause games to undergo big changes even after release, and this game is no exception. Many of the problems people had with the game when it came out are gone, and as a full package with all 4 DLC the game is fully realized and certainly worth your time and money.
This game is in a weird spot. If you're a shooter fan, it may feel like a fairly competent shooter, with some other weird turret things thrown in. If you're a Tower Defense player, it will feel very strange not always having a bird's eye veiw mainscreen (though there is a minimap and pressing a button will enlarge it so don't worry) and having these wierd variables of teammates and not having perfect aim all the time. If you like both, it is an outstanding blend of the two genres. And I recommend it to both fps and td fans. Fans of both sides may be dissapointed in the lack of this or that, but if you forget about games you've already played to compare it to for a minute, those things may not make sense in this hybrid.
That being said, the gameplay is phenomenal. A great blend of strategy and skill, but without requiring too many desicions and responsibilities that the player can easily become to overwhelmed. You build a maze, build towers (you choose what to bring beforehand) and then get to shooting. Mistakes are punished but don't mean the end until very late in the game. You have many ways to fix your holes and mistakes, even mid-wave. There is also an immense amount of freedom. Pro FPS-er? Take a bunch of perks that help you kill enemies and just let the towers clean up. TD Vet? Create a build that buffs your towers so you don't need to do much shooting. There's loads of combinations and styles of play that make the replay value even bigger. There's always that weird combo you want to try out for fun just to see if you can beat the level with it. The levels curve in very nicely, and there are enough modes and difficulty modifyers to keep you playing well after you've reached max level. Speaking of which, there's also a level up system where you unlock new weapons and perks. Early unlocks tend to be more general and easy to use, while still being powerful in their own right. Later unlocks are more specialized and require a bit more skill and familiarity with the game, and offer a slight better advantage if used correctly. No one unlock completely invalidates another, either. It's a very good system.
In addition, the single player and multiplayer are vastly different experiences. Play both. They're the exact same game but as soon as you have a team, its an almost completely different one. The way multiplayer and singleplayer seamlessly blend together is great as well, and usually only requires you to shift mindsets, not builds (at least in the middle of a map - organizing for the next one and specializing is one of the myriad ways the game becomes different).
The outstanding team at Coffeestain is one of the most hardworking and talented development teams I've seen from an indie studio in a long time. I often find myself drawing parallels between them and CDProjekt Red when they started out. You can see the level of attention to detail if you look at the game closely, how every little piece seems to sort of mesh together to make a very nice whole. The art and music direction is phenomenal, without saying anything and before the first wave even starts you get a feel for it, where you are, what you're doing, and the impact you're having. The comic book for loading screens just gives the right amount of context to understand what's going on, the environments, music, and enemies tell the real story.
The game isn't without its flaws though. Sometimes it can lag a little bit or disconnect you, but that could just be my bad internet. Many guns don't feel terribly satisfying to shoot because things don't have so much health, and many of the enemies look similar. It's hard to find to many criticisms for the game though.
Overall, I highly recommend you pick up the whole package. It isn't for everyone, I will concede, so I also recommend trying the demo and see how you like the first few levels. Then pick up the whole game and if you want to the season pass or individual DLCs. They're all fantastic additions to the game. One even includes a fifth playable character. Don't worry if your friends aren't getting it and you think you'll have no one to play with, the community here is also one of the friendliest I've ever encountered.
If you can get past the static character models, you may find that "RPG MO" has a certain charm.

One Sentence Summary- A high-end point and click adventure with great graphics for the time it came out.
***(If you encounter a bug where the game freezes on the world map, please see my last Con (-) bullet point for a fix)***
--MY THOUGHTS--
I got this game very cheaply as part of a bundle. I did not know what to expect. This game seems to follow a pseudo-historical timeline, meaning it takes place in a fantasy/historical setting. The graphics are great. This game comes from a time when developers were learning various tricks to make games look amazing with little processing power. Think back to the early ps1 days when they used 3d polygonal characters with pre-rendered backgrounds (Resident Evil, Final Fantasy 7 thru 9). This allowed developers to make games with graphics way more detailed than what would be possible with real-time 3d rendering. Then, even later, developers improved upon that with making these pre-rendered backgrounds more lively like a cinematic video. This game is very much a point and click adventure with 360 degree living/moving pre-rendered backgrounds. For example, you can look every which way. You can see soldiers moving, animals moving, and things happening all around you (quite beautifully, too). When you talk to a person, it moves to a much closer view of the person speaking to you in the similar form of the cinematic vidoes of the past (about xbox360 graphics). The impressive thing about this is, is that this is a game that can run on a 400mhz processor and 128 mb ram.
This game should take most players about 7-10 hours to complete. Below are pro's and con's:
--PROS--
+You can get this game cheaply in game bundles on various game bundle websites. (I've seen it twice so far)
+The game has very low minimum system requirements.
+The graphics are quite good.
+ The voice acting is pretty good for the most part, with few moments of exceptions.
+The story looks to be interesting.
+The game has pretty high production values.
+The setting is a fantasy/historical setting, which is pretty creative.
+There are some pretty creative puzzles that will make you think.
--CONS--
-The game seems to be a bit dark on it's storyline and setting (some people may like this)
-Pretty much all of the characters are selfish, greedy people. Even the protagonist, Spendius, seems to have few redeeming qualities.
-The game graphics and style is dated (but it has aged fairly well, IMO)
-There are a few puzzles where the solutions are simply too obscure. For example, in one puzzle, the player would need to know that apparently Carthaginian writing is from right to left, from bottom to top, and that the grid without numbers has an opposite order of how numbers appear on a phone (1-3, 4-6, 7-9, etc.). There are one or two other similar puzzles. I would recommend consulting an online walkthrough if you spend more than 30 minutes on any puzzle.
-There seem to be a few bugs or compatability problems (I am using win 8). When I changed the resolution, things got really messed up and I had to verify the installation to replace a file. Another time, the game crashed. The biggest error I saw (and others have experienced it as well) is one where after you acquire a animal to ride, you have a map where you can choose where you want to go. After choosing the location, the game simply stops. After an internet search, I found a post on the steam community board where one person mentioned a workaround. If you encounter this bug, press f5 repeatedly, and you will see the cursor slowly move towards the destination. If you have a laptop, you may need to press shift and f5 or another similar button combination. Very strange, but it worked.
--SUMMARY--
All in all, the game seems pretty interesting. The asking price ($4.99) is not bad, but I would recommend picking it while on sale or in part of a bundle.

Based on the historic novel by Gustave Flaubert the team at Cryo Interactive (Rereleased by Anuman & Meridian4) made a first person point & click game with some combat in it to tell the story of how Carthage fell. Now before I start I want to get the negatives out of the way before I say anything good about it. The interface is god awful/annoying, the story is kinda linear but follows the original novel pretty well without being boring, the puzzles are easy except for a few hard ones (Perfect game for the new adventurer), the music is decent but it's inaccurate whenever the game plays it & depending on how good you are with puzzles (There's mini games like War Chess but that doesn't last too long) the game will last around 7 hours.
Now with that out of the way I'll start by saying for a 12 year old game it's got a weird & gorgeous art style it's just a unique piece of animation done well, the voice acting is very good, the humans look like aliens & demons, the atmosphere has that science fiction (Or Fantasy I dont know what Cryo was targeting) heavy metal type style you would see on music albums like Mastodan or GWAR for example & overall I would just wait for the game to go on sale since the game was only an average experience.
Bonus: The original story is on Good Reads if you want to check it out
Bonus 2: Another influence for this game is Phillippe Druillet (the website is in french)

The developers contacted me by email asking me to give this game a thumbs up, telling me it does not matter what I actually write about the game so long as I rate it positive. So here is my (negative) review.
Consortium is a first person shooter/action/adventure game.
The game is all very fourth wall, where you yourself are transported into the game world via a satellite. You're a "Bishop" in the Consortium, aboard the ZENLIL ship, where everyone has ranks matching the game of chess.
Your task is to stop rebellion forces attacking the ship and ensuring it safely reaches its destination. However things go south and you're tasked with trying to uncover which person on the ship is a traitor to your cause, using a speech system similar to most RPG games.
The game is incredibly short, at around 1-2, maybe 3 hours, with some minor replayability. The game ends abruptly, which left me incredibly disappointed. I was extremely excited for this game and even pre-ordered, but once the game ended I suddenly saw that it's episodic. This is something the developers never indicated which left a -very- sour taste in my mouth. I was incredibly let down which is why I cannot recommend this game. I'm sure the sequel will also be just as short with an ending just as abrupt.
Wait for the next two episodes to release, and pick all three up on a sale. Maybe Consortium as a whole will be good as all three games, but this sole entry is too short and lacks the depth for me to recommend a purchase.

The rules are very simple, be respectful, don't cheat, and if you're going to talk about something that is considered an adult topic then go to the 18 chat. The combat system is simple to understand, magic adds to your next melee hit. The UI has been frequently updated over the past several months on things making the game more and more enjoyable.
The only thing I have a problem with on here is that I believe the tutorial system needs to be updated to include directions on how to use the wiki as I find myself answering the same questions daily to new players as well as the tutorial system should be updated to include the current version of the game.

- Casual gamers will hate this game as it stands now.
Look. Capcom tried to appeal to casual gamers while appeasing the 3rd strike crowd by removing 1-frame links and making the game entirely based around footsies. The problem is that competative players like me still dominate online matches, and because everything is so basic, matches are boring to watch and stale as a result of most match-ups consisting of close quarters guessing games. If you analyze even Tokido vs Daigo matches, most hits are actually random and not based on skill.
A HUGE PROBLEM WITH THE GAME IS THAT IT'S BORING TO WATCH.
I want you to really think about this for a second. Every match boils down to two players standing next to each other, pressing a slow normal, and one players normal randomly connects, leading to a frame advantage. You can call this reads, footsies, whatever. It's extremely boing to watch compared to melee or USF4. Capcom really screwed up here, and I think Combofiend (developer) was so busy making it a great way to measure skill between two players, that he forgot the magic ingredient that a fighting game needs. He did accomplish perhaps the best way to measure the skill of two players ever - the better player always wins, but somehow too many other ingredients were sacrificed in the process.
The main problem for Capcom with SF5 since launch day, is that the game just doesn't appeal to casual gamers. It had a terrible launch, and MKX and other recent fighting games makes SF5 look like an early alpha. They could have easily averted this, and I think it will be their downfall. I predict a massive shrinking of the fighting community and a slow decline in tournament participants and viewers. I will continue to enjoy this game, and I love playing it as a competative player, but I'm sorry Combofiend, those aren't the most important aspects of a fighting game.
No upsets, no excitement, no FGC.
