So... ok I have no idea why I'm going back to edit this review but I feel some need to share a bit more on the game. So here be my list (or what I can at least remember) of PROs and CONs. Be advised that these can be different from person to person and will possibly be missing A LOT of things in between.
PROs:
>>The game is ADDICTIVE.
>>You can buy houses. Own a stall. Be the governor of your own island and captain of your own crew and king/queen of your own flag.
>>Over the years more puzzles have been added as well as challenges. For example, there's Treasure Haul, Foraging, Weaving, Patching and that other sailing puzzle I keep forgetting about. There might be a furniture crafting related puzzle in the future but that's just me and my wishful thinking. As for challenges there's Kraken Hunts, Brigand Hunts, Atlantis- I am naming all these things that came out over the years and not just recent but yeah you get the point.
>>Tutorials... well I don't know how that works now but in the past (ok fine, over a decade ago) your newly shipwrecked pirate's whisked away on a crew ship where you're spoon fed all you need--- about puzzles. Yeah, no real clue about the other details of the game such as starting a crew, governing an island, owning a building and other things but basically, there IS a tutorial and I might just be stating this after seeing a review about the game not having a tutorial.
>>It... actually has some replay value. Sure the game's not much different- (well not at all) since the day I first started, however, new features, games, seals, trophies, etc. make the game something worth coming to. And you'll be surprised at how easily you'll get lost in playing it again after a while, but of course, that differs from person to person.
>>You CAN play and experience every feature in this game even WITHOUT paying real money for it. Of course, this still requires the use of dubloons, grabbing badges, etc. etc. The dubloon exchange exists to allow players to exchange pieces of eight for dubloons to use in buying badges necessary to unlock certain features of the game like Kraken Hunting, Atlantis, stall jobs, job puzzles, those cards/drink/swordfighting/rumble puzzles and officer privelages. Just know that the dubloons aren't being sold cheap and depending on your luck and the times, they could be running from 2.5k to 5k (pieces of eight mind you). Trust me... I was surprised to see how expensive they are now too.
>>Following up on the puzzles, certain puzzles are available on certain days. Wanna go play Smithing? Wait until Tuesday. Foraging? Wait until Wednesday. Rumble and Swordfighting? That's on Monday! DISCLAIMER: I DO NOT REMEMBER THE DAYS THESE PUZZLES ARE ACTUALLY OPEN. The badges are basicaly just there to allow you to play the puzzles at your own leisure and earn even more pieces of eight via jobbing. Of course, this does not apply to hunts, flots, etc. which require the Bravery Badge.
>>The community... well. Let's just say the community is... SPECIAL. There are those that are weird. Those that are down right rude. Those that are friendly. Those that are- basically just your average online community. You might have to be a tad bit lucky and a hella bit persistent if you wanna find a goodcircle to indulge in but, trust me, if you find the perfect crew you won't be sorry. Course, times change and people do come and go in the game so expect to see new faces and miss old ones over time, especially when you're the type that tends to disappear for long periods of time like I do. (Read, years.)
>>There is this thing called GREETER PILLAGES. As people know, some pirates hold greenie pillages, or pillages for green users. These pirates usually have pink names and are called greeters and are players who spend some time to help acquaint people to the game. They can take these new pirates on trial pillages, hunts, etc. and teach them about the usual game etiquette and jargon used in the middle of a game... Actually, this is the best the game has to offer when it comes to tutorials. And it can be fun, especially when the greeter's got some good sense of humor in them.
>>You can always STOP. I think this might be the most important part. You can stop playing the game at your leisure. It's FREE for crying out loud and you can enjoy it fully just by- well, enjoying it. All the features are within arm's reach if you just keep playing. And if you get tired of it, you can just put it down. No need to waste money and all that if you feel it's not worthit.
CONs:
>>The game is ADDICTIVE.
>>You'll end up playing for hours on end and might end up with a huge migraine from staring at your screen for too long or from the puzzles.
>>The game reminds you to take a break from playing.
>>It DOES get repetitive after a while, and to a mind numbing level at that. Addictive and repetitive does not go well together.
>>Inactivity CAN lead to DELETION. I don't particularly know or remember how long it'll take before your pirate gets deleted from inactivity but one review said it only takes 6 weeks. Now, before anything, you are sent an email before your account is deleted and all you need to do to keep that from happening is to log on for... just over a minute. Or well, not even that long. After that you can close the game and say goodbye to it until your next warning. Now, as for what happens when your pirate is deleted- well, obviously EVERYTHING goes poof. Badges, pieces of eight, dubloons, ships, crew, achievements, trophies, pets, houses, EVERYTHING. So it's usually a good idea to log in every two months or something to make sure this doesn't happen. ESPECIALLY if you actually care about losing progress.
>>The... community lol. Ok as I said earlier, the place is a hotpot of people. There are good, and of course there are the bad ones. There are plenty of scammers EVERYWHERE in this game. At least from when I first started. These days, I haven't seen a single one though that can be accounted for my lack of activity but not many have talked much about any scammers recently. The other thing, are elitists who only pick pirates based on their reputation or skill level as depicted on their pirate page. This has often times dissuaded a few people from playing the game or trying out a new feature, and other times, most especially in a hunt where everyone's cooperation is needed, these people who are in charge can get... a little out of hand. You can'tentirely blame them due to the losses you can suffer in these hunts but still, that is what greeter pillages are for.
>>Lags and glitches. Lags and glitches everywhere when you least expect it.
OTHER THINGS??
>>I won't call it a pro or a con, but the graphics of the game are... well fine. Walk animation- what is that? lol. Minimal interaction with your environment? Yeeeeerp. Puzzles bright as heck and burns the eyes? Yeeeeep. Basically, the graphics... well they aren't perfect, but they're a decent fit to the game.
So... TL;DR
The game introduces new puzzles and pillages/hunts every now and then. You also have events that give you one time trophies as well as monthly seals that might be out of reach if you don't have badges sometimes or a good crew that would take you in. All the features are unlockable either through insane amounts of effort or minimal effort depending on whether you're lucky, have good friends, or money you feel like throwing at the game. Aaand you can quit at any time.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In it's simplest and purest form, this Strategy game proves once more that bigger / complicated isn't always better. Unlike some other Tower Defense games, you can really influence the game because you have to make a path for the units. It's not liked the locations for the towers are fixed. Whenever a Tower Defense game makes use of this type of Tower Placement, it already scores a lot of points on my list.
The core of the game is very solid, the levels are very challenging ( Depending on one of the three difficulties ) and the amount of control you can practise on the battlefield is amazing. This can be done by making complicated choices between Quanitity and Quality. For Example: Do i want to build 4 more chaingun towers? Or do i want to build a tower that slows units down, thus giving the excisting towers more time to destroy them. And do i want to spread the towers out over the map or do i want a very dense 'killing zone'?
I can certainly recommend this game. Even to people that aren't into Tower Defense games. If you're doubting, just do it!

A big improvement over the first game. I'm about halfway through the second "act," and I've yet to encounter an enemy so moronicly undefeatable as the bobbleheads from Sanctum. In Sanctum 2, instead of choosing two weapons to compliment your "trusty" pistol, you choose a character class (which locks your primary weapon) and a secondary weapon. Meh. It's the same, they just call it something different. The difference is that the weapons are much more effective, and don't get upgraded.
In Sanctum, you had to pull off this frustrating balancing act between building blocks, putting towers on top of those blocks, upgrading towers and upgrading your guns. You never had enough money to do quite enough. In Sanctum 2, blocks are free but you only get a certain number of them per round. And since your guns don't get upgraded, all your money is divided between building and upgrading towers.
In addition, they've got rid of the televators. To get up on top of your walls, you juts jump. One less thing to spend money on.
Sanctum 2 looks better (I always felt that Sanctum was blindingly bright, but the colors in S2 are a bit more muted, making the game a lot easier on the eyes), plays easier (it's easier to play, not easier to win), and is all-around more fun than its predecessor. Haven't had the chance to check out the co-op mode yet, but I imagine it will be a bit like Dungeon Defenders.
Towers and guns in S2 are far simpler, and therefore much easier to use. Instead of lengthy, fluffy explanations of each tower and weapon, there are two lines. Something like "Deals damage in an area. Good againt swarms." That's something that always troubled me about Sanctum; it took a lot of experimentation (and dying) to figure out how to use the different towers. Sanctum 2 gets rid of that issue by essentially giving you the classic TD towers you're already familiar with and giving them simple explanations so you immediately understand that "Kairos" means "slow tower."
All things considered, Sanctum 2 is a big improvement over Sanctum. I am very impressed. Clearly, the developer took into account user feedback from the original game.
This doesn't happen very often, but I'm giving Sanctum 2 a grade of A. The game fixes almost all (if not all) of the problems from the first game and changes things up enough to still be interesting to a player who spent a lot of time playing the original. Not a simple task in a genre so over-done as Tower Defense.
Orcs Must Die 2, for example, is essentially a glorified DLC map pack. I haven't had the good fortune to playtest Defense Grid 2, but I expect essentially a new coat of paint and some interesting new enemies. Sanctum 2 is a great follow-up to a game that wasn't quite as good as it might have been. Along with Defense Grid, Sanctum 2 is now a staple of my "Defense" category.
Update: I have accidenteally tried co-op, and it's pretty cool. It's not really like Dungeon Defenders. In DD, things tended to shake out to "I'll watch this door, you watch that one." S2 co-op is much more team-oriented. Since most maps have only one enemy entrance, you have to actually collaborate on maze-building and placement of towers. I don't recall if each player gets a certain number of blocks to plop down each round or if you share from a pool, but whichever way it is, it works just fine.
Co-op seems to be drop-in/drop-out, meaning that at any point in the match you might gain or lose players. It also seemed that the difficulty (toughness and quantity of enemies) scales according to the number of players.
In short, co-op good. I'll still spend most of by time solo, but I will ocassionally start an open co-op game, if only to see how other people handle a map that's troubling me.

Now, this is one game almost solely dedicated to the notion of SPOOKY.   The other recurring theme is MODELS:  No, not the wafer-thin things that caper about on cat-walks, but rather a three-dimensional model of the title building and its attendant rooms/sections (an absolutely ingenious device which you'll just have to play the game to "spoil" for yourself), as well as some of the hands-down scariest bronze statues/art models you will ever have the good fortune to be terrorized by.
I gotta say, it's always nice to be so pleasantly surprised by a game you didn't even know existed until it was already available in the Steam store (the last such game for yours truly was perhaps Outlast, so this title is in mighty good company therein). This isn't to say there aren't a few problems, however...
Firstly, the Steam asking price is a tad silly for a game which even I managed to complete in under two hours ('cause believe me, I play games kinda sloooooow).  The project is apparently the product of university students graduating from a game design course, so within those parameters it's impressive as hell, but it doesn't hurt to recognise that even the very best of such projects can't exactly go head-to-head with the "big boys", especially price-wise.
Secondly, there's a few glitches...on more than one occasion, I had a particular enemy permanently freeze on me; which might almost sound like a "good"/opportunistic thing, but decidedly less so when you require said enemy to cause damage to something in order for you to progress.
Also, I had a hell of a time getting a couple of objects to successfully interact with what they were SUPPOSED to interact with.  I especially had no end of fun trying to get a round ornamental medal thing to go into its appropriate slot in a wall...thought I must be missing something...looked up a video walkthrough and lo and behold, the dude playing it gets it in first go without even trying.  One game reboot later and I finally managed it, but again not quite as promptly as Mr Walkthrough did, so...yes, problems, it had a few.  I did however break with my usual cheapskate tradition (of waiting for a decent sale) and bought this game smack-dab on its release date, so perhaps these little bugs will be corrected with time...
On the whole, though...VERY impressed.  Expect big, big things from the people involved.  For now, this one merely qualifies as just a single "big", but there's no doubt there's some talent involved here.  If I were their teacher, I would definitely give them an "A" (but not quite an "A+")...but since I'm not a teacher, I'll simply rate them in my standard manor (whoops, make that "manner"), and round off my review with the customary:
Verdict: 8.5/10.

Pros (+) & Cons (-) in short:
- difficult to understand
+ incredibly big variety in build startegies (Unit types, units, defense, experimental buildings)
- no fractions
+ good balancing (no fractions)
- no skilltrees
+ good balancing (no skilltrees)
- still some (minor) ai bugs
+ Titans (Prototypes)
- no story mode
+ challenging singleplayer mode (skirmish like, but with changed settings like with skill trees)
+ System (Map) designer
+ more content than comparable (all?) RTS games
- long term game (you need to play it a lot)
+ long term game (you are able to play it a lot!)
- game is almost dead
Conclusion: Well made game that is still fun to play, has much content, uncountless strategies and deserves more attention, sadly many people are still mad for reasons that don't change the actual game.
People expect too much, and are easily offended by various strategies of companies. It is a bad thing, that the game has to be bought twice, but it had the price of a dlc for owners of the original game (13$ something).
Also the game is balanced, there are too many reviews about the balance of the game, while the player played only a few hours.The game is big. Incredibly big!
Unlike other RTS Games like Starcraft you won't find the perfect build orders. The game offers you way too many possibilities to play, to find a perfect strategy. And this is one of the reasons why this game is so good, and i recommend it. The game offers much more content than any total annihilation or supreme commander did, with a few exceptions: the skilltree and the fractions.
I liked the skills in SC2 but that they are missing is not too bad, as you can build improved factories, that more or less replace the skilltree.
Then there are no fractions. And even the different commanders are only different in thier look and behave all the same. This also sounds bad, but on the other hand you have now all buildings and units available at once. You don't need to fear that your opponent has walking ships and you mostly low-range units. Well actually this sounds pretty balanced to me, as you can adjust your strategy while playing. In SC2 you were quite f*cked when you realized mid-game that you would have needed another skilltree and mid-game turns end-game suddenly.
The more possibilities in building, adjustment, units, defense system, orbital units, planets & asteroids etc. make it quite difficult to play und understand the game as a beginner. And also, the tutorial sucks. You need to take the time to discover the game by yourself.
That's a reason why many people dislike the game and give bad reviews. Their complaints are mostly about "buying the game twice",  "this should has been the game in the first place", "It's not balanced" (from users that played <3hrs), "Paid update" etc. Those reviews have nothing to do with the game itself and should be avoided, while still some arguments are true. Like the bad ai, when it comes to movement. Sometimes the units get stuck and need to recalculate the route because they didn't walk around obstacles. But thats bugs that mostly won't bother you when playing. I've never seen someone losing because 2 of 50 walking units got stuck and arrived a bit later.
The only real problem with the game is not in the game itself. And that problem is a really sad one:
The Game is dead. Almost.
Log in any time you want, you won't find more than 5 active online games and the queue for ranked games is most likely empty for a while.
And even most of the active multiplayer parties are using PA, and not PA: Titans which makes owning Titans useless in most public parties.
I love the game and you should give it a try, maybe when it's a sale.
Improvement in my opinion:
The game should have the turn-based singleplayer mode (galactic war) available for online parties. Including real and ai players, that try to expand and gain improvements from wins. It could be more like the singleplayer from rome, or other total war games, the possibility is there

I really like this game. I am absolutely addicted to it, but it has its fair share of problems. Firstly, modding. When a game's experience becomes boring and repetitive, I like to spice things up with mods. I wish people were given the ability to easily create animations, wavebanks, texturepacks, and the like. Its kind of depressing going to the steam workshop only to find skins that either replicate more powerful items or are just terminally boring. There's another problem with this game, experience. Im talking both levelling up, and the experience that the player has. While I do understand that you need to make money somehow, you shouldnt force players into paying real money just to enjoy a game. If that were the case, it might be a better idea to just charge money from the get-go, with all of the content unlocked, and more easily obtainable. This game is challenging, and has quite a bit of replayability, if you know where to look. At times, though, it can seem kind of boring. When you go to the next world, there isn't anything new. It feels like "artificial difficulty." There isnt really anything new to do in the new world when you rank up. The only things that change are: enemies gaining more health and defense and dealing significantly more damage, much less cornerstones, and more powerful weapons that become useless  because they deal significantly less damage than your current weapon, at least where I am in the  game's progression. Thats about it. There are no new enemies to fight, just the same enemies, except beefier. The game needs optimization. Badly. Even on computers with really high specs, and all of the graphics setting turned to low, all of the framerate-hungry setting turned off, R.E.T.R.O.M.O.D.E activated, VFX turned off, the game STILL lags! And even then, with all of the VFX turned off, the game becomes less exciting to look at, and more difficult to play. Especially with the servers. Chunks take an eternity to load, Im often teleporting spontaneously, getting killed spontaneously, healing potions not registering, AI walking off without me because I'm apparently standing still when I'm not, just a plethora of bugs and issues that I wish would be fixed.
Like I said, I really like this game. I think the voxel art style is adorable. I just wish I could enjoy it without all of the pixelation and lag.

As a fighting game player for 20 years now, I grew up on VF2, Tekken 2 and the like. Never really liked the 2D fighters, but I appreciate what they bring to the table. So I picked up Street Fighter V to keep the fire going with the friends.
That was a mistake...
It's painfully, painfully clear that Capcom released this game far before it was ready for purchase. The purpose was to meet the requirements for EVO, a very popular fighting game competition. And in offline mode, I'm sure it's fine. Again, I'm no 2D fighter expert, and cannot comment on the mechanics.
But holy hell is the online aspect broken. I've tried every conceivable combination of online matches, from friends to joining randoms to hosting randoms. Every match ends with a disconnection within the first two rounds. If it gets that far. Not a single private match with friends has connected, hosting or joining. Every random match I've joined, I've randomly disconnected from within a minute. These are not issues I ran into with fighting games ten years ago, I have no idea why I'm facing this wall now.
As it stands, this is absolutely a Beta game. The ability to host more than one other player in a 'room' is a month away. The ability to fight another player online is a perilous journey. The practice mode lacks features introduced a decade ago. The entire experience is extremely frustrating, and I wouldn't wish it up any player, unless you're playing exclusively offline.
In that case, you have a fraction of the eventually available characters, which will likely make the game a $100+ purchase. Let's ignore the costumes and outfits for a moment, we're talking about gameplay elements here. And this won't be SFV Super Ultra Ultimate Alpha Omega, this will be the exact game you purchase at full price, yet incomplete. Future additions will arrive, unbalanced and not included in the price of entry.
This is the first and last time I purchase a SF game that isn't more than 50% off. This is more than likely the last time I purchase a SF game. I long for the arcade days, when a game felt complete, even if it had less features. But in the meantime, I'll hope for a real fighting game, like Tekken or Virtua Fighter, to come to PC..

The story is slightly sophisticated, describing difficulties in negotiations to bring factions together for a common goal.
It is a full length game and story.
The inability to easily see which direction one can move is a critical downfall of the game, detracting so much from gameplay that I regret having played.
Figuring out which exits are possible is a methodical process of scanning each direction with the mouse.
It is very easy to overlook a possible exit and get stuck only for this reason.
Much time is wasted backtracking and double checking scans for possible exits.
The map is of no help at all in this regard.
The other downfall of the game is grossly unintuitive puzzles, that make little sense even in retrospect after consulting the walkthrough.
Even worse, some of the most difficult puzzles are timed events, where one must make a series of correct decisions in rapid succession to succeed.  An absolute clickfest requiring many maddening repeats, even if one stares at the walkthrough knowing what to do.
If I was chained to the computer for 24 hours I would have NEVER gotten past some puzzles without the walkthrough.  That's terrible.
Some of the story and art is interesting, but from a gameplay and puzzle perspective I cannot recommend this game.

Sanctum 1 was a great fusion of Tower defence and First person shooter material. The enviroments were spectacular, and it was a generally good game.
Sanctum 2, is an improvement of almost all aspects. First off, the teleport barriers that warped you back to spawn if you walked too far are gone. Meaning you can now fully explore each enviroment between waves, and this is great, because Sanctum 2 is absolutely gorgeous!
The loadout system has been slightly tweaked too, employing a new Class based system with preset weapons, and perks too. These are all unlocked through a progressive levelling system, which rewards playing, but can also be a little annoying at times. I feel most people will find it restrictive, but i personally think it allows you to specialise your character better, which is important, because combat has a much bigger role in this iteration.
Towers can get the job done, yes. But they are now also quite weaker, meaning if you want to hold off all waves you need to get down there yourself and take part in the fighting. Again, many will not enjoy this, and Tower Defence purists may be annoyed.
Pretty much the entire game has also been simplfied too. Towers now only have 3 levels, but you can insert more resources in order to "overcharge" them and increase their stats more. Weapon levelling is now gone, instead relying on your loadout more. Standard block towers and offensive towers themselves now take seperate resources, meaning you can now build an effective maze and not worry about running out of resources.
All in all, i thoroughly enjoy Sanctum 2, and highly recommend you purchase it if you own the first!

XCom 2 is pure TBS joy.
I played the original UFO Enemy Unknown for DOS, loved it to pieces.  I played the XCom reboot and was thoroughly impressed with how well they modernized the game and made it interesting.  So I went into XCom 2 with high expectations, and it did not disappoint.
It's a tough as nails TBS that gets you emotionally attached to your soldiers, so that when you inevitably make that one small mistake that leads them to their doom, you kick yourself in the balls and spew a string of explitives.  This game knows how to pull just the right level of emotion out of me.
One of the biggest problems in the first XCom was that there no time limit, which meant there was exactly one strategy that was superior to all others:  Move a soldier up, overwatch, move another up, overwatch.  Play it safe, play it slow.  It would get you through just about every mission.  Especially when you get to the other big problem, which was static maps, which you'd inevitably memorize, leaving the game with no surprises left.
XCom 2 fixes both of those problems.  And while some people gripe about the timed missions, I think they do a great job at exactly what they were designed to do.  They take you out of your comfort zone, make you take risks every now and then, and prevent you from ever getting too comfortable.  They stop the game from ever getting too easy.
It's not without its share of problems.  Class balance seems to be one of them.  Rangers are a bit overpowered, and sharpshooters (in an attempt to correct how overpowered they were in XCom 1) got nerfed a bit too much.  Snipers want to park on a perch and pick guys off, but when you have a time limit you're never really able to do that, which makes the sniper tree only useful in very specific instances.
Also the enemy designs are kind of bland compared to XCom 1.  Most of the enemies you fight are just soldiers in slightly different armor designs, and only ocassionally are some of the cool aliens thrown in.
But those problems are not deal breakers by any means.  The game is still great.  It's tons of frustrating fun, if you're into that kind of thing.

I will give XCOM 2 a qualified thumbs up. I didn't really care for the initial release of the game, largely because I ran into problems with some of the strategic map (mission timers going negative and other bugs like that), some issues with overly strict mission timers (mostly unfortunate map configurations where you couldn't really fight because you had to spend all of your movement to get to the extraction point), and extremely poor game optimization that made mission load times almost unbearable. I enjoyed the game enough to play through to the end, but then I put it down and didn't come back to it very often. I tried coming back to play through after the post-launch DLC was released, but I found them underwhelming and was especially unhappy to see that the devs hadn't learned anything from the poorly received XCOM1 story mission DLCs.
However, with the release of War of the Chosen, XCOM 2 feels like a completely different game. The game runs and performs better, while the inclusion of additional options seems to have added just enough extra strategic and tactical elements to the game to make it more engaging and enjoyable experience.
If you buy XCOM 2 on sale I think you'll get your money's worth out of it, but it really won't shine unless you commit to picking up War of the Chosen, too. They have managed to build on the strengths of the first game, and I'm interested to see what direction they take XCOM 3 when that game inevitably makes an appearance.

Some may pass off Starbound as another attempt to cashe in on the "Build your own world" style of gameplay similar to minecraft (Which is solely the only reason to play that game) or terraria (Where you feel as if the only reason to build is to store your things). It is not though. I may have few hours into the game when I first got it, but I can tell, it is different. Each planet feels so real, and you grow to love your little human/apex/star kid/ect... In the first coulple of days, a rainstorm happened. A pretty nasty one. I was content to wait out the rain inside, interacting with all the furnature (a great touch BTW) and planning how to build my hut as it did rain, instead of go out and fight or explore as my little starkid got drenched. It was a feeling of satisfaction that my house protected me from the elements that I never got in the other games like this.
Starbound also does combat much better than the others I gave examples of. The system of firearms and bows being powered by energy gives a concept of saving ammo, without having to go buy ammo. Melee weapons not only burst hard, but your character seems to have heft from them, with your melee weapon appearing to have weight to them, as two handed axes seem to take more to swing from you than a knife would. Also starbound allows for dual wielding of any two one-handed weapons or shields, something i wondered why the other games couldnt get that right.
Lastly, the final reason people come to theese kind of games is the exploration, and this is the best of all. Starbound does a great job of making you feel like a space explorerer, with each planet a unique experience. You will find yourself in beautiful hilly forest plannets, or boiling desert plannets. You will brave frozen wasteland plannets, to asteroid fields rich with resources. In most planets there is also expansive underground cave systems, with things such as a dead kings tomb, to portals to pocket dimensions that lead you to a special challenge with powerful rewards.
Starcraft has been the first game to not only make me excited to leave home for an adventure, but upset aswell. Starbound has all I mentioned and more. As the game gets updated, all three of theese points strengthen even more. Bossfights are intense and truly test your skills, and colonated planets allow you to interact with the many interesting NPC's. As well, your ship's AI is quite adorable. Would I reccomend Starbound? When it was still a young game, just a skeleton, I would have not. But now? Within a heartbeat I would reccomend it to someone who is new to the "Build your own world" game style, or someone who the magic of them died out due to the lacking of satisfaction with the other games. If you are going to spend your money on any open beta, do it on Starbound. (The soundtrack is also beautiful BTW)

I really like this game. I am absolutely addicted to it, but it has its fair share of problems. Firstly, modding. When a game's experience becomes boring and repetitive, I like to spice things up with mods. I wish people were given the ability to easily create animations, wavebanks, texturepacks, and the like. Its kind of depressing going to the steam workshop only to find skins that either replicate more powerful items or are just terminally boring. There's another problem with this game, experience. Im talking both levelling up, and the experience that the player has. While I do understand that you need to make money somehow, you shouldnt force players into paying real money just to enjoy a game. If that were the case, it might be a better idea to just charge money from the get-go, with all of the content unlocked, and more easily obtainable. This game is challenging, and has quite a bit of replayability, if you know where to look. At times, though, it can seem kind of boring. When you go to the next world, there isn't anything new. It feels like "artificial difficulty." There isnt really anything new to do in the new world when you rank up. The only things that change are: enemies gaining more health and defense and dealing significantly more damage, much less cornerstones, and more powerful weapons that become useless  because they deal significantly less damage than your current weapon, at least where I am in the  game's progression. Thats about it. There are no new enemies to fight, just the same enemies, except beefier. The game needs optimization. Badly. Even on computers with really high specs, and all of the graphics setting turned to low, all of the framerate-hungry setting turned off, R.E.T.R.O.M.O.D.E activated, VFX turned off, the game STILL lags! And even then, with all of the VFX turned off, the game becomes less exciting to look at, and more difficult to play. Especially with the servers. Chunks take an eternity to load, Im often teleporting spontaneously, getting killed spontaneously, healing potions not registering, AI walking off without me because I'm apparently standing still when I'm not, just a plethora of bugs and issues that I wish would be fixed.
Like I said, I really like this game. I think the voxel art style is adorable. I just wish I could enjoy it without all of the pixelation and lag.

Consortium is one of those games that (a) defies a strict pigeon-hole; and (b) slips under the radar at release, but comes to be seen as a classic in time, like Hostile Waters or Sacrifice.
Set in the sealed environment of a futuristic plane in an alternative reality, your connection to the world is through the mind and body of Bishop Six, a sort of peacekeeping commando belonging to the Consortium, this world's UN/global goverment.
However, not all is as it seems. You are actually accessing this reality from our own via iDGi's proprietary technology- a satellite link across multiple realities. ( This is an excellent plot device for explaining the "gaming-ness" of your visuals, they claim not to have perfected the technology yet). As a result, none of your colleagues know that you are controlling Six, and in order to not arouse suspicion you must play along, learning the story-and your past- as you go.
To further complicate matters, shortly after your arrival a murder is committed, and with the suspect sealed on board, time is running out for you to find them before things get worse. Much worse.
Where this game succeeds is in creating an incredible sense of place. The environment, the crew, the world building- all of it combines to make a believable future- if somewhat overwhelming. Keeping apace of all the new information can get a little much at times, although there are extra materials available outside of the game to give you a little more grounding.
Hands down the best thing about this game is the voice acting. One or two dodgy accents aside, the pace, delivery and impact of the cast is outstanding- you really do start to feel the personalites shine through. Add to that a conversation system that is timed, and you have to think carefully and quickly about what you say- making enemies on board probably isn't wise...
Combat- of which there is little- is not particularly satisfying, and mercifully avoidable. Despite being FPS, it just doesn't seem to have the kick you'd expect it to. However, this is a minor gripe, as the game really should be played more in the style of a police procedural, finding clues, teasing information from crewmates and suspects, and choosing whether you can trust someone enough to reveal your existence- without dropping Six in trouble.
The game does finish on a high note, albeit a cliffhanger- this is the first in a trilogy, with the second due to hit Kickstarter this year.
It's a bit of an oddity, Consortium, but when it gets it right it's worth the price. Most reviews were for a release that had quite a few bugs, but the support from the developers since has rendered the game stable and enjoyable.

I had my doubts about this game - there is quite a lot of negative reviews regarding game's performance, mechanics, stability. But during the last winter sale I've decided to give it a try. And the only thing I regret is not playing it earlier.
It may not be a game for everyone. There are games that are longer, prettier, even deeper. But what "Consortium" IS - it's a great role-playing game. Not in the sense of tweaking your character's characteristics, but rather of living another life, while remaining yourself (literally - you are playing as yourself, only after being implanted into a different body). You choose your own actions and behavior, line of actions - and face the consequences.  Act kindly, aggressively, funny, try to flirt or impose discipline - and see the crew of Zenlil-2 react. You can even choose to reveal your true identity. Or act neturally, learning of how this new world works and adapting to its rules.
Second part of the game is coming to KS soon - and I myself am waiting for a possibility to live in that world a bit more.

I'll assume you read the description blurb for the game.  And now onto the review.
Was it worth it?  Yes.
When you think about a game occasionally over the course of *years*, you know they did something right.  (Forgetting about the fact I've been waiting for a sequel for AGES)
Too many games are forgettable in my opinion.  Especially when Steam has SO MANY.  This one however, was totally worth it ;)
Let's skip to the breakdown:
+ Great background music by Jeremy Soule and free soundtrack download
+ Stanley's Parable level of unique choices with different outcomes
+ Unique setting (it's on a plane?)
+ Great voiced characters
+ Detailed story with lively characters
+ Did I mention the story?
- The graphical style is unusual.  It's not BAD, it just doesn't look real
- Fights while few, are fast, frantic and unwieldy
- I ran into some weird graphical issues when I first played, restarting worked for me
- A single playthrough is SHORT!  And the sequel, well I've been waiting forever!!
+ The sequel is about to make its kickstart debut... FINALLY!
The real fun of this game is in blindly throwing yourself into a detailed new universe, the game admitting that, and enjoying how the world reacts to your choices.
Spoiler example:
What would happen if you started a new game, and didn't know much about your environment, who the NPCs were, ... even what your name was?  lol Actually that's typical, but expect this game to call you out on it if you're obvious.
I recently played Undertale and it reminded of this game, choice-wise.  That's praise.
Anyway, I say it's definitely worth a shot if it sounds at all interesting to you.  With TallTale taking the lead on games like this, it's nice to have new blood.  Especially since you have SO much more control over your choices compared to traditional adventure games.

Fun and addictive. These should be the key elements to any basic game such Salem. Quickly log onto your account and jump into a game in less than a minute with games lasting roughly 10-30 minutes, or you could leave upon fulfilling your part. What makes this game amazing is that it's an 'arena' style game with quick ‘play and leave’ ability, busy and just want to have a quick game, well, play Salem! Maximum 15 player based multiplayer game, in which you re-live the medieval era that was the Salem days. The Salem witch trials were a series of hearings and prosecutions of people accused of witchcraft in colonial Massachusetts between February 1692 and May 1693. Bear witness to the horrors of our past, re-live these horrors in a virtual reality with a top down view of a town of people who are in control of their fate or not based upon what role you're designated and what the mission of your game is. Free to play online, or purchase for a low price on Steam (quicker load times and you're given free coins.)
The game has no real progression besides its aesthetics aspect of developing the appeal of your avatar in game, purchasable aesthetic gear on their store or play the game and progress through collecting coins at the end of each session. I mention this because it's the main scope of progression in this game.
The second scope of progression, I would say, is your win/loss ratio and you ranking in game (if you want to play in the competitive scheme.)
The game types range from the standard game you play with town members, mafia members and neutral members to the absurd All Any mode whereby no one’s role is known in game.
The objective of the game, what ever you damn well please as an 'objective: Troll, kick back,  go AFK, play competitively, choose a side that is against your own roles objectives, help 'townies' win, help 'mafia' win etcetec, you'll have to decide or let the game decide for you based on the role you're given.

Definetly a recommendation for anybody interested in futuristic settings. People who are not as enthuisastic about just experiencing a really interesting world through texts and dialogue, might find the gameplay elements a bit rough and the game overall too short to completly justify the full price. In that case, it is definetly worth getting during a sale!

Blackwake is the best first person pirate simulator on the market right now, in my opinion. While it's still in early access, it still has plenty of entertainment to be had at the reigns of your very own pirate ship.
PROS
-------
+Graphics - This game looks great, from the water to the chracters. The graphics are not very intensive, and it looks and feels like an immersive pirate world.
+Gameplay - There is an endless amount of ridiculous fun to be had, whether you are the captain or a crew member. From loading cannons to intense melee battles, the possibilities are endless.
+Developers - The tiny team of developers has done and continues to do great updates for their game. Just recently, they have added new ship models and fixed some annoying bugs. They can only do so much with their team, but they haven't given up, and this being EA, that means something.
+Design - The ship design down to the muskets are authentic and immersive. Lots of care was definitely put into this aspect of the game.
+Realism - While this game definitely has its silly moments, such as blowing people hundreds of feet up in the air to the hilarious voice acting, there is an amount of realism here that deserves to be appreciated. Loading cannons takes time as well as reloading your gun. It's serves to enhance the already immersive game design.
+Optimization - I have a fairly high end system, but the game runs extremely well for me with no stutter or FPS issues. For an EA game, this is definitely a plus.
CONS
-------
-Content - While the ship battles are fun, there are some lackluster moments. They are planning to add new game modes soon, so this part of the review may be removed upon their addition.
-Bugs - There are occasional crashes, and the server menu is currently not working very well (This is being fixed).
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who wants to scratch their pirate itch. It has everything you need to feel like an authentic pirate. Welcome to the high seas!

I spent over 500 hours on Trove and I must say, this is one of the only games I'm writing a review for. The game is AMAZING until you get to late game. It isn't coop anymore at that point. It becomes a competition. The marketplace is controlled by the few for an example, I was able to buy all the pearls at the market and then sell at a higher price and it some how worked. It demonstrates the weakness of the marketplace. Of course, I'm not that high in the game because I am only 15k PR with 1m flux. Though, I would like to point out the pros and cons of this game.
Pros:
-Lots of options and modifications to suit your taste
-Lots of unique classes that are truly amazing
-Many dungeons to explore
-Open World
-Adventurer Friendly
-Side skills such as ring crafting and gardening
-Club worlds to suit the needs of guilds
-Player Friendly UI and Tutorial
-Challenging and Unique bosses
-Moderately nice community
-Player driven with dungeons and gear being player made
Cons:
-The few rule the market
-Repetitive
-Servers sometimes are laggy ping wise
-Weekly challenges are ruled by the few (Classes anyway)
-Grinding
-Bad decisions
I want to expand on the bad decisions that Trove has made because it makes up half of the problem with Trove as well as the other half with disconnects and laggy chunks. The first thing I've noticed is that when I was playing in 2015 ~ 2016, people were gaining momentum and there was no outlet with flux in order to balance to growing amounts of flux as a monster reward therefore causing inflation. Of course there is forging but it didn't provide enough leverage to sustain the inflation status. Along with that, I would like to point out that they decided to make classes credits only therefore making it seemingly a monopoly for the few to sell tradable class coins at a skyrocketing rate. The new inventory system allows the inflation to continue because there is no need to store things at all therefore allowing more space for loot from mobs.
Also grinding is insane. You need about 1k gem boxes to make a slight upgrade to your characters. Maybe they should add new mobs if possible and allow players to make monsters because seeing the same faces makes it limited. I was hoping for maybe a Sky Realm boss of some sort but I guess it never happened lol.
I would recommend this game if they attempted to fix their server lag as well as provide a fix to their inflation. Next thing I know, I'm going to come back to Trove and 1m will be worth nothing lol. Grinding needs to lessen.
But then again, this is just my opinion~ :)

Update Review:
'The little dinghy that could' should define this game. Is it in its prime? No. Does the player count immerse you in dangerous seas? No. But for a game that launched in 2003, do you expect it to? I hope not. The boat still sails and this game is still alive. You can still enjoy the fun puzzles and get on a ship to enjoy the core game. It might take awhile to get the bigger ships filled depending on the time of day, literally needing dozens of people at times. But the navy ships are auto pilot by AI and can teach you the puzzles whenever, so don't fear testing the game out. The updates (monthly uniques and events) still rollout like clockwork, quite literally clockwork actually, so don't think the game never gets new things added either!
I said it at the end of my original review, which I am leaving below, and I will say it again here because it is a good point to be made:
It's a free to play game, why not at least try it?
**Original Review**
Ignore the 'hours played' displayed, I have been playing this game off and on for eight years. I don't know when it came to Steam but I always forget to load it through here when I decide to play. Hence the little time Steam thinks I've put into this game. I won't claim to play too much recently, but it is still a game I can come back to and pick up in no time and enjoy myself.
For most purposes it is still the same game it was when I started, some massive overhauls to features and many new minigame additions have occured but it is still the same base game. Think of Puzzle Pirates as a game full of minigames where sailing a ship is a compilation of various stations with different games each with different goals (get it, PUZZLE Pirates). There are easy to learn minigames that you can enter the game and pick up quickly but enough intricate details and strategies in each and some harder minigames to master to strive to be the best on the Ocean. There are some competitive 'PvP' (not to kill but you can bet money) minigames for direct competition steaming from a simple swordfight to a ship battle with cannons ending in a sword fight or rumble minigame (note the minigame word you will not run at another pirate with a sword or your fists).
There is a quirk, as with any able to be free to play game, to encourage spending real money to make things in game easier to obtain. These are not neccessary to buy by any means and can be obtained in game for in game money, though it takes work and it based on the player market. The game is fully playable and enjoyable without spending any real life money and (I believe) every item can be obtained in game without having to spend real money.
Eight years later and I still enjoy this game, I only sporadically play it because it's hard not to play for hours once you start. I can go on about this game and do a full review but who wants to read that?
It's a free to play game, why not at least try it?

Trove is an MMO with an N64-esque style, and endless pay to win microtransactions and... um... I really don't know how to start a review, do I?
Trove on the surface is very easy to get into, you pick out a class
, jump around a bit, kill a monster, and get a cool new weapon. Then you go to the hub, and there is so much to do. You can look at other people's houses, you can look at items you can't afford yet, you can see how many people are better than you
, you can look at a menu that shows you what your buttons do, you can destroy grass to get money, all that good stuff. But after a while, you go through a gren portal, and you are thrust into a whole new world, with caves, other players, wild creatures, dungeons, weapons, ore, and different enviroments. Then, your adventure slowly gets more difficult...
There isn't much of one, although there may be hints towards it in certain dungeons.
The combat is solid, although some classes are clearly better than others
, and some bosses are way harder than others. Every class has a standard attack, 2 abilities, an extremely powerful third ability, a roll, and health potions. Every class can hold a different type of weapon, with some weapon types being more commonly shared than others.
The microtransactions, however, are not so solid. They are pretty pay to win oriented (however, it's thankfully the less annoying type of pay to win, where buying stuff makes you "win" way more easily, but you can still "win" without them). If you don't buy some stuff, then you are going to have to do quite a bit of grinding to get decent items and every class.
Also there is an economy, and it can seem complex at first, but after you get used to it it's mostly just a lot of buying for cheap and selling for less cheap and taking advantage of events.
Also the game has subpar servers, so lag will be common.
This game looks pretty nice, taking obvious inspiration from the n64 era and Minecraft. Also it's really vibrant, which I think fits the game well. However, the double jump effects which look like they were ripped right out of Super Smash Bros feel really out of place.
Mods are easy to install and use, and there are only visual/sfx mods for obvious reasons.
Trove is a fun MMO with a nice visual style and amazing mod support, however suffers from pay to win elements and servers that are mediocre at best. I'd recommend trying this game despite it's flaws, as it is still a fun experience (and is free).

In a short summary this is rally well done story driven JRPG which tackles a bit darker themes - revenge, failure, loss.
- The whole story, it ranges from funny skits to some really dramatic, emotional, dark material. There will be moments which will tug your feels and deliver some real emotions. And there will be some daily life funny stuff which usually is in the right place at the right time. The main story is worth it. And the light stuff helps building the characters.
- Characters, their interactions and personalities. This is a strong one. Everyone on your party has their own unique personality and views, many times they have really nice chemistry and interactions. For some reason I really liked Rokurou and Laphicet banter, those two looked like they are getting along very well. But there are more of them and their stories are unveiled pretty well when the game progresses.
- General feel of the game, quests and tasks. It's a tricky one to explain, but it kept me enganged the whole time. Each new main story point was intriguing enough to progress it and go where you need to go. There's not that much pointless wandering and backtracking. Also if you want, you can do few side quests which also felt that you are doing something rather than being an item delivery service as so many RPG's have with their fetch quests.
- As this is a heavily story driven game, you progress a story. And I liked that, where you can kinda get comfy and enoy it. There were no noticeable story breaking quests or tasks to do. You can do a bit of exploration, but at particular story point you will have only one right path to go at the end. So there will be no situations where you feel lost or don't know where to go.
- Generally fun combat. Combat is a big thing in this came as you can tweak and tune it in many ways. You can upgrade your weapons by getting better ones or improving existing ones, you can create your combo moves and customize attacks, you can performs various special attacks at specific conditions and as in most japanese games, you will get grades for your fights. But if you don't want to delve deeply into this mechanic, you can enhance your gear adequately, level up a bit and you will be good to go. This is not challenging game and generally combat is not that hard. If you want, you can make your characters auto-fight for you if you are feeling lazy.
- Combat doesn't break story. Well, this happened for with few other games in this genre. As this is story driven game, you will have to lose some battles as the story is written. And the game makes sure you won't accidentally win or do good on these battles. Or if you need to have a hard battle, it will be hard. So there will be no situations, where you are just blasting enemies and after some point you will get a cutscene, where your characters will look beat and tired and talk how hard this battle is and you probably won't win. So here you won't have such moments and story driven combat will flow with the story.
- Generally good voice acting with one exception. More or less all main characters have good voiceovers, sometimes they have really nice dialogues or simple banter. Yet Velvet's voice can be improved.
- One thing that stood out for me was Velvet's english voice acting. The lady voicing Velvet is really good delivering super dramatic or calm, natural lines. But when she has to do generic angry or nervous lines, they sound a bit forced. And well, Velvet's character is kinda angry most of the time.
- Combat system is a matter of taste, but for me it tried to be more complex than it is. If you want, you can tune and optimize your skills, but generally you will be good with a bit optimized defaults.
- Background music could be made bit better. Although there were some good emotional pieces, but generally it has this synthetic orchestral sound, which is kinda generic sounding.
Generally it's really well done story driven game and if you like stories and some combat, this one is really good choice. Don't rush it and you will have some good entertainment.

It's a decent enough recording software, probably the best I've used due to ease of access. When O.B.S. (another decent recorder) decided to freeze after the first few seconds of recording, and with no solution, I was led to Xsplit by a friend of mine.
NOTE: Before you get this software, keep in mind that I have noticed a bug that may or may not affect you if you are running this on Windows 7 64Bit.
After recording once, I am good. Clips look good and everything. But when I stop recording one game and start recording another in the same session (or even the same game after one recording session), the entire computer's audio becomes tinny and distorted for me. It affects ALL sound, and apparently the distortion cannot be recorded as evidence (unless you use a phone or some other method, which isn't a good way to gather evidence of this bug).
The ONLY way to fix this that I know of is restarting the computer or turning it off then on. That way, sound driver can reset. I suspect this is an Xsplit problem since I have never encountered this problem prior to using Xsplit, and since it only occurs when I am using or have recently used the program. Both Steam and Non-Steam versions do this. I've even checked to see if it is a headset problem. No, the distortion plays through speakers as well.
So, be on the lookout for that if you get this program. I recommend this as an easy-to-use and high-quality* recording software.
*May take tweaking to get desired results in quality, but nothing too complicated like OBS's interface is.

CONSORTIUM is one of those games that I wish I'd bought earlier.  It's so well rated, so well reviewed, by so many people, and seems right up my alley.  I like story-based single-player games.  I like quirky games, with inside jokes and external references.  There was no reason for me to avoid buying this game, other than fear that the game would suck.  I eventually bought it, the game was fun - albeit short - with the possibility of a sequel coming out at some point.  The game also has a lot of achievements, so if you're into those, great! I'm used to playing games where a lot of the exposition is extracted by asking NPCs questions - and NPCs in other games are happy to oblige (that is their main purpose in life!) by talking for hours on-end.  CONSORTIUM is different, in that if you treat NPCs like you'd normally treat NPCs, the game mechanics change.  Overall, I'd say buy this game, and you'll enjoy it, if you like unique games that are quirky and fun.  It's like a pseudo-space murder-mystery game you can play over and over again!

What is the main driving force behind indie game development? Inovation. And that is what Sanctum and now Sanctum 2 provides.
The Sanctum series is a tower defense first person shooter. Those are two generas you would never see a AAA company make. But thankfully we have indie studies that are willing to get their hands dirty and try new things. Sometimes they fail, but other times, like with this game, they succeed.
Now I wouldn't call Sanctum a ground breaking game. Perhaps it is the somewhat lack of story but it doesn't really suck you in, at least not in my opinion. However, this is a great game to play for the sake of playing games. If you're bored open this game up. Each level is challenging, giving you different map arrangments to deal with. Perhaps enemies come from more than one location or that the area you have to build your maze and towers is quite small.
On top of a pretty solid tower defense mechanic, this game provides a very satisfying FPS aspect to the fight. When the next wave starts (and sometimes you don't ge to control that) you pull out your guns and join in the fight. Success of failure might ride on your ability to know which enemies to focus on or when to abandon one area to support another.
However, I would highly recommend that you watch some youtube videos of the game first before you click that purchase button. I find that no matter the game, always watch game play videos of it. It can help you make your final decision on whether or not you buy it.

This game might lag a lot after your city has passed 300'000 inhabitants. I didn't experience this because I stopped to play before that point, as I got enough of the game after 10 hours.
Interesting & decent city building, although with less charm than the old Sim City 4 (2003) ; it is however more realistic, as planting a couple of trees between your industrial zone and your residential zone isn't enough to clean the air, so it requires a more thoughtful approach to build a functioning city.
But there's a big issue : most companies require high "quality of life", but neither the tutorial, the manual nor the in-game heat-maps explain nor show what it is ! Looking on Internet, I found a guy theorizing it was a mix of air pollution and noise nuisance.
Nonetheless, I'd still recommend the game if you can get it with a discount (if you check the other reviews, it seems the concurrence is better, but a bit more expensive ;-) ), as it's pleasant enough for a while.
- Decent visuals
- Can build non-orthogonal cities
- Advanced planning required to build a functional city
- I started to have some slowdown with my city reaching 300'000 inhabitants
- Different buildings that do the exact same thing and need to catch the tip during loading to know that
- Very perfectible GUI usability ; eg: the road selection always go back to the cheapest road, instead of showing your last selection ; some description text missing ; etc.
- In-game Ads for a famous french supermarket chain... :-/
- Crashed a couple of times in 10 hours of play
- A lot of things lack of clarity, and it can get hard to understand some aspects ; eg: the silo enhancing the farms efficiency requires freight ; but shouldn't it actually create the freight it needs if the roads are there ?
- It's hard to build a polyvalent city, as the game is designed to make you create several cities that will trade with each other (and I don't have that kind of time ! ;-) )

Very good game, but full of bugs you will hate.
Pros:
XCOM 2 is an extreme tactical game, and you can spend a lot of time thinking through just 1 turn to make your moves perfect. If you like turn based strategy, something a little bit like the old "commandos" you will love it. Watching gameplay footage on youtube will only give you a glimpse of the feeling you get playing it yourself. Countless possibilities to engage the enemy, to upgrade your soldiers in different ways and classes. Very complex.
Cons:
Very annoying at times. Way too many bugs. After loading a saved game enemies where no longer visible. I blew away a cover with a grenade. The cover was blown away, but still counted as cover for the enemy and so on...
And then there is the luck factor. If you move too much in one direction while fighting one squad of enemies you might trigger another squad of enemies. Or the other enemy-squad is appearing out of nowhere because they where patrolling the area. Then it might be impossible to win the mission, you lose all your soldiers. And then comes the worst thing: You can NOT play the mission again. Maybe you have a save or an autosave way back in time, before the mission. Then you start the mission again, the landscape and the enemy squads get generated completly new and different, and then you walk through this mission as if nothing happend.
Note: Always save before the mission and also a lot during the mission. Auto-save can be problematic because you might lose them.
Sometimes you think: Ok, I can kill this enemy easily because he is standing completly in the open. But after moving to flank him you will notice: Only 25% chance to hit.
It would be a big improvement if you could see the hit chances before you move to the tile.
Also the interface could be way more user friendly. Usability is not something they where thinking of when making this game. You have to find out too many things through try and error because its nowhere explained.

Some may pass off Starbound as another attempt to cashe in on the "Build your own world" style of gameplay similar to minecraft (Which is solely the only reason to play that game) or terraria (Where you feel as if the only reason to build is to store your things). It is not though. I may have few hours into the game when I first got it, but I can tell, it is different. Each planet feels so real, and you grow to love your little human/apex/star kid/ect... In the first coulple of days, a rainstorm happened. A pretty nasty one. I was content to wait out the rain inside, interacting with all the furnature (a great touch BTW) and planning how to build my hut as it did rain, instead of go out and fight or explore as my little starkid got drenched. It was a feeling of satisfaction that my house protected me from the elements that I never got in the other games like this.
Starbound also does combat much better than the others I gave examples of. The system of firearms and bows being powered by energy gives a concept of saving ammo, without having to go buy ammo. Melee weapons not only burst hard, but your character seems to have heft from them, with your melee weapon appearing to have weight to them, as two handed axes seem to take more to swing from you than a knife would. Also starbound allows for dual wielding of any two one-handed weapons or shields, something i wondered why the other games couldnt get that right.
Lastly, the final reason people come to theese kind of games is the exploration, and this is the best of all. Starbound does a great job of making you feel like a space explorerer, with each planet a unique experience. You will find yourself in beautiful hilly forest plannets, or boiling desert plannets. You will brave frozen wasteland plannets, to asteroid fields rich with resources. In most planets there is also expansive underground cave systems, with things such as a dead kings tomb, to portals to pocket dimensions that lead you to a special challenge with powerful rewards.
Starcraft has been the first game to not only make me excited to leave home for an adventure, but upset aswell. Starbound has all I mentioned and more. As the game gets updated, all three of theese points strengthen even more. Bossfights are intense and truly test your skills, and colonated planets allow you to interact with the many interesting NPC's. As well, your ship's AI is quite adorable. Would I reccomend Starbound? When it was still a young game, just a skeleton, I would have not. But now? Within a heartbeat I would reccomend it to someone who is new to the "Build your own world" game style, or someone who the magic of them died out due to the lacking of satisfaction with the other games. If you are going to spend your money on any open beta, do it on Starbound. (The soundtrack is also beautiful BTW)

Allrighty. So youre looking at this game and thinking if you should buy it.
Scroll to bottom for pros and cons if youre not up for the massive reading
First off ill go ahead and mention that TITANS is an expantion on the original game: Planetary Annihilation, this expansion adds 5 Titan class units and a dozen or so other smaller units, the original game is probably one of the best RTS games currently for its price. If you dont know it allready, theres quite a few of bugs and smaller glitches currently on TITANS but they are working on fixing them with roughly monthly updates
Before i begin you should know the Titans
There are 5 Titans currently in the game (dont know if more are coming)
They consist of 3 land units, 1 orbital, and 1 air
The Titans are:         Ragnarok (after finishing the build it will make the planet it is built on go boom within a minute)
Ares (basically a moving fortress, near impossible to kill without air, has extreme range and can move across ocean)
Atlas (The most commonly seen Titan, it can move through ocean and land and causes minor nukes whenever something stands in its way, not as tanky as the Ares but has more damage and is very vulnerable to kiting and air)
Zeus (the second most commonly seen Titan is probably this one, its an air unit, meaning it can fly over any terrain and cant be hit by regular tanks and such, it has a massive damage AOE attack with relatively short range, very vulnerable to airfighters or orbital)
Now that you know the titans you should also know that they all have weaknesses, allthough most of the time one is built its gameover for the other player(s) unless they have one or more to counter it. This means that much of mid-lategame is just rushing a Titan. Other than that the Multiplayer is very stable for the most part and i have not experienced many issues other than a few bugs here and there. The original game is extremely well balanced, i havent yet settled for wether or not TITANS is balanced
Now then, the singleplayer, or Galactic War as the game calls it is VERY fun compared to alot of other RTS games singleplayer modes. The AI is very well programmed for newbies, but can also be ramped up by alot to fit better players.
Anyway, the general theme of Galactic war is that you have very limited options that expand as you conquer and annihilate, for example you will start with vehicle factories only, but when you conquer a solarsystem you get 3 random techs to choose one of, that tech will then unlock something for you, for example; Advanced Vehicle factories, and then you basically keep going, fighting bots untill you find their HQ and destroy him.
The learning curve isnt too steep, you can just learn the basics in Galactic War before you run into Multiplayer, that way you wont have teammates going full CAPSLOCK-heavybreathing-rage

I've started playing this game back in November and managed to finish my first playthrough before 2017 ended. I can say that this game is really enjoyable not just because of its graphics, BGMs, animations, battle scenes and the likes, but also because they added back some new features like cooking system and minigames which the previous franchise (Tales of Zestiria) lacked. They also added new feature which allows you to deploy your own pirate ship to gather ingedients for cooking and salvaged items, while you are doing your quests.
I really love the way how they incorporated fun minigames in the world of TOB because it offers the players the feeling of being relaxed and chill after doing some dark quests revolving around assassination, arson and so forth - this is the first game that I've played which involves heinous activities but Velvet and the gang aren't doing these things just because they want to.
As for for the artes and fight scenes, I definitely enjoyed thinking thoroughly and customizing which arte goes where and also, the directional buttons play a big role on where you want to land your artes at. At first, it was very confusing for me because Zestiria didn't allow such customization to happen if I recall correctly, (played it back it 2015) then Berseria came in and it blew my mind of. Every battle I fought was engaging because of this.
With regard to the skills, they really did a fine job in showcasing it. I cannot help but to compare every thing that I disliked about Zestiria's artes and skills systems in view of the fact that Berseria finally had it the easier and more convenient way - Zestiria's skills system was so convoluted that I almost ignored how they worked. In this game, all equipment have skills attached on them, and you just have to wear and fight using those until you master the skills. The skills you learned will be passive and you don't have to worry about it anymore after learning.
And finally concerning the story of the game, there were parts that almost made me cry which I didn't saw coming. It's very unlikely for me to cry over trivial things, even when watching sad movies and animes but this game did it. The game was really thrilling that I did every single sub quests available just to prolong my playthrough and to learn every single aspect of the stories involved on the game. Two to three years from now, I would most probably play Zestiria and Berseria again just to experience all the good and bad things that these games had offered me.
I highly and REALLY recommend this game, especially to those who love and seek adventure - JRPGs. This game is a work of art, a must have game, sitting on your Steam library :)

This game is incredibly fun. Whether you're working on your bluff skills or just the strong silent type, it's a game that involves very little luck and a lot of observation. I like that. I play a lot of games that have luck as one of the primary deciders and it's nice to sit back and play a game about observation. Manipulation is one of the keys here, having information or just knowing how to lie your way to victory is quite an adrenaline rush.
I was apprehensive about this game at first because I'm not really the multiplayer type (though I do play Armello), but it's very easy to  just focus on remembering what you learn each night-even if you're the first to die, you can still keep tabs on what's going on. It's also nice that, even if you die, if you're town and town wins, you win, likewise with mafia, if you die but mafia wins, you win. This gives the game a good amount of "loyalty" based on which side your class is on.
The game is simple to play, but difficult to master since it requires quite a few skills to make things work in your favour. Sanctum 2 is an unusual tower defence game, where the player will usually do as much or more killing than their towers do.
The gameplay involves the player building a maze of walls within certain confines set by the current map, these walls then have towers built onto them which (mostly) attack enemies that get within range, other types of towers provide other small bonuses.
during each wave the player then needs to attack the enemies themselves, using various guns available to them.
The game requires a unique strategy which takes some getting used to, some of the maps have a considerably high difficulty the first few times you play them.
The storyline is a decent length, with additional challenges, steam achievements etc. along with the infinite "survival" mode which is available on any map making up most of the end-game content.
Overall the game is good, best played with friends though expect many arguments unless you're all pros at the game before you team up. 8/10.
A really unique game and a hidden gem for RPG fans with a great story, just a tad stort but hopefulluy a sequel will be funded soon on Kickstarter.

I wanted to like this one, but after almost an hour the issues with the game just kept building up and I ended up getting a refund from Steam.
I think that Consortium has potential on offer. For a 2014 game it doesn't look that great, but graphics aren't what makes or breaks a game for me, so that's liveable. What I saw of the plot seemed interesting and the voice acting was more than passable. It made me smile to get a reference to one of my favourite TV shows, Continuum, early on.
The problem was that the game was unstable and buggy for me from the get-go. The very first time I fired it up it crashed when trying to load a new game. When it did load the loading times were quite long and appeared to freeze, so I was never sure if it really had froze or not. But you know, this wouldn't be the only game I've played with this kind of problem. Major titles can suffer from this too (I personally find Fallout: New Vegas to be extremely unstable, especially once modded, as a random example). This alone isn't enough to make me throw in the towel.
The deal-breaking problems came when the game was actually 'working'. Firstly there's this strange effect on the graphics that comes up at seemingly random times that makes the screen look really distorted (I've uploaded a screenshot to my account which demonstrates this problem). From what I can tell by skimming the Steam forums for the game, this is by design. It wasn't a major issue for a while as the interference appeared and faded again quite quickly, but then the effect seemed to get stuck on, pretty much rendering the game unplayable until I quit and reloaded it, which did fix the issue.
The final straw came during the combat training sequence, which bugged on me and couldn't be completed. What happened was that the game expected me to pick up a weapon and ammo from where it spawned them for me. Only I grabbed the nearer ones dropped by the previously taken out enemies from the previous objective. The game did not recognise this, and broke my progress. I guess I could have reloaded and made sure I didn't pick up a dropped weapon instead, but really I shouldn't have to. What difference does it really make if I take Gun A or Gun B, if Gun A & B are exactly the same?
Expecting more problems to make themselves apparent, I applied for and got a refund for the game. A part of me would have liked to play it some more, but as we all know the Steam refund window isn't exactly long (not a criticism), and I could see me easily overrunning the two hour window due to the long loads and repeating sections due to bugs.
All in all, it just didn't seem worth the hassle. A shame, as this one did genuinely look interesting.
Update: at some point this was given away for free after my refund so I grabbed it again, but haven't felt like going back to it for another go yet. Any additional playtime is from getting its Steam cards).
