It took me a little while to get past Consortium's fairly ugly, Reboot-esque graphics, but I'm glad I did, because it's a pretty interesting game. In some ways, the game feels like a tutorial level for a bigger game - the game teaches you how to manage your health and armor and use one of five weapons, with loading screen tutorial texts to match, but there's almost no actual combat in the game, amounting to a single optional firefight and some VR training missions. But it also uses this to have a somewhat interesting setting - the entire game takes place on an airship on the way to your next mission, and along the way you deal with a locked room murder mystery and unearth conspiracies. The gameplay is mostly dialogue-based with occasional bits of action, and the dialogue offers enough variety to highly encourage multiple playthroughs with the amount of choices you get and secrets to find. The dialogue is made interesting by the fact that rather than just breaking the fourth wall, Consortium doesn't really have a 4th wall to begin with, and the player is recognized in the game as a person using the game (described in-universe as a software that allows you to view the future through someone else's eyes) to control the main character in the future. This also ties into a pretty extensive ARG that leads up to the game for those who find themselves wanting more of the game's lore, and if you don't want to play the entire ARG there's a free DLC package that gives you all of the documents to clue you in, but it's a pretty substantial read, running several hundred pages of PDFs. The game can be enjoyed without ever acknowledging the ARG, however.
Consortium is a game that feels like a smaller part of a bigger game while still holding its own as a standalone experience, and the next game, Consortium: The Tower, is currently in development and will presumably start off where this game ends. At the base price of $15 I'd consider Consortium to be a decent purchase, but at its current sale price of $1.50 I don't see any reason not to give it a try if you're into dialogue-based stories.

Admittedly, I did not finish the game (and as always, will update my review scores if I decide to complete it) due being completely bored with everything in the game. The story was dull, typical revenge/kill the bad guy type stuff of typical Shonen anime tropes. The combat was just button mashing. Occasionally when I fought a powerful enemy I had to inspect for their weakness and plan my Artes (moves) around that. Which leads me to another complaint, the Artes system is rubbish. Berseria tries to be a fighting game with an RPG. What ends up happening is the game is too easy on Normal/Moderate settings. So when I increase it to Hard, it’s basically button mashing for 2 minutes instead of 1.
The story I couldn’t care less about. It’s completely uncreative. There are tons of plot issues for the sake of gameplay. For example in one part Velvet (main character) ends up jumping and scaling a building. A few zones later, I can’t even jump down a 1 foot ledge, or jump up a latter that she can grab with her hands. I hate it when the gameplay zones are tailored as a contradiction of what we already know the main character is capable of doing.  Also, to expand on the story, I feel like almost everything I played was just filler for the sake of making the game longer.
Speaking of making the game longer. The constant backtracking is another thing that really made me dislike this game.
The final thing I’ll mention is the equipment. You just get completely showered in gear and almost all of it is useless or uninteresting. The mastery system for gear is just almost insulting for a mechanic after such iconic mechanics exist over a decade ago, like FF7’s Materia system for example. Overall, for an RPG, I felt as if I was making little to no progression with my characters from a statistical standpoint.
I cannot think of any positives about the gameplay other than the things I did not list which the game does them average.
Graphics are good, but a bit inconsistent and bland at times. Sometimes, they are so good it feels like I am watching an anime. Other times, the levels appear boring rehashes of copy-pasted dungeons.
Average. The music/sounds were not bad, but I heard nothing that made me think a lot of time or effort was put into the music. In fact, there were a few zones where the music was absolutely annoying.
All of the boring story content I have done in 20 hours felt like 2 hours of actual content and 18 hours of filler. The world building is atrocious and the game does zero effort to make me feel like I am playing in a unique world after the ~20 minute opening “tutorial.”
I am unable to provide an accurate rating since I did not finish the game.
This was my first Tales game, and possibly my last. I have heard so many good things about Berseria. How the story was dark and you play as the “bad guy” in a way. Unfortunately, I was sorely let down. I went into it expecting a Seinen-type experience, like Hellsing, Berserk, Ghost in the Shell, One Punch Man, ect. Instead, I got the lowest of Shonen anime. I felt the tones in the game were far from dark or shocking other than the characters trying their best to make it appear worse than it actually is. It could almost just be a Saturday morning cartoon. Overall I would recommend this game for people going into it expecting a younger, more lighthearted adventure, but I cannot recommend this game based off the numerous faults and aspects of gameplay elements that did not make me want to finish it.

Cannot belive I'm typing up a good review but it is what it is. I'm reviewing the product, not the company. Yes Uber made some shady moves, but I got PA for $10 last year during a sale and PA:Titans for $13.50 or so, so in total I got less than $25 into PA as a game. Some people paid $90 way back when, etc. Yes it's crappy Titans was not made free for some of the original backers from long long ago, yes it's crappy how the original PA isn't sold anymore so the negative reviews won't be shown. Uber as a company, well, let me just say it's a semi-positive thing that their kickstarter for another game didn't make it through. They are trying other things and trying to do right by Titans even though the $40 pricetag is still a bit high, but PA:T is actually an alright TA-derivative. Let me explain below.
If you are looking for traditional Total Annihilation gameplay, it's not here. Get Supreme Commander Forged Alliance, though I suggest you avoid the often recommended FAF lobby and it's toxic community since the Steam multiplayer works fine for me and my friends. PA:T is not traditional TA but it is based very heavily on TA, in fact most people will call it a spiritual sequel with extras like multiple planets and oribital plane added for extra tactical depth. I will describe to you what PA:T is in reality: it's a variant of TA that used to be played on 'Speedball' maps. These are maps in the old TA where all the ground is solid metal so you could lay down Mexes (metal extractors) anywhere you want and get massive metal income. Most maps were 'ball' or 'circle' shaped, as in a giant circle surrounded by water or two circles surrounded by water with a large land bridge in the middle. The extremely high amount of resources allowed players to just spam factories and units in large amounts and basically just have a gigantic brawl that is much faster paced than traditional TA. Speedball maps were made for TA:Spring/Spring RTS as well.
How is PA:T like Speedball in TA you ask? It's the same exact thing in every way except the metal on the ground, PA has the traditional metal hot-spots you have to build Mexes on and protect from the enemy taking them. Besides that it is the exact same thing. Most matches are much much shorter, this game is not defense oriented though making a turret-line for the enemy to run it's units against is still a valid tactic at times. This game is all about spamming factories which then spam units, as much as possible. The globe-shaped 'maps' on each planet take some getting used to but there is a noticeable thing here, no physical chokepoints. There are no land bridges etc. If there is water/lava in the way you can go around and still reach the target by ground, so you are always exposed to land assault with an enemy Com on the same planet and you cannot make a good chokepoint like in many TA/SupCom maps to repel ground attack and force the enemy to adapt, here you have to either go all offense and rely on units to keep enemy units away or if you do defense it must be full circle or those defenses you spent metal on could be completely bypassed. Defenses are actually used more in a semi-offensive role, push and gain ground then drop defenses, let your unit ball back up a bit to those defenses to thin enemy ball a little, push again and make another defense line closer to enemy base. You can even cut off an enemy and surround him with turrets to prevent expansion.
I could keep talking longer about various little tactics and tricks, this game is different from the original TA formula and is much faster paced. The singleplayer is alright, it's a bunch of skirmishes you can fight on a meta-map and you can unlock bonuses for your Commander to help beat the faction leaders in the Galactic War. Multi I tend to avoid, communities for TA-style are not nice in general most places you go and it's been like that since Cavedog was still around. It's not complete trollish hell like in Ark or DOTA 2, not that bad, but it's discouraging enough that I'm content doing bot-stomps against AI with friends or singleplayer against AI. Around $15 this is a good deal, do not pay the full $40 though since I feel it doesn't offer enough to warrant such a high price tag. I can get lots of enjoyment out of this game a little bit at a time, when I want Speedball-style TA this is what I reach for the rest of the time it's back to SupCom:FA.

I've been wanting to play Berseria ever since I played Zestiria a couple of years ago. Berseria certainly did not disappoint. There were multiple references in Berseria to Zestiria which increased the joy of playing this game immensely. Now if you haven't played Zestiria, it doesn't mean you can't enjoy this game. It's quite the opposite. Berseria is the prequel to Zestiria (1000 years difference), so that means that you'll get the references from Berseria the other way around, which is great for the Zestiria gameplay.
The story for this game is great, there's a lot of dialogue and a lot of backstory to dive in to. The characters are great and the voices (in Japanese) are awesome (except for Bienfu, sorry)
There is plenty of drama and plenty of humor (thank you Magilou) in the game, that will keep you playing this game.
Also, I did not find the game grindy at all. At no point in the storyline did I have the feeling 'my level is too low, I need to train a bit more' The battles sure were difficult at times, but playing the game normally without skipping to many monsters each region, will make the game feel just difficult enough.
I have to say that there are multiple difficulty levels, and I've played it through 'moderate'. The 'chaos' difficulty will probably make it a little bit more difficult, but that just a little bit of speculation on my side.
Now it's time to play something else again. Maybe Zestiria? Or New Game+.

Considering how the game got written off after its long and troubled development history and the general lack of marketing, it's quite amazing how great this game is. Graphically it's absolutely gorgeous for an open-world game, especially when you get caught in one of the rather heavy Hong Kong rainstorms, and the character animations and car models are all quite pretty as well. The game also boasts a fantastic soundtrack, both in-world and as radio selections, showing a huge diversity in styles ranging from modern hits to cantonese gangster rap.
The gameplay runs very similar in style to most other open-world games in the same vein, such as GTA and Saint's Row, but a noticeable deviation is the fact that the game is much, much more sparse with firearms, instead having fight enemies in hand-to-hand combat. That sounds kinda ill-advised, but the melee combat in Sleeping Dogs is good enough that it's enjoyable the entire way through. The amount of character progression gained both through levels and sidequests allows for the combat to become more and more nuanced and fun.
The story itself is quite good as well, at least much moreso than you'd expect at first. It hits the same kinds of story beats as most of the similar open-world games, as in having a heavy focus on criminal gangs and the like, but there's enough interesting story elements and plot twists that it keeps you interested the entire way through.

"3. No Interaction Between Multiple Accounts.

This also includes using accounts for storage space, and selling the resources gathered on one account to gain money on another. Any accounts that are found to be interacting with each other who have the same owner will be permanently jailed and banned. "
This is inane. Other than to make an acct for just PVP or something, there wouldn't be much use for 5 accounts in game in a game with theoretically three builds: mage, warrior, hybrid. Furthermore, no using accounts as extra storage is extremely discouraging- working to actively handicap the player from stockpiling resources and making money by giving them that little invo space may keep you in control of the market, but at the cost of making money a chore and forcing you to "play favorites" with your invo and trashing perfectly fine items. I also can't think of many MMOs that outright ban "trading across the same IP" meaning people (like those complaining in the forums for this game) can't trade with their family members or friends if they are playing LAN. It's ridiculous. Look at the forums, you have these people desperate to like the game but are being put off cause they can't do♥♥♥♥♥♥with their girlfriends or younger brothers.

The devs here have a lot of nerve pushing the blame of exploiting bugs onto the player themselves rather than their own oversight. Exploit of bugs doesn't give you unfair advantage over the rest of the community if those very bugs are theoretically accessible to the entire community. The bugs are you problem, not ours. These are mechanics discovered within the confines of the game, with no third party involved. You should either be more lenient or just patch and thank the damn players for calling attention to the exploits. Why would players go out of their way to test out exploits in an open beta if they could be punished? Why would you even punish them if you are not losing money? If a certain exploit was good enough to invalidate paid content, I would think it would come to the community's attention really fast. Instead of banning people, patch the stuff. The game is in EARLY ACCESS, how counterintuitive is it to ban for exploiting bugs in an open beta?

Why is this not allowed? What if I got sick of the terrible rules and my friend wanted to start playing so I let them pick up mine? Would that count? The rules, despite being so draconian, are also extremely vague.

When Valve initially released this, it was an unfinished game. Now, it's polished, but Valve killed the online community with the release of L4D2. There are still a handful of die hard players that cling to it, but most everyone else has moved on. It would still be a good game today had L4D2 not taken its place.

Edit: I actually have around 80 hours of play time, not 10. You can play this game through your internet browser as well, which is where I played most of the time. I found the game on Steam and then switched to browser once I found out about it.
Original Review:
Don't be decieved by the Steam release date. This game has been out for 4 years and only has 2 main developers. They are taking an incredibly long time to update the game and it doesn't look like it will be finished any time soon. Maybe in another 3 years it will be close to finished. There's lots of inbalance in gear, and their item store is very decieving. As a new player do NOT buy the Firelord gear in the store because although people in chat tell you that it is among the best equipment in the game, what they don't tell you is that it requires 15 upgrades to become the best gear in the game, and you'll never have enough coins to upgrade the gear unless you've been playing the game hardcore for over a year. The Firelord gear is only for veterans and new players are always sucked into buying it. It will help you as a new player for the first few weeks of playing, but after that when it's time to upgrade the equipment to level 2, you won't have anywhere near the amount of currency for even 1 upgrade, not to mention 14 upgrades after that for each piece of the set.
And everyone was right, mods are very sensitive and ban people for no good reason. At first I didn't have a problem with the mods and I figured only the people who deserve to be muted are muted by the mods, but then I started noticing very unfair calls by the mods, and very inappropriate bans. After just 4 days of seeing the way the mods were acting in chat, I felt very bitter toward them even without having talked to one personally.
On another note, chat is VERY sensored. Chat feels like the game is hosted in North Korea. Better watch what you say or off with your head! And I mean if the apple is red don't call it pink, or off with your head! And the community is very toxic more than 1/2 the time. It is a very small community and you better not make any suggestions to improve the game unless you're ready to get beat up. Want to cause an uproar? Mention something about the game's graphics being updated for higher quality, something along those lines. You will cause a riot.
There are a few very helpful players in the game and they are were incredibly nice to me. Those few helpful players reached out to me and answered all of my questions and even gave me very expensive items to start out with (expensive for me anyways). Those few players made the game very enjoyable, but unfortunately the community is toxic most of the time. If you play the game for hours on end you will see what I'm talking about. Or if you get lucky and only log in for 1-2 hours you might luck out and miss the toxicity.
Ultimately, it is the toxic community (moderators included) that made me quit this game and ask for a full refund on my credit card for all in-game purchases. Yes, it is the community that drove me away from this game, namely 45% players 55% moderators = 100% enough for me to quit.

It took me a bit to determine if I would recommend this game and the answer has to be no. In the end, the actual "game" is extremely lacking and the best bits really leave you wanting more. It might have a great sequel, but as it is, I can't recommend it.
The bad stuff. So there isn't really a game here. There are the concepts of a FPS intermixed and there are even a couple VR training sessions that show off a functional shooter. It's not great, but it's functional. Oh and there's a bug where apparently the AI cannot figure out where you are if you go up two ramps from the starting level.
In the game itself, there are at most two parts that can involve combat. If you play "correctly," there will be no combat though. If you don't, it's again not very good combat.
So the experience rests firmly on the story and the interactions. The actual writing of all of the lines is pretty good overall with respectable voice acting. There just isn't any real motivating force past either advancing the game or I don't have anything better to do to actually play along. There is a ton of information you clearly are left out of, but the game never really lets you into that. Maybe with some more context or something, I would care, but as presented, I just don't.
So that sounds like all of the game. Why would this be hard for me to say yes or no to the recommend to it? It sounds boring to bad overall.
There are glimmers of something great in here. The meta story could be actually pretty interesting. I would love for there to be more to it. At the end, it even seemed to be coming through a bit.
There actually seem to be characters in this game. People have glimmers of personalities and conflicts. That all seems great. No one happens to develop anywhere near enough for me to care about them, but I can see things there.
The entire game takes place on one (large) plane. I love that in such a condensed space, you can have quite a few interactions and it felt decently real (as in a reasonable series of events). Hell, even the plane felt appropriate where there were places for people to sleep and relax and eat and such while remaining very tight and small. Unfortunately those interactions all end up being boring.
So I really want to see what comes of the sequel which I believe starts kickstarting soon. This isn't the game I wanted to play, but it is a world I'm interesting in revisiting.

Town of Salem is good fun! I have a fan for werewolf or mafia or whatever the heck you call it. For people that don’t know what werewolf/mafia/whatever, what it is that there are at least two people within a group of at least 7 people that’s goal is to kill everyone but they have to make sure they’re not too suspicious because during the day the people vote to ‘lynch’ a person and if both bad guys die the survivors win.
This is usually a card game but Town of Salem has mixed it up a little. They’ve added a bunch of roles that changes the game drastically. 33 roles that are possible in custom games but the basic game gives only a few of these roles. A sheriff, a doctor the Investigator, jailer, medium, Mafioso godfather, framer, executioner, escort, lookout, serial killer, random town with a killing role, Jester, and just a random town role.
Allow me to explain these roles for you.
Sherriff shows the exact role of any town member except for the Godfather, they leads the mafia.
The doctor can nurse people back to health if they get attacked that night. If they think they’re going to get attacked, they can heal themselves only once.
The investigator finds clues that suggests the role of a town member.
The Jailor hauls someone to jail, and anonymously interrogates that town member, they can choose to execute that character, but that would be very foolish.
The medium is a role that can talk to the dead, this can extremely useful but it is prone to being useless to the fact that most people will leave as soon as they die, leaving you in silence until your inevitable death. (That got dark).
Mafioso is the killer of the mafia, the Godfather orders to kill someone and they do it. The Framer plants evidence in someone’s house for that night, so if the investigator looks into them, they will appear to be a part of the mafia, all mafia members get to talk to each other at night.
Executioner, this role is a neutral but is bit evil. Their goal is to get their target to get ‘lynched’. If they die at night they become a jester.
The Jester, is scum beggary at its finest. Their role is to get themselves lynched at all cost, if they do, they can possess one town member to kill themselves.
Escort role is to distract people and role block them, making their role useless for that night.
Lookout, they watch someone’s house and see if anyone comes to their house in the night, this role is extremely useful if that character turns up dead the next day.
Serial Killer, talk about a spanner in the works, their goal is to kill everyone, they are immune to death at night and if they get hauled off to jail, they will kill the jailor.
The random town killing role roles can be any role under that category, they can be the Jailor, Veteran, Vigilante and Vampire Hunter.
Finally the Random town role is any town role, I’d list them all out but I’m too lazy.
You see how many roles each person has and that’s just basic game. This game is great fun, locked at 25 frames a second, which can be bad for some people but it never diminishes the effect of the game, in fact it is built for the experience more than the AAA feel. And it being only $4.99 I’d happily recommend it.
Just be warey of the people you encounter, there are people that skype with other people in the game basically throwing the game in their favor or just people that lack logic, which is me sometimes but I try. But still, great game.

This is a great game. You play as the new security officer on a commandship tasked with monitoring global security. It goes a bit deeper than that, you are part of a mysterious time warp experiment who happens to take the body of the new security officer. Soon there is a murder on board and ransomers outside and you have to deal with the situation. Clues start adding up and you really wonder who is behind the conspiracy, what do they want from you, do they know your secret?
The developers really went all out in the writing and voice acting of this game. The characters all have their own personalities, quirks and back stories so you really feel like you are a part of a team. They go about their work day throughout the ship.  You can follow them and see what secrets they are hiding or you can joke around with them. I began to like these people and actually felt bad when I tried to do a jerk playthrough.
There is a combat simulator on board and two optional combat situations.
It is very short, the game world moves on with or without you so there is no real down time. Things happen fast so the game isnt long. Its worth multiple playthroughs tho and I enjoy the atmosphere. Plus there are from 3-4 responses to dialogue and the writers really fleshed it out so there are a lot of options to explore.
So if you want to take an afternoon to become an officer on a space ship, meet some new friends (or enemies), solve a murder and shoot some badies then I highly recommend this game. It will be memorable.

Groovy is a Marble Maze game that is similar to that of the old NES Classic
Marble Madness, Which I was very fond of growing up.
The main Difference is this is that game on steroids, Much more things to do, much more mechanics.
The Music is ok, its very soft and slow, Then picks up at times, But over all i'd label it closer to futuristic lounge music.
The mousefeedback, even when setting the sensitivity to high seemed off and sort of laggy in movement, at least in the menus, It doesn't seem to be this way when actually playing, but moving the mouse through the menus seemed laggy like it dragged to much.. I like the interface and menus, But that mouse lag on the menus is pretty bad.
Honestly the game needs one of the forced tutorials, if only for a minute, to at least tell what those things are your getting, and show controls.
Once I figured them out, The controls of this game were actually a hell of a lot smoother than marble madness, and I actually had fun flashing back to classic marble platforming.
I do with the levels had a little more color to them, as everything is a little bland and all looks similar.
The 3d environment itself is really nice besides the lack of vibrant coloring.
Not sure what happened on the 2nd level, But I Appear to have glitched inside of a spaceship? No way to pause or exit out of it? Had to quit, Must of been a glitch of some sort, Because when I went back and loaded it again, It beamed me from the ship down like it was supposed to.
Even tho its been used in many games, I like the 3 star system here, It works at rating you pretty well.
Overall if you like Marble Madness, you'll probably dig this at least to some extent.

Some may pass off Starbound as another attempt to cashe in on the "Build your own world" style of gameplay similar to minecraft (Which is solely the only reason to play that game) or terraria (Where you feel as if the only reason to build is to store your things). It is not though. I may have few hours into the game when I first got it, but I can tell, it is different. Each planet feels so real, and you grow to love your little human/apex/star kid/ect... In the first coulple of days, a rainstorm happened. A pretty nasty one. I was content to wait out the rain inside, interacting with all the furnature (a great touch BTW) and planning how to build my hut as it did rain, instead of go out and fight or explore as my little starkid got drenched. It was a feeling of satisfaction that my house protected me from the elements that I never got in the other games like this.
Starbound also does combat much better than the others I gave examples of. The system of firearms and bows being powered by energy gives a concept of saving ammo, without having to go buy ammo. Melee weapons not only burst hard, but your character seems to have heft from them, with your melee weapon appearing to have weight to them, as two handed axes seem to take more to swing from you than a knife would. Also starbound allows for dual wielding of any two one-handed weapons or shields, something i wondered why the other games couldnt get that right.
Lastly, the final reason people come to theese kind of games is the exploration, and this is the best of all. Starbound does a great job of making you feel like a space explorerer, with each planet a unique experience. You will find yourself in beautiful hilly forest plannets, or boiling desert plannets. You will brave frozen wasteland plannets, to asteroid fields rich with resources. In most planets there is also expansive underground cave systems, with things such as a dead kings tomb, to portals to pocket dimensions that lead you to a special challenge with powerful rewards.
Starcraft has been the first game to not only make me excited to leave home for an adventure, but upset aswell. Starbound has all I mentioned and more. As the game gets updated, all three of theese points strengthen even more. Bossfights are intense and truly test your skills, and colonated planets allow you to interact with the many interesting NPC's. As well, your ship's AI is quite adorable. Would I reccomend Starbound? When it was still a young game, just a skeleton, I would have not. But now? Within a heartbeat I would reccomend it to someone who is new to the "Build your own world" game style, or someone who the magic of them died out due to the lacking of satisfaction with the other games. If you are going to spend your money on any open beta, do it on Starbound. (The soundtrack is also beautiful BTW)
although it lacks in graphics it overall is an extremly fun game better than most games in the genre

I’m inexperienced Steam user and actually this is my first review here.
So, why do I think that ”GROOVY” is worth every cent of the price?
This is a catchy game that perfectly absorbed puzzle, strategy and action in one attractive pot.
I really never saw a similar game among platformers. Developers have managed to create two absolutely unique modes: third-person Arcade and side-scrolling Survive.
Even if you’re not a fan of “Marble Madness”, “Ballance” or “Switchball” there are many reasons for taste “GROOVY”. There are huge locations, a lot of levels and it’s really hardcore (for me truly hardcore started with level A-5 :)) But anyway levels are pretty beatable, it’s not too difficult to get 2 stars, for example. However, if you want receive three, you should earnestly try and create own strategy for every level. It’s possible, of course, but very-very difficult. It’s like: “You try, fail, try again, fail again, and then try another one time, but fail again, TRY AND FAIL, TRY AND FAIL, but can’t stop until you get it!” :) Withal game is really addictive and enjoyable.
“GROOVY” has got a truly superb graphics (glad that it runs on my far from the most powerful PC). Mechanisms, Groovy, every levels detail, platforms are well-made and look literally amazing.
Physics of the ball deserves special compliments. Jumps, inertia, torque – that’s all implemented perfectly.
Music should liked by every person who like techno and electronic. It’s dynamic, in game style, doesn’t distracts and isn’t annoying.
The system of customization of Groovy skins is remarkable, and I bet you’ll spend a lot of time changing the ball. Because you can change everything! Texture, HUE, saturation, gloss, emissivity etc.
Finally I’d say that I played with controller and it works fine.
+ Great graphics
+ Remarkable physics
+ Two radically different game modes
+ Large number of levels
+ Hardcore
+ Many gameplay hours
+ Cool music
+ Deep skin customization
+ 60 achievements
+ 12 languages are supported
+ Reasonable price
+ Controller support
Without doubt, “GROOVY” is one of the best platformer I ever met.

As an avid 'Tales of' fan, I was at first skeptical when first going into this game, as it didn't seem like your typical Tales game. Well, I'm 20 hours in now and I was right, but I was also wrong, so let me break it down for you.
- The main character's motivation is revenge, and she doesn't apologize for it. You're more or less playing the bad guy when you start out, but I imagine in proper Tales fashion your actions are justified in the end. I've been constantly hooked on "get the next step done" in the storyline aspect.
- Each character is well written, even by Tales standards, and each has their own motivations. When they join your party, it's because their goals align with yours and don't just join because you're the main character in a video game. Even minor characters seem to have somewhat flushed-out personalities, but you don't see much of them unless plot demands it.
- Definitely different from most Tales games. Instead of Artes and basic attacks, it works more like a fighting game. Emphasis is on performing high combos and exploiting enemy weaknesses rather than managing attacks/TP-consumption. It takes a bit to get used to, but it's pretty solid. Also, the world map is littered with enemies, so do yourself a favor and buy some Holy Bottles...
- There's a mastery system for equipment that helps you power up pretty easily, but can get tedious. Instead of just "Equip the most advantageous item", it's more of "Equip/Enhance/Master every weapon/armor to git gud." It can be frustrating at times, but can easily be used to your advantage if you take the time to do it.
- Loooooots of extras in this game. Cooking's there, and several mini-games here and there. My favorite part is the cosmetics system where you can dress up the characters how you please. Dressing people up like dude-bros and Mary Sues and seeing them in cutscenes is worth a laugh, at least. There are plenty of references to other Tales games within, so that's nice.
+ Solid writing / Compelling story (so far)
+ Detailed combat that's easy to learn, hard to master
+ Solid voice work
+ Easily-changed difficulties
+ Soundtrack is on point
+ Lots of game aspects to explore
+ Japanese audio for weebs

I'm not going to bother writing most of the downsides to this game, as literally every single thing I could bring up is already stated quite clearly in the rest of these reviews. Instead, let me cover the things that make this game fun to play despite all of its numerous issues.
The community can be amazing. I'm not saying it always will be, and honestly I may just be incredibly lucky, but here's my reason for saying this. I played the game for about two days before I stumbled across the recipe to make my own club. My close friend and I who were playing together did about four days of grinding and walked away with a club of our own. We built a few buildings just to get started, then I started inviting every single person I saw in the starting levels who didn't have a club yet, as well as everyone looking for a club invite in global. Within a month we had over 150 members, and a club world I am honestly proud of. All of our architects and officers are dedicated and friendly, helping new members learn game mechanics and running them through shadow towers on a regular basis. We ended up setting up a Discord channel recently, and I've grown to have real friends amongst the people in my club.
Everything is obtainable without paying a penny. Yeah, people talk endlessly in these reviews how you have to pay real money for classes, styles, mounts, tomes, everything. That just isn't true. The only things that you have to pay real money for are the styles you get for being a recurring customer, and honestly those look like♥♥♥♥♥♥ If you want to know more about how to get EVERYTHING for in game currency, no real money purchases, check at the bottom of this review.
It has the simplest combat of any MMO I have ever played, and that's nice. I've played a whole bunch of MMOs in my time, and Trove is awesome because there's just as much intensity in the combat as there is in a game like WoW, but you don't have to worry about two or three bars full of abilities for every character. Simple and fast paced combat makes everything better in my opinion.
There is a TON of content. It will easily take thousands of hours of playtime before you get your hands on the last of the cool mounts you want, or that last upgrade for your gear. You may turn around and say that's a bad thing, because it'll get boring after a while. Well, you'd be right if it wasn't for the fact that this game measures out its rewards in perfect doses. Every time you start to get bored, you'll reach a new zone or get a new item that makes you want to keep playing. I love a game that can keep me endlessly entertained.
All in all I'd recommend this game, despite all its MANY flaws. If you can't deal with the lag, the grind, and the bugs, then you aren't going to last more than a few hours. Get past that, join a good club, set a personal goal for yourself, build a sweet world, and you'll easily drop a few hundred hours before you realise it.
How to get EVERYTHING for free:
Classes: Craft them. That's right, you can craft classes. Most reviews that ♥♥♥♥♥ about this game being pay to play lean heavily on their claim that the classes have to be purchased in real money, when a few days of grind will get you the materials to craft any and all of the classes.
Credits: There are some things that can only be obtained by purchasing them from the in game store with a currency known called credits. Credits are usually obtained by spending real money, but here's two ways to get credits for free: level up or buy them in the market. Leveling up you mastery rank occasionally gives you some cradits, and when you add them all up there's enough there to buy a whole bunch of stuff from the shop. Run out of those? That's fine, with enough time and effort you can buy credits from the community market. Don't want to spend the time on that? Well guess what, there isn't a single goddamn thing that they sell for only credits that is actually essential to gameplay. Suck it up and farm♥♥♥♥♥♥the old fashioned way.
Patron passes: Not only do these drop from daily login rewards, but during every seasonal event (of which there are many) they give a patron pass to everyone who logs in on certain days. For instance, the St. Patricks day event goes on for two weeks, and 7 of those days they give you a free patron pass.
Comments or concerns? I am more than willing to edit this review as many times as I need, in order to provide the most accurate information possible.

This game is a masterpiece. I haven’t enjoyed myself with a JRPG like this since Kingdom Hearts 2 and that was years ago.
This review will be addressed to 2 kinds of people: the ones who have played tales of Zestria and those who haven’t.
In any cases expect 50 hours of gameplay for the main story.
Soundtrack is good to decent. It’s not FF X good but there are some nice themes.
Lore wise this game is a prequel to tales of Zestria like the prequel Star Wars trilogy is to the original one: you don’t
to have seen the original one to follow the story but you’ll miss all the references. In our case, it takes place a few thousand of games before Zestria and players will most likely notice them (places, characters, etc) For example ruins weren’t always ruins you know…
Story wise you will form a band of antiheroes in order to get revenge. It’s not a battle between good and evil like Zestria and instead of black versus white it will be gray versus gray or law versus chaos in D&D terms.
This game is simply put a better Zestria:
- combat system is roughly the same but AI characters will be actually useful when Zestria ones were dying all over and over with nothing you could do.
- Enhancement system doesn’t give you a headache and you don’t need to simulate your stats every single time you’re considering an upgrade. Stats and skills unlocked through enhancement are already predetermined
- Huge world with more towns.
- Characters are more ambiguous and enjoyable. Your team is a mix of heroes and antiheroes with different motivations and personality traits than “let’s save the world cause we’re the good guys”. I didn’t understand at first the hype for Magilou, considering her a joke character but 40 hours later I was amazed.
- You don’t have to look for Normins in order to get a special stat on your equipment
- Main story less foreshadowed. Without spoiling both of the games it’s hard to detail but at least the opening video isn’t spoiling you half the game.
Tales of Berseria is a JRPG with real time combat around combos. You will be controlling one character while up to 3 others will be under AI control. Each character has unique abilities and his own combat playstyle: for instance some are melee characters with fast hits, others use long range spells and heals and then some are a mix between the two.
You can swap at any moment between characters and on moderate and lower difficulty you won’t have to play every single character if you don’t want to, the AI doing a more than average job.
In the main menu there’s a submenu to adjust their actions for instance the use of special abilities using a gauge filled by previous encounters.
It’s strongly recommended to play with a controller since it’s a port from playstation.
Difficulty can be changed at any moment outside of combat with around 5 different settings.
You will alternate between exploration and combat phases. Equipment is looted from enemies and can be enhanced by sacrificing unwanted loot to get components.
You have to expect a huge world with areas you’ll more likely revisit for the main story, side quests or farming.
You’ll unlock cosmetics allowing you to change the aspect of your characters.
Tales of Berseria is an awesome game. 20 euros for 50h of deep story and quality content seems a good deal to me. I strongly recommend playing tales of Zestria first if you enjoy story content otherwise you’ll miss a lot of references.
If you’re experiencing freezes when moving consider changing FPS to 30 instead of 60. Worked for me.

Also the “I can’t feel the cold” to justify fan service on the 19 years old main character outfit seems wrong in so many levels, but you can always swap outfits on the fashion menu.
Lastly achievement system doesn't work offline.

First things first: Creation Club. It's awful, but it's not going away. You can ignore it.
Second: Main story line/vanilla launch. It's subpar, but there are WONDERFUL and free mods to change that with minimal "invasion" to the game.
With those out of the way, on to the review itself.
Is it like previous FO games? That depends on how you look at them. Compared to FO3 and NV, you have less dialogue options to make since they're now fully voiced, and the karma system is less diverse and invisible, but those are the only big pull-aways. I personally find the combat system fun and even improved. VATS feels more optional than "required to get out of a sticky situation," and is a slow-motion lag-free toggle rather than a bullet-time freeze-cam. There's no weapon/gear repair system, but that's for a reason. The materials you collect, including extra gear and weapons, is for a new system where you can build settlements (or you can just keep on making some caps at traders). This settlements building system is also optional. While it did feel overwhelming at first, within a short amount of time it sucked me right in. Even across multiple characters and saves I find myself rebuilding things differently than I had built them before because I found it could be fun!
Now, say you haven't played anything in this franchise before, so you're not here to compare. This is an open-world game, so you can stay on track or get as much off track as you want. Beat the game in a few hours or spend hundreds of hours on it, that's completely up to you. You can have traveling companions with you who are all enjoyable, and they're optional, so if you wanna fly solo, that's cool, too. There are four varying main endings to choose from, reflecting on who you interact with along the way. After you feel you've "beat" the game and want something more out of it, the modding community is vast and friendly, and has many surprising and fun things to offer.
Overall, I personally was pleasantly surprised with what I got, and I admit that I went in a harsh judge. Pick it up on sale if you're on the fence about it, and if you like it, buy the DLC. And remember: "Creation Club" is entirely optional, even if it is part of your download size. :-)

Street Fighter 5 has received a mix bag of reviews, mainly due to some initial problems on launch. Whilst these problems were a bit annoying, they did not take away from the core mechanics of the game, which are utterly fantastic.
Pros:
- Much better net-code and online play compared to Street Fighter 4, despite the initial server issues on launch
- Basic combos are far more damaging in general, which makes scoring damage a lot easier for a newer player
- No more "1 frame links", making the top damaging combos far more accessible for newer players
- A nice graphical upgrade from Street Fighter 4
- Ability to buy DLC with in game currency you earn for completing various tasks. (Once the store is fully released)
Cons:
- The story mode and other key modes are being released in March as free DLC. This has caused a lot of outrage in the community, and is the reason for many of the negative reviews you will read
- No tutorial mode to help new players figure out combos. This can be solved with a quick Google search, but it would've been nice to have it already in the game.
- Server issues. As mentioned, Street Fighter 5 has had some server issues on launch which are still being ironed out. It is still very playable online, but expect it to be more polished by next week.
To conclude, Street Fighter continues to raise the bar in terms of it's core mechanics. It's an absolute blast when it's all working, and I see it being a very entertaining iteration long term.  If you are new to the series, I would highly recommend doing a quick Google search for your character's basic combos to help get you started, and stick to the 'Survival' and 'Training' modes for now.
If you are familiar with the series and are having trouble finding good games online, try searching for 'your system' only, and make sure to set 'Network Settings' to 5 only. This gave me the best results.

Well, i've just completed my first playthrough and it was an insanely well-realized story, even just once through. But, much like Life is Strange, the meta-game explicitly encourages you to try different approaches. Perhaps it will be the first time i actually do go back to a game just to play another path.
Essentially it is a first-person narrative adventure, with a few FPS elements. You are thrown in completely blind, teased with reams of world-building text in the information console, but immediately confronted with situations and dialogs that push you to skip it with absolutely no idea what's going on. As you start to learn the story, there are a few clues that lead you back to that wall of text, and the story is so ♥♥♥♥ing intriguing by then that it no longer feels like a chore at all. The characters are believable, the mythology is one of the richest i have ever seen in a video game and the whole experience is great.
If there's one thing i didn't like, it's the FPS segments. These days i am much more into stealth and skillful one-shot-kills, but the shooting segments here are oldskool Doomguy bullet-sponge strafe-em-ups. Fortunately it seems there is only one of these, plus some training missions. The storyline is truly great, though, and totally makes the shooting worthwhile. Could it be better than Gemini Rue? Yes. Better than Mass Effect? A million times yes. Better than Deus Ex? Almost. Probably. If you like science fiction you owe it to yourself to play this game right now. Don't sit on it. This is excellent.

Just take a look at my hours played before reading this. 250+ hours. I've been through a lot, man.
Anyhow, if you don't know what Town of Salem is, it's a game where 7-15 random people (mostly 15) are in Salem with the witch hunts and crap like that. Before the game starts, you name yourself, and are given a role to follow, which can range from mafia all the way to a werewolf. You just follow your role and kill/lynch everyone else that's not on your side.
Seems simple, right?
Wrong.
Though you know what you are, most of the time, you don't know ANYONE else. Therefore, you can't really trust anyone else. Therefore, not every game is the same. Every time you play, it's a totally different experience. One game, your a Doctor trying to safe people from dying. The next game, your a Mafioso blasting the brains out of everyone.
You can even play with your friends in the same server, although sharing information outside the game completly ruins the fun. The rules of punishment aren't so bad. Basically, don't be a little crybaby when you die. Like I said, all it takes is one person to ruin it for 14 others.
With most of the positives aside, I really only have one issue with this game, and that's the fanbase. Not everyone is bad, but I've played over 500 games of this, and I've seen a lot. Spammers, people who can't spell proper engwish (:P), and, of course, gamethrowers. Though those are only a few reasons, it can really make you not want to play this game sometimes, which sucks.
In conclusion. I'd like to say it's worth the $5, and if your a broke college kid like me, you can even look it up online and play it for free, as long as you don't mind some ads every now and then. If you do buy it here, you have no ads, and the $5 is broken down into their in-game currency (1300 Town Points), which you can use to buy skins for you characters or house, get pets to follow you, or even scrolls, which increase the chance of you getting a certain role, and can be used until you get said role. So, you're not really losing $5 on this deal. Plus, NO ADS. C'mon, dudes.
Well, that about raps this up. If you ever get in a game and have issues, the creators of this game have a Facebook and Twitter account, to which you can message them. They usually respond, too.
Happy Hanging, boys and girls. ;D
P.S. This game is always updating, to which new features are always being added. For example, at the time of writing this, Vampire and Vampire Hunter are due to come out.

This game is what Sanctum should have been.  It improves on just about every aspect from the first game, and then some.
Pros:
- Customization.  With four different characters, each with their own unique primary weapon and dialogue, and a wide variety of towers and abilities to choose from, Sanctum 2 has something for just about everyone's playstyle.
- Enemies.  Like Sanctum and just about every good tower defense game, Sanctum 2 has a large number of enemies.  From miniature "runners" that will punch you if you get too close to dudes with an obscure "weak point", each enemy will give you a challenge regarding tower placement.  Bosses are a ton of fun as well, although they can be a little cheap.
- Difficulty.  Sanctum 2's difficulty is perfect, in my opinion.  It's not an easy game, yet it's no Dark Souls either.  You will be tested on how well you can utilize the space and resources given to you, and any weaknesses in your defenses can turn a "perfect run" into a failed mission pretty quickly.  Thankfully, resources are fully refunded when selling towers, so you can create different setups as each mission progresses.
Cons:
- Too much non-buildable space.  In many maps, at least half of the map is area that cannot be built on.  This can get pretty annoying, since in those areas there are crappy "prebuilt defenses" in the form of conscripts that die with 1-2 hits.
- Useless towers.  Some towers seem very out of place, and even pointless in some cases. For example, there's a tower that gives you one mine every wave.  Why?!  This should have been a secondary weapon!
- Scarce resources.  I think the idea of providing a relatively small amount of resources every turn is interesting and certainly ups the difficulty of the game, but it can be quite silly at times.  In the original Sanctum I could build entire corridors full of towers within a few turns; in Sanctum 2, the maximum is 15 towers, and you'll be lucky if you can build 1-2 towers every wave.  Some players may like this, and I do to an extent, but it's one part of Sanctum that I sort of miss.
I highly recommend this game to anyone with a remote interest in Tower Defense games, or to someone looking for a breath of fresh air in the Tower Defense genre.  If you didn't like the first Sanctum, I still recommend giving this game a shot when it goes on sale; it improves on enough of the original game to justify a reconsideration.

Quick summary: More FPS, Less TD, now it feels like another FPS with a gimmick.
Original Sanctum offered a nice blend of Tower Defence and First Person Shooter, where carefully planned blocks and tower layout was crucial to completing higher waves and individual skills as a shooter certainly contributing to keep the enemy mob under control. Sanctum 2 however seem to have watered down the strategy part and heavily leaned towards the FPS orientated game by applying constraints to the towers you can build.
In the original Sanctum, the aim of the game was in-line with the Tower Defence genre, building up your defence as much as your resource allows until you're overwhelmed by the enemy or until you ride out the wave. Sanctum 2 has made three major changes from the predecessor;
1.  blocks and towers now have separate resource pools
2. there is a limitation on the number of towers you can have built at anytime.
3. no more weapon upgrades.
The above changes diminishes the reward for carefully thought out, long-term planning and favour on-the-fly, impulsive decisions. With blocks, towers and weapons not sharing tje resource pool, there are no more dilemmas regarding the early game. There used to be a choice on how to begin the game. Should I start building the maze early?, Add more towers and supports? or perhaps upgrade your own weapon and take responsibility for the enemy to come? you had a choice. Now the guns you picked cannot have custom upgrades, you can build only certain amount of blocks per wave and have a pitiful amount to build maybe couple of towers. There really is not much you can do different. This also affect the mid-game where you are left with more blocks than you need with no resource to upgrade your tower. For a tower defence game where resource management is the key, it seems so wasteful.
The changes also shorten the length of the game. No weapon upgrade, limit on tower number and reduced resource for tower upgrades means the game cannot grow out for too long. In tower defence games it is a battle between how much and how fast you build your defence against how tough the enemies grow. Cripple the player's ability to upgrade and it is obvious that the waves count has to be reduced. To compensate and "up the difficulty", the big boss monster will walk straight through the maze you built, smashing away the beautiful defence you have planned and built. No tower defence for that part, just shoot.
For Multiplayer, Sanctum 2 has introduced player levels with towers, weapons and even the tower slots using the "unlock at this level" mechanism. At first it may seem that this may encourage players of equal progression to play together but it significantly reduces the amount a new player can contribute to the game. A new player would have to do a little grind before joining a match.
With that said, Sanctum 2 brought few nice ideas into the game.
Player Classes encourages the players to work as a team, each taking on a particular role to play. the idea is nice although some role may feel left out when their speciality is not required or ill fitted for the job at hand. The original allowed for 3 weapons, which gave a little more freedom and perhaps better backup weapon would have been nice. Sniper class especially can be frustrating when the team requires fire rate than firepower and even worse if you are fighting alone.
Sanctum 2 have lowered platforms and hostile enemies. This is one thing I actually commend and it feels like an improvement. In the original Sanctum, the enemies simply followed the shortest path to the core and players couldnt really be killed unless you stood in front of them. This time, the blocks are lowered in height and some of the monsters will actually chase you and attack you. It adds bit more action to the game without destroying the strategy of Tower Defence. No more of being lazy, letting towers do the work and watching the action as the overlord; you gotta get down there and contribute.
In conclusion Sanctum 2 feels like it has deviated away from the planned, strategy cored gameplay that made it so unique and interesting. The higher dosage of FPS was welcomed but to sacrifice the TD element for it is highly questionable in my opinion. Perhaps for those who prefer more shooting this maybe more enjoyable. But for me who enjoyed  the careful planning of the Lumen killing floor, can't help but compare it to the original Sanctum. The boundless possibilities of building your own defence was what I was after and I feel rather disappointed by the lack there of.

I wish steam gave us a neutral option just for games like this. I've always enjoyed the XCOM series but it seems as if this game was geared more toward veterans.
The odds are definitely stacked against the player. Right when you start to take control of a mission, something transforms into a huge monster, AND gets a turn to attack before you can even react to it. This inevitably screws over your set-up and/or kills one of your guys. Don't get me wrong, unpredictability is awesome on a battlefield. It adds a degree of realism that makes it fun and challenging. But this is a terrible design decision for two reasons:
1. On the contrary, as soon as you come into contact with enemies, they get to run for cover before you can act. But when an enemy can appear on the battlefield and attack you all in the same turn is a bit unfair.
2. I don't mind losing to a difficult game. I like it when things are fair and challenging for both parties. But unless you have a perfect mission every.single.time, you'll most certainly fall behind in the difficulty curve and it will quickly become overwhelming as your rookies continuously die over and over.
There are also still bugs left in the game that really demotivate the player. If you extract a VIP on the last turn, the game thinks the VIP died and you lose the mission. This bug was reported over a year ago and it's still in the game today.
I don't mind difficult games at all. In fact, I much prefer them over games that hold your hand and make you the ruthless hero. But unfair games are a different story, and XCOM is an unfair game.

(and in EU you had time to get the good gear before fighting them)  As early as the second mission your ‘Elite’ soldiers will be mind controlled against each other, if not killed in a single, impossible shot from across the map, and it only gets harder from there.

If you are a returning veteran XCOM 2 can be beat, and can be enjoyed, but have a replacement laptop on standby, because you will probably throw yours out the window.

Titans is what Planetary Annihilation always needed in order to make it a brilliant RTS. Whilst not charting the same depth of Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance, PA: Titans brings with it a lot of key and interesting features.
The addition of "these titans" is central. The Atlas, Zeus, Ares and Helios all have fantastic game buster qualities which can end stalemates and validate a lot of former "unviable" strategies. Moreover, the addition of other units (Mobile Nuke, Locusts, Kaiju) add plenty of diversity to the later game.
WIth that in mind, there is still a lot of boredom to the early game. It's either Dox or Bolos, with very few maps (e.g. Lock with sparks) offering any availability to deviate from spamming these 2 units with an accompanying air force early game. Ranked 1v1 is still relatively boring and short most games, with very few available opportunities to use the full arsenal at your disposal.
However, in general you will find a much stronger game complete with fun orbital gameplay. The interplanetary selling point of this game is finally worthwhile and viable. Orbital play is now diversified with the addition of the Omega, Artemis and Helios.
I strongly recommend this game unless you are looking for a 100% pro game, in which case go check out Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance.

TL;DR: Extremely solid game dragged down by time padding and mediocre presentation. If you can handle the above, thumbs up, otherwise wait for a sale.
Context: I used to really like the Tales games, although I have not played even close to all of them (prior to this title, I had played Symphonia, Vesperia, Abyss, DotNW, and Xillia). Xillia's half-baked plot and bland gameplay (I'd go into detail but that's a review unto itself) turned me off of the series for a while. When Zestiria was released for PC, I considered getting back into Tales, but word of mouth indicated that it was even more of a mess than Xillia, so I skipped on it.
Then, this game happened. All of my friends raved about it. But it was so *expensive*. The game sat on my wishlist for almost a year, before finally going on sale for 60% off on Black Friday, at which point I decided it was time to get my Tales on again. (Note that the fact that I purchased this game at a significant discount almost certainly colored my opinion of it positively.)
I really liked the battle system, for the most part. The basic concept is that you have Souls which dictate how many attacks you can string together and how long your spirit gauge lasts before needing to be recharged. Inflicting status ailments (which is easier if you use an attack the enemy is weak to) gives you souls, and receiving status ailments (which is more likely if you make a mistake, such as taking an attack while attacking or with an empty spirit gauge) loses souls, and also prevents the afflicted from being healed. This makes battles extremely unforgiving, as a mistake can seriously hamper your ability to mount an attack; by contrast, good play lets you build up momentum and flatten opponents.
Sometimes the game isn't designed well around this system, though. Some enemies are specifically purposed towards inflicting status, which is odd when the game in turn is built around status ailments being a punishable offense.
The potentite system is pretty excellent. It's nice to have a tangible reward for progressing through the game or seeking out powerful enemies.
The dungeons aren't quite as lifeless as in Xillia (I obviously can't compare them to more recent titles such as Zestiria), although they were still somewhat lacking. The only ones that left a positive impression on me were the forest with the toggleable gates (unfortunately, this gimmick is reused later in the game) and the water temple. A lot of the areas, particularly the second-to-last dungeon, are literally just giant hallways with no points of interest to speak of.
I felt like the game has a lot of padding. Pretty much every area feels somewhat too large for the amount of actual content therein, with actual points of interest being rather sparse. It gets particularly bad towards the end of the game; even the hoverboard you get about 2/3s of the way through feels agonisingly slow in the face of just how friggin' *gigantic* the final areas are.
On top of that, late-game enemies take ridiculously long to kill (a problem which may have been alleviated had I bothered to deal with the equipment upgrade system, but that's a problem unto itself), which combined with their tendency to attack in mobs of 6 or more makes even minor encounters take upwards of 2 minutes, which doesn't sound like much until you realise just how goddamn *many* there are.
Overall, while my final in-game time was about 50 hours, I'd estimate at least 8 of those were spent walking though sprawling empty corridors or beating up enemies that posed no real threat to me but just refused to freaking die.
The difficulty curve throughout the game is really random at times. The reef area is way harder than the actual dungeon afterwards simply by virtue of the enemies being more status-happy. There is a dungeon wherein I couldn't get past the midboss without turning the difficulty down to the lowest level, but beat the actual boss on my first try. The bosses of the last few dungeons are arguably less threatening than the random enemies in said dungeons.
The equipment system is pretty bad, being one part RNG grinding and one part endless clicking through menus. By the second-to-last dungeon, I wasn't even bothering with equipment upgrading at all. The skill system is also very bland, with all characters having the same pool of generic skills, none of which are very exciting.
The story was surprisingly excellent. Melodramatic and often corny as all get out, but that's basically my jam so I was fine with it. It had a strong motivation for its protagonist, didn't shy away from portraying the depths she'd sink to for revenge or her determination to see her goal through to the bitter end, and (surprisingly for a Tales game) kept its head on right up to the end, coming full circle in a very satisfying manner. "Why do birds fly?"
Eleanor was another strong point for me; I enjoyed seeing her journey from a model soldier who did and believed as she was told to someone who thinks for herself and fights for her own truth and ideals.
I also enjoyed Artorius. I personally don't think he's anything new for the series (hero who lost a loved one and his sanity along with it and proceeded to engineer a holocaust in the name of a twisted ideal of order before being foiled by the protagonist whose personal journey throughout the game reflects his own), but I found him to be quite well executed.
For the negative: Rokurou was disappointing; I kept waiting for him to have some kind of greater depth, but it just wasn't there. "I want to kill my brother and become the greatest swordsman, because uhhh something something youngest child something something inferiority complex? i dunno lol" Whee.
A couple plot points felt clumsily storyboarded, in particular many key moments with Laphicet (a bunch of them feel like the writers just decided "okay he grows as a person HERE" without bothering to give him an actual reason for it). Zaveid kinda... disappears without much actual resolution of the ideological conflict between himself and the party.
The graphics are nice. I like the character designs, although I can see people getting pissy over Velvet's outfit (there are options to take if it bothers you), and Magilou's book-skirt is probably the dumbest thing I've ever seen and that's coming from a Touhou fanboy (Keine's lunchbox-hat pales in comparison). Some tertiary characters have significantly lower-quality models compared to the main cast, which got distracting at times.
None of the areas really left an impression on me visually.
The music is really, really generic. The only tracks that left any impression are Hellawes and the Code Red enemy themes. The generic "ruins" BGM is really bad; there's no tension to it and it removes any sense of urgency from the scenario whenever it plays.
I appreciate the extensive voice work, but I question if it was actually worthwhile. Much of the voicing is bland at best, with no real standouts (Laphicet is terrible).
There's a lot of bad mo-cap in cutscenes et al. Magilou's is particularly jarring, since she relies on lots of big, sweeping gestures which mostly end up looking stiff or wobbly. Fortunately(?), this isn't that big an issue, since a very large amount of plot-important cutscenes are shown in the skit engine; as bland as it was, the cutscene direction and animation was so mediocre that I found myself almost grateful whenever a scene was played out by talking heads.
Overall, this game kind of leaves me wishing that Steam had a "Recommended, IF" option or something similar. IF the game had a better tempo without all the mind-numbing time padding and a crappy equipment system, or IF it had a lower price tag, then it would get an unqualified thumbs-up from me. However, it doesn't, so I would say to get this game at a discount if at all possible, UNLESS you have a tolerance for the above, in which case I can safely say you'll have a pretty good time.

This was my most anticipated game of 2017 (I don't play a lot of games, forgive me) and as a newcomer to the Tales series I played Symphonia as a background and I can tell you it was well worth it. Berseria does not reinvent the wheel but it's a crisp, beautiful game that anyone who loves RPGs should own just to support these kind of games on PC.
In this story you don't play as the good guys but as a rag-tag sort of team wrecking havoc in the world. This is a classic revenge story and to play as "bad guys" is a nice twist. You are all working towards one goal but everybody in you party has their own motivations. There are your usual cliches but the game is interesting enough that it doesn't diminish the overall experience. This is another 50 hour adventure that insists it's more about the journey than the destination.
Characters are where the game really shines. First you have a main character who is a good girl gone bad hellbent on avenging her brother. You have a samurai, a pirate, a witch and other colorful characters who join your team. The English voice acting is on point and I don't regret choosing it. The VA for Magilou is fantastic and you can tell she poured her heart into voicing her. The skits between the characters was well done and was held up by the phenomenal voice acting. Again, Magilou really stole the show. My personal favorite was Eizen/Eleanor.
The graphics were nice and clean for a RPG of today. You go through some beautiful environments. The animations of the characters (skits and models themselves) were great considering it's an "anime game". Menus look good and I really liked the pink color scheme that was used.
Now gameplay is where things get pretty standard. The fighting system does things to shake it up a bit but it can either be challenging or a walk through the park depending on what difficulty you set. The comboing is fun when you experiment with different elements but you'll find you will be button-mashing most of the time which could be good or bad. Regardless, Velvet screaming her special moves while swiping a group of enemies never gets old. The dungeons were pretty lackluster since almost all of them are just big empty rooms with hallways that will send you back and forth once in a while. I think the puzzles should have been harder.
The music is really solid but nothing out of the ordinary. Only one track that stood out to me was "Run Into the Horizon".
Plenty of extras to do in this game. Sending out your boat to gather materials was my highlight. Going to dangerous islands to mow down monsters felt great if you wanted to take a break from the story. The mini games are a nice touch and you can do them every town you went to. Regrettably the in-game costumes are nothing to talk about since the only good costumes you can get is through paid DLC. Speaking of DLC, you can get some extra consumables for free but I didn't use any of them because I played on normal. Oh and before I forget, there's plenty of collectibles!
I can't speak much about the Tales series as whole since this is my second but I can say with confidence this game didn't disappoint. I would definitely play this again.

Decent, but not life-changing action JRPG with a lot of weird humour.
Story:
Tries to do something new for the franchise by making your party the bad guys, which does lead to some fun. At it's heart, though, it's a pretty traditional Town > Dungeon> Town predictable RPG. A female protagonist is also a first, though sadly her default outfit is ridiculously skimpy for a badass  warrior. You can immediately switch into a more reasonable costume if this annoys you as much as it did me.
Characters:
The highlight of the game. There's a huge amount of quality (I was listening in Japanese)  mostly optional voiced dialogue between the party themselves as well as with NPCs. Priest confessions with your mass murdering demonic party are pretty funny and there are a lot of amusing moments in general. There are some weird Japanese things like the "mascot" character whose dialogue I found myself mostly mashing skip. Thankfully he's not a full party member and doesn't talk that much. The depth and growth of the main cast is well done with some interesting conflict.
Gameplay:
In theory the battle system is interesting, but at moderate and hard difficulty, spamming combos and breaksoul will do just fine. You are probably going to have a very large number of similar battles, though at least you have a lot of characters and possible combos to play with, You can choose whoever you control at any time. The dungeons are unfortunately a low point, with too many open fields and no real interesting design, just a few switch puzzles. There's a decent amount of side content, though I didn't find it interesting enough to fully complete.
Soundtrack:
Absolutely outstanding with many memorable themes.
Touching plot for a game with simplistic game play.  Easily one of my favorites.

I'm a huge fan of tower defense games, always have been, and so looking for interesting ones that do something new with the genre but that keep the meat of what makes a TD game a TD game is always enjoyable. I'll admit, I hadn't played the original Sanctum when I first found S2, but that didn't stop me from enjoying it. Sanctum 2 is a TD game mashed together with an FPS. The game feels similar to other games such as Orcs Must Die, but it has a few things that set it apart. The biggest one being it feels much closer to a classic TD game. Despite the fact that it's in a 3D rendering and seen from the first person view, you still use a block system and classic towers. That may be a plus or minus depending on how you feel about the genre, but it has a few things that set it apart and make it a ton of fun. Upgrades to your characters and multiple guns to unlock will have you playing for hours to see all the cool stuff you can do.
One thing I will say is this game was desgined to be played with friends, and so if you want to get anywhere in it I highly recomend having people to play with. You can join random parties of people, but nothing beats building up a strat with your friends and gunning down some big aliens. So if you're looking for an awesome tower defense game, or even a twist on your FPS style games, grab a few friends and get yourself a copy of Sanctum 2.

Just take a look at my hours played before reading this. 250+ hours. I've been through a lot, man.
Anyhow, if you don't know what Town of Salem is, it's a game where 7-15 random people (mostly 15) are in Salem with the witch hunts and crap like that. Before the game starts, you name yourself, and are given a role to follow, which can range from mafia all the way to a werewolf. You just follow your role and kill/lynch everyone else that's not on your side.
Seems simple, right?
Wrong.
Though you know what you are, most of the time, you don't know ANYONE else. Therefore, you can't really trust anyone else. Therefore, not every game is the same. Every time you play, it's a totally different experience. One game, your a Doctor trying to safe people from dying. The next game, your a Mafioso blasting the brains out of everyone.
You can even play with your friends in the same server, although sharing information outside the game completly ruins the fun. The rules of punishment aren't so bad. Basically, don't be a little crybaby when you die. Like I said, all it takes is one person to ruin it for 14 others.
With most of the positives aside, I really only have one issue with this game, and that's the fanbase. Not everyone is bad, but I've played over 500 games of this, and I've seen a lot. Spammers, people who can't spell proper engwish (:P), and, of course, gamethrowers. Though those are only a few reasons, it can really make you not want to play this game sometimes, which sucks.
In conclusion. I'd like to say it's worth the $5, and if your a broke college kid like me, you can even look it up online and play it for free, as long as you don't mind some ads every now and then. If you do buy it here, you have no ads, and the $5 is broken down into their in-game currency (1300 Town Points), which you can use to buy skins for you characters or house, get pets to follow you, or even scrolls, which increase the chance of you getting a certain role, and can be used until you get said role. So, you're not really losing $5 on this deal. Plus, NO ADS. C'mon, dudes.
Well, that about raps this up. If you ever get in a game and have issues, the creators of this game have a Facebook and Twitter account, to which you can message them. They usually respond, too.
Happy Hanging, boys and girls. ;D
P.S. This game is always updating, to which new features are always being added. For example, at the time of writing this, Vampire and Vampire Hunter are due to come out.
