First things first: Creation Club. It's awful, but it's not going away. You can ignore it.
Second: Main story line/vanilla launch. It's subpar, but there are WONDERFUL and free mods to change that with minimal "invasion" to the game.
With those out of the way, on to the review itself.
Is it like previous FO games? That depends on how you look at them. Compared to FO3 and NV, you have less dialogue options to make since they're now fully voiced, and the karma system is less diverse and invisible, but those are the only big pull-aways. I personally find the combat system fun and even improved. VATS feels more optional than "required to get out of a sticky situation," and is a slow-motion lag-free toggle rather than a bullet-time freeze-cam. There's no weapon/gear repair system, but that's for a reason. The materials you collect, including extra gear and weapons, is for a new system where you can build settlements (or you can just keep on making some caps at traders). This settlements building system is also optional. While it did feel overwhelming at first, within a short amount of time it sucked me right in. Even across multiple characters and saves I find myself rebuilding things differently than I had built them before because I found it could be fun!
Now, say you haven't played anything in this franchise before, so you're not here to compare. This is an open-world game, so you can stay on track or get as much off track as you want. Beat the game in a few hours or spend hundreds of hours on it, that's completely up to you. You can have traveling companions with you who are all enjoyable, and they're optional, so if you wanna fly solo, that's cool, too. There are four varying main endings to choose from, reflecting on who you interact with along the way. After you feel you've "beat" the game and want something more out of it, the modding community is vast and friendly, and has many surprising and fun things to offer.
Overall, I personally was pleasantly surprised with what I got, and I admit that I went in a harsh judge. Pick it up on sale if you're on the fence about it, and if you like it, buy the DLC. And remember: "Creation Club" is entirely optional, even if it is part of your download size. :-)

The first Sanctum was a first person tower defense game, with first person shooting aspects added to help give the players something to do during waves instead of simply watching your towers do all the work. It was a somewhat new concept in how well the tower balancing was executed while giving almost limitless designs and combinations. The drawbacks were simply trademarks of it being a new Indy title, a simple lack of content for missions and poor textures clearly showed the limitations of the budget and time they were working with. The first person shooting elements needed much more work to be entertaining in the long run however the game’s much heavier focus on the tower building distracted enough from this flaw that the game remained fresh with each new layout you created.
With the release of Sanctum 2, I was looking forwards to an updated version of the first giving more customization, towers, maps and maybe a few thrilling scripted events during the campaign missions. As I launched the game for the first time, ignoring the many technical errors of the initial release and completed the tutorial I started my first mission. As expected the graphics were considerably improved as they took on a more comic based look, similar to the art design of borderlands 2, although it has been done before it definitely gives sanctum 2 a much more unique appearance. The new addition of a progression system allows players to level up to unlock perks, new weapons and towers that rewards players who play on harder difficulty settings with a shorter grind.
Once I decided to get started building I suddenly realized I was only allowed to build seven blocks of wall, which meant I had to obey the map design when creating my maze for the enemies to pass through. This immediately felt very limiting, as one of the great aspects of the first is that it allowed you to create as many walls as you desired, and simply expecting you to create your own design within the map layout. With a limited number of wall blocks, the game forces you to take the basic route that the map often implies for you to take making it feel like I had little choice at all when it came to the design, just simply having to do what everyone else does within the same map. Speaking to my co-op partner on skype I found myself frequently saying, “I could do this amazing layout.. oh I don’t have enough blocks I guess this will have to do.” Constantly leaving missions with a feeling that it could have been better, and wasn’t complete, one of the worst feelings possible within a tower defense game. I decided to play a survival mission to get around this issue, where each wave I would be given more blocks. I would be able to finally create the layout I wanted, however I soon found myself no longer being given wall blocks after the first few waves, leaving me to keep the same incomplete design for the never ending survival mode.
After my second to third mission I started to notice in the end game statistics that I was dealing considerably more damage then all of my towers each game. With the new design you will notice a much stronger focus on the first person shooting then the tower defense, with many levels not even requiring the use of towers providing the use of the right equipment. The stronger focus on shooting would expect dramatic improvements to the design of shooting compared to the first game, however this is simply not the case and some elements of the weapons have been removed. You are no longer able to spend resources on your weapons to improve their performance as possible within the first game. A bigger selection of weapons allows you to focus on certain strengths or help cover flaws that your character choice may have. With the addition one weapon slot being fixed depending on your character choice, you only have access to change your secondary weapon. With such a strong focus on the shooting elements, it leave me to question why they forced this to be so limited during missions. It soon becomes a boring chore to shoot during waves, especially when weapons empty their clips so quickly and then demand a five second cooldown time to reload.
Within the game mechanics of Sanctum 2 the placement of a single block can often decide the success or failure of a wave on specific maps. Some maps are clearly much better designed then others, some of which only emphasize the first person aspects even more as you are not allowed to build along the enemies path at all. This just turns entire missions into a first person shooter with shooting that does little to excite. The new addition of boss waves simply takes all tower defense aspects and throws them out the window for the final wave. Bosses are able to destroy towers and wall bases, so on many maps a well designed layout will be instantly ruined as the boss targets a vital block and is soon followed by every other enemy in the wave.
Pros:
The character progression adds more value to replaying missions
Four player co-op
Colourful eye catching visuals
Cons:
A stronger focus on first person shooting, with little content within the shooting elements
Balancing issues, some characters and towers are simply sub-par to others
Boss waves completely ruin all aspects of tower defense
Limited resources often leave your base design incomplete before the end
Frame issues can sometimes cause huge frame rate drops
Sanctum 2′s attempts to become a stronger hybrid between tower defense and first person shooting by removing many tower elements of the first leaves Sanctum 2 with little identity. Becoming a jack of all trades, it simply becomes a case of “Anything I can do, you can do better.” If you want an action orientated defense game, Orcs Must Die 2 surpasses anything Sanctum 2 has to offer. For those who want a more traditional tower defense game then Defense Grid or Sanctum 1 have much more enjoyment to be had. The limitations of the new gameplay mechanics means nothing stands out, leaving a disappointing collection of “ok” and as such no reason to buy it over other titles available.

This game has some of the most satisfying feeling combat. The animations and sound effects are just right, making it feel extremely meaty. Very satisfying to land hits in this game. The Characters are all pretty different thanks to the v skill and v trigger system. Ken and Ryu are not just simple copy and paste jobs this time around.
Lack of single player content be damned - this is some of the most intense fun online experiences i've had in a while and i'm someone who is relatively new to fighting games (started with usf4 in august last year). The more lenient combo system really helps to get down the basics and bnb's (bread and butter) of a character really fast, while the game still offers plenty of depth with footsies and general mindgames.
One thing though - for players who are starting out with sf v as their first fighting game:
The tutorial will not really be helpful for you, at all. You will have to search online and in the steam guide section to get you started. You will also need a lot of frustration resistence, because being a beginner means you will get blown up a lot at the start. It will take a time for you to get a feel for the flow of the game and when to press buttons and when not etc. Don't get discouraged, it will get better if you put in the time :). Also, now that the game is new, it's probably one of the best times to enter because there are other new people as well. When i started out with us4 it was 8 years or something into it's lifecycle, so people with 1000hrs playtime were much more common then people with low playtime or even beginners who just started out, too.
Capcom is in it for the long run with this game. Content WILL come and this game will be played for years to come.
If you aren't flustered by the lack of sp content right now on launch and only care about the online (which admittedly does have some server probles at the moment,let's hope todays maintenance fixes some of them) this game is imo well worth the money - considering you'll get thousands of hours out of it. Or you could always join at a later date,when more content has been added. In the end it is up to what you value the most i guess, but this is a fine game at it's core that was a bit rushed but feels just so good to play.
I would definitely recommend this to every fan of fighting games and newcomers, because now is the best time to join and learn. Later on people will already be pretty good and have figured everything out, making it harder for you to start.
If you are looking for sparring partners you can also just add me - i'm always on the look out for more people to play lobbies with.

After having read lots of "professional" praise and lots of "player" hate, I decided, that the element the press praises is more important to me personally, than the element the players hate on. It's the fun of the “easy to learn, hard to master” gameplay versus the lack of basic and netherrealmy modes and bonus shenanigans. Considering the fact, that MKX online is a catastrophe, and its support has been ceased, SF5 online is a marvel, as it not only works like a charm, but it does so CROSSPLATFORM. Yes, if you wish, you can fight against people on the PS4, which widens the audience and potential competitors quite a lot.
The survivor mode is a string of single round fights and comes with added elements of strategy, due to several bonus options to choose from, if you can pay for them with accumulated points. The fact, that within this mode, the lifebar carries over makes this thing very spicy.  It took me a whole weekend to finish this thing on normal, and while you can noob yourself through the easy setting, you really have to learn to play to get to the finish on normal setting.
The added incentive to finish this mode are the bonus colors for your chosen character, as these are unlocked only via this mode - in SF4 you only had to play to unlock these colors, you did not have to achieve anything. Now my ego boosting and vanity is properly displayed, when I play online with a hard earned color palette, that not everyone has yet accessed.
What I also really love is the option to set up your readiness for online ranked an casual matches. If you (as I) don’t like to wait minutes and more for the system to team you up with an opponent, you simply configure your readiness for these matches and go play survivor mode, story mode or training mode, or whatever. Once someone knocks on your door or screen or whatever, your current mode will be interrupted and you will be sent to fight the opponent. Once this interruption match is over, you can choose to return to your previous mode and restart the last battle that got interrupted.
This has its downside, as you are not being asked, if you wish to accept that match… Once I finally achieved the Bison fight in survivor on normal (this was not easy for my noobiness), I had 3 online matches interrupt that one final fight, so I had to restart that FINAL battle four times!!… Twice I had the upper hand and once I was done for, so one interrupt actually saved my hide. The fourth time I got Bison to his knees. So if you are not ready for interruptions in your offline play, just set the options and it will not be a problem.
The other great thing is, you can set your preferences like stage, character, costume and color scheme. Once a match starts, all of this is already set and chosen… gone are the days, were you were ready to kick some, but had to wait for your opponent to choose a character and everything else (and some people tend to draaag this out)… you simply get down and dirty MUCH faster this time around!
Well, not really next gen, I can tell this much. It has great lightning and great designs which are very plastic, but I had wished for more sharpness. It is a small downside, but I think it is that one thing that holds its graphically back. Do not get me wrong, it is a gorgeous looking game, but the art style is a hit and miss, like with some Telltale games, where
for example looked amazing, yet
was less than impressive.
Now one thing is to be noted: Maybe the amount of bonus modes as seen in
is not really necessary, but a simple VERSUS mode with the option to fight against the CPU should be there. It is like the most basic (I dread to call this a feature, but ohh well…) It is like the most basic feature for any fighting game.  But I do not mourn the arcade mode, or tower mode, as the survivor mode is much more fun.
The same can be said about the story mode, which should rather be called the Prelude or Intro mode. In simple words, it is a laughably easy two to three fights interrupted with the usual capcomy cheesiness, but surprisingly ugly presented. You do not get cut scenes with character models, you do not get some great anime shorts… you really get ugly pictures with dialogue. There will be a free story mode some time down the line, but it is not why I PERSONALLY am here.
We do know, more content is to be made available over time, all of which will be purchasable with real world money and earned with ingame money. That is actually great, cause you can unlock what you REALLY want for free, if you do not intend to spent more on this game. Those with the cash will have it easier, but there is something special in earning something as opposed to buying something, so I am going to max out two or three favorite characters, while leaving the rest with the basic set ups.
The story mode is due later this year, so there is no need to get into that.
I personally hope for more stages, as the provided selection might not be bad, but I found only one or two stages to be to my liking. (In MKX all looked great, but not one really won my heart over).
As bonus fighters go, I am a one kind of gal type of guy… So I try to get good with a max of three characters per fighting game, so I doubt the additional fighters will make me get them… we will see… but I NEVER played the new characters in either MK9 or MKX. I just got them, so friends coming to play at my home could choose them.
In the long term a proper content stream might be keeping my attention for far longer, especially that it can be earned or purchased, but some of this stuff should be in game just to avoid the completely unnecessary launch “scandal”.
– if it's the fighting that counts...
If you want a great fighter that actually works in online play, is easy to learn, hard to master and DOES look gorgeous this is the game.  If you want offline play and proper next gen visuals, maybe try MKX first, and wait for SF5 to get more content and a better purchase price, because as far as PC fighting games go... this might not be the must have right now... but it will get there... trust me... IT WILL GET THERE!

Starbound: A game that lives to surprize you.
First and foremost this game created by a Legend Indy Company (Chucklefish) holds many great games as it is. That being said, Starbound is no exception. Ever since early beta release the game was developed and continuously growing.
After 200+ hours and MANY many restarts in this game with so many challenging aspects, the game only grows to be better with each patch. As of writing this, the Combat Patch just hit Unstable branch of the game and is shaping to be more amazing than the game already has.
So that leaves us with what the game is capable and what they hope to see:
In game:
Grow Crops, Fight enemies, Mine and Craft the world, Build colonies, Explore temples, dungeons, micro dungeons, and settlements all across an infinite galaxy.
Friends find something good? Join up in Multiplayer to show off the wonders of the universe.
Explore a Story driven quest system that even though has not been finish, still leads to a mystery of the universe and possibly a culture long gone.
Explore with one of six races in the game complete with pets and a combat system rapidly evolving.
Not In Game:
Combat not your thing? Don't worry the game is going to be viable for a builder just as much as some one Raging war across the stars. The choice is yours on how to proceed into the universe~!
Want more on this game daily? Then opt in for Nightly Builds and help the dev test content developed every day (WARNING these are not tested fully and are buggy. DO NOT expect Nightly to run with out bugs)
Not into the bug fest but could still want to see new content before it hits the Stable branch? Then opt in for the Unstable which is the final phase before live. This is where the end of bugs get hammered out but full patches are sent before the big release.
All in all this game is one for both combative adventure and those that just enjoy sitting back and creating a world to enjoy and live in.

Gave it a shot. Played Skirmish through wave 11. There's no variety whatsoever. The same 2 ships come at you by the dozen forever. Fly in, shoot, turn away, circle back. Hundreds of them forever, no change. There is exactly 1 boss type who does the same tactic, but with more health. And sometimes a destroyer that sits motionless and fires at you. New enemies spawn randomly with no discernable entrance, fly faster than you, and peck at you forever.
Which... ok. But meanwhile you have 3 weapons. 3 total, ever. Except that you don't, because you only have 1 weapon that just comes in three colors. Upgrades increase the numeric damage, but make absolutely zero difference to tactics, feel of the guns, or appearance. Even equipping more than 2 of the guns doesn't affect the effects. You never look like you're shooting more than 2. Never faster, never bigger, never spreading, never splashing. Just pewpewpew at level 1 or level 15.
Hey, there are multiple ships though, right? Wrong. You can start in a 2-gun ship. You can unlock the 4-gun and 1-turrent ship. Then you can unlock the 6-gun and 2-turret ship. But since the guns cap at looking like 2 guns, the only difference is damage numbers, never the feel of power. And of course turning slower so your only option is sitting there, pointing at ships that are flying toward you, and shooting back as they come to you because there are a dozen at a time and they are all faster than you are.
But wait! There are three factions of ships to choose from! Military, Outlaw, and Consortium! At least there's some choice there, right? Wrong again. They are reskinned, but statistically identical. So... just like the weapons are color choice but substantially the same, likewise the ships look unique but aren't.
So turn, wait, shoot, turn, wait, shoot, upgrade, turn, wait, shoot. Half an hour later, you'll realize you haven't had any fun and uninstall.
It looks nice. But awful controls, terrible lack of variety, monotonous AI tactics, and god just so boring.

Solar Struggle is one of those indie-games that tries to inject some fresh ideas into the space shooter genre, but ended up as WTH were they thinking?
Solar Struggle, or just SS from here on, is a 2D space shooter with a high-and-behind-chase view. Yes, you heard that right... It looks 3D, but the game's actually 2D only. There is no "up/down", only left and right. You can turn, and you can "side strafe" (i.e. fly forward and sideways).
What's more, the enemies move way too much for the weapons that you do have. You're almost always outnumbered and will score 10-30 kills per mission, but the enemies are twitchy and you'll need to hit them dozens of times to kill them. So you basically end up in the spray-and-pray mode as the "weak" guns you have is unlimited ammo and needs no cooldown. The big guns you have have limited shots, so you save those on really slow targets.
The controls barely make sense. Why have side strafe at all?
The cutscenes are just static text blocks, usually quite short.
Graphics are below average, sound is below average.
All in all, this game feels like someone's garage project that barely makes sense and is worth maybe $1.00 USD.

4 years ago I wrote a review for Solar Struggle: Survival, a $1 version of Solar Struggle for the Xbox Live Indie Games Service. I actually gave it a pretty high rating. Today I'm writing why this game isn't worth it. It's awfully strange, way back then I liked Solar Struggle, but now, I'm wondering if past me and current me played the same game.
Hmm. I suppose it's like this: When I originally reviewed Solar Struggle: Survival, I was comparing it to other games on the XBLIG service. XBLIG is home to many of the worst games of all time. Back then, if I happened upon something even half-way competent on that service, I'd probably say it was the greatest game since Super Mario Bros. 3. Solar Struggle is on Steam now, and...well....Steam is practically the inverse of XBLIG when it comes to quality gaming.
Or maybe I simply had no idea what I was thinking when I reviewed Solar Struggle: Survival.
In any case, SS is a space-shooter. There is a campaign that runs the usual gamut of missions. Destroy this, escort that, protect these, and so on. The most exciting aspects are the lousy translation, and the crazy twist ending where the main character dies...of boredom. Okay I might be wrong about that last part, but can you blame me? The missions are bland, shooting enemy ships down is more annoying than entertaining, and there's absolutely no challenge. Normally I wouldn't kick free achievements out of bed, but even I have standards.
The Survival portion aka "the part of SS I originally reviewed" doesn't hold up at all. On the outset, everything sounds alright. There are a variety of ships to unlock, upgradeable weapons, and standard wave-based action. However, there's no real challenge. Every time you sit down to play this mode you're going to do two things: 1) Hold the A button and Right Trigger down and 2) Aim at whatever happens to fly in your line of sight. My first Survival play lasted over an hour and a half. Staying awake is the real struggle here. The second time around I chose a better ship, and dropped my time by about 30 minutes.
It isn't until around wave 20 that dying becomes a possibility. The enemies start drowning your ship in bullets, shield upgrades (which also act as repairs) become too costly, and your thrusters no longer function, because all your energy is spent on weapons. The problem is, this doesn't happen until an hour or so of straight play. I didn't get this far through some winning strategy and tons of practice. I held down a couple buttons and pointed my ship towards anything explosive. It's a wonder that I never caught this in my original review. Solar Struggle is shallow and dull, but it also expects players to drag more than 5 minutes of compelling entertainment out of it.
The worst part? There STILL isn't an option to turn off rumble.
Honestly, I'm disappointed in myself, disappointed in the fact that I recommended this game in the first place.

So, I've been asked many times to write a review for Planetary Annihilation.
Be sure to check out
Should you have any feedback, comments, questions or suggestions, post them below and I'll try to answer them to the best of my ability!
It's a massive scale RTS game where you can command 1000s of units across a whole solar system with a variety of strategies open to you. A robust planet(map) generation system allows essentially unlimited map variation at your fingertips. Indeed there are a number of planet 'biomes' creating different strategic options themselves from desert and ice and oceanic biomes to earth, moon and lava and even the resource rich gas giants! Of course, as a new player you will need to allow some time to get used to the idea of spherical maps in an RTS game and how to navigate and orientate yourself. There are features to help with this; togglable Pole-Lock ensures that the planet's orientation remains constant. Gone are the days of turtling into a corner; you now have a corner of 360 degrees of approach.
In game, there are many modalities of combat; land (vehicles and bots), sea, air and even an orbital layer. Fancy building a base on that moon over there - go and do it, launch an attack from it at a beachhead you have established on a different planet - do it. It's all up to what you decide to do in any given game. There are many different mechanics in the game as well like Unit cannons, periodically available asteroids and planet destruction methods. Such include planetary engines, super-lasers and now the Ragnarok Titan. Of course there is the nuclear option, should you decide to invest the resources.
The game is also easily moddable with a thriving mod scene established since alpha. Visit the Uber forums to download PAMM (PA Mod Manager) to have instant access to UI and server mods created by the community as well as map packs from a variety of creators.
The unit pool has been expanded greatly with TITANS and is definitely worth the upgrade for existing PA owners and easily worth the purchase price for prospectives.  TITANS also brings improvements to terrain with a much better scaled than 'classic' PA, as well as a new 'Bounty mode' where you get economic bonuses depending on how many people you knocked out. The expansion also brings polish to the game, along with AI and Galactic War improvements. Let's not forget the host of new units, 21 to be precise as well as 5 badass titans
. This expansion also sees the return of unit wreckage, which players can reclaim for resources, as well as 'hover' units enabling new strategies to circumvent water and lava obstacles.
I will admit that PA, prior to TITANS was at a stage where, I believe, it was beginning to stagnate. Since release a number of big features were added that spurred discussion, introduced new possibilities and fun mechanics (Super-laser, Unit Cannons, Asteroids and full planet smashing) though aside from that PAs updates consisted mainly of general polish, bug-fixing, AI and pathing improvements etc. While this is not to say that these improvements haven't had a cumulative impact over time, I will say that the base game remained largely unchanged and unit balance was in a good place.
Then BANG, TITANS dropped 'outta nowhere'. If anything it shows that PA can definitely still be built on and drastically improved.
I did say I'd be balanced and here are the drawbacks of PA at the time of writing this review;
~The player-base is relatively small so thelikelihood is that in modes like 'Ranked 1v1' you will likely be waiting a long time for a game, and over time find that you recognise a lot of faces and may often be matched poorly due to the lack of players on that mode.
~Pathfinding still leaves much to be desired. In combination with a few annoyances involving the new terrain, such as units on low ground being able to shoot up, but units on high ground not being able to shoot down or over the edge of ramps, the result can be frustration.
~There are still a number of bugs (though being worked on, improved and fixed all the time) which may serve to lessen your play experience, such as lobby bugs, disconnects, crashes and more. All I can do here is urge patience and to help the devs fix these by reporting issues on their forums and bug tracking pages.
~With the host of new units, some may argue that there are a few balance issues - this is likely the case though by and large balance is in a good place at the moment where each unit, with a couple of exceptions, serve a purpose.
~There is still discussion on-going in the forums as to whether or not entire planet smashing (regardless of planetoid size - i.e. no leaving of craters / partial destruction of larger planet) is a good gameplay mechanic. The reason this was implemented was due to technical difficulties with pathfinding for craters. I'm sure given time, effort and money this issue may be resolved, but for the time being it is good that we have something that works, though may or may not be what would be 'best'. Again, this is debatable.
To comment on the general hate of Uber and PA; I believe TITANS shows irrefutably that Uber do not abandon their games, it shows that they are dedicated to pleasing fans, and reinforces that they are great people who love fun. For those hating PA because it was $90 at alpha, don't cut off your nose to spite your face! The package is worth the asking price easily.
I hope this has at least made you a little more aware of what a hidden gem this game is, even if it is still largely a diamond in the rough... who knows... maybe there's even more updates Uber have up their sleeves?

Alright, so if you've read the other comments about this game, you're going to notice one glaring fault that predominates most of the negative comments:  The mods are Nazis and will mute or ban your account at the slightest provocation, almost seeming to exist solely to torment you and make your life a living hell.
In almost 30 hours of gameplay, I have not seen this happen once.
I have seen people have their messages removed by a moderator.  These people broke the chat rules by posting profanity in EN chat or talking about other games, both explicitly big no-nos.  They asked for it.  What the moderators DIDN'T do is mute them or ban their accounts, instead erasing only the offending messages and warning the violator that what they posted isn't acceptable.
In other words, they did their jobs.
I have also seen these same moderators answering questions from newer players, farming items and offering to sell them at reasonable prices to new players to help them get their feet on the ground, offering to forge beginner equipment for people (sometimes free of charge), and otherwise being very helpful people.  The same can be said for most of the other players.  Overall, if you ask a question, you'll get a reasonable response, even if that response is to check the wiki (why wouldn't you?  It's a great source of information!)  Sometimes, the best way to respond to a question is to refer people to an outside source of information that answers that question, as well as the other couple of dozen frequently asked questions people might have about the game.  Answering questions one at a time doesn't teach people how to help themselves, it just teaches them to rely on other people, right?
Now, the downside...it's grindy.  Very grindy.  Runescape-level grindy.  If you like that, you're in for some fun.  If you don't like it, you're going to hate this game.  I personally don't mind it, it gives me something to do to pass the time, and there's a sense of accomplishment in finishing a goal in the game that's very satisfying.
My other complaint is the captcha system.  Now, I fully understand the purpose of the system.  It's designed to keep people from botting the game, requiring human interaction at random intervals, and I do appreciate the fact that the game actually rewards you for being there to answer the captcha in the form of free experience that you can assign to a skill of your choice (giving you an alternate way to get your first few dozen or so levels on a skill that's otherwise a severe pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to grind), but it feels like they're almost too frequent at times.  I've had a couple of occasions where I've been mining away, working on cooking dinner, I answer a captcha and think "okay I'm good for a while", get up for 5-10 minutes to go cook food, and come back to an angry message saying I missed a captcha and I'm at -1 reward points and if I hit -5 I'm effectively banned for botting (they call it jail, and admins/moderators can let you out of it, but I wouldn't imagine they'd tend to do that often.  If you miss that many captchas, you're doing something you shouldn't be).  It's a minor complaint, though.
Overall, the game so far has been satisfying.  It's free to play, that's always a bonus.  The community IS helpful, contrary to popular representation.  The moderators aren't sadistic, power-hungry maniacs looking to ruin the experience of newer players and only playing to their preferred cliques.  And the best part is, there's ways to earn MOS (that's the RL-purchasable currency that lets you buy premium items and/or account status) ingame, so you can earn some of those "pay-to-win" perks without even paying for them.  Granted, it'll take forever and a day, but hey, it's there, right?
Don't play into the hype that some of the negative comments are trying to feed you.  Those people either did something to deserve what they got, or they're playing a much different game than I have been.

What may be considered the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of Planetside 2 and Bloons Tower Defense, Sanctum 2 provides a great deal of fun for how much it costs (assuming you got it in a Humble Bundle, or on a Steam Sale).
While the campaign holds itself up in single player mode, it really shines in multiplayer, getting complete strangers to work together as a more tight-knit team than even Team Fortress 2, which has "team" in the title, even. After a couple matches with a random individual, it's more than likely that they'd share their resources with you if you ask them.
The only major complaint I have is that the difficulty ramps up rather quickly, making some levels very difficult if you're doing them by yourself, or with a team with poor planning. One level in particular I did probably half a dozen times before moving on to multiplayer, where the team I was with got it on the first try. It really depends on who you're with.
In all, I'd say the game is about an 8.5/10. It has its flaws, but plays and runs well while looking damn fine at the same time.

Terraria is very much a game of progression, a game where that is the main focus. That doesn't mean Terraria is bad and in fact I enjoy Terraria quite a lot, but Starbound tries to do something completely different with the genre. Starbound tries to encourage exploration, completetion, and the beauty of seeing the universe. While both game try to be light-hearted, Starbound separates itself from that kidding mood with a gaxaly rife with conspirators, and it is very much a game where you decide what to get out of it, which to me is the point of video games over other mediums. Atleast, I hope Starbound grows into that, for right now Starbound is a game of exploration appealing almost solely into that kind of experiance and forcing it into a different mold is incrediably hard.

Pros: Incredibly unique concept and done near-perfect, wide range of customizable features, refreshingly new style of game, overall visual quality
Cons: Lack of diversity for enemies, tower building only from first person
When I first heard about Sanctum and what the gameplay is like my initial reaction was “Yes! Yes! Yes!”, never did play Sanctum however as Sanctum 2 was just being released and whatever people may say about the first I have to say that the 2nd does not disappoint. Sanctum 2 is a unique and refreshingly new concept of mixing the tower defense / tower grid concept with FPS. It’s a bit of RTS as well in that you place your towers with the tower grid and then you play a unit in your own FPS and become a soldier on the ground during the battle.
There are a few main classes that have set perks and primary weapons, then a list of universal secondary weapons, towers, and passive perks. For sure there are lots of options with towers and perks to adapt to a very wide variety of play-styles. And the multiplayer coop allows for interesting blends of play-styles or an all-out stacking of a set style with synchronizing to get the most out of the various perks.
Overall it’s a brilliant game, and I for sure recommend it. I think the build phase being only in first person is a mistake however, would have liked the choice to view the grid and place turrets from a bird’s eye of the entire grid instead of having to constantly refer to the mini-map to make sure I’m placing things in the correct square. Also the enemy units are immediately redundant so while there is a huge range of variety on the player side with perks and weapons there is just the same few enemy units (the DLCs seem to address this – as well as add
weapons and perks!). No difficulty option but the game has five “Feats of Strength” options to make it both harder and give greater rewards, similar to Bastion’s “Idols”.
All in all the wide range of turret types, weapons, and perks are all blended and balanced nicely to make a very nice RTS / FPS blend that – and I cannot state this enough – was soooo refreshing to play. Indie games like this or something like Frozen Synapse that push the boundaries of the gaming development “norm” will forever be welcome in my gaming libraries, they are fantastic. The RTS to place the walls to funnel enemies into pinch points and U-turns while placing the proper turrets to take advantage of the situation then starting the wave and going into the battle yourself in an FPS with your own highly customized class unit is something that will not get old quickly for me.

The vacuum left by the SimCity series after 4 was a perfect opportunity for another developer to swoop in and claim the city-building throne. After all, as venerable as it was, SimCity never actually ventured into full 3D, and the rare competitors that did could never match the quality of the core simulation. Eventually the folks behind Cities XL stepped up to the plate, and while it ticks all the right boxes for a fine city builder, it also leaves a lot to be desired.
XL's pitch was that you could finally build the modern city of your dreams, as huge and sprawling as you want. To that end you lay roads, zone for residences and businesses, provide utilities and services, and manage the finances of your burgeoning burg, just as you would in a traditional SimCity. All of this is rendered in full 3D, with skyscrapers rising from the hills and valleys of your map, all while little cars and even people traverse your network of streets. From that perspective, it's pretty much what anyone wanted from a SimCity 5.
But Cities XL is more than just a copy of the old formula. The familiar residential, commercial, and industrial zones are split into types that demand specific resources of each other. Homes can be zoned for unskilled workers, skilled workers, executives, and "elites", whatever that means. Industries can be anything from farms to factories, tech centers to office complexes. Different industries require different proportions of worker classes, and then produce goods for your shops and trade outside the city. Some resources are limited by the map, such as having specific agricultural zones for farms or fields for oil. Not every map has every resource, either, so use of the trading system becomes necessary as you expand.
New buildings such as larger services and higher-density zones unlock at certain population levels. In a strange twist this happens at specific "ticks" that actually make XL play more like a turn-based builder than a real-time one. You can set the amount of time between each tick, but until it rolls over nothing will really change in the city. Income, trades, unlocks, and changes to building status are all held until the next tick. Honestly I found speeding up the ticks more useful than playing slow because it keeps the money rolling in at the pace you need to expand.
And boy howdy, will you be expanding. The specific balances of workers against workplaces is so fragile that you'll constantly be zoning new houses and factories to keep up with the alerts pouring in. This isn't the lazy suggestion of SimCity's RCI meter, this is the constant threat of businesses going bankrupt and citizens streaming out of your city. The way Cities XL is designed, your city will never be at peace or even equilibrium. You'll always be lacking something, and forever be pestered to fix it.
That brings me to my chief complaint about the game, the feel of it. Stripping away the complexity of the zoning and additional systems, you could almost mistake XL for a SimCity if not for the incredibly cheap feel of it. Every single menu is a simple blue gradient with text misaligned on it, like a developer's first mock-up of a UI. The building menus have teeny-tiny tooltips and titles, leaving you to rely on the blurry icons to figure out what you're building. You have several zoning tools at your disposal but they all map out fields of square zones mashed against each other at awkward angles or in boring grids. Sure, you can make curved, complex roads, but why bother if you're just going to be snapping cubes against them?
In the end, the shoddy presentation and the unnecessary complexity doom Cities XL to languish behind even the earliest SimCities. The graphics can't even save it, cursed with washed-out colors and bland models for even the largest skyscrapers. You can make enormous, sprawling cities but they're just going to be grids (or knots) of ugly, samey buildings, with little to even differentiate offices from condos. And honestly, if you can't build a city you can admire, there's just no point to building.

From the screenshots, I was expecting some nice arcadey space-shooter goodness. My hope was basically for a Star Fox knockoff with better graphics.
Unfortunately, what I got was a janky, poorly voice acted mess that runs far worse than a game of this grapical fidelity should.
The entire game is played on a flat plane. There is no 3-d movement or action. Ships turn very quickly. So quickly it's difficult to do fine maneuvers. Generally, this means that a dogfight consists of either a series of head-on passess, or flying behind a wiggling enemy fighter. It's incredibly hard to see where your shots are going. There's no sort of lead indicator, and your "Crosshairs" are basically useless. Your bullets are your best indicator, and even then, it's mostly "This is the general flightpath of the enemy ship, maybe he'll run into enough of them to die." I found one of the most effictive dogfighting techniques to be to sit still, and just point your gun at the incoming enemy fighters, as that's the only time they really flight striaght.
The campaign missions are frequently interrupted with poorly written cutscenes which basically consist of your ship hovering near other guy's ship. Then you skip them, and you're thrown against a timed wave of infinite enemy fighters. The voice acting comes in here, as the only things more repetitive than the sound of your guns constantly firing (there's barely any reason not to), and the music, are the death cries of enemy pilots. The frequent "Arghs!" and "Oh No!"s are delivered with the drama and gravitas of realizing you put slightly too much creamer in your coffee.
I was hoping the arrival of capital ships on the playing field would make things more interesting. Unfortunately, rather than doing things like take out individual guns, or subsystems like engines, they're just another life & shield bar. Actually, the ones I fought were easier than the fighters, because they're so much larger and easier to hit.
Finally, the options menus are limited. If you're in a mission they're limited to "Quit" or "Don't quit". Anything you change results in the game restarting. You can use a controller, but you get even less fine control. Sometimes the turn keys just plain didn't work, or your acceleration will get stuck on.
I didn't have high hopes for this game, yet it still managed to dash them. For that, bravo.

The best way to describe Sleeping Dogs is "A somewhat oblivious American team writes a story about cops in Hong Kong." It's exactly what you'd expect: Wei Shen is trying to infiltrate the Triads using his blank personality and his mastery of kung fu.
The fighting system is quite simple, but also quite complex. You'll learn enough to get yourself through the game, but mastery will make it so much better. You'd better master it too, because the game forces you to use your fists - you don't get your first weapon until about halfway through the main storyline. You'd think they are limiting that part of the game, but once you start obtaining weapons, there's a very good balance of weapons vs fisticuffs.
The story itself is pretty good, but nothing great. It has it's good moments, bad moments, and one very disgusting moment that can really take you off guard. Overall it is a very fun thing to play though and experience. There's also some DLC storymodes that you can play, but they seem to be on par with the main story: good, but not great.
With the exception of the Zodiac Tournament DLC, there isn't much to write home about. I'd avoid buying any DLC until you play the game at least once fully through, or else you may get some weapons or upgrades much earlier than you normally should.
Sleeping Dogs doesn't take itself really seriously, and it's an enjoyable midpoint between GTA and Saint's Row. It knows when to go easy on you, or when to throw everything it's got. It knows when to throw the best kung-fu sections at you, while also keeping the shooting alive and well. Missions are quite varied, and it is overall a very well polished game to play.

For those that have played Tales of Zestiria and are wondering how Berseria compares, the short answer is that it is improved and better in most ways.
Most importantly the story and characters are much more interesting and engaging this time around, something that I felt was Zestiria's weakest aspect.  The complex and aggrevating equipment customization system of Zestiria has been replaced with something much more managable and easier to understand.  There are other differences of course, but these two changes are the most important IMO.
The only thing that Berseria does worse is the battle camera.  It no longer stays behind the character that you are controlling and makes sure that the enemy that you are targeting is in view.  Instead, you have to manually snap the camera behind your character with a button press, which is just...odd.
I was planning to write a full review similar to my Zestiria review when the game was still fresh on my mind but never got around to it.  So if anyone has any questions or would like more information feel free to leave a comment.

The game can be too easy (even at top difficulty), apart from the rare times where the mob is unusually unbeatable because they can one shot you and your teammates in a blink of an eye, forcing you to go into the option screen at various times.
It's worth a purchase becoming the anti-hero in a Tales game and it was very refreshing, but I highly doubt it will emotionally engage or excite you anywhere close to Persona 5 or the Legend of Heroes Trails in the Sky series. The latter had stories and characters that spoke for itself outside of the general gameplay that seperate an ok JRPG (like this game) to a great JRPG (Persona 5).
It seems like BANDAI refuse to move forward and bring to the table something truly new to the series, especially in the form of game mechanics and general plot that are still the same since the series existed. I've only ever played since Vesperia but it feels to me they are still stuck in the past and have fallen into the habit of not taking any risks and then produce absolutely nothing in the form of innovation, just the same 'old' same 'old'.
There are only so many coats of paint you can put on an old buidling until you have to rennovate the whole building, foundations included and for me the Tales Series is heading in that direction, maybe not now, but in 5+ years they will be.

I really like the approach of making the user essentially a character in the story. It's a unique perspective for the game to take. The story is solid, the characters are interesting, and I like what they are doing here conceptually.
In practice, it doesn't make for a great game. It wants you to read through exhaustive articles to pick up little bits of information. It wants you to replay the same game multiple times in order to pick up on a reasonable chunk of the story and content. It can be confusing to navigate the ship when they frantically yell at you to go to some area with an unclear location. Other than to appear Mass Effect-like, I don't know why they chose to utilize a first person engine. The combat and inventory are exceedingly clunky. Going with an RPG style or even menu based system would probably fit the overall game better.
It's interesting and I'm glad that I played it, but I wouldn't recommend it to others. Without a smoother gameplay experience, I'm not eager to play the sequel to continue the story when it comes out.

Excellent concept and plot. Voice acting and music is top notch, especially for an indie game. That said, I couldn't help but feel as if the game were just a demo of something bigger. After the first real combat situation I picked up a bunch of extra hardpoint modules for my suit and... you never use them again. I also felt that the ending sequences felt a bit "phoned in".
I think the key positive in this game is that there are a TON of threads you can explore with each situation (and even sub-situations inside those situations!). Many RPG/FPS/Adventure hybrids give you two or three choices in a few situations in the game. The lazier ones just give you 3 choises at the end and call it a day. Consortium has TONS of choices presented at almost every turn. I have to respect the amount of design that had to go into that.
Obviously it was meant to have a sequel and hopefully the sequel will take what made Consortium great and expand upon it much more. I hate to be one of the people complaining that it didn't have enough action in it and ordinarily that wouldn't matter in an adventure game... but the action they did have was GOOD! So they should definitely capitalise on it in the future.

The best way to describe Sleeping Dogs is "A somewhat oblivious American team writes a story about cops in Hong Kong." It's exactly what you'd expect: Wei Shen is trying to infiltrate the Triads using his blank personality and his mastery of kung fu.
The fighting system is quite simple, but also quite complex. You'll learn enough to get yourself through the game, but mastery will make it so much better. You'd better master it too, because the game forces you to use your fists - you don't get your first weapon until about halfway through the main storyline. You'd think they are limiting that part of the game, but once you start obtaining weapons, there's a very good balance of weapons vs fisticuffs.
The story itself is pretty good, but nothing great. It has it's good moments, bad moments, and one very disgusting moment that can really take you off guard. Overall it is a very fun thing to play though and experience. There's also some DLC storymodes that you can play, but they seem to be on par with the main story: good, but not great.
With the exception of the Zodiac Tournament DLC, there isn't much to write home about. I'd avoid buying any DLC until you play the game at least once fully through, or else you may get some weapons or upgrades much earlier than you normally should.
Sleeping Dogs doesn't take itself really seriously, and it's an enjoyable midpoint between GTA and Saint's Row. It knows when to go easy on you, or when to throw everything it's got. It knows when to throw the best kung-fu sections at you, while also keeping the shooting alive and well. Missions are quite varied, and it is overall a very well polished game to play.

This game is the perfect example of getting out of something exactly what you put into it. You can cruise through and miss most of it, or you can dive face first in, and be absorbed for a long time.
If you can invest in the characters and the story, it will pay off in dividends. Each character is lovingly written, with strong arcs and believable interactions. You'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll get angry with your faavorites, and sympathize with the worst. You'll be forced to make deisions you question, and then question it all over again before the end. You'll wonder not only if you CAN win, but whether or not you SHOULD win.
If you challenge yourself to play through at frustrating difficulty, you will get your time out of it. Some of these reviews say they finished in 30 hours or so, but I've been at this for 200+ hours and only recently finished my first run, including post-game content. I play on the highest difficulty, and I am trying for all trophies, so there's that too. I also used very little internet to find out how to get them, so I was also using trial and error.
If you take the time to delve into the combat system, you'll find the perfect style for you. Each character is unique in their style, specializing in different aspects, and while I didn't enjoy all of them, I'm sure there are people who would. Combat is fast and visceral, and can have as much depth as you want it. I personally found combos I liked and strung them together, but there is optimization in chaining moves, and the Break Souls add more ways to have fun. All that being said, combat can be really frustrating as well. If you've played Tales Of games before, you'll probably be familiar with the SP system, which takes kind of a back seat here, and kind of interferes with the new style they've gone with. It can be really disheartening when, in mid battle, you find yourself being constantly interrupted,  inflicted with status effects, and reduced to only being able to use one move at a time. However, as I've said before, if you invest time into your equipment, you'll find it easier and easier to overcome a lot of these problems.
If you can become interested in the world, the depth will amaze you. I played a bit of Zestiria before this, which bored me to the point of quitting. This is the same world, several thousand years before, and the writers do a much better job of making you care about the different races, and appreciating just how horribly people treat each other in it, and above it, to the point where you'll want to do something about it.
If you play games for the story, buy it. If you play games for the combat, buy it, but be prepared to study.

This is the first Tales game I have played fully, and after seeing Zesteria I was originally offput by the franchise, opting to try this game out on sale. I'm glad I did because this game is a hell of a step up from Zesteria all round.
The combat is a bit unusual to me as it uses a system generally used by turn based games (despite being real time combat) in the way that you put abilities (or artes as they call them in Berseria) into combo slots and branch between slotted attacks. The combat is good but a little hard to get used to if you haven't played this kind of game before. By the end of the game I was still figuring out some of the battle controls, either because they were never explained or because I somehow skipped past there explanation.
The allied AI is functional in battle but can do some questionable things like wasting there ultimate artes on enemies that are a single generic attack away from dying. Enemies tend to be all over the place for difficulty, some generic enemies can take massive amounts of damage whereas some bosses can be combo'd start to finish without them ever getting an attack in.
There is a huge amount of customisation from how your allies fight in battle, to your own combos setup, to your equipment (which all have there own unique models) and "fashion" (basically outfits and attachments).

The main draw of this game is the story, while it can be boiled down to a generic revenge story, it's the character interactions and events that happen in between the story that makes it stand out. It's really hard to say much about it without putting in spoilers.
I've had a lot of fun with this game even though the end was a bit of a grind for me. New game plus is a little unusual in how you select what you get to carry over, but I don't really see myself playing the game many times over, since I played for the story. It's a solid JRPG and worth your time.

What's up everyone? Giving the current situation of Street Fighter V I feel obligated to speak up, so here it is:
Firstly, I apologize for the length of this, however, I do want to be thorough.
Is this a good game? Is my sweaty money worth it?
Well, the answer is simple, and it is a big fat NO. Stick around and I'll tell you exactly why.
Although I choose to believe that CAPCOM did not want to trick people into buying the game, they were also not very forthcoming with the release state of the game. I for one, pre-ordered it and have been following the betas and every piece of information they've put out since then, so yeah, I knew what I was getting into. In conclusion, no, this game is not worth your money in its current state if you are expecting the amount of content you encounter in other fighting games, or even, some of the basic features rooted in the genre such as the Arcade Mode.
On the other hand, if you ask me 'Is this a good fighting game?', then I strongly believe that the answer is suddenly not so simple. Since CAPCOM is selling a "PLATFORM", which means, all future updates, DLC's, and characters for free (characters being unlocked with in game currency), I have to say that this IS a good purchase despite all of its flaw and rocky launch. Don't get me wrong, I do not think it's excusable to have the launch that it did, but I reckon the game redeems itself with rock solid fighting game mechanics and, as oppose to its competitors, AMAZING ONLINE CONNECTION. In other words, never has it been a better time to play Street Fighter. What's more, this IS the time for people who want to become good at the game to start playing. If that's not your case, then by all means, sit and wait until July when the game will receive a massive update according to CAPCOM, and will finally reach a much more attractive and rich state as far as content is concerned.

This game certainly surprised me. It is very short but has a high replay value. It's a bit of a mix of Sci-Fi RPG à la Deus Ex and Mystery Crime Adventure. Therefore, your (dialogue) choices matter and there are many of them. This allows you to replay the game several times and see many different outcomes.
The setup is that in the game, you are playing an Augmented Reality game in which you take control of a real person in a parallel Earth universe in the year 2042 (iirc). You take control of this person, who is a "Bishop" on a (military?) aircraft, where the ranks are named after chess figures (Pawns, Rook, Knights, Bishop etc.). While you are controlling him, you do not know his name, his past, his background, nothing... which results in interesting dialogues where you try to converse with people who know more about you than you do.
All of the game plays on this aircraft. You need to know that they have planned this game as a trilogy and this is the introduction. It took me around 4 hours to play through and the ending is a real cliffhanger. Howevery, the second game, called Consortium: The Tower Prophecy, will be out soon and you are able to take your save game (= all your decisions) with you into the new game. (like in Mass Effect)
The graphics are a bit dated (the new game will be on UE4 and the trailers suggest that it looks way better than this one) but that did not lessen my enjoyment of this game. It was full of surprises, there was a lot of background info to find out (and to read, yes, read! If you don't like reading in videogames, this is maybe not ideal for you... the dialogues are voiced), the story was incredibly well written, the choices really mattered (and I'm very anxious to find out what their influence will be in the future Consortium games) and it motivated me enough to play through in one swift session - which is rare nowadays for me.
While I really enjoyed Consortium, it may be off-putting to people who expect an action FPS (there aren't many shooting sequences and they are very short, it's more an adventure than a FPS), who do not like to "play detective" and find out what's going on on their own or to people who expect a huge skilltree and character modifications (there are none, except the items you equip). Consortium is an adventure game first and foremost, with RPG-elements in it.
If you like adventures, mysteries, solving crimes, exploring every crook and nanny, meaningful dialogue choices and a futuristic setting, this game is for you and I recommend it highly. I'm already looking forward to the next episode of this intruiging story.

I don't usually do a pro/con list for my reviews, but in this case, I feel like whether or not you should by Cities XL should be dependent on how you feel about four key points.
Good:
+Great graphics (for a city-builder)
+You can make your city HUUUUGE. Like, your metropolis actually looks like a metropolis. I'm not kidding when I say that your city can reach a NYC level of scale (though not population-wise, since it does that thing that all city-builders do where it makes population way lower than it seems your city should be able to accomadate).
Bad:
-I'm only exagerrating a little bit when I say that it has the depth of a mobile city-builder. There's virtually no challenge from the get-go and I was almost expecting to have to tap buildings for coins.
-When your city gets to a certain size, the game will start to struggle with processing everything and you'll get lag. Personally, the lag I dealt with was nothing too bad, but I didn't grow my city as much as other people did before I got bored and stopped playing; I heard many people say that the lag gets unbearable at a certain point.
Those are the four main points, the things that'll really make you either like or dislike it. I know you see the red thumbs down, but I'm not not recommending it, per se. If you think the pros outweigh the cons, then you should totally buy it. I wouldn't have recommended this game to my past self however, because this game is a little too shallow for my taste.

Consortium is a very different beast to review.
The game is short, and as other have said, it's a proof of concept game. Mystery is abound, secrets and a lot of lore.
The game is simple, you are allowed to try out a machine that not only let's you go to the near future, but take the mind of someone there. So who is the subject of this new futristic mind control, a peace keeper enforcer with armor and weapons costing billions of dollars. Let that sink in.
Of course, being stuck in that role, you have not damn clue what is going on. So you right there, you can replay the game if you want. What's even more intresting is that you have the option to say nothing, at all. So points right there for true neutrals out there.
The major plot is simple, there is a murder and a traitor onboard, as well as mercs who are out to destroy the plane. All while you hear voices in your head, an archive lore that you can read or not.
Gameplay:
Gameplay is solid but shallow. The combat works, but you barely use it, unless you test the simulation mode out. The interactive interface is good, but with everything glitching on purpose, you are force to pull yourself out again and again as you can't handle everything.
Character interaction is based on points. Say things the right way and you get favor,♥♥♥♥♥♥them off vice versa. This doesn't mean much unless you are after achivements or just want to. Either way, you do get options where you can do peaceful alternatives, or blow stuff up.  Overall my first run was 'play by the rules' cop, and then I went renegade on my next.
Story:
By far, the major pushing force. It's a classic murder mystery, just in the future. The game really wants to make you think one guy is the killer. All I will say is think with your head, use proper deduction, and keep trying.
The story features some solid lore on a master AI, political issues, and even hints of a great war and cultist inthe background. I am kind of angry that it was so short, because I am dying for more.
Music:
Music flowed well. Proper timing and good score made sure that I can listen to this even after the game is over. I enjoyed it and really did put some epic feelings in what you do.
Overall: Should you play CONSORTIUM?
If you like a good murder mystery, dialogue, decent voice acting and story that is also complimented by a great score. Then YES.
If you feel you can't handle this game being too short and with a big fat " To be continued." Then I would advise to move on.

It's...not bad.  This game is, for the most part, the same as Sanctum, but with a few differences in how enemies move and the maze you send them through is constructed.  You can now choose more characters, which each specialize with a different type of weaponry to destroy the aliens with.
Alright, so let's get down to the nitty-gritty.  Sanctum 2, like its predecessor, is an FPS-TD, which stands for First Person Shooter-Tower Defense.  Yes, it is *both* at once.  You construct your maze for the ugly aliens to get through and then, once it's built and they start marching in, you pull out your gun and start pulverizing them yourself as well!  It's a cool concept that I haven't seen before (and frankly, hadn't even thought of until the original Sanctum came around).
The graphics are neatly and nicely done, the gameplay itself is cool, and this one even has a slight story element to it as well (as opposed to its predecessor, which was purely maps and killing aliens).  But the problem with it is that it is almost identical...to the point where I kind of wish this game was just an update to the original and not another $15 to purchase (rest assured that I took advantage of sales, and you should too).
If you've never played a Sanctum, get this one.  You'll have more fun than you would purchasing the original for sure.  But if you have Sanctum, I hesitate to tell you to buy it unless the price gets cut drastically.

Еще со времен античности люди начали задумываться о том, что их окружает. Бессознательно, хотели они того или нет, они стали стремиться к познанию мира вокруг себя. Сейчас принято разделять такие термины, как "любопытство" и "познание", потому как последнее в наше время вовсе не бессознательно. Ученые всего мира объединены высшей идеей: сделать мир лучше. Ради этой идеи они приносят жертвы, чаще всего эта жертва их собственная жизнь или жизнь их близких в широком и узком значениях. Но нужно ясно понимать, что в бесконечном стремлении к познанию, жертвой может стать и наша с вами планета, а вместе с ней и мы.
Итак, игра представляет собой шутер от первого лица с элементами научной фантастики. Играем мы за Гордона Фримена, доктора философии в области теоретической физики, который работает в научно-исследовательском комплексе "Черная Меза". В лаборатории, в которой проводит свои дни молодой ученый, работают с аномальными материалами. И вот в один из таких обычных рабочих дней и начинается эта игра.
Эта игра не сможет впечатлить вас графикой, искусственным интеллектом персонажей и противников, наличием скриптованных сцен, даже если вы неискушенный геймер. Но тем не менее, эта игра шедевральна. Но почему, скажете вы? Потому что в этой игре вы не будете бежать и раскидывать десятки монстров направо и налево из своего многоствольного пулемета. Потому что в этой игре есть над чем подумать. Потому что в этой игре вы будете бегать туда-сюда с мыслью "Черт, почему кнопка на этой панели неактивна?". Потому что основное оружие - монтировка. Потому что в этой игре есть отличный сюжет. И если вас не пугают названия вроде "антимасс-спектрометр" или "каскадный резонанс" и вы жаждете поиграть в игру с замечательной музыкой, сюжетом и геймплеем, то я настоятельно рекомендую не проходить мимо этой игры, даже не смотря на дату ее выхода и на "квадратность" ее графики.
О чем же на самом деле эта игра? В начале своего обзора я писал о познании, о том что кроме технологий, которыми мы можем пользоваться сегодня, оно может привести человечество к его закату. Вот об этом и рассказывает нам игра. А еще - это трагедия, молчаливая трагедия одного человека, который по чистой случайности оказался не в то время и не в том месте. И о мире, который потерял свободу - свободу выбирать и "свободу жить".
Это потрясающая игра, которая по праву стала игрой года. И я ставлю ей

I came into this game because it mentioned runescape classic and Ultima Online in the very beginning, and when I first started it indeed felt like them... Atleast, at first. After playing for some time and learning about the game I found it to be quite lacking sadly.
While the game does boast multiple skills that are reminiscent of runescape/UO, its execution is quite lacking. Typically one of the most iconic skills from UO is the taming system... This has none. Instead it has Breeding, which is a neat concept, except for the fact that pets feel more like equipment rather than, well, pets. I can't train my pet, but I can mate him and get a good mix that I can use and/or sell off, it actually reminded me of a game called Chicken Jockey where you bred and raised chickens to sell..
The death system is similar to runescapes in that you keep 2 most valuable items, but in this game, the rest of your items are destroyed. Furthermore the value is based on poorly listed prices in game, so an item that could take you 5 hours of real grinding, is worth peanuts compared to something simple you can buy off an npc in the starter town, causing you to have a panic attack should you happen to almost die.
The game does stop bots by incorporating a captcha system, however the mods go over the top by also banning those who trade between accounts on the same IP. Sorry brothers and sisters, dads/moms and sons/daughters, helping out each other is punishable by losing all your accounts tied to your home should you choose to help each other out.
Its further laughable that the game makes the point to compare themselves to runescape and UO in the very description of the game on the store page, but don't you dare mention those games, or any others for that matter, in chat unless you like being yelled at by a mod for "advertising other games".... Seriously? You listed them in your bloody description, why point out your game is similar to these others and then stop people from talking about the similarities?
If the furer's secret police don't daunt your spirit from liking this game, the unbelievable grind will. The skills are hardly balanced out, some increasing so quickly in exp that you would expect to become a master in mere days from focusing on, while others are so horrendously slow you want to punt a rabbit across a football field *cough, woodchopping, cough*
The monsters all seem to be static, glued in place like pieces on a chestboard, always spawning back in the exact same square they appeared before, and their loot seems to be wildly unbalanced as the drop rates are set horrendously low for the most oddest of items. You need 6 dorpat souls to make a potion that teleports you to the starter town... With a drop rate of 0.25% from all mobs found on that map. How very rare... Oh, or heres a teleport to dorpat scroll on this merchant npc in town for a mere 1k gold.
No archery? Oh no! Wait... Magic! Yay.....Oh... Its not ranged? Of course not, the monsters can't move, so being a mage is pretty much... I'm sorry, whats the point? I mean seriously? Having to use magic as if its a sword is just.. Ugh, don't get me started on that, just don't.
Alot of things need to change and be added for this to even touch either of those titles mentioned in its description, if anything

The Story (A little predictable) and gameplay is good. But my goodness, the brother obsession is real. It took me a while to actually sit down and immerse myself. Reason? Looking at Laphi only makes me remember my personal experiences. I had nothing but older sisters around me...and all it did was remind me of how annoying it was when they were so clingy, nitpicky, invasive and judgemental when i showed interest in other girls.
With that said, there is a limit to how edgy a character can be for me and  Velvet passed that threshold.  I've watched too much anime, played too many jrpgs, played all the tales games to the point where i have question my life choices. So i have come across plenty of edgy characters.
I mean ok I get it, you are out for revenge, of course you're going to be edgy. In her circumstances it was her niche but it never felt new to me.
I understand that it was mostly to cope with the lost of her brother. But it only shows how obsessed she was with him. I couldn't personally relate to any of the characters but Laphi (in a negative way). My favorite character out the bunch is Magilou, almost reminds me of Jade from Abyss. Being that comedic troll of the game.
The direction they took the story is a breath of fresh air and that alone is a good reason to try it out. I bought the game when it was on sale, so if you're skeptical wait until then. The game isn't MY cup of tea, but its not bad in any means.

I'm having a lot of fun with this game. I made the mistake of playing my first galactic war on Normal difficulty, which should be renamed Easy. (And no, that's not a humblebrag, I'm far from a pro at these types of games.) On Normal difficulty, I don't think the AI ever even attacked me. They just stood around and waited to be killed. So I played my second galactic war on Hard, thinking I was going to get my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me. But it turns out Hard difficulty simply means that the AI will attack you, although the attacks are predictable and mostly pathetic. Only the faction commander battles were any kind of challenge, and even then only minimally.
At that point I was ready to give up on this game, but commenters suggested I try it on a higher difficulty or with AI mods, so I started up another galactic war but on Relentless difficulty. Bingo! That difficulty seems just about right for me. The AI is challenging, and even overwhelming if I don't get to them fast. So now I'm looking forward to playing this co-op with friends against the computer!
The battles are pretty fast and furious, so if you're looking for a slower game with tons of upgrade options and a myriad of tactics you can dive into, you probably won't be happy here. The upgrade trees are shallow, and everything in an entire tree tends to unlock with a single tech upgrade, so you only get strategic variety early on in a galactic war, when you don't have every option at your fingertips and you have to improvise a strategy based on what you have access to.
This game does a great job with interplanetary combat, and making it feel like you're really on a planet zipping around a solar system. It has a very stylized/minimalist art style which I don't care for because it's too cartoony for me, but I get why people like it. I don't think the art detracts from the game, it's just not my favorite style. The explosions are quite nice, and the game does a really good job of making you feel powerful.
So in the end, I recommend this game for those who are looking for a real-time strategy designed for fast matches and fairly simple strategic depth. It's a great game for when you have 30min - 1hr for a match against the AI. But if you get frustrated and think the AI is just too stupid, stick with it and turn the difficulty up to Relentless or Absurd. You'll eventually find the challenge you're looking for. :)

This game looks pretty poor and has remarkably long loading times. It's also a pretty short game; I finished it twice in about 11 hours.
With that said, this game is worth playing twice if you enjoy this type of game. What type is that? An RPG with lots of decisions and consequences. Note that, the decisions you make are actually quite impactful, and the game entirely allows you to make "bad" decisions (the game itself describes this as there being no bad decisions). Beyond that, the game explores some fairly cool science fiction themes and does a fairly good job in making those themes interesting and plausible.
Just a small addendum: I said this game is largely based around decisions and consequences. Let me elaborate on this a little. During the game you'll be trying to solve a sort of mystery. You will not be spoon-fed the answers to your questions and your suspicions will not easily be confirmed. Even if you do a pretty thorough job of the 'investigation', there's a good chance you won't figure it out. However: That is okay. If you don't figure it out the game doesn't become less fun after that point.
I would absolutely recommend this game, with one sidenote: This is a short game. If you think a game costing 15 euro or dollar or whatever, should net you ~15+ hours of gameplay, then you should buy this game when it's on sale. I myself bought it at 65% off, but feel like I wouldn't have been upset if I'd bought it at full price.

Okay, so the previous review I had up here was... a little 'cringy'. To be fair, it was my first review. STARBOUND!
Do you like space? Do you like exploration? Do you like open world sandbox building?
Starbound handles all these surprisingly well! It's an awesome game!
