You play as Rover, the friendly and intelligent family dog. You are the biggest corgi the world has ever seen, and you must eat all the sausages in the kitchen, until you can fight no longer, and you become the Sleeping Dog. Really now, you play as a Jackie Chan double who is actually a sleeper agent (hence the name, hurr durr) and you want no trabble. You fight your way through several ladder factories while holding several different babies, in your fight against slightly bigger asian people that look like they're straight out of Fast and Furious. You go through several losses, in this trainless society, and sleep with many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, although it is wisely disguised as if you are getting a massage from a massage parlour. You go through several girlfriends, and lose none of the perks that came with them after you pump and dump through all of them, essentially leaving the world with several Jackie Chan babies. You also learn many secret hidden techniques by picking up some sort of Chinese takeout food, or something along those lines, I don't really recall because it was unmemorable, but that's besides the point. The game has you fighting in a very enticing combat system that allows you to have fun while you steamroll everybody as if you were a train. What this game lacks in trains, it makes up for in witty dialog, enticing story, and fun gameplay. The main character is likeable, and most of the game is played through his eyes where he's constantly at odds of being caught by the criminals he associates with. Overall, if you want a fun, and mindless beat 'em up game, with a karaoke minigame in it that frankly deserves its own review, you should get Sleeping Dogs, because who doesn't want to be an oversized corgi, fighting sausages in the kitchen?

It's...not bad.  This game is, for the most part, the same as Sanctum, but with a few differences in how enemies move and the maze you send them through is constructed.  You can now choose more characters, which each specialize with a different type of weaponry to destroy the aliens with.
Alright, so let's get down to the nitty-gritty.  Sanctum 2, like its predecessor, is an FPS-TD, which stands for First Person Shooter-Tower Defense.  Yes, it is *both* at once.  You construct your maze for the ugly aliens to get through and then, once it's built and they start marching in, you pull out your gun and start pulverizing them yourself as well!  It's a cool concept that I haven't seen before (and frankly, hadn't even thought of until the original Sanctum came around).
The graphics are neatly and nicely done, the gameplay itself is cool, and this one even has a slight story element to it as well (as opposed to its predecessor, which was purely maps and killing aliens).  But the problem with it is that it is almost identical...to the point where I kind of wish this game was just an update to the original and not another $15 to purchase (rest assured that I took advantage of sales, and you should too).
If you've never played a Sanctum, get this one.  You'll have more fun than you would purchasing the original for sure.  But if you have Sanctum, I hesitate to tell you to buy it unless the price gets cut drastically.

As a fan of the original Sanctum, playing this game can feel a little weird. Firstly, you're far more limited on towers, with you starting off only being able to deploy/upgrade 1 kind of tower and can get a max of 4 as you progress. You also only have 2 weapons. Before you had a giant blank canvas to develop into a maze of towers with your core WAY off at the end, now your core is almost in the middle of things. So if you've developed tactics from the first game, they won;t fly in this one. Instead of a ton of towers, you're better off with a few that get a lot of upgrades. And instead of only really needing to shoot a few special enemies, now you're gonna be in the thick of it, so pick your weapons carefully.
Honetly, from what I've seen this game takes Sanctum in a direction that it seemed to be heading for anyway. The first was almsot all about tower placement and maze formation, while this game gives the FPS elements more of the spotlight. The two work well together despite what you'd think, and it adds a level of tactical gameplay with the limiting of towers and weapons not to mention character selection since each has their own signiture weapon and defauly bonuses.

This game basically has a lot of the same skills like RS, for example AT/STR/DEF/HP and prayer.
From my point of view, graphics aren't important. This game looks colourful, has nice backgroundmusic and plays smoothly once you get used to the mechanics (like "you can only eat food when you're DONE fighting or after running away).
It really throws you back into the days of grinding those stats, crafting that junk till you could make better junk, looking for rare drops/random events...
Now this game is Early Access, so the interface feels very basic and looks a bit unfinished. But that's not a big deal, because the game itself is already very enjoyable to play. I have faith they're going to bring nothing but improvements to this game.
And hey, even if they don't: it's Totally Free 2 Play! No member-restricted areas or member-only items or events or any of that bullcrap. You can explore the whole world. I think this game ain't even 200Mb in size, so it's installed in like 10 seconds. Just give it a go and if you think it's boring, then no harm done.
So if you (used to) like Runescape, you should definitely give this a try!

The reason why I am writing this review before finishing the game is because of this is a tales game and because it received overwhelming positive responses. I played 3 tales games so far. First tales of legendia, then tales of abyss and finally this one. To be honest, this is the least original one. It is purely because of the characters. They are not memmorrable, they are not fun and the dialogues are sooooo unneccesery i feel like watching a filler episode of an anime each time I begin a conversation. The character progression is too slow that the first 10 hours you need to be a masochist to have fun.. Which was never a case in abyss or legendia. I loved those games. Especcially Abyss.. All time favorite. However berseria excells in combat system. It is fresh and my blood pumps like hell in chaotic combat situations. It is fast, sometimes strategic and most of the time feels very enjoyable..
There are a couple of major factors why the game sucks. One of them is the graphics. Hell it's from PS3 era. You cannot jump, you cannot pass the invisible walls and stuff, which is like... bleh.. You can't hear velvet at all but in combat her voice is like uber high you cannot hear any♥♥♥♥♥♥other than that. The environment is blatant and boring AF. The Orb Chamber is a fairly challenging Puzzle-Platformer game, especially if you are starting anew in this category of games. I’ve started with a few frustrating attempts at level 1, had quit and then watched some gameplays to understand the gist of the controls and tactics to use for playing.
To start off, our objective is as any other Platformer game – get from Point A, to Point B. There are obstacles such as spikes, boxes and (partially) the bombs, as they do aid in destroying the former obstacles, but also can kill the player if they are too close in range of the explosion. Then there are checkpoints and respawn orbs that we can collect so we spawn from where we last left them when/if we die. A neat row of levels is presented to the player, plus a hard mode for each that will unlock when completing the normal level.
The controls are were things get challenging. Your mouse is your only sense of control of where your character goes. When you click and drag on the screen near the ball, this will push the ball away from your cursor; similar to a slingshot. Arrows will also appear, pointing to which direction your ball will go when you click. I suggest proceeding slowly and consistently. Don’t send your character flying across the map if you don’t know how to halt their movement completely or properly. My experiences aside, here is what the downside(s) of the game were.
The art style was rather messy. There is a mix of tile patterns as the backgrounds, differing from levels. All the foreground objects share a flat, monotone colour, which largely contrasts with the background, since the BG tiles all have a detailed form of texture and shading. Level 10 was the most confusing level for me, because the background tiles were quite similar, if not exact, as the colour of the ball itself!
The level menu also shared its mediocre design. In the background, you see an overly of a gradient colour, with what appears to be a wheat field, and a tree. There are forms of plant life present, but in the game itself there was probably one or two total. (One of them being on the very first level) It’s slightly misleading to the overall theme of the game, if any.
I also question why our ball looks so sad? :C
But, on the bright side, the menu music wasn’t bad. As a fan of Electronic music, I give kudos to the BGM. This, as well as any other effects in the game can be turned on/off too, on the level menu.
Overall, this game has its challenges for being a platformer. While the graphics weren’t as good, the developers did include some interesting visual effects, plus a trail line for our cursor. Is it worth the price? Not really unless it goes on sale. It is still worth trying out, though, and I give it a thumbs up for that.

Burnout Paradise is an arcade, open-world racing game developed by Criterion Games (an EA-owned developer since 2004) and published by EA circa 2008. This game was released before the massive average drop in quality surrounding EA-affiliated games around 2010-2012, so it has plenty of potential for being a solid game, more than most would expect of a similarly modern EA title.
Well, first things first. Paradise is a surprisingly great game for the usually underdog racing genre. In fact, I would go as far as to say that Burnout Paradise is one of the best racing games ever made.
Burnout Paradise's gameplay uses an impressively effective combination of open-world exploration, high-speed arcade racing, and aggressive vehicular combat. Paradise is primarily a single-player game, as almost all unlocks are acquired in the single-player mode, but it comes with a well-integrated multiplayer mode where you can enter another player's world at any point and place and race, collide or play various minigames with him and other players in the party (max of 8).
In this game, the player is given a car and put in a large city, entirely unlocked from the beginning. Then it's left up to the player to drive around, find missions and activities, and unlock more content (cars, missions, license upgrades etc). This system is simple and highly effective, giving players substantial freedom to progress through content at their own pace, without being punished for choosing to do things in a specific way that the game's developers didn't intend. There are a handful of game modes available besides the standard overworld exploration, and while not much direction is given to players upon first playing, most of the gameplay is pretty self-explanatory, so not much instruction is needed. Among these gametypes, there is: A standard point A to point B race (the trick is that the whole map is unlocked in the race so the player has to learn the city to be able to get to anywhere rapidly), an aggressive "Road Rage" gametype where the objective is to takedown (IE fucҝing destroy) as many other cars as possible, Stunt runs where the player has to get points by doing stuns (air time, jumps, flips, fetching objects, etc) and getting combos without crashing, and Marked Man, where the player has to get to a specific point on the map while avoiding being killed by constantly respawning, ominous black vehicles. Kind of like The Terminator 2, but with less Schwarzenegger. There's also a special game mode available only once for each unlockable car, where you have to use that car to get to a spot very fast in order to unlock an upgraded version of that car.
In addition to the normal mission types and drop-in/drop-out multiplayer, there are also a lot of collectibles to get in the open-world map, in the form of billboards that require taking jumps to get to, and glowing yellow fences that the player smashes through to get shortcuts. There's also a time trial on each street where the player has to drive from one end of the street to the other end as fast as possible to get the minimum time on it.
The primary objective of the game is to upgrade your license to the maximum level. (And also to smash through every single yellow fence piece on the map. Good luck you autist.) Starting from a D-level training license, the player moves up the license upgrade ladder as they beat missions on the overworld. Each license level requires the player to beat a certain number of missions to unlock, and when their license is upgraded, all the missions on the map reset. In here lies one of the shortcomings of Burnout Paradise. The constantly resetting missions and requirement to beat them all again several times contributes to making Paradise seem like a very repetitive game. However, I believe that the core gameplay within Paradise is strong enough to make the game remain consistently enjoyable despite the repetition of the overworld missions.
The cars handle very smoothly and move at very acceptable speeds, with a lot of variation between them. In Paradise City you can find vehicles of all types suitable for all play styles, whether it be supercharged glass cannons, tiny Asian imports that turn on a dime, or gigantic unshakable bricks on wheels. Not all vehicles are suitable for all mission types (don't bring a van to a drag race, dummy), but there's enough of them that you can find at least one car of every type that you'll like.
While the gameplay is extremely strong in both quality and amount of content, that's not the only strong point of Burnout Paradise. Although the game lacks any sort of story to speak of ("Welcome to Paradise City, now fucҝ off") and thus cannot really be judged on an aspect like that, the game is really legit on both graphical and audial levels. I'm not normally a stickler for graphics in video games, but I have to complement the technical graphics of Paradise, as the game is very pretty to look at (both in and out of motion) and also surprisingly well optimized, especially given that it's both a console port and an EA game. I was able to get a consistent 60 frames per second on max settings from the beginning, without having to do an excessive amount of optimization and tweaking for my system. There's also an ENB available for this game, which can be found on the main ENB site. Beware though, it gives the game a somewhat noticeable blue tint, if that's not to your tastes. The amount of graphical detail is quite impressive at times, especially when it comes to the car damage system. Every collision/impact that your vehicle is involved in generates damage on it, depending of course on factors such as speed, angle, the car you're driving and the car you hit.
From a sound standpoint, Burnout Paradise is a pleasure to listen to. Both sound effects and music fit into the game very well. Car engines sound powerful, and are unique to almost every vehicle, and impacts sound brutal and destructive. The soundtrack is pretty exceptionable as well, as expected from a 2000s EA racing game. While not every track is a 5 star hit, the game still contains a good amount of solid tracks from several genres, including classic rock, pop, and modern metal, presenting a good amount of variety in the OST. Included is a large amount of tracks from previous Burnout games, which helps keep series consistency. It also has Avril Lavigne's "Girlfriend" which you can play on loop if you're clinically insane, and "Paradise City" by Guns n Roses is the first track that plays when you launch the game, which, in my opinion, is incredibly cool. Pretty punny too.
Overall, one of the best games I've ever played.

Updated review to better reflect how the past year has fared for Capcom and this game.
Opinions on Street Fighter V are clearly polarizing, and that's not without good reason. There's still missing quality of life features and a lack of single-player offerings.
There have been clear improvements over the game's poor state at launch, but whether or not the game is for you depends on what you want out of a fighter and how experienced you are with the genre.
Street Fighter V feels very narrow compard to other fighting games. I think this can be both a good and bad thing. It's good because the game isn't too daunting to approach and it doesn't require a ridiclous amount of time spent to stay sharp. It's bad because what you can actually do in the game to outplay your opponent can feel stifled and restricted.
Most of it's going to come down to whether or not you like the gameplay and meta. I personally enjoy it more than SF4, but that's more of a personal preference than it is an argument of quality (I think Skullgirls is one of the most quality fighting games available, but it's gameplay just isn't for me unfortunately).
For experienced fighting game folk: the game is read heavy and wakeup pressure still reigns supreme in the current patch. Defensive options are lacking, so the best defensive options are either godlike footsies or relentless offense to prevent your opponent from getting started.

Current state at near launch is quite miserable.
- No arcade mode.
- No quick vs CPU mode.
- Story is very short, very barebones.
- No shop.
- Long loading times.
- Online lobby is limited to only 2 players.
- Online server is kinda broken, lots of issues.
However, the gameplay is really fun!
- V-Skills and V-Trigger give each character a unique gimmick, it's like Street Fighter got inspirations from BlazBlue. Even Ken now plays very differently than Ryu!
- V-Trigger can be used to cancel moves, creating very cool and devastating combos.
- V-Reversal system to get you out of long blockstrings, basically it's Street Fighter Alpha's Alpha Counter.
- 16 characters with upcoming 6 DLC characters which can be unlocked for free!
- Karin Kanzuki, Rainbow Mika, and Charlie Nash from Street Fighter Alpha finally made a return!
- Great soundtrack! From old songs remix, electronic and dubsteps, to great new rock songs.
Conclusion:
At its core, SFV is a great fighting game, but it suffers from severe lack of contents and messed up online mode. Also, the Steam digital price in my region (Indonesia) is very expensive! I got it retail from a nearby store and it was around Rp300.000 ($25) cheaper.
Gameplay-wise it's probably the best Street Fighter ever. But unless you're a big megafan of Street Fighter series and absolutely can't wait, you might want to wait until June, when the big patches finally came out.
It's hard to decide, but I guess I'll give this game a thumb up because I still have faith in the developers. If by June everything's still broken, I'll change it to thumbs down :P

I bought this game a few minutes ago, and I regret my purchase. I'm having tons of issues, and I'm quite upset about this. If I cannot get the game working, I will ask Steam Support for a refund. ;(
EDIT (2 Days Later): I have gotten the game working. Bugs (mostly) aside, here's my ACTUAL review below.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
For years, I'd heard little blurbs about this racing game called Burnout Paradise here and there. I'd seen it used at GameStop back when I was primarily a console gamer, but I never really paid it any attention. After seeing a popular YouTuber named NerdCubed do a video on it with his dad, I was sale hunting for this game.
The Steam Summer Sale came, and the game was $9.99 USD. A few of my close friends had the game, and loved it to death. I thought I'd pick it up, but it didn't just come with the game, nor just the DLC. I got an unwelcomed bonus - A NONFUNCTIONAL GAME. Multiple reinstalls, a lot of Googling, and hours of tinkering came before I got to properly experience this game. One problem after another bit me in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ the infamous DMV screen, crashing at the loading screen right when you start up the game... yada, yada. I got the game to open occasionally; sometimes, rarely, the game would launch flawlessly, and let me play just fine. The other 8 out of 10 times, it crashed. Until I fixed it, I'd only successfully launched the game three times in two days. I probably made 30+ attempts to launch the game. I tried every fix I could find on the internet, and none worked. I eventually thought to try Windows 95 Compatibility Mode "again," or so I thought. I thought I'd tried it already, but I must not have! After applying that fix (some people can only get it to work on certain compatibility modes; some XP SP3, some Vista only, some Win2000 only, etc.), the game launches flawlessly. Now, the only bug I get is the game freezes when I try to quit. Saves fine, just I have to manually kill the process on exit.
Steam claims I've played 8 hours of this game. I don't know how many hours of that (probably about 2) are just me trying to get it to launch properly. The game is phenomenal! The world is pretty large, with about 400 gates to smash (which lead you to backroads and alternate routes), and about 200 (I think, I'm not exactly sure) billboards to smash. Many of these billboards require you to do jumps on ramps to get to them, many of these jumps being at the end of the alternate routes that lie past those gates I told you about. I usually overlook elements like that in games, but in Paradise, I like going around and smashing them! Every intersection with a spotlight is a new race. You simply do a burnout (hold both triggers) to start one of these events; you have events where you must takedown other cars, races, events where you have to get somewhere without getting taken down, and more. There's plenty to do in Burnout Paradise!
There are over 75+ cars to choose from, as well as four bikes (which I think are more fun than the cars) added by the Burnout Bikes update included in The Ultimate Box. Allow me to note that TUB was a collection of all DLCs released up to that point; Criterion had no intention to keep making more expansions when they released TUB, but they did, The Burnout Store is down, so you can't buy the other DLCs if you don't go onto either Amazon or GreenManGaming and buy a code. The racing style is very arcadey, but you can also do barrel rolls and stuff when you do jumps, which feels very good and solid. On the cars (and cars ONLY, not bikes) you can boost your vehicle. You have different types of cars like Aggression (for takedowns and strength for when you crash) and Stunt (which are faster and more for doing stunts, but crash and are wrecked very easily). The driving in this game is great, and feels amazing.
The graphics in this game are pretty good, as well as the overall feel. My 650m cannot run it at maximum settings, but my buddy's dual Titans smoke it. It is a pretty good-looking game, especially when you crank it up. The visuals department is top-notch!
The soundtrack is amazing, although there's only one song I really pay attention to - "Paradise City" by Guns 'n' Roses. That song alone makes the soundtrack AWESOME....!
Overall, Burnout Paradise is a great game. Bugs aside, I give it a 8.5 out of 10. However, with the bugs in the mix, I give it a 2.5 out of 10. I would not recommend it; it may or may not work for you. I don't think it's worth the risk unless you get it off Origin, so you can return it within 24 hours with their Great Game Guarantee.

It's a lot of fun!  If you have never tried this game and it goes on sale - grab it!  You can easily spend 100 + hours on this game and still never explore the whole thing.
PROS:
1) Easy to Learn
2) Great Graphics for an older game
3) Fun tutorial... creatively funny
4) There is a TON TO DO!
5) Trade with other cities that you have built! You can have one city be a farming community while another has industry.
6) Hours of enjoyment
7 ) Definitely SATISFIES your desire to be a CITY BUILDER , MAYOR, and Planner in a similar but yet different way than SIM CITY.
8) Direct relationships with class of people and business's success is interesting.
CONS:
1) Graphics engine does not run as well as SIM CITY.  Your computer will BOG down the closer you get to a million plus citizens
2) Road systems are a little screwy and VERY EXPENSIVE.  You will be paying 1000 credits for just a small patch of EXPRESSWAY.
3) Citizens are NEVER HAPPY - at least not for very long.  They will either always not be able to find a job or you will not have enough housing to contain them all.  THere is always an immediate shift even if just one business goes bankrupt.
4) Businesses will go bankrupt for different reasons that just POP UP even if there have been no changes.  It makes it interesting on one hand ... on the other it is a little aggrevating that a balanced city only stays that way for a very short period of time.
5) BUILDINGS - The buildings do not change over time like in SIM CITY.  Rather than the businesses growing to towering mega structures because they are so successful, they are what they are when you plant them.

If you know Tales, you'll see pretty quick what Berseria does and doesn't. Typical plots of Tales are here-- a villain who you can sympathize with, enemies who have personal motives for fighting, and a main character who has to overcome their lack of self-worth. All of it is there as it is in every Tales, except for Vesperia. But that's neither here nor there.
It would ruin the effect to go into great detail. Instead, fans of the Tales series should find a lot here to love and without ruining more, I think it's one of the more compelling Tales games, plot- and character-wise.
The gameplay is kind of atrociously simple, since they've done away with mana and you now simply spend combo points to enact any skills whatsoever. This means that there can be some unnecessarily stifling moments in the game where there doesn't seem to be a lot you can do but as Namco is well known for, you can solve a lot of problems by being impeccably practiced with guarding.
All the same, solid game and worth seeing the plot if you're a fan of the series. If not, maybe you don't want to bother. Vesperia is a better entry point and has a far more compelling main character for those not as heavily invested in the series, and its unfortunately weeaboo habits.

I came for the singleplayer, then stayed for the multiplayer. This game has three strong points:
HL1 is a great game fundamentally and objectively. It's story is not over-bearing like normal games these days and it's just enough to host the gameplay and keep you going. Doom 2016 did their story similarly and I'd consider that game one of the best games that has come out in the past few years. The best way to make a singleplayer game is to let the story be the platter for the gameplay. If your game is all story and no interesting gameplay it's just going to be boring. Looking at you, Call of Duty...
Speaking of story, the game's plot is not told through cutscenes. One of the greatest things this game has to offer is it's immersion. It doesn't feel like a story. It feels like you're living it. This is because the game never takes control away from your character and it lets the events play out around you while you're still able to move and look for yourself. The game makes you feel like YOU were the one responsible for the destruction of Black Mesa, not your character. It makes you feel like YOU are dealing with the consequences of the resonance cascade scenario, not your character. It sets you up to feel like a badass.
Moving on to functionality. The GoldSrc engine let's you bunny-hop and build speed in all kinds of ways which makes this game very fun game for speedrunning. Another thing is the response time. The response time and snappy-ness is what makes all Source games great.
In the end, I love this game and all but I can't say most people would enjoy this game simply because of the looks. Lets be real, this game looks gross next to something like Doom 2016. However even if you can't get past the game's 1998 graphics, I have just the thing! For the best singleplayer experience of this game, check out Black Mesa. It's a HL1 remake in Source 2 so it looks beautiful and functions great. It's the same game and same levels(basically) but it utilizes technology that wasn't available in 1998 and makes the game look sexy.
There's not much to say about this, and most people won't be interested so I'll keep this short. Everything about this game makes it perfect for speedrunning. All Source games are good for speedrunning and GREAT for learning to speedrun on. Bunnyhopping is almost a sport in some Source games so it's fun to apply it to singleplayer and utilize it to beat the game as fast as possible. In addition to bhopping, there are some interesting glitches that make running the game really satisfying.
Half-Life 1 objectively has
multiplayer experiences in the entire Steam store. Playing deathmatch mode is a very unique experience for many reasons...
The first major reason is the community servers. There is no matchmaking like we have nowadays. The effect of not having matchmaking is that you see the same people on the same servers(generally) and this allows you to get familiar with them and become friends. (shout-out to Discosuperfly and the rest of the Hootersgaming crew :P)
Second reason is the weapon selection. Every weapon is good for different situations, and it allows people to develop unique play-styles. On top of that, you get the satisfaction of watching your scores get better over time as you learn what weapons to use and when.
It's a very no-mercy type of multiplayer. At first, you will get beaten and battered simply because there is no tutorial or guide. You join a server in the midst of an all out free-for-all war and you're left to figure out how to fight for your life or lose trying. If you're not willing to put some effort into learning new skills to git gud at a game, don't buy this game and consider buying a Call of Duty title :)

I'd never played Werewolf or Mafia so I was new to this concept. Basically, it's the Town vs the Mafia and some roles you can get work only for themselves (Jester has you trying to trick the town into hanging you, the Serial Killer wants everyone dead, etc). No one knows each others' roles and revealing your role opens you up to being killed. It's a lot to explain while still being pretty simple, but there are two phases - night and day. The town (everyone) is active during the day, the Mafia and certain other roles are active during the night. What you do is obviously very dependent on your role - choose a person to watch overnight, jail one person a night, set yourself to alert to kill anyone who visits your house, turn into a Werewolf and slaughter people.
This game has lots of variety that allows for some crazy moments. The dev team's active, too, and there's microtransations that won't win anyone any games but do add a little something to the game.
Support these devs and pick this one up. I'm pretty sure it's free, so just click the ♥♥♥♥ing button. Then buy a pirate avatar or something, I don't know, this is a cool♥♥♥♥♥game.

Street Fighter V is a great game.
When it works.
The launch for this game has without a doubt been a rough one, from disconnects, to really dumb synch issues (when you alt-tab) and Battle Lounge (the custom games) not working for about the entire first day.
Capcom obviously released this game early than they should've to give players an edge for the upcoming Capcom Pro Tour, but they obviously messed up technically.
That said, even though these problems exist (and definitely suck) SFV is a solid game and probably the best Street Fighter to date.
It's still solid Street Fighter, where you need your fundamentals, footsies and execution to succeed, and it's a goddamn mountain to climb, but every combo you successfully hit, every ranked match you win, makes you feel so good. This has somehow been bumped up in this iteration. Everything does a lot of damage, the V system is a great evolution of the comeback mechanic in Street FIghter IV, where each character has their own set of buffs or utilities in their V-Gauge, that you fill up, just like Ultras. but these are a lot more interesting, and you can use this meter for V-Reversals to get you out of bad situations.
These new mechanics somehow make this game even more of an emotional rollercoaster, for some reason this game seems to be very emotionally challenging in comparison to IV, and I love it.

So yeah. Street Fighter V. This is a game that excels in many ways and is extremely disappointing in many others. The fighting is fast, fluid, and powerful. The input buffer makes combos manageable (no combo requires inputs faster than 1/10 of a second. Believe me, this is quite doable with a little practice). The characters are well balanced, and I actually like that there are only 16 fighters as it means each character had tons of time put into them and they all feel very distinct. Even Ryu and Ken are the most different of any SF I've played.
However, this is a major failure on the part of Capcom. Why? Because they desperately wanted to get new players into the series but chose to omit any features new players would find useful. The in game tutorial is a joke, the AI modes are dumb, and there's very little to unlock in game and unlocking what is there is a pain. It's a real shame, too, since SFV has some of the most accessible fighting mechanics I've ever seen.
If you didn't know, Capcom released the game as early as they did so the game would be ready for their eSports season. This is a good idea as the actual fighting is finished and polished, so competetive/hardcore fans can enjoy getting their hands on it and watching a compelling year of tournaments ending in the Capcom Cup. However, since the team put almost all of their efforts into getting the characters done on time, there is a severe lack of modes to ease new players into the experience. When a scrub goes online and gets bodied button mashing, they're not going to want to keep playing. You have to introduce them to the higher level strategy of fighting games so they can analyze their mistakes and stay motivated. Like, look at the Skullgirls tutorial. There's a part where they tell you what a mixup is and then you have to successfully guard against an AI throwing out some blockstrings. That's amazing! Now that player knows about how he or she should be throwing out their own moves. Plus the tutorials go into BnBs for each character. Actual, useful, helpful information instead of "Every character has a unique V-System! Figure it out yourself! Okay bye."
I think Capcom, in chasing that MOBA money, could have done better with actually learning from Dota 2's release. Essentially, the version they released now should have been a "Beta" or "Early Access" or whatever catchy name they decided to use that you would have to buy. That way hardcore players can immediately play and the tournaments can still go on. Then, in a few months once they finished up the single player, newbie focused stuff, release the game for real. Either fully free-to-play (those costumes are going to make so much money anyway) or just on the cheap. Everyone would win this way: casuals/reviews don't buy in until there's stuff that casuals/reviews would like, the FGC gets the game for the Capcom Pro Tour, and Capcom makes money hand over fist.

This is a very different, very cute game!
It definitely FEELS like a first game from a new developer. They had a million good ideas, but couldn't make time to really make good use of all of them.
Much of it is a murder mystery (with interrogations), which is rather solid. Some of the voice acting is a little rough-hewn, and parts of how dialogue/plot plays out feels either obvious and heavy-handed, or a bit amateur. The majority, however, is extremely servicable, and downright good at times.
The mystery part of it is great -- it was 100% unpredictable and honestly, a real challenge to figure out. I got it on the first try, but really only because I save-scummed a couple times in important conversations to see how dialogue/actions would play out if I said X or Y. You have to REALLY pay attention to the small stuff.
My only real complaint about the murder mystery is that it went by too fast. I wanted more time to hunt for clues, get to know the characters, and piece details together.
There IS fighting in this game -- extremely basic FPS stuff (with a way overcomplicated item management system). It's just extremely scant, and actually almost 100% avoidable. The devs put all this work into this FPS system, and had you go through basically two sets of tutorials on how to do it, and then they butter you up by saying that "oh wow you're going into something REALLY dangerous!! You're gonna need these skills!!!" ... And then the episode ends.
I get that there will be another episode, hopefully, someday, but TBH it would have been REALLY nice if the devs had tossed in one big battle at the end to make the FPS tutorial stuff worth your time.
All the negative stuff aside, I recommend the game (if it is <$10) ... If only because of how extremely DIFFERENT it is. I've played a lot of games that it had elements of, but I've never played a game that had this particular combo of elements.

A Good Upgrade.
Some people are not happy that Planetary Annihalation: TITANS exists since they depricated the original Planetary Annihilation.   Most of the time I would agree, however here are some considerations:
1. The origional Planitary Annihailation was on sale for a steal of a price often (and you get a nice discount if you have it).
2. The Devs are continuing to support the people who did the kickstarter backing (not me I came in later) yet in a way that does not give them an unfair advantage.
3. The content that has been added is substantial.  The titans are an nice addition with each one filling a good niche.  They have also added quite a few other buildings and units to give you a more diverse army.
4. You can still play the original Planetary Annihalation with people who get Titans.  While this may seem like something that not too many people want to do, I have to give the devs credit for attempting some type of backwards compatbility.
In all I think the devs have done a great job.  While I do not condone the practice of re-hashing a game with new content as a complete new game, I do thing that the devs were trying to help people out with the process.
In some ways I would rather it be this way instead of an expensive DLC that you are not sure who has.  Stuff like that makes it difficult to get new players in.  "hey man I picked up PA!" "oh great did you pick up the TITANS DLC?" "No, I was trying to save some cash and I didnt know I needed it to play with you guys"  "Bummer, looks like you're going to have to wait until the next sale to jump in our big games"  ...see with this option you dont have that problem.

It may not be quite as good as the Batman: Arkham series of games, but it's fighting system is still briliant in it's own right. Think of a GTA world with a Batman: Arkham-esk fighting system.
The gunplay isn't nearly as good as it's fighting system, but is still respectable and acceptable.
To think, this game was originally a 'Streets of LA' title before being dropped and eventually picked up by another developer / publisher.
Here's to the possibility of a Sleeping Dogs 2.
In short; Regardless of it being on sale or not, it's a must-buy.

Don't let my low amount of time on this game fool you; it's basically the same game as its previous iterations; this is just the one now solely available on Steam.  I put dozens of hours into the 2012 edition and got this for about three bucks.
Now then, that said.  Is this game anywhere near as good as Cities: Skylines (my 2015 Game of the Year)?  Of course not.  Not by half.  But there's more to it than that.
See, XL has one thing Skylines doesn't; a beautifully interconnected resource economy that makes building specialized cities so much more rewarding.  You can build a breadbasket city on a map with a ton of fertile land, an oil town, a manufacturing center, a tourist paradise...and the oversupply in one city is demand in another.  Is the trading sim as robust as Grand Ages Medieval or any of Gaming Minds' maritime trade sims?  No, but it's not supposed to be.
Skylines is the builder I reach for when I'm after a "classic" SimCity-like experience.  I go for XL when I want to build something on a bigger scale, more like a nation than a city (in that sense, "XL" is an appropriate word for it.  Extra-large, indeed.)
As I write this, it's on sale for four bucks.  Anything from about $7 downward is a good value proposition for any game in this series.  It's not as good as Skylines (not much is), but it's still worth playing for what it gets right.

RPG MO is a very simple game that is similar to old school games. Not only in design but in mechanics as well.
tl;dr at bottom.
EDIT: As I go on playing longer and longer, I still enjoy the game but the chat and the people talking in the default chat are seriously irritating. This is a fair warning about some in the community, they just don't know when to stop. I'm finding the ignore command coming right in handy.
Pros:
-It's free to play and actually free.
-In game wiki. (This is great, search prices, informatino about items, NPCs etc.)
-In game map that states how to get to all areas.
-No cap on Skills
-Decently large amount of items, enemies and places
-Global 2x experience when someone uses a 2x experience buff (This makes it less of a "Pay to win" game.)
-Completely player run economy
-Mods that make the User interface more friendly and makes multiple actions possible. (Mods are maintained by players.)
-Cross platform. ( Runs through browsers, Steam, a Downloadable .exe, and an app on Android. Can be played literally anywhere.)
-Most experienced players help out by answering questions to those who ask.
-All items that can be bought with real money can also be bought with ingame currency from other players. (You don't have to spend real money to get the paid items.)
-Party questing, as well as PvP.
-The ability to subscribe and unsunscribe to multiple chat rooms. (Less annoying when you don't see bothersome people.)
On that note. There are some people who complain about the mass amount of bans/mutes that happen in the chat. That is in the basic chat and usually it's full of people trolling and asking to get banned or muting by blatantly disregarding the rules. It is possible to change chats and go to chats where the rules are much more lax. The mods are all pretty friendly and only bring down the hammer when completely needed.
Cons:
-It is a huge grind (That is the intent of the game though so if you don't like grinds this game is not for you.)
-The community is pretty small (Some may see this as a good thing, making it more tight knit.)
-The antibot system is seriously annoying. (However, the do compensate the annoyance with experience which means you can train other skills and use the captcha experience to train other things.)
-There is little to no animation in the game.
-Can't cut all trees even though they are shown (This is more of a minor annoyance of mine as someone who Woodcuts mainly.)
tl;dr: It's a casual, grindy game that you can sink 100s of hours into playing with a small-ish community that is generally pretty friendly. Only a few minor annoyances.

-Headache inducing for the impatient or intolerant. I'm very patient and decided I was straight up wasting my time after 6 straight hours. Those hours feel like they disappeared really fast.
-Grindfest, timesink, and nothing else. This game is excellent for anyone who likes grinding and being mindless. This game IS grinding.
-The market is kinda fun but that's about it. I enjoyed selling materials to get some good starter items but.. meh.
-There isn't really any combat that takes place unless you consider trading a single attack with enemies until you or they die to be fighting. There are no abilities or mechanics. It's click and wait just like everything else.
-I played to level 30 and couldn't figure out how to make anything more than the tutorial items. Maybe I missed something. This wasn't a big deal as I wouldn't waste a minute crafting. The system, UI, and inventory already deterred me from that.
-Inventory space is a big problem. Materials do not stack so after 10 minutes of AFK farming a node you get to run back to the bank to unload/sell. Items need to stack at least somewhat.
-Collecting materials would be an idle task if it weren't for their awful bot-prevention system. You get captchas randomly and if you miss 5 in a row, you get permabanned so you can't just afk while you collect resources slower than mollasses. Most of your experience collecting is resources is watching "You failed..." messages roll up your chat box.
-Completing the captchas gives you a point that you can allocate to any of your skills. If you miss a captcha, you've essentially missed out on 2 of these points. This is the first and last time I play a game that shoves captchas in my face.
Also, I wouldn't exactly look to this game for immersion but popping up a captcha is an easy way to break it. You're playing a fantasy game and then suddenly your looking at a picture of a house number. Apparently they're so afraid of botters that they're willing to do this. A bot would be better off playing this game anyway since players basically replicate one.
1/10 Stay away.

I haven't reviewed a lot of games on Steam (if any) but after seeing so many negative reviews and having my own opinions, I felt a need to review Street Fighter V.
People have been expressing concern with many things from online gameplay, to controller issues, and lack of content.  I totally agree with the rage quitting and controller issues, and it's good that people are voicing their concerns so Capcom notices (although to be fair, my Qanba Q4 works just fine).  What frustrates me though is seeing how many people are annoyed by the lack of content.
If you look at SFV from a game design standpoint, it's VERY well thought out and removed a lot of the things people didn't like in SFIV (vortex, 1 frame links, powerful option selects, etc).  Yes there is a lack of one player content, but that's not what we should be complaining about and it doesn't mean they need to offer it less than full price.
What Capcom has done is like League of Legends or DOTA. They sell are selling you an expanding platform, and this was expressed many times by Capcom representatives.  They never said this game will be decked out with features at the start, neither did Riot, and neither did Valve. The only difference is how these companies are selling the product.
Riot and Valve give it for free and make you pay for what you want on the way. Capcom makes you pay for the platform and receive everything free. Same business model, different method of receiving money.  Considering the backlash Capcom has received for paid DLC before and the eSports route they're looking to take, this makes a lot of sense.  Also keep in mind the majority of features people are begging for will be here in a few weeks (arcade, trials, more characters, etc).
If you want to buy this game next month with Arcade mode, then go ahead and do that.  Want to wait until story mode in June? By all means!  But personally I want to enjoy a great game now and receive the content as it comes.

Town of Salem is another Mafia and Werewolf, chat-based game. It's addicting, I don't even know why.
Gameplay revolves around lie and deceit, sometimes on trust, but expect that trust to be shattered on random occasions. As such,
Use every caution when playing with teens. Thankfully there's a filter and report function for deterring such toxicity.
To win, you need to see your role and objectives, then act accordingly. More often than not, this requires plenty of experience on examining people's behavior and try to adapt or manipulate them to get your goal done. While it seems easy, in reality it's not. You will see people's reaction very different than you have hoped, thus failing your objective. There are bunch of roles to learn, ranging from good roles e.g Jailor, Medium to badasses (is that even a word?) e.g Mafia, Serial Killer. The roles contradict each others, heck even good guy can kill good guy in chaos, making it confusing. Logic is necessary before you judge.
It's recommended to read the roles carefully and check the wiki every now and then if you get lost somehow.
There are basically two game modes, normal (fun sessions) or ranked (oh-so-damn serious sessions). You need to get certain threshold to unlock the ranked match, which is expected  as thorough knowledge of the game is necessary so you don't ruin others' experience during ranked match.
This version of Town of Salem on Steam is coded on Adobe AIR of which naturally has different issue than, say, outdated graphic/sound drivers. The most common complaint is the inability to even launch the game due to Adobe AIR issue. I honestly think they should've coded this with different engine/programming language. However, due to low requirements, even toasters can run the game. I've had success launching the game on Intel HD-based machine myself.
Some other annoying issues for me personally are:
- inability to minimize the game completely, as it runs on borderless window that can't be minimized. Can be forced into background/inactive window, but that's all.
- You'll also get kicked if you're AFK in normal menu (not in a match with other players) something that I can't understand myself.
- Also, there are random disconnects that force you to restart the game because you stuck in one menu and unable to open, say, lobby or join match.
- Soundtracks are repetitive and boring.
- Microtransactions are shoved on your face. While it's not required to play the game or give any advantage whatsoever, it is annoying to see the pop up every time.
Salem has the data saved on cloud/server-based, so you won't have to worry about your game data unless they shut down the server. You just need to take care of your Steam login and you're set. And to date, the game's still being developed. As of today, I read the news post about new role update about Vampire/Vampire Hunter, which is good knowing it'll add another layer of strategies and... lies.
A bit note of game's replayability - it's very high. Although the mechanic stays the same from session to session, it's not similar experience as you're dealing with different people every time on different sessions (unless you're playing with all friends). Good stuff really.
Now for pricing, for me it seems to be appropriately priced. This Steam version contains in-game coins equal to 5 USD, while the free version (browser version) does not offer such. I got the copy from recent Bundlestars' bundle, though, very cheap around 5 USD for like 9 games.
So, while generally I can appreciate and recommend this game, there are several negative points that must be addressed above. Overall, it will be fun session should you try to play the game.

This is an updated review as I now have the game working and my old review isn’t really relevant anymore.  Originally thumbs downed.  After troubleshooting, I found the issue with running PA:Titans on Windows 10 was caused by Crossfire.  You can find the details of this issue on Ubers forums:
And now for the review (completely subjective and separate from any opinions I have of Uber as a developer):
Now that I have actually played Titans, I can finally talk about the game itself.  I have to say, I am thoroughly enjoying this game.  The gameplay is better.  The UI is better.  The new units are good and create a lot of new tactical possibilities that simply don’t exist in vanilla PA.  A couple units are pretty much throwaways, but others you will find to be integral and regular fielders.  Such as the Tesla bot.  As a tier one bot unit, it's cheap, has high health, great damage and is relatively fast.  Making it an excellent early game spam rush unit.  The new naval units drastically improve naval combat.  The new orbital units are a very welcome inclusion. The new titans themselves, are well implemented.  They’re powerful, but not overpowered.  They’re both game changers and not game changers.  They can sometimes seem like they are a little too easy to build too early.  But they can be countered.  However, as much as I’ve grown to love it, the Ragnarok Doomsday Titan is a little too easy to build.
Seriously, this is probably the most devastating unit in the game.  But has created one of the funniest scenarios I’ve ever experienced in a game.  I was playing AI Skirmish against 3 AI’s in a huge solar system.  Two of the AI’s were on the planet with me pounding me from both sides.  I’m losing the battle on the starting planet.  I’m cutting my losses and going to bail out.  But by this point, they’ve taken orbital superiority of the planet and I’m not getting off the planet by launching into orbit.  Thankfully, early on in the match I had sent a couple orbital fabricators to the metal planet to build a stargate on it.  So I have a couple fabricators building a stargate on the starting planet and any others I can spare building a Ragnarok Titan.  The stargate on the metal planet finally finishes.  I activate the link and send my commander through with a few units and fabricators for defense while I rebuild.  Just as this is happening the Ragnarok finally finishes.  My going away present for the 2 victors is about to be unwrapped.  At this point I realize that I’m now wearing rather sadistic grin on my face.  I close the gate behind me and 60 seconds later, the planet pops.  Eliminating both of the AI commanders that were kicking the crap out of me in one shot.  Needless to say I was lmao for a few minutes.  Then focused on fighting the last AI.
I had repeated games where I was finding that I would win, but I would often win by a different method each time.  Sometimes, by covertly building a stargate in an unoccupied spot on a planet, bring in fabricators, build a Ragnarok and leave before they ever knew I was even there.  Some times by smashing moons or asteroids into planets.  Sometimes with the annihilaser on the metal planet.  Sometimes with traditional warfare.  I never felt forced down any one path.  And it was devilishly fun every time.
Simply put, this game is outstanding. This is the definitive version of Planetary Annihilation. Do I recommend this game.  Absolutely!

Here are some notes and context on the current situation between Uber and its community and how the situation is affecting Titans:
This so called expansion is damn expensive considering what it offers. It should've been marketed as DLC and not a full standalone game/expansion.  Although I can understand why they did it.  The original PA caught a lot of flak and it showed in the reviews.  But it caught that flak, not due to the quality of the game (which admittedly still needed a lot of work), but because of the way Uber treated its community.  Such as Uber attempting to start up another kickstarter without actually finishing PA.  And then in an attempt to call a technical, they claimed PA as fully launched, but released it without key promised features, such as offline mode, requiring an always online connection in order to play the game.  If that wasn’t bad enough, they would flat out refuse to answer the community when they were questioned about these issues.  And on top of that, the people who were talking to the community were often aggressive, offensive and overtly rude.  As a result, a lot of the original PA store page reviews showed the bad blood between the community and Uber and reflected how the community felt about this treatment by Uber.  The thing is, Uber did eventually come around.  They finally released offline mode for PA, replaced the people responsible for interacting with and working with the community (and for the better might I say.  A huge improvement) and continued adding and updating content to PA.  Uber has for quite a while now been mending fences and turning their act around.  The problem, is that the reviews on the PA store page were never updated by the original writers to reflect this and painted a picture of the game that was no longer representative of the games current state.  So, as I said, while I don’t agree with the way they’ve marketed this standalone expansion, I do understand why they took the approach they did.
Fast forward to today and Uber again have put themselves at odds with the community.  Look, I understand that they as a developer need to make money.  We get that.  Everyone gets that.  But Uber need to understand that they are where they are because of the community.  Because when they asked for help, the community rose up and backed them.  Then during early access (EA), new members kept them going by buying the game in EA.  But they didn’t simply support the game for the cost of a game for released retail prices.  They paid well over the value of the game to get EA with Uber charging more during EA than any other developer I’ve ever seen.  There’s no bones about it.  The prices Uber was charging were downright extortionate.  So you can imagine how people would feel when Titans is released, Kickstarter backers get it free, but EA backers are charged for it.  They should’ve given it for free to their Alpha and Beta EA buyers as well.  Their Alpha EA buyers at the very least.  Given what Alpha purchasers paid during EA, it’s insulting for them to be told that they need to pay for the Titans upgrade.  It’s wrong and this is not how you should treat your community.  The alpha buyers gave you a lot and they kept you going through EA.  They deserve to be treated a hell of a lot better than that.  They need to be treated with the respect they deserve.  It’s as simple as that.
To put it quite blunt, you’re shooting yourself in the foot Uber.  It’s a contradiction to release Titans as a standalone expansion in order for it to get up-to-date reviews that are representative of the games current state and then pull what is quite frankly, a d**k move.  You wanted a clean slate and then immediately pulled the same kind of stunt and recreated the exact same scenario that resulted in the state of the reviews on the original PA store page.  The very thing you are trying to distance yourselves from now.  The reviews on the store page are not made by professional reviewers who are required to stay on point and maintain a professional level of objectivity.  They are made by the community and the community is an emotional beast.  Treat them right, and your store page will glow from the love.  Treat them poorly and your store page will show the communities wrath.  You shot yourselves in the foot.  But you still have time to mend the situation.

I paid $40 for this game.  I didn't get the previous game, and didn't kickstart Planetary Annihilation, and never played Total Annihilation or SupCom or SupCom2.  My most similar game to PA is "AI War", which has a similar economy but more tech, way more turrets, and per-unit pop limits.
PA is unlike most other RTSes in many ways: you can zoom all the way out to a solar system view, with multiple orbital bodies that are all useful.  You have picture-in-picture.  You can give factories not just a waypoint for newly built units but also actions ("patrol this area; patrol the entire planet; go through this teleporter; assist this unit"), and put them on continuous build.  You lose when your commander dies rather than when all of your structures die, and your commander can build and fight and move (and move underwater, and fire a super weapon with AoE, and fire guided missiles at aircraft).  You have no 'supply' to limit the number of units you can have.  Resources are not exhausted.  There are no factions except in the storyline (or vignetteline since the only narrative appeal are the amusing backstories about the various commanders).  Units have (wildly) varying sight ranges and moving-while-firing is the norm.  You can achieve sea, air, and space dominance.  You can reclaim the metal left by your own and your enemy's wrecks on the batlefield.  You can build a conga-line of Manhattans (slow moving groundbourne nukes that explode on death), have one die, and then watch the chain reaction of explosions reach all the way back to your base and kill your commander.  You can design solar systems with a time limit: in ten minutes, the only two planets will smash into each other, so either prevent that or win the game by then.  There are 'bad spawns', 'good spawns', and 'godly spawns'.  There are spawns which encourage you to develop one way or another - for example, if you spawn on an island in a big ocean, you might want a navy.  There are spawns which are relatively easily fortified, with ramps that you can wall off.
PA is like other RTSes in many ways: you're playing from the word 'go', balancing early econ with early defenses and combat ability.  You can rush, be rushed, and can defend against rushes.  You can scout, see that the other guy has gone straight to building a Tech 2 structure, and can either match him with your own greedy construction or can punish his greed by sending an early, Tech 1 attack force.  You can try to contain an enemy, surrounding him with your forces and preventing him from expanding.  You can attack an enemy's econ and try to starve him out.  You can see that your enemy has invested in a unit and, in response, focus production on a unit that fares well against it.
The real game seems to be multiplayer with a dozen players on multiple worlds.  I'm still gearing up for that.  There's also 1v1 ranked matches.  I've played only one of those so far and quite enjoyed it.  There are also AI skirmish matches and Galactic War.  Galactic War seems to have a bad rap, but it's just a series of AI skirmish matches with limited tech, but also techs unique to this mode, like an AI ally, a tech that improves the combat capabilities of your commander, a tech that makes your vehicles twice as fast, and so on.  On Normal, it is so easy that it's basically just an extended tutorial that lets you try different things out.  I just wish that the unlock system were less random, so that you could more easily shake things up with different Commander loadouts.  The most charming bit of Galactic War, again, are the Commander backstories.  Such-and-such commander hears voices... probably because his brain was stitched together from the parts of five different enemy commanders.  This other commander does this thing which "is super annoying".
I hope that Uber continue to develop PA.  How about multiplayer with random Galactic War 'techs'?  How about real factions?  I hope that people get tired of 'reviewing' Titans based purely on unhappiness with Uber.  Waah, why don't they work for free?  Why don't I get a pony for paying $80 when Uber was promising that prices would lower, but that they only wanted the most invested players at the time?  Why aren't Uber so much better devs that they could've made this game a year ago instead of more recently?
If you're looking for video of this game, check out 'MasterofRofleness' on Youtube.  Large, skillful games with a lot of players on VOIP, with a lotta banter.

If you are as confused by the explanation of this game as I was, pull up a chair.
First things first, though: the review. Did you like Mass Effect or (insert equivalent Bioware game) and, like me, took every possible opportunity to find as much of the dialog as possible? Are you a person who would let a really interesting plot, story and characterization apologize for lacking gameplay? Can you play a game like To the Moon and end thinking "Wow, can’t wait to play it again" rather than "This 'game' cheated me out of the 'game'"? If you answered yes to one or more of these, buy this "game."
Kinda spoiler, but not really since they tell you this all before even starting the game. Since nobody says these things, I was incredibly confused about what the game really was before purchasing and almost didn’t. Read on so that doesn’t happen to you...
The game is a strangely absorbing, 4th-wall-breaking interactive story where you, the player, body snatch (v) a dude in one of an infinite number of alternate dimensions (meaning you can reload or start over from scratch as much as you want, but the setting/characters/whatnot all stay the same) and play through a series-of-unfortunate-events scenario through his eyes, yet maintain your memories and are fully capable of telling everybody you’re just a body pilot playing a video game. Think Outer Limits or Twilight Zone and you won’t be too far from the truth. There is an organization on the far end of this dimensional rift called Consortium that thinks it’s cute to name all its members after chess pieces and then expect the "pawns" to be emotionally stable members of the team. Honestly, I think the concept is clever, but it makes it very difficult to remember who everybody is; kind of a big issue with characterization this strong.
Anywho, the problem most people had with this game is that it’s not complete. The game abruptly ends damn near without warning in what I would consider to be the climax and then tells you "To be continued..." They do kinda mention this in the description, but don’t make it as obvious as other similar games like the Walking Dead, Broken Age or Life is Strange. They say it’s a "trilogy," which implies three complete games. No, this game is not complete. Again: nothing wrong with an episodic method of release, but that ending really did deflate my balloon in a very anticlimatic way...
I still recommend this, though, even though it’s incomplete because it’s still an enjoyable experience and I am very much looking forward to the sequel/continuation announced just this January.

It's not Grand Theft Auto and that's also not an criticism. A spiritual successor to the 'True Crimes' series, Sleeping Dogs is a rebirth of what the True Crimes game SHOULD have been like. An open world game of this genre that takes place outside of the United States (or an implied) is a fresh and nice change of scenery. Sleeping Dogs takes place in Hong Kong, the home base of the Chinese Triads. You play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop that walks a very thin line between loyalites. Sleeping Dogs takes on the Hong Kong cop genre and does a fantastic job of telling you a story backed with fun gameplay.
The visuals of the game is solid and it is to be expected out of any game with Square Enix label on it. Especially in cutscenes, everything is crisp. Which is important for a story driven game such as this one. In game graphics shows the enviroment very well. When it rains, the clothing on Wei does get wet and it shows. Little details, like blood and bruises after getting into a brawl shows up on Wei's face and on his clothing as well.  Damage to cars is admittedly, pretty standard in these games. Paint will be scratched up if you brush up too closely to another car and bullet holes will show up if shot at. Visuals are at its finest at the most important aspects of the game, while some little details could have used a little more work.
Gameplay might be a little different from what people expect from an open world game of this type of genre. While you can go on shooting rampages and crime spree when you are free roaming, it isn't anything like the calibur of GTA. You don't start out with a gun or have any places to buy weapons, melee combat is the name of the game in Sleeping Dogs. You'll be punching, kicking and slamming your enemies down on the ground alot. The melee combat is fairly firmilar to the Arkham games, but isn't as stylish. They mix it up a bit by throwing different types of enemies, like certain enemies cannot be grabbed and certain enemies dish out more damage than others. Enemies could have used more work and variations. You can upgrade your melee skins by collecting Jade Statues, which unlocks new melee combo strings or get triad upgrades which you get buffs and more combo strings. Combat is passable in this game and you shouldn't be detered by the fact it isn't just like the Arkham games.
Sleeping Dogs is a very story driven game. You play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop on a mission to infiltrate the ranks of the Triad. Wei throughout the game is faced with conflicting loyalities, he has a personal vendetta to settle with one of the members and has to deal with his growing attachment towards the triads. The story and setting really does feel like a hong kong cop drama.
Overall, Sleeping Dogs is a solid buy. It has enough side missions to extend gameplay. Some of the best side missions are the street races. It is a nice change of pace from triple A titles. Its definitely a cult hit. Definitely worth putting in your library of games. Sleeping Dogs is an experience that won't disappoint you.
Sleeping Dogs has quite a few DLCs with it, here is a list of DLCs that is worth getting.
1. Year of the Snake. A post game DLC that gives Wei a police mission to stop something big going down in the Chinese New Years.
2. Nightmare on North Point. A stand alone DLC that has Wei fighting Chinese vampires and a vengeful spirit of a dead and forgotten triad leader.
3. Zodiac Tournament. A DLC that is intergrated with the main game. A throwback to the 70s with corny Kung Fu action that pits Wei with some of the worlds finest martial artist and a corny plot. (Story has nothing to do with the main story)
4. Street Racer Pack. Adds 3 more challenging races to the game. (Not worth getting at full price, wait for a sale on this one)
The rest of the DLC are almost all cosmetic, unless you really want more outfits and access to certain guns for Wei, its better to buy them when there is a sale. Not worth getting at full price.
It's just a great game.

It's fun, but there are easily fixable problems that have been flat out neglected.
Pros:
+Good gameplay
+Large land area
+Decent variety of roads
+Decent variety of buildings
+You can zoom in to get a close look of your city, which I find appealing
Cons
-Bad public transport menu. It is WAY too confusing to build a metro line. Also, the terminuses are not needed in my opinion.
-HORRIBLE OPTIMIZATION!! i5-4690K and a GTX 970 and this thing still lags like crazy! I swear enabling anti-aliasing broke the game! Also, with graphics not that good, you would expect it to run better.
-Leisure. Leisure. Leisure. This is one problem that will never go away. I feel like a Six Flags every block would not satisfy the citizens.
-No free-flowing traffic options. I did my best to make an interchange, but nope. It looks like crud. I wish I could install a mod to fix this, but....
-No Steam Workshop support. The game you get is the game you get. Nothing to add on to it to make it optimized for modern machines or for a McDonalds in your town. You get none of that.
-Towns can be slow to grow. Not a huge problem for me, but it just takes a little longer then I would like.
-OmniCorp. F**k you, OmniCorp. Trading with them is like selling your soul to the devil. Unless you build another town to trade with, but then they have to trade with someone, right?
-What is this "Can't build below the water table" crap? I can't make any tunnels in my downtown because of this, which leads traffic to just suck.
Overall, just get something better. Cities XL Platinum is a decent game, and it has fine gameplay. However, there are too many things wrong with it to justify paying $20 for it. It is fun and runs smooth at first, but upon advancing to 250,000 population, you will see many graphics problems, many leisure problems, many problems in general. Of course, I could just be bad at the game. But I think not.
Fair warning: If you do decide to get this game, it will not run well on modern machines. It doesn't matter whether you have a GeForce 8800, TITAN X or Fury X, performance will be the same crap across the board.
I would recommend Cities:Skylines. That game is a city builder done right.

Though this game is not for everyone, it's got a multitude of activities to do besides combat. Unlike in some other free-to-play MMOs. Though these activites aren't very interactive. Fishing for example; a popular thing people in this game do is cook and sell fish for money. You fish by equiping your fishing rod and walking up to a fishing hole. Then, you wait for your inventory to be filled with fish, and walk away. Eventually your fishing skill will increase, and you'll be able to catch more expensive fish. So, yes, this game is a grindfest. But, due to the areas you can visit. The rewarding level system, and many options with those activities; it feels like you're doing more then grinding most of the time. There are many skills to learn and upgrade in this game, such as mining, farming, breeding, etc. They level up the more you do them, and every now and then, a point is rewarded to you, and you may give it to what ever stat you like. A combo that works suprisingly well, as both tend to feel rewarding. The music in this game is exellent, and feels medieval. The graphics are lovely, if you're in to 2D retro graphics. The game's main flaw, is how it gets boring after you get to high leveled. Though thanks to the many play styles you can take, it has some replay ability. There's more stuff to this game I did not touch on. Such as player housing, and the player market. But, I want you to discover the rest of the game for yourself. If you deside it's your cup of tea.

Starbound is, in my opinion an amazing game, even though it is in early access. The music is some of the best I have ever heard in a video game, it fits the theme well and doesn't annoy me or give me a metaphorical headache, it feels victorious, creepy or exploratory.
The game itself has a lot of care put into it, and it shows, even though it is not yet fully released, a lot of bugs are fixed in each release as well as careful consideration given to the design, in my opinion.
One of the best things about this game though is that it has fully working mod support from the get go, therefore allowing anyone to add anything into it, and the creativity of the community has truly astounded me with the races, ships, extra items, clothing changes, colour additions, quests etc etc etc.
All in all, I fully recommend this game, especially if you like Sci-Fi, but even if you don't, staring up at the stars at night on a far-flung planet whilst emotive music plays can give one some very genuine, relaxing and/or euphoric feelings as it did for me.
Finally, it's avaliable on all major operating systems and will be avaliable on a few of the consoles on release, you have no excuse not to buy it if you have the money and this is your genre/type of game, in my opinion. ^^

Town of Salem is another Mafia and Werewolf, chat-based game. It's addicting, I don't even know why.
Gameplay revolves around lie and deceit, sometimes on trust, but expect that trust to be shattered on random occasions. As such,
Use every caution when playing with teens. Thankfully there's a filter and report function for deterring such toxicity.
To win, you need to see your role and objectives, then act accordingly. More often than not, this requires plenty of experience on examining people's behavior and try to adapt or manipulate them to get your goal done. While it seems easy, in reality it's not. You will see people's reaction very different than you have hoped, thus failing your objective. There are bunch of roles to learn, ranging from good roles e.g Jailor, Medium to badasses (is that even a word?) e.g Mafia, Serial Killer. The roles contradict each others, heck even good guy can kill good guy in chaos, making it confusing. Logic is necessary before you judge.
It's recommended to read the roles carefully and check the wiki every now and then if you get lost somehow.
There are basically two game modes, normal (fun sessions) or ranked (oh-so-damn serious sessions). You need to get certain threshold to unlock the ranked match, which is expected  as thorough knowledge of the game is necessary so you don't ruin others' experience during ranked match.
This version of Town of Salem on Steam is coded on Adobe AIR of which naturally has different issue than, say, outdated graphic/sound drivers. The most common complaint is the inability to even launch the game due to Adobe AIR issue. I honestly think they should've coded this with different engine/programming language. However, due to low requirements, even toasters can run the game. I've had success launching the game on Intel HD-based machine myself.
Some other annoying issues for me personally are:
- inability to minimize the game completely, as it runs on borderless window that can't be minimized. Can be forced into background/inactive window, but that's all.
- You'll also get kicked if you're AFK in normal menu (not in a match with other players) something that I can't understand myself.
- Also, there are random disconnects that force you to restart the game because you stuck in one menu and unable to open, say, lobby or join match.
- Soundtracks are repetitive and boring.
- Microtransactions are shoved on your face. While it's not required to play the game or give any advantage whatsoever, it is annoying to see the pop up every time.
Salem has the data saved on cloud/server-based, so you won't have to worry about your game data unless they shut down the server. You just need to take care of your Steam login and you're set. And to date, the game's still being developed. As of today, I read the news post about new role update about Vampire/Vampire Hunter, which is good knowing it'll add another layer of strategies and... lies.
A bit note of game's replayability - it's very high. Although the mechanic stays the same from session to session, it's not similar experience as you're dealing with different people every time on different sessions (unless you're playing with all friends). Good stuff really.
Now for pricing, for me it seems to be appropriately priced. This Steam version contains in-game coins equal to 5 USD, while the free version (browser version) does not offer such. I got the copy from recent Bundlestars' bundle, though, very cheap around 5 USD for like 9 games.
So, while generally I can appreciate and recommend this game, there are several negative points that must be addressed above. Overall, it will be fun session should you try to play the game.
