Overview: First Person RPG/Adventure
The Good
+The main selling point of this game is that the choices you make affect the story in multiple ways. These choices have a significant impact in how things play out and what scenarios you are put in. Something that is very lacking in today's modern games. Too many games claim to give you freedom of choice however many of these games lead you to the exact same place/story segment and it feels cheap. Consortium however is different, decisions you make in the beginning of the game can adversely affect you later on without you knowing it. I have played through this game a few times now and I am very impressed with the degree of how the decisions you make have a major impact on what goes on.
+ Its one thing to have choices, but if the scenarios are boring the game wouldn't be interesting. Consortium does a great job of putting you in some really great situations. These situations will really make you think and the outcomes are not always so obvious.
+ The developers really wanted to explain everything in the game. The game features an in-game console that explains a lot of the history /characters/story to really immerse you in the game. In addition all the characters seem to act realistically given their surroundings. It wasn't until I went online and read what other people were seeing that it made me go back into the game to see how much attention to detail the developers put into such a small game.
+Good replay value, play the game again and choose different options, speak to people differently and see what happens!
+ Good voice acting
+ I was very surprised by how good the music is.
+ Included is a virtual reality mini game, it is completely optional and provides a nice change of pace to a game that is mostly about talking to people.
The Average:
The developers included partial controller support, sadly the controller doesn't seem to work in menus/inventory making controller support rather useless. You are given two choices of button layouts, you cannot remap any buttons for the controller. Just stick with keyboard/mouse.
The art style is rather ugly. It just doesn't look right, the game isn't very impressive technically either. I understand this is an independent developer and they don't have a big budget but that doesn't really excuse them for choosing such a poor art style.
User interface looks cheap.
Most of the back story is hidden behind information console.
Somewhat short if you don't bother to read anything in the information console.
The Bad
In a game that is all about making choices and replaying the game to see how things play out differently, it would be nice to skip dialogue. Having to listen to the same things over and over again is awful.
Conclusion
I really want the is game to do well because the game has some really good design decision wrapped up in a poor looking presentation.

Let's face it; this is quite similar to all the other city games; so there is not really that much to say on the gameplay.
I enjoy play this game, because it is extremely simple. You start, get your buildings unlocked and wait that people get in the city; then they start to demand jobs, and you create industrial areas; then you unlock the skilled workers (office people), and once they flock in your city, you give them some office areas, and so on until you unlock the whole array of buildings.
There are plenty, but mostly they are the same type, just with higher density. It is fun to see how the city grow, but at one point you hit the wall, where you have no more money to continue to grow. The biggest flaw of this game is that it give you plenty to start, but then it doesn't teach you how to get revenues. You may want to try various tactics before you get what you expect; this is time consuming at times, so the newbies may get surprised to see the city grow so fast, and then see that they can't do anything else because the money coming in are barely covering for the structures that you have (in particular public structures take quite a lot of resources...open few hospital and you will see the bill!).
Gameplay is fun; not sure why peopllpl don't enjoy the game...if you expect to get a masterpiece, keep in mind that not even Sim City from Maxis was able to give you a decent experience. The game is worth the discounted price, but if you pay it full price, you may be a bit disappointed.
Performances are great; some framerate drop happens here and there but no crash nor problems that cause you to get stuck. Graphics are great; compared to Sim City from Maxis and most of the other city games. Zoom in at street level and you will get a smile on your face.
City size is not an issue, and you can trade too, which is something interesting to do; here you don't have meteorites but you have to deal with class balancing; waste management and overall keep an eye to not make a residential area close to a dump and expec that people won't complain.
AI is quite good too, looks realistic, and respond to changes; although keep in mind that it is still a sim city AI type, so keep that in mind.
OVerall, if you never played Cities XL, give it a try, it is worth 10 bucks. If you want something super polished and optimized; there is actually not really that much out there, beside Cities Skyline, which is another good game but it is not leap and bounds ahead of this.

Buy This:
If you love Grand Theft Auto or Saints Row styled games
If you want to experience some of the best hand to hand fighting in an action game
If you're looking for a unique locale for a game
Sleeping Dogs is a game in the Grand Theft Auto vein set in Hong Kong. It features a solid story with good voice acting, and some of the best hand to hand fighting I've experienced in a game of this genre. Often the player will find themselves in some kind of back alley brawl where several thugs will need to be dispatched by throwing them through phone booths, smacking them with huge fish or throwing them from a rooftop. It's incredibly satisfying and rarely got old.
Like all games of this genre, Sleeping Dogs features a ton of different mechanics and things to do in the city. There is racing,♥♥♥♥♥♥fighting, brawling, car and cloths shopping, etc. The amount of extracurricular aren't overwhelming as they can sometimes be in a game like this, and most can be ignored entirely if you're not a completionist.
The plot follows an undercover cop who works his way through the ranks of a local triad. He has to constantly battle with whether to serve the triad or the police as the plot continually goes through murky grey areas. In the end, there are some very memorable characters, and some moments are very powerful.
If you're looking to get something slightly more dialed back and a little different than Grand Theft Auto, I can't recommend this game enough. As a side note, however, I would strongly suggest having some kind of gamepad to play on.

It's story, characters, and world are just so full of heart and meaning. Every member of your party is an individual with their own dreams and desires, as well as their own problems and flaws. Over their journey, they struggle to overcome them, and being there as they change and grow is something magical.
I recommend this game not for its graphics or its combat, both which can be easily beaten by other games - but for the journey it takes you on. It's a journey full of emotions, morals, and creeds. It's a journey of violence, selfishness, and cruelty. But, most of all, it's a journey of logic versus emotions, and the divide between them.
This game balances its themes very well with its story and its characters, and it never loses track of itself. Things will happen that will leave your mouth hanging in surprise or wishing they never happened. There are moments of disaster and moments of crisis, but there are also precious moments of respite and joy. This balance will keep you going through thick and thin, and the way the game handles its emotional experience is what makes it beautiful.
+Great story. It shines with emotion, meaning, and purpose. One of the most impactful storylines I've experienced in a game in a long time.
+Great characters. Each one is incredibly different. You'll definitely find a favorite among them.
+Fantastic dialogic. I never skipped a line. Interactions are full of personality.
+Meaningful sidequests. Each one is very rewarding to go through and finish.
+Lovely music. By Motoi Sakuraba, the composer of Dark Souls.
+Amazing cutscenes. By ufotable, the studio behind Unlimited Budget Works.
-Early environments can be underwhelming.
-Combat can feel too mashy early on.

Pro:
----
+ Some refreshing ideas and game mecanics
+ nice story
+ some freedom on the map
+ no need to manually control time like in the old X-com games
Con:
----
- Accuracy: Extremely low accuracy will ruin your day. The guy who programmed this thought it was ok you could be body against body with an enemy, put a MINIGUN to its forehead and still not kill it, meaning you will still get eaten.
- Wallhacks: The enemy can stick weapons through walls and kick your teeth in from unexpected angles.
- Timer: The timer is way too short and puts so much pressure on the game it's not even enjoyable. It's not about having a cosy turn-based game like in the old games. It's about making ONE wrong move, costing you an hour of your life because you failed the map and you made zero progress because of it.
- Fake Freedom: The idea you have the freedom to pick the mission you like is an illusion. If you don't pick the preprogrammed path, you will fail the story goal and you will fail the game. I'm already 2 missions behind and lacking the points to unlock them.
- Snipers who couldn't hit the floor if they fell on it.
- Range: There is only 1 range in XCOM2, and it's called mid-range. You can't get a hit on anything else than mid-range, you can't even get a partial hit (Jagged-alliance does this much better).
Conclusion:
------------
If you think it's hard trying to cross a map while fighting 4 VS 4 against enemies who have AOE attacks while you have only 2 places to hide while controlling a 4 man team (/facepalm), then it will become harder when a shuttle lands behind you surrounding your team with another 3 or 4 enemies, all while having 3 turns to cross the map and reach the mission target, essentially making it impossible.
The A.I. is super strong in Xcom2 and your team of rookies has the accuracy of a bunch of drunks, while having to complete missions in literally a few turns.
I find it far from enjoyable.

Street Fighter IV in all its flavours, colours and editions is one ofn my favourite games ever. I've sunk hundreds of hours into each edition across a range of platforms, splurged on expensive arcade sticks and submitted fully to its beauty. So you can imagine my anticipation for Street Fighter V.
And you can imagine my disappointment.
Now, the game plays absolutely beautifully, it has to be said. But I'm not going to talk about that for two reasons: 1) its been pretty well artilcuated elsewhere and 2) you amount you will actually play the game will be limited as I'll explain below.
Its widely acknowledge that there is a paucity of game modes. Anyone who has been following this game will know this. I pre-ordered knowing it would be pretty barebones at launch.
What I didn't expect was how lousy connections would be. On release night I couldn't connect to Capcoms servers at all. The next night I managed to connect and despite being disconnected twice managed to get some games in. Since then I've not been able to get a match, whether waiting on the menu with fight request on or by selecting one of the 3 matchmaking options.
This is utterly unacceptable.
What infuriates me more is that several mainstream sites are following the lead from @SFV_server on twitter and their constant proclamations that the game is fixed. Its not. Its an absolute mess.
This is an online game where the online component does not work. That should tell you everything you need to know about picking this up.
As for Single Player, theres an atrocious story mode with overlong cut scenes consisting of awful scripts and concept art quality images. You get 2 - 3 fights, each fight lasting just one round, not two. You also get an frightfully dull survival mode. Oh and if you want to waiting for an online game in between, good luck! Matches tend to last around 20 seconds (difficulty is set painfully low) and fight request is paused during anything other than an actual match!
Its breaks my heart to write this, but I had to if for no other reason than to warn prospective Steam users and in the vain hope that something might be done about fixing it.

I bought this game intending to play versus people online. I have to say, even though there was a bit of a rocky start with the online servers, the game completely delivers on the multiplayer aspect of the game. The single player content is lacking.
The two main gripes I have with this game so far:
1. You are forced to play the tutorial. This was a really stupid decision, the tutorial is incredibly shallow and should be optional.
2. To unlock costume colors, you are forced to play the games survival mode. I would much rather unlock character items through multiplayer gameplay.
Gameplay is fun and easy to jump into. After several hours of playing, it really surpised me how different each character feels to each other. It doesn't feel like any character is a clone of another, even Ryu and Ken have very different playstyles. Even though some may say 16 characters aren't enough, I feel that each character feels complete and varied. I would much prefer a small roster of characters that are different, rather than a large roster of clones with minute differences.
As for the seemingly unanimous consensus that this game is a beta, I completely agree. I don't really feel that is a negative for this game however, it gives me hope that there will be fairly regular updates by Capcom, but we'll see how it plays out. They seem to have a number of general dates for character releases and content updates, but I am always skeptical of release schedules from gaming companies.
Now the mulitplayer. I love the fight request system and the ability to restrict fight request via connection type. The connections I have had to other players are generally very good. The net code seems drastically overhauled from USF4, but don't expect it to fix poor internet connectivity or poor attitudes (rage quitters).
Overall, I am quite happy with my purchase and would recommend that others do the same if they are looking for a solid multiplayer fighting experience. If you are looking for single player content, I would wait for some time or even recommend giving this game a pass.
Update:
1. Reliability of the netcode definitely didn't hold, I can only imagine what my opponents were dealing with if my connection seemed solid. (1-Sided rollback and lag spikes. It's a thing in this game.)
2. Constant server maintainence for no increase in CFN reliability. Disconnects are unpredictable and at times frequent. At least two days a week, the game is unavailable due to maintainance. If I hadn't ever worked in creating and designing network infrastructure I would say they are trying to fix it, but either Capcom is incompetent and hired a gerbil to find the reset button or they have seriously underfunded and underdeveloped the infrastructure they force everyone to use.
3. Always online required to use the DLC you have purchased (the previous issue doesn't help this). Definitely a software design issue, an incredibly very poor implementation for paid content.
4. Significant increase of microtransations and prices are definitely out of control.
5. Timed DLC releases for costume packs with "no plans for rerelease", a collector's nightmare.
6. No real way to gain fight money without grinding hours on ALL characters in single player modes and constantly playing ranked matches (for eternity).
7. Constant excuses for consistently missed delivery of pre-paid content.
8. Unwilling to listen to the community for the pre-paid content. (Purchase a season pass, find out months later that none of the upcoming or current content is what you wanted.)
9. Can easily be double charged for content bought (with money) on the CFN and then DLC containing the same content on Steam within less than a week timeframe (bought the CPT 2017 costumes before they were available as a DLC bundle pack on Steam). Steam holds Capcom responsible for refunding in-game purchases, Capcom support claims they don't know how to refund. I stopped buying from Ubisoft and EA because I didn't want to spend my time in the lab sorting through their DLC to figure out what I get. My time in the lab should be spent improving my game (It definitely needs it).
Definitely a drastic change in opinion of this game. I may have just been riding the high of having a fighting game released to Steam within the same timeframe of the console release and playing against a larger community due to cross platform gameplay. I was definitely being optimistic about their promises in hindsight, because I thought they had learned from their experience with Street Fighter X Tekken.
Capcom has proved they...
1) ...cannot create infrastructure to support paid online transactions with integrity.
2) ...are willing gouge their customers for EVERYTHING in the game like it's owed to them.
3) ...are unwilling to let their customers collect all the content within the game. (This isn't an MMO, why is anything a timed exclusive? Why not re-release the content every year for the same event with new content as well? No plans to re-release digital items is ridiculous this isn't a stock issue.)
4) ...are unable to learn from previous games they have created and re-introduce the same problems that have existed in their previous titles at the expense of their consumers.
I was very hopeful that the microtransactions from this game would lead to a regularly updated and improved experience. A year later and this has yet to be seen, tweaking balance changes aren't really what I am referring to (though many would argue that isn't being done either). I still enjoy the game, but I have realized how much I have spent with the hopes of funding better netcode, better optimization, better matchmaking, etc.
Unfortunately, I have already pre-purchased MvCi for Steam and if it is even slightly a similar experience, I will not purchase another game with a microtransaction model from them. They are not capable of integrity and supporting basic business practices. Capcom seems to want to be payed and treated like a AAA publisher at the consumer's expense, without investing into the creation of a AAA experience.

I completely recommend the game to any previous PA user, and to any user interested in RTS games.

I like the idea. I like slow open RPGs (both SP and MMOs) where main focus is on crafting. I also like the aesthetics.
The things I really don't like is the extremely tedious UI. I don't think that every game needs to solve UI problems the same way as other games, but I really can't get used to the inventory system: In order to put anything from your inventory to your stash you need to click on the object in question in STASH and click on "deposit" in stashes lower right corner... And If you do it wrong (click on your inventory like in any other game) you might destroy your eqipment.
The battles are very simple (I didn't mind that) but very unreactive. Once you are in the battle it's extremely difficult to escape... And you die... And you have to recraft your equipement. When it comes to dying in games I am of a very strong opinion that you need to deserve your death: When you die it should be always because YOU as a player didn't make the challenge. Accidental deaths simply doesn't do it for me. And every single death in this game was accidental. I accidently started a battle with wrong equipement in my hands and wasn't given a chance to change it mid combat, or I accidently started a battle with strong opponent. I never felt that I died because lack of my skills.
The whole core of the game is crafting. It's not interesting enough.
But the absolutely worst design decision in the game is definitely the captcha leveling system. During my whole play time I got about 20-30 captcha tests when my character progressed in skills. If you fail the test you will not "level up" and if you fail 5 times you will get banned. To begin with it's extremely tedious. Second: The game playes itself in your absence while you make the test. You will continue mining too long... And sometimes fight a opponent you want to escape from. Third: This system messes with the controlls. If you press "enter" one time too many and use arrows to move (or escape) you will be changing languages in chat instead. It's very hard to notice that. For most users it will simply look like you can't use your keybord any more.

A truly fantastic open world action game set in the refreshingly colorful city of Hong Kong. You play the role of an undercover cop trying to take down a notorious group of Triads.
The story is something to take note as there is no simple good cop / bad criminal side to it. The game does a fantastic job of showing you the side of what it means to be part of a Triad family and that the police isn't necessarily the enemy here, nor are the Triads. Doing missions and assignments for both sides will test your moral standings and alignment. The story is good enough and has enough twists and turns to make you stay interested in finding out what happens at the end.
Gameplay wise, you will primarily be falcon punching your enemies or killing them with your horrible karaoke singing skills. The game does include guns but is primarily fighting focused. As per open world style, you can drive around the city looking for stuff to do. Options include but not limited to: driving for fun,♥♥♥♥♥♥fighting, dating, looking for shrines of health, delivering vehicles, participating in street races, learning fighting moves, hacking street cameras, karaoke, beating down groups of gangs, eating pork meat, drinking herbal tea, getting an erotic massage, buying clothes, yachting and I've probably missed half of the others.
So if you're in it for fighting, the drama of becoming a Triad gang member, the colorful Hong Kong city lights or just want to listen to some fantastic Chinese radio stations - be sure to pick up Sleeping Dogs, you will not be sorry.

A great game for those that love interactive stories in their games. Good writing, good characterization, and good voice acting come together to make a solid piece of video game storytelling. There are plenty of permutations in the story to justify multiple playthroughs, and your choices genuinely affect the way the story plays out. Considering the fact that there are so few games like this that focus on player choice, it's good to not only see it released, but to see that it is done very well, and in a unique way. For this alone, I would recommend the game.
Though the game contains combat, there isn't very much of it. This is a bit odd considering how much detail they tried to put into the system. In the higher difficulty levels, individual parts of your suit and body can be damaged, and you can repair/heal those specific parts. There's even an inventory system, wherein you can trade energy (which is used for repairs and energy weapons) for physical space to carry guns, ammo, etc.
Despite this level of detail, it isn't particularly polished. The AI spews fire everywhere while running around like headless chickens, and the inventory system is more annoying than it's really worth. The creators of the game either had a grander vision than they were able to actually execute, or they are just trying to establish the skeleton of the combat system for the future titles.
Don't get me wrong, the combat isn't unplayable or unfun, it's just nothing particularly special. This is not a AAA FPS.
It's also worthy to note that, when this game was first released, it had several game-breaking bugs. However, the vast majority of the bugs have been mopped up now, and I have had no trouble since the first few patches they released to fix the major bugs.

I bought Consortium after a favourable writeup on Rock Paper Shotgun, however I am inclined to disagree with that article.
Consortium is essentially two things. It is both a game, and an interactive art piece. And deserves to be looked at in terms of each.
As a game, Consortium is incredibly forgettable. The animations are jerky, the graphics are dated, and the bugs are frequent and irritating. There are a lot of interesting ideas there re: combat, with customisable loadouts that change how you play. And besides one possible battle there's not really anywhere in the game where combat exists, outside of the VR training sim. Which is a shame.
As a piece of art, it walks the line between being a meaningful experience and pretentious. Unfortunately this one falls on the side of being pretentious. It has a "play this game a thousand times with tiny variations to see all it has to offer" rhetoric, which would be fine if the game part worked well. But it doesn't. And attempting to experience other parts of the story through the experience of others actually gets censored by the developers on the steam forums. Want to know who the murderer was, but can't piece it together? Play the game repeatedly until you find out! No thanks devs, just let someone else tell me what I've missed. That's MY choice, not yours; thinking otherwise shows that the developers have no real understanding about creating art for the consumption of others.
Consortium gets the concept right, but the execution is not quite there. It is ultimately a forgettable experience that is begging for someone else to take the core idea and do it justice. Not worth buying, not worth playing. Skip it.

Despite all of the negativity from launch day, I had a coupon from Greenmangaming in my e-mail to get this at 25% off.  I was torn because there was a chance my arcade stick wouldn't work and that I wouldn't even really be able to play but I bought it anyway after reading about the potential:
* Cross Platform play from PC and PS4 meant I didn't need to buy a PS4 just to play with my friends.  Wish more games did this.
* No more Hyper, Turbo, Ultra since Capcom will be releasing base system changes to everyone and the only upgrades will be new characters and outfits.
* Needing to pay for new characters everytime wouldn't be the end of the world but Capcom is going the route of more recent games where you can use in game "fight money" currency to unlock characters that you want or pay to quick unlock if you don't have the patience or time.
Most confusing thing from the start was actually trying to get past the Terms and Conditions page.  I was mashing keys on my keyboard expecting Enter or Space to accept but as it turns out after talking to my friend, I had to press B because this was mapped to A or Ok.  Input mapping was pretty terrible but once I learned GHJ were punches and BNM were kicks, I was able to get by.
Could the launch have been better? Of course, but with that said, I was able to set up my old x360 Hori DoA4 stick to my PC and connect it to Joy2Key so I could play.  Hooked up with a friend in a battle lounge and played 10 straight matches without any lag or issues.  I was disconnected a few times randomly just playing story mode and this would have been much more upsetting if I was doing survival mode since you lose all of your progress which is very disheartening and until the servers are more stable, I won't plan to even attempt this yet.
Looking forward to having more 1p content like challenge mode and the store to buy outfits but they say it's coming so I'll remain optomistic for now.
I then proceeded to try out ranked and casuals.  Won a few and lost a few.  It takes a little time after finding an opponent to actually connect and start the match (maybe 1-2 minutes) but having set the connection minimum to 4-5, I haven't experienced any major lag.
I also started exploring the Capcom network and I was happy to see I could pull replays from the currently top ranked players as well go through my history to see what I went wrong in my losses.
Would I recommend this to everyone? No.  But if you're into Street Fighter and want to get in for the long haul, I'd say it's worth it as there's only one way to go and hopefully that's up.  Again optomistic that the servers will be stable, there will be more characters and outfits and content in the near future.

Game feels Barebones at release.  You're basically paying $60 for an early access of the game, because most of their content will come out at March/June.

-Fighting feels nice, controls are responsive.
-(When matchmaking works*) You can get into online matches fairly quickly and improve upon one character as you play.
-(when you've got decent connections to your opponent*) Netcode is decent, no weird issues.  I noticed some weird crossplay issues if I ever got console users however.  felt like frames would skip or they would teleport for a few frames. It was weird to try and get used to.
-Story mode at the moment is basically just a tease of the promised story mode.  (Coming in June)
-Shoddy netcode/server connections.  If you disconnect you're booted out of whatever mode you are currently in. Long matchmaking, etc. (Being worked on apparently)
-No penalties for ragequits/disconnects at the moment.
-Game will sometimes fail to upload your match stats to the server.
-Lack of lobby selection.
-Weak steam integration,you cant invite or join other steam users. (wouldve been awesome to have this with some nice lobbies, with spectating; Mortal Kombat X-esque lobbies.)
-Character select is quirky, you have to select a main beforehand to play ranked. instead of being taken to a character menu. This also means you're going in blind as to who your opponent is playing.
-Survival mode is pretty boring. You have to grind all of the difficulties in order to unlock your color customizations for every character. The difficulty doesnt seem to change, you're just killing a ton of fodder.  The perks you can purchase with your survival score is a pretty neat idea, but it doesnt change anything up drastically. (Wouldve been awesome to see a BlazBlue Chronophantasma survival mode, where you can pick a character and customize them through the ordeal with equippable buffs or something.)
I have to not recommend this game at the moment. For the price point and what you're actually getting,  No.
If you're a die-hard fan of fighters and want to jump right into some online matches, sure. but even then, you're paying $60 for a 16 character roster and some iffy netcode issues/server issues.

I have 300+ hours on the Steam client, which came out in my 7th year of play, and toward the end of my hardcore playing days. From the time this game out on Steam, I've spent maybe 10% of my total hours on the Steam client. My best guess has me at over 10,000 hours. That's well over a year of game play. Not even kidding you.
The game has been in a state of "dying" for about 5 years now. At its peak it saw 5 free servers, 2 sub servers, 2 foreign servers, and 1 kid server, with ~5,000 concurrent players daily. Now it's down to 1 sub, 2 free, and the 2 foreign servers, with ~800 daily. The Spanish and German servers are literally down to 10 people.
As a game to get started in, things are pretty daunting. There is a bit of a tutorial experience for players, but the real fun stuff begins once you've amassed experience/money.
There are puzzles for every type of player. There are 2 combat puzzles, one similar to Tetris, the other similar to any ball-pop game you've played before. There are 3 shipboard station types: Sailing, Carpentry, and Bilging. Sailing and Carpentry both have an alternate puzzle. There is also a Navigation puzzle. The Battle Navigation Puzzle is where the person in charge moves the ship to outmaneuver their opponents, and is the most important role on the ship. There are 5 "Carousing" type puzzles, including Poker, Hearts, Spades, and two puzzle PvP games. There are 6 "Labor" type puzzles, that require a labor badge on the free oceans. These puzzles are uniquely tailored to fuel the game's economy system, as every puzzle helps produce labor that produces products you can buy throughout the game.
With all of these puzzles, you can take on a variety of personas. There are the hard-core puzzlers, the ship-masters (they run pillages, sea monster hunts, etc.), the carousers, the traders, and many more. It's really up to you to decide who you are.
The best part about this game has to be the social aspect. There is literally a chat function for almost every group imaginable. I've met so many great and wonderful people playing this game. You can get the best experience imaginable if you 'put yourself out there' so to speak, find a crew, open yourself up to voice-communications, and amass a list of 'hearties'.
This game will suck up your time. You just have to dedicate maybe 30 hours to getting used to the puzzles and interactions, and it opens up completely.
There is an extensive experience/rating system for each puzzle. There are hundreds of trophies to mark your adventure with. There are thousands of items to collect. Dozens of ships, with many 'limited edition' versions to collect, each with their own, fun, and unique niche. Still hundreds of people to meet, across a number of oceans. Hundreds of Islands with their own unique histories.... the list goes on.
You can pillage the high seas; fighting brigands, barbarians, hoards of monkeys, Brigand Kings & Queens, The Infamous Black Ship; exploring Treasure Wrecks, Forage Spots; Raiding Vikings, Imperial Outposts. You can explore Sea Monster Lairs including: Atlantis, The Cursed Isles, The Haunted Seas, and The Kraken. You can engage Brigand Kings at their very own Flotillas. You can job for flag vs. flag or flag vs. Brigand King Blockades. You can join the navy to gain experience. You can spend your time at the inn, playing poker or settling disputes with a swordfight. You can collect pets, familiars, ships, houses, trinkets, swords, trophies, whatever you'd like. You can make ships, potions, clothes, MONEY. You can sit on the docks and harass random players. You can do absolutely nothing. You can do absolutely anything.
Seriously.
Play this game.
10/10 would spend another year+ of game time on this game.

To start, I want to say that I absolutely love the gameplay in the XCOM series.  The small squad turn-based combat is both challenging and rewarding.  I have beaten both XCOM: Enemy Within and XCOM 2 on console, and now, I bought and have been enjoying playing through XCOM 2 on PC.  The game can be difficult at times, but remains fair, and beating it feels like a real accomplishment.
All of this considered, there are a couple of things that desperately need to be addressed...
The game runs like garbage.  Ran awful on consoles with regular crashes, but I still managed to limp through.  Imagine my suprise when I switch over to PC with an i7 and a GTX1080 and the game still runs like garbage.  Constant frame stutters and huge amounts of hesitation during actions, especially when there are a lot of units on screen.  A new problem that  I have encountered on PC is a hard crash during the cutscene before the last mission that completely power cycles my computer.
Another smaller issue that I have found on PC is that sometimes the controls bug out.  You will go to select an option for a unit to perform, and the game will then register the wrong command, or after you select a command, will automatically target the closest enemy rather than allowing you to select the enemy you want to attack.  While this problem can be combatted by regularly saving and reloading when it happens, I will sadly never attempt the Ironman mode on PC, as these issues can easily cause a mission to go completely wrong, and leave you with no way to take it back.  Imagine how depressing it would be to have a 20+ hour playthrough ruined because of a misclick you cannot control.
Again, I really love XCOM 2 and think that it is one of the best strategy games in the genre, but there are severe performance issues and UI bugs that can be frustrating, and should not be overlooked when considering purchasing this game.

Originally, I didn't think this game was as bad as everyone said it was. Sure, it wasn't perfect, but I had fun with it, and that's what matters. If I made this review last year, I would have recomended it. However, a recent update have started to negate my ability to have fun with this game. That update being the Creation Club update.
I could go on for hours, and trust me I have, about how scummy bethesda are for implementing this, how stupid they are for trying this again after the last time and how they've lied to and continue to lie to us about pretty much everything when it comes to this service, but that would be leaving a review of bethesda and not Fallout 4, so I won't. What I will complain about, however, is the way that this negatively impacts the modding community we had before Creation Club, and why this has ruined the game for me.
"But you don't have to buy anything from the Creation Club so why do you care?" I hear someone say. Well, person with either more money than sense or no knowledge of the way Creation Club actually works, allow me to explain:
"Creation Club content" (which, let's be honest here, is paid mods despite bethesda's insistance that it isn't) works much in the same way as on-disk DLC does. The content gets rolled out in an update, everyone installs that update, and that content that you just installed is then locked until you pay up for it. This is scummy in itself, but it isn't the part that I'm the most disappointed about. A large number of the old mods used a thing called Fallout 4 Script Extender, or F4SE for short, to help the mods run. The issue is every time there is a Fallout 4 update, F4SE has to update as well, and because F4SE isn't made by bethesda there's a period of time where F4SE is outdated while the creators are working on updating it to work with the newest version of Fallout 4. With particularly game changing mods, this means that some people's saves can't be played while F4SE is outdated.
With the introduction of creation club, this means that the game will have to be updated more frequently with more paid mods that are locked behind the creation club paywall. More frequent updates means that F4SE is outdated more often, which means some people won't be able to use their saves while that is the case. With non Creation Club mods being outdated more often than not, this just intices people to get their mods from the Creation Club.
To any modders/future modders out there, go mod a game where the devs actually care about you. To anyone thinking about playing the game, mods are what give this game replayability. Without them, this is a one shot thing. If you feel like buying it, get it on sale. It's not worth full price by a long shot.
Bethesda, stop this. It's not healthy, and one of these days it's going to kill your company. Stop it.

Cities XL Platinum is a interesting city building game that strikes a decent balance between fun and challenging.
Positives:
- Good supply/demand balance.
- Fairly deep resource system.
- New buildings and things to strive for early-to-late game, including notable landmarks.
- Nice interface, allows for new users to jump right in.
- Ability to trade between cities allows for specilization.
- Very 'pretty' with easy zoom and camera functions.
Negatives:
- Ingame lag when playing for 1+ hours, building 'fastlanes', and on large cities (restarting the game helps).
- Horrible road snapping, especially when creating an intersection with little room. The road curves instead of going straight.
- Later game is very difficult to play without having at least Expressways on major throughfairs. The problem is that these are not unlocked until at least 100k population when your city is fairly large (using low population residences). I can plan ahead for larger buildings, but it is hard to change street sizes without completely rebuilding the city.
- Confusing/annoying traffic model. Why wont citizens use the new bypass i built to avoid that terrible intersection? This makes larger cities 1mill+ hard to handle.
- Fast Lanes suck. These need to reworked. Fixing snapping and placing interchanges would help. Shortening interchanges would help. As it stands i ignore them.
- Pollution model is very aggressive.
Note: Would not recommend purchasing if you own other Cities XL titles.

Previously, Tales of Xillia was the standout in this series. The story line was complex, and believable given the context. The next one in the series was pale by comparison. Tales of Berseria, however, is the new champion. Each of the 6 companions has his or her own story that develops throughout the game. This is also true of the most important NPC's (of which there are quite a few), who are portrayed as real people, rather than 2-dimensions villains/allies.
For people who play RPG's mainly for the story, this game sets the standard. The combat is there - lots of it. But if you don't care about that, just set it to Auto and let the AI take care of it. Surprisingly, the AI is effective for most enemies even on the hardest mode. For those few where it's not, dial the AI back to Simple, and Bob's your uncle.
As a result of this, it may be less interesting to those who are primarily interested in combat. However, you can certainly play on manual, and there's enough complexity in available actions, equipment, and settings to keep most people happy.
The world is large, and semi-open. By that I mean that sometimes there are certain places you've been to that you can't yet go back to, and sometimes there is only one place you can go next. Most of the time there is a fair amount of freedom though.
As with others in the series, the game has an augmented replay option, which allows you to carry over a limited amount of earned items and characteristics, depending how well you did on the previous run.
My biggest criticism is that crafting is rather lame. But then, there are very few RPG's that do any better - I can't think of one offhand.

Holy wow, I had only just heard of this game a few weeks before the December 2014 Steam Holiday Sale, so I didn't have a lot of expectations going in. However, even if I'd set my expectations sky high, I don't think this game would have disappointed me.
First off, the game is rather pretty; the cel shaded graphics will likely help the game retain playability for a long time, so if you don't have the money to spend now, you can always wait for the next sale. Bonus: The developers have said there will be future episodes of Consortium that build upon the events of this game, so waiting for that may be in your best interest if you're a binge gamer.
As for the story, it feels pretty natural. If you're unfamiliar, the game puts you in the body of a person in the future. The game itself pretends that this is actually happening, so when you have to pretend you know what is going on, it feels legitimate. However, that also means that on future playthroughs, you can react to situations differently as you are more familiar with the game's lore. The game is built with this concept in mind, which makes it extremely replayable. On that note, I recommend playing the game through, living with each decision you make, rather than reloading to see how consequences change. In the amount of time I spent watching the loading screen, I probably could have played the game through at least one or possibly two more times.
The situtations the game puts you in have the feel of action-packed, suspensful movie scenes, and the game does a darned good job making you feel as if you were really in the thick of things. Also, since you're not the captain, you're not always the center of attention. In my opinion, this feeling adds another layer of deptht to the game as it made me feel more like a part of the crew, as opposed to having me order people around, Kirk-style.
I can't speak much for the combat because the game gives you the options to not have to fight, except for one "air combat" mission. The controls in general felt solid. There's nothing that felt innovative here, but nothing that felt broken.
The only time the game didn't feel smooth were when I accidentally triggered an event that moved the story forward before I meant to. This is a chronic issue I have in games and may speak more about me than it does about the game.
Bottom Line/TL;DR: If you want to feel like you're actually in a futuristic crew on a ship flying around on missions, then this game is likely to be right up your alley. The conversation choices and reactions to actions you take feel natural and make you feel like you really are hijacking the body of someone in the future.

Game feels Barebones at release.  You're basically paying $60 for an early access of the game, because most of their content will come out at March/June.

-Fighting feels nice, controls are responsive.
-(When matchmaking works*) You can get into online matches fairly quickly and improve upon one character as you play.
-(when you've got decent connections to your opponent*) Netcode is decent, no weird issues.  I noticed some weird crossplay issues if I ever got console users however.  felt like frames would skip or they would teleport for a few frames. It was weird to try and get used to.
-Story mode at the moment is basically just a tease of the promised story mode.  (Coming in June)
-Shoddy netcode/server connections.  If you disconnect you're booted out of whatever mode you are currently in. Long matchmaking, etc. (Being worked on apparently)
-No penalties for ragequits/disconnects at the moment.
-Game will sometimes fail to upload your match stats to the server.
-Lack of lobby selection.
-Weak steam integration,you cant invite or join other steam users. (wouldve been awesome to have this with some nice lobbies, with spectating; Mortal Kombat X-esque lobbies.)
-Character select is quirky, you have to select a main beforehand to play ranked. instead of being taken to a character menu. This also means you're going in blind as to who your opponent is playing.
-Survival mode is pretty boring. You have to grind all of the difficulties in order to unlock your color customizations for every character. The difficulty doesnt seem to change, you're just killing a ton of fodder.  The perks you can purchase with your survival score is a pretty neat idea, but it doesnt change anything up drastically. (Wouldve been awesome to see a BlazBlue Chronophantasma survival mode, where you can pick a character and customize them through the ordeal with equippable buffs or something.)
I have to not recommend this game at the moment. For the price point and what you're actually getting,  No.
If you're a die-hard fan of fighters and want to jump right into some online matches, sure. but even then, you're paying $60 for a 16 character roster and some iffy netcode issues/server issues.

Left 4 Dead is a zombie apocalypse game where players take control of four different and unique characters who work together to escape the rotting clutches of the fallen. The game is very insistent on tight teamwork, purposefully creating situations that set up teams for failure should they decide to work individually instead of pooling their efforts into one.
The environment in Left 4 Dead is akin to one of a typical suburb while some portion of the game does take place in more rural and business areas. The game has a darker, colder feel to it as it takes place in the night and brings with it, a sense of death and decay, what with all the former residents dead. While it may seem that all hope is lost, players are greeted with the hope that they can make it, defeating any challenges along the way.
In general, Left 4 Dead is best suited towards those seeking a four player cooperative game. It's a great introduction into first person shooters, and plays just as well for veteran gamers.

XCom 2... This one took me a while to review.  XCom 2 is a successor to the recent XCom reboot, which are spiritual successors to the XCom Series in the 90s.  Both of these have been a successful reboot of the franchise, emphasising smaller groups, more customization options, faster gameplay for this day and age, and better use of technology to give it a much needed refresh.  XCom 2 does not follow the original series' terror from the deep, but rather follows the most recent XCom release as though the main mission were unsuccessful, which draws a few interesting playing elements to the game.  Namely the units and the look/feel of the game is that you're sometimes stealthy freedom fighters against a near omnipotent enemy.
The new mechanics are engaging, but also can be ignored for the core draws of the XCom series, a ant-hill style base/research/technology development with growth of potential combined with a turn based strategic shooter.  Get new things in the field, get excited to research them, which gives you new things to use in the field to get more things to research, rinse and repeat.  Sometimes, the tactical aspects can get a little boring, especially if you've exhausted playing the original series or the recent XCom remake, but it's to be expected from the next game in a series to offer similiar mechanics.
The recent War of the Chosen DLC was performed in incredibly similar fashion to the new XCom's Enemy Within.  While the core gameplay is the same, there have been new creatures, new technology, more intense play style, more mechanics, and more options.  It is less of a conventional DLC where you see a new hat/weapon/whatnot, and much more of an entire new take on the gameplay.  War of the Chosen leveraged heavily from the popular Long War mod for XCom, introducing fatique, more missions, and squad development opportunities.  To call it a DLC is almost a misnomer when you see other games like Dungeon Defenders offering new classes as DLC... this is more like a complete rewrite within the same engine, and much more like an XCom 2.5.
This game is an XCom game... Turn based tactical shooter with anthill style base development, paired with splatterings of missions in various forms.  It doesn't completely break the mold, but adds some bells and whistles to the end product.  I recommend this game heavily to people that have played the recently rebooted first XCom.  If you are completely new to the series, I would recommend the recent remake of the initial Xcom before this one, predominantly because of the price, and the core mechanics being so similiar.

X-Com 2 is a great turn based strategy game that has a lot of customisability. Strategy is the core aspect of the game and the rogue-like aspect compliments the strategic gameplay of the game. This is a hard game to master so because if its “Permadeath” mechanic even on easy difficulty, it’s a game of trial and error so don’t expect to win on the 1st playthrough. The game does have a lot of visual bug glitches (these don’t really effect the game it just makes the game look funny) and there are so game breaking glitches that will break the game so keep an eye out for those on the forums for the most common game breaking bugs (I stopped playing for a long time because I got hit by one but luckily it was patched by the devs so I can play again).
The game will feel completely unfair at time and sometimes you just want to throw your keyboard out the window because of it mechanics (seriously standing next to and enemy with 90% accuracy and the shot misses because he shot the floor 0_o) but if you stick with it and figure out the overall scheme of thing you will find enjoyment in this game.
The DLC’s for the game are a bit of a hit and miss, Shens last gift is good and adds a new unit type which gives a lot more possibilities to play with, War of the Chosen adds more game content to the base game which makes the already long game even longer. The other DLC’s in my honest opinions are not worth anything since they mostly consist of cosmetic upgrades which I think you are better off just going on to Steam Workshops and getting cosmetics mods from there (I recreated Delta Squad from Star Wars: Republic Commando just because I miss the characters).
So, overall good hard to master strategy game with some decent DLC with a lot of customization and moddability. This is a game that you need to try first and see if it’s your cup of tea, but if you’re a veteran turn based strategy player from the Civilization series or Fire Emblem series this might just be up your alley.
Can’t comment on the multiplayer skirmish modes since I never tried them.

The basic plot (as you've probably read) is that demons are taking over and it's up to you to fix things. Doing this is a long and convoluted journey involving several countries and islands visited via sea, meeting a range of party members along the way and fighting an organisation run by your newfound arch-enemy.
My biggest problem with it is that I think it's been mislabeled. This is a CRPG and a full on one at that. Think FF7 on steroids with a side of monsters.  It's almost at the level of a fighting game and at least part of the combat and XP/reward mechanic reflects that. To be fair you can avoid some of the en-route fights if you choose but you still have to focus or it finds you. This gets tiresome pretty fast unless you're really into your CRPG's.
The second negative was the storytelling. Not the story itself which although pretty standard fare for a JRPG was at least in depth with some good twists and turns here and there. No, my problem was how it was told. You will be trying to get somewhere and picking and choosing your fights when out of the blue you're interrupted by a cut scene. Some of these make sense e.g when you're entering a key area or discovering a plot point but a lot of them are just 'character' stuff that you generally have no interest in at the time as you're trying to actually get something done. I ultimately got the sense these were actually just filler to break up the seemingly endless combat and give you a reason to plough on.
The third thing, which is probably a 'love it or hate it' deal is the characters themselves. Some are exactly what you'd expect. The stoic leader, the brave but foolhardy sword swinger etc etc. Forgettable but not a problem. On the other hand, some are just downright annoying. On it's own you could probably swallow this but as you plough on through the game putting up with the other flaws it starts to grate. You really start to wish they'd just shut up and let you get on with it. I'm not sure if this is a deliberate game design choice to test you in some way but if it is it's a strange one.
With all that said the game itself ran well with no issues. The actual mechanics of it work better than many games I've played recently. You've got a huge amount of choice in how you set up and equip your own character and your companions and the crafting and cooking options are pretty in-depth and interesting.
If you're in the market for a super-grindy CRPG then this may be for you. If you want a more traditional JRPG then I'd give it a wide berth frankly. It's almost nothing like previous Tales games I've played and was a big dissapointment.
Edit: Oh, and a significant number of dungeons being some kind of gateway puzzle? That's a nope. It's horribly tedious and ends up feeling 'get it out the door' lazy.

Don't let the screenshots fool you. They do not give this gem justice.
Tales of Berseria is fantastic. A great step up from Zestiria. Good dialogue. Fantastic voice acting;  I played with English audio. The story was in depth with amazing character development. The minigames (card games, fishing, ship missions and more) is a fantastic addition and gave you something else to do other than work on the storyline. The PC port in itself is very good, running at a maximum of 60FPS.
-Not much of a variety of items, felt like you were looting the same thing on the ground over and over again. With that said, not a huge fan of the gear system. Would like to see more variety/unique items.
-As a person who doesn't play with a controller, the keyboard and mouse felt a little awkward during combat until you get used to it.
-Combat might be a little difficult to grasp. Tutorials and hints are kind of thrown at you making it a bit overwhelming, so it was easy to forget lessons previously learned. I know I had some problems with it. Reading a few guides online helped.
-Once you find the Geoboard, I found it annoyingly difficult to control. I almost preferred not using it at all. (Afer getting the hang of it, I found it easier to forget using the keyboard to steer, just use the mouse and it's not so jerky.)
-Towards the end of the game, most notably during the side quests, I noticed a whole ton of errors in the text that didn't line up with the English audio. Made me laugh a few times reading some of the weird words that popped up.
I picked up Berseria on sale, but for me, I would have easily enjoyed this all the same if I had purchased it at full price. Highly addicting and will definitely revisit for another playthrough in the future!

I'm about an hour into my first playthrough of the game - I hear a single playthrough is about two hours long. As soon as I'm done, I want to start the game again and try different things. This game is incredibly successful at engaging a lot more of my brain and 'gut feelings' than most. I'm not sure that I've ever played a game that gave the player such respect while also commanding so much responsibility.
Without revealing too much; you're thrown (somewhat 'naked') into a key role during a specific series of events. Your decisions and actions can sway how events unfold and also how the game is to be played. In most games, if you stray too far from what they want to show you, the game tugs harshly at your leash or essentially shuts down and waits for you to come back. Not so, here! As far as I can tell, the only time you're really yanked out of the proceedings is if your character dies. Then, you can load up an auto-save from earlier and try something else. That's only happened to me once so far. Basically, if you bumble, the game unfolds in a logical way as it would if someone in your position bumbled in an actual situation like this, if that makes sense.
What kind of a game is it? Well, it's a shooter if you want it to be...I guess. It's a missile defense game sometimes. It's a 'cool special agent on a plane' social simulator. It's an alternate future reality quantum leap homage thingiemadoop.

How to review a game like Consortium that is packd with so many great ideas? Well first off I will say that I really enjoyed the play throughs I have made so far.
Consortium puts you - Quantum Leap style - in the body of an operative called Bishop-6 onboard a high tech aircraft flying to Dublin. The entire game takes place during the flight and can play out differently every time depending on your actions. There are no right or wrong actions, just different versions of reality. You are confronted with a number of plots to solve - or ignore - which I won't spoiler. What I will say is that they are excellent, and enjoyable.
Consortium is an excellent example of the "One Block RPG" where everything takes place in a small area with well developed characters but within that scope the player has great freedom. Consortium benefits from many play throughs as you explore diferent possibilities and in fact the game makes a virtue of this and saves them as detailed versions for you to look back on.
Oh did I mention it has a soundtrack by Jeremy Soule?
The game had a rough launch - the team who developed it are very small - but they stuck with ut  and turned it into a gem that should not be missed.
If you like good, thoughtful RPGs: buy it. If you love interesting sci-fi setups: buy it. If you like good writing: buy it, If you like soundtracks by Jeremy Soule: buy it.

Fighting games are about mechanics mastery. Street Fighter has always been about mastering the fight system of each iteration and using your mastery to compete with other humans. The reason that people buy fighting games is the same reason people play MOBAs, to 'git gud' at them and become able to beat other players. I bought Street Fighter V for this reason.
Many are concerned about the lack of singleplayer modes. I can sympathize with this, but I must mention that if your goal is to gain mastery of the fight system in order to beat better and better players, your time is better spent fighting other humans rather than AIs. As it stands, if your goal is mechanics mastery, the game has what you need it to have in it right now. If you're choosing not to buy this game because it lacks singleplayer content, you probably weren't going to play it for more than a month. I presume that those who are declining purchasing the game because it lacks singleplayer content are those who already don't see the value, don't see the depth in what the game already has to offer in its multiplayer mode. If you don't see the value in that, then I assume you want to play Street Fighter V because it's the Next Big Game coming out. It's something to occupy your time for a short while before the Next Big Game after it comes out. This is a mistake. Fighting games, like MOBAs, are not about occupying you for a short amount of time. If you want to get any meaning out of this game, it is not such a game that you play for two hours after work before you go to sleep for the next day, forgetting about it once Dark Souls 3 comes out. It is a game that you must not forget about if you wish to gain the fullest amount of value from it. It is a game that will take many hundreds of hours to gain a respectable level of skill for. It is a game that requires a time commitment that is daunting compared to many other video game genres. If you do not have the patience to put the time in to get good, I do not think this game will be worth 60 dollars to you. And assuming you are waiting on the game already until it has its singleplayer modes patched in, you will get about 8 hours or so of playtime out of that. Then you might try online and get absolutely wrecked. You might spend two or so weeks trying to get good at online play, and then you'll quit because you're unwilling to put in the amount of time you will realize is necessary to beat these players. This is not meant to be a put down, or to be dismissive. This is just the experience of a vast majority of people when they first play fighting games. It was my experience. It will likely be yours as well. Most Steam users are at least familiar with DoTA, so I'll use it as a similar case. Street Fighter is a game that asks even more time of the player than DoTA does in order to get the most out of it. Please consider this fact before you make your purchase.
In summary:
This game is not for you if you're not interested in player versus player and are unwilling to put in the time required to harden muscle memory/gain general knowledge of the fighting system. I am, so that's why I'm recommending this game. This game is likely not for you if you only want to play singleplayer modes. I may be wrong on this point. You may find 60 dollars of enjoyment in the singleplayer modes the game will patch in within a few months that will likely only last 6-8 hours. If you feel that's the case, of course spend 60 dollars on the game, but if you find yourself wanting, don't say I didn't tell you so. ;)

This is a very strange game. Your first clue is that it claims to be real. The deal is, you used a system by iDGi to take control of Bishop-6, a general-operations crewmember aboard the Zenlilth in the year 2043. The Zenlilth is a highly advanced plane containing a chess-based heirarchy, all working for the leaders of Consortium, King and Queen. Your purpose is to do stuff, and try not to screw up the plane too badly through traitors, mercenary attacks, and intrigue. There's even a section where the high leader of Consortium calls you specifically to tell you not to kill the guy you're controlling. It is, in my opinion, well-written and creative, and if Bioware RPG's are too busy for you, this is much more story-focused and less shooting and picking flowers.
The combat is unique, and takes backstage. As a "Bishop", you are supposed to know how to fight, but in the only big combat scene of the game people get a bit annoyed if you kill too many people (especially the leader). Story is unique and immersive, the ending is incredibly strange and yet not out of place. So much detail is put into a facade of reality that the same section of a game might be experienced with bad space/time continuum connection the first time, and some static the next. There's a lot more to learn and I've played through the game twice. Is it worth 20$? Maybe. Is it worth the money you pay when on sale for 33% off or more? Definitely.

Void Source is quite a fun little game, whereby you fly your spaceship along a linear path, shooting various enemies (on the ground and in the air - and even in the water).
In story mode, most of the levels have a enemy boss (except for the volcano level, which makes you do some hard flying and weaving instead).
It's an amusing bit of shooting fun, the graphics are quite reasonable, the sound effects are fine, and the music is OKish (at least at first, although you might want to turn it off after you've been playing for a while).
It's in Early Access at this stage, so not all parts of the game are fully working. For example, you need to Alt-F4 to exit out of Classic Mode, and the Level Editor is only very bare bones.
However, the main part of the game, Story Mode, is working fine - so don't let the Early Access label stop you from buying it.
It costs $4 (although I picked it up with a Steam discount coupon for $1) - either way, its cost is quite reasonable.
It's nothing amazing, just another linear space-shooting game (an updated version of those games that have been around since the 1990s), but it provides some cheap entertainment - so I can recommend it on that basis.

Let me start off by sayign that this game is ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic. I have to give the developers a ton of credit for taking a bunch of characters that I intially didn't like or was merely indifferent towards and slowly turning them into a wonderful and super likable cast of misfits.
The Good
- The combat system may be the best its ever been, I haven't played every Tales game (I've played 5 others), but this one has the best combat system I've experienced by a mile. Your moves are fast and enemy damage is super punishing even on the lower difficulties. Getting to a boss or "dire foe" is a genuinely exciting experience as they are all simply a joy to fight (There's one sorta ♥♥♥♥♥♥ one, but hey, that's just one amoung tons of good ones)
- The characters for the most part all get a chance to have their archs all come to logical and satisfying ending in a way that doesn't feel rushed or forced. This required that the game be super long (60+ hours), but in the end I didn't feel robbed of my time since the pay-off for each character made the time spend building them more than worth it. The voice acting for the characters is pretty solid, although there are a few cringe-worthy lines in the first half of the game, but nothing too bad.
- The story has tons of little call backs and references to Tales of Vesparia and the two games combined serve to tell a wonderful story. It was pretty enjoyable to see this game fill in the cracks and holes left behind by Vesparia. The added benefit of being able to play as the villains for a change was a great change of pace from playing the almost sickening lawful good characters that the Tales series usually puts you in the shoes of
- Very little grinding required. Experience can be gained super fast by triggering dangerous encounters (Luring two enemies close together an then fighting both) which causes the experience gained from the fight to be multiplied by what I think is 10x. I did this to most of the enemies that naturally spawned in my path through the dungeons and never felt under-leveled
The Bad
- The environments in the game are a bit boring. Very few of them are interesting to look at and some are so dull that you can't wait to get out of them. I would have liked the scenery to be more enjoyable to look at and explore, instead you mostly hug the wall of a map and just walk around it.
- Very few side quests. Side quests aren't something the Tales series is really known for, but it seemed like this time there were barely any. I would have liked a few more to bring more variety to questline.
- The story. I know I listed that in the Good section, but here's the thing, this game kinda assumes that you have played Tales of Vesparia before this one. Without playing Vesparia a lot of the big moments and reveals of Berseria fall pretty flat as the player doesn't have enough context. Normally this wouldn't be much of an issue, but Vesparia is a vastly inferior game to this one and I wouldn't recommend playing one without the other. (It would be interesting to hear the thoughts of someone who played Berseria first and then played Vesparia.)
All in all, this game is truely wonderful and well worth the price. I won't say that you HAVE to play Tales of Vesparia before this one, but you won't be able to get everything out of the plot unless you at some point play both games since they are basically two sides of the same coin.

To me personally this was an incredibly interesting game. It completely subverted my expectations about it when I started playing it. I am so used to getting into a game, listening to 10-15 min of expostition and story content that isn't developed or focused on again until the end, that when I went past that point with CONSORTIUM I was slightly taken aback and realized that this truly is a story focused RPG. And best of all it managed to hold my attention to the story throughout the whole game, and only games with great stories have managed that (sadly, there aren't too many of those). Perhaps this is only a side effect of the fact the game is unexpectedly short, even the story itself doesn't have a good conclusion. It is very much dependant on a sequel, however it is not yet clear if we are going to get one.
The game also has an FPS element to it, which is very much underdeveloped. You have an inventory and equipment system, which you manage throughout the game, so that you will be optimally prepared for combat when the need arises for it. But sadly, that moment doesn't ever come. Not really that is, there are two seperate instances in the game where you can use weapons, in the first one it is clear that the game is pushing you towards the non-violent path. The second one is a bit more mandatory, however you can win that fight simply by waiting it out...
CONSORTIUM reminded me of the times when you are aboard the Normandy in the Mass Effect games and you go around talking to your crewmembers, getting to know them and their story and actually progressing the overall story somewhat. I enjoyed that part in the Mass Effect games, it made me connect with the characters. This game only has that part, but it does it so much better. It would appear they also tried to make the combat part, but given how little importance it has I would imagine they simply didn't have the budget for it.
There are two major disappointments I have with the game. Firstly, its short lenght, and secondly, the present but never developed FPS portion of the game. Seeing all the possibilities this game has on offer I was starting to think this game would be something truly amazing, with a meaning story that made you care about the characters within it, which would connect all the different missions you would embark upon. However, the sad fact is, the game ends before the first mission truly begins.
With that said I can also now reveal that the whole story in the game takes place aboard an airplane (supposedly also a spaceship), and you are fully confined within it throughout the game. All the story elements come from interacting with the people within it (well, almost all), and so it is a good thing that, for the most part, they are well written and voice acted. And with a multitude of dialogue choices and possible story paths there is never a single clear choice to take, there are only the choices you want to make. That is what is most appealing about this game, and it is also what gives it replayability, despite being so heavily story focused. I am a bit disappointed with how it ended and so I won't be replaying it any time soon, only when the sequel comes out (hopefully).
Perhaps the game I envisioned after a couple of hours of play could only have been achieved with a large budget, or perhaps we will get that game after all with multiple sequels of this one. Despite this, CONSORTIUM is worth buying and playing, you just need to be prepared for a fully story focused game and you'll enjoy yourself.

Just got done playing CONSORTIUM after picking it up in the humble bundle, I heard good things about it and this is what I took away from my experience.
Great-Characters, pacing, atmosphere
The characters are written well with their own motives and quirks, without being transparent enough to feel like an NPC. Pacing of these interactions and the overall plot are not bad at all, and when combined with the setting deliver a game you can jump into and feel hooked. I personally enjoyed the voiceacting and sound design.
Alright-Play length and amount of content to experience on a single playthrough leaves something to be desired, don't blow your horn about a trilogy if they're all going to be this quick and rely on multiple playthroughs to deliver full circle. Content is one thing, double handling gets old after awhile. I appreciate that we have many choices, but some of them lack follow through if you play certain types of characters. Sometimes there is no foothold for a player with too much intuition that will scour out of the way areas.
Lore dumps-the lore contained in this game is handcrafted and certainly interesting. The only problem outside of limited audio broadcasts/conversations is that if you want to experience any of it-have fun reading codex lore dumps in the menu. No offense but it was more fun to fly by the seat of my pants than do that and try to figure anything out, which seems to be a huge waste. Why gate so much great stuff behind one of the dullest interactions in your game?
Plain bad-Shooting, Inventory management, sense of progression, jaggy shadows
This is a game worth playing but it feels at times if it is grasping for too many things to have that "feature list" that tends to accompany recent steam releases. The shooting is just plain bad(especially if you want to play non-killing), the hud sucks for it. If you want to play a decent shooter don't come into Consortium expecting even that. To make the matter worse any inventory management feels like it is there just to be there. Most of the items I encountered had no practical use inside the story, and anytime I did use a weapon/ammo/armor it was unintuitive, a huge hassle, and most of all not even fun. These two areas need some polish or even to be redone completely if you want to really tout them as cornerstones of the gameplay experience.
Which leads to my next point-progression. At the end of the day I felt like I made a difference, and was a set piece for some cool stuff. Even though I kept being swept along to the next issue there were a few "AHA" experiences in the plot or character interactions which left me wanting more. But you still feel very gated off from what is really happening, with few avenues to approach it in an otherwise very thoughtful and ambitious setup.
Also the shadow jaggies are downright terrible, expect them to be a bit jarring even if you have a nicer PC.
My final comments will be aimed at the developer review-you need to decide on what you want and get it right the first time, and budget the appropriate timelines and resources to it. There is a vocal audience that bought into this game when it released, and you can tell they felt let down by the compromises and changes you made to the content and schedule. I can believe how buggy the initial playthroughs probably were. You can't look back and say "Well I should have done it that way" or "Well we have this awesome system, but the way it was presented in the first game didn't suit it well"
I don't say this to be harsh, but to let you know those were both areas of your responsibility during game production, and to say it didn't work or wasn't presently appropriately falls on you. It is easy to say how you would change past design decisions or player encounters at the end of the day, for obvious reasons. Perhaps a wiser approach towards future projects would be to set clear, concise goals on how to approach past issues while being mindful of what worked well.

Let's face it; this is quite similar to all the other city games; so there is not really that much to say on the gameplay.
I enjoy play this game, because it is extremely simple. You start, get your buildings unlocked and wait that people get in the city; then they start to demand jobs, and you create industrial areas; then you unlock the skilled workers (office people), and once they flock in your city, you give them some office areas, and so on until you unlock the whole  array of buildings.
There are plenty, but mostly they are the same type, just with higher density. It is fun to see how the city grow, but at one point you hit the wall, where you have no more money to continue to grow. The biggest flaw of this game is that it give you plenty to start, but then it doesn't teach you how to get revenues. You may want to try various tactics before you get what you expect; this is time consuming at times, so the newbies may get surprised to see the city grow so fast, and then see that they can't do anything else because the money coming in are barely covering for the structures that you have (in particular public structures take quite a lot of resources...open few hospital and you will see the bill!).
Gameplay is fun; not sure why peopllpl don't enjoy the game...if you expect to get a masterpiece, keep in mind that not even Sim City from Maxis was able to give you a decent experience. The game is worth the discounted price, but if you pay it full price, you may be a bit disappointed.
Performances are great; some framerate drop happens here and there but no crash nor problems that cause you to get stuck. Graphics are great; compared to Sim City from Maxis and most of the other city games. Zoom in at street level and you will get a smile on your face.
City size is not an issue, and you can trade too, which is something interesting to do; here you don't have meteorites but you have to deal with class balancing; waste management and overall keep an eye to not make a residential area close to a dump and expec that people won't complain.
AI is quite good too, looks realistic, and respond to changes; although keep in mind that it is still a sim city AI type, so keep that in mind.
OVerall, if you never played Cities XL, give it a try, it is worth 10 bucks. If you want something super polished and optimized; there is actually not really that much out there, beside Cities Skyline, which is another good game but it is not leap and bounds ahead of this.
